### PREFACE.
---

Having undertaken to prepare a course of lectures on <term>natural philosophy</term>, to be delivered in the theater of the Royal Institution, I thought that the plan of the Institution required something more than a mere compilation from the elementary works currently existing; and that it was my duty to collect from original authors, to examine with attention, and to organize into one system, everything relating to the principles of the <term>mechanical sciences</term>, that could lead to the improvement of the arts that serve the conveniences of life. I found also, in delivering the lectures, that it was most appropriate to write down, as nearly as possible, everything that was required to be said on each subject; and that, even when an experiment was to be performed, it was best to describe that experiment without interruption, and to repeat the explanation while it was being shown. Hence it became necessary that the written lectures should be expressed as clearly and thoroughly as possible, and in a language adapted as much to the understanding of a mixed audience as the nature of the investigations would allow; and that each experiment which was to be performed should also be minutely described in them. If, therefore, there was any novelty either in the subject matter or the arrangement of the lectures as they were delivered for two successive years, it is obvious that they must have possessed an equal claim to the attention of a reader had they been published as a book; and upon resigning from the position of Professor of Natural Philosophy, I immediately began to prepare them for publication.

I had in some measure committed myself, in the printed <term>syllabus</term> of the lectures, to make a catalog of the best works already published on

# PREFACE.

the various subjects; with references to such passages as seemed most important. It was therefore necessary, both for this purpose and to obtain all possible information that could contribute to the improvement of the work, to examine a select library of books specifically with this goal in mind, taking notes on the main subjects discussed in them, and carefully examining those parts that seemed to deserve more than ordinary attention. From this emerged a catalog of references; regarding which it is sufficient to say that the labor of arranging about twenty thousand articles in a systematic form was by no means less significant than that of collecting them. The transactions of scientific societies, and the best and latest periodical publications—which have so greatly increased the number of sources of information—formed a significant part of the collection, which was thus to be consolidated into a single body of science.

With the addition of the materials acquired in making this compilation, and the results of many original investigations to which they had given rise, it became almost essential to rewrite all the lectures once more and to replace some of them with others that were entirely new. At the same time, every possible effort was made to discover and correct any lack of clarity in expression or argument. Drawings were also made to represent the apparatus and experiments shown at the time the lectures were delivered, to show the construction of various machines and instruments related to the subjects being explained, and to illustrate them in many other ways. These figures have been expanded to more than forty plates, very finely engraved, and the production of the engravings has been carefully supervised. However, the text of the lectures has been made so independent of the figures that the reader is never interrupted in the middle of a line of reasoning, but is instead referred, at the end of a paragraph, to a plate which always has a sufficient explanation on the opposite page.

# PREFACE.

The size of this work is not so large that reading it in its entirety would require an unreasonable amount of time or effort. However, there may be some people who would be satisfied with focusing on those parts where it differs most from previous publications, without having the leisure or inclination to study the whole thing. For such readers, it may be helpful to point out those subjects which the author considers most worthy of their attention.

First, the fundamental principles of motion have been more directly linked to purely mathematical axioms than has been common until now; and the application of these principles to practical purposes has perhaps, in some instances, been made easier. The passive strength of materials of all kinds has been very thoroughly investigated, and many new conclusions have been drawn regarding it. These are of immediate importance to the architect and the engineer, and they appear to contradict the results of some very complex calculations.

The theory of waves has been greatly simplified and somewhat expanded, and their motions have been illustrated by experiments of a unique nature. A similar method of reasoning has been applied to the circulation of the blood, to the propagation of sound (either in fluids or in solids), and to the vibrations of musical strings <note>The original text uses the term "chords" to refer to musical strings.</note>. The general principle of a velocity, corresponding to half the height of a certain <term>modulus</term>, is shown to be applicable to all these cases. A connection has also been established between the sound obtained from a given solid and its strength in resisting <term>flexure</term> of any kind; or, in the case of ice and water, between the speed of sound in the solid and the compressibility of the fluid state. The theory of sound and of sounding bodies in general has also received some new illustrations, and the theory of music and of musical intervals has been specifically discussed.

# PREFACE.

the images formed by lenses and mirrors have been correctly investigated, and the inaccuracy of some former estimates has been demonstrated.

In the department of physical optics, the phenomena of halos and parhelia <note>Also known as sun dogs.</note> have been explained using principles that are not entirely new, but which had been long forgotten. The functions of the eye have been minutely examined, and the way it adjusts to perceive objects at different distances has been determined. The various phenomena of colored light have been extensively described and accurately represented by colored plates; and some new instances of the production of colors have been pointed out and attributed to the general law of double lights <note>The principle of interference.</note>, which also explains many experiments by earlier opticians. Furthermore, this law has been applied to establish a theory on the nature of light that satisfactorily resolves almost every difficulty that has previously surrounded the subject.

The theory of the tides has been simplified into a very basic form, which seems to agree better with all observed phenomena than the more complex calculations usually thought necessary. Regarding the cohesion and capillary action of liquids, I have had the good fortune to anticipate Mr. Laplace in his recent research, and I have attempted to show that my assumptions apply more universally to the facts than those used by that rightly celebrated mathematician. I have also tried to shed new light on the general properties of matter in other forms and on the theory of heat, which is significantly involved in them. Additionally, I have drawn some useful conclusions by comparing various experiments on the elasticity of steam, evaporation, and the readings of <term>hygrometers</term>. I have listed, in a concise and systematic way, the principal facts that have

The historical part of the work can scarcely be called new, but several of the circumstances which are related have escaped the notice of former writers on the history of the sciences.

Besides these improvements—if I may be allowed to give them that name—there are others, perhaps of less importance, which may still be interesting to those who are particularly engaged in those departments of science, or of mechanical practice, to which they relate. Among these may be ranked, in the division of <term>mechanics</term> properly so called: a simple demonstration of the law of the force by which a body revolves in an <term>ellipsis</term>; another of the properties of <term>cycloidal pendulums</term>; an examination of the mechanism of <term>animal motions</term>; a comparison of the <term>weights and measures</term> of different countries; and a convenient estimate of the effect of human labor. With respect to <term>architecture</term>: a simple method of drawing the outline of a column; an investigation of the best forms for arches; a determination of the curve which affords the greatest space for turning; considerations on the structure of the joints employed in carpentry and on the firmness of wedges; and an easy mode of forming a <term>kirb roof</term> <note>Commonly known today as a curb or mansard roof.</note>. For the purposes of machinery of different kinds: an arrangement of bars for obtaining <term>rectilinear motion</term>; an inquiry into the most eligible proportions of wheels and pinions; remarks on the friction of wheelwork and of balances; a mode of finding the form of a tooth for impelling a pallet without friction; a <term>chronometer</term> for measuring minute portions of time; a <term>clock scapement</term> <note>Now spelled "escapement."</note>; a calculation of the effect of temperature on <term>steel springs</term>; an easy determination of the best line of draft for a carriage; and an

In the hydraulic and optical parts, the following may be enumerated: an overflowing lamp; a simplification of the rules for finding the velocity of running water; remarks on the application of force to hydraulic machines; a method for releasing air from water pipes; an analysis of the human voice; and some arrangements for solar microscopes and for other optical instruments of a similar nature.

In the astronomical and physical division of the work, there will be found: a general rule for determining the correction for aberration; a comparison of observations on the figure of the earth; a table of the order of electrical excitation; a chart of the variation of the compass and of the trade winds; formulas for finding the heat of summer and winter; remarks on the theory of the winds; and a comparative table of all the mechanical properties of a variety of natural bodies.

A few of these subjects have been more fully discussed in the miscellaneous papers which have already been published in the *Philosophical Transactions* and elsewhere, and which are now reprinted with corrections and additions; others are briefly investigated in the mathematical elements that form a part of the second volume, or in the remarks that are inserted, in their proper places, in the catalogue of references.

# PREFACE.

value, especially in a work intended to serve as a key, by which access may be gained to all the widely scattered treasures of science; and which will enable those who are eager to extend their research in any specific department to quickly obtain all the information that books can provide.

It will not be considered surprising that the implementation of this plan—allowing for some other professional commitments and for various incidental interruptions—should have occupied more than three years from the resignation of the professorship to the publication of the work. Some part of it is, by its nature, incapable of permanent perfection, since the catalogue must be continually expanded by the listing of new publications; and it might perhaps be desirable for an appendix to be added to it at least every ten years. However, the lectures themselves may be expected to remain reasonably adequate to the state of the sciences for a much longer period; since, in investigations so closely connected with mathematical principles, fundamental improvements will always bear a very small proportion to the number of innovations. I do not, however, mean to claim that the catalogue is by any means complete, even regarding older works, but I believe that the references it contains are at least sufficient to lead those who may consult the quoted passages to the works of every prominent author who has treated the respective subjects. Nor do I claim to have excluded all references of little importance; but I trust that the number I have included will be found insignificant; and it would have been very difficult to have rejected any of them without some chance of omitting others of greater value.

Whatever the deficiencies of this work may be, I think it right to observe that my current pursuits will not allow me to look forward to any time at which I shall be able to correct them, or even to attend to the proofreading or the revision of the engravings, in case

...regarding the necessity of a second edition. I have already begun to collect materials for a work, in a very similar form, relating to every department of medical knowledge. This work will not, however, be ready for publication soon; it will be relatively more concise than these lectures, in proportion to all that has been said and written regarding medicine, but, I hope, much more complete with regard to everything that is known with certainty and can be applied with utility.

Welbeck Street,
30th March, 1807.

# ADDITIONS AND CORRECTIONS.

P. 40. L. 5 from the bottom; for "therefore," read, afterwards.
P. 71. L. 5 from the bottom; for "IV," read, V.

P. 87. After l. 4, insert,
When an insulated body revolves around an axis in any direction, the state of revolution cannot be permanent unless the axis is situated so that the centrifugal forces on each side of it balance each other. It is obvious that this must happen in a homogeneous sphere, whatever the position of the axis may be; and it has been demonstrated that when the body is of an irregular form, there are at least three different axes, situated at right angles to each other, around which the body may revolve in an equilibrium that is either stable or unstable. It can also be shown that if a body, revolving around any axis, receives at the same time an impulse which would cause it to revolve around a second axis in another direction, the two revolutions will be combined and will form a single revolution around a third axis, in an intermediate position. This axis will remain at rest until it is displaced by some new force, provided that it is one of the axes of permanent revolution; so that no body can revolve around a moveable axis without a continual disturbing force. And when an irregular body begins to move on an axis incapable of equilibrium, its revolution will be gradually altered, so as to approach continually to a revolution around one of the natural axes; but it will never pass beyond the state of equilibrium, as in many other cases of deviation from such a state; since the momentum produced by the excess of centrifugal force in one part of the revolution is destroyed in another. For a similar reason, if a stick is thrown in a horizontal position with a rotary motion, it will fall in the same position much more certainly than if it were thrown without any rotation; for any small disturbing force, which might be sufficient to turn it into a vertical position during its flight, will only produce, when combined with the rotary motion, a slight change in the direction of the rotation, which will confine the deviation of the stick from a horizontal position within narrow limits.

They have supposed these to act in the same manner as the sun's attraction operates in slowing the moon’s motions. But the fact is that, according to Mr. Laplace, the disturbing force of the sun produces this effect on the moon only in proportion as it increases her distance from the earth; consequently, no such slowing can possibly be produced by the force of gravity in the rotation of the sea or of the atmosphere, and the entire effect must be attributed to meteorological causes. These causes first produce the trade winds, and secondly, by means of the friction of these winds, cause a similar motion in the sea. In the case of Jupiter's atmosphere, the effects of heat can indeed hardly be supposed to be very noticeable; and as the rotation of this planet is extremely rapid, it is not at all impossible that the satellites may exert an action on the atmosphere somewhat similar to the slowing of the moon’s motion by the disturbing force of the sun.

But the difficulty may be removed by returning to the general principle of superficial cohesion, and by comparing the common surface of the liquid and solid with the surface of a single liquid whose attractive power is equal only to the difference of the respective powers of the substances concerned. In this manner it may be shown that if the attractive power of the solid is equal to that of the liquid, or even greater, it will be wetted by the liquid, which will rise until its surface acquires the same direction as that of the solid; and that in other cases, the angle of contact will be larger in proportion as the solid is less attractive. A similar comparison is also equally applicable to the contact of two liquids of different densities.

### LECTURE I.
### INTRODUCTION.

It is to be presumed that most of those who honor the theater of the Royal Institution with their attendance are already acquainted with the nature of the goals which its founders and promoters have been endeavoring to attain; yet it appears to be by no means superfluous that I should accurately define my own views of the utility that is likely to be derived from it, and of the most effective means of accomplishing its purposes. This is in order that we may be able to distinguish, without difficulty, the most suitable path for our common progress through the regions of science, and so that those who are desirous of accompanying me on the journey may know precisely what route we are to follow and which departments will more particularly capture our attention.

Societies that are merely literary and philosophical have, in general, principally proposed to themselves to enlighten the understanding by the discovery of unknown phenomena, and to exercise the reasoning powers by

<sig>B</sig>

<summary>This lecture introduction outlines the speaker's goals for the course and describes the intended utility of the Royal Institution. The author aims to define a clear path for scientific study to help the audience understand the specific topics and methodologies that will be covered.</summary>
<keywords>Royal Institution, Natural Philosophy, science education, scientific societies, philosophy, research methodology, introduction</keywords>

# LECTURE I.

opening new fields for inquiry. Other associations have been more particularly intended for the encouragement of the arts, <term>manufactures</term>, and <term>commerce</term>. The primary and specific goal of the <term>Royal Institution of Great Britain</term> is avowedly of a humbler, but not of a less interesting nature. It is to apply the improvements which have been made in <term>science</term> to domestic convenience, and to introduce into general practice such mechanical inventions as are of clear utility. But while it is chiefly engaged in this pursuit, it extends its views, in some measure, to the promotion of the same ends which belong to the specific domains of other literary societies; and it is all the more impossible that such objects should be wholly excluded, as it is upon the advancement of these that the specific objects of the Institution must ultimately depend. Hence, the dissemination of the knowledge of <term>natural philosophy</term> and <term>chemistry</term> becomes a very essential part of the design of the Royal Institution: and this department must, in the natural order of arrangement, be prior to the application of the sciences to practical uses. To exclude all knowledge except that which has already been applied to immediate utility would be to reduce our mental faculties to a state of servitude, and to thwart the very purposes which we are working to accomplish. No discovery, however remote in its nature from the subjects of daily observation, can with reason be declared wholly inapplicable to the benefit of mankind.

It has therefore always appeared to me to be not only the best beginning, but also an objective of high and permanent importance in the plan of the Institution, to direct public attention to the cultivation of the basic doctrines of <term>natural philosophy</term>, both theoretical and practical. Those who possess the genuine spirit of <term>scientific investigation</term>, and who have tasted the pure satisfaction arising from an advancement in <term>intellectual acquirements</term>, are content to proceed in their research without inquiring at every step what they gain by their newly discovered insights, and to what practical purposes they are applicable: they receive sufficient gratification from the expansion of their views of the structure of the universe, and experience, in the immediate pursuit of knowledge, that pleasure which others wish to obtain more indirectly by its means. And it is one of the principal advantages of a <term>liberal education</term> that it creates a capacity for an enjoyment so elegant and so rational.

# INTRODUCTION.

A considerable portion of my audience, to whose instruction it will be my particular ambition to adapt my lectures, consists of that sex which, by the customs of civilized society, is in some measure exempt from the more laborious duties that occupy the time and attention of the other sex. The many leisure hours which are at the command of females in the higher ranks of society may surely be devoted, with greater satisfaction, to the improvement of the mind and to the acquisition of knowledge, than to such amusements as are only designed to facilitate the dull consumption of excess time. The hours spent in this way will unquestionably become, through a little habit, as much more agreeable at the moment as they must be more capable of providing self-approval upon reflection. And besides, like the seasoning which reconciled the Spartans to their uninviting diet, they will even heighten the relish for those pursuits which they interrupt; for mental exercise is as necessary to mental enjoyment as physical labor is to physical health and vigor. In this point of view, the Royal Institution may in some degree supply the place of a subordinate university to those whose sex or situation in life has denied them the advantage of an academic education in the national institutions of learning.

But notwithstanding the necessity of frequently introducing speculations of a more general nature, we must not lose sight of the original objects of the Royal Institution; and we must therefore direct our attention more particularly to the theory of practical mechanics and of manufactures. In these departments, we shall find some deficiencies which may, without much difficulty, be supplied from scientific principles; and by an ample collection and display of models, illustrative of machines and of inventions of all kinds, we may proceed in the most direct manner to contribute to the dissemination of that kind of knowledge which is most particularly our object. So that we must be more practical than academies of sciences and more theoretical than societies for the improvement of arts; while we endeavor at the same time to give stability to our proceedings by an annual return to the elementary knowledge which serves the purposes of both; and, as far as we are able, to apply to practice the newest insights which may, from time to time, be thrown on particular branches of mechanical science. It is thus that we may most effectively perform what the idolized sophists of antiquity but

<header>LECTURE I.</header>

To those who are engaged in the practical cultivation of various arts that serve the conveniences of life, these lectures may be of some utility by providing them with well-established principles applicable to a variety of cases that may occasionally occur to them, where a slight deviation from the ordinary routine of their profession may be necessary. Unfortunately, the hands that execute are too often inadequately supported by the head that directs; and much labor is lost for want of a little previous study of the fundamental doctrines of the mechanical sciences. Nor is an excessive amount of time or industry necessary for this purpose; for it happens, strangely enough, that almost all practical applications of science depend on principles easily learned; and, except in astronomy alone, it has seldom been found that very obscure investigations have been of great importance to society. Our most refined analytical calculations are far too imperfect to apply to all possible cases of mechanical actions that can be proposed; and those problems which occur most frequently may, in general, be solved by methods that are sufficiently obvious; although, from a lack of proper order and clarity in the treatment of first principles, it has often happened that the most elementary propositions have been considered to require great study and application.

We may also be able to perform an important service to society, and to confer a still more essential benefit on individuals, by restraining the premature zeal of unskilled inventors. We need only read over the monthly accounts of patents—intended to secure the financial advantages of useful discoveries—in order to be convinced of how much time and fortune is continually wasted on the feeblest attempts to innovate and improve. If we can succeed in convincing such reckless enthusiasts of their real ignorance, or if we can show them that even their own "fairy ground" has already been occupied by others, we may save them from impending ruin, and may relieve the public from the distraction of having its attention constantly stirred by unworthy objects. The ridicule associated with the name of a <term>projector</term> <note>A term used historically for a person who forms speculative schemes or designs; often used dismissively for an impractical inventor.</note> has been, in general, only too well deserved; for few—very few—who have aspired to make improvements have ever had the patience to submit their inventions to such experimental tests as common

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

We may venture to affirm that out of every hundred imagined improvements in arts or in machines, at least ninety, if not ninety-nine, are either old or useless; the object of our research is to enable ourselves to distinguish and to adopt the hundredth. But while we prune the excessive shoots of youthful invention, we must remember to perform our task with leniency, and to show that we wish only to give additional vigor to the healthy branches, and not to uproot the parent plant.

The Repository of the Royal Institution, as soon as it can be properly furnished, will be considered a supplementary room for apparatus. In it, the most interesting models exhibited and described in the lectures will be placed for more frequent inspection, and a few other items may perhaps deserve admission that do not require such a detailed explanation. To those who have profited by the lectures, or who are already too far advanced to need them, our rooms for reading and literary conversation may be a source of mutual instruction. Our Library, in time, must contain all those important works that are too expensive for the private collections of most individuals, which are necessary to complete the knowledge of particular sciences, and to which references will occasionally be given in the lectures on those sciences. Our Journals, free from commercial constraints, will present the public from time to time with concise accounts of the most interesting novelties in science and the useful arts; they will also provide a constant incentive for their editors to adopt, as much as possible for their own improvement, whatever is valuable in the publications of their contemporaries. When all the advantages that may reasonably be expected from this Institution are fully understood and impartially considered, it is hoped that few people of liberal minds will be indifferent to its success, or unwilling to contribute to and participate in it.

I shall always most willingly submit to and most punctually follow that regulation which forbids the introduction of any discussions connected with the learned professions. It requires the study of a considerable portion of a person's life to qualify them to be of use to mankind in any of those professions; and nothing can be more harmful to individuals or to society than attempting to act practically based on an incomplete understanding of only a few first principles.

<header>LECTURE I.</header>

In medicine, the wisest can do only a little, and the ignorant can do worse than nothing; and just as we are eager to seek whatever relief the learned and experienced may be able to offer us, we should be equally cautious to avoid the harmful interference of the half-trained amateur. In politics and in religion, we need only look back at the history of kingdoms and republics to be aware of the mischief that follows when “fools rush in where angels fear to tread.”

Deeply impressed by the importance of mathematical investigations, both for the advancement of science and for the improvement of the mind, I considered it my primary and essential duty to provide the Royal Institution, in my Syllabus, with a connected system of <term>natural philosophy</term>, following a plan rarely, if ever, executed before even in the most comprehensive treatises. Starting from the simplest axioms of abstract mathematics, the syllabus contains a rigorous demonstration of every proposition I have found necessary to use throughout the entire field of natural philosophy. Only in the astronomical section do some observations appear that are not supported by mathematical evidence; here, however, it was as impractical as it would have been useless to attempt to delve into investigations which, in many cases, have been extended far beyond the limits even of Newton’s researches. But for the sake of those who are not inclined to undertake the labor of following, with mathematical accuracy, all the steps of the demonstrations on which the doctrines of the mechanical sciences are founded, I shall try to avoid, throughout this whole course of lectures, any complexity that might be perplexing to a beginner and every argument more suited for private study than for a public lecture hall. In this setting, I propose to support the same propositions with experimental proofs—not because I consider such proofs to be the most conclusive, or more interesting to a truly scientific mind than a deduction from general principles, but because there is satisfaction in discovering how theories align with visible effects, and because physical objects are helpful in assisting the imagination to comprehend and the memory to retain what might fail to hold enough attention in a more abstract form.

This combination of experimental and analogical arguments constitutes the primary merit of modern science. And here, I hope the citizen of the world will excuse the bias of an Englishman if I take pride in, and congra-

# INTRODUCTION.

I congratulate my audience on the clear superiority of our own country in the first establishment and in the subsequent cultivation of the true philosophy of the operations of nature. I admit that we have at times been culpably negligent of the labors of others; that we have lately allowed our neighbors to excel us in abstract mathematics and perhaps, in some instances, in the patient and persevering observation of plain phenomena. We do not have a Lagrange or a Laplace at this moment; what we do have, I do not think it necessary to enumerate. But there is a certain combination of theoretical reasoning with experimental inquiry in which Great Britain, from the time of the reformation of philosophy, has never been inferior to any existing nation. I need only refer to the Transactions of the Royal Society for many instances of the mode of investigation to which I refer; and I will venture to assert that their recent publications are equal in importance to any that have preceded them. It was in England that a Bacon first taught the world the true method of the study of nature and rescued science from that barbarism in which the followers of Aristotle, by a too servile imitation of their master, had involved it; and with which, even lately, a mad spirit of innovation—under the name of the critical philosophy—has again been threatening it in a considerable part of Europe. It was in this country that Newton advanced, with one gigantic stride, from the regions of twilight into the noonday of science. A Boyle and a Hooke, who would otherwise have been deservedly the boast of their century, served only as obscure forerunners of Newton's glories. After these, a crowd of eminent men followed, each of great individual merit; but, absorbed in the pursuit of the Newtonian discoveries, they chose rather to be useful through their humble industry than to wander in search of the brilliance of novelty. It is difficult to judge our contemporaries; but we appear at present to possess more than one philosopher whose names posterity will be eager to rank in the same class as the few who have been listed. But it is not our present business to enter into the history of science; regarding what is supposed to be wholly unknown, we can have little curiosity. A short sketch of the progress of each branch of <term>natural philosophy</term> will be more properly introduced after we have finished our investigation of the principal doctrines belonging to it.

By bearing in mind this observation, I hope to be able to render my lectures more and more intelligible and familiar—not by passing over difficulties, but by endeavoring to make the task of overcoming them easier; and if at any time I appear to have failed in this attempt, I shall think myself honored by any subsequent inquiries that my audience may be disposed to make.

We have to extend our views over the whole circle of natural and artificial knowledge, to consider in detail the principles and application of the philosophy of nature and of art. As to the practical importance of philosophical theories of the arts, it may have been overrated by some, but no one is authorized to claim that it has been too highly estimated unless he has mastered everything that theory is capable of achieving; such a person, although he may in some cases be forced to admit the insufficiency of our calculations, will never have reason to complain that they are false.

The division of the entire course of lectures into three parts was originally suggested by the periodic schedule in which the appointed hours recur; however, it appears to be more convenient than any other for the regular classification of the subjects. The third part relates to the specific history of the phenomena of nature and of the properties of bodies actually existing in the universe independently of human art; it includes astronomy, geography, and the doctrine of the properties of matter and of the most general and powerful agents that influence it.

For once these laws are established, each fact, as soon as it is known, assumes its place in the system and is retained in the memory through its relation to the rest as a connecting link. In the analytical mode, on the contrary—which is absolutely necessary for the initial investigation of truth—we are obliged to begin by collecting a number of isolated circumstances. These lead us back by degrees to the knowledge of original principles, but until we arrive at those principles, they are merely a burden to the memory. For the phenomena of nature resemble the scattered leaves of the Sibylline prophecies: only a word or a single syllable is written on each leaf, which, when considered separately, conveys no instruction to the mind. But when, through the labor of patient investigation, every fragment is replaced in its appropriate connection, the whole begins at once to speak a clear and harmonious language.

Proceeding, therefore, in the synthetical order, we set out from the abstract doctrines of mathematics relating to quantity, space, and number. We pass over these, assuming they are previously understood or sufficiently explained in mathematical elements, and move on to their immediate application to mechanics and hydrodynamics, or to those cases of the motions of solids and fluids that depend on arbitrary assumptions—that is, where we do not confine our inquiries to any particular cases of existing phenomena. By means of principles that can be deduced in a satisfactory manner from mathematical axioms, with the assistance only of the general logic of induction, we shall be able to draw conclusions that can provide us with very important information regarding the operations of nature and art. We shall also be able to lay down laws that, to an uninformed person, would appear to be beyond the powers of reason to determine without the help of experiments. The behaviors of falling bodies and of projectiles, the phenomena of bodies revolving around a center, the motions of pendulums, the properties of the center of gravity, the equilibrium of forces in various kinds of machines, the laws of preponderance, and the effects of collision—all these are wholly referable to axiomatic evidence and are frequently applicable to important practical uses. Upon these foundations, we shall proceed to the general principles of machinery and the application of different kinds of forces. All these subjects are partly preparatory to the direct examination of the <term>mechanical arts</term> and manufactures, which are so numerous and complicated that they are difficult to arrange regularly without some difficulty. In these departments, it is often of the utmost importance for the mechanic—especially in works of great magnitude—to return to philosophical principles. In the same manner, while taking a general view of other arts and manufactures, we may be able to explain their principles where theory is concerned and to show practical examples where the nature of the subject requires no complex investigation.

The general theory of such motions will be introduced under the headings of hydrostatics, or the states of liquids at rest; pneumatostatics, or the properties of elastic fluids at rest; and hydraulics, or the theory of fluids in motion. The practical application of this theory to hydraulic and pneumatic machines is of very considerable importance, and is as interesting to the philosopher as it is necessary to the engineer. The employment of the force of water and wind to the best advantage, the draining of lands and mines, the supply of water for domestic convenience, the maneuvers of seamanship, and the construction of the steam engine are all dependent upon hydrodynamical principles, and are often considered as included in the science of hydraulics. Harmonics and optics, the remaining parts of this division, are more distinct: the doctrine of sound, the theory of music, and the construction of musical instruments are as pleasing to the intellect in theory as they are gratifying to the senses in practice; but the science of optics is no less interesting, and at the same time far more useful. The instruments which it provides are of almost indispensable necessity to the navigator, to the naturalist, to the physiologist, and even to the person of business or pleasure. It is perhaps in this science that many individuals of the greatest genius have been most successfully employed. The reasons for which it is classified as a division of hydrodynamics will be explained hereafter.

The contemplation of the particular phenomena of nature, as they are displayed in the universe at large, contributes perhaps less to the perfection of any of the arts that are immediately subservient to profit or convenience than the study of mechanics and hydrodynamics. In all these respects, the science of astronomy holds the first rank; its uses in assisting navigation and in regulating chronology are beyond all calculation. Electricity and magnetism are partly attributable to the properties of matter, and partly to the actions of substances that seem to share some properties with common matter while differing in others. The phenomena produced by these agents often excite a high degree of curiosity to investigate their causes, although the inquiry too often ends only in astonishment; but we have reason to expect significant progress in these sciences from the remarkable discoveries of modern chemists. The usefulness of the study of electricity is well demonstrated by the widespread introduction of conductors to protect us from lightning, not to mention the occasional use of electricity in medicine; and since the important discovery of the compass, we can only regret that the changing nature of magnetic effects so greatly limits the utility of that instrument for nautical and geographical purposes. Our knowledge of meteorology and geology is still very imperfect; despite many extensive treatises written about them, we cannot claim to have reduced them to any definite laws; and yet there are some meteorological facts that well deserve our attention. Natural history is the last of the sciences we need to mention; some may think it unnecessary to attempt such a superficial sketch of this vast subject as our plan allows; but it is still possible to select some general observations regarding methods of classification, as well as the principles of natural history, which, though very brief, may still be somewhat instructive. This third division of the course would properly include, along with the general properties of matter and the specific actions of its particles, the entire science of chemistry; but the variety and importance of chemical research require a separate and detailed discussion; and the novelty and beauty of many of the experiments provided by the work of our contemporaries, which will be shown in the theater of the Royal Institution by the Professor of Chemistry, are enough to make this branch of natural philosophy the most entertaining of all the sciences.

Such is the complete outline of our plan, and these are the practical uses to which the arts and sciences included in it are mainly applicable.

INTRODUCTION. 15

Before we proceed to examine its various parts, we must pause to consider the mode of reasoning that is most generally to be adopted. It depends on the <term>axiom</term> which has always been essentially involved in every improvement of <term>natural philosophy</term>, but which has been increasingly employed since the revival of learning under the name <term>induction</term>, and which has been sufficiently discussed by modern <term>metaphysicians</term>. That like causes produce like effects, or that in similar circumstances similar consequences ensue, is the most general and most important law of nature; it is the foundation of all analogical reasoning and is gathered from constant experience by an indispensable and unavoidable inclination of the human mind.

It does not seem that we can have any other accurate conception of <term>causation</term>, or of the connection between a cause and its effect, other than a strong impression from observation and uniform experience that the one has constantly followed the other. We do not know the inner nature of the connection by which gravity causes a stone to fall, or how the string of a bow pushes the arrow forward; nor is there any inherent absurdity in supposing it possible that the stone might have remained suspended in the air, or that the bowstring might have passed through the arrow as light passes through glass. But it is obvious that we cannot help concluding that the stone's weight is the cause of its fall, and that every heavy body will fall unless supported; and that the pressure of the string is the cause of the arrow's motion, so that if we shoot, the arrow will fly. If we hesitated to make these conclusions, we would often pay dearly for our skepticism. This explanation is sufficient to show that these two expressions are identical: that like causes produce like effects, and that in similar circumstances similar consequences follow. And such is the basis for arguments based on experience, the simplest principle of reasoning after pure mathematical truths—which appear to be so far prior to experience that their contradiction always implies an absurdity offensive to the imagination.

In the application of induction, the greatest caution and carefulness are necessary; for it is obvious that before we can infer with certainty the complete similarity of two events, we must be perfectly assured that we are acquainted with every circumstance that can have any relation to their causes. The error of some of the ancient schools consisted principally in the

# LECTURE I.

...lack of sufficient precaution in this respect; for although <term>Bacon</term> is quite rightly considered the author of the most correct method of <term>induction</term>, yet, according to his own statement, it was primarily the cautious and gradual application of this mode of reasoning that he worked to introduce. He remarks that the <term>Aristotelians</term>, based on a hasty observation of a few similar facts, immediately proceeded to deduce universal scientific principles and fundamental laws of nature. They then derived from these, by their <term>syllogisms</term>, all the specific cases that should have actually served as intermediate steps in the investigation.

We can easily find a familiar example of such an error. We observe that, generally, heavy bodies fall to the ground unless they are supported; it was therefore concluded that all heavy bodies tend downward. Since flame was most often seen to rise, it was inferred that flame was naturally and absolutely weightless. If enough care had been taken in observing the effects of fluids on falling and floating bodies, in examining the relationship of flame to the surrounding atmosphere, and in determining the <term>specific gravity</term> of air at different temperatures, it would have been easily discovered that the greater weight of the colder air caused the flame to rise. While flame is less heavy than air, it has no inherent tendency to move upward. Accordingly, the <term>Epicureans</term>—whose arguments regarding matter and motion were often more accurate than those of their contemporaries—had corrected this error; for in the second book of <term>Lucretius</term>, we find a very accurate explanation of the phenomenon.

> “See with what force that river’s crystal stream
> Resists the weight of many a massive beam.
> The more we vainly struggle to sink the wood,
> The higher it rebounds with a swift recoil.
> Yet no man would rashly venture to claim
> That the beam would rise on its own.
> Thus, flame also has weight, though it is very thin,
> And it only rises when forced up by heavier air.”

It may be appropriate to mention here those axioms which <term>Newton</term> called <term>rules of philosophizing</term>; though it must be admitted that they offer us very little immediate help in our investigations. The first is,

# INTRODUCTION.

that “no more causes are to be admitted as existing in nature, than are true, and sufficient for explaining the phenomena to be considered;” the second, “therefore effects of the same kind are to be attributed, as far as is possible, to the same causes;” thirdly, “those qualities of bodies which cannot be increased nor diminished, and which are found in all bodies within the reach of our experiments, are to be considered as general qualities of all bodies existing;” fourthly, “in experimental philosophy, propositions collected by <term>induction</term> from phenomena, are to be esteemed either accurately or very nearly true, notwithstanding any contrary hypotheses, until other phenomena occur, by which they may either be corrected or confuted.”

As an illustration of the remark that these axioms, though strictly true, are of little real utility in assisting our investigations, I shall give an instance from the subject of electricity. Supposing that we wish to determine whether or not the <term>electric fluid</term> has weight; we are to inquire whether or not <term>gravitation</term> is one of those properties which are described in the third rule, and whether that rule will authorize us to apply it to the <term>electric fluid</term> as one of those qualities of bodies which cannot be increased nor diminished, which are found in all bodies within the reach of our experiments, and which are therefore to be considered as general qualities of all bodies existing. Now it appears to be, in the first place, uncertain whether or not the increase and diminution of gravity resulting from a change of distance is strictly compatible with the terms of the definition; and in the second place, we are equally at a loss to decide whether or not the <term>electric fluid</term> can with propriety be called a body, for it appears in some respects to be wholly different from tangible matter, while it has other qualities in common with it. Such are the difficulties of laying down general laws on so comprehensive a scale, that we shall find it more secure to be contented to proceed gradually by closer inductions in particular cases. We shall, however, seldom be much embarrassed in the choice of a mode of argumentation. The <term>laws of motion</term>, which will be the first immediate subjects of discussion, have indeed sometimes been referred to experimental evidence; but we shall be able to deduce them all in a satisfactory manner, by means of our general axiom, from reasonings purely mathematical, which, wherever they are applicable, are unquestionably preferable to the imperfect evidence of the senses employed in experimental investigations.

# LECTURE II.

## ON MOTION.

The whole science of mechanics depends on the laws of motion, either actually existing or suppressed by the opposition of the forces that tend to produce it. The nature of motion therefore requires a particular examination at the beginning of the science of mechanical philosophy; and although the subject is so abstract as to demand some effort of attention—being seldom capable of receiving much immediate illustration from objects of sense—yet we shall find it indispensable to our progress in the investigation of many particular problems of importance to first obtain a clear conception of the properties and characteristics of all kinds of motions.

One of the ancient philosophers, on being asked for a definition of motion, is said to have walked across the room and to have answered, "You see it, but what it is, I cannot tell you." It does not, however, appear absolutely necessary to appeal to the senses for the idea of motion: for a definition is the resolution of a complex idea into the simpler elements that compose it. In the present instance, these elements are the existence of two points at a certain distance, and, after a certain interval of time, the existence of the same points at a different distance. The difference of the distances is assumed to be determined according to that postulate of geometry which has generally been tacitly understood, but which I have expressly inserted in the geometrical part of my syllabus; this requires that the length of a line be capable of being identified, whether by the effect of an object on the senses or merely in the imagination.

Motion, therefore, is the change of rectilinear distance between two points. Allowing the accuracy of this definition, it appears that two points are ne-

This may seem in some measure paradoxical, but it is the necessary consequence of our definition, and the paradox is only due to the difficulty of imagining the existence of a single atom, unsurrounded by the innumerable points of a space which we represent to ourselves as immovable.

It has been for want of a precise definition of the term motion that many authors have fallen into confusion with respect to absolute and relative motion. For the definition of motion, as the change of rectilinear distance between two points, appears to be the definition of what is commonly called relative motion; but, on a strict examination, we shall find that what we usually call absolute motion is merely relative to some space which we imagine to be without motion, but which is so in imagination only. The space which we call quiescent is in general the earth's surface; yet we well know, from astronomical considerations, that every point of the earth's surface is perpetually in motion, and that in very various directions. Nor are there any material objects accessible to our senses which we can consider as absolutely motionless, or even as motionless with regard to each other; since the continual variation of temperature to which all bodies are liable, and the minute agitations arising from the motions of other bodies with which they are connected, will always tend to produce some imperceptible change in their distances.

Therefore, when we assert that a body is absolutely at rest, we only mean to compare it with some large space in which it is contained; for we cannot positively affirm that there exists a body absolutely at rest, in as strict a sense as an absolutely straight line may be conceived to exist. And if such a quiescent body did exist, we have no criterion by which it could be distinguished. Supposing a ship to move at the rate of three miles in an hour, and a person on board to walk or to be drawn toward the stern at the same rate, he would be relatively in motion with respect to the ship, yet we might very properly consider him as absolutely at rest. But on a more extended view, he would be at rest only in relation to the earth's surface; for he would still be revolving around the axis of the earth, and with the earth around the sun; and with

Now, regarding any effects within the ship, all subsequent relations are of no consequence; the change in his <term>rectilinear distance</term> from the various parts of the ship is all that needs to be considered when determining those effects. In the same manner, if the ship appears—by comparison with the water only—to be moving through it at a velocity of three miles per hour, and the water is moving at the same time in the opposite direction at the same rate due to a tide or current, the ship will be at rest relative to the shore. However, the mutual actions of the ship and the water will be the same as if the water were actually at rest and the ship were in motion.

It is not enough to observe the increase or decrease in the distance of a moving point from only one other point: we must compare its successive positions with many other surrounding points. For this purpose, these points must be at rest relative to each other so that they can be considered part of a <term>quiescent space</term> or surface. This may be defined as a space or surface in which all points always remain at equal distances from one another, without any external influence. In this sense, we must call the deck of the ship a <term>quiescent surface</term>, whether the ship is at anchor or under sail. However, we must not consider a surface revolving around a center as a quiescent surface; for it will be shown later that no such motion can exist without the influence of a <term>centripetal force</term>, which makes it unsuitable for determining the properties of a moving body.

When a point is in motion relative to a <term>quiescent space</term>, it is often simply called a <term>moving point</term>, and the straight line joining any two of its positions that are immediately next to each other is called its direction. If it remains continuously in one straight line drawn in the quiescent space, that line is always the <term>line of its direction</term>. If it travels along several straight lines, each line is the line of its direction for as long as it continues along it. But if its path becomes curved, we can no longer consider it to be perfectly coinciding with a straight line at any time; instead, we must return to the literal definition by assuming a straight line is drawn through two successive points where the object is found. If these points are then conceived to approach each other without limit, we will have the line of its direction. Now, in geometry, such a line is called a

Having formed an accurate idea of the nature of motion and of the meaning of the terms used when speaking of its properties, we may proceed to consider the mechanical laws to which it is subject. These laws are derived from the core of the definitions that have already been established. The first law is that a moving point never leaves the line of its direction without a disturbing cause. Since a straight line is the same with respect to all sides, no reason can be imagined why the point should lean toward one side more than another; and the general law of induction requires that the moving point should maintain the same relationships toward points similarly situated on every side of the line. This argument appears to be satisfactory enough to give us ground for asserting that the law of motion stated here may be considered independent of experimental proof. 

It was once proposed as a prize question by the Academy of Sciences at Berlin to determine whether the laws of motion were necessary or accidental—that is, whether they were to be considered mathematical or physical truths. Maupertuis, then president of the academy, wrote an elaborate dissertation in which he endeavored to derive them from a complicated principle: that every effect is produced in the manner which requires the <term>least possible action</term>. He supposed this principle to be most consistent with the wise economy of nature. But this principle has itself been shown to be capable of adapting to any other imaginable laws of motion, and the complexity of the theory tends only to wrap the subject in unnecessary obscurity. The laws of motion appear to be easily demonstrable from the simplest mathematical truths, provided we grant the homogeneity or similarity of matter with respect to motion, and allow the general axiom that similar causes produce similar effects. If, however, anyone thinks differently, they are at liberty to call these laws experimental axioms gathered from a comparison of various phenomena; for we cannot easily reduce them to direct experiments, since we can never remove the influence of all disturbing causes from our experiments. Either <term>gravitation</term> or the contact of surrounding bodies will interfere with all the motions which we can examine.

Having established the <term>rectilinear</term> direction of undisturbed motion, we

come to consider its uniformity. Here, the idea of time enters into our subject. To define time in general is neither easy nor necessary, but we must have some measure of equal periods of duration. Our abstract idea of time depends on the memory of past sensations; however, it is obvious that the results of an intellectual measure of the duration of time would be subject to the greatest uncertainty. We may observe that, on a journey, the perpetual succession of various objects will often make a week appear, in retrospect, as long as a month spent in a series of uniform activities that are not laborious. The multitude of new impressions not only serves to increase the apparent length of the interval by filling up its gaps, but also tends to diminish the clarity of the ideas they replaced, giving them the character of the fainter recollections of an earlier date. We are, therefore, obliged to estimate the passage of time by the changes in external objects. Of these changes, the simplest and most convenient is the apparent motion of the sun—or rather of the stars—derived from the actual rotation of the earth on its axis. This is not indeed an undisturbed rectilinear motion, but it is equally applicable to every practical purpose. From this we obtain, through astronomical observations, the well-known measures of the duration of time implied by the terms day, hour, minute, and second.

Now, with the equality of time being thus estimated from any single motion, all other bodies moving without disturbance will travel across equal successive parts of their lines of direction in equal times. And this is the second law of motion, which, along with the former law, constitutes Newton’s first axiom or law of motion:

> “that every body persists in its state of rest or uniform rectilinear motion, except insofar as it is compelled by some force to change it.”

It appears that this second law is strictly deducible from the axioms and definitions which have been established, and principally from the consideration of the relative nature of motion and the total lack of a criterion for absolute motion. For, since the velocity of a body moving without resistance or disturbance is only a relationship to another body, if the second body has no mechanical connection with the first, its state with respect to motion can have no effect on the velocity of the first body, however great its comparative size may be. And if a body is at rest, there is nothing to cause it to begin to move either to the right hand or to the left; if it is at rest with respect to any other bodies, it will remain in the same condition, whatever the relative

the motions of those bodies may be understood when compared with surrounding objects; and these relationships can only be preserved by their continuance in uniform straight-line motion. This law is also confirmed by its perfect agreement with all experimental observations, although it is too simple to allow for an immediate proof. For we can never place any object in such circumstances as to be totally exempt from the operation of all accelerating or retarding forces; and the conclusions from such experiments as we can perform would generally require, for the accurate determination of the necessary corrections, a prior knowledge of the law which we wish to demonstrate.

Indeed, when we consider the motion of a projectile, we only have to account for the disturbing force of gravity, which so modifies the effect that the body deviates from a straight line but remains in the same vertical plane. From this we may infer that, in the absence of the force of gravity, the body would continue to move in every other plane in which its motion began, as well as in the vertical plane, since in that case all these planes would be equivalent to it; it must therefore remain at their common intersection, which could only be a straight line. So, by thus combining reasoning with observation, we may obtain a confirmation of the law of the straight-line direction of undisturbed motion, founded partly on direct experiment. Its uniformity is, however, even less subject to immediate examination; yet, from a consideration of the nature of friction and resistance, combined with the laws of gravity, we may ultimately show the perfect agreement of the theory with experiment. The tendency of matter to persist in this manner in a state of rest or of uniform straight-line motion is called its *inertia*.

In all these cases it is important to attend to the composition of motion, or the joint effect of more than one motion existing at the same time. The existence of two or more motions at the same time in the same body is not easily understood at first. It is, in fact, only a combination or separation of relationships that is considered: in the same manner as by combining the relationship of son to father and brother to brother, we obtain the relationship of nephew to uncle, so by combining the motion of a man walking on a ship with the motion of the ship, we determine the relative velocity of the man with respect to the earth’s surface. <header>LECTURE II.</header>

motion, and to examine how it may move in the simplest manner with respect to another space.

If any number of points move in parallel lines, covering equal distances in equal times, they are at rest with respect to each other; for it can easily be demonstrated that the rectilinear distance of each, from every other point, remains unchanged. And if all the points of a plane move in this manner on another plane, either plane may be said to be in rectilinear motion with respect to the other. This is easily exemplified by causing one plane to move on another, so that two or more of its points shall always remain in a given straight line on the second plane: as when a square is made to slide along the straight edge of a board, the surface of the square is in rectilinear motion with respect to the board. (Plate I. Fig. 4.)

If, besides this general motion of the plane, any point is supposed to have its own specific motion within it, the point will have two motions with respect to the other plane: the one in common with its plane, and the other specific to itself. The joint effect of these motions with respect to the second plane is called the result of the two motions. Thus, when a carriage moves on a perfectly level road, all its points describe parallel lines, and it is in rectilinear motion with respect to the road: its wheels share this motion, but also have a rotatory motion of their own; and the result of the two motions of each point of the wheels is the <term>cycloid</term> or <term>trochoid</term> that it describes in a stationary vertical plane. (Plate I. Fig. 5.)

When an arm is made to slide upon a bar, and a thread, fixed to the bar, is made to pass over a pulley at the end of the arm next to the bar, to a slider which is movable along the arm, the slider moves on the arm with the same velocity as the arm on the bar. But if the thread, instead of being fixed to the slider, is passed again over a pulley attached to it, and then brought back to be fixed to the arm, the motion of the slider will be only half that of the arm; and this will be true in whatever position the arm is fixed. Here we have two motions in the slider: one in common with the arm, and the other specific to itself, which may be either equal or unequal to the first; and by tracing a line on a fixed plane, with a point attached to the slider, we may easily examine the joint result of both the motions. (Plate I. Fig. 6.)

<header>ON MOTION.</header>

The joint result of any two motions is the diagonal of the parallelogram whose sides would be traveled, in the same amount of time, by the separate motions. That is, if we have two lines representing the directions and velocities of the separate motions, and from the far end of each we draw a line parallel to the other, the intersection of these lines will be the position of the moving body at the end of the given time. This is the necessary consequence of the coexistence of two motions in the sense that has been defined; it can also be fully illustrated by the apparatus that has been described. (Plate I. Fig. 7.)

Any given motion may be considered the result of any two or more motions capable of composing it in this manner. Thus, the line traced by the pointer of our apparatus will be exactly the same whether it is simply moved in the given direction, or made to move along the arm at a speed equal to that of the arm, or—when the arm is in a different position—at only half that speed. (Plate I. Fig. 8.)

This principle constitutes the important doctrine of the resolution of motion. There is some difficulty in imagining a slower motion to contain, as it were, within itself, two faster motions opposing each other. However, in fact, we only have to imagine ourselves adding or subtracting mathematical quantities, and we must set aside the prejudice, derived from our own feelings, which associates the idea of effort with that of motion. When we conceive a state of rest as the result of equal and opposite motions, we use the same method of representation as when we say that zero is the sum of two equal quantities with opposite signs; for instance, plus ten and minus ten make nothing.

The law of motion established here differs very little in its wording from the original words of Aristotle in his *Mechanical Problems*. He says that if a moving body has two motions that maintain a constant proportion to each other, it must necessarily travel along the diagonal of a parallelogram whose sides are in the ratio of the two motions. It is obvious that this proposition includes the consideration not only of uniform motions, but also of motions which are similarly accelerated or slowed down. We would hardly have expected that, from the time when the subject began to be so clear—

<header>LECTURE II.</header>

...ly understood, two thousand years would have passed before this law began to be applied to determining the velocity of bodies moved by deflecting forces, which Newton has so simply and elegantly deduced from it.

In the laws of motion, which are the main foundation of the *Principia*, their great author immediately introduces the consideration of forces; and the first corollary is stated this way: “a body describes the diagonal of a parallelogram by two forces acting together, in the same time in which it would describe its sides by the same forces acting separately.” It seems, however, to be more natural and clear to delay the consideration of force until the simpler doctrine of motion has been separately examined.

We may easily proceed to the composition of any number of different motions by combining them successively in pairs. Therefore, any uniform motions represented by the sides of a polygon—that is, a figure consisting of any number of straight sides—which are supposed to occur in the same movable body in directions parallel to those sides, and in the order of going around the figure, cancel each other out, and the body remains at rest. We may understand the truth of this proposition by imagining each motion taking place in succession for an equally small interval of time; then the point would describe a small polygon similar to the original one and would be found, at the end of every such interval, in its original position.

When the motions to be combined are numerous and diverse, it is often convenient to resolve each motion into three parts, reduced to the directions of <term>three given lines perpendicular to each other</term>. In this manner, it is easy to find the general result of any number of motions by addition and subtraction only. We may describe the flight of a bird, ascending in an oblique direction, by estimating its progress northwards or southwards, eastwards or westwards, and at the same time upwards; we may thus determine its location as accurately as by ascertaining the immediate bearing and angular elevation of its path, and its velocity in the direction of its motion.

<header>LECT. III.</header>

# LECTURE III.

## ON ACCELERATING FORCES.

We have until now only considered motion as already existing, without any regard for its origin or alteration. We have seen that all undisturbed motions are uniform and straight, and that two motions represented by the sides of a parallelogram cause a body to move along its diagonal through their combined effect. We are now to examine the causes that produce or destroy motion. Any cause of a change in the motion of a body, with respect to a space at rest, is called a force; that is, any cause that produces motion in a body at rest, or that increases, diminishes, or modifies it in a body that was previously in motion. Thus the power of gravitation, which causes a stone to fall to the ground, is called a force; but when the stone, after descending a hill, rolls along a horizontal plane, it is no longer impelled by any force, and its relative motion continues unaltered until it is gradually destroyed by the retarding force of friction. Its persistence in the state of motion or rest due to the inertia of matter has sometimes been expressed by the term *vis inertiae*, or the force of inertia; however, it appears somewhat inaccurate to apply the term force to a property that is never the cause of a change of motion in the body to which it belongs.

It is a necessary condition in the definition of force that it must be the cause of a change of motion with respect to a space at rest. For if the change were only in the relative motion of two points, it might happen without the operation of any force. For example, if a body is moving without disturbance, its motion relative to another body (not in its direct line of travel) will be constantly changing; and this change, considered by itself, would suggest the existence of a repulsive force. On the other hand, two bodies may be subjected to the action of an attractive force while their distance remains unchanged, as a result of the centrifugal effect of a rotating motion. (Plate I. Fig. 9.)

<header>LECTURE III.</header>

The exertion of an animal, the unbending of a bow, and the transfer of motion by impact are familiar examples of the actions of forces. We should not imagine that the idea of force is naturally linked with that of labor or difficulty; this association comes only from habit, since our voluntary actions are generally accompanied by a specific effort, which leaves an impression almost inseparable from that of the force it calls into action.

It is natural to ask in what direct way any force acts so as to produce motion; for example, how the earth causes a stone to gravitate toward it. In some cases, indeed, we are inclined to imagine that we understand the nature of a force's action better; for instance, when a moving body strikes another, we believe that the impenetrability of matter is a sufficient cause for the transfer of motion, since the first body cannot continue its course without displacing the second. It has been supposed that if we could discover any similar impact that might be the cause of gravity, we would have a perfect idea of how it works. However, the reality is that even in cases of apparent impact, the colliding bodies do not actually touch each other. If any analogy between gravity and impact is ever established, it will not be by referring them both to the impenetrability of matter, but to the intervention of some common agent, perhaps weightless. Newton observed that a considerable force was necessary to bring two pieces of glass into a degree of contact that still was not quite perfect, and Professor Robison has estimated this force at a thousand pounds for every square inch. These extremely tiny intervals have been determined by observations on the colors of the thin plate of air trapped between the glasses. When an image of these colors is shown using a solar microscope, it is very easily demonstrated that the glasses are separated from each other by the operation of this repulsive force as soon as the pressure of the screws holding them together is reduced; the rings of colors, which depend on their distance, contract their dimensions accordingly. Therefore, it is obvious that whenever two pieces of glass strike each other without applying a pressure equal to a thousand pounds on a square inch, they may affect each other’s motion without actually coming into contact. Some people might perhaps be inclined to attribute this repulsion to the elasticity of air particles sticking to the glass, but I have found that the experiment works equally well in the vacuum of an air pump. We must therefore be satisfied to ac-

<header>ON ACCELERATING FORCES.</header>

...acknowledge our total ignorance of the fundamental nature of forces of every kind; and we must first examine the effect of forces, considering only their magnitude and direction, without any regard to their origin.

It was truly asserted by Descartes that the state of motion is as natural as the state of rest. When a body is once in motion, it requires no external power to maintain its velocity. If, therefore, a moving body is subject to the influence of any force acting in the direction of its movement, its motion will be either accelerated or slowed down, depending on whether the force's direction aligns with or opposes the motion. For example, a stone that begins to fall, or is thrown downward, does not maintain the same velocity during its descent but gains more and more motion every instant. We know well that the higher a body falls from, the greater the risk that it will destroy whatever stands in its way. Similarly, when a ball is thrown upward, it gradually loses its motion due to the effect of gravitation, which is now a retarding force, until it eventually begins to descend again.

It is appropriate here to ask what the precise meaning of the term <term>velocity</term> is; while we seem to understand how the word is commonly used, it is not easy to provide a correct definition. The velocity of a body can be described as the quantity or degree of its motion, regardless of its mass or size. It could always be measured by the distance traveled in a specific amount of time—for example, a second—if all motions were undisturbed or uniform. However, velocity can vary significantly within that second, so we must find a measure other than the distance actually traveled in any finite span of time. If, however, we assume the time intervals are infinitely short, the tiny increments of space covered can be considered the true measures of velocities. These increments, though smaller than any measurable amount, can still be accurately compared to one another. They provide a true standard for velocity because the change in velocity during such a short interval must be completely insignificant compared to the total velocity. Thus, the increment of space becomes a true measure of the instantaneous velocity, just as a larger distance would measure a uniform velocity.
