### LECTURE III.

When the increase or decrease of the velocity of a moving body is uniform, its cause is called a uniform force. The distances that would be traveled in any given time, if the current velocity continued uniformly, are always equally increased or decreased by the action of such a force. For example, if the velocities at the beginning of any two separate seconds are such that the body would travel one foot and ten feet in those respective seconds if undisturbed, and the distances actually traveled become two feet and eleven feet—each being increased by one foot—the accelerating force must be called uniform.

The power of gravitation, acting at or near the earth’s surface, may be considered as such a force without noticeable error. Thus, if a body begins to fall from a state of rest, it travels about 16 feet—or more correctly 16 1/12—in the first second; if it begins a second with a velocity of 32 feet, it travels 32 and 16, or 48 feet, in this second. The decrease of the force of gravitation in proportion to the squares of the distances from the earth’s center is barely perceptible at any heights within our reach, even by the most precise tests that we can employ.

The velocity produced by any uniformly accelerating force is proportional to the magnitude of the force and the duration of its operation combined. When the forces are the same, a little consideration will convince us that, since every equal portion of time adds equally to the velocity, the total velocity produced or destroyed must be in proportion to the total time. When the forces differ, the velocities differ in the same ratio, for the forces are only measured by the velocities they generate. Thus, a double force acting for a double amount of time produces a quadruple velocity. That a force producing a double velocity is properly called a double force can be shown from the laws of the composition of motion; for when the equal sides of a parallelogram representing two separate forces or motions approach each other and finally coincide in direction, the diagonal of the parallelogram, representing their joint effect, becomes equal to the sum of the sides. (Plate I. Fig. 10.)

It is also a centrifugal force that is the foundation of the amusement of a boy driving a hoop. A hoop at rest, placed on its edge, would very quickly fall to the ground; but when it is moving forward, a slight inclination toward either side causes the parts to acquire a motion toward that side, those which are uppermost being most affected by it; and this lateral motion, assisted sometimes by the curvature of the surface of the hoop, causes its path to deviate from a <term>rectilinear direction</term>, so that instead of moving straight forward, it turns to that side toward which it began to incline; and in this position, its tendency to fall still further is counteracted by the centrifugal force, and it generally makes several complete revolutions before it falls. The motion of a bowl <note>A ball used in the game of lawn bowls</note>, with its bias, is of a similar nature; the centrifugal force counteracting the tendency to <term>curvilinear motion</term>, so as to diminish it very considerably, until the velocity is so much reduced as to allow it to describe a path evidently curved, and becoming more and more so as the motion is slower.

When a body is retained in a circular orbit by a force directed to its center, its velocity is everywhere equal to that which it would acquire, in falling—by means of the same force, if uniform—through half the radius, that is, through one-fourth of the diameter. This proposition affords a very convenient method of comparing the effects of central forces with those of simple accelerating forces, and deserves to be retained in memory. We may in some measure demonstrate its truth by means of the whirling table: an apparatus which is arranged on purpose for exhibiting the properties of central forces, although it is more calculated for showing their comparative than their absolute magnitude; for according as we place the string on the pulleys, the two horizontal arms may be made to revolve either with equal velocities, or one twice as fast as the other. The sliding stages, which may be placed at different distances from the centers, and which are made to move along the arms with as little friction as possible, are in a certain proportion to the weights, which are to be raised, by means of threads passing over pulleys in the centers, as soon as the centrifugal forces of the stages with their weights are sufficiently great; and the experiment is to be so arranged, that when the velocity, having been gradually increased, produces a sufficient centrifugal force, both stages may raise

From this proposition, we can easily calculate the velocity with which a sling of a given length must revolve in order to keep a stone in its place in all positions. Assuming the motion is in a vertical plane, it is obvious that the stone will tend to fall when it is at the highest point of the orbit, unless the <term>centrifugal force</term> is at least equal to the force of <term>gravity</term>. Thus, if the length of the sling is two feet, we must find the velocity acquired by a heavy body falling through a height of one foot, which will be eight feet per second, since eight times the square root of 1 is eight. This must be its velocity at the highest point; at this velocity, it would complete each revolution in about a second and a half, but its motion in other parts of its orbit will be greatly accelerated by the <term>gravitation</term> of the stone.

It may also be demonstrated that when bodies revolve in equal circles, their <term>centrifugal forces</term> are proportional to the squares of their velocities. Thus, in the <term>whirling table</term>, when the two stages are equally loaded, one that is made to revolve at twice the velocity of the other will lift four equal weights at the same instant the other raises a single one. But when two bodies revolve with equal velocities at different distances, the forces are inversely proportional to the distances; consequently, the forces are, in all cases, directly proportional to the squares of the velocities and inversely proportional to the distances.

If two bodies revolve in equal times at different distances, the forces by which they are retained in their orbits are simply proportional to the distances. If one of the stages of the <term>whirling table</term> is placed at twice the distance of the other, it will raise twice as great a weight when the revolutions are completed in the same time.

<header>LECTURE IV.</header>

In general, the forces are directly proportional to the distances, and inversely proportional to the squares of the times of revolution. Thus, the same weight revolving in double the time at the same distance will have its effect reduced to one-fourth; however, at double the distance, the effect will be increased again to half of its original magnitude.

From these principles, we may deduce the law discovered by <term>Kepler</term> regarding the motions of planetary bodies, which was first demonstrated by <term>Newton</term> through mechanical considerations. Where the forces vary inversely as the squares of the distances—as in the case of <term>gravitation</term>—the squares of the times of revolution are proportional to the cubes of the distances. Thus, if the distance of one body is four times as great as that of another, the cube of 4 being 64 (which is the square of 8), the time of its revolution will be 8 times as great as that of the first body. It would be easy to show the truth of this proposition experimentally by means of the <term>whirling table</term>, but the proof would be less striking than those of the simpler laws already established.

Until now, we have assumed the orbit of a revolving body to be a perfect circle. However, it often happens in nature—for instance, in all planetary motions—that the orbit deviates more or less from a circular form. In such cases, we may apply another very important law also discovered by <term>Kepler</term>: that the straight line joining a revolving body and its center of attraction always describes equal areas in equal times; therefore, the velocity of the body is always inversely proportional to the perpendicular line drawn from the center to the tangent. (Plate I. Fig. 14.)

The demonstration of this law, developed by <term>Newton</term>, was one of the most elegant applications of the <term>geometry of infinites</term> <note>often referred to today as the geometry of infinitesimals</note> or <term>indivisibles</term>. This is a branch of mathematics for which <term>Archimedes</term> laid the foundations, which <term>Cavalieri</term> and <term>Wallis</term> greatly advanced, and which <term>Newton</term> brought near to perfection. Its truth may be shown to some extent by an experiment on the revolution of a ball suspended by a long thread and drawn toward a point immediately under the point of suspension by another thread. This second thread may either be held in the hand or have a weight attached to it. When the ball is made to revolve, its motion evidently becomes more rapid when it is drawn by the ho-

It was also discovered by <term>Kepler</term> that each of the planets revolves in an ellipse, of which the sun occupies one of the foci. It is well known that an ellipse is an oval figure, which may be described by fixing the ends of a thread to two points and moving a tracing point so that it may always be at the vertex of the angle formed by the thread; and that the two fixed points are called its foci. The inference respecting the force by which a body may be made to revolve in an ellipse was first made by <term>Newton</term>; that is, that the force directed to its focus must be inversely as the square of the distance. We have no other experimental proof of this theorem than astronomical observations, which are indeed perfectly decisive, but do not need to be anticipated here. (Plate II. Fig. 16.)

There is another general proposition which is sometimes useful in the comparison of rectilinear and curvilinear motions. If two bodies are attracted in the same manner toward a given center—that is, with equal forces at equal distances—if their velocities are once equal at equal distances, they will always remain equal at equal distances, whatever their directions may be. For instance, if one cannonball is shot obliquely upward, and another perpendicularly upward with the same velocity, the one will describe a curve and the other a straight line, but their velocities will always remain equal—not at the same instants of time, but at equal distances from the earth's center, or after having ascended through equal vertical heights, although in different directions. This proposition has usually been a step in the demonstration of the law of the force by which a body is made to revolve in an ellipse; but there is a much simpler method of demonstrating that law by using some properties of the curvature of the ellipse.

In treating of the motion of projectiles, the force of gravitation may, without significant error, be considered a uniform force acting in parallel lines perpendicular to the horizon. On the other hand, a body that is not <term>specifically heavier</term> than water gains more in apparent weight—due to the diminished density of the atmosphere at great elevations—than it loses by the increase of its distance from the earth. But both these differences may be wholly disregarded in all common calculations. The direction of gravity is always exactly perpendicular to the horizon—that is, to the surface of the earth, which is somewhat curved because of the earth’s <term>spheroidal shape</term>; however, any small portion of this surface may be practically considered as a plane, and the vertical lines perpendicular to it as parallel to each other.

The oblique motion of a <term>projectile</term> may be most easily understood by resolving its velocity into two parts: one in a horizontal direction and the other in a vertical direction. It appears from the doctrine of the <term>composition of motion</term> that the horizontal velocity will not be affected by the force of gravitation acting in a direction perpendicular to it, and that it will therefore continue uniform; furthermore, the vertical motion will be the same as if the body had no horizontal motion. Thus, if we let fall a weight from the head of a ship's mast that shares in the ship's forward motion, the weight will descend by the side of the mast in the same manner, and with the same relative velocity, as if neither the ship nor the weight had any horizontal motion.

We may therefore always determine the greatest height to which a projectile will rise by finding the height from which a body must fall in order to gain a velocity equal to its vertical velocity (its velocity of ascent). This is calculated by squaring one-eighth of the number of feet that it would rise in the first second if it were not slowed down. For example, suppose a musket is tilted so that the muzzle is higher than the butt-end by half of its length—that is, at an angle of 30°—and let the ball be discharged with a velocity of 1000 feet per second. Its vertical velocity will then be half as great, or 500 feet per second. The square of one-eighth of 500 is 3906; consequently, the height to which the ball would rise, if unresisted by the air, is 3906 feet, or three-quarters of a mile. But in fact, a musket ball actually shot upward with a velocity of 1670 feet per second—which would rise six or seven miles in a <term>vacuum</term>—is so slowed by the air that it does not reach the height of a single mile.

We may easily find the time of the body’s ascent from its initial velocity; for the time of ascent is directly proportional to the velocity, and may be found in seconds by dividing the vertical velocity in feet by 32; or if we divide by 16 only, we shall have the time of both ascent and descent; and then the horizontal range may be found, by calculating the distance described in this time, with the uniform horizontal velocity. Thus, in the example that we have assumed, dividing 500 by 16, we have 31 seconds for the whole time of the range; but since the hypotenuse of our triangle is 1000, and the perpendicular 500, the base will be 866 feet; consequently the horizontal range is 31 times 866, that is, nearly 28,000 feet, or more than 5 miles. But the resistance of the air will reduce this distance also to less than one mile.

It may be demonstrated that the horizontal range of a body, projected with a given velocity, is always proportional to the sine of twice the angle of elevation: that is, to the elevation of the muzzle of the piece <note>A "piece" refers here to a piece of artillery or a gun.</note> in a situation twice as remote from a horizontal position as its actual situation. Hence it follows, that the greatest horizontal range will be when the elevation is half a right angle; supposing the body to move in a vacuum. But the resistance of the air increases with the length of the path, and the same cause also makes the angle of descent much greater than the angle of ascent, as we may observe in the track of a bomb. For both these reasons, the best elevation is somewhat less than 45°, and sometimes, when the velocity is very great, as little as 30°. But it usually happens in the operations of natural causes, that near the point where any quantity is greatest or least, its variation is slower than elsewhere: a small difference, therefore, in the angle of elevation, is of little consequence to the extent of the range, provided that it continues between the limits of 45° and 35°; and for the same reason, the angular adjustment requires less accuracy in this position than in any other, which besides the economy of powder, makes it the best elevation for practice. (*Plate II. Fig. 17, 18.*)

The path of a <term>projectile</term>, supposed to move without resistance, is always a parabola. This interesting proposition was first discovered by Galileo: it follows very readily from the doctrine of the <term>composition of motion</term>, combined with the laws which that philosopher established concerning the fall of heavy bodies. (Plate II. Fig. 19.)

In practical cases on a large scale, where the velocity of a projectile is considerable, the resistance of the atmosphere is so great that it makes the Galilean propositions of little or no use; a complete determination of the path, including all the circumstances which may influence it, is attended with almost insuperable difficulties. It appears from Robins's experiments that the resistance of the air to an iron ball 4¾ inches in diameter, moving at the rate of 800 feet per second, is equal to four times its weight, and that where the velocity is much greater, the resistance increases far more rapidly. But what must greatly diminish the probability of our deriving any major practical advantage from the theory of gunnery is an observation, also made by Mr. Robins, that a ball sometimes deviates three or four hundred yards laterally without any apparent reason; thus, we cannot be absolutely certain of coming within this distance of our target in any direction. This circumstance is probably due to an accidental rotatory motion communicated to the ball as it passes through the gun, which causes greater air friction on one side than on the other; it may be remedied to some extent by using a rifle barrel, which controls the rotation of the ball so that its axis initially coincides with the ball's path, ensuring that the same face of the ball is turned in every direction in succession. ### LECTURE V.

#### ON CONFINED MOTION.

We have so far considered the principal cases of motion, either undisturbed or simply subjected to the action of an accelerating, retarding, or deflecting force. We now proceed to examine the effects of an additional modification, which is introduced when the motion is limited to a given line or surface of any kind. This occurs when the body is either supposed to slide on the surface of a solid that is actually extended, or is confined to an imaginary surface by its attachment to a thread, or even more narrowly restricted by means of two threads, which allow it to move only in a given line. Suspension is the most convenient method for conducting experiments on confined motion; however, it is not always easy to cause the body to remain on the required surface, and to confine it in this manner to a perfectly flat surface is impossible. When we allow a body to slide along any surface, there is a loss of force from friction, from the production of rotary motion, or from both of these causes combined. The effect of friction is obvious and well known; and we may be convinced of the retardation following the production of rotary motion by allowing two cylinders of equal dimensions to roll down an inclined plane. One is covered with sheet lead, while the other has an equal weight of lead in its axis and is covered with paper; both have similar projecting surfaces at the ends which come into contact with the plane. We may easily observe that in the first cylinder, much more of the force is consumed in producing rotary motion than in the second, and it therefore descends much more slowly. (Plate II. Fig. 20.)

When a body is placed on an inclined plane, the force urging it to descend in the direction of the plane is to the total force of gravity as the height of the plane is to its length. This is demonstrable from the principles of the composition of motion and may also be shown experimentally with

Thus, if a plane is inclined one inch in every 32, a ball will descend on it in two seconds—instead of the 64 feet it would fall vertically, it travels somewhat less than two feet.

It may be deduced from the laws of accelerating forces that when bodies descend on any inclined planes of equal heights, but of different inclinations, the times of descent are proportional to the lengths of the planes, and the final velocities are equal. Thus, a body will acquire a velocity of 32 feet per second after having descended 16 feet, either in a vertical line or in an oblique direction; but the time of descent will be as much longer than one second as the oblique length of the path is greater than 16 feet. This may be shown by experiment, as nearly as the obstacles already mentioned will permit, with the times being measured by a pendulum or by a stop watch. (Plate II. Fig. 21.)

There is an elegant proposition of a similar nature which is even more capable of experimental confirmation; that is, that the times for falling through all chords leading to the lowest point of a circle are equal. If two or more bodies are placed at different points of a circle and allowed to descend at the same instant along as many planes which meet at the lowest point of the circle, they will arrive there at the same time. (Plate II. Fig. 22.)

The velocity of a body descending along a given surface is the same as that of a body falling freely through an equal height, not only when the surface is a plane, but also when it is a continuous curve in which the body is retained by its attachment to a thread or is supported by any regular surface supposed to be free from friction. We may easily show, by an experiment on a suspended ball, that its velocity is the same when it descends from the same height—whatever the form of its path—by observing the height to which it rises on the opposite side of the lowest point. We may alter the form of the path in which it descends by placing pins at different points so as to interfere with the thread that supports the ball and to form in succession temporary centers of motion; and we shall find, in all cases, that the body ascends to a height equal to that from which it descended, with a small deduction on account of friction. (Plate II. Fig. 23.)

->LECTURE V.<-

From this is derived the idea conveyed by the term **living** or **ascending force**; for since the height to which a body will rise perpendicularly is proportional to the square of its velocity, it will maintain a tendency to rise to a height proportional to the square of its velocity regardless of the path in which it is directed, provided that it encounters no abrupt angles, or that it rebounds at each angle in a new direction without losing any velocity. The same idea is expressed somewhat more concisely by the term **energy**, which indicates the tendency of a body to ascend or to penetrate to a certain distance in opposition to a retarding force.

The most important cases of the motion of bodies restricted to given surfaces are those relating to the properties of pendulums. Of these, the simplest is the motion of a body in a cycloidal path. The cycloid is a curve with many unique features; we have already seen that it is formed by tracing the path of a given point on the circumference of a circle that rolls along a straight line. Galileo was the first to consider it attentively, but he failed in his attempts to investigate its properties. It is quite remarkable that the principal cause of his lack of success was an inaccurate experiment: in order to obtain preliminary information regarding the area it contains, he cut a board into a cycloidal shape and weighed it; he inferred from this experiment that the area had some irrational proportion to that of the generating circle, whereas it is actually exactly triple. In the same way, it happened in later times that Newton, in his study, determined the shape of the earth more accurately than Cassini did from actual measurement. It was Huygens who first demonstrated the properties of the cycloidal pendulum, which are even more important for solving various mechanical problems than for the immediate purposes of timekeepers, to which that eminent philosopher intended to apply them. (Plate I. Fig 5.)

If a body is suspended by a thread swinging between two cycloidal cheeks, it will describe another identical cycloid through the unwinding of the thread, and the time of vibration will be the same, regardless of the part of the curve from which it begins to descend. Consequently, the vibrations of a body moving in a cycloid are called **isochronous**, or of equal duration. This equality can be demonstrated by releasing two pendulum balls at the same moment from different points on the curve and observing that they meet at the lowest point. (Plate II. Fig. 24.)

The absolute time for the descent or ascent of a pendulum in a cycloid is the time in which any heavy body would fall through half the length of the thread, in the same ratio as half the circumference of a circle relates to its diameter. It is, therefore, nearly equal to the time required for the descent of a body through $\frac{\pi^2}{8}$ of the length of the thread; and if we allow the pendulum to descend at the same moment that a body falls from a point elevated one-fourth of the length of the thread above the point of suspension, this body will meet the pendulum at the lowest point of its vibration. (Plate II. Fig. 24.)

From this, it may readily be inferred that since the times of falling through any distances are proportional to the square roots of those distances, the times of vibration of different pendulums are proportional to the square roots of their lengths. Thus, the times of vibration for pendulums of 1 foot and 4 feet in length will be as 1 to 2: the time of vibration for a pendulum 39.13 inches in length is one second; the length of a pendulum vibrating in two seconds must be four times as great.

The velocity with which a pendulous body moves at each point of a cycloidal curve may be represented by imagining another pendulum revolving uniformly in a circle, starting from the lowest point at the same time that the first pendulum begins to move and completing its revolution in the time of two vibrations; then the height reached by the uniformly revolving pendulum will always be equal to the distance traveled by the pendulum vibrating in the cycloid. (Plate II. Fig. 24.)

It may also be shown that if the pendulum vibrates through the entire curve, it will move everywhere with the same velocity as the point of the circle which is supposed to have originally formed the cycloid, provided that the circle rolls forward with a uniform motion.

All these properties depend on the fact that the relative force driving the body to descend along the curve is always proportional to its distance from the lowest point; and it happens in many other instances of the action of various forces that a similar law prevails. In all such cases, the vibrations are isochronous, and the distance traveled corresponds to the versed sine of a circular arc increasing uniformly—that is, to the height of any point

The cycloid is the curve in which a body may descend, in the shortest possible time, from a given point to another point positioned obliquely below it. It can easily be shown that a body descends more rapidly in a cycloid than in a straight line joining the two points. This property is of little practical use; the proposition was formerly considered somewhat difficult to demonstrate, but recently, through the invention of new methods of calculation, theorems of a similar nature have been greatly extended with much ease. This experiment naturally suggests a familiar proverb, which cautions us against being led away too hastily by an appearance of brevity and ease. (Plate II. Fig. 25.)

It has been found that the inconveniences resulting from the complicated apparatus needed to introduce a cycloidal motion for clock pendulums outweigh the theoretical advantage of perfect <term>isochronism</term>. Since the curvature is nearly constant in small cycloidal arcs, the vibration time of a simple circular pendulum must ultimately be the same as that of a cycloidal pendulum of the same length; however, in larger arcs, the time must be somewhat greater, because the circular arc falls outside the cycloidal one and is less inclined to the horizon at equal distances from the lowest point. This can be shown by comparing two identical pendulums vibrating in arcs of different sizes. It can also be observed through an experiment with two simple pendulums of different lengths that their vibration times—just like those of cycloidal pendulums—are proportional to the square roots of their lengths; a half-second pendulum is only one-fourth as long as a pendulum that vibrates in seconds.

We have been forced to assume that both the weight and the <term>inertia</term> of a pendulum are concentrated at a single point, since we are not yet prepared to examine the effects of the slight differences in position and velocity between various parts of the materials used in our experiments. It is remarkable that the isochronism of pendulums, which is a property so important in its application, can still be preserved despite the interference of a constant retarding force, such as friction is found to be in many cases. It has been shown by Newton that each complete vibration of a cycloidal pendulum, slowed by a resistance of this nature, will be shorter than the preceding one by a certain constant distance, but that it will be completed in the same amount of time.

There is a strong analogy between the vibrations of pendulums and the revolution of balls suspended from a fixed point. If a body, suspended by a thread, revolves freely in a horizontal circle, the time of revolution will be the same whenever the height of the suspension point above the plane of revolution is the same, regardless of the length of the thread. Thus, if several balls are fixed to threads (or rather, wires) connected to the same point on an axis that is made to rotate using a whirling table, they will arrange themselves so as to remain very nearly in the same horizontal plane. (Plate II. Fig. 26.)

The duration of each revolution of the balls is equal to the time taken for a double vibration of a pendulum whose length is equal to the height of the suspension point above the plane in which they revolve; consequently, all the revolutions will be nearly isochronous as long as the threads or wires deviate only slightly from a vertical position. In fact, we may imagine such a revolution to be composed of two vibrations of a simple pendulum occurring at the same time in directions at right angles to each other; for while a pendulum is vibrating from north to south, it is subject to the influence of any force capable of causing a vibration from east to west. The combined result of both vibrations will be a uniform revolution in a circle if the vibrations are equal and properly combined; but if they are unequal, the resulting vibration will ultimately be an ellipse, with the combined force directed toward its center and always proportional to the distance from that center. (Plate II. Fig. 27.)

The same laws are applicable to many other cases of rotary motion. For instance, if we wish to determine the height at which a ball, revolving with a given velocity, will be held in a spherical bowl; or the inclination of a circular road capable of counteracting the centrifugal force of a horse running around it. For the horse, like the ball of the revolving pendulum, has a centrifugal tendency that increases as his velocity increases. This centrifugal force, combined with the force of gravity, creates a resultant force which, in the case of the pendulum, is completely counteracted by the tension of the thread or wire and must therefore act in the direction of the thread. This force obliges the horse to position his legs in a similar direction, as if proceeding from an imaginary point of suspension above; otherwise, he would be liable to fall outward if his velocity were sufficiently great. But in order to withstand the pressure of the horse's legs, the road must be in a direction perpendicular to them; otherwise, its materials will naturally be forced outward until they produce an elevation sufficient to give the road the required form. Thus, if the diameter of the ring were 40 feet and the horse moved at the rate of 12 miles an hour, he would perform about 500 revolutions in an hour, and half a revolution in three and a half seconds. Now, the length of a pendulum vibrating in 3.5 seconds must be 39 inches multiplied by the square of 3.5, or a little more than 80 feet. The road must therefore be perpendicular to the direction of a line drawn to it from a point 80 feet above the center of the ring, and its outer circumference must be higher than its inner circumference by one-fourth of its breadth. It would, however, be improper to have a road of this form in a <term>manege</term> <note>a riding school or arena for training horses</note>, since the horse must be taught to perform all his maneuvers on a perfect plane.

There is a general principle of curvilinear motion which is in itself of little importance or practical utility, but which deserves to be noticed because it has been magnified by some philosophers into a fundamental law of nature.

# ON CONFINED MOTION. #

Among all the curves that a body can describe in moving from one point to another, it always selects the one in which—if its velocity is supposed to be everywhere multiplied by the distance that it describes—the sum of the infinitely small products will be a minimum; that is, less than in any other path that the body could take. For example, if a body moves freely, and therefore with a uniform velocity, across any regular curved surface, it will pass from one part of the surface to another by the shortest possible path. This has been called the principle of the least possible action; it is, however, merely a mathematical inference from the simpler laws of motion, and even if those laws were different from what they are, the principle would be true in another form, and in another sense of the word action.

# LECTURE VI.

## ON THE MOTIONS OF SIMPLE MASSES.

**HITHERTO** we have considered the motions of only one or more single points or atoms, without any regard to the bulk or mass of a movable body; but it now becomes necessary to also consider the difference in the masses of bodies in motion. This may be done, however, without considering the actual magnitude or extent of the body. We may easily conceive different masses or bulks to be concentrated in a mathematical point; and it is most convenient to define a movable body as a movable point or particle composed of other elementary particles that differ only in number, thereby constituting the proportionally different mass or bulk of the body.

Although we must rely on material bodies in our experiments on motion, and although such bodies differ considerably from this definition of a single movable body, they still serve well enough to represent such bodies—especially when they are small and regularly formed. We are considering the doctrine of motion here in a mathematical rather than a physical sense, so we are able to neglect all properties of matter that are not immediately necessary for our purpose. Indeed, although the general properties of matter are usually placed at the beginning of elementary works on mechanics, it has still been found necessary to omit the consideration of their effects when examining the laws and properties of motion. For example, the forces of cohesion and repulsion generally act in a very complicated manner in almost all cases where motion is communicated; however, to consider these operations minutely when treating collision would involve the subject in very great and unnecessary difficulties. Furthermore, a complete investigation of these properties of matter would require the use of various branches of mechanical and hydrodynamical science. Therefore, we may take a much simpler course by entirely deferring all theoretical consideration of actual

matter; but in the meantime, we must have some measure of the mass or bulk, as defined here, for our experimental illustrations. We might use spherical bodies made only of homogeneous substances—that is, substances of the same kind—and we might estimate the mass by their relative size, imagining all the particles of each sphere to be concentrated at its center. But it is more convenient to derive a measure of mass from weight, anticipating the effects of gravity, since it can be proved that the weight of a body is proportional to its absolute quantity of matter, assuming all matter behaves similarly in relation to motion. So, instead of counting the particles of each body, the same purpose is served by determining their relative weight.

Inertia, or the tendency to persist in a state of rest or of uniform straight-line motion, is a property of all matter and may be considered proportional to the mass or weight of a body. When considering the motions of a system of bodies, their inertia may in some respects be referred to a single point, which is called the <term>center of inertia</term>. The center of inertia of two bodies is that point on the straight line joining them which divides it into two parts such that the ratio of one part to the other is the same as the ratio of the mass of the distant body to that of the nearby body. For example, if one body weighs a pound and another two pounds, and they are a yard apart, then the center of inertia is two feet from the smaller body and one foot from the larger; and the distance of each from the center is to the total distance as the weight of the other is to the total weight. Also, the products obtained by multiplying each weight by its distance from the center are equal: thus, two multiplied by one is equal to one multiplied by two (Plate II, Fig. 29).

This point is most commonly called the <term>center of gravity</term>; it has also sometimes been called the <term>center of position</term>. Because it has many properties independent of gravity, it should not derive its name from gravitation, and the term center of inertia is now, quite properly, beginning to be generally adopted.

For it may be shown, from the principles of the composition of motion, that any force acting in this manner will cause each of the two bodies to move through a distance proportional to the magnitude of the other body: thus, a body of one pound will move through a space twice as large as a body weighing two pounds, and the remaining parts of the original distance will still be divided in the same proportion by the original center of inertia, which therefore still remains the center of inertia and is at rest. And it also follows that if the center of inertia is at first in motion, its motion will not be affected by any reciprocal action of the bodies.

This important property is very capable of experimental illustration; first observing that all known forces are reciprocal, and among the rest the action of a spring: we place two unequal bodies so as to be separated when a spring is released, and we find that they move, in any given interval of time, distances which are inversely proportional to their weights; and that consequently the location of the center of inertia remains unaltered. They may either be made to float on water or may be suspended by long threads; the spring may be released by burning a thread that confines it, and it may be observed whether or not they strike two obstacles at the same instant, placed at such distances as the theory requires; or if they are suspended as pendulums, the arcs which they move through may be measured, the velocities being always nearly proportional to these arcs, and accurately so to their chords. (Plate II. Fig. 30.)

The same might also be shown for attractive as well as for repulsive forces. For instance, if we placed ourselves in a small boat and pulled a rope tied to a much larger one, we would draw ourselves toward the large boat with a motion as much more rapid than that of the large boat as its weight is greater than that of our own boat; and the two boats would meet at their common center of inertia, supposing the resistance of the water to be negligible.

Having established this property of the center of inertia as a law of motion, we may derive from it the true estimate of the quantity of motion in different bodies in a much more satisfactory manner than it has usually been explained. The quantity of motion must always be measured by the joint ratio of mass to mass and velocity to velocity; that is, by the ratio of the products obtained by multiplying the weight of each body by the number expressing its velocity; and these products are called the *momenta* of the bodies. We seem to have deduced this measure of motion from the most undeniable arguments, and we shall have occasion to apply the *momentum* thus estimated as a true measure of force; while at the same time we allow for the practical importance of considering, in many cases, the effectiveness of forces according to another criterion—multiplying the mass by the square of the velocity to determine the *energy*: yet the true quantity of motion, or *momentum*, of any body is always to be understood as the product of its mass multiplied by its velocity. Thus, a body weighing one pound, moving with a velocity of one hundred feet per second, has the same momentum and the same quantity of motion as a body of ten pounds moving at the rate of ten feet per second.

We may also demonstrate experimentally, by means of Mr. Atwood's machine, that the same momentum is generated in a given time by the same preponderating force, regardless of the quantity of matter moved. Thus, if the preponderating weight is one-sixteenth of the total weight of the boxes, it will fall one foot in a second instead of 16, and a velocity of two feet will be acquired by the entire mass, instead of a velocity of 32 feet, which the preponderating weight alone would have acquired. And when we compare the centrifugal forces of bodies revolving in the same time at different distances from the center of motion, we find that a greater quantity of matter compensates for a smaller force; so that two balls connected by a wire, free to slide either way, will retain each other in their respective positions when their common center of inertia coincides with the center of motion; the centrifugal force of each particle of the one being as much greater than that of an equal particle of the other as its weight, or the number of particles, is smaller.

But it is not enough to determine the center of inertia of only two bodies considered as single points, since in general a much greater number of points is involved: we must therefore define the sense in which the term is to be applied in this case. We proceed by considering the first and second of three or more bodies as a single body, equal to both of them and placed in their com-

We may always represent the motion of the center of inertia of a system of moving bodies by supposing their masses to be united into one body, and this body to receive at once a momentum equal to that of each body of the system, in a direction parallel to its motion. This may often be done most conveniently by referring all the motions of this imaginary body to three given directions, and collecting all the results into three sums, which will represent the motion of the center of inertia of the system.

We have already assumed this proposition when we employed material bodies of finite magnitude—that is, systems of material atoms—to represent imaginary bodies of the same weight condensed into their centers; and it now appears that the velocity and direction of the motions of such bodies as we have used agree precisely with those of our imaginary material points. We cannot attempt to confirm this law by experiment, because the deductions from the observable consequences of an experiment would require nearly the same processes as the mathematical demonstration.

It is obvious that the result of any number of uniform and <term>rectilinear motions</term>, thus collected, must also be a uniform and rectilinear motion. The center of inertia of a system of bodies moving without disturbance is, therefore, either at rest or moving uniformly in a straight line.

The mass, or weight, of each of any number of bodies being multiplied by its distance from a given plane, the products, collected into one sum, will be equal to the whole weight of the system multiplied by the distance of the common center of inertia from the same plane. This property is particularly applicable to the consideration of the center of gravity, and also provides the easiest means of determining its location in bodies of complicated forms. (Plate III. Fig. 32.)

We have already seen that the location of the center of inertia of two bodies is not affected by any reciprocal action between them; and the same is true of the actions of a system of three or more bodies. We might easily apply our experiment on the reciprocal action of two bodies to a larger number, but it would not clarify the subject further, and the method for reaching that conclusion would be somewhat complicated.

All the forces in nature that we know of act reciprocally between different masses of matter, so that any two bodies repelling or attracting each other are made to move away from or toward each other with equal momenta. This circumstance is generally expressed by the third law of motion: that action and reaction are equal. There would be something strange, and almost inconceivable, in a force that could affect similar particles of matter unequally, or in the particles themselves if they possessed such different degrees of mobility that they were equally movable with respect to one force and unequally with respect to another. For instance, a magnet and a piece of iron, each weighing a pound, will remain in equilibrium when their weights are balanced against each other; they will be separated with equal velocities if impelled by the release of a spring placed between them, and it is difficult to conceive that they should approach each other with unequal velocities because of magnetic attraction or any other natural force. The reciprocity of force is, therefore, a necessary law in the mathematical consideration of mechanics, and it is also perfectly supported by experience. The opposite supposition is so highly improbable that the principle may almost as justly be termed a necessary axiom as a phenomenon gathered from observation.

Sir Isaac Newton observes, in his third law of motion, that "*reaction is always opposite and equal to action, or that the mutual actions of two bodies are always equal and directed in opposite ways.*" He continues, "if any body

If a horse is drawing a weight tied to a rope, the horse is also equally drawn backward toward the weight: for the rope, being stretched throughout, will in the same attempt to contract, urge the horse toward the weight, and the weight toward the horse, and will impede the progress of the one as much as it promotes the advance of the other.” Now, although Newton has always applied this law in the most irreproachable manner, yet it must be admitted that the illustrations quoted here are phrased in such language as to have too much the appearance of a paradox. When we say that a thing presses another, we commonly mean that the pressing thing has a tendency to move forward into the place of the thing pressed, but the stone would not noticeably advance into the place of the finger if it were removed; and in the same manner, we understand that a thing pulling another has a tendency to recede further from the thing pulled and to draw this after it; but it is obvious that the weight which the horse is drawing would not return toward its first position, with the horse in its train, even if the exertion of the horse should entirely cease; in these senses, therefore, we cannot say that the stone presses or that the weight pulls, and we have no reason to offend the reasonable prejudices of a beginner by introducing paradoxical expressions without necessity. Yet it is true in both cases that if all friction, and all connection with the surrounding bodies, could be instantaneously destroyed, the point of the finger and the stone would recede from each other, and the horse and the weight would approach each other, with equal amounts of motion. And this is what we mean by the reciprocity of forces, or the equality of action and reaction.

The quantity of action of two attractive or repulsive bodies on each other is partly dependent on their magnitude. When the bodies are of the same kind, their mutual action is in the compound ratio of their sizes; that is, in the ratio of the products of the numbers expressing their sizes. For instance, if two bodies, each containing a cubic inch of matter, attract or repel each other with a force of a grain <note>A grain is a traditional unit of weight.</note>, and there are two other bodies, one containing two inches and the other ten of the same matter, then the mutual attraction or repulsion of these will be expressed by 20 grains; for each of the 10 inches is attracted by each of the two with a force of a grain. And the mutual action of 3 and 10 will be 30, and of 4 and 10 will be 40; so that when one of the bodies

Therefore, the quantity of matter in every body surrounding us is considered proportional to its weight; for it is inferred from experiment that all material bodies are equally subject to the power of gravitation toward the earth and are, in respect to this force, of the same kind. The apparent difference in the velocity with which different substances fall through the atmosphere is only due to the resistance of the air, as is sometimes shown by an experiment with a feather and a piece of gold falling in the vacuum of an air pump; but the true cause was known long before the invention of this machine, and it is clearly explained in the second book of Lucretius:

> "In water or in air when weights descend,
> The heavier weights more swiftly downward tend.
> The limpid waves, the gales that gently play,
> Yield to the heavier mass a readier way,
> But if the weights in empty space should fall,
> One common swiftness we should find in all."

We are therefore to suppose that the different weights of equal volumes of different substances depend merely on the greater or lesser number of particles contained in a given space, independently of any other characteristics that may constitute the specific differences of those substances.

In some cases, it is necessary to consider the sum of the masses of two bodies in order to estimate their mutual action—that is, when we wish to know the total relative motion of two bodies with respect to each other; for here we must add together their individual motions with respect to the <term>centre of inertia</term>, which are inversely in the same proportion. This consideration is sometimes useful in determining the action of the sun on the various planets.

If two bodies act on each other with forces proportional to any power of their distance—for instance, to the square or the cube of the distance—the forces will also be proportional to the same power of either of their distances from their common centre of inertia. # LECTURE VI.

To determine the effect of attraction as directed toward a fixed point, we consider the force as residing in the common <term>center of inertia</term> of the two bodies, which remains at rest as far as the mutual actions of those bodies only are concerned. It may be shown that the force diminishes as the square of the distance of the bodies—either from this point or from each other—increases. The reciprocal forces of two bodies may therefore be considered as tending toward or away from their common center of inertia as if it were a fixed point. However, it often happens that because the difference in size is very great, the motion of one of the bodies may be disregarded. Thus, we usually ignore the motion of the sun when treating the planetary motions produced by its attraction, although, by means of very precise observations, this motion becomes detectable. But it is utterly beyond the power of our senses to discover the reciprocal motion of the earth produced by any terrestrial cause, even by the most massive eruption of a volcano; although, speaking mathematically, we cannot deny that whenever a cannonball is fired upward, the whole globe must suffer a tiny depression in its course. The boast of Archimedes was therefore accompanied by an unnecessary condition: "Give me," he said, "but a firm support, and I will move the earth." But even granting him his support, he could only have displaced the earth imperceptibly by the properties of his machines; and without any such support, when he threw rocks upon the ships of Marcellus, he actually caused the walls of Syracuse and the island of Sicily to move northward with as much <term>momentum</term> as carried his projectiles southward against the Roman armaments.

## LECTURE VII.

### ON PRESSURE AND EQUILIBRIUM.

**WE** have now examined the principal cases in which a simple force is employed in the production of motion; it is of equal importance to consider the opposition of forces, where they prevent each other’s action. A force counteracted by another force, so that no motion is produced, becomes a pressure: thus we continually exert a pressure, by means of our weight, upon the ground on which we stand, the seat on which we sit, and the bed on which we sleep; but at the instant when we are falling or leaping, we neither exert nor experience a pressure on any part.

It was very truly asserted by the ancients that pressure and motion are absolutely incommensurable as effects; for according to the definition of pressure, the force appears to be what is called in logic a **potential cause**, which is not in a state of activity. Since an interval of time must pass after the removal of the opposing force before the first force can have caused any actual motion, this effect over a finite time cannot with justice be conceived to bear any proportion to the pressure, which is, as it were, merely a nascent effect. It is true that a large weight, pressing on a spring, may keep it bent in exactly the same position into which a smaller weight, falling on it with a certain velocity, would bend it; but to retain a spring in a certain position and to bend it into that position are effects absolutely incommensurable. The one is a measure of the constant repulsive force of the spring when bent to a certain point; the other is the sum of the effects of the same spring, in various degrees of <term>flexure</term>, over a certain time. Hence, the smallest possible <term>momentum</term> is said to be more than equivalent to the greatest possible pressure: a very light weight, falling from a very minute distance, will force back a very strong spring, although often through an imperceptible space only. But the impulse of a stream of infinitely small particles, like those of which a fluid is supposed

Nothing, however, forbids us from comparing two pressures by considering the initial motions they would produce if the opposition were removed; nor is there any difficulty in extending the laws of the composition of motion to the composition of pressure. For since we measure forces by the motions they produce, it is obvious that the composition of forces is included in the doctrine of the composition of motions. When we combine three forces according to the laws of motion, there can be no question that the resulting motion is accurately determined in all cases, whatever its magnitude may be; nor can any reason be given why it should be otherwise when this motion is evanescent (fading away) and the force becomes a pressure. The case is similar to that of a fraction, which may still retain a real value even when both its numerator and denominator become smaller than any assignable quantity. Some authors on mechanics—indeed, the most eminent, such as Bernoulli, Dalembert, and Laplace—have deduced the laws of pressure more directly from the principle of the equality of the effects of equal causes. This demonstration may be found in an improved form in the article "Dynamics" in the *Supplement of the Encyclopaedia Britannica*, though its steps are still tedious and intricate.

We are, therefore, to consider the <term>momentum</term>, or quantity of motion, which would be produced by any force in action as the measure of the pressure it causes when opposed. We should understand equal or proportionate pressures to be those produced by forces that would generate equal or proportionate <term>momenta</term> in a given time. It may be inferred that two contrary pressures will balance each other when the <term>momenta</term> that the forces would separately produce in opposite directions are equal. Furthermore, any one pressure will counterbalance two others when it would produce a <term>momentum</term> equal and opposite to the <term>momentum</term> derived from the combined result of the other forces. For instance, if we suppose that each of two opposing forces acts for an instant and remains inactive for the next equal instant while the other force is exerted, it is obvious that these effects will neutralize each other so that the body on which they are supposed to operate will maintain its position. However, such an action is precisely half of the continued action of each force; consequently, since the halves completely counteract...

It follows from the laws of the <term>composition of motion</term>, that the result of two pressures, expressed by the sides of a <term>parallelogram</term>, will be represented by its diagonal, and that, if a body remains at rest by means of three pressures, they must be related to each other in magnitude as the sides of a triangle parallel to their directions. This may be very completely shown by experiment. We attach three weights to as many threads, joined at a single point and passing over three pulleys; then by drawing any triangle, of which the sides are in the directions of the threads, or in parallel directions, we may always express the magnitude of each weight by the length of the side of the triangle corresponding to its thread. (Plate III. Fig. 33.)

The most important of the problems relating to equilibrium are those concerning the machines which are usually called <term>mechanical powers</term>. We are not, however, to enter at present into all the properties and uses of these machines; we have at first only to examine them in a state of rest, since the determination of their motion requires additional considerations, and their application to practice belongs to another subdivision of our subject.

There is a general law of <term>mechanical equilibrium</term>, which includes the principal properties of most of these machines. If two or more bodies, connected together, are suspended from a given point, they will be at rest when their <term>centre of inertia</term> is in the vertical line passing through the point of suspension. The truth of this proposition may easily be illustrated by the actual suspension of any body, or system of bodies, from or upon a fixed point; the whole remains in equilibrium when the centre of inertia is either vertically below the point of suspension, or above the point of support, or when the fixed point coincides with the centre of inertia. And whatever may be the form of a compound body, it may be considered as a system of bodies connected together, with the situation of the common centre of the inertia determining the <term>quiescent position</term> of the body. (Plate III. Fig. 34..38.)

Hence the centre of inertia is called the <term>centre of gravity</term>; and it may be practically found by determining the intersection of two lines which become

Thus, if we suspend a board of an irregular form from any two points successively, and mark the position of the vertical line in each position, we may find the location of the <term>center of gravity</term> by their intersection; and it will appear that this intersection will be the same, whatever positions we employ. (Plate III. Fig. 39.)

The consideration of the degree of <term>stability</term> of <term>equilibrium</term> is of material importance in many <term>mechanical operations</term>. Like other variable quantities, the stability may be positive, negative, or evanescent. The equilibrium is positively more or less <term>stable</term>, when the <term>center of gravity</term> would be forced to ascend more or less rapidly if it left the vertical line. The equilibrium is <term>tottering</term>, and the stability is negative, when the <term>center of gravity</term> would descend if it were displaced; but when the <term>center of gravity</term> coincides with the <term>center of motion</term>, or when its path would be a horizontal straight line, the equilibrium has been called "insensible," but may more properly be termed <term>neutral</term>, and the body will rest in any position without tending either to fall or to return to its original situation. It is obvious that the <term>center of gravity</term> cannot move without descending when it is vertically over the fixed point, nor without ascending when it is immediately below it; so that in the one case the equilibrium is tottering, and in the other stable. From this, we may understand the reason for fixing the movable handles of any kind of vessel at its upper part, in order that the <term>center of suspension</term> may always be above the <term>center of gravity</term>. If they are fixed too low, the vessel will be liable to overturn, unless there is sufficient friction to retain it in its proper situation. (Plate III. Fig. 40.)

An oval surface, placed on a horizontal plane, is capable of a stable equilibrium when it rests on its side or on the extremity of its shorter axis, and of a tottering equilibrium when it stands on the extremity of its longer axis. But the equilibrium of a circle or a sphere is always neutral, for, when disturbed, it neither recovers its first position nor deviates further from it. A flat body, resting on a sphere, will have its equilibrium tottering or stable, depending on whether its <term>center of gravity</term> is more or less than the <term>semidiameter</term> of the sphere above the point of contact. (Plate III. Fig. 41, 42.)

The <term>stability</term> of a body supported on a flat base of a given extent is of a different kind and is independent of <term>equilibrium</term>. For here, if the <term>center of gravity</term> moves either way, it must begin its motion in an inclined direction, instead of describing a curve which is initially horizontal. The <term>stability</term> of such a body becomes less and less as it is more and more inclined, until, when the <term>center of gravity</term> is vertically over the margin of the base, there is a <term>tottering equilibrium</term>; and if the inclination is still further continued, the body will fall. (Plate III. Fig. 43.)

The broader the base and the lower the <term>center of gravity</term>, the steeper the path of that center must be, and consequently the greater the <term>stability</term>. Thus, the disposition of the weight in a carriage may considerably affect its <term>stability</term> by altering the place of the <term>center of gravity</term>. A wagon loaded with iron is much less easily overturned than when it is loaded with an equal weight of hay; supposing an inequality in the road, or any accidental obstacle, elevates one side of the wagon, it will always recover its position, provided that the <term>center of gravity</term> remains within the vertical line passing through the point of contact of the lower wheel and the ground; and it is obvious that the higher the <term>center of gravity</term> is situated, the sooner it passes this line. If the speed of the motion were very great, the wheel which is elevated might be lifted off the ground by the <term>momentum</term>, and the <term>center of gravity</term> might thus be carried beyond the vertical line by means of an obstacle which would not have overturned the wagon if it had been moving slowly. (Plate III. Fig. 44.)

If a person is sitting or standing in a carriage, the part of the carriage on which he sits or stands may be considered as representing the place of his weight, provided that his posture is always perpendicular; but if the motion is rapid, he will not be able to remain constantly in a posture perfectly erect, and the <term>center of gravity</term> of the carriage, with its passengers, will be somewhat more elevated than it would be on this supposition.

The direction of the initial motion of the <term>center of gravity</term> readily explains the suspension of a weight, or a bucket of water, on a rod resting on the end of a table, when another rod is employed to keep the bucket at such a distance from the end of the first that the <term>center of gravity</term> may be under the table;

# LECTURE VII.

For although the bucket seems suspended by its handle, yet if the handle began to descend, the center of gravity would be obliged to rise; consequently, the whole will retain its position and remain at rest. (Plate III. Fig. 45.)

The apparent ascent of a loaded cylinder on an inclined plane, and the motion of a roller composed of two united cones with a common axis, resting on the edge of a triangle which is inclined to the horizon, may be easily understood from the same consideration. (Plate III. Fig. 46.)

We may also observe many circumstances illustrative of the properties of the center of gravity in the equilibrium of animals. When a person stands on one foot and leans forward, in the attitude usually exhibited in the statues of Mercury, the other foot is elevated behind in order to bring back the center of gravity so as to be vertically over some part of the foot on which he stands. But on account of the convex and irregular form of the foot, the base it affords is really very narrow; hence, when we attempt to stand on one foot, we often find it necessary to use muscular exertion in order to bring the point of support to that side toward which we are beginning to fall. When the base is still more contracted, the body never remains at rest, but—by a succession of actions of this kind, sometimes too minute to be visible—it is kept in a state of perpetual vibration without ever attaining such a position as would give it any degree of positive stability. Thus, it may be conceived to be supported even on a single point, recovering its position from time to time by means of a slight degree of rotary motion, which is produced by its flexing and by the changes of the position of the limbs. Hence, through habit, the arts of rope-dancers and balancers are acquired. Sometimes, however, the position of the balancer is not as difficult to preserve as it appears, as the curvature of the wire in contact with the foot tends materially to assist him.

When we attempt to rise from a seat, we generally draw our feet inward in order to bring the point of support into, or near, the vertical line passing through the center of gravity, and to create a tottering equilibrium, which is favorable for beginning motion. And before we rise, we bend the upper part of the body forward in order to procure a momentum capable of carrying the center of gravity beyond the vertical line passing through the point of support.

When a horse walks, its center of gravity is sometimes supported by only two feet on the same side, yet for such a short time that its tilt toward the other side is easily corrected once the legs on that side resume their movement. Some authors have thought it impossible for a four-legged animal to stand for even an instant with both feet on one side raised from the ground; however, when a horse walks quickly, it can often be observed that the print of the hind foot is significantly further forward than that of the front foot, which was raised to make way for it.

From the general law of the equilibrium of the center of gravity, we can derive the properties of all types of levers. It follows from the definition of this point that if two bodies are attached to a straight rod of negligible weight, they can be held in equilibrium by a fixed point, or <term>fulcrum</term>, which divides the distance between them into parts that are inversely proportional to their weights. And it is obvious that if any other equivalent forces are substituted for weights—acting at the same distance from the fulcrum and at the same angle to the rod or lever—the conditions for equilibrium will remain exactly the same. Also, if either of the forces is moved to an equal distance on the other side of the fulcrum and acts there in the opposite direction, the equilibrium will still be maintained. Thus, we have two primary kinds of levers: the first, where the fixed point or fulcrum is between the points where the forces or weights are applied; and the second, where the forces are applied in opposite directions on the same side of the fulcrum. (Plate III, Fig. 47.)

There have been many different demonstrations of the fundamental property of the lever. Archimedes himself provided two. Huygens, Newton, Maclaurin, Dr. Hamilton, and Mr. Vince have all explained the same subject using different methods. Archimedes' demonstration, as improved by Mr. Vince, is clever and elegant, but it is neither as general and natural as one of Dr. Hamilton’s, nor as simple and convincing as Maclaurin’s, which is worth our attention. Suppose two equal weights of one ounce each are attached to the ends of equal arms on a first-class lever; in this case, it is obvious that there will be equilibrium, as there is no reason for either weight to outweigh the other. It is also evident that the fulcrum supports the total weight of two ounces, disregarding the weight of the lever itself; consequently, we may substitute for the fulcrum

Here, therefore, the weight remaining at the other end of the lever counterbalances a force of two ounces acting at half the distance from the new <term>fulcrum</term>; and we may substitute for this force a weight of two ounces acting at an equal distance on the other side of that fulcrum, provided the lever is sufficiently lengthened, and there will still be an equilibrium. In this case, the fulcrum will sustain a weight of three ounces; and we may substitute for it a force of three ounces acting upward and proceed as before. In a similar manner, the demonstration may be extended to any commensurable proportion of the arms—that is, any proportion that can be expressed by numbers—and it is easy to show that the same law must be true of all ratios whatever, even if they happen to be incommensurable, such as the side of a square compared to its diagonal, which cannot be accurately expressed by any numbers whatever. The forces remain always in equilibrium when they are to each other inversely as the distances at which they are applied.

It is sometimes more convenient to have a series of levers acting on each other, with a moderate increase of power in each, than to have a single lever equivalent in its effect. We may also bend either arm of a lever in any manner that we please without altering its power, provided that the direction of the force is perpendicular to the line drawn to the fulcrum; or if the force is applied obliquely, it may always be imagined to act at the end of a lever equal in length to the perpendicular line dropped from the fulcrum on the direction of the force. Thus, if two levers are connected by a rope or bar, when the direction of one of them nearly coincides with that of the rope, a force applied transversely to the lever acts with a great mechanical advantage against the rope; but as the inclination increases, the advantage gradually diminishes, and changes, at last, to an equal advantage on the side of the rope and the other lever to which it is attached. When, therefore, a great force is required in the beginning of the motion, and afterward a much smaller force with a greater velocity, this apparatus may be extremely convenient: thus, in opening a steam valve, the pressure of the steam is at first to be overcome, and after this, little or no additional force is required; and Mr. <term>Watt</term> has very ingeniously applied this arrangement of levers to the purpose in his steam engines. In the

In the same manner, it is necessary that the platen of a printing press, or the part which presses the paper onto the types, should descend from a considerable height, but a great force is required only at the instant of taking the impression; both of these goals are achieved by similar means in a press recently invented by Lord Stanhope. (Plate III. Fig. 48, 49.)

The wheel and axis bear a very strong resemblance to the lever. If two threads, or perfectly flexible and inextensible lines, are wound in opposite directions around two cylinders, drums, or rollers, which move together on the same axis, there will be an equilibrium when the weights attached to the threads, or the forces operating on them, are inversely proportional to the radii of the cylinders, or to the diameters of which they are halves. It can easily be understood that the weights have the same power in turning the cylinders as if they were directly attached to the arms of a lever equal in length to their radius [semidiameter], and that the conditions of equilibrium will be the same. The demonstration may also be more directly deduced from the position of the center of gravity, located immediately below the axis of the cylinders, which requires the weights to be inversely proportional to the radii. With respect to stability, the equilibrium is neutral, and the cylinders will remain at rest in any position. A single cylinder is also often combined with a lever or winch, and in this case the radius of the cylinder is to be compared with the length of the lever or winch. (Plate III. Fig. 50.)

Systems of wheels and pinions of various kinds resemble, in their mechanical properties, either a series of levers or the combination of cylinders that constitutes the wheel and axis; but the form of the teeth may produce a difference in their action, which will be mentioned when the practical construction of wheelwork is discussed.

Sometimes the axis connected to a winch is composed of two cylinders, with one end of the rope being uncoiled from the smaller while the other end winds around the larger; the weight is supported by a pulley running in the angle of the rope. Here, the conditions of equilibrium are easily determined from the location of the center of gravity, and the effect of the machine is the same as if the weight were attached to a rope coiled around a simple cylinder with a diameter equal to half the difference between the diameters of the double axis. # LECTURE VII.

The machine is, however, much stronger than such a cylinder would be, and does not require such a great curvature in the ropes employed. (Plate IV. Fig. 51.)

The laws of the equilibrium of pulleys have been referred, by some writers on mechanics, to those of the lever; but the comparison is both unnecessary and imperfect. In the simple case of two equal weights attached to a thread passing over a single pulley, which is the only case that allows us to return to the properties of the lever, the conditions of equilibrium are axiomatically evident without any further reasoning; and in more complicated cases, the calculations proceed on completely different grounds. We are, therefore, to consider a pulley as a cylinder moving on an axis, merely in order to change the direction of a thread without friction; for whatever can be demonstrated regarding pulleys or their combinations would be equally true of as many perfectly smooth grooves, which do not bear the slightest analogy to the lever.

Now, when the direction of a thread is altered by passing over any perfectly smooth surface, it communicates the whole force acting on it; for the resistance of a surface without friction can only be in a direction perpendicular to itself and to the thread, and the operation of any force remains undisturbed by a resistance which is always in a direction perpendicular to it.

A fixed pulley, therefore, has no effect in gaining a mechanical advantage; but by means of a movable pulley, it is obvious that a weight may be supported by two forces, each equivalent to half the weight, applied in a vertical direction to the ends of the thread. These forces may be derived from two weights if the thread is made to pass over two fixed pulleys in a proper position; and if one of the ends is attached to a fixed point and the other remains connected to its weight, the equilibrium will continue unimpaired, with each portion of the thread still supporting one half of the original weight. So, by means of a single movable pulley, one body may maintain in equilibrium another of double its weight. (Plate IV. Fig 52, 53.)

The modes of arranging pulleys are very various, but the advantage which they provide may always be estimated from the consideration that every part of the same thread must be equally stretched; and where there is only one thread, the weight will be divided equally among all the portions which help

In common ship blocks, the pulleys or sheaves are equal in size and placed side by side; here, their number cannot conveniently exceed two or three without causing an obliquity in the block when the force is applied to the rope. For this reason, Mr. Smeaton invented a system of pulleys arranged in two rows in each block, one larger and the other smaller. With the force being applied in the middle, the rope passes over the larger pulleys until it arrives at the last one, then returns through the entire series of smaller pulleys to the opposite side, and comes back again on the larger pulleys to be finally attached in the middle. (Plate IV. Fig. 54 .. 56.)

If the diameters of all the pulleys in both blocks are set in the ratio of the number of portions of the thread intervening between them and the fixed extremity, their angular velocity will be equal, with each of them turning on its axis in the same amount of time. They may, therefore, be fixed to a single axis in each block; in this case, because the axis is longer, there will be less accidental friction from a lack of steadiness, and even the necessary friction may, perhaps, be somewhat diminished. (Plate IV. Fig. 57.)

If one end of a thread supporting a movable pulley is fixed, and the other is attached to another movable pulley, and the threads of this pulley are similarly arranged, the weight will be counterbalanced by a power found by halving it as many times as there are movable pulleys; for it is obvious that each of these pulleys doubles the effect of the power. (Plate IV. Fig. 58.)

There are also other arrangements by which the effect of pulleys may be increased or diversified: for instance, where one end of each rope is attached to the weight to be moved, or where two of the pulleys are connected by a rope passing over a third; but these methods are of little practical utility. (Plate IV. Fig. 59, 60.)
