A force may also be applied obliquely to a wheel and axle. Suppose a rope is coiled obliquely around the axle; to maintain equilibrium, it will require a force that is as much greater than what would be sufficient if it were simply applied in the direction of the motion, as the length of any part of the uncoiled rope is greater than the perpendicular distance of its end from the axle. So, when the rope becomes very oblique, a great force is required to counteract a much smaller one acting perpendicularly. This observation may be illustrated to some extent by considering the method used by joiners and stonecutters for keeping a saw straight: two ropes or braces are twisted together by means of a pin or lever passing between them, and they serve as an axis for each other around which they are coiled obliquely, so that they act with great force when they are sufficiently tight and not too much twisted. (Plate IV. Fig. 62.)

It appears from the laws which have already been established respecting the motions of bodies on inclined surfaces, that a weight acting vertically will hold in equilibrium another weight resting on an inclined plane, without friction, when the first is to the second as the height of the plane is to its slanted length. In this case, the pressure on the plane is to the weight resting on it as the horizontal length of the plane is to its slanted length. This pressure may be measured experimentally by substituting for the resistance of the plane that of a thread perpendicular to it. (Plate IV. Fig. 63.)

# ON PRESSURE AND EQUILIBRIUM.

The same principles are applicable to the equilibrium of the wedge. A wedge is a solid which has three plane faces inclined to each other, and two triangular ends; and we suppose the faces to be perfectly polished, so as to be free from friction, and that no force can act on them except in a perpendicular direction. Now, in order that three forces acting on the faces or sides of a wedge may hold each other in equilibrium, each of them must be in proportion to the length of the side on which it acts. They must also be applied at such points that their directions may meet in one point; for otherwise they will not be completely opposed to each other, and a rotational motion will be produced. (Plate IV. Fig. 64.)

If each face of the wedge were conceived to be capable of receiving a pressure, not only in a perpendicular direction but in any other direction at will, as some authors have supposed, the instrument would lose its essential character as a wedge; but in such cases, the proportion of the forces required for the state of equilibrium may always be determined by drawing a triangle with its sides parallel to their directions.

It happens, however, quite often that the force actually operating on the wedge is derived from another force acting in a direction more or less oblique—such as when a heavy body rests on one of the faces of the wedge which is inclined to the horizon. The body is retained in its position by an obstacle or a thread which confines it to a vertical line, and the sliding away of the wedge is prevented by a horizontal force. A wedge so situated, and supposed to be capable of sliding without friction on a horizontal surface, is sometimes called a movable inclined plane, and it will support the weight resting on it if the horizontal force is to the weight as the height of the plane is to its horizontal length. If the thread, or the obstacle helping to support the weight, is placed in any other direction, the magnitude of the forces must be determined from the general law of the composition of three pressures. (Plate IV. Fig 65.)

The action of a screw depends on the same principles as those of an inclined plane; for by rolling a thin and flexible wedge—for instance, a triangular piece of card—around a cylinder, we form a screw. We may consider the force tending to turn the screw around its axis as being applied horizontally to the base of the wedge, and the weight which is to be raised as acting vertically on its inclined surface. The circumference of the cylinder will represent the horizontal length of the wedge, and the distance between the threads, measured in the direction of the axis, will be its height, provided that the threads are single; consequently, the forces required for equilibrium are in the same proportion to each other as the height of one spire is to the circumference of the screw. But besides these forces, it is necessary that some obstacle be present which may prevent the body on which the screw acts from following it in its motion around its axis; otherwise, there can be no equilibrium. (Plate V. Fig. 68.)

The cylinder, which is the foundation of a screw, may be either convex or concave, creating a cylindrical or a tubular screw; and these, when fitted together, are sometimes called a screw and a nut. The nut acts on the screw with the same mechanical power as a single point would do, since it only divides the pressure among the different parts of the spire. In general, the screw is applied in combination with a lever in order to gain an advantage in overcoming friction, which is always considerable in the simple screw and nut, and which would resist a force applied immediately at the circumference without any reduction of its power. Sometimes the spires of a screw are made to act on the teeth of a wheel when a very slow motion of the wheel, or a very rapid motion of the screw, is required for the purposes of the machine. (Plate V. Fig. 69, 70.)

In all the kinds of equilibrium that we have considered, and in all other cases that can be imagined, it will be found that the forces, or rather weights, opposed to each other, are so arranged, that if they were put in motion, their <term>momenta</term> in the direction of gravity would, in the first instance, be equal and contrary, the velocity being as much greater as the magnitude of the weight is smaller. Thus, if an ounce weight, placed on a lever at the distance of four feet from the fulcrum, balances a weight of four ounces at the distance of one foot, the velocity with which the ounce would descend, if the lever were moved, would be four times as great as that with which the weight of four ounces would descend. A single movable pulley ascends with half the velocity of the end of the rope which is drawn upwards, and acts with a force twice as great; a block of three sheaves <note>OCR "shieves"; the wheels in a pulley block</note> enables a weight to sustain another six times as great; but the velocity with which this weight ascends is only one-sixth of that with which the smaller weight must descend. When a weight rests on an inclined plane, of which the height is one-half of the length, it may be retained by the action of a weight of half its magnitude, drawing it up the plane by means of a thread passing over a pulley; here if the weight ascended or descended along the oblique surface, its velocity, reduced to a vertical direction, would be half as great as that of the smaller weight which balances it.

In the kind of equilibrium that we have been considering, the weights or other forces are arranged such that, if they were moved, their velocities would be in the inverse proportion of their magnitude. In this situation, the velocities are said to be inversely as the weights; thus, if an ounce were placed at one foot, and four ounces at three inches from the fulcrum of a lever, the velocity of the ounce would be four times as great as that of the four ounces; and four ounces moved through one inch would require as much force as one ounce moved through four inches. A similar proportion may be observed in the pulley; the end of the rope which is drawn by the hand is pulled with a force as great as that of the block which supports the weight, but it moves six times as fast; but the velocity with which the weight ascends is only one-sixth of that with which the weight would fall if it were not held. In the case of an inclined plane, where the height is one-half of its length, a weight held by the tension of a weight of half its magnitude—drawing it up the plane by means of a thread passing over a pulley—the weight ascending or descending along the slanted surface, its velocity reduced to a vertical direction, would be half as great as that of the smaller weight which balances it.

### ON COLLISION.

Having examined the laws and properties of motion and rest in single bodies under the influence of one or more forces, and the equilibrium of these forces in various circumstances, we are next to examine some simple cases of the motions of various movable bodies acting reciprocally on each other. In all problems of this kind, it is important to remember the general principle already established regarding the <term>center of inertia</term>: that its position is not affected by any reciprocal or mutual action of the bodies that make up the system.

Whenever two bodies act on each other to change the direction of their relative motions—by means of any forces that maintain their activity undiminished at equal distances in every direction—the relative velocities with which the bodies approach or move away from each other will always be equal at equal distances. For example, the velocity of a comet as it passes near the Earth during its descent toward the sun is the same as its velocity of ascent on its return, even though its velocity undergoes considerable changes at different distances. In this case, the force acts continuously and attracts the bodies toward each other; however, the force involved in <term>collision</term>—when one body strikes or impels another—acts only during the period of more or less close contact and tends to separate the bodies from each other. When this force acts as powerfully in causing the bodies to separate as it did in destroying the velocity with which they met, the bodies are called <term>perfectly elastic</term>. When the bodies meet each other without a <term>reaction</term> of this kind, they are called more or less <term>inelastic</term>. Ivory, metals, and elastic gum <note>natural rubber</note> are highly and almost perfectly elastic; clay, wax mixed with a little oil, and other soft bodies are almost inelastic; and the effects

# LECTURE VIII.

of inelastic bodies may be imitated by elastic ones, if we cause them to unite or adhere after an impulse, so as to destroy the effect of the repulsive force which tends to separate them.

When two bodies approach each other, their form is in some degree changed, and more so as the velocity is greater. In general, the repulsive force exerted is exactly proportional to the degree in which a body is compressed; and when a body strikes another, this force continues to increase until the relative motion has been destroyed, and the bodies are for an instant at rest with respect to each other; the repulsive action then proceeds with an intensity which is gradually diminished, and if the bodies are perfectly elastic, they resume their original form, and separate with a velocity equal to that with which they before approached each other. Strictly speaking, the repulsion commences a little before the moment of actual contact, but only at a distance which in common cases is imperceptible. The change of form of an elastic substance, during collision, is easily shown by throwing a ball of ivory on a slab of marble, or a piece of smooth iron, colored with black lead, or printing ink; or by allowing it to fall from various heights: the degree of compression will then be indicated by the magnitude of the black spot which appears on the ball. It may be shown, from the laws of pendulums, that, on the supposition that the force is proportional to the degree of compression, its greatest exertion is to the weight of a striking body, as the height from which the body must have fallen, in order to acquire its velocity, to half the depth of the impression.

For making experiments on the phenomena of collision, it is most convenient to suspend the bodies employed, by threads, in the manner of pendulums; their velocities may then be easily measured, by observing the chords of the arcs, through which they descend or ascend, since the velocities acquired in descending through circular arcs are always proportional to their chords; and for this purpose, the apparatus is provided with a graduated arc, which is commonly divided into equal parts, although it would be a little more correct to place the divisions at the ends of arcs, of which the chords are expressed by the corresponding numbers. (Plate V. Fig. 72.)

When a ball at rest is struck by another equal ball, it receives a velocity equal to that of the ball which strikes it, and this ball remains at rest. And if two equal balls meet or overtake each other with any unequal velocities, their motions will be exchanged, each rising to a height equal to that from which the other descended.

The effect of collision takes place so rapidly that if several equal balls are arranged in a straight line, in apparent contact with each other, and another ball strikes the first of them, they will all receive in succession the whole velocity of the moving ball before they begin to act on the following ones; they will then transmit the whole velocity to the succeeding balls and remain entirely at rest, so that only the last ball will fly off.

In the same manner, if two or more equal balls, in apparent contact, are in motion and strike against any number of others placed in a line, the first of the moving balls will first drive off the most distant ball, and then the second moving ball will drive off the second-to-last ball of the row which was at rest: so that the same number of balls will fly off together on one side as descended to strike the row of balls on the other side, while the others remain at rest.

If the line of balls, instead of being loosely in contact, had been firmly united, they would have been impelled with a smaller velocity, and the ball striking them would have been reflected. For when a smaller elastic body strikes a larger one, it rebounds with a velocity less than its first velocity, and the larger body also proceeds with a lower velocity than that of the body striking it. But if a larger body strikes a smaller one, it still proceeds with a lower velocity, and the smaller body advances with a greater one.

# LECTURE VIII.

...of inelastic bodies may be imitated by elastic ones, if we cause them to unite or adhere after an impulse, so as to destroy the effect of the repulsive force that tends to separate them.

When two bodies approach each other, their form is changed to some degree, and more so as the velocity increases. In general, the repulsive force exerted is exactly proportional to the degree to which a body is compressed; and when a body strikes another, this force continues to increase until the relative motion has been destroyed and the bodies are for an instant at rest with respect to each other. The repulsive action then proceeds with an intensity that is gradually diminished, and if the bodies are perfectly elastic, they reassume their original form and separate with a velocity equal to that with which they previously approached each other. Strictly speaking, the repulsion begins a little before the moment of actual contact, but only at a distance that in common cases is imperceptible. The change of form of an elastic substance during collision is easily shown by throwing an ivory ball onto a marble slab or a piece of smooth iron colored with black lead or printing ink, or by letting it fall from various heights; the degree of compression will then be indicated by the size of the black spot that appears on the ball. It may be shown, from the laws of pendulums, that—on the assumption that the force is proportional to the degree of compression—its greatest exertion relates to the weight of a striking body in the same way the height from which the body must have fallen to acquire its velocity relates to half the depth of the impression.

For conducting experiments on the phenomena of collision, it is most convenient to suspend the bodies being used by threads like pendulums; their velocities may then be easily measured by observing the chords of the arcs through which they descend or ascend, since the velocities acquired in descending through circular arcs are always proportional to their chords. For this purpose, the apparatus is provided with a graduated arc, which is commonly divided into equal parts, although it would be slightly more accurate to place the divisions at the ends of arcs where the chords are expressed by the corresponding numbers. (Plate V. Fig. 72.)

When a ball at rest is struck by another equal ball, it receives a velocity equal to that of the ball which strikes it, and the striking ball remains at rest. And if two equal balls meet or overtake each other with any unequal velocities, their motions will be exchanged, each rising to a height equal to that from which the other descended.

The effect of collision takes place so rapidly that if several equal balls are arranged in a straight line, in apparent contact with each other, and another ball strikes the first of them, they will all receive in succession the whole velocity of the moving ball before they begin to act on the succeeding ones; they will then transmit the whole velocity to the succeeding balls and remain entirely at rest, so that only the last ball will fly off.

In the same manner, if two or more equal balls, in apparent contact, are in motion and strike against any number of others placed in a line, the first of the moving balls will first drive off the most distant, and then the second will drive off the second to last of the row of balls which were at rest: so that the same number of balls will fly off together on one side as descended to strike the row of balls on the other side; the others remaining at rest.

If the line of balls, instead of being loosely in contact, had been firmly united, they would have been impelled with a smaller velocity, and the ball striking them would have been reflected. For when a smaller elastic body strikes a larger one, it rebounds with a velocity less than its original velocity, and the larger body also proceeds with a lower velocity than that of the body striking it. But if a larger body strikes a smaller one, it still proceeds with a lower velocity, and the smaller body advances with a greater one.

<header>LECTURE VIII.</header>

...its impulse, and the second body acquires a momentum nearly twice as great as that of the first. When a larger body strikes a smaller one, it communicates to it only as much momentum as it loses.

In the transfer of motion between inelastic bodies, the lack of a repulsive force capable of separating them with an equal relative velocity is probably due to a permanent change of form; such bodies receive and retain an indentation at the point of contact. When the velocity is too small to produce this change of form, the bodies, however inelastic, may usually be observed to rebound a little.

Bodies that are perfectly inelastic remain in contact after collision; they must, therefore, move forward with the same velocity as the center of inertia had before the collision. Thus, if two equal balls meet with equal velocities, they remain at rest; if one is at rest and the other strikes it, they move forward with half the velocity of the ball that was first in motion. If they are of unequal dimensions, the joint velocity is as much smaller than that of the striking ball as the weight of this ball is smaller than the sum of the weights of both balls. In a similar manner, the effects of any given velocities in either ball may be determined.

It follows immediately from the properties of the center of inertia that in all cases of collision—whether of elastic or inelastic bodies—the sum of the momenta of all the bodies in the system (that is, of their masses or weights multiplied by the numbers expressing their velocities) remains the same when adjusted for direction after their mutual collision as it was before their collision. When the bodies are perfectly elastic, it may also be shown that the sum of their energies or ascending forces in their respective directions also remains unaltered.

The term *energy* may be applied with great appropriateness to the product of the mass or weight of a body multiplied by the square of the number expressing its velocity. Thus, if a weight of one ounce moves with a velocity of one foot per second, we may call its energy 1; if a second body of two ounces has a velocity of three feet per second, its energy will be twice the square of three, or 18. This product has been called the living or ascending force.

Some have considered this the true measure of the quantity of motion; but although this opinion has been almost universally rejected, the force estimated in this way still deserves a distinct name. After the considerations and demonstrations already presented on the subject of forces, there can be no reasonable doubt regarding the true measure of motion. Nor can there be much hesitation in admitting at once that since the same force, continued for twice the time, is known to produce twice the velocity, then twice the force must also produce twice the velocity in the same amount of time. Despite the simplicity of this view, Leibnitz, Smeaton, and many others have chosen to estimate the force of a moving body by the product of its mass and the square of its velocity. Although we cannot admit that this estimation of force is correct, it may be conceded that many of the observable effects of motion—and even the advantage of any mechanical power, however it is used—are usually proportional to this product, or to the weight of the moving body multiplied by the height from which it must have fallen to acquire that specific velocity. For example, a bullet moving at twice the velocity will penetrate to four times the depth in clay or tallow. A ball of equal size but one-fourth the weight, moving at twice the velocity, will penetrate to an equal depth; and, with a smaller quantity of motion, it will make an equal excavation in less time. This appears somewhat paradoxical at first glance; but on the other hand, we must consider the resistance of the clay or tallow as a uniformly retarding force. It will then be obvious that the motion which it can stop in a short time must be less than the motion which requires a longer time to stop. Similarly, when overcoming the resistance of an object to a force that might break it, the power of any moving body to break it is proportional to the energy of its motion (or its weight multiplied by the square of its velocity), assuming that the distance the object can be bent before breaking is known, along with the force exerted at every point across that distance.

In almost all cases involving forces used in practical mechanics, the labor expended in producing any motion is proportional not to the momentum, but to the energy obtained. This is because these forces are seldom considered uniformly accelerating forces; instead, they generally act at some disadvantage when the velocity is already significant. To obtain a certain velocity by letting a heavy body descend from a height, we must first carry it up a flight of steps. If we wish to double that velocity, we must ascend four times as many steps, and this will cost us nearly four times as much labor. Similarly, if we apply a specific force to the shorter end of a lever in order to move a weight located at a greater distance on the other side of the fulcrum, a certain portion of the force is used up in the pressure supported by the fulcrum. Consequently, we do not produce the same momentum that would have been gained by applying the same force directly to the body we wish to move.

An elastic ball weighing 2 ounces, moving at a velocity of 3 feet per second, possesses an energy—as we have already seen—that can be expressed as 18. If it strikes a 1-ounce ball that is at rest, its velocity will be reduced to 1 foot per second, and the smaller ball will gain a velocity of 4 feet per second. The energy of the first ball will then be expressed as 2, and that of the second as 16, totaling 18 as before. The momentum of the larger ball after the collision is 2, while that of the smaller is 4, and the sum of these equals the original momentum of the first ball.

Assuming the size of an elastic body at rest to be infinite, it will receive twice the momentum of a small body that strikes it; however, its velocity—and consequently its energy—will be negligible, since energy is expressed by the product of the momentum and the velocity. If the larger body has a finite size but is still much larger than the smaller one, its energy will be very small. The energy of the smaller body, which rebounds with a velocity nearly equal to its original speed, is only slightly diminished. For this reason, a man with a heavy anvil placed on his chest can endure the blow of a large hammer striking the anvil without much discomfort, whereas a much lighter blow from the hammer, if it struck his body directly, would have fractured his ribs and killed him. The anvil receives a momentum nearly twice as great as that of the hammer; however, its tendency to overcome the strength of the bones and crush the man is proportional only to its energy. This energy is less than that of the hammer in nearly the same proportion that four times the hammer's weight is less than the weight of the anvil. Thus, if the weight of the hammer were 5 pounds and that of the anvil 100, the energy of the anvil would be less than one-fifth as great as

When a body strikes another in a direction which does not pass through its center of gravity, the effect produced involves the consideration of rotational motion, since in this case the body is made to revolve on an axis. But this can never happen when the body is spherical and its surface is perfectly polished; since every impulse must then be perpendicular to the surface, and must consequently be directed to the center of the body. If the motion of a ball which strikes another is not directed to its center, the surface of contact must be oblique with respect to its motion, and the second ball will only receive an impulse in a direction perpendicular to this surface, while the first receives, from its reaction, an equal impulse in an opposite direction, which is combined with its original motion. The magnitude of this impulse may be determined by breaking down the motion of the first ball into two parts: the one parallel to the surface of contact, and the other perpendicular; the first part remaining always unaltered, while the second is modified by the collision. If, for example, the balls were equal, this second part of the motion would be destroyed, and the remaining motion would be in the direction of the surface of contact, and perpendicular to that of the ball being struck.

Hence it follows, that if we wish to propel a billiard ball in a given direction by the stroke of another ball, we have only to imagine a third ball to be placed in contact with the first, immediately behind it in the line of the required motion, and to aim at the center of this imaginary ball: the first ball will then be propelled in the required direction, and the second will also continue to move in a direction perpendicular to it.

By a similar analysis of the motion of an elastic ball, we may determine its path when it is reflected from a fixed obstacle. That part of the motion which is in a direction parallel to the surface of the obstacle remains undiminished: the motion perpendicular to it is changed for an equal motion in an opposite direction, and the joint result of these constitutes a motion in a direction which is equally inclined to the surface as the first motion,

Those who are desirous of pursuing the investigation as a mathematical amusement will find all the assistance they require in the profound and elegant works of Maclaurin.

## LECTURE IX.

### ON THE MOTIONS OF CONNECTED BODIES.

**T**HE motions of single bodies acting on each other in any way—which we have been considering as they relate to the effects of collision—are of less importance to practical mechanics than the properties of such bodies that are joined together, so as either to revolve around a common center or to share in each other’s motions through some kind of machinery.

It is only within the last fifty years that the phenomena and effects of rotatory motion have been sufficiently investigated. Newton made a mistake, which is now universally acknowledged, in his calculation of the precession of the equinoxes because he did not attend sufficiently to this subject; and it is important in the calculation of many of the effects of mechanical arrangements that it should be treated in an accurate manner.

The effect of a moving body in producing motion in any other bodies—so connected as to be able to turn freely around a given center—is jointly proportional to its distance from that center and to its momentum in the direction of the motion to be produced. Thus, a body of one pound weight, moving with a velocity of one foot per second, will have three times as great an effect on a system of bodies (to which its whole force is communicated) at the distance of one yard from the center of their motion as if it acted only at the distance of a foot on the same system of bodies; a double weight, or a double velocity, would also produce a double effect. For, supposing two unequal bodies to be connected by an inflexible line and to move with equal velocities in a direction perpendicular to that of the line, it is demonstrable from the principles of the composition of motion that they may be completely stopped by an obstacle applied to the center of gravity; consequently, their effects in turning the line around this point are equal; here the mo-

<summary>This lecture introduces the mechanics of connected bodies and rotatory motion, noting that these principles are more practically important than simple collisions. The author highlights a historical error by Newton regarding the precession of the equinoxes and explains that the force exerted on a rotating system depends on both momentum and distance from the center.</summary>

Hence, in a connected system of bodies revolving around a given point with equal angular velocities, the effect produced by the rotatory motion of each body, as well as the force which is employed in producing it, is expressed by the product of the mass multiplied by the square of the velocity, since the velocity is in this case proportional to the distance from the center; and this product is the same that I have named the <term>energy</term> of a moving body.

These propositions are of great use in all inquiries respecting the operations of machines; and it is of importance to bear in mind that, although the equilibrium of a system of bodies is determined by the equality of the products of their weights and their effective distances on each side of the center, the estimation of the mechanical power of each body, once in motion, requires the mass to be multiplied by the square of the distance, or of the velocity. For this reason, together with some others which have been already mentioned, some have considered the square of the velocity as providing the true measure of force; but the properties of motion concerned in determining rotatory power are in reality no more than necessary consequences of the simpler laws on which the whole theory of mechanics is founded.

The effects of rotatory motion may be very conveniently examined by means of an apparatus similar to that which was employed for the same purpose by Mr. Smeaton. A vertical axis is turned by a thread passing over a pulley and supporting a scale with weights; the thread may be applied at different parts of the axis having different diameters, and the axis supports two arms on which two leaden weights are fixed at distances which may be varied at pleasure. The same force will then produce, in the same time, only half the velocity in the same situation of the weights when the thread is applied to a part of the axis of half the diameter; and if the weights are removed to a double distance from the axis, a quadruple force will be required in order to produce an equal angular velocity in a given time. (Plate V. Fig. 74.)

...magnitude, is made to revolve around a center, it is sometimes necessary to inquire into what point their masses might be supposed to be concentrated, so as to preserve the same rotatory power with the same angular velocity. This point is called the <term>center of gyration</term>. In a circle, or any portion of a circle, turning around its center, the square of the distance of this point from the center is half the square of the radius; and the total effect of the momentum of the circle upon an obstacle at its circumference is exactly half as great as that of an equal quantity of matter striking the obstacle with the velocity of the circumference.

There is another point, the determination of which is of considerable utility in many mechanical problems: this is the <term>center of percussion</term>; or the point at which an obstacle must be applied in order to receive the full effect of the impact of a body that is revolving around a given center, without producing any pressure or strain on the center or axis of motion. In a straight line, or a slender rod fixed at one end, the distance of this point from the center of motion is two-thirds of the total length.

The same point is also the <term>center of oscillation</term>, the distance of which determines the time of oscillation, or vibration, of the body when suspended as a pendulum on the given center of motion. It may easily be shown that a rod a yard long and of uniform thickness, suspended at one end, vibrates in the same time as a ball suspended by a thread two feet long. But if the rod were suspended on a center at some point within its ends, the time of its vibration would be prolonged, so as to become equal to that of a simple pendulum of much greater length. This may be illustrated by two balls fixed at the ends of a rod, with a center of suspension that is movable to any part of the rod; as the center approaches the middle of the rod, the vibrations are rendered extremely slow. (Plate V, Figure 75.)

The rotatory motion of bodies not fixed on an axis might be considered here, but the subject involves some complex calculations in its full extent, and, except in astronomy, the investigation is scarcely applicable to any problems that occur in practice. However, if the fulcrum is applied to any other part of the line, one of the bodies will move forward and the other backward, with a velocity that can easily be determined by calculating their rotatory power in relation to the fulcrum. If the fulcrum is applied at a point on the line extended beyond the bodies, one will lose and the other will gain velocity, since the quantity of rotatory power will always remain unchanged; only that point called the center of oscillation will retain its original velocity. Now, the same inequality in the motion of the bodies, and consequently the same angular velocity of rotation, will be produced if the connected bodies are initially at rest and the fulcrum is applied to them with the same relative velocity. For example, if a straight rod or wire receives an impulse at one end in a transverse direction, the center of oscillation—which is at a distance of two-thirds of the length from the end struck—will remain at rest at the first instant. Consequently, the center will move with one-fourth of the velocity of the impulse; this must be the velocity of the progressive motion of the rod, since the center of gravity of any body that is free to move always moves with a uniform velocity in a straight line, while the whole rod will also revolve uniformly around its center, except for such slowing as may arise from outside causes. In a similar manner, the calculation may be extended to bodies of a more complicated form. Thus, it has been calculated at what point on each planet an impulse must have acted in order to give it, in a single blow, both its rotation and its progressive motion in its orbit.

Those who have asserted that the motion of a body's center of gravity can only be produced by an impulse directed either wholly or partly toward it have obviously been mistaken. The center of oscillation is the only point that remains at rest regarding the first effect of the stroke, and the center of gravity—which never coincides with the center of oscillation—moves in the direction of the impulse, while the parts beyond the center of oscillation begin to move in an opposite direction. The subject of preponderance—or the action of weights or forces counteracted by other forces and burdened with extra matter to be put in motion—requires for its discussion a previous knowledge of the simple operation of forces, the conditions of equilibrium, and the estimation of rotatory power. The consideration of the effects of preponderance enables us to determine, in some circumstances, the best possible proportions of the powers of machines to produce the required effects in the most advantageous manner. For, in order that motion may be produced, it is not sufficient for there to be an equilibrium (in achieving which only a part of the power is spent); there must be an excess of force above that which would be necessary for equilibrium. It is often important to know what portion of the power must be employed in each way so that the greatest effect may be produced in a given time. We are sometimes told that what we gain in power, we lose in time. In one sense, this remark is true; for example, one man can do no more with a powerful machine in ten hours than ten men can do with a weaker machine in one hour. But in other senses, the assertion is often incorrect; for by increasing the mechanical advantage to a given degree, we may in some cases considerably increase the performance of a machine without adding to the force.

According to the nature of the force employed and the construction of the machine, a different calculation may be required for finding the best proportions of the forces to be used; but a few simple instances will serve to show the nature of the determination. Thus, in order for a smaller weight to raise a greater one to a given vertical height in the shortest time possible by means of an <term>inclined plane</term>, the length of the plane must be to its height as twice the greater weight is to the smaller, so that the acting force may be twice as great as that which is simply required for equilibrium. This may be shown experimentally by causing three equal weights, supported on wheels, to ascend three inclined planes of the same height but of different lengths at the same time, by means of the descent of three other

If the weights begin to rise at the same time, the first will arrive at the top before either of the others. (Plate V, Figure 76.)

If a given weight, or any equivalent force, is used to raise another equal weight by means of levers, wheels, pulleys, or any similar mechanisms, the greatest effect will be produced if the acting weight is capable of sustaining, in equilibrium, a weight about two and a half times as great as itself. This proposition can be very satisfactorily illustrated by an experiment. Three double pulleys are placed independently of each other on an axis around which they move freely. The diameters of the two cylindrical portions that compose the first are in the ratio of 3 to 2, those of the second are as 5 to 2, and those of the third are as 4 to 1. Six equal weights are attached to them in pairs, so that three may be raised by the descent of the other three, according to the principle of the wheel and axle. If we then hold the lower weights by threads, or otherwise, and release them so that they begin to rise at the same instant, it will be clearly evident that the middle pulley raises its weight the fastest. Consequently, in this case, the ratio of 5 to 2 is more advantageous than either a much smaller or a much larger ratio. If the weight to be raised were very great in proportion to the descending weight, the arrangement should be such that this weight could maintain in equilibrium a weight about twice as great as that which is actually to be raised. If the descending weight were a hundred times as great as the ascending weight, the greatest velocity would be obtained in this case by making the descending weight capable of holding in equilibrium a weight one-ninth as great as itself. (Plate VI, Figure 77.)

The proportion required for the greatest effect is somewhat different when the heights through which both weights must move are limited, as they usually must be in practical cases. Here, if we suppose the operation to be continually repeated, the effect will be greatest in a given time when the ascending weight is between two-thirds and one-half of the exact counterpoise to the descending weight. If, however, the force were accumulated during the action of the machine, there would be no limit to the advantage of

Thus, if we have a stream of water filling a single <term>reservoir</term>, which is to raise a weight by means of its descent, the proportion assigned here will be the best for performing the most work in a given time; but if we chose to double our machine, so that one <term>reservoir</term> should be filled during the descent of another, it would be proper to proportion the weights in such a manner that the whole time required for filling one of the <term>reservoirs</term> should be occupied in the descent and the reascent of the other.

In all these cases, if great accuracy were required, it would be necessary in the calculation to add to the mass to be moved the quantity of movable matter in the machine, reduced to a mean distance from the <term>fulcrum</term> or center, according to its <term>rotatory power</term>, in the same manner as the <term>centre of gyration</term> is determined. But there is seldom occasion for such a degree of precision. The magnitude of the pressure which is exerted on the <term>fulcrum</term>, during the motion of the connected bodies, may always be determined by comparing the actual velocity of the <term>centre of gravity</term> with that of a body descending without resistance.

These propositions and experiments must be admitted to require attentive consideration from those who are engaged in <term>practical mechanics</term>; and it is natural to suppose that the proportions laid down may be adopted with safety and employed with success, and that we may sometimes derive important advantages from their application. But on more mature consideration, we shall find some practical reasons for caution in admitting them without material alterations.

If a machine were constructed for raising a solid weight, and so arranged as to perform its task in the shortest possible time with a given expense of power, the weight would still possess, when it arrived at its destination, a considerable and still increasing velocity: in order that it might remain in its position, it would be necessary that this velocity should be neutralized; if it were suddenly neutralized, the machinery would undergo a strain which might be very injurious to it; and if the velocity were gradually diminished, the time would no longer be the same as is supposed in the calculation. In the second place, the forces generally employed are by no means uniformly <term>accelerating forces</term>, like that of <term>gravitation</term>, to which the propositions which

# LECTURE IX.

...we have been considering are adapted: they are not only less active when a certain velocity has once been attained, but they are often capable of a temporary increase or decrease of intensity at will. We have seen the inconvenience of producing a great final velocity, on account of its endangering the structure of the machine; if, therefore, our permanent force is calculated according to the common rule—so as to be able to maintain equilibrium and overcome friction—the <term>momentum</term> or <term>inertia</term> of the weights, when once set in motion, will be able to sustain that motion steadily. It will not be difficult to give them a sufficient <term>momentum</term> by a greater exertion of the moving force for a short time at the beginning; and this is, in fact, the true mode of operation of many machines where <term>animal strength</term> is employed. Other forces—for instance those of wind and water—regulate themselves to some extent, at least with respect to the relative velocity of the sails and the wind, or the <term>floatboards</term> and the water; for we may easily increase the resistance until the most advantageous effect is produced. Many authors, considering the pressure of a stream of water as analogous to the impulse of a number of unconnected particles striking the <term>floatboards</term> and then ceasing to produce any further effect, have inferred that the force obtained by such an impulse must be proportional to the square of the relative velocity, and that the effect of an <term>undershot wheel</term> must be most advantageous when its velocity is one-third that of the stream; but it will appear hereafter that this estimation of <term>hydraulic force</term> is by no means accurate. If we compare the greatest velocity with which a man or a horse can run or walk without fatigue to the velocity of the stream, and the actual velocity of that part of the machine to which the force is applied to the velocity of the <term>floatboards</term> of a water wheel, the strength which can be exerted may be represented—according to the experiments of some authors—by the impulse of the stream, as supposed to be proportional to the square of the relative velocity. Consequently, the same velocity would be most advantageous in both cases, and the man or horse ought, according to these experiments, to move, when his force is applied to a machine, with one-third of the velocity with which he could walk or run when unburdened. This, for a man, would be about a mile and a half an hour; for a horse, two or three miles; but in general, both men and horses appear to work most advantageously with a velocity somewhat greater than this.

# ON THE MOTIONS OF CONNECTED BODIES.

Where a uniformly accelerating force, like that of gravitation, is used in machines, it might often be advantageous to regulate its operation so that it acts nearly in the same manner as the forces we have been considering: at first with greater intensity, and later with enough power to maintain equilibrium and overcome friction alone. This could be done by means of a spiral barrel, like the <term>fusee</term> of a watch; and a similar modification has sometimes been applied by making the ascending weight, when it arrives near its destination, act on a <term>counterpoise</term> that resists it with a continually increasing force through the operation of a barrel of the same kind, so as to prevent the shock that a motion that is too rapid would cause.

Overall, we may conclude that, because of the limited velocity usually allowed in the operation of machines, a very small portion of the moving force is spent on producing <term>momentum</term>; a velocity of 3 miles per hour would be generated in a heavy body descending by its own weight in one-seventh of a second, and a very short time is generally enough to achieve a motion as rapid as the machine or the nature of the force permits. Once this has been achieved, the entire force is used to maintain equilibrium and overcome resistance. Thus, the common opinion—which was probably formed without examining the subject in detail and which appears to lead to significant errors when we first examine its foundation accurately—is largely justified by a more thorough investigation.

Searching for a source of motion within the construction of a machine reveals a total ignorance of the principles on which all machines operate. The only interest we can take in the projects attempted to achieve <term>perpetual motion</term> must arise from the opportunity they afford us to observe the weakness of human reason: to see a man spending entire years chasing an object that a single week's study of sound philosophy could have shown was unattainable. The most satisfying refutation of the idea of the possibility of <term>perpetual motion</term> is derived from considering the properties of the <term>center of gravity</term>. We only need to examine whether it will begin to descend or ascend when the machine moves, or whether it will remain at rest. If it is placed so that it must either remain at

LECTURE IX.

rest or ascend, it is clear from the laws of equilibrium that no motion derived from gravitation can occur. If it can descend, it must either continue to descend forever with a finite velocity, which is impossible, or it must first descend and then ascend with a vibratory motion. In that case, the situation would be reduced to that of a pendulum, where it is obvious that no new motion is generated, and that friction and air resistance must soon destroy the original motion. One of the most common fallacies by which superficial inventors of perpetual motion machines have been deceived arises from imagining that any number of weights ascending by a certain path on one side of the center of motion, and descending on the other at a greater distance, must cause a constant preponderance on the side of the descent. For this purpose, the weights have either been fixed on hinges that allow them to fall over at a certain point so as to become more distant from the center, or made to slide or roll along grooves or planes that lead them to a more remote part of the wheel, from which they return as they ascend. However, it will appear upon the inspection of such a machine that although some of the weights are more distant from the center than others, there is always a proportionally smaller number of them on the side where they have the greatest power; so that these circumstances precisely counterbalance each other. (**Plate VI. Fig. 78.**)

## LECTURE X.

### ON DRAWING, WRITING, AND MEASURING.

Having investigated all the general principles and laws of motion and of mechanical power, we may now proceed to the consideration of particular departments of practical mechanics. But before we can satisfactorily compare the various forces which we are to employ or to oppose, we must have some mode of determining their magnitude; and we must begin by examining the spaces which are measures of their action. A knowledge of the instruments employed for drawing, and of the rules of perspective projection, is also necessarily required as a previous step in the study of practical mechanics. We have therefore to consider, as preliminary subjects, first the arts which may be expressed by the terms instrumental geometry, or the geometry of mechanics; secondly, statics, or the mode of ascertaining the magnitude of weights and of other active forces; and thirdly, the examination of the passive strength of materials of various kinds, and of the negative force of friction.

The art of drawing can scarcely be distinguished by any correct definition from painting. In its simplest state, when we merely imitate an original laid before us, it is called copying; and in writing, we only copy the letters of the alphabet. If we proceed in a mathematical manner in the operation of drawing, we require a number of geometrical instruments, which are still more necessary for the first construction of diagrams or figures. In modeling and sculpture, a solid is simply imitated; but when a solid is represented on a plane, the principles of perspective are employed in determining the position of the lines which are to form the picture. The productions of the arts of drawing and writing are multiplied and perpetuated by means of engraving and printing—inventions which have been the sources of inestimable advantage in the instruction and civilization of mankind.

<header>LECTURE X.</header>

In drawing, we may employ the pen, the pencil, chalks, crayons, inks, watercolors, or body colors; we may paint in miniature, in distemper, in fresco, in oils, in varnish, in wax, or in enamel; and we may imitate the effects of painting by mosaic work or by tapestry.

The first step in copying a drawing or in painting is to procure a correct outline. A master of the art can do this with sufficient accuracy by estimating the proportions of the figures using only his eye, especially if he is assisted by lines that divide the original into a number of squares. These lines enable him to transfer their contents to the corresponding squares of the copy, which may in this manner be reduced or enlarged as required. But a copy may sometimes be more quickly made by tracing immediately from the original, when the materials employed are sufficiently transparent to allow the outlines to be seen through them. Alternatively, where the original is of no value, one may prick a number of points through it to mark the copy, either all at once or by means of charcoal powder rubbed through the holes, which is called *stenciling*; for this purpose, an intermediate copy may be formed on semi-transparent paper. Another method is to put a thin paper, rubbed with the powder of <term>black lead</term> <note>graphite</note> or of red chalk, between the original and the paper intended for the copy, and to pass a blunt point over all the lines to be traced, which produces corresponding lines on the paper; this is called *calking*. Where the work is large, it may be covered with a thin gauze and its outlines traced on the gauze with chalk, which is then placed on the blank surface and the chalk shaken off, in the same way that a carpenter marks a board with his line.

The pen was formerly much used for making rough sketches, and it is still sometimes employed for the same purpose, as well as for assisting the effect of the pencil. The appearance of uniform light and shade must necessarily be imitated in drawings with the pen, as well as in engravings, by a mixture of the whiteness of the paper with the blackness or color of the ink. The eye is too far away to minutely distinguish the separate lines by which the effect is produced, although they do not entirely escape its observation. In this respect, drawings in pencils and chalks have an advantage over engravings; these substances, after being applied in lines, are spread by means of rubbers, or *stumps*, made of paper, leather, or linen, so as to produce a greater

Of black chalks, the Italian is harder and more generally useful than the French: <term>red chalk</term> has the disadvantage of not being easily removed, either by bread or by Indian rubber, without leaving a brownish mark. Sometimes a gray paper is used, which serves for a middle tint and lessens the labor, with the lights and shades only being added in white and black chalks.

<term>Crayons</term> consist of colors mixed with <term>gum water</term>, or other adhesive substances, and usually also with some chalk, plaster, or pipe clay, so as to be of a proper consistency for working in the manner of chalks. The principal inconvenience attending them is their lack of adhesion to the paper: the paper must therefore not be too smooth.

For drawings washed in light and shade only, the materials employed are <term>Indian ink</term>, the black liquid of the cuttlefish, or <term>bistre</term>, which is extracted from soot: both of these last produce a browner and richer tint than the Indian ink. ## LECTURE X.

When colors are used, there is less difficulty in producing a uniformity of tint than with watercolors, as each coat of color is applied in sufficient quantity to cover everything beneath it without mixing; thus, it becomes easier to make any required alterations. For watercolors of all descriptions, a certain amount of gum is used, and sometimes a size made of isinglass with a little sugar candy. Body colors contain less gum than other watercolors. Besides paper, wood, silk, and cotton velvet are sometimes used for watercolor drawings.

In miniatures, the most delicate tints are applied in dots with simple watercolors; but for the draperies, body colors are sometimes used. These are commonly executed on ivory.

For painting in distemper, the colors are mixed with a size made by boiling shreds of untanned leather or parchment for several hours; this method is mainly used for coloring walls or paper, but sometimes for painting on cloth. For more delicate purposes, the size may be made with isinglass.

When a wall or ceiling is painted in fresco, the rough coat of the plaster is covered with a coat of fine sand and lime, as far as it can be painted before it dries; the colors are partially absorbed by this coat, and thus become durable. Once they have been applied, no alteration can be made without removing the last coat of plaster, and each part must be completed at once. It is, therefore, always necessary to have a finished drawing to copy; this is usually executed on paper and is called a cartoon. The colors can only be made from earths or metallic oxides; they are prepared as they are for painting in distemper. The only paintings of the ancients that have been preserved were executed in fresco.

The art of oil painting was first discovered by Van Eyck of Bruges toward the end of the 14th century; it has now become almost the only method by which large-scale paintings are produced. The colors are mixed with linseed or nut oil, and sometimes with poppy seed oil, along with a small portion of turpentine oil to help them dry, and the occasional addition of other oily and resinous substances. The work may be executed on wood, cloth, silk, paper, marble, or metals; these substances

The glare of the oil colors, or of the varnish, which is added in order to give them brilliance, is considered an inconvenience attending oil paintings; and some of the colors are too liable to fade or to blacken by the effect of time.

The encaustic paintings of the ancients were imperfect approximations to the art of painting in oil. Wax or resins were employed for retaining the colors in their places; and they were applied by means of a moderate heat. An effect nearly similar is produced by dissolving the resins in spirits of wine, as is done in painting in varnish. A much greater degree of heat is required for paintings in enamel: for this purpose the colors are mixed with a glass of easy fusion, and, when finely powdered, they are usually applied with oil of turpentine, or sometimes oil of lavender, to a ground of metal or porcelain; they are afterwards fixed and vitrified by exposure to the heat of a furnace.

Mosaic work is performed by putting together small pieces of stone, or baked clay, of various colors, so as to imitate the effects of painting: in tapestry, and in embroidery, the same is done by weaving, or working in, threads of different kinds.

The art of writing is very ancient, but it is probably in all countries, and certainly in some, of a later date than that of drawing representations of nature. The Mexicans, at the first arrival of the Spaniards in South America, are said to have employed drawings as a mode of conveying intelligence; some of them simply resembling the objects to which they related, others intended as hieroglyphics; that is, like the ancient Egyptian characters, of a nature intermediate between drawing and writing. The Chinese have always used arbitrary marks to represent whole words, or the names of external objects, not resembling the objects to which they relate, nor composed of letters appropriated to constituent parts of the sound, although they are said to be combined from a few hundred radical characters expressive of the most simple ideas. The art of writing with alphabetical letters must have been sufficiently understood, in the age of Moses, to serve the purpose of the promulgation of laws and of religion: it is generally supposed to have been invented

<header>LECTURE X.</header>

...by the Phoenicians. Among the Greeks, it was in a very imperfect state until the time of the siege of Troy, about 3,000 years ago. The Chinese write from top to bottom, beginning on the right side; other Eastern nations have always written from right to left. The most ancient Greek inscriptions are oriented alternately backward and forward, with the letters being reversed in the lines that begin on the right side; but the Greeks soon restricted themselves to the method that has since been adopted by all European nations, and which appears to be the most natural, at least for writing with a pen and with the right hand.

The earliest methods of writing were probably those that deserve the name of engraving, with the letters being cut into stone, wood, sheets of lead, bark, or leaves. For temporary purposes, they were formed on tablets of wax with a point called a *stylus*, and this practice was long continued for correspondence and was not entirely out of use in the fourteenth century. The *stylus* was made of metal or bone; its upper end was flattened for the purpose of erasing what had been written. According to Varro, Egyptian papyrus was first used for writing at the time of the founding of Alexandria; before then, palm leaves, the inner bark of trees, or sometimes linen cloth had been employed. The export of papyrus was forbidden by Ptolemy, and as a result of this prohibition, skins of parchment or vellum were first used for writing at Pergamus for the library of King Eumenes, which is why they were called *membrana pergamena*. To make the best paper, the widest and finest leaves of the papyrus were matted together, joined by a vegetable glue, and pressed until they became sufficiently smooth; the coarser kinds were not used for writing but for commercial purposes. In China, paper is sometimes made of a thin and almost transparent membrane taken from the bark of a tree. Cotton paper was introduced into Europe from the East in the Middle Ages; it has since been replaced by paper made from linen rags, which is also an Eastern invention. For coarse and strong paper, old hemp ropes are also used, and sometimes many other vegetable substances have been employed. The strength and consistency of paper are due to the lateral adhesion derived from the interlocking of the fibers, assisted by a glutinous size, which is also useful for counteracting the absorbent quality of the paper by filling up its pores.

# ON DRAWING, WRITING, AND MEASURING.

<term>Ivory</term> and prepared <term>ass’s skin</term> <note>specially treated donkey hide</note> are sometimes used for writing with a <term>black lead pencil</term> <note>graphite pencil</note>; for slates, a pencil made of a softer type of slate is used. Ancient mathematicians usually constructed their diagrams in sand to instruct their pupils.

Pens made from <term>goose quills</term>, <term>swan’s quills</term>, or <term>crow quills</term> were known as early as the seventh century. In Europe, they have generally replaced the <term>reeds</term> that were used for writing by the ancients; but in India, <term>reeds</term>, <term>canes</term>, and <term>bamboos</term> are still in use. In China, a <term>hair pencil</term> <note>a small brush</note> is used instead of a pen.

The inks of the ancients are said to have been made of a carbon-based substance, and modern <term>Indian ink</term> owes its blackness to similar materials. Common writing ink consists of <term>iron gallate</term> suspended by means of a little <term>gum</term>; the <term>sulfuric acid</term> that remains mixed with it is probably of no consequence to its blackness. It has been observed that an abundance of <term>gallic acid</term> produces a much blacker color than is obtained when this acid is used in a smaller proportion. Mr. Ribaucourt’s method of making ink is to boil eight ounces of <term>galls</term> and four of <term>logwood</term> in twelve pounds of water until the liquid is reduced by half; and, after straining the decoction, to add to it four ounces of <term>sulfate of iron</term>, one of <term>sulfate of copper</term>, three of <term>gum arabic</term>, and one of <term>sugar candy</term>. But for ordinary purposes, it is enough to soak three ounces of <term>galls</term> for a day or two in a pint of water, and to add to it an ounce of <term>gum arabic</term>, half an ounce of <term>green sulfate of iron</term> (or <term>copperas</term>), and a <term>dram</term> of <term>sulfate of copper</term> (or <term>blue vitriol</term>), or even a much smaller quantity of gum and of copperas if a very fluid ink is required. The <term>sulfate of copper</term> produces a durable stain, but it does not immediately add to the blackness of the ink; its principal use is to counteract the tendency of the ink to become moldy. Sometimes a <term>mercurial salt</term> is used for the same purpose, and a little cotton, if the inkstand is too open, is also useful in preserving the ink; but the addition of <term>spirits</term> <note>alcohol</note> is often insufficient and is liable to make the ink run.

It has been proposed to use inks of different colors for indicating different numbers, so that by using ten kinds of ink applied in different ways, any numbers could be expressed as desired. Thus, in making an index of an author’s words, each page could be easily covered with lines of different colors...

### LECTURE X.

An ingenious instrument has lately been constructed, by means of which copies may be multiplied with great ease; it is called the <term>polygraph</term>, and consists of two or more pens, so connected by frames and springs as to move always in parallel directions, each having its own inkstand and a sheet of paper. In this manner, five copies may be made at once with tolerable ease, and the method may perhaps hereafter be extended to a much greater number.

A mode of writing, perfectly different from any of those which have been mentioned, is performed by means of the <term>telegraph</term> <note>an optical telegraph or semaphore system</note>, which is justly considered the invention of the ingenious Dr. Hooke. The ancients had attempted something similar by the display of torches on elevated locations; but Dr. Hooke observes that the addition of the <term>telescope</term> is absolutely necessary for the practical success of the process. The directions which he gives for its performance differ very little from the plan which has since been generally adopted, first in France, and afterwards, with some variations, in this country <note>Great Britain</note>. Dr. Hooke proposed the employment of alphabetical and other arbitrary characters; at present, it is usual to have six boards, each turning on its axis so as to appear or disappear at pleasure: these admit of sixty-four combinations, which are sufficient for every purpose that can be required, in addition to indicating the letters of the alphabet. (Plate VI. Fig. 80, 81.)

Pens for drawing lines and figures sometimes differ from those used for writing; they are made of two plates of steel inclined toward each other and adjusted by a screw; or sometimes of a plate of tin folded up so as to include a receptacle for the ink; or of a glass tube drawn to a very fine point and still remaining perforated. In all these pens, as well as in common pens, the ink is retained by its cohesion and by the <term>capillary attraction</term> of the pen; and it attaches itself to the paper by the operation of similar forces.

It is by no means easy to comply strictly with that postulate of geometry which requires us to draw a straight line from one point to another. # ON DRAWING, WRITING, AND MEASURING.

We judge the straightness of a line by the well-known property of light, which moves only in straight lines; thus, if we look along the edge of a ruler, we easily discover its irregularities. This can be done with even greater accuracy if we look through a small hole made with a pin in a card. Rulers made of silver, brass, or ivory have a significant advantage over those made of wood, as they are not liable to be ruined by warping. A pen filled with ink cannot be placed close to the edge of a ruler without difficulty; therefore, for diagrams requiring great accuracy, it is best to draw the lines first with a steel point or a very hard graphite pencil, finishing them with ink if necessary. The paper should also be fixed to a drawing board; for very delicate work, plates of lead or copper may be used instead of paper. The carpenter’s chalk line is a useful tool that takes the place of a very long ruler; it becomes straight when stretched because a straight line is the shortest distance between any two points.

To draw a circle of a specific radius, we use <term>compasses</term>, usually with one metal point and the other of various types. Compasses are sometimes made with a spring instead of a joint and are opened or closed by a screw. Sometimes a graduated arc is fixed to one leg and passes through the other; when great accuracy is required, <term>hair compasses</term> may be used, which have a spring joint in one of the legs that can be slightly adjusted with a fine screw. <term>Beam compasses</term> are useful for drawing circles with larger radii; they also have the advantage of being steadier than common compasses and easily allow for the attachment of a graduated scale to indicate the measurement of the radius of the circle being drawn. Sometimes, to draw portions of very large circles, two wheels with slightly different diameters are fixed onto a common axis; this causes them to revolve around a point that is further or closer depending on how far apart the wheels are set on the axis, with the wheels tracing circles on the paper. Alternatively, two rulers joined to form an angle can be made to slide against two points or edges projecting from a third ruler, so that the vertex of the angle always stays within the arc of a circle. For drawing a line perpendicular to another, we often use a square; and if we use a rectangular drawing board, there is an added convenience in making the square slide along its edge. Rulers of various types are also commonly made rectangular so they can occasionally serve the same purpose.

Triangular compasses are sometimes used to lay down a triangle equal to a given triangle; by repeating this process, any figure that can be divided into triangles may be copied without having to intersect arcs. However, the same result is more commonly achieved by pricking off the figure with a steel point. (Plate VI. Fig. 86.)

Various properties of parallel lines are used in constructing parallel rulers. A parallelogram with jointed angles is the most common type; two equal rulers are joined by equal crossbars placed at an angle and turning on pins fixed in the rulers. The instrument is much improved by adding a third ruler, joined to the second in a similar way, because the angle of one of the two movements can then be made to correct the other. A simple cylinder, or a round ruler, serves the purpose in a rough way, and two small rollers fixed on the same axis are also sometimes attached to a flat ruler, causing it to move so that it always stays in parallel positions. A very useful instrument for drawing parallel lines at any given distance is now generally known by the name <term>Marquois's scales</term>, although it is by no means a recent invention; by sliding a triangle along a graduated ruler, one can read the divisions on an enlarged scale with great accuracy. However, where the distances between lines are large, the angle of this motion is a significant inconvenience. The pantograph is used for copying figures while simultaneously reducing or enlarging them. It consists of four rulers: two of them are joined at their ends and connected at their midpoints to the other two, which are only half as long. These are also joined together to form a jointed parallelogram with the others, with two of the sides extending beyond the angles. If holes are made in these and in one of the shorter rulers, positioned so that they lie in the same straight line in any position of the instrument, they will remain in a straight line in any other position and will always divide this line in the same proportion. Thus, if one of the holes is placed on a fixed axis or pin, a tracing point is inserted in another, and a pencil is placed in the third, any figure drawn by the pencil will be similar to the one traced by the point. Instead of holes in the rulers, they may be equipped with sliding sockets to hold the axis, the point, and the pencil. (Plate VI. Fig. 89.)

Proportional compasses are also very useful for reducing lines and figures to a different scale. This instrument consists of two legs, pointed at each end and rotating on a center pivot that slides in a groove shared by both legs and is equipped with an index. The divisions of the scale are arranged so that the center may divide the length of the legs from point to point in a specific proportion. Sometimes a screw is added to adjust the center with greater precision; it is common to include scales for dividing the circumference of a circle into a specific number of parts, among other purposes. The use of the <term>sector</term> depends also on the properties of <term>similar triangles</term>. The scale of equal parts, which is laid down on each leg, beginning from the center, serves to determine the length of the legs of two <term>equilateral triangles</term>, in any required proportion to each other, according to the division which we mark, and the transverse distances from the corresponding points are necessarily in the same proportion. Thus, if we have any line in a figure which we wish to call three feet, or three inches, we may take the interval with a pair of common compasses, and open the sector to such an angle that it may extend from the third division of one leg to that of the other; then all the other divisions of the scale will furnish us with the lengths corresponding to any distances that we may wish to lay down. The other scales usually engraved on the sector are principally intended for trigonometrical calculations on similar principles. (Plate VII. Fig. 91.)

<margin>#</margin>
The magnitude of angles admits an easy determination and description, by the comparison of the respective arcs with a circle, or with a right angle. We may divide an angle geometrically, by continual <term>bisection</term>, into parts as small as may be required, and by numbering these parts, we may define any angle with an error smaller than any assignable quantity. Bisections of this kind are sometimes actually employed in the construction of instruments; for instance, in one of the arcs of the <term>mural quadrant</term> of the observatory at Greenwich, the right angle is divided into 96 parts, by the continual bisection of one-sixth of the circle. There are also some practical methods of dividing angles into three or more equal parts, which are sufficiently accurate for many purposes, although it is well known that in theory the perfect <term>trisection</term> of an angle is beyond the reach of <term>plain geometry</term>. This trisection is necessary in the common division of the circle into 360 degrees, a number which was probably chosen because it admits a great variety of divisors, and because it nearly represents the diurnal and annual motion of the sun among the stars. The circle being divided into 6 parts, the chord of each of which is equal to the radius, these parts are divided into 60 degrees, each degree into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds: further than this we can—

Whole circles, or <term>theodolites</term>, divided into degrees and their parts, <term>quadrants</term> and <term>sextants</term>, are usually employed in measuring angles; and <term>protractors</term>, semicircles, and lines of chords, in laying them off. The most convenient of <term>quadrants</term> for general use is <term>Hadley’s reflecting instrument</term>, which is in fact an <term>octant</term> or a <term>sextant</term>, but in which, for reasons depending on optical principles, each degree of the arc is counted as two.

For the graduation of all instruments of this kind, of moderate dimensions, Mr. <term>Ramsden’s dividing engine</term> is of great utility; the instrument being fixed on the revolving plate of the engine, its arc is made to advance under the cutting tool by very small steps, regulated by the turns of a screw, of which each revolution is divided into a considerable number of equal parts. The largest and finest instruments are, however, still usually divided by hand, that is, by means of compasses. Some artists have first divided a straight plate, and then made a hoop of it, which has served as a standard for further processes. An arc of 7° 10’, of which the chord is one eighth of the radius, may be employed as a test of the accuracy of the work. A <term>micrometer screw</term> is often used in large instruments as a substitute for the smallest divisions; a movable part of the index being brought to coincide with the nearest point marked in the arc, by turning the screw through a part of its revolution, which is measured by means of a graduated circle. But a simpler method of reading off divisions with accuracy in common instruments is the application of a <term>vernier</term>, an apparatus so called from its inventor. The space occupied by eleven divisions of the scale being divided into ten parts on the index, the coincidence of any of the divisions of the index with those of the scale shows, by its distance from the end, the number of tenths that are to be added to that of the entire divisions.
