# LECTURE X.

...above the horizon; at sea, the apparent horizon, formed by the surface of the water, provides the most convenient measurement. However, since the spectator is somewhat elevated above the curved surface of the sea, the apparent horizon is necessarily lower than the true horizon, and a correction is therefore required according to the height. In the open sea, this correction may be determined by measuring the whole angle above and below the apparent horizon, and taking one-fourth of the difference for the <term>dip</term> or depression. On shore, a <term>plumb line</term> is the simplest instrument for determining the position of the horizon, and its accidental vibrations may be prevented by suspending the weight in water or in oil. For small instruments, a spirit level—the operation of which depends on hydrostatic principles—is capable of greater precision than a plumb line. When well made, it easily indicates an error of a single second, but it requires some attention to avoid temperature fluctuations, which would tend to distort its shape. Well-purified ether is found, because of its perfect fluidity, to be the best liquid for a spirit level. An <term>artificial horizon</term> is a reflecting surface used to obtain an image as far below the horizon as the object is above it, and for measuring the angular distance of this image from the object. Sometimes a flat mirror (<term>speculum</term>) of glass or metal is used for this purpose, after being previously adjusted by a spirit level; at other times, the surface of mercury, molasses, or tar is used, protected from the wind by a vessel with holes in it or by a glass cover, which is either separate or simply floating on the mercury when that liquid is employed.

It is in many cases simpler and more convenient to estimate angles not by the arcs spanning them, but by their <term>sines</term>, or the perpendicular lines dropped from one side to the other. Thus, it is common among miners to say that the ground rises or falls one foot, or one yard, in ten, when the sine of the angle of its inclination to the horizon is one-tenth of the radius. Angles of different sizes are indeed proportional to the arcs and not to the sines, so in this sense the sine is not a true measure of the comparative size of the angle; however, in making calculations, we are more often required to use the <term>sine</term> or <term>cosine</term> of an angle than the angle or arc itself. It is, however, easy to convert one of these values to the others by means of either trigonometric tables or the scales engraved on the <term>sector</term>.

The same purpose is served by <term>Gunter’s scale</term>, by the <term>sliding rule</term>, and by the <term>logarithmic circles</term> of Clairaut and of Nicholson, which are employed mechanically in the same manner as a table of logarithms is used arithmetically; the proportion of any two numbers to each other is determined by the distance of the corresponding divisions on the scale. Thus, if we wish to double or to halve a number, we have only to find the distance from 1 to 2 and lay it off from the given number in either direction. (Plate VII. Fig. 93, 94.)

The measurement of angles is directly applied to the estimation of distances in the <term>dendrometer</term> or <term>engymeter</term>. A part of the instrument forms a base of known dimensions, and since the angle at each extremity of this base is measured with great accuracy, the distance of the object may be inferred from an easy calculation or from a table. The most complete instruments of this kind have two speculums for measuring the difference of the angles at once, in the manner of <term>Hadley’s quadrant</term>. <term>Telescopic scales</term> or <term>micrometers</term> are also sometimes used for measuring angles subtended by distant objects whose magnitude is known or may be estimated—for example, by the height of a rank of soldiers—and inferring immediately the distance at which they stand.

Arithmetical and even <term>algebraical machines</term>, of a much more complicated nature, have been invented and constructed with great labor and ingenuity; but they are to be considered as mathematical toys rather than as instruments capable of any useful application.

An angle, once measured, can be verbally and numerically described by reference to the whole circle as a unit. However, for the identification of the measure of a straight line, we have no natural unit of this kind, and it is therefore necessary to establish some arbitrary standard with which any given lengths and surfaces may be compared. It might be advantageous in communication between different countries to fix one single standard to be employed throughout the world, but this does not appear to be practically possible, even if it were determined what that standard ought to be. “The observation of the <term>isochronism</term> of the small vibrations of a pendulum, and the ease and certainty with which the length of a <term>pendulum</term> vibrating seconds...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the need for universal standards of measurement, specifically referencing Pierre-Simon Laplace's advocacy for a system based on natural constants and decimal division.</meta>

<header>LECTURE X.</header>

...may be determined, have suggested," says Mr. Laplace, in his account of the system of the world, "the idea of using this length as a universal measure. We cannot reflect on the massive number of measures in use—not only among different nations but even within the same country—their arbitrary and inconvenient divisions, the difficulty of determining and comparing them, and the embarrassment and frauds they cause in commerce, without considering the adoption of a system of measures to be one of the greatest benefits that scientific improvements and civil government ordinances can provide to humanity. Such a system, with uniform divisions, could be easily used in calculations and derived in the least arbitrary way from a fundamental magnitude indicated by nature itself. A nation that would introduce such a system of measures would combine the advantage of reaping the first fruits of the improvement with the pleasure of seeing its example followed by other countries, to which it would thus become a benefactor. For the slow but irresistible rule of reason must eventually prevail over national jealousies and all other obstacles opposed to a measure whose convenience is universally felt. Such were the motives that led the Constituent Assembly to entrust the Academy of Sciences with this important task. The new system of weights and measures is the result of the Committee's labors, supported by the zeal and knowledge of several members of the national representation.

"The fact that the calculation of decimal fractions is identical to that of whole numbers leaves no doubt regarding the advantage of dividing all kinds of measures into decimal parts. To be convinced of this, one only needs to compare the difficulty of compound multiplication and division with the ease of the same operations when only whole numbers are involved—an ease that becomes even greater through the use of logarithms, which may also be made extremely popular by using simple and cheap instruments. The decimal division was therefore adopted without hesitation; and in order to preserve the uniformity of the whole system, it was decided to derive everything from the same linear measure and its decimal divisions. The question was then reduced to the choice of this universal measure, which was to be called the metre."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of scientific standards for measurement, specifically comparing the use of a pendulum versus the Earth's meridian to define a universal unit of length.</meta>

# ON DRAWING, WRITING, AND MEASURING.

The length of the pendulum and that of a meridian of the earth are the two principal standards that nature provides us for fixing the unit of linear measures. Because both of these are independent of social and political revolutions, they cannot undergo a noticeable alteration without very great changes in the physical makeup of the earth. The first method, which is easy to carry out, has the disadvantage of making the measure of length depend on two elements that are unrelated to it and to each other: gravitation and time; furthermore, the division of time into small portions is entirely arbitrary. It was decided, therefore, to employ the second method, which," says Mr. Laplace, "appears to be of very high antiquity; it is so natural for man to relate measures of distance to the dimensions of the globe which he inhabits, so that, in traveling from place to place, he may know, simply by the naming of the distance traveled, the relationship of this space to the entire circumference of the earth. This method also has the advantage of making nautical measures correspond immediately with celestial ones. The navigator often has occasion to compare the distance he has traveled with the arc of the heavens corresponding to that distance; it is therefore important that these measures should be easily obtained from each other, by changing only the placement of the units. But, for this purpose, the fundamental unit of linear measures must be an <term>aliquot</term> <note>a part of a number that divides the total exactly without a remainder</note> part of the terrestrial meridian, which must correspond to one of the divisions of the circumference of a circle. Thus, the choice of the metre was reduced to that of the unit of angular measure, and the right angle, as it constitutes the limit of the inclination of two lines to each other, was considered entitled to the preference.

> "The arc which was measured in 1740, from Dunkirk to the Pyrenees, might have served for finding the magnitude of the quadrant of the meridian; but a new and more accurate measurement of a larger arc was more likely to excite interest in favor of the new measures. Delambre and Méchain were therefore entrusted with the direction of the operations for measuring an arc from Dunkirk to Barcelona, and after making a proper correction for the <term>ellipticity</term> <note>the degree to which the Earth's shape deviates from a perfect sphere</note> of the earth, according to the measurement of the arc in Peru, the quadrant was determined to be equal to 5,130,740 of the iron <term>toise</term> <note>an old French unit of length equal to approximately 6.39 feet or 1.949 meters</note> used at the equator, its temperature being 61 ¼° of Fahrenheit: the ten-millionth part

# LECTURE X.

...of this quadrant was taken as the unit, or metre. A standard was placed in the custody of the legislative body, adjusted at the temperature of melting ice. In order to be able to always identify this length without returning to an actual measurement of the arc, it was important to compare it very accurately with the length of a pendulum swinging at the rate of one second; this has been done with great care by Borda at the Paris Observatory. The unit for measuring land is the "are," or 100 square metres. A cubic metre of wood is called a "stere," and a cubic decimetre (a cube with sides of one-tenth of a metre) is a "litre," or the measure for fluids.

> “Uniformity seemed to require that the day should be divided into ten hours, the hour into a hundred minutes, and the minute into a hundred seconds. This division, as useful as it will be to astronomers, is of less advantage in civil life, where arithmetical operations are seldom performed on parts of time; and the difficulty of adapting it to clocks and watches, together with our commercial relations with foreign countries, has suspended its introduction for the present. We may, however, expect that it will ultimately be brought into general use.”

Such is Mr. Laplace’s account of the new system of measures, the result of the collaborative work of many of the most capable mathematicians on the continent. There is not at present any great probability that it will ever be employed in this country. It is of little consequence from what source the original unit was derived, unless we can with ease and accuracy refer back to its origin; and whether a standard was first adjusted according to the circumference of the globe or to the foot of an individual hero, the ease of comparing other measures with it remains the same. It is admitted that the pendulum provides the readiest method of recovering the standard if it is lost; and if it was necessary for the Committee of the French Academy to determine an entirely new unit, it would perhaps have been preferable to fix on one that was independent of any further comparison, rather than to seek an ideal perfection by attempting to copy from a more grand original—to say nothing of the uncertainty regarding the ellipticity of the earth and the probable irregularity of its form in various respects. On the other hand, it must be allowed that the correct determination of the length of the pendulum has sometimes

# ON DRAWING, WRITING, AND MEASURING.

...has been found more difficult than Mr. Laplace’s statement would lead us to suppose, and we cannot depend on any measurement of it as being totally exempt from an error of one ten-thousandth part of the whole.

The <term>metre</term>, as definitively established by the government of France, is equal to 39.371 English inches, measured (as has been usual in this country) on a standard scale of brass at a temperature of 62° Fahrenheit; while the French, on the contrary, reduce the length of their measures to the length they would have at the freezing point. Hence, ten thousand inches are nearly 254 metres, and a thousand feet are 305 metres. The length of a <term>pendulum</term> vibrating seconds in London was found by George Graham—from an average of several experiments, all agreeing very closely—to be 39.13 inches. This is also nearly an average between the length that may be deduced, with proper corrections, from Borda’s experiments in Paris and Mr. Whitehurst’s experiments made in London with the apparatus invented by Mr. Hatton, where the length determined is the difference between the lengths of two pendulums vibrating at different times. Mr. Whitehurst’s measurements, however, require some corrections, which Mr. Nicholson has pointed out. The fall of a heavy body in the first second appears, from this determination of the length of the pendulum, to be sixteen feet, one inch, and one-tenth.

Of the old French measure, 15 inches made nearly 16 English inches, and 76 were, very exactly, 81; the <term>toise</term> was 76.736 inches. In Germany, the <term>Rhineland foot</term> is generally used; 100 of these feet make 103 English feet.

A wine gallon contains 231 cubic inches; an ale gallon is the capacity of 10 yards of a pipe with a one-inch diameter.

A variety of instruments are used for the direct comparison of the standard measure, or its parts, with other lengths or distances. Such are scales (simple and diagonal), <term>verniers</term>, <term>micrometer screws</term>, <term>beam compasses</term>, rods, lines, chains, and measuring wheels. It has generally been supposed that the greatest accuracy in measuring large distances is obtained by means of rods made of glass or of platinum, which are less susceptible to the changes produced by variations in temperature; General Roy, however, found that a steel chain was as little liable to error as any method he could em—

### LECTURE X.

...employ; and those who have continued the extensive survey which he began even prefer it to every other. For the comparison of standards and for determining small distances with great precision, beam compasses—or scales with sliding indices equipped with microscopes and crosshairs—have been constructed by the instrument makers of this country. In France, a lever has sometimes been introduced; its longer arm has a wide range of motion, corresponding to a very minute difference in the length of the substance acting on the shorter arm.

But for common purposes, the diagonal scale is sufficiently accurate and may be applied without an error exceeding one-thousandth of an inch. In cases where a very delicate <term>vernier</term> or a <term>micrometer screw</term> is used, a magnifier is usually required. Mr. Coventry has, however, succeeded in making simple scales that are accurate enough to measure one ten-thousandth of an inch. He draws parallel lines on glass at this distance, which are in some parts sufficiently regular, although they can only be seen with the help of a powerful microscope; but those which are at the distance of one five-thousandth of an inch are much more accurate and distinct. For dividing rectilinear scales of all kinds, Mr. Ramsden constructed a machine that operates by the turns of a screw; others have used an apparatus resembling Marquois's parallel rulers (Plate VII. Fig. 95 to 97).

The motion of a ship at sea is measured by a <term>log line</term>—a rope divided by knots into equal parts and attached to a <term>log</term>—which is kept nearly at rest by the resistance of the water. Attempts have also been made to cause a small waterwheel to turn by the motion of the ship, in order to measure both the speed and the distance traveled. An instrument has also been invented for doing the same based on hydraulic principles; it raises water in a gauge to different heights using the pressure caused by the relative motion of the ship and the water, while simultaneously discharging a small stream into a reservoir at a velocity proportional to that of the ship.

# LECTURE XI.

## ON MODELLING, PERSPECTIVE, ENGRAVING, AND PRINTING.

We have examined the principal instruments and materials used for drawing and for measuring; we are now to consider, first, the methods of copying solids and of projecting their images on a plane surface; and secondly, the arts of preserving the works of the pen and of the pencil through engraving and printing.

When it is required to make a copy of a solid of an irregular form—as, for example, a statue—we must determine the position of a sufficient number of points to guide us in our work with accuracy. This is done by means of an instrument capable of being fixed in any required position, so that the end of a sliding bar, or pin, may be in contact with each point in the original, and then removed to a similar part of another frame on which the copy is placed; a hole is made, by degrees, in the block, so as to allow the pin to reach its proper place, where it stops. (Plate VII. Fig. 98.)

The model of a statue is generally first made of clay, and a cast of this is taken immediately in plaster of Paris, since the clay would crack and change its shape in drying. This mode of copying, by means of plaster, is exceedingly useful in various departments of the mechanical arts: the original is well oiled and placed in a suitable vessel; a mixture of prepared plaster and water, with the consistency of cream, is then poured on it; this in a short time hardens and is divided into several parts in such a manner as not to damage the original figure during its removal. These pieces, being joined together again, form a mold for the final cast. Sometimes a small figure is first modeled in a mixture of wax, turpentine, and oil; and a mold being formed on this,

the final cast is made either of plaster, or of a composition of wax with white lead and a little oil, which serves as an imitation of marble.

We have, however, much less frequent occasion to make an exact copy of a solid object of any kind than to represent its appearance by means of perspective drawing. Assuming we are provided with the proper materials for drawing, we can easily imitate—with the help of a correct eye and a well-practiced hand—the shapes and relative positions of objects actually before us by sketching them in the same form as they would appear to be projected on a transparent surface placed before the eye. Considering the simplicity of this process, it is almost surprising that the theory of perspective should have been thought to require such serious study, and that significant errors should have been committed regarding it by men whose general talents in other areas of painting are by no means insignificant. But it must be admitted that when, instead of imitating objects directly before us, the pencil is used to embody imaginary forms—intended for either beauty or utility—a great degree of care and attention may be necessary to produce a true representation of objects that are either absent or do not exist. In these cases, memory and imagination alone will rarely be sufficient without resorting to mathematical principles. To architects, therefore, and to mechanics in general, a knowledge of perspective is almost indispensable whenever they wish to convey, through a drawing, an accurate idea of their planned projects.

If any assistance is required for the drawing of an object actually before us, it may easily be obtained mechanically by means of a frame with cross-threads or wires placed between the eye and the object. The eye is applied to an opening, which must be fixed in position to preserve the proportions of the picture; and this opening must be small so that the threads and the more distant objects may be viewed at the same time with enough clarity. With the paper being marked with corresponding lines, we may observe in what section of the frame any noticeable point of the object appears, and may then represent its image by a point similarly situated among the lines drawn on our paper; and having obtained, in this manner, a sufficient number of points, we may complete the figures by adding

Sometimes, for the outlining of large objects requiring close inspection, it has been found useful to employ two similar frames, one slightly smaller than the other, and placed at a certain distance from it, so that every part of the object, when seen through the corresponding divisions of both frames, appears in the same manner as if the eye were located at a very distant point. The elegant anatomical figures of Albinus were created in this way. (Plate VII. Fig. 99.)

But if it is required to lay down, on the plane of a picture, the projection of an object whose actual dimensions and position are known, we may obtain the required measurements from the properties of <term>similar triangles</term>, and the consideration of the <term>rectilinear motion of light</term>. We may consider our picture as a reduced copy of a projection formed on an imaginary plane, which, like the picture, is generally supposed to be in a vertical position, and which stands on the horizontal plane at the point where the objects to be represented begin. In order to find the position of the image of a given straight line, we must determine the point in which a line parallel to it, passing through the position of the eye, intersects the plane of the picture; this is called the <term>vanishing point</term> of the given line, and of all other lines parallel to it, since the image of any such line, continued infinitely, will be a straight line directed toward this point, but never passing it. When the lines to be represented are parallel to the picture, the distance of their vanishing point becomes infinite, and their images are also parallel to the lines and to each other. The <term>centre of the picture</term>, or that point which is nearest to the eye, is the vanishing point of all lines perpendicular to the picture; through this point it is usual to draw a horizontal and a vertical line: we may then mark downwards on the vertical line the distance of the eye from the picture, in order to find the <term>point of distance</term>, which serves to determine the position of any oblique lines on a horizontal plane: for if we draw a ground plan of any object, considering the picture as a horizontal surface, we may find the vanishing point of each of its lines by drawing a line parallel to it through the point of distance, until it meets the horizontal vanishing line. (Plate VII. Fig. 100, 101.)

When it is required to determine a point in a line parallel to the picture, we may imagine a line drawn through it perpendicular to the picture; by finding the image of this line, we may intersect the former image at the point required. It is in this way that the height of any number of columns or figures at different distances may be easily determined. (Plate VIII. Fig. 103.)

The projection of <term>curvilinear figures</term> is most conveniently achieved by drawing parallel lines across them to form small squares or rectangles, putting these divisions into perspective, and tracing a curve through the corresponding points. There are also methods of determining mathematically, or of drawing mechanically, the <term>ellipse</term> which results from the projection of a circle in a given position, but they are considerably intricate, and a steady hand is seldom in need of them. (Plate VIII. Fig. 104.)

This system of perspective must necessarily be employed when we wish to represent objects which appear to us under angles of considerable magnitude, and to give them as much as possible the appearance of an imitation of nature. But for almost all purposes of science and of mechanical practice, the most convenient representation is the <term>orthographical projection</term>, where the distance of the eye from the plane is supposed to be increased without limit, and the rays of light passing to the eye are parallel to each other. In order to represent any object in this manner, we must assume one line for the direction of the center of the picture, to which the images of all lines perpendicular to the plane of projection must be parallel, and another for that of the point of distance, by means of which we may measure the first lines as if that point were actually within reach; and in this manner, we may determine the place of any number of points of the object to be delineated. (Plate VIII. Fig. 105.)

If we wish to apply the mechanical method of drawing by the assistance of a frame to this mode of representation, instead of a fixed opening for an eyepiece, or a second frame of smaller dimensions, we must use a second frame of the same size as the first, in the manner that has already been described. Professor Camper has criticized Albinus for not adopting this method in his figures: but subjects as large as those he represented would have looked less natural if they had been projected orthographically; nor would such projections have been significantly more instructive.

It frequently happens that in geographical and astronomical drawings, we need to represent the whole or part of a spherical surface on a flat plane. Here, if we use the <term>orthographical projection</term>, the distortion will be such that the parts near the apparent circumference will be so contracted that it becomes impossible to show them clearly. It is, therefore, more convenient in this case to use the <term>stereographical projection</term>, where the eye is assumed to be at a moderate distance from the object. The position of the eye may be placed either inside or outside the sphere as desired; and depending on the size of the portion we wish to represent, the point from which the sphere may be viewed with the least distortion can be determined by calculation. But in these cases, all circles situated obliquely on the sphere must be represented by ellipses. However, there is one point where the eye can be placed that has the unique and important advantage that the image of every circle, whether large or small, remains a circle. This point is on the surface itself, at the end of the diameter perpendicular to the plane of projection. This is the point usually employed in the stereographical projection of the sphere, which is used for the geometrical construction of problems in <term>spherical trigonometry</term>. The projection of the entire surface of the sphere would occupy an infinite space, but within the limits of the hemisphere, the maximum distortion of linear measurement is only in a ratio of 2 to 1—each degree at the circumference of the figure occupying twice as much space as at the center. The angles that the circles form when crossing each other are also correctly represented. (Plate VIII. Fig. 106.)

The arts of writing and drawing, in all their varieties, are expanded in their practice and preserved in their duration by means of engraving and printing. If there is any single circumstance to which we can particularly attribute the more rapid progress of general civilization in modern times compared to ancient times, it is the ease of multiplying copies of literary works of all kinds with the help of these arts. The defining characteristic of printing consists in the use of movable types; the art of engraving is simpler and, in some of its forms, more ancient. The Romans were in the habit of using seals and stamps for marking letters and words on wax and pottery; it was common in the Middle Ages to use perforated metal plates as patterns for guiding a brush, by which capital letters were inserted in some manuscripts; and the Chinese are said to have long possessed the art of printing books from wooden blocks. It was in this form that printing was first introduced into Europe at the beginning of the fifteenth century. There seems to have formerly been a method of engraving on wood with greater ease and accuracy than is now practiced; the hatching in old woodcuts can be seen to cross each other more frequently and with greater freedom than in modern works, although some have conjectured, with a high degree of probability, that these old engravings were actually etched in relief on metal. The art of wood engraving is, however, currently at a high level of perfection in this country, and blocks are still frequently used for mathematical diagrams and other simple figures; for although they are somewhat more expensive than copper plates, they last much longer, and they have the advantage of being printed at the same time as the letterpress and of being included on the same page as the text to which they belong, since the ink is applied only to the raised parts of both these cuts and the common printing types.

The drawing, if it is not executed in <term>black lead</term> <note>graphite</note>, is generally prepared by passing a pencil over its principal features, and the outline is transferred to the plate—which has a thin coat of white wax laid on it—by placing the drawing on it and rubbing it with a <term>burnisher</term>. Sometimes a drawing in <term>Indian ink</term>, especially if freed from some of its gum, may be transferred in this manner without using a pencil. When written characters are to be engraved, the plate is laid on a cushion so as to be easily turned under the <term>graver</term> <note>a sharp tool for cutting metal</note>, which is a great convenience when forming curved lines.

In laying on even shades over a large area, much labor is saved by using a <term>ruling machine</term>, which enables us to draw lines, at any required distance, very accurately parallel, and either straight or following each other’s gentle waves, in order to avoid a stiff appearance. This machine, like the <term>dividing engine</term>, is sometimes adjusted by the turns of a screw, and sometimes by the diagonal motion of a triangular slider. Besides the <term>cutting graver</term>, which has a prism-like form ending in a slanted surface, other instruments are occasionally employed; the <term>dry needle</term> <note>drypoint needle</note> makes a very fine line and leaves the metal that it has displaced to be rubbed off by another tool. Sometimes a number of separate pits are formed by a pointed instrument, and the raised parts are afterwards removed; this is called <term>stippling</term>. A <term>burnisher</term> and some charcoal are required for erasing the strokes of the graver when necessary and for polishing the surface. It is seldom, however, that a plate is begun and completed by dry engraving alone.

For engraving in <term>mezzotinto</term> <note>mezzotint</note>, the plate is roughened by scraping it in every direction with a tool made for that purpose, so that an impression from it in this state would be entirely dark; the highlights are then inserted by removing the roughness of the surface in specific parts using a smooth <term>scraper</term> and a <term>burnisher</term>. As the plate wears down during printing, some of these parts are liable to have the grain raised slightly again, so that the highlights are less clear in the later impressions than in the proofs. It is well known that in common engravings, the proofs are usually the darkest throughout.

When the drawing is traced with a wooden point, the chalk adheres to the varnish in the form of the outline. Alternatively, if it is required that the final impression faces the same way as the drawing, an intermediate outline must be made in the same manner on a separate paper and then transferred to the plate. All the outlines marked this way are traced with needles, which create furrows in the varnish and leave the copper bare; the shades are inserted with the assistance of the <term>ruling machine</term> wherever parallel lines can be used. The plate, once prepared and fitted with a raised border of a suitable consistency, is subjected to the action of diluted <term>nitric acid</term> until all the parts are sufficiently corroded. Care is taken during this time to sweep off air bubbles as they collect and to "stop out"—or cover with new varnish—the lighter parts, which are completed first. When the varnish is removed, finishing touches are added with the <term>graver</term>. If the plate requires further corrosion, the varnish can sometimes be reapplied without filling the lines by applying it with a ball or cushion, taking care to avoid any slanted motion. It is said that the acid sometimes works so as to undermine the metal on each side, making the furrows wider as they become deeper; for this reason, in etchings as well as in <term>mezzotintos</term>, the later impressions are sometimes darker than the proofs, but this is by no means always true. It is well known to chemists that glass can be corroded in a similar manner by means of <term>fluoric acid</term> <note>hydrofluoric acid</note>.

An etching can also be quickly executed by using a varnish mixed with mutton fat and drawing upon a paper laid on the plate; the varnish then adheres to the back of the paper under the lines that are drawn and is immediately removed when the paper is taken off, without the use of needles. Sometimes only the outlines are etched, and the plate is finished in <term>mezzotinto</term>.

At times it is varnished with a spirituous solution of resin, which cracks throughout while drying; and if a strong line is required anywhere, it may be traced with a mixture of whiting and some adhesive substance before the varnish is applied. This method of engraving works very well in imitating the effect of drawings, but the plates are soon worn out. In order to judge the state of the work, an impression of any part of the plate may be taken by pouring a little plaster of Paris mixed with water onto it.

Musical characters are usually stamped with punches; in this country, on plates of pewter, but in France generally on copper. Mr. Rochon has invented a machine for stamping letters on copper instead of printing, but the method does not appear to have been used in practice.

Regardless of how the plate may have been engraved, when an impression is to be taken from it, it is covered with printing ink of the finest kind using stuffed balls and then wiped, mainly by hand, so that the ink is completely removed from the polished surface. It is then placed, along with the moistened paper, on a board between flannels and strongly pressed while passing between two wooden rollers. Through frequent use, the plate loses its sharpness and sometimes needs to be retouched; this is the reason for the greater value of first impressions; however, with proper precautions in cleaning the plate, its delicacy may be preserved for a long time.

An impression, while it is moist, may be reversed by passing it through the press with another sheet of paper. And by writing with a special ink, even common letters may be copied this way onto thin paper, and the impression will be legible on the opposite side. Mr. Montbret proposes putting some sugar candy into the ink and taking a copy on unsized paper using a hot iron.

<page-num>122</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XI.</header>

...nature, somewhat like a stone marl. When the drawing is finished, the stone is moistened and absorbs so much water that the printing ink will not stick to it, except in the parts where the crayon or the ink has been applied; and in this manner an impression is obtained, which has much of the freedom and spirit of an original drawing. When the ink is used, a little acid is afterwards applied to the stone in order to corrode its intermediate parts; and the bold style of the impression much resembles that of the old woodcuts.

The art of printing with separate types was invented soon after the introduction of wooden blocks into Europe. The improvement was great and important. The year 1443 or 1444 is considered the date of the oldest printed book; but the precise time and place of the invention remain somewhat doubtful; the art, however, advanced toward perfection with very rapid steps. The letters are first cut, in a reversed form, on steel punches; with these, a copper matrix is stamped, and the matrix forms the lower part of the mold in which the types are cast. The metal is a composition of lead and antimony, which is easily melted. Thus, the printed sheet is the fourth form of the letter, counting from the original engraving on the punch; in stereotype printing—recently invented, or rather improved and revived—it is the sixth. In this method, when a form for the side of a sheet has been composed, arranged, corrected, and locked by wedges in the chase, or iron frame which contains it, a mold of the whole is made in fine plaster, and as many repetitions of it may be cast very thin in type metal as will serve to print for the use of a century, without the expense of keeping a large quantity of types set up, or of providing paper for a large print run all at once.

The methods of arranging the types in boxes or cases, of setting the separate lines on the stick, and building them up by degrees into pages and forms, of correcting the proofs, of applying the ink, and taking the impression, are entirely designed for the simplicity and convenience of the manual operations involved, and require little or no detailed explanation.

# LECTURE XII.

## ON STATICS.

The examination of the magnitude of various forces used in practical mechanics constitutes the doctrine of statics. In a strict sense, the term statics implies only the determination of weights; however, it may appropriately be extended to the estimation of all kinds of forces—especially active forces—that can be compared to weights, just as the term hydrostatics encompasses everything relating to the equilibrium of fluids. The measurement of the passive strength of materials used, the changes produced in them by the forces they resist, and the laws governing the negative force of friction are also subjects that serve as an immediate introduction to the specific construction and use of machinery, and are closely connected to the field of statics.

The art of weighing is particularly important because it provides us with the only practical method of determining the quantity of matter in a given body. We could, in fact, cause two bodies to collide with known velocities and, from the effects of that collision, determine their relative momenta and the proportion of their masses; however, it is obvious that this process would be extremely difficult and incapable of great accuracy. Therefore, we rely on the well-known law of gravitation—that the weight of every body is proportional to the quantity of matter it contains—and we judge its mass by its weight. If all bodies were of equal density, we could determine their masses from their external dimensions; however, we rarely find even a single body of uniform density throughout. Even if we had such a body, it would generally be much easier to weigh it accurately than to measure it.

The weight of a body is commonly determined by comparing it directly

...with other weights of known dimensions; however, sometimes the flexing of a spring is employed for the comparison. Standard weights have generally been derived from a specific measurement of a known substance, particularly water. According to the most accurate experiments, when the barometer is at 30 inches and Fahrenheit’s thermometer is at 62°, 12 wine gallons of distilled water weigh exactly 100 pounds avoirdupois, with each pound containing 7,000 troy grains; and a cubic inch weighs 252 1/2 grains. A hogshead of water, by wine measure, therefore weighs 525 pounds, and a tun weighs 2,100 pounds, which is nearly equal to a ton weight. Mr. Barlow assumes that the tun measure of water originally contained 32 cubic feet and weighed 2,000 pounds, which was also called a ton weight; at that time, the gallon was somewhat smaller than it is at present, and the cubic foot weighed exactly 1,000 ounces, or 62 1/2 pounds. A quarter of wheat weighed about a quarter of a ton, and a bushel weighed as much as a cubic foot of water. A chaldron of coals was also considered equivalent to a ton, although it now weighs nearly half as much more. However, at the average temperature of this climate, or 52°, a cubic foot of distilled water weighs only 998 ounces. The avoirdupois ounce appears to correspond very closely with the ancient Roman ounce. Of the old French weight, 100 pounds equaled 108 English pounds avoirdupois. The gramme of the new weights is a cubic centimeter of pure water at its maximum density—that is, at a temperature of about 39° Fahrenheit; it is equal to 15 2/5 English grains. Therefore, the chiliogramme is 2 1/5 pounds, and five myriagrammes are nearly a hundredweight. Five grammes of silver, including one-tenth alloy, make a franc, which is one-eightieth more valuable than the old franc or livre and is intrinsically worth nearly nine pence and three farthings in English currency.

The instruments usually employed for the comparison of weights are either balances or steelyards. In a common balance, the weights of the substances being compared are equal. In a compound weighing machine, we use weights that are smaller, in a certain proportion, than those which they represent. In the steelyard, a single weight acquires different values at different parts of the arm, and in the bent lever balance, the position of the arms determines the magnitude of the counterpoise. The spring steelyard measures the weight by the degree of flexion that it produces in a spring.

The beam of a common balance must have its arms precisely equal. The

Scales, being freely suspended from fixed points in the beam, always act on them in the direction of gravity; the effect is the same as if the entire weight were concentrated in those points. The beam supports the scales and is itself supported by fine edges of hard steel working on steel, agate, or garnet, so that the motion may be free and the distances of the points precisely defined. The best beams are made of two hollow brass cones joined at their bases; they are lifted off their supports when the balance is not in use to avoid accidental damage. The scales are also supported so that they do not hang from the beam until they have received their weights. Depending on the position of the fulcrum relative to the points of suspension of the scales, the equilibrium of the balance may be either stable, neutral, or tottering; or if the beam is too flexible, it may pass from one of these states to another under the influence of the weights. Stable equilibrium is the most common and the best, because it allows us to determine the degree of weight inequality by the position in which the <term>centre of gravity</term> rests, or by the midpoint of the beam's vibrations, which are sometimes measured by an index pointing to a graduated arc. If, however, the <term>fulcrum</term> is elevated too far above the centre of gravity, the equilibrium may be too stable and may require a large difference in weight to produce a noticeable imbalance. If, on the contrary, by elevating the points where the scales are suspended, the equilibrium is rendered tottering, the lower scale will not rise even if it is somewhat less loaded than the upper one; <term>steelyards</term> of this construction have sometimes been used to deceive the purchaser with the appearance of full weight. Where great accuracy is desired, it is necessary to bring the equilibrium very close to a state of neutrality and to make the vibrations of the beam slow and wide, whether the scales have weights in them or not. For this purpose, a small weight is sometimes enclosed within the beam, which is raised or lowered at will by a screw to bring the centre of gravity of the entire moving apparatus as close to the fulcrum as the occasion requires. Mr. Ramsden’s balance, made for the Royal Society, is capable of weighing ten pounds and reacts to one ten-millionth part of the weight. (Plate VIII. Fig. 107–109.)

For example, if one arm of the <term>beam</term> were only three-fourths as long as the other, the counterpoise to a weight of twelve ounces would be nine ounces in one scale and sixteen in the other, making together twenty-five instead of twenty-four ounces. Supposing the beams of a <term>balance</term> to be accidentally unequal, either in length or in weight, we may still weigh in it with accuracy by making a perfect counterpoise of any kind to a weight, and then removing the weight and putting in its place as much of the substance to be weighed as is sufficient to restore the <term>equilibrium</term>.

The weights may also be reduced or increased in proportion to the length of the arms; if they differ from each other, care being taken to put the weights always into the same scale. This is actually performed in <term>weighing machines</term>, where a combination of <term>levers</term> is employed in order to enable us to determine the weight of large masses by means of weights of moderate dimensions. (Plate IX. Fig. 111.)

When the effective lengths of one or both arms of the beam are capable of being varied by changing the points of suspension according to the divisions of a scale, the instrument is called a <term>steelyard</term>. Where one weight only is used, it is not necessary that the two arms should exactly balance each other, since the divisions may be so placed as to make the necessary adjustment; but it is sometimes convenient to have two or three weights of different magnitudes, and for this purpose the instrument should be in equilibrium without any weight. In such cases, great accuracy may be obtained by applying a small weight at the end in the form of a <term>micrometer screw</term>. (Plate IX. Fig. 112.)

The center of gravity being, in the common balance, very nearly in a straight line between the weights, the arm must have a very significant angular motion for even a slight inequality of the weights in order for the center of gravity to be immediately below the fulcrum; but in the bent lever balance, the center of gravity is at such a distance from the fulcrum that a moderate motion of the arms may bring it into the vertical line. This motion is measured by an index on a graduated arc, which gives the instrument a considerable range; and where speed is particularly desired, it may often be used with advantage; but if the weights to be determined are large, the scale becomes very compressed, and the instrument requires to be leveled with great accuracy. A counterpoise acting on a spiral or conical barrel has also been applied to a similar purpose; it is capable of a scale somewhat more extended than a bent lever balance, but it is less simple and hardly more accurate. (Plate IX. Fig. 113.)

A spring, which is usually of a spiral form, being made to support a hook by the intervention of a graduated bar, the divisions of this bar, which are drawn out beyond the fixed point, indicate the weight supported by the hook. This instrument is called a spring steelyard. Mr. Hanin's spring steelyard has a long index, which revolves on a center and shows at once the weight according to the standards of different countries. The divisions of the scales in moderate flexures of the spring are nearly equal: hence it may be inferred that the distance through which a spring is bent, and consequently its curvature or change of curvature, is simply proportional to the force which acts on it, and that the vibrations of a weight supported by a spring must, like those of a cycloidal pendulum, be performed in equal times, whatever their magnitude may be. The strength of all springs is somewhat diminished by heat, and for each degree of Fahrenheit that the temperature is raised, we must deduct about one part in five thousand from the apparent weight indicated by the spring steelyard. (Plate IX. Fig. 114.)

The spring steelyard provides us with the most convenient method of measuring the immediate intensity of the forces exerted by animals of different kinds in the labor which they perform. All animal actions, or, at least, all the external actions of animals, are ultimately dependent on the contractions and relaxations of the fleshy parts, which are called <term>muscles</term>. The operation of the particular muscles belongs properly to the science of <term>physiology</term>; but their mechanism may in general be understood from the properties of the <term>lever</term> and of the <term>center of gravity</term>. The bones are the levers, the joints the <term>fulcrums</term>, and the force is applied by the muscles, which are usually attached to the bones by the intervention of tendinous cords. When a muscle contracts in the direction of its fibers, it becomes at the same time thicker, and its total bulk is little if at all diminished: when it relaxes itself, it is merely passive, for the fibers, being extremely flexible, can have little or no effect in separating the parts to which they are attached; this separation is generally performed by the action of other muscles, which are called the <term>antagonists</term> of the first, but sometimes by elastic ligaments, or by other means. The bone forms a lever of the second kind, where the two forces opposing each other are on the same side of the fulcrum. In general the insertion of a muscle is much nearer to the fulcrum than the point of action, and the obliquity of its direction gives it a still greater mechanical disadvantage with regard to rotatory power; but it is more convenient in the animal economy to produce a great contractile force, than a great extent in the original motion. For instance, when the arm is raised by the exertion of the <term>deltoid muscle</term> of the shoulder, a very strong contraction takes place in the muscle, but the action is only continued through a short space; had the contractile power been weaker and more extensive, the shoulder must have been made higher, in order to give it sufficient purchase, and the projection would have been inconvenient.

<term>Borelli</term> has calculated that the immediate force of the <term>biceps</term>, or double-headed muscle which bends the arm, is equivalent to about 300 pounds, and that of the muscles which raise the lower jaw, above 500 in man, but in beasts of prey far greater. It is obvious that in muscles of the same kind, the strength must be as the number of fibers, or as the extent of the surface which

# ON STATICS.

The weakest man can lift with his hands about 125 pounds, a strong man 400. Topham, a carpenter mentioned by Desaguliers, could lift 800 pounds. He rolled up a strong pewter dish with his fingers; he lifted with his teeth and knees a table six feet long, with a fifty-six-pound weight at the end. He bent a poker, three inches in circumference, to a right angle by striking it upon his left forearm; another he bent and unbent around his neck and snapped a hemp rope two inches in circumference. A few years ago, there was a person at Oxford who could hold his arm extended for half a minute with a fifty-six-pound weight hanging on his little finger. A young gentleman, who has distinguished himself as a pedestrian by walking 90 miles in 19 hours, has also lifted two hundredweight weights, one in each hand, and made them meet over his head.

Sometimes feats of strength that appear extraordinary have been exhibited by men who did not actually possess any significant physical superiority. Desaguliers relates that one of them used to withstand the force of two horses pulling at a belt passed around his waist, while his feet were braced against a firm obstacle. By falling suddenly backward into an oblique position, he broke a rope that was fixed a little before his feet. He supported one or two men by forming his body into an arch; and by a harness fitted to his hips, he sustained a cannon weighing two or three thousand pounds. In all these cases, the muscles principally employed are the extensors of the legs and thighs, but the passive strength of the bones is more involved than the active force of the muscles. In the instance mentioned by Lahire, of a young man who raised a donkey from the ground by cords tied to the hair of his head, the sensitivity of the nerves of the skin must have been diminished by habit, so as to allow the hair to be so forcibly pulled without immoderate pain.

The application of animal force is usually performed by means of a forward motion. The muscles employed in this process are generally, if not always, the strongest in the body, both by nature and by habit; so that when force alone is required, it is most advantageously obtained from their exertion. In walking, the <term>center of gravity</term> is moved forward with a nearly uniform velocity. If the legs were perfectly inflexible, the center of

### LECTURE XII.

gravity would describe, in succession, portions of circles, of which each leg would alternately be the radius: but if the velocity were great enough to create a centrifugal force more than equivalent to the force of gravity, the pressure would be removed from each leg after the first instant it touches the ground; the path would become parabolic instead of circular, and walking would be converted into running: for the difference between walking and running is this, that in running, one foot is removed from the ground before the other touches it; while in walking, the rear foot is only raised after the front foot has touched the ground. Now, supposing the length of an inflexible leg to be three feet, the centrifugal force would become equal to the weight at a velocity that would be acquired by a heavy body falling through a foot and a half—that is, nearly 10 feet per second, or 7 miles an hour; and this is the maximum velocity with which it would be mechanically possible to walk with inflexible legs. But the flexibility of the legs makes the forward motion much more uniform by softening the angles of the path described by the center of gravity, and rendering it either more or less curved at will; so that it becomes mechanically, if not physically, possible to walk with a velocity somewhat greater than 7 miles an hour, and to run or dance with as low a velocity as we please, since we may make the path of the center of gravity somewhat less, or much more curved, than a circle centered on the point of the foot. (Plate IX. Fig. 115, 116.)

The flexing and extending of the legs are also almost the only means by which momentum is given to the body; if the legs were perfectly inflexible, it would be extremely difficult, although not absolutely impossible, to achieve forward motion. The center of gravity is principally propelled forward at the beginning of the ascending part of the curve it describes: in walking, by the action of the leg left behind; but in running or hopping, by the action of the only foot touching the ground at any one time. When we push against any obstacle or pull a rope in a horizontal or downward direction, the body leans forward, and in some cases, its action is limited by the effect of the body's weight relative to the direction of the <term>line of draft</term>; but we much more usually draw or pull in an upward direction, so that our entire muscular force may be exerted without any limit of this kind.

## ON STATICS.

However, it happens very frequently that we require motions of such a nature that they are more conveniently performed by the hands and arms than by walking or running. Where precision is required rather than strength, the form of the human hand and fingers gives our species a great superiority over all other animals, though this is by no means—as some authors have supposed—an advantage equal to that of our higher intellectual powers. It is true, as we can see in the factories of this country, that machinery has been invented by which power of any kind can be converted to purposes that seem most intricate and refined. After all that has been achieved by men like Watt and Arkwright, it is difficult to set a definite limit on the ingenuity of mechanical invention.

In examining various sources of motion, it is necessary to consider not only the immediate magnitude of the forces they produce, but also the speed at which they are capable of acting and the duration for which that action can be continued. The daily work of a healthy, middle-aged laborer will serve as a convenient unit for comparing all types of moving powers. It may be most easily remembered in this form: a man can raise a 10-pound weight to a height of 10 feet in one second, and he can continue this labor for 10 hours a day. The actual speed of the man’s motion must vary according to how his force is applied, but we assume that speed to be whatever produces the greatest effect under the specific circumstances of the machine. This is a moderate estimate of a laborer’s work, without subtracting for friction. Desaguliers states that the performance of a man working at a winch, assisted by a fly <note>A flywheel used to regulate motion.</note>, is considerably greater, but he does not provide any accurate experiments to support his estimate. However, Professor Robison mentions a hydraulic machine in which the effect was actually more than one-tenth greater, without making any allowance for friction. Therefore, considering the loss from both friction and the momentum with which the water must have been released, it is probable that the immediate performance was at least one-third more than this unit. That machine was operated by a light man carrying a weight and walking back and forth on a lever. According to Mr. Buchanan’s experiments, an action like ringing bells produced an effect about one-third greater than turning a winch, and rowing produced an effect four-ninths greater; however, it does not appear that these experiments were continued for a

It is indeed rare that the muscles employed in forward motion are exerted as much as in the arrangement described by Professor Robison. A Chinese man, in the operation called sculling, is said to beat a European at his oar.

For a short time, a much greater effect than this may be produced by a great exertion: thus, a man weighing over 160 pounds can ascend by means of steps at the rate of more than three feet in a second for a quarter, or perhaps half a minute; and this is an effort five times as great as that which can be continued for a day. Usually, however, where the hands are chiefly employed—whether in turning a winch or in pumping—it is only possible to exert a double or, at most, a triple action for a minute or two. Thus, although a machine may only enable a man to raise a hogshead <note>A large cask, typically containing 54 to 63 gallons.</note> of water in a minute to the height of ten feet for a whole day, it is easy to work it so rapidly for a single minute as to raise double the quantity, or to raise a single hogshead to a height of twenty feet. The total exertion of force must be slightly greater than what is thus estimated, because a certain degree of extra momentum must be generated in moving weights from one position to another; but this loss is usually negligible.

The action of carrying a load horizontally requires an exertion of a different kind and allows for no direct comparison with the application of a constant force to overcome the gravity of a weight, or any other immediate resistance. The work of a laborer thus employed is, however, confined within moderate limits. A strong porter can carry 200 pounds at the rate of three miles an hour; and, for a short distance, even 300 pounds. A chairman <note>A person who carries a sedan chair.</note> carries 150 pounds and walks four miles an hour; and in Turkey, it is said that there are porters who, by stooping forward and placing the weight very low on their backs, are enabled to carry from 700 to 900 pounds. The subjects of Mr. Coulomb's experiments appear to have been either weaker or more inactive than the majority of porters in this country; he calculates that the most advantageous load for a man of common strength is about a hundredweight <note>112 pounds.</note>; or, if he is to return without a burden, 135 pounds.

# ON STATICS.

It is generally supposed that in pulling up a steep ascent, a horse is equivalent to only 3 or 4 men; for this reason, the use of horses in walking wheels <note>A type of treadmill where an animal or person walks to provide mechanical power.</note>, where the action is similar to ascending a hill, has been condemned. For men, on the contrary, an ascent of any kind appears to provide a favorable mode of exertion. But perhaps the weight of the carriage, and of the horse itself, has not always been sufficiently considered in the comparison. The strength of a mule is equal to that of three or four men. The expense of keeping a horse is generally about two or three times as great as the wages of a day laborer; therefore, the force of horses may be considered about half as expensive as that of men. The horse Childers <note>Flying Childers (1714–1741), a famous and undefeated English Thoroughbred often cited as the fastest horse of his era.</note> is said—though perhaps without sufficient authority—to have run an English mile in a single minute; in this case, his velocity must have been 88 feet per second, which would have been sufficient to carry him up a frictionless inclined plane, or in a very long sling, to a vertical height of 120 feet.

A large windmill, upon which Mr. Coulomb conducted many experiments, was capable, on average, of working eight hours a day; its total performance was equivalent to our estimate of the daily labor of 34 men, with 25 square feet of the sails performing the work of one laborer. The expense of the machinery, including its repairs, would probably amount to less than half the expense of a number of horses capable of exerting the same force. Where a stream of water can be obtained, its force is generally more convenient because it is more regular than that of the wind.

A steam engine of the best construction, with a thirty-inch cylinder, has the force of 40 horses; and, since it acts without intermission, it will perform the work of 120 horses or 600 men, with each square inch of the piston being nearly equivalent to one laborer. According to Mr. Boulton, the consumption of a bushel (or 84 pounds) of coal will raise 48,000 cubic feet of water 10 feet high, which is equivalent to the daily labor of 8 1/3 men, or perhaps more. The value of this quantity of coal is seldom more than the wages for the work of a single laborer for a day; however, the expense of the machinery generally makes a steam engine slightly more than half as expensive as the number of horses for which it is substituted. The force of gunpowder is used advantageously where a very powerful action is required for a short distance, such as in splitting rocks or in generating great velocity in a projectile. As a source of momentum or energy alone, this power is by no means economical; the daily labor of a man is equivalent to the effect of about 40 pounds of gunpowder. However, the advantage of artillery consists in having the force communicated by means of an extremely thin elastic fluid <note>Gas produced by combustion.</note>, which is capable of generating very great velocity in the ball alone, without any waste of power in producing useless momentum in any other substance.

The relative force of different kinds of gunpowder is determined by an *eprouvette*, or *powder proof*: the effect is measured by the angular motion of a small wheel; a projecting part of the wheel is struck by the explosion of a small quantity of the powder, while the friction of a spring or weight creates a resistance that can be adjusted if necessary. The absolute force of a given quantity of powder may be determined either by suspending a cannon like a pendulum and measuring its angular recoil, or by shooting into a large block and finding the velocity imparted to it by the ball.

To measure very small attractive or repulsive forces with great accuracy, the most convenient test is provided by the effects of twisting. An arm or beam is suspended horizontally by a long wire; once the force required to make the beam complete one or more revolutions is determined, we may divide the circle traced by its ends into as many parts as we wish. The force required to bring the beam into any position will always be proportional—without any noticeable error—to the size of the arc between that position and the point where the arm would naturally rest. When the force is of a nature capable of producing a vibration—and the body on which it acts is suspended by the thread of a silkworm or a spider—we may compare its magnitude with that of gravity by observing the time required for each vibration and determining the action of the force according to the laws of pendulums. It is in this manner that the forces involved in the effects of electricity and magnetism have been measured by Mr. Coulomb <note>Charles-Augustin de Coulomb (1736–1806), known for his work on torsion and electromagnetism.</note>.

# LECTURE XIII.

## ON PASSIVE STRENGTH AND FRICTION.

The passive strength of the materials used in the mechanical arts depends on the cohesive and repulsive forces of their particles, and on the rigidity of their structure. Considering the fundamental nature of these forces belongs to the discussion of the physical properties of matter; however, estimating their magnitude and their relative value in various circumstances is of undeniable importance to practical mechanics and must be examined as a continuation of the subject of statics. The retarding force of friction is very closely allied to some kinds of passive strength and may be largely explained by similar considerations.

The principal effects of any force acting on a solid body may be categorized into seven types: extension, compression, detrusion, flexure, torsion, alteration, and fracture. When a weight is suspended below a fixed point, the suspending substance is extended, or stretched, and maintains its form through its cohesion, assisted by its rigidity. When the weight is supported by a block or pillar placed below it, the block is compressed and resists primarily through a repulsive force, but secondarily also through its rigidity. The effect called detrusion <note>The act of pushing or thrusting away; in mechanics, specifically referring to shear stress or the displacement of parts of a solid in a direction parallel to the plane of the force.</note> is produced when a transverse force is applied close to a fixed point, in the same way the blades of a pair of scissors act on the pin; the force resisting this action is mainly the rigidity or lateral adhesion of the layers of the substance, though it could hardly be effective without some degree of cohesive and repulsive force. When three or more forces are applied to different parts of any substance, they produce flexure—that is, they bend it—as some of its parts are extended while others are compressed. In torsion, or twisting, the central particles remain in their natural state, while those in opposite parts of the circumference

The operation of forces applied in any of these ways may produce a permanent alteration, or change of shape, in substances that are sufficiently soft, and perhaps, to a certain degree, in all substances: this change is sometimes called by workmen "settling," or "taking a set." But the limit of all these effects is fracture, which is the consequence of applying any force capable of overcoming the strength of the substance, and to which the majority of writers on mechanics have hitherto confined their attention.

The forces by which the form of any substance is changed may also be divided into two kinds: simple pressure and impulse. However, it is only with regard to fracture that it will be necessary to take the force of impulse into consideration.

Extension and compression follow laws so similar that they may be best understood by comparison with each other. The cohesive and repulsive forces which resist these effects depend almost as much on the solidity or rigidity of the substances as on the attractions and repulsions which are their immediate causes; for a substance that is perfectly liquid, although its particles are in full possession of their attractive and repulsive powers, may be extended or compressed by the smallest force that can be applied to it. Indeed, it is not certain that the actual distances between the particles of all bodies are increased when they are extended, or diminished when they are compressed; for these changes are generally accompanied by opposite changes in other parts of the same substance, although probably to a smaller degree. We may easily observe that if we compress a piece of elastic gum <note>Natural rubber or caoutchouc.</note> in any direction, it extends itself in other directions; and if we extend it in length, its breadth and thickness are diminished.

If the rigidity of a body were infinite, and all lateral movements of its particles were prevented, the direct cohesion alone would be the measure of the force required to produce extension, and the direct repulsion would be the measure of the force required to produce compression. In this respect, the actual rigidity of some substances may be considered as infinite whenever the extension or compression is moderate and no permanent alteration of form is produced; and within these limits, these substances may be called perfectly elastic. If the cohesion and repulsion were infinite and the rigidity limited, the only effect of force would be to produce an alteration of form. Such bodies would be perfectly inelastic, but they would be harder or softer according to their degree of rigidity.

It is found by experiment that the measure of the extension and compression of uniform elastic bodies is simply proportional to the force that causes it—at least when the forces are relatively small. Thus, if a weight of 100 pounds lengthened a steel rod by one-hundredth of an inch, a weight of 200 would lengthen it by very nearly two-hundredths, and a weight of 300 pounds by three-hundredths. The same weights acting in the opposite direction would also shorten it by one, two, or three-hundredths respectively. The former part of this law was discovered by Dr. Hooke, and the effects appear to be perfectly analogous to those more easily observable in elastic fluids.

According to this analogy, we may express the elasticity of any substance by the weight of a certain column of the same substance, which may be called the modulus of its elasticity. The weight of this column is such that any addition to it would increase it in the same proportion as the added weight would shorten, by its pressure, a portion of the substance of equal diameter. Thus, if a rod of any kind, 100 inches long, were compressed 1 inch by a weight of 1,000 pounds, the weight of the modulus of its elasticity would be 100,000 pounds—or more accurately 99,000, which is to 100,000 in the same proportion as 99 to 100. In the same manner, we must suppose that the subtraction of any weight from that of the modulus will also diminish it in the same ratio that the equivalent force would extend any portion of the substance. The height of the modulus is the same for the same substance, whatever its breadth and thickness may be: for atmospheric air, it is about 5 miles, and for steel, nearly 1,500. This supposition is sufficiently confirmed by experiments to be considered at least a good approximation. It follows that the weight of the modulus must always exceed the utmost cohesive strength of the substance, and that the compression produced by such a weight must reduce its dimensions to one half. I have found that a force capable of compressing a piece of elastic gum to half its length will usually extend it to many times that length, and then break or tear it; and

The property of stiffness is fully as useful in many works of engineering as the ultimate strength with which a body resists breaking; for example, for a shelf, a lintel, or a chimney piece, a great degree of bending would be almost as inconvenient as a rupture of the material.

When a beam is supported at both ends, its stiffness is twice as great as that of a beam of half the length firmly fixed at one end; and if both ends are firmly fixed, the stiffness is again quadrupled. For if the whole beam were inverted and supported by a fulcrum in the middle, each half would resemble a separate beam fixed at one end, and the fulcrum would bear the sum of two equal weights placed at the ends, disregarding the weight of the beam itself; and consequently, the same bending will be produced by placing a double weight on the middle of the beam in an inverted position. If both ends were firmly fixed, the curvature would everywhere be proportional to the distance from the middle of each half, the whole being in the same state as four separate beams fixed at their ends. Each of these beams would be eight times as stiff as beams of twice the length, and the whole beam, in this state, would be eight times as stiff as if the ends were simply supported. It is, however, difficult to fix the ends of a beam so firmly as to increase its resistance in this proportion, unless it is continued in both directions considerably beyond the supports.

It is evident that a tube, or hollow beam of any kind, must be much stiffer than the same quantity of matter in a solid form; the stiffness is indeed increased nearly in proportion to the square of the diameter, since the cohesion and repulsion are equally exerted with a smaller curvature, and also act on a longer lever.

Torsion, or twisting, consists of the lateral displacement, or <term>detrusion</term>, of the opposite parts of a solid in opposite directions, with only the central particles remaining in their natural state. It can be shown that the whole wire would be shortened by one-fourth as much as the external fibers would be extended if the length remained unchanged, and that the force would vary as the cube of the angle through which the wire is twisted. However, the force of torsion, as determined by experiment, varies simply as the angle of torsion; it cannot, therefore, be explained by the action of longitudinal fibers alone. Instead, it seems to depend principally, if not entirely, on the rigidity, or lateral adhesion, which resists the <term>detrusion</term> of the particles. If a wire is twice as thick as another of the same length, it will require sixteen times as much force to twist it once around; the stiffness varies as the fourth power of the diameter—that is, as the *square of its square*. But if the length varies, it is obvious that the resistance to the force of torsion will be inversely proportional to the length.

A permanent alteration of form is most noticeable in substances that are most lacking in rigidity and most closely approach the nature of fluids. It limits the strength of materials for practical purposes almost as much as fracture does, since, in general, the force capable of producing this effect is sufficient, with only a small addition, to increase it until fracture occurs. A smaller force than the one that first produced an alteration of form is seldom capable of either increasing or removing it—a circumstance that gives materials susceptible to this kind of alteration a great advantage for many purposes of convenience and art. The more capable a body is of a permanent alteration of form, the more ductile it is said to be. Pure gold and silver, lead, annealed iron and copper, warm wax, red-hot glass, and moist clay possess considerable ductility. Wood allows for little permanent change of form, except when it is green, although it sometimes settles slightly when it has been exposed to pressure. Even stone will become permanently bent over the course of years, as we may observe in old marble chimneypieces. But the most ductile of all solid substances seems to be a *spider’s web*. Mr. Bennet twisted a thread of this kind many thousand times and shortened it by more than a fourth of its length, yet it showed no tendency to untwist.
