The degree of <term>flexure</term> or <term>torsion</term> required to produce a further alteration also appears to vary little. For example, if a spider’s web could initially be twisted only half a turn while still retaining the power to return to its original state without any permanent alteration of form, it would never acquire the power of returning more than half a revolution, no matter how much it might be twisted. Due to a lack of attention to this consideration, a recently esteemed author has questioned, without sufficient reason, the accuracy of Mr. Bennet’s experiments.

A variation of <term>ductility</term> in any substance does not appear to depend on any change in the magnitude of the ultimate powers of <term>cohesion</term> and <term>repulsion</term>. Steel, whether perfectly hard or of the softest temper, resists bending with equal force when the deviations from its natural state are small. However, at a certain point, soft steel begins to undergo an alteration of form; at another point, it breaks if it is very hard. But when the hardness is moderate, it is capable of a much greater curvature without either permanent alteration or fracture. This quality, which is valuable for the purposes of springs, is called <term>toughness</term> and is opposed to <term>rigidity</term> and <term>brittleness</term> on one side, and to <term>ductility</term> on the other. 

There may, however, be an apparent difference in the stiffness of some substances in different states, arising from the greater ease with which their dimensions are extended in one direction while they are contracted in another. For instance, <term>elastic gum</term> <note>natural rubber</note> appears to possess a much greater degree of stiffness when its hardness is increased by cold than when it is at a higher temperature. But the change produced in this case by heat is not an increase of that ductility which facilitates a permanent alteration of form, but rather of the toughness which allows a temporary change of shape, lasting only while the force is applied. The effects of forging and of wire-drawing tend to lessen the ductility of metals and to render them tough, and even rigid. Thus, in hammering copper and brass, and in drawing wire, it is necessary to <term>anneal</term> the metals more than once by fire in order to restore their ductility, which is reduced by the operation. The corrosion of the surface of a metal by an acid is also said to render it brittle, but it is not impossible that this apparent brittleness may be caused by some irregularity in the action of the acid.

### ON PASSIVE STRENGTH AND FRICTION.

The final effect of force on solid materials is their <term>fracture</term>, which, like the previously mentioned changes, can be produced either by <term>impulse</term> or by <term>pressure</term> alone. The action that resists pressure is called <term>strength</term>, and the action that resists impulse may properly be termed <term>resilience</term>. The strength of every object is in the combined ratio of its immediate <term>cohesion</term> and <term>repulsion</term> (or <term>elasticity</term>) and its <term>toughness</term>—the degree to which it may be extended, compressed, or otherwise distorted without its parts separating. Resilience is jointly proportional to its strength and its toughness; it is measured by the product of the <term>mass</term> and the square of the <term>velocity</term> of an object capable of breaking it, or by the mass and the height from which it must fall to acquire that velocity. In contrast, strength is simply measured by the maximum pressure that the object can support while at rest.

The simplest way an object can be broken is by tearing it apart. The cohesive force continues to increase as long as the <term>tenacity</term> of the substance allows the particles to be separated from each other without a permanent change of form. Once this change has occurred, the same force—if its action is continued—is generally capable of causing a total loss of continuity; sometimes, a separation occurs without any prior observable change of this kind.

It follows from the nature of resilience that a one-pound object falling from a height of one yard will produce the same effect in breaking any substance as a three-pound object falling from a height of one foot. Thus, here—as well as in the estimation of mechanical power—it is the <term>energy</term>, and not the <term>momentum</term>, that should be considered the measure of the effect. If we know the strength of any substance and the extent to which it can be stretched, we may easily determine its resilience by considering the laws of pendulums. For the same weight that would break it through pressure will gain enough impulse to break it if it falls from a height equal to half the distance the substance can be extended, assuming the direction of the impact is horizontal so that its effect is not increased by the force of <term>gravity</term>. For instance, if the pressure of a 100-pound weight broke a given substance after stretching it by one inch, the same weight would break it by striking it with the velocity acquired from the fall of a heavy body from a height of half an

It is obvious that the <term>cohesive strength</term>, as well as the <term>resilience</term>, of any substance must be simply proportional to the magnitude of its <term>transverse section</term>, that is, of the <term>surface of fracture</term>. Some experiments appear to show that it increases in a greater proportion than this surface, others that it increases in a smaller proportion; but it is probable that in both cases some accidental irregularities must have interfered, and that a wire two inches in diameter is exactly four times as strong as a wire one inch in diameter. The length has no effect either in increasing or in diminishing the cohesive strength; but the resilience is proportional to the length, since a similar extension of a longer fiber produces a greater elongation.

There is however a limit beyond which the <term>velocity</term> of a body striking another cannot be increased without overcoming its resilience and breaking it, however small the bulk of the first body may be. This limit depends on the <term>inertia</term> of the parts of the second body, which must not be disregarded when they are impelled with a considerable velocity. For it can be demonstrated that there is a certain velocity, dependent on the nature of a substance, with which the effect of any <term>impulse</term> or <term>pressure</term> is transmitted through it; a certain portion of time, which is shorter according to how much more elastic the body is, being required for the <term>propagation of the force</term> through any part of it. If the actual velocity of any impulse is in a greater proportion to this velocity than the <term>extension</term> or <term>compression</term>—of which the substance is capable—is to its whole length, it is obvious that a separation must be produced, since no parts can be extended or compressed which are not yet affected by the impulse, and the length of the portion affected at any instant is not sufficient to allow the required extension or compression. Thus, if the velocity with which an impression is transmitted by a certain kind of wood is 15,000 feet in a second, and it is susceptible to compression to the extent of 1/200 of its length, the greatest velocity that it can resist will be 75 feet in a second, which is equal to that of a body falling from a height of about 90 feet. And by a similar comparison we may determine the velocity which will be sufficient to penetrate or to break off a substance in any other manner; if we calculate the velocity required to convey the impulse from one part of the substance

It is easy to understand, from this statement, the different qualities of natural bodies regarding hardness, softness, toughness, and brittleness. A column of chalk, capable of supporting only a pound, will perhaps be compressed by it only by a thousandth part of its length; a column of elastic gum <note>rubber</note>, capable of suspending a pound, may be extended to more than twice its length; the elastic gum will therefore resist the energy of an impulse incomparably greater than the chalk. A diamond, so hard that it resists an enormous pressure, may be broken by a moderate blow from a small hammer. A weight of 1,000 pounds, moving with a velocity of one foot per second and acting on a small surface of a board, may possess sufficient energy to break or to penetrate it; at a velocity of 100 feet per second, a weight of 1/10 of a pound will possess the same energy and produce the same effect if it acts on a similar surface. But if the wood is so constituted as to be wholly incapable of resisting a velocity of 100 feet per second, it may be penetrated by a weight of 1/100 of a pound as easily as by one-tenth, and by a moderately soft body as well as by a harder one. The whole board, however, if at liberty, would receive a much greater momentum from the impulse of the large weight than from that of the small one, as its action is continued for a much longer time. And it is for this reason that a ball shot from a pistol will perforate a sheet of paper standing upright on a table without overturning it.

The strength, or rather hardness, of a substance exposed to the action of a force that tends to compress it must not be confounded with its resistance to a force applied longitudinally and tending to produce <term>flexure</term> <note>bending</note>. A slender rod of wood, when it yields to a longitudinal pressure, commonly bends before it breaks, and gives way at last to the force by a transverse fracture; but a column of stone or brick, and even a thick pillar of wood, is crushed without bending, and generally by a smaller force than that which would produce or continue a flexure. In this case, the parts slide away laterally; and in a rectangular pillar, if the texture of the substance is uniform and not fibrous, the surfaces of fracture will make nearly a right angle with each other, assuming the resistance arising from the <term>lateral adhesion</term>, in the direction of any surface or section, to be simply proportional to that section: but if this force,

<header>LECTURE XIII.</header>

The power of the force of lateral adhesion in resisting fracture is considered by Mr. Coulomb to be nearly equal to that of the direct cohesion of the same substance, or a little greater; while Professor Robison considers it twice as great. If, however, this force is supposed to be simply equal to the direct cohesion, it may be inferred that the strength of a square bar in resisting compression is twice as great as its cohesive strength, assuming that the fracture takes place on the surface of least resistance. It is, however, rare that the strength with which a body resists compression is in such a high proportion to its cohesive strength; and where the substance is in any degree composed of fibers, they must naturally produce great irregularities through their flexure <note>bending under a load</note>. The strength in resisting compression must, according to this statement, be simply proportional to the size of the cross-section of the substance, although some experiments on freestone <note>a type of stone, such as limestone or sandstone, that can be cut easily in any direction</note> appear to indicate that when the cross-section is increased, the strength increases in a greater proportion; and there is no reason to suppose that it can be influenced either way by the length. A cylindrical or prismatic form is therefore the best that can be given to materials of a specific volume in order to enable them to resist a force that tends to crush them, except that the additional pressure of their own weight on the lower parts requires that those parts be a little stronger than the upper parts. It also appears that something is gained by making the outline slightly convex externally; for it can be demonstrated that for a column or upright beam to be cut out of a slab of uniform thickness, assuming the strength is independent of pressure, the strongest form is a circle. (Plate IX. Fig. 126, 127.)

When a body is broken by a transverse force applied very near to a fixed point, its lateral adhesion is overpowered by the effect that we have called detrusion <note>the act of pushing or thrusting down; a type of shear stress</note>, and its strength in this case is therefore generally somewhat greater than its direct cohesive strength. But when the part to which the force is immediately applied is at a distance from the fixed point greater than about one-sixth of the depth, the fracture is no longer the immediate consequence of detrusion, but of flexure.

<header>ON PASSIVE STRENGTH AND FRICTION.</header>

Flexure <note>bending</note> is the most common way in which fracture is produced; the surface parts on the convex side are most extended and usually give way first, except in soft fibrous substances, such as moist or green wood, which is more easily crushed than torn. In this case, the concave side fails first and becomes buckled, though the piece still remains held together by the cohesion of the fibers. After the convex surface has been cracked, the entire substance is usually separated, but not always; for example, a triangular beam, with one of the edges facing upward, may be loaded with such a weight that the upper edge may be divided while the lower part remains entire.

When a column or rafter is broken by the application of a longitudinal pressure, once the stiffness of the column is overcome, a small addition of force is usually sufficient to produce a fracture, unless the pressure has been applied to a part more or less distant from the axis; for in this case, a moderate force may produce a moderate flexure, and a much greater force may be required to break the column. But in general, the stiffness of columns is of more consequence than their strength in resisting transverse <note>crosswise</note> fracture.

The strength of beams of the same kind, fixed in the same manner, in resisting a transverse force, is simply proportional to their breadth, the square of their depth, and inversely proportional to their length. Thus, if a beam is twice as broad as another, it will also be twice as strong; but if it is twice as deep, it will be four times as strong: for the increase in depth not only doubles the number of resisting particles but also gives each of them a double power by increasing the length of the levers on which they act. Increasing the length of a beam must also obviously weaken it by giving a mechanical advantage to the force that tends to break it; and some experiments appear to show that the strength is diminished in a proportion somewhat greater than that in which the length is increased.

The strength of a beam supported at both ends, like its stiffness, is twice as great as that of a single beam of half the length which is fixed at one end; and the strength of the whole beam is again doubled if both the ends are firmly fixed.

### LECTURE XIII.

...a law very different from that which determines its strength, for it is simply proportional to the bulk or weight of the beam, whether it be shorter or longer, narrower or wider, shallower or deeper, solid or hollow. Thus, a beam ten feet long will support only half as great a pressure, without breaking, as a beam of the same breadth and depth which is only five feet in length; but it will bear the impact of a double weight striking against it with a given velocity, and will require that a given body should fall from a double height in order to break it.

It is therefore of great consequence in determining the form and quantity of the materials to be employed for any mechanical purpose that we should consider the nature as well as the magnitude of the forces which are to be resisted. Stiffness, strength, or resilience may be separately or jointly required in various degrees. For a ceiling, stiffness would be principally desirable; for a door, strength; for the floor of a ballroom, resilience; for a coach spring, resilience and flexibility—that is, resilience without stiffness. An observatory should be as stiff as possible, a ship as strong as possible, and a cable as resilient as possible.

It is a common remark that a floor which shakes is the strongest; and, improbable as it appears at first sight, it may perhaps be based in truth: for if the absolute strength of a stiff and a shaking floor were equal, the shaking floor would bear the effects of motion with the least injury. It is possible that a stiff floor, which would support a numerous assembly, might give way at a ball; while a more resilient one, which would be suited for dancing, might be destroyed by a crowded concert.

A coach spring, divided into plates, has the same power of resisting, without being broken, the momentum of the carriage arising from sudden elevations and depressions as it would possess if it formed one entire mass, while its greater flexibility allows it to regulate these motions in a much more gradual and gentle manner. A single piece of timber may perhaps sometimes have too much of the flexibility of a coach spring, its strata <note>layers</note> sliding in some degree on each other: in such a case, its stiffness and strength may be increased by binding it very firmly with hoops.

# ON PASSIVE STRENGTH AND FRICTION.

The transverse strength of a perfectly elastic substance, fixed at one end, is to its direct cohesive strength as the depth of the substance is to six times its length. This proportion is equally applicable to such substances as resist compression more strongly than extension; for their immediate repulsive force is probably not greater than their cohesive force when their dimensions are changed equally, so that the middle of the beam is always in its natural state. When the curvature is sufficient to overcome the cohesive force, the whole beam must give way. When, however, the substance is less capable of resisting compression than extension, the concave surface gives way first, and the strength depends immediately on the repulsive strength of the substance. This is perhaps the reason why, in experiments on beams of oak, the transverse strength has seldom been found in a greater ratio to the total cohesive strength than that of the depth to nine times the length.

It may be inferred from the consideration of the nature of the different kinds of resistance which have been explained, that if we have a cylindrical tree a foot in diameter, which is to be formed into a prismatic beam by flattening its sides, we shall gain the greatest stiffness by making the breadth or thickness 6 inches and the depth 10½ inches; the greatest strength by making the breadth 7 inches and the depth 9¾ inches; and the greatest resilience by making the beam square. The stiffness and the strength of the beam may be much increased by cutting the tree into four pieces, turning their edges outward, and uniting them so as to make a hollow beam. However, it will require great strength of union to make the whole act as one piece, and the resilience of the beam will be diminished rather than increased by the operation.

The adoption of the hollow masts and beams which an ingenious mechanic has lately introduced requires, therefore, some caution. For where an impulse is to be resisted, such a mast is no stronger than a solid mast of the same weight, and much weaker than a solid mast of the same diameter. The force of the wind is, however, rather to be considered as constituting a pressure than a finite impulse, except when a sudden squall carries a loose sail before it with considerable velocity. A similar caution may also be extended to some other attempts to make improvements in naval architecture: it is a common opinion, and perhaps a well-founded one, that flexibility is of great

We have up to this point supposed the beams, whose strength has been compared, to be prismatic—that is, of equal breadth and thickness throughout. This is not only the simplest form in theory, but the most generally useful in practice. If, however, we have the power of giving any form we please to materials of a certain weight—which may often be done where several smaller pieces are to be cut out of a larger one, or a larger one is to be composed of several smaller ones, or where the materials are either ductile or fusible—it is frequently possible to determine a more advantageous form than that of a uniform <note>equable</note> beam or column. Since the extension that the parts of a substance allow without giving way is the limit of their strength, if the depth of a beam is everywhere equal and the curvature is unequal, the fracture will first take place where the curvature is greatest, and the extra strength of the other parts will be lost. Therefore, in order to achieve the greatest strength that a given quantity of material can provide in a beam of a given length, the form must be such that the strength is everywhere equal, with the tension of the surface being equal throughout; the depth must also be smaller where the curvature is greater. 

It is also necessary to consider whether the substance is likely to be crushed, and whether it is liable to be broken by detrusion <note>shearing</note> rather than by flexure <note>bending</note>. Sometimes the depth of the beam may be limited, and sometimes its breadth; or it may be required that the breadth and depth always be equal or proportional to each other. The force may be applied at one end of the beam, or it may be equally divided throughout its length; it may also depend principally on the weight of the substance itself. The strongest form will vary according to the different conditions of its application. In the most common cases, the outline must be either triangular or parabolic, as if the point of the triangle were rounded off; however, the curves required are sometimes much more difficult to investigate. (Plate X. Fig. 128 . . 147.)

In order to investigate the strength of the various substances employed for the purposes of the mechanical arts, it is most convenient to use a machine equipped with proper supports, and grips, or vices, for holding the materials, and with steelyards for determining the magnitude of the applied force, while the extension or compression is produced by a screw or a winch, with the use of a wire, a chain, or a cord: provision should also be made for varying the direction of the force when the bending of the materials makes such a change necessary. (Plate XI. Fig. 148.)

According to the experiments of various authors, the cohesive strength of a square inch of razor steel is about 150,000 pounds; of soft steel, 120,000; of wrought iron, 80,000; of cast iron, 50,000; of good rope, 20,000; of oak, beech, and willow wood, in the direction of their fibers, 12,000; of fir, 8,000; and of lead, about 3,000 pounds: the cohesive strength of a square inch of brick is 300, and of freestone, 200. Teak wood, the *tectona grandis*, is said to be even stronger than oak.

The weight of the modulus of elasticity of a square inch of steel—or that weight which would be capable of compressing it to half its dimensions—is about 3 million pounds; hence it follows, that when a square inch of steel is torn apart by a weight of 150,000 pounds, its length is first increased to one-twentieth more than its natural dimensions.

The strength of different materials in resisting compression is liable to great variation. In steel, and in willow wood, the cohesive and repulsive <note>compressive</note> strength appear to be nearly equal. Oak will suspend much more than fir; but fir will support twice as much as oak, probably on account of the curvature of the fibers of oak. Freestone has been found to support about 2,000 pounds for each square inch; oak, in some practical cases, more than 4,000.

### LECTURE XIII.

Although iron is much stronger than wood, it is more liable to accidental imperfections; and when it fails, it gives no warning of its approaching fracture. The uniform quality of steel may be determined by corrosion in an acid; but there is no easy way of detecting internal flaws in a bar of iron, and we can only rely on the honesty of the workman for its soundness. Wood, when it is stressed to the point of failure, "complains" or emits a sound; after this, although it is much weakened, it may still retain enough strength to be useful. Stone sometimes throws off small splinters when it is beginning to give way; it is said to be capable of supporting by far the greatest weight when it is placed in the same orientation, relative to the horizon, in which it was found in the quarry.

It is obvious that when the bulk of the substance used becomes very large, its weight may become so great a proportion of its strength as to add significantly to the load to be supported. In most cases, weight increases more rapidly than strength, and this causes a practical limit on the size of our machines and buildings. We also see a similar limit in nature: a tree never grows to a height of 100 yards; an animal is never strong enough to overturn a mountain. It has been observed that whales are often larger than any land animals because their weight is better supported by the pressure of the medium <note>the water</note> in which they swim.

The force of friction, which resists the sliding of different bodies against each other, seems to be intimately connected with that lateral adhesion, or rigidity, which opposes the internal displacement of the parts of a single body through the effect which we have called <term>detrusion</term>; and when friction is considered as resisting pressure rather than motion, it is even more similar to that same force. It is probably derived in great measure from the strength of the protruding particles, which must be broken, bent, or compressed by the motion of the bodies against each other. However, the existence of such particles cannot always be confirmed, much less can they be made perceptible to the senses, and we can only examine the effects they are supposed to produce through direct experiments on the forces required to counteract them. Such experiments have been conducted on a very extensive scale by Musschenbroek and Coulomb, and many of their results have been confirmed by Mr. Vince in a simple and elegant manner.

### ON PASSIVE STRENGTH AND FRICTION.

With a few exceptions, the friction of all solid bodies is either perfectly or very nearly a uniformly retarding force, neither increasing nor decreasing when the relative velocity of the bodies involved is changed. The friction of some rough substances increases a little with velocity, but as they become more polished, this variation disappears. However, when the motion is completely stopped and the bodies remain in contact with each other, their adhesion is usually greater than the friction; and by continuing the contact, it may become twice or even three times as great, especially where the surfaces are large and the substances are only moderately hard.

The truth of the assertion that friction is a uniformly retarding force may be shown very conveniently by using Atwood’s machine for experiments on accelerated motion. By allowing the axis of the pulley to rest on the surface of any fixed substance, we may subject it to friction, the magnitude of which may be varied by different methods. We shall find that the motions of the boxes still indicate the action of a uniformly accelerating force, as the distances traveled are always proportional to the squares of the times of descent. It follows, therefore, that since the operation of gravity is uniform, the friction which is subtracted from it at each instant must also be uniform so that the resulting acceleration follows the same law.

The uniformity of the force of friction may also be shown by the descent of a flat substance on an inclined plane. If the body is made to begin its descent with a certain velocity, it will be slowed down when the resistance is greater than the relative force of gravity. In this case, the slowing will continue until it is completely stopped, as the resistance does not decrease with the velocity. If, on the contrary, the relative weight overcomes the resistance at first, the motion will be continually accelerated, as the resistance is not increased by the increase in velocity. But since every experiment of this kind must be performed in the presence of air, the resistance of this fluid—which follows a different law—will eventually prevent further acceleration.

It may in general be asserted, with some exceptions, that the force of friction is simply proportional to the weight or pressure that brings the substances involved into contact, regardless of the size of their sur-

By calculating these forces separately, we may probably always determine the total resistance with sufficient accuracy. This constant portion is usually much smaller than that which varies with the weight, and in all common cases it may be safely neglected. The friction of stone on stone may be considered equal to one-half of the pressure, that of wood on wood one-third, and that of metal on metal one-fourth; this may serve as an estimate sufficiently accurate for calculating the effects of machines. Although, if their parts were perfectly adjusted to each other and all the surfaces well polished, the friction would not in general exceed one-eighth of the pressure, regardless of the nature of the materials. The application of oily substances <note>The original uses "unctuous substances."</note> lessens the friction in the first instance; but unless they are frequently renewed, they sometimes tend instead to increase it.

The simplest way to determine the magnitude of the friction of two bodies is to tilt their shared surface relative to the horizontal until one begins to slide on the other. This point determines the magnitude of their adhesion; but in order to find the magnitude of their friction when they are in motion, they must first be separated and then allowed to move over each other while the whole apparatus is gently shaken. The friction will then be to the pressure as the height of the inclined plane is to its horizontal length, when the tilt is barely enough to allow the continuation of any motion imparted to the substance placed on the plane.

It follows from the principle of the resolution of forces <note>The original uses "resolution of force."</note> that when any body is to be drawn along a horizontal surface which produces a resistance proportional to the pressure, a part of the force may be effectively used to diminish the pressure produced by the weight of the body. Therefore, for the most effective application of the force, its direction must be tilted relative to the horizontal; it can be demonstrated that this tilt must be the same as that of a plane on which the relative weight of the body is exactly equal to the friction. Thus, if we can determine the inclination of a road that is barely sufficient for a carriage to descend on it by its own weight, the same inclination will be the best possible for the appli-

It is obvious that an inclined plane, on which a weight rests because of an adhesion proportional to the pressure, can never be forced backwards by any increase of that pressure, since the resistance increases in the same proportion and remains always sufficient to prevent the relative motion between the weight and the inclined plane. Two such planes, put together, would form a wedge, which would be equally incapable of giving way to a pressure applied to its opposite surfaces, as each of them possesses similar properties regarding friction. Thus, if the friction or adhesion were exactly one-eighth of the pressure, the height of the inclined plane would be one-eighth of its length, and the back of the wedge would be one-fourth. Such a wedge would therefore possess perfect stability regarding any forces acting on its inclined surfaces. However, the effects of agitation and the minute tremors produced by percussion have a strong tendency to diminish the force of adhesion by interrupting the intimacy of contact. Therefore, where a pin, a nail, or a screw is required to stay firmly in its position, the inclination of the surfaces must be smaller than the angle of a wedge that is barely capable of providing sufficient resistance in theory.

It appears, therefore, that the force of lateral adhesion acting between two bodies in contact is of great importance in all mechanical arts; the stability of architecture and carpentry depends largely on it. Since this kind of resistance is equally powerful when the force is applied in the direction of the surface—regardless of which part of the surface it acts upon—it follows that any body subjected to friction on all sides will remain in its position with the same force used to overcome the friction in order to bring it into that position. In fact, it will hold with a greater force, since lateral adhesion is generally slightly greater than friction. Consequently, a cylindrical wire cannot be withdrawn from a hole in a board by any direct force less than the force employed to insert it. This kind of stability, along with that of a wedge or nail resisting lateral pressure, provides the security for the lighter structures of carpentry, while those of architecture receive a great part of their stability from the accumulation of weight, which

### LECTURE XIII.

...makes the resistance of their lower parts to any lateral motion almost impossible to overcome.

When a hard body penetrates another, or when a substance is ground away by the attrition of another, the force that opposes the motion is to be considered a uniformly retarding force, much like the force of friction. There is no reason to imagine that the stiffness of a bar, whether longer or shorter, depends on the velocity of the body that bends it; additionally, the distance through which it may be bent without breaking is also limited only by the toughness of the materials. In the same manner, when the internal parts of a solid are broken and displaced by the penetration of another, or its external parts are worn away (abraded) by its attrition, the resistance is the same regardless of the velocity. The distance covered by the body before its velocity is spent is always proportional to the square of that velocity, or to the energy which results from a combination of the proportions of the velocity and the momentum.

# LECTURE XIV.

## ON ARCHITECTURE AND CARPENTRY.

The subjects that we have recently examined are to be considered as preliminary to the particular departments of practical mechanics. The first division of these is to consist of those employed in resisting forces of various kinds, but they may almost all be referred, without difficulty, to the general heads of architecture and carpentry, of which the principal business is to resist the force of gravity. Architecture, in its most extensive sense, may be understood as including carpentry, but the term is more usually applied to the use of those materials which are only required to resist the effects of a force tending principally to produce compression, while the materials used by carpenters are frequently subjected to the operation of a force which tends to stretch or to bend them. The works of architects are commonly executed in stone or brick, and those of carpenters in wood, in addition to the occasional use of iron and other metals in both cases.

The simplest problem in the mechanics of architecture appears to be to determine the most suitable form for a column. Assuming the length and weight are specified, it is important to investigate the form which provides the greatest possible strength; but it is somewhat difficult to determine the precise nature and direction of all the forces which are to be resisted. If we considered the column as a beam fixed in the ground and moved by a transverse force, it should be significantly tapered and reduced almost to a point at its end; but it is rare that any force of this kind can be powerful enough to do more than overcome the weight of the column alone, and it is only necessary to consider the load which presses vertically on it. Whether we consider the force as tending to bend or to crush it, the forms commonly employed will appear to be sufficiently suitable. Mr. La-

# LECTURE XIV.

Lagrange seems to have been misled by some intricacies of mathematical investigation—too far removed from physical accuracy—when he calculated that a cylinder was the strongest form for resisting flexure; in reality, that form approaches much more nearly to an oblong spheroid, whose outline is elliptical. The consideration of the flexure of a column is, however, of little practical importance in architecture; for, based on a rough estimate of the properties of the materials usually employed, it can be calculated that a stone column must be about forty times as high as it is thick to be capable of being bent by any weight that would not otherwise crush it; however, a bar of wood or iron may be bent by a longitudinal force if its length exceeds about twelve times its thickness. The force may therefore be considered as tending only to crush the column. Since the lower parts must support the weight of the upper parts in addition to the load pressing on the whole column, their thickness should be somewhat increased. Based on a consideration of the direction in which a fracture is most easily caused, it appears that the outline should be made a little convex on the outside and more curved above than below, which is the usual, though not universal, practice. An elliptical arc is perhaps the most suitable outline, or a curve formed by bending a ruler fixed at the top of the column. Sometimes the form is made to differ little from a cone, but such a shape is very inelegant. The reduction in thickness generally amounts to about one-sixth or one-seventh of the whole, and sometimes to one-fourth. (Plate XI. Fig. 149.)

For a lighthouse, where a great force of wind and water had to be resisted, Mr. Smeaton chose a curve with its concavity turned outward. If we calculated the best form for a wooden pillar intended to remain constantly immersed in water to a certain depth, we would find that a cone or pyramid would possess the greatest possible strength for resisting the motion of the water; and a cone more acute than this would be equally capable of resisting the force of the wind, assuming the wind to be less powerful than the water. Therefore, the part below the water might be widened to become a portion of a more obtuse cone, while the upper part remains more slender. Since the greatest agitation of the sea occurs near its surface, the base of the pillar might be slightly narrowed, so that the outline of the lower part is a little convex outward, if the depth of the water were

But in the case of a stone building, the strength often depends as much on the weight of the materials as on their cohesive power; and the lateral adhesion, which is significantly influenced by the weight, constitutes a very important part of the strength. To resist a force that tends to overturn the building, the form in which the weight provides the greatest strength is that of a conoid, or a solid whose outline is a parabola, concave towards the axis. However, to achieve lateral adhesion through weight that is proportional to the force at every point, the form must be cylindrical. Therefore, in a building situated like the pillar we have supposed, there appears to be no reason for making either part of the outline convex toward the axis when considered separately, although the angular junction of two cone sections might appropriately be rounded off; additionally, the upper parts might be slightly enlarged if it were desirable to reduce the thickness of the walls. 

But the Eddystone Lighthouse is entirely above sea level, even though in stormy weather every part of it is exposed to the action of the waves, with water sometimes thrown up to a much greater height than that of the lighthouse itself. Consequently, it may be considered as exposed to the force of a fluid that becomes increasingly powerful closer to the foundation. From this perspective, its form differs very little from what the most accurate theory would suggest, although it is probably a bit weaker around the middle of its height, or slightly lower, than in any other part. (Plate XI. Fig. 150.)

A wall must decrease in thickness as it rises, for the same reason that a column is tapered. If the wall is part of a house, it must be reduced even further, since the load it supports at different heights varies greatly due to the weight of the floors and the contents of the rooms. However, sometimes the slant of the wall surface may become inconvenient by encouraging the growth of moss and weeds. In building a wall, the first necessary precaution is to dig deep enough to determine the nature of the ground; the next is to lay a sufficiently wide and firm foundation. It has been very rightly recommended that, if a well is needed, it should be dug before the house foundations are laid to examine the qualities of the various strata which are to support them. Hence, the <term>reticulated walls</term>, sometimes employed by the ancients, in which all the joints were oblique, possessed very little durability. If the materials are thrown together without order, they press on the parts in contact with them; but occasionally, as in the case of piers or quays, this circumstance may be of some advantage in opposing external pressure; or at least the effect of such a pressure may remove the inconvenience which would otherwise arise from the irregularity of the structure.

In some cases, it is necessary to unite the stones of a building mechanically, either by cramps of iron fixed by means of melted lead, or by other methods similar to those more usually employed in carpentry. <term>Mr. Smeaton</term> was obliged to fix the stones of his lighthouse to the rock and to each other by <term>dovetail joints</term>, and to connect each horizontal tier with the tier below it by pins of wood passing through the stones, with wedges driven in at each end to make them expand and tie the stones fast together. But, in general, it is sufficient to employ mortar made of lime or *<term>terras</term>* <note>a volcanic ash used in hydraulic cement</note> and sand, the utility of which depends principally on the firmness and cohesive strength that it acquires as a result of its chemical properties. Sometimes the whole structure is composed of a mass which is at first soft but hardens as it dries; mud walls are built in this manner, and the materials called *<term>pisé</term>* <note>rammed earth construction</note> are of a similar nature. (Plate XI. Fig. 151.)

The wall or column, when raised, must in general help to support a single <term>lintel</term> or beam, an arch, a dome, or a roof of carpentry. The strength of the lintel depends more on the nature of the substance than on any art employed in forming it, except for the precaution of giving it as much depth as is convenient—especially toward the middle, if the depth is anywhere unequal. However, the construction of an <term>arch</term> affords considerable scope for the application of mechanical science.

The simplest theory of the <term>arch</term> supporting itself in equilibrium is that of <term>Dr. Hooke</term>, the greatest of all philosophical mechanics. When an arch has only its own weight to bear, it may be considered as the <term>inversion of a chain</term> suspended at each end; for the chain hangs in such a form that the weight of

Each link is held in equilibrium by the result of the two forces acting at its ends; these forces or tensions are produced, one by the weight of the part of the chain below the link, and the other by that same weight increased by the weight of the link itself. Both of these forces originally act in a vertical direction. Now, assuming the chain is inverted to form an arch of the same shape and weight, the relative positions of all the lines indicating the directions of the forces will remain the same. The forces act only in opposite directions, so they are combined in a similar way and balance each other under the same conditions, with this difference: the equilibrium of the chain is stable, while that of the arch is unstable. This property of equilibrium makes an accurate experimental proof of the proposition somewhat difficult, but it can be shown that a small amount of friction is enough to keep an arch formed by an inverted chain of beads in equilibrium. The shape is called a <term>*catenaria*</term> <note>a catenary curve</note> when the links are assumed to be infinitely small and the curvature is sharpest at the middle of the chain. It is not at all necessary for the experiment that the links of the chain are equal; the same method can be applied to determine the shape required for equilibrium, regardless of the length or weight of the arch’s individual parts. When the arch is to be loaded unevenly in different parts, we can include this factor in the experiment by hanging proportional weights from different parts of the chain. In this way, we can use wires or other chains to represent the pressure, adjusting them gradually until their ends hang in a specific line. Thus, we can find the shape that will best support the weight of the materials; the upper surface, or <term>*extrados*</term>, of the arch is represented by the same line in an inverted position, while the original chain shows the shape of the <term>*intrados*</term>, or the curve required for the arch stones themselves. In typical cases, the shape determined this way will differ little from a circular arc spanning about one-third of a full circle. It rises from the abutments at a 30° angle from the vertical line and never takes a direction much closer to being perpendicular to the horizon. It usually becomes more curved at some distance below the summit and then less curved again. (Plate XI. Figs. 152–154.)

But the assumption that an arch resists a weight acting only in a vertical direction is by no means perfectly applicable to cases that generally occur in practice. The pressure of loose stones and earth, moistened as they

This precaution is, however, entirely unnecessary in every respect, because the effect it is intended to prevent causes no inconvenience, except for requiring the skill of the architect. The effect of such a pressure only requires a greater curvature near the <term>abutments</term>, reducing the form nearly to that of an ellipse, and allowing the arch to rise at first in a vertical direction.

A bridge must also be calculated so as to support itself without being in danger of falling due to a lack of the lateral adhesion of its parts. In order that it may be of equal strength throughout in this respect, its depth at each point must be proportional to the weight of the parts beyond it. This property belongs to the curve called logarithmic, where the length corresponds to the logarithm of the depth. If the strength were provided by the arch stones only, this condition might be fulfilled by giving them the required thickness, independently of the general form of the arch; but all of the materials used in the construction of the bridge must be considered as adding to the strength, and the magnitude of the adhesion depends in great measure on the general outline.

We must examine next what is the most advantageous form for supporting any weight which may occasionally be placed on the bridge, particularly at its weakest part, which is usually the middle. Supposing the depth at the summit of the arch and at the abutments to be fixed, it may be reduced considerably in the intermediate parts without impairing the strength, and the outline may be composed of parabolic arcs, having their convexity turned towards each other. This remark also would be only applicable to the arch stones if they provided the whole strength of the bridge, but it must be extended in some measure to all of the materials forming it.

The tier of bricks cut obliquely, which is usually placed over a window or a door, is a real arch, but so flat as to allow the apparent outline to be horizontal. Mr. Coulomb observes that the greatest strength is obtained by causing all the joints to point toward a single center; but little reliance can be placed on so flat an arch, since it produces a lateral thrust which may easily overpower the resistance of the wall. For the horizontal force required to support each end of any arch is equal to the weight of a quantity of the materials which are supported by its summit, assuming them to be continued, at their actual depth, for the length of a semidiameter of the circle of which the summit of the arch is a portion. This simple calculation will enable an architect to avoid such accidents as have too often happened to bridges for want of sufficient firmness in the <term>abutments</term>. The equilibrium of a bridge, so far as it depends only on the form of the arch, is naturally unstable, and the smallest force which is capable of deranging it may completely destroy the structure; but when the stones or blocks composing it have flat surfaces in contact with each other, it is necessary that the line representing the direction of the pressure be so much disturbed as to exceed the limits of these surfaces at some part before the blocks can be displaced. When this curve, indicating the general pressure which results from the effect of a disturbing force combined with the original thrust, becomes more remote from the center of the blocks than one-sixth of their depth, the joints will begin to open on the convex side, but the arch may still stand while the curve remains within the limits of the blocks.

At this distance, it would be appropriate to use either a chain or some external pressure to maintain stability, since the weight itself would need to be increased infinitely if it were the only source of pressure on the lower parts. (Plate XII. Fig. 157.)

The dome of St. Paul’s Cathedral is elliptical and is built of wood, secured by strong chains consisting of iron bars. That of the Pantheon at Rome is nearly circular, and its lower parts are so much thicker than its upper parts that they provide sufficient resistance to their pressure. They are supported by walls of great thickness and are furnished with many projections which serve the purpose of abutments and buttresses. (Plate XII. Fig. 158, 159.)

A knowledge of the parts and proportions usually assigned to columns and to buildings in general, along with their technical names and divisions, belongs more to the subject of ornamental architecture than to functional architecture. Furthermore, the consideration of symmetry and elegance is largely outside the scope of the mechanical properties of bodies, which it is our present business to investigate. The five orders of ancient architecture are found to differ considerably in their proportions across the various remains of Greek and Roman edifices, yet certain characteristic distinctions always remain. The Tuscan is known by its strength and simplicity, without any specific ornament; the Doric by its <term>triglyphs</term>, or triangular grooves, above each column, which were intended to represent the ends of beams; the Ionic by its large <term>volutes</term>; and the Corinthian by the foliage surrounding its <term>capitals</term>. The Composite is usually identified by the combination of both these characters. Each order is lighter than the one preceding it and is sometimes employed above it in the upper parts of the same building. In general, the length of the Tuscan column, including its capital, is equal to about seven diameters of the base; that of the Doric is eight, the Ionic nine, and the Corinthian and Composite ten diameters. (Plate XII. Fig. 160–164.)

# LECTURE XIV.

The Gothic architects seem to have been superior to the Greeks in the mechanical arrangement of the parts of their buildings, so as to produce the most effective results in maintaining overall equilibrium. They made every essential part of their buildings an integral component of their system of ornament; even those decorations which a casual observer might think useless or detrimental are often designed—either through their strength or their weight—to serve a beneficial purpose. The pointed arch is not always ideal for equilibrium, but when it has a pillar resting on its summit, it is exceptionally strong. The most famous modern architects have sometimes been less successful than those of the Middle Ages; for lack of paying sufficient attention to mechanical principles, they have committed such errors in their attempts to achieve equilibrium that the results have been disastrous. Examples of this could be pointed out in the bridges of our own country and the churches of others; but if we master the true theory of pressure, we will be able to avoid similar errors without needing to examine the specific details that caused these accidents. (Plate XII. Fig. 165.)

The principles of equilibrium employed in architecture are equally applicable to many cases in carpentry. Where the work is mainly designed to withstand a thrust, there is little difference in how the forces operate; however, when a tie is introduced—that is, a piece which resists primarily through its cohesive strength—the parts often require to be arranged in a different manner. The general principle—that for three forces to remain in equilibrium, they must be proportional to the sides of a triangle corresponding to their directions—is sufficient for determining the distribution of pressure in almost every possible case. The conclusions drawn from this principle and from other similar considerations regarding the strength of materials will also be very useful in helping us determine the best shapes for beams, rafters, and all kinds of timbers, and how to arrange and connect them most effectively.

The use of the cohesive strength of materials in carpentry introduces a difficulty that hardly exists in architecture. Two blocks, placed

For this purpose, it is generally necessary to sacrifice a considerable portion of the strength of the materials employed. The most usual mode is to place the ends of the pieces side by side, first reducing their dimensions where a regular outline is required, and to procure a firm adhesion between them by means of external pressure, or to employ the natural adhesion of some parts which are made to project beyond the rest in each piece and receive in their spaces the corresponding projections of the other piece.

Where the adhesion is produced by external pressure only, it is advantageous to subdivide the joints into a considerable number of parts, as is usually done in the masts of ships, and to make the junction of any two pieces following each other in the same line as distant as possible from any other junction; for in this manner, the loss of strength may be diminished almost without limit, provided that the distance between the joints is great enough to afford a firm adhesion to each part. The junction may also be formed by an oblique line; but the slope must be so great that any lateral pressure may increase the stability of the wedge, the length being in a greater proportion to the depth than the pressure is to the adhesion that it causes; and the pieces must be pressed together very forcibly by means of hoops or bolts. (Plate XIII. Fig. 166.. 168.)

Where the natural adhesion of some projecting parts in each piece is employed, the projections must be long enough to secure their strength, and they must be as little prominent as possible, partly because the adjacent piece must be hollowed out to receive them, and partly because their strength is diminished when they project more than one-sixth of their length. A beam united to another in this manner is said to be <term>scarfed</term>. (Plate XIII. Fig. 169.)

In order to preserve the strength of a compound beam intended to resist a transverse action in a particular direction, it is necessary to avoid, as much as possible, reducing the depth of the beam in that direction, and to secure

strength unimpaired, by splicing or fishing it on the convex side; and if the
depth of the piece added be only half as great as that of the original beam,
the strength will be somewhat increased by the operation, supposing the two
ends to meet each other without any connection. Such pieces require, how-

or <term>joggles</term> let in to a certain depth, in order to prevent their sliding on each
other; and this mode of union is stronger than <term>scarfing</term> them, because it does
not diminish the depth. (Plate XIII. Fig. 170, 171.)

Where the pieces to be connected together are in different directions, the
end of one of them is usually reduced in its size, and becomes a <term>tenon</term>, while
a <term>mortise</term> is cut in the other for its reception, and the joint is also often se-
cured still more firmly by a <term>strap of iron</term>. If a <term>joist</term> be let into a beam, at its
upper edge, and made very tight by wedges, the strength of the beam will
not be materially diminished; but the changes of moisture and dryness
may very much impair the firmness of the union, and the end of the joist
may fail in dry weather to afford sufficient resistance to the bending of the
beam: so that in some cases it might be more advisable to cut the mortise
near the middle of the depth of the beam. If two pieces meet obliquely, and
one of them exerts a thrust against the other, the simplest mode of opposing
this thrust is to bind them together by a strap of iron fixed to the second
piece; this strap renders it impossible for the first to advance without having
its extremity crushed; it is also common to make a mortise in the second
piece, a part of which serves as an <term>abutment</term> for the first: and for this pur-

projection sufficient force of adhesion, a condition which is the more easily
fulfilled when the action of the strap produces a pressure on it. The assist-

each other, and the force tends to draw one of them away from the other: in
this case the mortise may be made a little wider at the further part, and the
end of the tenon may be made to fit it by driving in wedges, in the same
manner as <term>Mr. Smeaton</term> united his blocks of stone; but a large mortise would
weaken the beam too much, and a strong strap or hoop is usually required for

additional security. Such a strap ought always to be as straight as possible, so as to act only in the direction of the force to be resisted: it has been too common to adapt the strap to the form of the beams, or to make it deviate in other ways from a straight line. But wherever a strap is bent in any direction to a distance from a straight line equal only to its depth in that direction, its strength is so reduced that it does not exceed one-seventh of what it would have been if it had remained straight. (Plate XIV. Fig. 172 .. 174.)

It is equally necessary in all other cases that occur in carpentry to avoid a transverse strain as much as possible. The disadvantage of this is obvious from the great inferiority of the strength of any substance resisting a transverse force compared to its original cohesive or repulsive strength. For similar reasons, it is proper to avoid using a very wide angle at a point where a load is supported; the great slant of the two pieces forming the angle requires them to exert a great force in order to oppose a much smaller one. Allowance must also be made for the contraction of the timber, and care must be taken that it does not so alter the arrangement of the parts as to bring a disproportionate strain on a point not intended to support it. If the two pieces forming an obtuse angle consisted, either wholly or partly, of wood cut across the grain, and the piece joining their ends were cut in the usual manner, the slanted pieces would contract considerably more as they became drier, and the angle would become more obtuse, so that the strain produced by a given weight would be greater than in the original state of the triangle. Sometimes the work is liable to be disrupted by the operation of a lateral force, which may have appeared too trifling to produce any significant effect, but which may still destroy the greater part of the strength by causing the resistances to deviate from the plane of the forces they are intended to oppose.

The framing of a roof is one of the most common and most important subjects for the application of the theory of carpentry. If the rafters were simply to lean against the walls, they would push them outwards; a tie beam is therefore necessary to counteract this thrust. In order to enable the tie beam to support a weight, a king post is suspended from the rafters; and frequently braces are again erected from the bottom of the king post to sup-

Sometimes a flat or less steeply inclined portion is placed in the middle, forming a <term>curb</term> or <term>mansard roof</term>, which somewhat resembles an arch. This form has the advantage, when properly proportioned, of lessening the transverse strain on the rafters by making them shorter; however, this purpose is served equally well by adding the braces previously mentioned. A curb roof provides more interior space than a plain roof of the same height and also produces somewhat less strain on the <term>tie beam</term> or the abutments. The tie beam may be suspended from it by a <term>king post</term> and two <term>queen posts</term> descending perpendicularly from the joints; the place of the king post may also be supplied by a crossbeam uniting the heads of the queen posts and keeping them at a proper distance. This beam may also be suspended by a shorter king post from the summit. Such a roof appears to be more advantageous than is commonly supposed. (Plate XIII, Figures 175–177.)

The angle of inclination of a roof to the horizon usually varies in different climates. In Italy, the height is generally less than one-fourth of the width. In England, it was formerly three-fourths, but it now commonly approaches the Italian proportion much more closely. In northern climates, a steep roof is required because of snowfall, which greatly increases the lateral thrust of the rafters. The horizontal force exerted by a roof is always proportional to the length of a line perpendicular to the rafter, descending from its end until it meets another similar line drawn from the opposite rafter; this perpendicular is obviously much increased when the roof becomes very flat. But for resisting the transverse strain, which tends to break the rafters themselves, a low roof is stronger than a high one, assuming the number of braces and queen posts is equal on both. If we have to support a given weight by a beam or rafter—whether it is placed in the middle or equally divided throughout its length—we neither gain nor lose force by lengthening the beam and raising it higher while the horizontal span remains the same. This is because the obliquity <note>the slant or angle of the beam</note> reduces the effect of the weight in precisely the same ratio that the length of the beam diminishes its strength. However, by lengthening the beam, we also add to the weight that must be supported, and we thus diminish the strength of the roof. It must be observed, when calculating the strength of a rafter, that the slight bending produced by the transverse strain has a material

Wooden bridges, and the temporary <term>centering</term> (centers) on which stone arches are supported during their construction, depend on nearly the same principles as roofs: the external parts usually support a thrust, and the internal parts act as ties; but the abutments are generally capable of withstanding a horizontal thrust without difficulty, so that through their assistance, the strain on the ties is considerably diminished. Great strength may also be obtained where it is practical to support each part of the centering by two beams in the direction of chords, bearing directly on the abutments. (Plate XIV, Figures 178, 179.)

The various items of household furniture belong to subordinate branches of carpentry, but their form is generally adapted more for convenience and elegance than for strength and durability. Yet even in making a chair, there is room for error and for improvement; the same principles that guide us in framing a roof are applicable here; but if they were followed strictly, they would lead us to use bars crossing each other in an unattractive manner. Doors, gates, locks, and hinges are either parts of the carpenter’s work or appendages to it; and it is possible that, through careful consideration, improvements might be made in all of them. Mr. Parker has devoted much time and labor to the subject of gates, along with their hinges and fastenings, and has presented a very useful collection of models to the Royal Institution, which show the results of his investigations.

## LECTURE XV.

### ON MACHINERY.

Having taken a general view of those branches of practical <term>mechanics</term> in which forces are to be resisted, we are next to consider the modifications of forces and motions. First, we will examine the modes of applying forces, of changing their direction and intensity, and of communicating them to different parts of our machines through the intervention of rods, joints, cranks, wheelwork, ropes, or other flexible substances. Second, we will look at the structure of these substances and the methods by which the joining of flexible fibers in general may be achieved. Third, we will consider the regulation and equalization of motion by means of clocks and watches.

The modes of applying mechanical forces are almost as varied as the machines that are constructed and the purposes for which they are employed. However, in general, the strength of men is applied by means of levers, <term>winches</term>, or <term>walking wheels</term> (which slide beneath them as they attempt to climb); and the strength of other animals is applied by a horizontal arm projecting from a vertical axis to which they are harnessed, and sometimes also by causing them to walk on or inside a movable wheel. Many of these arrangements may, however, be very conveniently considered as belonging to the particular objects for which each machine is constructed, especially the methods for raising weights by <term>cranes</term> and grinding substances by <term>mills</term>.

When motion is simply communicated to a substance placed before the moving body, materials must be used that are capable of exerting a repulsive force, or a thrust; these are generally of the same kind as those sometimes involved in the operations of architecture, but more commonly in those of carpentry—particularly metal and wood. But when the body to be moved is behind the moving power and is pulled along by it,

chains or ropes are sometimes more convenient. In the joining of wood for movable machinery, it is generally advisable to avoid using metal pins or bolts; for these, by their greater weight and hardness, sometimes damage the wood in contact with them and become loose.

When the direction of the communicated motion must also be changed, levers or cranks may be used, joined by various kinds of joints or hinges. Sometimes a long series of connected rods is suspended by other rods or chains so as to convey the effect of the force to a considerable distance; in this case, the motion is generally alternating—for example, when pumps are operated by means of a waterwheel at a distance from the shaft in which the pumps are placed. In this arrangement, there is no necessary loss of power due to the alternating motion of the rods; for if they are suspended at equal distances from several fixed points, they will move backward and forward like a single pendulum. However, the amount of friction is the main drawback caused by the weight of the series. Where a lever is used for changing the direction of a great force, its strength may be increased by adding a frame projecting in the direction of its depth; and if the lever is bent, a crosspiece joining its arms is even more necessary. (Plate XIV. Fig. 180 . . 182.)

For the communication of a rotary motion, Dr. Hooke’s universal joint is sometimes useful, especially when the angle of inclination does not need to be significantly changed; but if the angle is large, the rotation is not transferred evenly to the new axis at all points of its revolution. This joint is formed by a cross making the diameters of two semicircles, one of which is fixed at the end of each axis. (Plate XIV. Fig. 183.)

The best way to connect a rotary motion with an alternating one is, in all common cases, to use a crank acting on one end of a long rod that has a joint at the other end. If the rotary motion of the crank is steady, the progressive motion of the rod will be gradually accelerated and slowed down, and for a considerable part of the revolution, the force exerted will be nearly uniform. However, if we attempted to give the rod its full velocity in each direction all at once—as has sometimes been done by inclined planes or by wheelwork—the motion would become extremely

On the other hand, it must be noted that the force applied to a machine can, in general, be divided into two portions: one employed in opposing another force so as to produce <term>equilibrium</term> only, and the other in generating <term>momentum</term>. With respect to the first portion, a single <term>crank</term> has the inconvenience of continually changing the <term>mechanical advantage</term> of the machine. With respect to the second, its motion in the second quarter of its revolution is accelerated instead of being slowed by the <term>inertia</term> which this portion of the force is intended to overcome; and from a combination of both these causes, the motion must necessarily be rendered very irregular. These issues may, however, be completely removed by always employing cranks in pairs, with one of them fixed so as to make a right angle with the other. This is also the best position for two <term>winches</term> to be turned by two laborers, since the point of the circle in which a man can exert his greatest strength is nearly at the distance of a right angle, or a little more, from the point at which his force is smallest.

An <term>alternate motion</term> may be communicated to a rod so that the force may be either uniformly exerted or varied according to any given rule, by means of an inclined surface formed into a proper curve and acting on a <term>friction wheel</term> fixed to the rod; a single plane surface, placed obliquely, would answer sufficiently well for this purpose. But in such cases, as well as when a crank is used, it is necessary to employ other means for supporting the rod in its proper position; this may either be done by additional friction wheels or, in a more elegant manner, by an arrangement of <term>jointed rods</term> that will cause the end of one of them to move in a curve which does not significantly differ from a straight line. If we fix two pins in a beam so as to connect two equal rods to it, the ends of which are joined by a third rod, and the end of this third rod nearest to the center of the beam is connected to a second beam of a proper length, the opposite end of the rod will initially describe a straight line. For this purpose, the length of the second beam must be to the distance of the nearest pin from the center as that distance is to the distance of the pins from each other. The same effect may also be produced by means of a frame made of two pieces, each a

The proportions of the rods may also be made more convenient than these, and others may be added to them if required, which may make a line move so as to remain always in parallel directions. (*Plate XIV. Fig. 185–188.*)

But of all the modes of transmitting motion, the most extensively useful is the employment of wheelwork, which is capable of varying its direction and its velocity without any limit.

Wheels are sometimes turned by simple contact with each other; sometimes by the use of cords, straps, or chains passing over them; and in these cases the minute bumps on the surfaces, or whatever else may be the cause of friction, prevent them from sliding against each other. Where a broad strap runs on a wheel, it is usually kept in its place not by making the edge of the wheel protrude, but, on the contrary, by making the middle prominent: the reason for this may be understood by examining the manner in which a tight strap running on a cone would tend to move toward its thickest part. Sometimes pins are also fixed in the wheels and inserted into holes in the straps; a method only practical where the motion is slow and steady. A smooth motion may also be obtained, with considerable force, by forming the surfaces of the wheels into brushes of hair. (*Plate XV. Fig. 189.*)

More commonly, however, the circumferences of the adjacent wheels are formed into teeth, pushing each other as if with the ends of so many levers, either exactly or nearly in the common direction of the circumferences; and sometimes an <term>endless screw</term> is substituted for one of the wheels. In forming the teeth of wheels, it is important to determine the curvature which will achieve a steady transmission of motion with the least possible friction. For the steady transmission of motion, two methods have been recommended: one, that the lower part of the face of each tooth should be a straight line in the direction of the radius, and the upper part a portion of an <term>epicycloid</term>, that is, of a curve described by a point of a

a circle rolling on the wheel, the diameter of which must be half that of the opposite wheel. In this case, it can be demonstrated that the plane surface of each tooth will act on the curved surface of the opposite tooth so as to produce a uniform angular motion in both wheels. The other method is to shape all the surfaces into portions of the involutes of circles (the curves described by a point on a thread that has been wound around the wheel as it is uncoiled). This method appears to serve the purpose in an easier and simpler manner than the first. It can be experimentally demonstrated that a uniform motion is produced by the action of these curves on each other: if we cut two boards into shapes terminated by these curves, divide the surfaces by lines into equal or proportional angular sections, and fix them on any two centers, we shall find that as they revolve, whichever parts of the surfaces may be in contact, the corresponding lines will always meet each other. (*Plate XV. Fig. 190 – 192.*)

Both of these methods may be derived from the general principle that the teeth of one wheel must be of such a form that their outline is described by the revolution of a curve upon a given circle, while the outline of the teeth of the other wheel is described by the same curve revolving within the circle. It has been supposed by some of the best authors that the epicycloidal tooth also has the advantage of completely avoiding friction; however, this is by no means true, and it is even impossible to invent any shape for gear teeth that will allow them to act on other teeth without friction. In order to diminish friction as much as possible, the teeth must be as small and as numerous as is consistent with strength and durability; for the effect of friction always increases with the distance of the point of contact from the line joining the centers of the wheels. In calculating the amount of friction, the velocity with which the parts slide over each other has generally been used as its measure. This is a slight conceptual inaccuracy, for, as we have already seen, the actual resistance is not at all increased by increasing the relative velocity; however, the effect of that resistance in retarding the motion of the wheels can be shown, from the general laws of mechanics, to be proportional to the relative velocity determined in this way. When it is possible to make one wheel act on teeth fixed in the concave surface of another, the friction may be reduced in the proportion of the difference of the diameters to their sum. If

If it is desired to produce a high angular velocity with the smallest possible quantity of wheelwork, the diameter of each wheel must be between three and four times as large as that of the pinion on which it acts. Where the pinion drives the wheel, it is sometimes made with only three or four teeth; but it is much better in general to have at least six or eight; and considering the additional labor of increasing the number of wheels, it may be advisable to assign more teeth to each of them than the number resulting from the calculation; so that we may allow 30 or 40 teeth to a wheel acting on a pinion of 6 or 8. In works which do not require a high degree of strength, the wheels sometimes have a much greater number of teeth than this; and on the other hand, an endless screw or a spiral acts as a pinion of one tooth, since it moves the wheel through the width of only one tooth in each revolution. For a pinion of six teeth, it would be better to have a wheel of 35 or 37 than 36; for each tooth of the wheel would thus act in turn upon each tooth of the pinion, and the mechanism would wear more evenly than if the same teeth continued to meet in each revolution. The teeth of the pinion should also be somewhat stronger than those of the wheel, in order to support the more frequent recurrence of friction. It has been proposed, for the coarser kinds of wheelwork, to divide the distance between the middle points of two adjoining teeth into 30 parts, and to assign 16 to the tooth of the pinion, and 13 to that of the wheel, allowing 1 for freedom of motion.

The wheel and pinion may either be situated in the same plane, both being commonly of the kind named spur wheels, or their planes may form an angle: in this case one of them may be a crown or contrate wheel, or both of them may be beveled, the teeth being cut obliquely. According to the relative size of the wheels, the angle of the bevel must be different, so that the velocities of the wheels may be in the same proportion at both ends of their oblique faces: for this purpose, the faces of all the teeth must be directed to the point where the axes would meet. (*Plate XV. Fig. 193, 194.*)
