### LECTURE XV.

In cases where a motion that is not perfectly uniform is required—as sometimes happens in the construction of <term>clocks</term>, but more frequently in <term>orreries</term>—the <term>wheels</term> may either be divided slightly unequally, or the <term>axis</term> may be placed slightly off-<term>centre</term>. These <term>eccentric wheels</term> may either act on other <term>eccentric</term> <term>wheels</term> or, if they are made as <term>contrate wheels</term>, upon a lengthened <term>pinion</term>. (Plate XV. Fig. 195, 196.)

An arrangement is sometimes made for separating <term>wheels</term> that are intended to turn each other and for reconnecting them at will; through these operations, the <term>wheels</term> are said to be thrown out of <term>gear</term> and into <term>gear</term> again.

When a <term>wheel</term> revolves around another and is fixed so that it remains nearly in a parallel direction, causing the central <term>wheel</term> to turn around its <term>axis</term>, the apparatus is called a <term>sun and planet wheel</term>. In this case, the circumference of the central <term>wheel</term> moves as fast as that of the revolving <term>wheel</term>, each point of which describes a circle equal in diameter to the distance between the <term>centres</term> of the two <term>wheels</term>. Consequently, when the <term>wheels</term> are equal, the central <term>wheel</term> makes two revolutions every time the exterior <term>wheel</term> travels around it. If the central <term>wheel</term> is fixed, and the exterior <term>wheel</term> is caused to turn on its own <term>centre</term> during its revolution by the effect of the contact of the <term>teeth</term>, it will make one more turn in every revolution relative to the surrounding objects than it would make if its <term>centre</term> were at rest during one turn of the <term>wheel</term> which is fixed; and this circumstance must be remembered when such <term>wheels</term> are employed in <term>planetariums</term>.

<term>Wheels</term> are usually made of <term>wood</term>, of <term>iron</term> (either cast or wrought), of <term>steel</term>, or of <term>brass</term>. The <term>teeth</term> of metal <term>wheels</term> are generally cut by means of a <term>machine</term>; the <term>wheel</term> is fixed on an <term>axis</term> which also carries a plate furnished with a variety of circles, divided into different numbers of equal parts and marked by small excavations. These are brought in succession under the point of a <term>spring</term>, which holds the <term>axis</term> firm, while the intervals between the <term>teeth</term> are quickly cut out by a <term>revolving saw</term> of steel. The <term>teeth</term> are afterward finished by a <term>file</term>; and a <term>machine</term> has also been invented for holding and working the <term>file</term>. (Plate XV. Fig. 197.)

This is generally achieved by allowing a weight to descend that has been previously raised, or a spring to unbend itself from a state of forced <term>flexure</term>, as is exemplified in the weights and springs of <term>clocks</term> and <term>watches</term>. The common <term>kitchen jack</term> is also employed for prolonging and equalizing the operation of a weight; in the <term>patent jack</term>, the same effect is produced by an alternating motion, the <term>axis</term> being impelled backward and forward, as in <term>clocks</term> and <term>watches</term>, by means of an <term>escapement</term>, and the role of a <term>balance spring</term> being supplied by the twisting and untwisting of a cord.

In these machines, as well as in many others of greater magnitude, the <term>flywheel</term> is a very important part; its velocity is increased by the operation of any part of the force that happens to be superfluous, and its <term>rotatory power</term> serves to continue the motion when the force is diminished or withdrawn. Thus, when a man turns a <term>winch</term>, he can exert twice as much force in some positions as in others, and a <term>fly</term> enables him in some cases to do nearly one-third more work. In the <term>pile engine</term> also, without the help of the <term>fly</term>, the horses would fall for want of a <term>counterpoise</term> as soon as the weight is disengaged. Such a <term>fly</term> ought to be heavy, and its motion must not be too rapid; otherwise, the resistance of the air will destroy too much of the motion. But in the <term>kitchen jack</term>, as well as in the striking part of a <term>clock</term>, where the superfluous force is purposely destroyed, the <term>fly</term> is made light and strikes the air with a broad surface. An effect similar to that of a <term>fly</term> and a <term>spring</term> is sometimes produced in <term>hydraulic machines</term> by the introduction of an <term>air vessel</term>; the air contained within it is compressed more or less according to the intensity of the force, and it exerts a more uniform pressure in expelling the fluid that is forced irregularly into it.

## LECTURE XVI.

### ON THE UNION OF FLEXIBLE FIBRES.

**T**HE strength of cordage, and of other substances which are employed in the transmission of motion where flexibility is required—as well as the utility of other flexible materials which serve for furniture or for clothing—depends principally upon the lateral adhesion produced by twisting, or by the intermixture of fibres. The union of flexible fibres, therefore, being frequently useful for the transmission of motion, and the machinery usually employed for producing it belonging directly to the subject of the modification of motion, we may properly consider at present, as far as our plan will allow us, those important branches of the mechanical arts whose object is to achieve a union of this kind.

When a chain is made of wire, each link is separately bent and remains united with the neighboring links because of its rigidity; but the fibres of vegetable and of animal substances must be united by other means. For this purpose, we have recourse to the force of friction, or rather of lateral adhesion, and the fibres are so disposed that, besides the mutual pressure which their own elasticity causes them to exert, any additional force applied in the direction of the length of the whole aggregate tends to bring the parts into closer contact and to augment the adhesion, in the same manner as we have already seen that a wedge and a screw may be held in their positions. The simple art of tying a knot, and the more complicated processes of spinning, ropemaking, weaving, and felting, derive their utility from this principle.

When a line is coiled around a cylinder—for instance, in letting down a weight by means of a rope which slides on a post, or on such a grooved cylinder as is sometimes employed to enable a person to lower himself from a window in cases of fire—the pressure on the whole circumference

Or, if the weights acting on the different ends are different, the adhesion may be a little greater or less than in this proportion, according to the manner in which the rope is applied. If such a rope made two or three coils, it would be impossible to apply a force sufficient to cause it to slide in the grooves.

From considering the effect of a force which is counteracted by other forces acting obliquely, we may understand both the effect of twisting in binding the parts of a rope together and its drawback in causing the strength of the fibers to act with a mechanical disadvantage. The greater the obliquity of the fibers, the greater their adhesion will be, but the greater also will be their immediate tension as a consequence of the action of a given force in the direction of the rope. Thus, after employing as much obliquity and as much tension as is sufficient to connect the fibers firmly in all cases of relaxation and flexure, and to prevent the penetration of moisture to some degree, any further twisting only tends to overpower the original cohesion of the fibers along their length.

The mechanism of simple spinning is easily understood; where the hand is used, care is taken to intermix the fibers sufficiently and to engage their ends as much as possible in the center. It is obvious that if any fiber were entirely on the outside of the rest, it could not be held in the yarn; in general, however, the materials are already in such a state of intermixture as to render this precaution unnecessary. Where we have a number of single continuous fibers, as in reeled silk, they are sufficiently connected by twisting, and we have no need of spinning. In both cases, such machinery has been invented for performing the necessary operations as is both honorable and lucrative to the British nation.

But if two such threads are held in contact at a specific point on the circumference of each, this point is made stationary by the opposition of equal forces acting in contrary directions. It becomes the center around which both threads are carried by the remaining forces, so that they continue to twist around each other until the new combination creates a tension capable of counterbalancing the remaining tension of the original threads. Three, four, or more threads may be joined in nearly the same manner: a <term>strand</term> consists of a significant number of yarns thus twisted together, generally from sixteen to twenty-five; a <term>hawser</term> consists of three strands, a <term>shroud</term> of four, and a <term>cable</term> of three hawsers or shrouds. Shroud-laid <term>cordage</term> has the disadvantage of being hollow in the center, or of requiring a greater change of form in the strands to fill the empty space; in undergoing this change, the cordage stretches and is strained unequally. The relative position and the comparative tension of all the fibers in these complicated combinations are not very easily determined by calculation. However, experience shows that it is most advantageous for the strength of the ropes to twist the strands—when they are being combined—in a direction that untwists the yarns they are made of; that is, to increase the twist of the strands themselves. Probably, the greatest strength is achieved when the final slant of the individual fibers is minimal and most consistent. This advantage is largely achieved by Mr. Huddart’s method of adjusting the length of the strand to its position in the rope, and his "registered cordage" appears to derive a clear superiority from this arrangement of the strands. A very strong rope may also be made by twisting five or six strands around a seventh as an axis. After much use, the central strand, or "heart," is often found to be worn down to <term>oakum</term>. It should be twisted more than the rest to allow it to stretch slightly; however, such ropes are unsuitable for running rigging or any use where they are frequently bent.

Ropes are most commonly made of <term>hemp</term>, but various other plant materials are occasionally used. The Chinese even use woody fibers, and the bark of trees provides cordage for other nations. Indeed, in this country, we have an example in the use of lime tree bark, which is used for garden matting. The finest hemp is imported from Riga and St. Petersburg. The

The male and female flowers of hemp are on different plants; the male plants ripen earliest and require being pulled first. They are prepared for dressing by being exposed to the air, and the fibrous part is separated from the dry pulp by beating and hackling. In spinning the yarn, the hemp is fastened around the waist; the wheel is turned by an assistant, and the spinner, walking backward, draws out the fibers with his hands. When one length of the walk has been spun, it is immediately reeled to prevent its untwisting. The machines employed in continuing the process of rope-making are of simple construction, but both skill and attention are required in applying them so as to produce an even texture in every part of the rope. The tendency of two strands to twist, as a result of the tension arising from the original twist of the yarns, is not sufficient to achieve equilibrium because of the friction and rigidity that must be overcome; therefore, it is necessary to employ force in order to assist this tendency, and the strands or ropes afterward spontaneously retain the form which has thus been given to them; even the largest ropes require external force in order to make them twist at all.

The individual ropes that make up a common cable, when separate, are stronger than the cable itself in a proportion of about 4 to 3; and a rope worked up from yarns 180 yards in length down to 135 yards has been found to be stronger than when reduced to 120 yards, in a ratio of 6 to 5. The difference is due partly to the slant of the fibers and partly to the unequal tension produced by twisting. Mr. Huddart's ropes of 100 yarns lose only about one-eighth of the total strength of the yarns; and his experiments appear to show that similar ropes made in the common manner retain only one-half of their original strength. The tarring of ropes, although sometimes necessary for their preservation from decay, is found to lessen their strength, probably because it produces partial adhesions between some of the fibers, which cause them to be disproportionately strained. A rope is also said to be weaker when wet than when dry, perhaps because the water enables the fibers to slide more easily against each other, or because the presence of water is generally favorable to separation of any kind. A good hemp rope will support, without danger, one-fifth as many tons as the square of its circumference in inches.

# LECTURE XVI.

[Cultiva]tion is encouraged in this country by a bounty from the government, and a large quantity is also imported from Northern Europe. The plant, while green, is laid in water for ten days and undergoes a chemical change which softens the pulpy part without injuring the strength of the fibers; this makes it easier, once it has been dried and exposed to the air for two weeks, to separate the two substances during the processing stage. This is performed by beating it with the edge of a flat piece of wood—using angled strokes that run nearly in the direction of the fibers—and afterwards combing it in order to arrange the fibers into a regular order and prepare them for spinning. The refuse, consisting of the shorter fibers, is called tow.

Cotton is a fine fibrous substance that encases the seeds of a plant. The best is brought from the Isle of Bourbon, but by far the greatest quantity comes from the West Indies, although the Turkish territories as well as the East Indies furnish us with a considerable supply. It is usually white, but there is a yellow variety which is used for nankeens. It is separated from the seeds by means of rollers, between which it passes, leaving the seeds behind. It is then beaten on a flake, or a stool covered with a texture of cord. Next, it is carded, either by hand—the fibers being drawn into regular order by cards (brushes made of fine pointed wire)—or, more commonly, by machinery, where the cards are arranged on cylinders that revolve nearly in contact with each other. The drawing or roving machine then pulls it into long flakes to prepare it for spinning by Sir Richard Arkwright's machines or spinning jennies, which produce forty threads at once through the labor of a single person.

The silkworm is bred in the greatest abundance in Italy and in Asia; it has lately been introduced very successfully into the British possessions in the East Indies. The principal food of the caterpillar is the white mulberry tree, which is too delicate to thrive well in northern climates; in Italy, the trees are planted in beds, like willows, and the foliage is cut as it is needed. The room in which the worms are fed is kept at a temperature of 80 degrees Fahrenheit. The eggs from the previous year are hatched either by body heat or by the heat of the sun. At six weeks old, the caterpillars begin to spin—first, a light external texture, which is carded and spun for coarse silk, and afterwards, a compact oval pod or cocoon made of one continuous thread. The silk is either yellow or white, but the white is only an accidental variety. Through repeated washings, the yellow silk is bleached, and that which is originally white acquires a more perfect whiteness. Soap is also used to remove a gummy substance that accompanies the silk of the cocoons.

Wool is categorized into two principal varieties: long and short wool. The longest comes from Lincolnshire; it is combed by means of instruments equipped with a double row of long, sharp teeth made of iron or steel. It is repeatedly drawn from one comb to the other, with heat and a little oil being used in the process. The fleeces of long wool are generally heavier than those of short wool, but less valuable because of their coarseness; they are used for worsteds and for cloths in which the individual threads remain visible, such as stuffs, shalloons, serges, and tammies. Short wool, on the contrary, is carded and used for cloths in which the individual threads are hidden by the projecting fibers.

The primary use of thread and yarn, once spun, is for weaving. The same force of lateral adhesion that holds the twisted fibers of each thread in place is also employed here to give firmness to the cloth; and this adhesion is generally increased by the action of any external force that tends to strain the entire texture.

The first step in weaving is to form a warp, which consists of threads placed side by side, running the length of the piece and sufficient in number to make up its breadth. Once this is wound on a beam or roller in the loom, the threads are drawn through a harness consisting of loops made of twine fixed to bars or frames. This harness raises and lowers the threads in succession using treadles moved by the feet, in an order that varies according to the nature of the intended work. Crape is composed of threads that are so strongly twisted they have a tendency to curl; in weaving it, moisture is sometimes used to prevent this tendency during the process. Woolen cloth, once woven, is made stronger and more compact by using a fulling mill, in which it is beaten by heavy wooden hammers, while fullers' earth or alkaline substances of animal origin are applied to cleanse it. In this operation, both its length and breadth are reduced, and it is brought to a texture similar to that of felt. The reason for this contraction is likely that all the fibers are bent by the action of the hammer, though not all equally; those that have been bent the most are prevented from returning to their original length by their adhesion to neighboring fibers. After fulling, the cloth is roughened using teasels, which are grown for this purpose, and the most prominent fibers are cut away through the operation of shearing.

The lateral adhesion of various kinds of fibers also provides strength to felted substances, assisted, as some claim, by tiny barbs with which the fur fibers are said to be equipped. However, its overall strength is much lower than that of cloth, partly because the fibers are generally much shorter and partly because their arrangement is less precisely organized.

The materials commonly used for felting are rabbit and beaver furs, mixed with each other and with sheep's wool in various proportions, depending on the required quality. A very fine fur has recently been discovered on the skin of a species of seal, mixed with its hair; it has been used not only for felting but also for spinning and weaving into a cloth resembling East Indian shawls. Rabbit fur is also mixed with coarser hair, which is separated by first being pulled from the skins with a sharp knife. The materials to be felted are thoroughly mixed through the process of bowing, which relies on the vibrations of an elastic string; the rapid alternating motions are particularly well-suited to removing all irregular knots and tangles among the fibers and arranging them in a very

The black dye is composed of logwood, sulfate of iron, and a little acetate of copper, or verdigris; and the stiffening is a thin glue.

The texture of paper is hardly different from that of felt, except that its fibers are less visible to the naked eye. To make white paper, linen rags are ground with warm water in a mill into a paste with the consistency of cream; a portion of the paste is taken up in a wire sieve, which is passed diagonally through it. After being shaken slightly, the paste settles into a sheet, which is turned out onto a piece of flannel. Once a number of sheets have been formed in this way, they are then pressed—first with flannel placed between them, and afterward on their own while they are still moist. For thick paper, two or more sheets are laid on top of each other before the first pressing. To fill the pores of the paper and to increase its strength, a size is used, which is generally made by boiling shreds of parchment or untanned leather. Sometimes the size is added after printing on the paper, but this is only done in works of lesser quality, and not at all in this country.

These are the principal examples of the union of flexible fibers for various purposes of strength or convenience. Their importance is such that they might be considered worthy of more detailed study; however, we are not likely to make any significant improvements in these areas of mechanical art through the application of theoretical refinements.

### LECTURE XVII. ON TIMEKEEPERS.
2

The measurement of time using clocks and watches is a very important and interesting branch of practical mechanics. This subject is closely connected to the study of astronomical instruments, but it does not rely essentially on astronomical principles.

Time is measured by motion; however, for motion to be a true measure of time, it must be uniform. Currently, a motion that is perfectly free and undisturbed—and therefore uniform—is impossible to achieve because of the resistances inherent in the nature of physical materials. Therefore, it is necessary to seek some method of approximating such a motion. Determining time through astronomy, which is the most accurate method, can only be done under specific conditions, and even then, it is of little help in dividing time into small intervals.

The earliest timekeepers somewhat resembled the hourglasses that are still used occasionally; they measured the flow of a specific quantity of water, rather than sand, through a small opening. In these <term>clepsydrae</term> <note>ancient water clocks</note>, Vitruvius's account indicates that geared mechanisms were used, and the hour was displayed on a graduated scale. These markings were also likely adjusted to correct errors caused by changes in velocity, which occurred as the water level in the reservoir varied. However, this problem was sometimes entirely avoided by using a constant stream to keep the vessel full or, more elegantly, by using the siphon of Hero. This was a curved tube supported by a float, ensuring that its lower opening—where the water was released—remained at a constant distance below the surface. Dr. Hooke proposed to keep the reservoir full by using a

Various other modes might also be devised for making cheap and simple timekeepers on similar principles, dependent on the motion of various liquids or gases; but great accuracy could scarcely be expected from them. A candle sometimes serves as a coarse measure of time; and by burning a thread which passes through it, it may easily be made to answer the purpose of an alarm.

Clocks and watches are machines in which wheelwork is employed for the measurement of time, being driven by a weight or by a spring, and regulated by a pendulum or a balance. Watches differ from clocks in being portable, and this condition excludes the pendulum and the weight from their construction.

It is conjectured that the Saracens <note>a historical term for Muslims</note> had clocks which were moved by weights as early as the eleventh century. Trithemius mentions an <term>orrery</term> <note>a mechanical model of the solar system</note>, moved by a weight and keeping time, which was sent in 1232 by the Sultan of Egypt as a present to the Emperor Frederick II. Wallingford, in 1326, had made a clock which was regulated by a <term>fly</term> <note>a rotating fan used as a governor to regulate speed through air resistance</note>. The use of such a fly in equalizing motion depends on the resistance of the air, which increases rapidly when the velocity is increased, and therefore prevents any great inequality in the motion, as long as the moving power varies but little. If the action of the weight were transmitted with perfect regularity by the wheels, and the specific gravity of the air remained unaltered by pressure or by temperature, a fly clock might be a perfect machine; the weight would always be exactly counterbalanced by the resistance of the air attending a certain velocity of the fly. It might even be possible to regulate the inequalities of the action of the weight by causing the fly to open and shut, or to turn on an axis by means of a spring, according to the magnitude of the resistance. The unequal density of the air would, however, still remain uncompensated; and in this respect, a liquid would be a better medium than a gas. For experiments which are but of short duration and which require great precision, a <term>chronometer</term> regulated by a simple fly is still a useful instrument. Mr. Whitehurst’s apparatus for measuring the time occupied in the descent of heavy bodies is governed by a fly; the index is stopped by the

The alternating motion of a balance, thrown back and forth by the successive actions of a wheel impelling its pallets, is also capable of producing a degree of uniformity in the motion of the wheel; for the force operating on the pallet is consumed in destroying velocity in one direction, and in generating velocity in the opposite direction; and as the space in which it acts is nearly the same in all cases, the velocity generated will also be nearly the same at all times, as long as the force remains the same. The addition of a balance to a clock was made soon after the year 1400, for Arnault, who died in 1465, describes a planisphere <note>a map of the celestial sphere projected onto a flat surface, often part of an astronomical clock</note>, constructed by his master De Fondeur, which had a balance with an escapement like that of a common watch, but without a spring. Such a balance vibrates much more slowly than a balance provided with a spring; if the balance spring of a common watch is removed, the hands will pass over the space of about twenty-eight minutes in an hour.

It is said that before the pendulum was used, a balance wheel was sometimes suspended in a horizontal position by a thread passing through its axis, which coiled around it and caused it to rise and fall as it oscillated back and forth. This mode of regulation differed but little in principle from modern pendulums, but it was more complicated and less accurate. Huygens, in somewhat later times, constructed a clock with a revolving weight, which rose higher and increased the resistance whenever an increase of the force increased the velocity; and he caused the thread which supported the weight to bend around a curve of such a form as to preserve the equality of the revolutions.

A chronometer may be constructed on this principle for measuring small portions of time, which appears to be capable of greater accuracy than Mr. Whitehurst’s apparatus, and by means of which an interval of a thousandth part of a second may possibly be rendered perceptible. If two revolving pendulums are connected with a vertical axis in such a manner as to move two weights back and forth according to whether they fly off to a greater or smaller distance, the weights sliding, during their revolution, on a fixed sur-

It may be turned by a string wound around the upper part, and this string may serve as a support for a barrel that slides on a square part of the axis, which will consequently descend as it rotates. Its surface, being smooth, may be covered with either paper or wax, and a pencil or a metal point may be pressed against it by a fine spring, so as to always trace a spiral line on the barrel—except when the spring is forced slightly to one side by a gentle touch, either by hand or by means of any object whose motion is to be examined, whether it is a falling weight, a vibrating <term>chord</term> <note>a string or cord used in musical instruments or physics experiments</note> or rod, or any other moving substance. In this manner, assuming a barrel one foot in circumference rotates every two seconds, each hundredth of an inch would correspond to the six-hundredth part of a second; the scale could be further enlarged if it were necessary. (Plate XV. Fig. 198.)

By using this instrument, we may measure, without difficulty, the frequency of the vibrations of sounding bodies by connecting them with a point, which will trace an undulating path on the roller. These vibrations may also serve in a very simple manner for the measurement of the smallest intervals of time; for if a body, whose vibrations have a certain frequency, is caused to vibrate during the revolution of an axis and to mark its vibrations on a roller, the traces will serve as a correct index of the time occupied by any part of a revolution. The motion of any other body may then be very accurately compared with the number of oscillations marked, during the same period, by the vibrating body. For many purposes, if the machine is heavy enough, it could be turned by a handle alone, provided care is taken to keep the balls in a proper position; it would also be convenient to have the descent of the barrel regulated by the action of a screw and capable of being stopped at will.

But for the general purposes of timekeepers, all other inventions have been almost universally superseded by the pendulum and the balance spring, or pendulum spring. About the year 1000, Ibn Junis and the other Arabian astronomers were in the habit of measuring time, during their

### LECTURE XVII.

The equality of the times occupied by these vibrations, whether larger or smaller, was known to <term>Galileo</term> in 1600, and some time before 1633, he proposed that they should be applied to the regulation of clocks. But <term>Sanctorius</term>, in his commentary on <term>Avicenna</term>, describes an instrument to which he had himself applied the pendulum in 1612. <term>Huygens</term> made the same application only in 1658, which is the date of his work on the subject. In the same year, <term>Hooke</term> applied a spring to the balance of a watch; and soon after, he conceived the idea of improving <term>timekeepers</term> sufficiently for ascertaining the <term>longitude</term> at sea, but he was interrupted in the pursuit of his plan. <term>Hooke</term> was also probably the first who employed for a clock a heavy weight vibrating in a small arc—an arrangement from which the peculiar advantages of a pendulum are principally derived.

The objects which require the greatest attention in the construction of <term>timekeepers</term> are these: to preserve the moving power, or sustaining force, as steady as possible; to apply this force to the pendulum or balance in the most suitable manner; and to employ a pendulum or balance of which the vibrations are in their nature as nearly <term>isochronous</term> <note>occurring at equal intervals of time</note> as possible. In clocks, the sustaining force, being generally derived from a weight, is already sufficiently steady, provided that care is taken that the line by which it is suspended is of equal thickness throughout and acts on a perfect cylinder. But in some clocks, and in all watches, the moving power is a spring. One of the first clock springs is said to have been an old sword blade; a clock with such a spring was recently preserved at Brussels. The spring which is currently used is a thin elastic plate of steel, coiled into a spiral form. Every spring exerts more force the more it is bent; in order to correct this inequality, the chain or cord by which it acts on the mechanism is wound on a spiral <term>fusee</term> <note>a cone-shaped pulley used to equalize the pull of a mainspring</note>; so that, as the force is lessened, it is applied to a larger cylinder or a longer lever. The general outline of the <term>fusee</term> must be nearly such that its thickness at any part may diminish in the same proportion as it becomes more distant from the point at which the force would cease altogether—the curve being that which is denominated a <term>hyperbola</term>; but the workmen generally have no other rule for this than habitual estimation. (Plate XV. Fig. 199.)

# ON TIMEKEEPERS.

Despite all possible precautions in the direct application of the weight or spring, the irregular action of the gear teeth, the increasing stickiness of the oil normally used, and other accidental disturbances make it still desirable to achieve a further equalization of the force. This is sometimes achieved in clocks by raising the weighted arm of a lever to a specific height, from which it may descend; and in watches, by bending a spring into a specific position, from which it may return, so as to limit with great precision the propelling force used in each vibration. The need to apply oil is sometimes largely removed by jeweling the holes in which the axes or <term>verges</term> <note>the spindles or shafts of the wheels</note> run; a hole is made in a plate of ruby, and a diamond is placed against this, in contact with the end of the axis; the hardness and high polish of these stones tend very significantly to reduce friction.

<insert><image-desc>Blue oval library stamp: THE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</image-desc></insert>

There are also various methods for maintaining the action of the force while the clock or watch is being wound: a spring is placed between the <term>fusee</term> <note>a conical pulley used to equalize the force of the mainspring</note> and the wheel it drives; this spring is slightly weaker than the original weight or spring so that it stays wound until the pressure of the mainspring is removed. At that point, it begins to act upon a fixed point on one side and the wheel of the fusee on the other, so that it drives the mechanism for a short time with a force nearly equal to that of the mainspring. Sometimes the spring is also wound by causing a small wheel to revolve around the center of the fusee, with its teeth engaged on one side with a wheel that is part of the fusee, and on the other side with the internal teeth of a hoop connected to the mechanism, so that the same pressure used to wind the spring also tends to turn the hoop and continue the motion. (Plate XVI. Fig. 200.)

The <term>escapement</term>, through which the sustaining force is transferred to the pendulum or balance, requires more skill and accuracy than any other part of a timekeeper. Occasionally, the back-and-forth motion of the pendulum has been produced by the action of a crank, but this construction subjects it too much to the irregularities of the wheelwork and is prone to several other issues. A crank cannot properly be called an escapement because, according to the etymology of the term, the pendulum must "escape" for a time from the action of the wheelwork; and in general, the more indepen-

The simplest forms in common use are the <term>crutch escapement</term> for a clock, and the <term>pallets</term> with a vertical wheel for a watch; the <term>dead beat escapement</term>, and the <term>cylinder</term> with a horizontal wheel, are improvements on these; and the <term>detached escapement</term> is a still further refinement.

The <term>crutch escapement</term>, called by the French the <term>anchor escapement</term>, is an arch in the plane of the <term>escape wheel</term>, and parallel to that in which the pendulum vibrates, supporting at each extremity a <term>pallet</term>, of which the face is a plane, and which is pushed in its turn by the teeth of the <term>escape wheel</term>. The faces are so inclined that the <term>pallets</term> are alternately forced, by the action of the teeth, to move away from the center of the wheel: and great care is taken in making the teeth exactly at equal distances, so that they may fall regularly on the pallet immediately after the release of the teeth on the other side from the opposite <term>pallet</term>. (Plate XVI. Fig. 201.)

In the common watch, the axis of the balance is parallel to the plane of the <term>escape wheel</term>, which is a <term>contrate</term> or <term>crown wheel</term>, and the flat <term>pallets</term> are fixed on the axis of the balance, at opposite parts of the circumference of the <term>escape wheel</term>. (Plate XVI. Fig. 202.)

In both these cases, the impulse given to one <term>pallet</term> carries the opposite <term>pallet</term> with some force against the approaching tooth, and drives the wheel a little backwards, with a visible <term>recoil</term>. Here the sustaining power, being applied principally at the ends of the vibrations, disturbs their <term>isochronism</term>, or the equality of the times in which they are performed, by partially increasing the force. We may recall that, in order for all vibrations, of whatever magnitude, to be performed in equal times, the force must be exactly proportional to the distance from a given point; consequently, if an additional force is applied near the extremities of the vibration only, the longer vibrations will take less time than the shorter ones. We may observe that, by increasing the force of the spring of a common watch with the key, we may accelerate its motion, at the same time that the angular magnitude of the vibration is increased. The motion of the balance also, being slowest at the extremities of its vibration, where the sustaining force is applied, is more affected by the inequalities of this force than if it were subjected to its

Yet a good clock with this construction may keep time without an error of a ten-thousandth part of the whole, and a watch within a two-thousandth. In the common watch <term>escapement</term>, there is little friction, for the force acts almost perpendicularly on the <term>pallet</term>; it appears to have been the oldest <term>escapement</term>, and was employed before the application of springs to <term>balances</term>. It requires a considerable range of motion in the <term>balance</term> and cannot, therefore, be easily applied to clocks with such <term>pendulums</term> as vibrate in small arcs. The <term>crutch escapement</term>, on the contrary, cannot be applied directly to a vibration in a very large arc; but by the interposition of a <term>lever</term> with a <term>roller</term>, or of a part of a wheel with a <term>pinion</term>, it may be adapted to the <term>balance</term> of a watch; and some watches thus constructed by Emery, Letherland, and others, appear to have succeeded very well.

To avoid the inconveniences of the recoiling <term>escapements</term>, Mr. Graham invented or introduced the <term>dead beat</term> for the clock, and the <term>cylinder</term> for the watch. In both of these, the tooth of the <term>escape wheel</term> rests, during the greater part of the vibration, on a cylindrical surface, and acts on the inclined plane for a short time only, in the middle of each vibration; so that a change of the sustaining power scarcely produces a noticeable derangement of the <term>isochronism</term>. Whichever way we turn the key of a <term>horizontal watch</term>, as long as it continues to run, the frequency of its vibrations is hardly affected. A good <term>horizontal watch</term> will keep time within about a ten-thousandth part, especially if a little oil is frequently applied to it, or if the <term>cylinder</term> is made of a <term>ruby</term>; and the <term>timekeeper</term> in the observatory at <term>Greenwich</term>, with a <term>dead beat escapement</term> made by Graham, varies from true time only two parts in a million. (Plate XVI. Fig. 203, 204.)

If the friction were perfectly uniform, it would scarcely disturb the <term>isochronism</term>, but friction is always increased by an increase of pressure; hence, therefore, the effect of any addition to the sustaining force must tend in some degree to retard the vibrations; and to avoid this, the surfaces on which the teeth rest have sometimes been so

Friction can, however, be considerably reduced by the <term>duplex escapement</term>, apparently so named because of the double series of teeth used. The teeth of the more prominent series are held on a cylinder so small that it is unsuitable for receiving an impulse from them; the <term>balance</term> is therefore moved by the other series of teeth, which act on a <term>pallet</term> at a greater distance from its axis. The French have sometimes used a construction that is somewhat similar, which they call the <term>comma escapement</term>, where the teeth first rest on a small arch of repose and then drive the curved surface of a <term>pallet</term> extending a considerable distance beyond it. In both these cases, the single <term>pallet</term>, which is driven by a simply shaped tooth, requires less labor in its manufacture than a series of larger teeth that each must be finished with great accuracy. However, watches with these designs—especially those with the <term>comma escapement</term>—are too liable to be stopped by any sudden motion, although the <term>duplex escapement</term> is beginning to be frequently used for pocket timekeepers. (Plate XVI. Fig. 205.)

Mr. Harrison avoided all friction on the <term>pallet</term> by connecting it with the <term>pendulum</term> by means of a slender spring, which was flexible enough to follow the motion of the <term>escape wheel</term> to a sufficient extent without sliding on its teeth. But the construction most usually employed when the greatest accuracy is required is the <term>detached escapement</term>, in which the teeth of the <term>escape wheel</term> always rest on a <term>detent</term>, except for a short interval when it is unlocked in order to drive the <term>pallets</term>. Mr. Mudge employed a <term>detached escapement</term> driven by a subsidiary spring, the force of which is hardly subject to any variation; the <term>detent</term> is unlocked by the motion of the <term>balance</term>. Mr. Haley has refined this construction even further by causing the subsidiary spring to unlock the wheel during its return, so that the <term>balance</term> is relieved from this action, which can sometimes produce a slight irregularity. These constructions are, however, much too delicate for common pocket watches. In a clock, Mr. Cumming has employed a <term>detached escapement</term> in which a lever is raised to a certain height by each tooth of the <term>escape wheel</term> and acts immediately on the <term>pendulum</term> as it descends in the middle of its vibration. The <term>escape wheel</term> is unlocked by the <term>pendulum</term> during its ascent, and a variation in pressure may, therefore, produce a very slight inequality in the motion of the <term>pendulum</term>. This escapement cannot, therefore, by any means be considered as detached. It is, however, easy to remove the defect of Mr. Cumming's escapement—if it can be called a defect—by a method similar to that which Mr. Haley has applied to watches: each tooth of the wheel is unlocked by the descent of the lever on the opposite side at the moment that it ceases to act on the pendulum, and it remains inactive until the pendulum meets it. (Plate XVI. Fig. 206, 207.)

The detents of the escapements of Mudge and Cumming are parts of the pallet; but in the timekeepers now commonly made by Arnold, Earnshaw, and others, the tooth is detained by a <term>pallet</term> or pin projecting from a lever, the point of which is forced back by the balance at the moment that the pallet presents itself to another of the teeth. Mr. Arnold employs an <term>epicycloidal</term> tooth acting on a single point of the pallet; Mr. Earnshaw makes a flat surface of the tooth first act on the point of the pallet, and then the point of the tooth acts on a flat surface of the pallet. In other respects, there is little difference in these escapements, and both makers have been judged worthy of a public reward for their success. (Plate XVI. Fig. 208, 209.)

The last of the three principal objects requiring the attention of the watchmaker is to employ a pendulum or balance whose vibrations are, by their nature, perfectly <term>isochronous</term>. For this purpose, the weight of the pendulum ought to move in a <term>cycloidal arc</term>, but the difficulty of producing such a motion in practice is much greater than the advantage derived from it; and a circular vibration, confined to a small arc, is sufficiently isochronous for all practical purposes. The error of such a vibration is nearly proportional to the square of the arc described by the pendulum, and amounts to a second and a half in a day of 24 hours for a single degree on each side of the point of rest. Thus, a pendulum keeping true time in an arc of three degrees would gain 13½ seconds if the arc were very much contracted or made cycloidal, and would lose 10½ seconds by having the vibration extended to an arc of four degrees. In order to avoid the friction which would be occasioned by the motion of the pendulum on an axis, it is usually suspended by a flexible spring, which is wholly free from friction.

The elasticity of this spring adds a tiny force to the power of gravitation acting on the pendulum, and this force must be considered when the length of a simple pendulum is compared with the frequency of its vibrations. It does not, however, interfere with the consistency of the vibrations among each other; for in all springs, Dr. Hooke’s general law—that the force increases in proportion to the degree of bending—is found to be perfectly accurate for moderate oscillations. Such a force, therefore, accelerates the larger and the smaller vibrations in exactly the same degree.

But in balances, it is desirable to have the velocity and the extent of the vibration as great as possible so that the motion is less influenced by the irregularities of the sustaining power. In large movements, Dr. Hooke’s law is not so precisely true; there must also necessarily be some inaccuracy from the loss of a certain portion of the force in generating the <term>momentum</term> of the spring itself, which, when the form is spiral, adds great complexity to the calculation of the properties of the vibration. Yet it has been found by experiment that a specific length can be determined for almost every spring that will provide vibrations that are either perfectly or very nearly <term>isochronous</term>.

In order that the weight or inertia of the spring may interfere less with the regularity of its motion, it is sometimes tapered and made thinner at the end. It is also now common in the best watches to use a spring coiled into a cylindrical form, like that of a bell spring, the motion of which appears to be somewhat more regular than that of a flat spiral. This was actually the original design, but it was likely abandoned because of the space it required. The balance springs are made of the finest steel, and the best are manufactured in this country, although the French are said to possess the skill of tempering their mainsprings better than ours. Sometimes the balance spring is made of an alloy of gold and copper; these springs are very elastic, but they are too prone to breaking. Mr. Earnshaw observes that the strength of a spring always diminishes slightly as it wears. He attempts to compensate for this loss of strength by using a spring shaped so that vibrations in small arcs are slightly more frequent than in larger ones; thus, when the presence of dust and the stickiness of the oil reduce the extent of the vibrations, this reduction may tend to produce an acceleration which compensates for the spring's weakened force. But it is perhaps better to make every compensation, as far as possible, independent of circumstances external to

It sometimes happens that, from a sudden motion or from some other accidental circumstance, the balance of a timekeeper may be thrown beyond the point at which the pallets are impelled by the scape wheels, and the entire motion may be interrupted for this reason. To prevent this accident, a small bar or pin is usually fixed on the balance spring; this is carried outwards when the vibration begins to extend too far and stops the further progress of the balance by intercepting a pin that projects from it. This arrangement is called banking the balance.

We have already seen that the squares of the vibration times of two pendulums are proportional to their lengths; so that if we add one-hundredth of its length to a pendulum, we increase the time of its vibration by very nearly one-two-hundredth. But since all bodies are expanded by heat, the variable temperature of the atmosphere must necessarily produce changes of this kind in the motions of pendulums, and it may be observed that a clock runs somewhat more slowly in summer than in winter. The same expansion has a similar effect on the motion of a balance, and the increase of temperature also produces a reduction in the elastic force of the spring itself. There is, however, a great difference in the expansibility of various substances; dry deal <note>pine or fir wood</note> is one of the least expansible and is therefore often used for the rods of pendulums. Brass expands one part in a hundred thousand for every degree Fahrenheit—or a little more or less than this, depending on whether it contains more or less zinc. Glass and platinum are less than half as expansible as brass, iron about two-thirds, and mercury three times as much. A brass pendulum would, therefore, make one fewer vibration in ten thousand at 70° than at 50° and would lose 8 1/2 seconds in a day; a balance regulated by a spring would lose much more. For I have observed that vibrations governed by the elasticity of steel have lost as much as one-ten-thousandth part in frequency for a single degree Fahrenheit; and Berthoud informs us that where a clock (probably with a steel pendulum) loses 20 seconds due to heat, a watch loses eight minutes.

This mode of compensation is still sometimes practiced with success; but the <term>gridiron pendulum</term> is more commonly used: it was the invention of Harrison, who combined seven bars, of iron or steel, and of brass, in such a manner, that the bars of brass raised the weight as much as the bars of iron depressed it. At present five bars only are usually employed, two of them being of a mixture of zinc and silver, and three of steel. Mr. Ellicott suspended a pendulum at the extremity of a lever, which was supported by a pillar of brass, much nearer to the fulcrum; as the pendulum expanded, the end of the lever was raised in the same degree, and the weight remained at its original distance from the point of suspension, which was determined by a fixed plate, transmitting the slender spring, as usual, between two opposite edges. The same effect is produced more simply by suspending the pendulum from the summit of a bar nearly parallel to it, and of the same substance with itself, resting on a fixed support, and either of the same length with the pendulum, or a little longer, accordingly as the distance of the fixed plate from the point of support of the bar, is determined by materials which may be considered as nearly of an invariable length, or as liable to a certain degree of expansion. (Plate XVI. Fig. 210.)

All these methods of compensation are peculiar to clocks; for watches, it is usual to unite together two metals which differ in expansibility, so as to form a compound plate; one side of the plate is commonly of steel, the other of brass, and it is obvious that any increase of temperature, by causing the brass to expand more than the steel, must bend the whole plate. Such a plate is variously applied; the most accurate method, which is employed by Arnold and other modern artists, is to make it a part of the balance itself, fixing a weight on its extremity, which is brought nearer to the centre, by the increase of curvature of the plate, whenever the expansion of the arms of the balance tends to remove it further off. The best way of making the plate appears to be to turn a ring of steel, and to immerse it in melted brass, and then to turn away what is superfluous of the brass. The magnitude of the weight, and the length of the plate, may easily be so regulated, as to com-

<note>This completes the word "compensate" from the previous page.</note> compensate not only for the expansion produced by heat, but also for the reduction of the spring's elasticity. Sometimes a plate has also been applied in such a way as to shorten the spring when the temperature increases, using a method similar to how a common watch is regulated; the clip, which determines the effective length of the spring, is moved backward and forward. A similar effect has also been produced by dividing this clip into two parts, one of which is fixed to a compound plate and is made to approach the other so as to confine the spring more tightly, and thus shorten its length, upon an increase in temperature. (Plate XVI. Fig. 211.)

The bending of a compound plate has also been applied in a simple and elegant manner by Mr. Nicholson to the pendulum of a clock, by using it to support the upper end of the pendulum. The plate is placed horizontally, with the brass on top, and supports the pendulum in the middle while the ends rest on two fixed points. The distance between these points can be adjusted with great accuracy so that when the temperature increases, the curvature of the plate raises the pendulum rod enough to keep the weight, or bob, at a constant distance below the fixed point that defines its upper end. (Plate XVI. Fig. 212.)

The resistance that air offers to the motion of a pendulum affects its velocity to some degree, and variations in atmospheric density must therefore also produce some irregularities in timekeepers; these are, however, too small to be noticeable. Derham found that air resistance accelerated the motion of a half-second pendulum by about four vibrations per hour by decreasing the arc in which it vibrated; yet, when the vibrations were restored to their original size, air resistance caused a delay of eight vibrations in the same amount of time. However, a heavy pendulum vibrating in a small arc is very little affected by this resistance.

Besides these more essential parts of the watchmaker’s art, there are several secondary considerations that require his attention. The striking mechanism, in particular, occupies a significant portion of the bulk in clocks and repeating watches. However, the apparatus used for these purposes requires neither refinement of invention nor delicacy of execution.

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>202</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XVII.</header>
<warning>ghosting from reverse page</warning>

In old clocks, the number of hours struck is usually determined by the rotation of a specific part of a wheel that supports an arm and allows the hammer to strike until, at the proper time, it falls into a notch. In watches and more modern clocks, the same effect is produced by means of a spiral of 12 teeth, rotating once every 12 hours.

It is very important for the accurate performance of a good clock that it be firmly fixed to a solid support. Any unsteadiness in the support causes the point of suspension to follow the motion of the pendulum and enlarges the diameter of the circle along which the pendulum describes an arc; therefore, this generally tends to slow the motion of the clock. Sometimes, however, an unsteady support may be of such a nature as to accelerate the motion. An observation of this kind, made by Berthoud, suggested a theory of compound vibrations to Bernoulli, which may perhaps be true in some cases but is by no means universally applicable to every situation. Due to circumstances of this kind, it happens that when two clocks are placed near each other and rest to some degree on the same support, they often have a remarkable effect on each other's vibrations. They can continue running for several days without varying by a single second, even when they would have differed considerably if they were situated otherwise. It sometimes happens that the clock that runs more slowly of the two will set the other in motion and then stop itself. This circumstance has been explained by the greater frequency of the vibrations of a circular pendulum when confined to a smaller arc; the tendency of the pendulums to vibrate in the same amount of time causes the shorter arc to become continually larger and larger, and the longer arc to contract its vibrations, until at last its motion entirely ceases. This "sympathy" resembles the alternating vibrations of two scales hanging from the same beam, where one may often be observed to stop vibrating when the other begins to move, and then resumes its motion once its companion is at rest. However, it is even more similar to the mutual influence of two strings, or even two organ pipes; although they may not be separately tuned to a perfect unison, they still influence each other's vibrations in such a manner as to produce exactly the same note when they sound together.

# LECTURE XVIII.

## ON RAISING AND REMOVING WEIGHTS.

The methodical arrangement of our subject leads us, after having considered the modifications of force, to those machines which are intended for counteracting it, or for producing motion in opposition to an existing force. The simplest of the forces to be counteracted is gravitation, and it is one of the most common uses of mechanical powers to raise a weight from a lower to a higher position. This operation is also closely connected with the methods of overcoming the corpuscular force of friction or adhesion, which constitutes the main difficulty in moving bodies horizontally from place to place; for if we only had to produce motion in a mass of matter that offered no resistance, a loaded wagon might eventually be pulled along by a silkworm's thread. The raising and removing of weights, therefore, together with the methods of avoiding friction in general, form the first part of the subject of the counteraction of forces, and the remaining part relates to the machinery intended for overcoming the other corpuscular powers of bodies by such operations as are designed to change their external forms.

Machines for raising weights, which involve only the mechanics of solid bodies, are principally levers, capstans, wheels, pulleys, inclined planes, screws, and their various combinations in the form of cranes.

A lever is a very simple instrument, but of most extensive utility in raising weights to a small height. We may recall that levers are divided into two principal kinds, depending on whether the power and weight are on different sides or on the same side of the fulcrum; the forces counteracting each other being in the one case in the same direction, and in the other, in opposite directions. Thus, when a man lifts a stone by means of a lever of the first kind, resting on a fulcrum between himself and the stone, he presses down

the end of the lever, and the greatest force that he can apply is equal to the entire weight of his body: but when he thrusts the lever under the stone, so that its end rests on the ground, it becomes a lever of the second kind, and in order to raise the stone, he must now draw the end of the lever upwards. In this direction, a strong man can exert a force equivalent to twice his weight; consequently, the second kind of lever possesses here a temporary advantage over the first; although, if the operation were continued, the workman would be more fatigued by raising even the same weight by this method than if he could conveniently apply his weight to a lever of the first kind; and for this purpose, crossbars have sometimes been added to levers in order to enable several workmen to stand on them effectively at once. A bent lever operates with exactly the same power as a straight one, provided that the forces are applied in a similar manner with respect to its arms: and in all cases, the forces capable of balancing each other are inversely proportional to the distances of the points of action from the fulcrum. Some addition of force is necessary for overcoming the equilibrium and producing motion, but as the velocity of the motion is seldom of much consequence, a small surplus of force is usually sufficient.

The principal inconvenience of the lever is the short range of its action: this may, however, be overcome by means of the invention of Perrault <note>Claude Perrault (1613–1688), a French architect and physicist</note>, in which two pins are fixed in the lever at a short distance from each other, sliding in two pairs of vertical grooves provided with ratchets, so that when the long arm of the lever is pulled by means of a rope, the nearer pin serves as a fulcrum, and the more distant one is raised at the same time as the weight, and is held in its place by the click <note>A catch or pawl used in a ratchet mechanism</note>; but when the rope is slackened, the weight sinks a little and raises the pin, which first served as a fulcrum, to a higher place in its groove. The same effects may also be produced by catches or clicks resting upon ratchets on the opposite sides of a single upright bar, which passes through a perforation in the lever. There must, however, be a considerable loss of force from the continual interruption of the motion. (Plate XVII. Fig. 213.)

An axis with a winch—that is, a lever bent at the end—is familiar from the common machine for raising a bucket out of a well. A vertical or upright axis, with two or more levers inserted into it, becomes a capstan. In these

In these cases, if we wish to estimate the force with accuracy, we must add half the thickness of the rope to the radius of the axis when we compare it with the arm of the lever.

Sometimes the weight of a reservoir or bucket of water is employed for raising another bucket, filled with coal or other materials, by means of a rope or chain coiled around a cylinder or drum, or two drums of different sizes. This machine is called a <term>water whimsey</term>: when the bucket of water has reached the bottom, a valve is opened by striking against a pin, which lets out the water. In a machine of this kind, employed in the Duke of Bridgewater's coal works, the water descends thirty yards and raises a smaller quantity of coal from a depth of sixty. In such cases, assuming the action to be single and the stream of water to be unused during the descent of the reservoir, a considerable preponderance of weight may be advantageously employed to give velocity to the loads, provided that the machinery is not liable to be damaged by their impact.

An upright axis or drum, turned by the force of horses walking in a circle, is used for raising coal and other weights; it is called a <term>gin</term>, probably as a corruption of the word "engine." The buckets are attached to the opposite ends of a rope that passes around the drum and is drawn by means of its friction against the drum. One of the buckets descends empty while the other is drawn up full; and when the motion of the buckets needs to be changed, the horses are turned, or the wheels are made to drive the axis in the opposite direction when any other moving power is employed.

When a ship's anchor is weighed, the cable itself would be too large to be coiled around the capstan; it is therefore connected to it by means of an endless rope called the <term>messenger</term>. As the messenger is coiled around the lower part of the capstan, it leaves the upper part, so that its position becomes lower and lower until it eventually has no more room on the capstan. It is therefore necessary to force it up from time to time; this is called <term>surging the messenger</term>. It is commonly done by beating it, and to facilitate the operation, the capstan is made somewhat conical. It has been proposed to employ lifters in different parts of the circumference which are raised once in each revolution by passing over an inclined plane with the use of friction wheels; a patent has been taken out for this invention, and it has already been intro-

The <term>capstan</term>, which consists of two cylinders of different sizes on the same <term>axis</term>, with a rope passing from the smaller one over a <term>pulley</term> (which is connected with the weight) and returning to be wound up by the larger one, is very powerful in its operation; but it requires a great length of rope for a small amount of motion. (Plate IV. Fig. 51.)

<term>Wheelwork</term> is employed in a variety of ways for raising weights: its power is in all cases derived from the same principles as the action of <term>levers</term>. Each wheel and <term>pinion</term> can be considered as composed of a series of bent <term>levers</term>, of which the <term>axis</term> is the common <term>fulcrum</term>, acting in succession on the teeth of the next wheel. The simplest combination of <term>wheelwork</term> used for this purpose is a <term>jack</term>: a bar furnished with teeth on one side, which is raised by the final <term>pinion</term>. Such instruments were not unknown even to the ancients; the *<term>barulcus</term>* described by *<term>Hero</term>* <note>Heron of Alexandria, a Greek mathematician and engineer</note> was a machine of this type.

A series of buckets connected by ropes and passing over a wheel is often employed for raising water to a small height, and sometimes even for solid substances in powder form—specifically for raising flour in a <term>corn mill</term>. In this case, the flour must be brought within reach of the buckets by means of a <term>revolving spiral</term>, which pushes it gradually forward. When a weight of any kind is raised in buckets distributed around the circumference of a wheel, the force required to keep the weight in <term>equilibrium</term> is as much less than the weight as the diameter of a circle is less than half the circumference; the rest of the weight is supported by the <term>axis</term> of the wheel.

<term>Pulleys</term>, and their combinations in <term>blocks</term>, are universally used on board ships. They are very convenient where only a moderate increase of power is required; but to obtain a very great advantage, the number of separate <term>pulleys</term> or <term>sheaves</term> must be greatly multiplied. A great length of rope must also be used; and it is said that in a pair of <term>blocks</term> with five <term>pulleys</term> in each, two-thirds of the force is lost by friction and the

A fixed <term>inclined plane</term> is often useful in assisting the elevation of great weights by means of other machinery. It is believed that in all the buildings of remote antiquity where great masses of stone were used—as in the pyramids of **Egypt** and the Druidical temples of this country—these vast blocks were raised on inclined planes of earth or scaffolding, with the assistance of levers and rollers as well. Inclined planes are frequently used for drawing boats out of one canal into another; and sometimes the local conditions are such that this can be done very conveniently, simply by allowing a loaded boat to descend and turn the axis that raises an empty one. An example of this can be seen on a large scale in the **Duke of Bridgwater’s canal**. This canal extends above ground for forty miles on one level; an underground navigation twelve miles long joins it at **Worsley**, leading to the coal mines under **Walkden moor**. At a height of 35½ yards above this is another subterranean section, nearly six miles in length. The connection between these levels is formed by an inclined plane: the boats are lowered while loaded and proceed three miles along the tunnel into the open canal. Inclined planes are also universally employed for making the ascent of heights easier for men or for animals; they may either be uniform, like roads, or the general inclination of the surface may be replaced by the formation of separate steps or stairs. The inclination of the surface may be determined by the proportion of the animal's strength to its weight, as the force required to support any weight on a plane relates to the total weight just as the height of the plane relates to its length; and if the plane is a little less inclined than exact equilibrium would require, the animal will be able to gain enough velocity at first to carry it easily up the ascent with a nearly steady motion. The strength of a laborer may be advantageously employed by ascending a given height via a flight of steps and placing himself on a platform which may raise a weight by its descent; but it appears that the force of other animals is less suited for efforts of this kind.

The screw is not often applied directly to the lifting of weights; although sometimes a number of screws have been used for raising a large and unmanageable weight by slow degrees—for instance, that of an obelisk—and a <term>perpetual screw</term> <note>A worm gear designed to rotate a toothed wheel.</note> is frequently employed to give motion to wheelwork. Such machines possess a considerable mechanical advantage, but they are subject to much friction and lack durability. **Mr. Hunter’s** double screw might be applied with advantage if the extent of the motion required were extremely small; but this limitation restricts its usefulness within very narrow bounds.

A <term>crane</term> is a machine for raising weights by means of a rope or chain, descending from an arm which is capable of horizontal motion, and passing over a pulley to be wound up on an axis. The axis is turned, either directly or with the intervention of wheelwork, by a winch, by the horizontal bars of a <term>windlass</term>, or by a <term>walking wheel</term> <note>A treadwheel turned by a person or animal walking inside it.</note>, and sometimes by the force of wind, water, or steam. A walking wheel is an advantageous way to use the strength of a laborer, but the size of the machine is

A walking wheel must be provided with some method of preventing the dangerous consequences of a rapid descent of the weight in the event of an accidental fall of the laborer. For this purpose, a catch is usually employed to prevent any backward motion; a bar has also sometimes been suspended from the axis of the wheel, on which the man may support himself with his hands, and other similar precautions have been adopted. Sometimes the plane of a walking wheel is only slightly inclined toward the horizon, and the man walks on its flat surface. In either case, the labor of horses, donkeys, or oxen may be substituted for that of men. However, for cranes, this substitution would be very disadvantageous, since much force would be lost in frequently stopping such a bulky machine as would be required. The use of a turnspit dog is a humble example of the same operation, and even goats appear to have been sometimes made to climb in a similar manner. In a walking wheel used for raising water at Carisbrook Castle, in the Isle of Wight, the work was performed by the same individual donkey for the entire forty-five years preceding 1771. Walking wheels have also been invented on which horses were to act externally with their forefeet or hindfeet only, but they have seldom, if ever, been applied to practical purposes. In general, it is advisable that walking wheels for quadrupeds should provide a path as level as possible; and it might probably be of advantage to harness them either to a fixed point, or to a spring or weight, which would enable them to exert a considerable force even in a horizontal direction. However, they might likely be more effectively employed in a circular mill walk. (Plate XVII. Fig. 217.)

Mr. White's crane provides a good example of an oblique walking wheel; the force may be varied depending on whether the laborer stands at a point more or less distant from the center. A model of a <term>crane</term> was shown several years ago to the Royal Society, in which a large wheel fixed to a short axis was made to roll around on a plane, while the lower end of its axis was connected by a joint to another axis in a vertical position. Then the wheel, having to traverse a circumference somewhat larger than its own, was turned slowly, and therefore powerfully, around its axis, and the motion was communicated to the fixed axis. The machine, however, appears to be more of a curiosity than of practical use.

Sometimes a <term>steelyard</term> has been combined with a crane for weighing goods at the same time they are being raised by it. A small crane, fixed to a carriage, is convenient for loading and unloading goods. In France, the carts used on the wharfs are generally so long that they reach the ground at the back when tilted down, providing an <term>inclined plane</term> along which the goods are raised by a lever and axis, or a type of <term>capstan</term>, fixed at the front.

To grip stones that are to be raised by means of a rope, a hole is sometimes carved into them—wider inside than at its opening—and into this a <term>lewis</term> is inserted. This consists of two inverted wedges separated by a plug, to which they are fastened by a pin. (Plate XVII. Fig. 219.)

When a rope or chain used to raise a weight is so long that it requires a <term>counterpoise</term>, the effect of this may be adjusted according to the length of the unwound rope by hanging it on a second rope or chain; this second rope acts on a spiral <term>fusee</term>, which is slowly turned by a wheel and <term>pinion</term>.

The use of cranes is so widespread and essential that their designs have often been diversified due to local circumstances or even mere whim; however, the constructions described here appear to be of the most general utility, and from them it will be easy to evaluate others.

Another method, the most natural and obvious if the objects are portable, is to carry them. There is, however, some scope for theory even in this common operation. We have seen that calculations have been made to determine the most advantageous burden for a porter to carry, but the experience of a few trials would generally be a better guide. Some carry weights on their heads, others on their shoulders, and others low down on their backs; depending on the position of the burden, they bend forward or backward so that the common center of gravity of the weight and the body falls immediately, or very nearly, over some part of the ground between their feet.

The difficulty of carrying a weight at the end of a long rod is easily understood from the properties of the lever, and these same principles will allow us to determine the distribution of a load between two porters, in whatever way they may carry it. Suppose the weight is placed on a porter's horse, or a hand barrow, at an equal distance from both ends; each of the men will support an equal portion of it. But if it is closer to one than to the other, the load will be distributed in the same proportion as the poles are divided by the center of the burden. For instance, if the weight were 300 pounds, and it were one foot away from one porter and two feet from the other, the first would have to carry 200 pounds and the second 100.

If the porters ascend a hill or a flight of steps, the distribution of the load will remain the same, provided that the center of the weight lies in the same plane as the poles. But if the weight consists of a large body placed on that plane, with the center of gravity being above it, the effect of an incline relative to the horizon may significantly change the distribution of the load. This is because the pressure will always be determined by the distance of the ends of the poles from the line passing perpendicularly through the center of gravity; so that, if the elevation were steep enough, the entire burden might rest on the lower porter. In the same manner, if the weight were suspended below the poles, the incline would cause a greater proportion of the load to be carried by the upper porter. The force is, however, only distributed this way as long as the arms of the porters remain parallel to each other. This inequality would naturally be lessened by a change in the directions in which they act; it would only be necessary for those directions to meet in some part of the vertical line passing through the center of gravity. The magnitude of each force would then be determined by the length of the side of a triangle corresponding to its direction, and the load might be either equally or un-

A man can carry, in general, a weight four or five times as great as that which he can raise continually in a vertical direction at the same speed; therefore, we may consider the resistance to be overcome as a kind of friction which amounts to about a fourth or a fifth of the weight. If we attempted to pull a weight along a horizontal surface, the resistance of the surface would often not only impede the motion but also damage the texture of the object being moved. This injury may, however, be avoided by the introduction of a simple frame or dray, and the dray may be reinforced with a material subject to little friction, such as iron. Friction may also be somewhat further diminished by making the underside of the dray slightly convex, so that a slight agitation may be continually produced during its motion. Sometimes the simple method of placing a load on two poles of elastic wood—where the thickest ends are supported by the horse and the thinner ends drag on the ground—is useful both in diminishing friction, by confining it to a smaller and smoother surface, and in steadying the motion through the flexibility of the poles.

It often happens that agitation of any kind enables us to considerably lessen the friction between two bodies, especially when they are elastic. If we wish, for instance, to pull a ring along an iron rod using a thread that is nearly perpendicular to it, we may exert all our strength in vain if we apply it gradually, since the increase of force continues to increase the adhesion. But if we pull the ring suddenly and then slacken the thread, the ring rebounds from the rod because of its elasticity; in this manner, it slides easily along through a series of these movements. In such a case, however, it would be more natural—if the thread were heavy enough—to give it a serpentine motion, which would pull the ring in a more oblique direction. It is said that when a screw is fixed very firmly in a piece of iron, it may be removed much more easily while the iron is being filed in a nearby part. The vibration thus produced probably operates in a manner somewhat similar to that of the rod.
