It is necessary to pay attention to the chemical properties of the oil and to ensure that it is not of such a nature as to corrode the metals used, especially where the work requires great accuracy. Tallow is liable to lose its lubricating quality unless it is frequently renewed. Between surfaces of wood, soap is sometimes applied, but more commonly black lead <note>graphite</note>, which becomes highly polished. The advantages of canals, and of navigation in general, are principally derived from the ease with which the particles of fluids move out of the way for the motion of bodies floating on them.

The placement of rollers or of balls bears some resemblance to the application of fluids. Assuming the surfaces are flat and parallel, a roller moves between them without any friction; but it still has to overcome the resistance caused by the depression it produces in the substance on which it moves, which is greater or lesser according to the softness and lack of elasticity of the substance. If the substance were perfectly elastic, the temporary depression would produce no resistance, because the tendency to rise behind the roller would be exactly equivalent to the force opposing its progress in front; and the actual resistance only arises from a greater or smaller lack of elasticity in the materials involved. The constant change of position of the rollers is often a significant objection to their use; their action may in some cases be prolonged by fixing wheels on their ends, as well as by some other arrangements; but these methods are too complicated to offer much practical utility. Rollers may also be placed between two cylinders, one convex and the other concave, and friction may be completely removed in this manner, regardless of the size of the rollers. (Plate XVII. Fig. 222, 223.)

The effect of friction in any machine is always reduced in proportion as the velocity of the parts sliding against each other is reduced; it is therefore obvious that by reducing the dimensions of the axle of a wheel as much as possible, we also reduce the friction. When the pressure on the axle is derived mainly from the weight of the wheel itself, the friction may be lessened by placing the wheel in a horizontal position and making the axle vertical:

#### LECTURE XVIII.

For in this manner, the weight may be supported on an axis ending in a very small surface, and the effect of the friction on this surface will be about one-third less than if it acted at the circumference. The speed of the parts sliding against each other may be reduced even further by placing each end of the axis on another wheel, or between two wheels, upon which the axis rolls as they turn around; in this way, the friction is transferred to the axis of these wheels, where the motion is very slow. However, when a heavy weight must be supported, it is necessary for the friction wheels to be very strong and very accurately formed; for if their surface were irregular, they might stop moving, and their purpose would be defeated. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 224.)

Perrault attempted to avoid all friction by supporting the axis of a wheel within the coil of a rope, which allowed it to turn while the entire wheel rose and fell; however, the stiffness of a rope generally causes even greater resistance than the friction for which it is substituted.

Carriage wheels owe a great part of their usefulness to the reduction of friction. This friction is as much less in a carriage than in a dray as the diameter of the axle is smaller than that of the wheel, even assuming the dray slides on a greased iron surface. The wheels also help us in pulling the carriage over an obstacle, for the path that the wheel's axis follows is always smoother and less abrupt than the surface of a rough road on which the wheel rolls. It is obvious that both of these advantages are more fully achieved by large wheels than by smaller ones; the dimensions of the axle do not increase in the same proportion as those of the wheel, and the path of the axle (to which the path of the center of gravity is similar) consists of segments of larger circles and is consequently less curved. If the wheels are elastic and rebound from an obstacle, the difference is even more pronounced. It is, however, just possible that the curvature of the obstacle to be overcome might be between that of a larger and a smaller wheel; in this case, the taller wheel will touch a more distant part of the obstacle, so that the path of the axle will form a sharp angle, while the smaller wheel follows the curve and produces a more even motion. This, however, is a rare occurrence and an advantage of little importance. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 225, 226.)

The greater part of the resistance to the motion of a carriage very frequently arises from the continual displacement of a portion of the materials of the road. These materials do not react on the wheels with perfect elasticity, but instead undergo a permanent change of form proportional to the loss of force. Hence, in soft sand, although the axles of the wheels may move in a perfectly horizontal direction, the <term>draught</term> <note>the force required to pull a vehicle</note> becomes extremely heavy. The more the wheel sinks, the greater the resistance is; and if we suppose the degree of elasticity of the materials and their immediate resistance at different depths to be known, we may calculate the effect of their reaction in retarding the motion of the carriage. 

Thus, if the materials were perfectly inelastic—acting only on the front half of the submerged portion of the wheel—and if their immediate pressure or resistance were simply proportional to the depth (like that of fluids or elastic substances), the horizontal resistance would be to the weight nearly as the depth of the submerged part is to two-thirds of its length. However, if the pressure increased as the square of the depth, which is a more probable supposition, the resistance would be to the weight as the depth is to about four-fifths of the length. The pressure may even vary still more rapidly, and we may consider the proportion of the resistance to the weight as no greater than that of the depth of the submerged part to its length, or of half this length to the diameter of the wheel. If the materials are in any degree elastic, the resistance will be lessened accordingly. 

But on any of these suppositions, it may be shown that the resistance may be reduced to one-half, either by making a wheel a little less than three times as high, or about eight times as broad as the given wheel. This consideration is of particular consequence in soft and boggy soils, as well as in sandy countries. Thus, in moving timber in a moist situation, it becomes extremely advantageous to employ very high wheels; they have the additional convenience that the timber may be suspended from the axles by chains, without the labor of raising it so high as would be necessary for placing it upon a carriage of any kind. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 227.)

But the magnitude of wheels is practically limited by the strength or the weight of the materials of which they are made, by the danger of overturning when the <term>centre of gravity</term> is raised too high, and—in the case of the first pair of wheels of a four-wheeled carriage—by the inconvenience that would arise in turning a corner with a wheel which might interfere with the body of the carriage. It is also of advantage that the draught of a horse should be in

In order to apply the force in this manner to both pairs of wheels, where there are four, the line of draught ought to be directed to a point halfway between them, or rather to a point immediately under the <term>centre of gravity</term> of the carriage; and such a line would always pass above the axis of the front wheels. If the line of draught passes immediately through this axis, the pressure on the rear wheels will remain unaltered; and if the traces or shafts are fixed even lower, the pressure on the rear wheels will even be somewhat increased by the draught. It is evident, therefore, that this advantage cannot be obtained if the front wheels are very high; we may also understand that in some cases the common opinion of the suitability of placing a load over the front wheels, rather than the rear wheels, may have some foundation in truth. When several horses are employed, the draught of all but the last must be nearly horizontal; in this case, the bending of the chain brings it into a position somewhat more favorable for the action of the horses; but the same cause makes the direction of its attachment to the wagon unfavorable; further than this, there is no absolute loss of force, but it appears to be advisable to cause the shaft horse to pull in a direction as much elevated as possible; and on the whole, it is probable that horses drawing singly have a material advantage, when they do not require additional attendance from the drivers.

The practice of making broad wheels conical obviously has the disadvantageous effect of producing friction at each edge of the wheel when the carriage is moving in a straight line; for such a wheel, if it moved alone, would always describe a circle around the vertex of the cone to which it belongs. Since the axles are slightly conical so that they do not become loose, or so they can be easily tightened as they wear, it is necessary for them to be bent downward so that their lower surfaces remain horizontal; otherwise, the wheels would press too much against the <term>linchpin</term> <note>a fastener used to prevent a wheel from sliding off its axle</note>. For this reason, the distance between the wheels should be slightly greater at the top than at the bottom, making their surfaces naturally somewhat conical. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 228.)

It has been proposed to fix the wheels to their respective axles, extending the axles only to the middle of the carriage and allowing them to turn on <term>friction wheels</term> or rollers; this is a plan that might succeed if the apparatus is not too complicated for use, but in fact, the direct friction on the axles is not significant enough to make this refinement necessary. If both opposite wheels were fixed to a single axis, one of them would be dragged backward and the other forward whenever the motion turned away from a straight line; a similar effect actually occurs in those carriages that are supported on a single roller.

The effect of the suspension of a carriage on springs is to equalize its motion by ensuring every change is communicated to it more gradually through the flexibility of the springs, and by absorbing a certain portion of every sudden impulse to generate a degree of <term>rotatory motion</term>. This rotatory motion depends on the oblique position of the straps suspending the carriage, which prevents it from swinging in a parallel direction; a vibration like the one that would occur if the straps were parallel would be too extreme unless they were very short, in which case the motion would be somewhat rougher. The obliquity of the straps also tends to some extent to keep the carriage in a horizontal position; for if they were parallel and both vertical, the lower one would have to support the greater portion of the weight—at least according to the common way of fixing them to the bottom of the carriage—and the spring, being flexible, would be depressed even further. But when the straps are oblique, the upper one always assumes a more vertical position and consequently bears more of the load; for when a body of any kind is supported by two oblique forces, their horizontal thrusts must be equal, otherwise the body would move laterally; and in order that the hori-

The reason for dividing the springs into separate plates has already been explained: the beam of the carriage, which unites the wheels, supplies the strength necessary for forming the connection between the axles. The ease with which a carriage moves depends not only on the elasticity of the springs, but also on the slight instability of its <term>equilibrium</term>, which we may judge to some extent by tracing the path that the center of gravity must describe when the carriage swings. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 229.)

The ways of attaching horses and oxen to carriages vary in different countries, and it is not easy to determine the most eligible method. When horses are harnessed to pull side by side, they are usually attached to the opposite ends of a bar or lever; and if their strength is very unequal, the bar is sometimes unequally divided by the <term>fulcrum</term>, the weaker horse being made to act on the longer end of the bar, and thus being enabled to counteract the greater force of his companion. But even without this inequality, a compensation takes place, for the center on which the bar moves is always considerably behind the points where the horses are attached; and when one of them falls back a little, the effective arm of the lever becomes more perpendicular to the direction of his force, and gives him a greater power, while the opposite arm becomes more oblique, and causes the other horse to act at a disadvantage: so that there is a kind of stability in the equilibrium. If the fulcrum were further forward than the end of the bar, the two horses could never pull together conveniently. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 230.)

In mining regions and in collieries, it is common, to facilitate the motion of the carriages employed in moving ore or coal, to lay <term>wheel-ways</term> <note>early forms of railway tracks</note> of wood or iron along the road on which they are to pass; and this practice has recently been extended in some cases as a substitute for the construction of navigable canals. It is possible that roads paved with iron may hereafter be employed for the purpose of rapid travel, since there is scarcely any resistance to be overcome except that of the air, and such roads would allow the speed to be increased almost without limit.

For removing earth from one location to another, a series of baskets has sometimes been hung on two endless ropes, moving on pulleys of such a form as to allow the bars supporting the baskets to pass freely over them; the baskets are moved by means of a winch, acting on the rope by a wheel like one of the pulleys. Sometimes also a series of small carts has been connected by ropes and drawn in a circle or oval up and down an inclined plane. These methods may be adopted in making roads where a hill is to be leveled and the materials are to be used in filling up the valley below; but in such cases, two carts connected by a cylinder or windlass are generally sufficient; and they may be arranged in the same manner as the carriages for removing boats on an inclined plane.

->LECTURE XIX.<-

### ON MODES OF CHANGING THE FORMS OF BODIES.

The corpuscular forces by which bodies retain their peculiar forms of aggregation require, in many cases, to be counteracted or modified by mechanical processes. Thus, we have frequent occasion to compress bodies into a smaller space, to augment their dimensions in a particular direction, to divide their substance—either partially or totally—along given lines or surfaces, or to destroy their general form by reducing them into more minute portions. We may consider these subjects as principally relating to the effects of compression, extension, penetration, division, attrition, digging, boring, agitation, trituration, and demolition. The first two of these articles depend on such a change as we have examined while considering the strength of materials under the name of alteration; the remainder depend on fracture.

The instruments particularly intended for compression are in general of the description of presses, and the most common operate by means of a screw. The friction on the screw interferes considerably with the power of the machine, but it is of use in keeping the press fixed in a position into which it has been brought by force. The screw is always turned by a lever; for without this assistance, however powerful it might be, the friction would render it almost useless. When great force is required, the screw is made as close as is consistent with the strength of its spires. Mr. Hunter's double screw may also be used with advantage where only a small extent of motion is required. The screw of a printing press, or of a stamping press, is, on the contrary, open, and it is caused to descend with considerable momentum, the handle being loaded with a weight. Wherever a force is so employed as to produce an impulse which acts on any body, the momentum, which is the result of the action of the force for a certain time, is usually much more powerful than the

simple pressure; the degree of its efficacy depends, however, on the degree of compressibility of the substance. Thus, if a heavy body falls from a certain height so as to acquire a momentum in consequence of the force of gravity, it will ultimately exert on the substance upon which it falls a force nearly as much greater than its weight as the space through which the surface of the struck substance is depressed by the impulse is less than twice the height from which the body has fallen; and unless either the substance is very compressible or the height is very small, this force must be incomparably greater than the pressure of the weight alone.

For a printing press, a single heavy roller is sometimes made to pass over the paper once it has been laid on the type; and since the whole action of such a roller is confined to a small area at any one time, it is said to exert sufficient force and to perform its work more evenly than a common press; however, its operation must be comparatively slow. A common mangle for linen acts in a nearly similar manner. In calendering mills, the force of a spring is employed to exert pressure on the block with which the materials are glazed.

The copperplate printing press and the machine for copying letters are composed of two rollers, parallel to each other, pressing on the substance which is placed between them, and which is brought into position partly by the friction of the surface of the roller and partly by external force.

The rollers by which sugar canes are pressed are generally positioned vertically, with the middle one of three being turned by horses, mules, or water, and the canes being made to return around it so as to pass through both gaps in succession. It appears to be of some advantage in presses of this kind that all the rollers should be turned independently of their action on the materials placed between them, since the friction of two rollers may tend to draw the materials into the space between them with more regularity and greater force than the action of a single roller would. For this reason, it may be advisable to retain the toothed wheels turning the rollers, even when their axes are not firmly fixed but are held together by an elastic hoop. (Plate XVIII, Fig. 231.)

### LECTURE XIX.

In oil mills, an even greater momentum is applied for the purpose of compression than in the printing press: hammers, or long wooden beams placed vertically, are raised by a water wheel and allowed to fall on wedges, which act very forcefully on the materials contained in bags on each side.

Compression is also sometimes performed by the operation of hammering: thus, cast brass is generally hammered before it is used in order to increase its strength; the hammer renders it so much stiffer that if it is necessary to preserve its ductility, it must be frequently annealed by exposure to heat. Anvils and vices are necessary appendages to the hammer; their use depends principally on their firmness, which is chiefly derived from weight in the one case, and from strength in the other; and pincers may be considered as portable vices.

For the purpose of producing a continued pressure on such substances as have a tendency to contract their dimensions under the operation of a press, a spring has been interposed between the press and the materials, which is capable of pursuing them with a certain degree of force: the utility of such an arrangement must, however, be extremely limited. Mr. Bramah has applied a well-known law of hydrostatics to the construction of a very useful press, which is simple, powerful, and portable.

Extension is seldom performed by forces that tend immediately to increase the dimensions of the substance only: it is generally procured by reducing the magnitude of the substance in another direction, sometimes by means of pressure, but more effectively by percussion. The rollers of the press employed for laminating metals are turned by machinery and are capable of being moved backwards and forwards in order to repeat the operation on the same substance; their distance is adjusted by screws, which are turned at once by pinions fixed on the same axis, in order that they may be always parallel. In this manner lead, copper, and silver are rolled into plates, and a thin plate of silver being soldered to a thicker one of copper, the compound plate is submitted again to the action of the press and made so thin as to be offered at a moderate expense. The glazier’s vice is a machine of the same nature for forming window lead: the softness of the lead enables it to assume the re-

In drawing wire, the force is originally applied in the direction of the extension, but it produces a much stronger lateral compression by means of the conical apertures through which the wire is successively drawn. For holding the large wire, pincers are at first used, which embrace it strongly while they pull and open when they advance to a new position; the interruption is perhaps of use by enabling the pincers to acquire a certain momentum before they begin to extend the wire. But afterwards, when the wire is finer, it is simply drawn through the aperture from one wheel or drum to another. During the operation, it requires frequent annealing, which causes a scale to form on its surface; and this must be removed by rolling it in a barrel with proper materials, for the application of an acid is said to injure the temper of the metal. Copper is sometimes drawn into wire so large as to serve for the bolts used in shipbuilding, especially for sheathing ships' bottoms. Silver wire, thinly covered with gold, is rendered extremely fine and then flattened in order to be fit for making gold thread: the thickness of the gold is inconceivably small, much less than the millionth part of an inch, and sometimes only a ten-millionth.

In order to form the handles of vessels of earthenware, the clay is forced through a hole of a proper shape in an iron box. The operation of the potter's wheel consists in great measure of compression and extension performed by the hands; the vessels are finished, when they are partly dry, in a lathe or by other instruments; some kinds of earthenware are formed in a mould only.

When a thread or a plate of glass is extended in a semifluid state, it has a tendency to preserve a uniform thickness throughout: this is derived from the effect of the air in cooling it, the thinnest parts becoming immediately a little colder than the rest and consequently harder, so that they retain their thickness until the neighboring parts are brought into a similar state.

common operation of the smith’s hammer. In forges, the hammers are raised by machinery and thrown forcibly against a spring, so as to recoil with great velocity. With the help of this spring, the hammer sometimes makes 500 strokes in a minute, its force being many times greater than the weight of the hammer. Such forges are used in making malleable iron, in forming copper plates, and in manufacturing steel. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 233.)

Gold is beaten between the intestines of animals on a marble anvil; for this purpose, it is alloyed with copper or silver. It is reduced to a thickness of little more than one three-hundred-thousandth of an inch. Silver leaf is about one one-hundred-and-sixty-thousandth; it is made of silver without alloy.

The operation of coining also depends principally on an extension of the metal into the recesses of the die; it is performed by strong pressure, united with a considerable impulse communicated by a screw like that of a printing press; and sometimes the impression is formed by the repeated blows of a hammer alone.

Thin plates of silvered copper are molded into any figure that may be required by being placed between two corresponding stamps, of which one is fixed and the other attached to the bottom of a heavy hammer. The hammer is raised and allowed to fall in a straight line by means of pincers, which open when they have reached a certain height. Sometimes the contact produced by the forcible impulse of a die is sufficiently close to cause a thin plate of silver to cohere permanently with a surface of iron; and this mode of uniting metals is actually employed in some manufactures.

The operations of perforating, cutting, turning, boring, digging, sawing, grinding, and polishing resemble each other in great measure with respect to the minute actions of the particles of bodies which they must overcome. Penetration is generally performed in the first instance by the effect which we have called <term>detrusion</term> <note>the act of displacing or shearing material by pushing it out of the way</note>, where the magnitude of the penetrating substance is considerable; but when a fine point or edge is employed, it probably first tears the surface where it is most depressed, and then acts like a wedge on the portions of the substance left on each side, with a force so much the

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of mechanical physics and the forces involved in altering the forms of bodies, specifically focusing on the relationship between velocity, energy, and penetration.</meta>

<page-num>225</page-num>
<header>ON MODES OF CHANGING THE FORMS OF BODIES.</header>

greater as the edge is thinner. The resistance offered by a solid, or even by a soft substance, to the motion of a body trying to penetrate it, appears to resemble the force of friction to some extent; this resistance is nearly uniform, whether the motion is slow or rapid, consuming a certain quantity of momentum in a certain time, regardless of what the total velocity may be or how much space is covered. From this arises the advantage of giving a high velocity to a body that is intended to penetrate another, as the distance to which a body penetrates is proportional to the square of its velocity, or to its energy; and a certain degree of energy is required in order to make it penetrate at all. It is true that when we exchange a slow motion for a more rapid one through the immediate action of any mechanical power, we can only obtain the same energy from the same power, because we must diminish the mass in the same proportion as the square of the velocity is increased. However, only a very small part of the force consumed in the operation of any kind of machine is employed in generating momentum; by far the greatest part is spent in overcoming resistances which vary very little with velocity. Only a small portion of the resistance increases in proportion to the square of the velocity; so that by applying triple the force, we may obtain more than double the velocity and more than four times the effect. Furthermore, it has already been observed that when the velocity begins to exceed a certain limit, the effect is increased in a much greater proportion than the square of the velocity. The same work is also performed with less pressure and less strain on the machinery when a high velocity is employed. It is because of the efficacy of velocity in facilitating penetration that soft substances, when moving very swiftly, will readily perforate much harder ones; for the same reason, a gunshot wound, or even the loss of a limb, can occur with so little disturbance to the neighboring parts that it is sometimes scarcely felt. The advantage of an impulse, however small, over a pressure, however great, may be easily understood by the ease with which a moderate blow from a hammer causes a nail to penetrate a substance into which the full force of the arm could not have pushed it.

In the engine for driving piles—the upright beams used for the foundations of buildings in water or in soft ground—the weight is raised slowly to a considerable height so that, in falling, it may acquire sufficient energy to propel the pile effectively. The same force, if applied by very powerful machinery directly to the pile, would perhaps produce an equal

For example, supposing a weight of 500 pounds, falling from a height of 50 feet, to drive the pile 2 inches at each stroke; then, if the resistance is considered as nearly uniform, its magnitude must be about 150 thousand pounds, and the same moving power, with a mechanical advantage of 300 to 1, would perform the work in the same time. But for this purpose, some parts of the machinery must be able to support a strain equivalent to the draft of 600 horses. In the pile-driving engine, the forceps, or tongs, sometimes called the **monkey**, or **follower**, is opened as soon as the weight arrives at its greatest height; and at the same time a lever detaches the drum, employed for raising the weight, from the axis or windlass, at which the horses are drawing; the follower then descends after the weight, uncoiling the rope from the drum, and the force of the horses is employed in turning a fly wheel, until the connection with the weight is again restored. (Plate XVIII. Fig 234.)

When we throw a stone, or a missile weapon of any kind, with the hand, the stone can acquire no greater velocity than the hand itself, accompanied by the neighboring part of the arm: so that the whole velocity must be produced in a mass of matter comparatively very large. A sling enables us to throw a stone or a ball much farther; for here the stone may be moved with a velocity far greater than the hand that impels it, although the action of the force on the stone is indirect, and the resistance of the air considerable. An elastic bow, furnished with a strong and light string, enables us to apply to an arrow or to a ball the whole force of our arms, unburdened by any considerable portion of matter that requires to be moved with the arrow; hence a very great velocity may be obtained in this manner. An air gun possesses the same advantage in a still greater degree, and the force of fired gunpowder excels perhaps all others, from its concentrating an immense force in the form of an inconceivably light elastic fluid; of course a ball impelled by this force, becomes a most effectual instrument in penetrating the most refractory <note>Refractory here refers to substances that are stubborn or highly resistant to penetration.</note> substances. The action of a whip, whether on the air or on a solid body, depends on the increase of velocity caused by the successive transmission of motion from a thicker to a thinner portion of its flexible substance, so that at last, the energy of the lash and of its knots gives it a sufficient capability of producing sound or of inflicting pain.

The instruments generally employed for the division of solid bodies are wedges, chisels, knives, and scissors; they sometimes act by pressure alone, but they are more powerful when impulse is added to it. Hatchets, planes, saws, and files always act with some rapidity. Cutting instruments are in general very thin wedges, but the edge itself is usually much more obtuse; Mr. Nicholson has estimated the angle formed ultimately by the surfaces constituting the finest edge at about 56 degrees. Knives are sometimes fixed on wheels so as to revolve in a direction oblique to their edges, as in some machines for cutting chaff, where the straw is also drawn forward through a space that can be adjusted as desired during each revolution of the knife. An instrument of a similar nature has also been invented for the purpose of cutting weeds underwater.

Steel is principally employed for the edges of all cutting instruments. After being hardened by plunging it into cold water when red hot, it is tempered by laying it on a heated iron or, more accurately, by Mr. Stodart's method of immersing it in a molten metallic alloy. When its surface has acquired a yellow tinge, it is fit for edge tools, and the degree of heat proper for watch springs is indicated by a blue color. The backs of knives are often made of iron, which is less brittle than steel; these substances are generally welded together by hammering them when red hot, but sometimes, in large instruments, a back of iron is only riveted on.

The lathe is an elegant instrument, in which a considerable relative velocity is produced between the tool and the substance to be cut, by the revolution of this substance on an axis, while the tool is supported by a rest. Ornamental lathes admit of a great variety of mechanical contrivance, but they are of little practical use, except for amusement. Picture frames are, however, sometimes turned in oval lathes; and in the manufacture of buttons, machines of a similar nature are occasionally employed. The effect of every lathe of a complicated construction depends on a certain degree of motion of which its axis is capable: if this motion be governed by a screw, a screw of any diameter may be turned by its assistance; if by a frame producing an elliptic curve, any number of ovals, having the same center, may be described at once; and if a movable point connected with the work, be pressed by a strong spring against a pattern of any kind, placed at one end of the axis, a copy, of the same form, may be made at the other end of the axis.

The process of boring is a combination of penetration and division, and sometimes of attrition. Awls, gimlets, screws, augers, and center-bits, are various forms of borers. The drill has the advantage of a rapid motion, communicated by the drill bow, which turns it round by means of a little wheel or pulley. In boring cannon, the tool is at rest, while the cannon revolves, and by this arrangement the bore of the cannon is formed with much more accuracy than according to the old method of putting the borer in motion; perhaps because the inertia of so large a mass of matter, as constitutes the cannon, assists in defining the axis of revolution with more accuracy. The borer is pressed against the cannon by a weight, hung on the arm of a bent spring, and during the operation, the outside is also turned into its intended shape by the application of proper instruments. Plows, spades, pickaxes, mattocks, harrows, and other agricultural instruments, resemble the chisel and the wedge in their operation. The numerous varieties in their form and the complications of their structure are determined more by the various modifications of their action required for particular purposes than by any significant difference in the way the principles on which they depend are applied. (Plate XVIII. Fig. 236.)

The process of mining is a combination of boring and digging. Shafts are sunk, levels are driven, and drains are carried off with the help of picks or pickaxes, wedges, and hammers; the rocks are also sometimes loosened by blasting with gunpowder. In searching for coal, a shaft is sunk through the uppermost soft <term>strata</term>, and the rock is then bored by striking it continually with an iron borer ending in a steel edge, which is meanwhile turned partly around; at proper intervals, a scoop is lowered to draw up the loose fragments. In this manner, a perforation is sometimes made for more than a hundred fathoms, the borer being lengthened by pieces screwed onto it. It is then partly supported by a counterweight and is worked by machinery; if it happens to break, the piece is raised by a rod equipped with a hollow cone, like an extinguisher, which is driven down onto it. Sometimes the borer is equipped with knives, which are made to act on any part as desired and to scrape off a portion of the surrounding substance, which is collected in a suitable receptacle.

For sawing wood on a large scale, sawmills are very advantageously employed, usually being driven by water. Several saws are generally fixed in a frame parallel to each other; they are worked up and down by a crank, and at every alternation, a wheel is drawn around a little by a catch, or click, and moves the frame that supports the timber forward. When the machine is used for cutting the <term>fellies</term> <note>The outer rim of a wooden wheel, to which the spokes are attached.</note> which form the circumference of wheels, the frame supporting the timber is made to turn around a center. A circular saw is used in the construction of blocks and pulleys; and in order to make the motion more secure from the effect of accidental irregularities, the wheels are made to turn each other by contact only, without teeth. The advantage of a saw that revolves continually appears to be very considerable, since a much greater velocity may be given to it than can be obtained when the motion is alternating. Such a saw has also sometimes been applied to cutting off piles underwater.

In mills for sawing marble into slabs, the saws are drawn backward and forward horizontally: they are made of soft iron without teeth; and when sand is applied to them with water during the operation, the sand is partly embedded in the iron and grinds away the marble.

<margin>*</margin>
Granite is worked by driving a number of thin wedges very gradually into it at various parts of the desired section; and sometimes wooden wedges are employed, which, when moistened by water, expand and separate the parts from each other. It is also said that many stones may be divided by drawing lines on them with oil and then exposing them to heat. Perhaps some processes of this kind might be performed with advantage underwater; it is well known that glass may be cut in a rough manner underwater without much difficulty by a common pair of scissors.

To reduce the size of a substance in a particular part, instruments of attrition are used: rasps, files, grindstones, and hones; and the immediate actions of all these appear to resemble those of chisels and saws. The teeth of files are cut with a hard chisel while the steel is soft, and the files are afterward hardened. In using the grindstone, water is applied to avoid the inconvenience produced by too much heat, and sometimes tallow is substituted for water with equal advantage. However, oil is not found to serve the same purpose; and it has been conjectured that the cold continually caused by the melting of the tallow at the point of friction serves as a substitute for the cooling effect of the water’s evaporation. For grinding and polishing steel, the grindstones are made to revolve either vertically or horizontally with a velocity so great as to traverse sometimes as much as 60 feet in a second. Various substances, chiefly of mineral origin, are also used, on account of their hardness, as intermediate materials for grinding and polishing others. These are diamond dust, corundum, emery, tripoli, putty, glass, sand, flint, red oxide of iron, or <term>crocus martis</term>, and prepared chalk; they are sometimes applied in loose powder, and sometimes fixed on leather, wood, or paper. Cuttlefish bone and sealskin are furnished by the animal kingdom, and Dutch rushes by the vegetable; these are employed chiefly in polishing wood or ivory.

Marble is made smooth by rubbing one piece on another, with the interposition of sand; the polishing blocks are sometimes caused to revolve by machinery in a trough in which the marble is placed underwater, and are drawn at the same time gradually to and from the center; or the slab itself, with the frame on which it rests, is drawn slowly backward and forward while the blocks are working on it. Granite is polished with iron rubbers, by means of sand, emery, and putty; it is necessary to take care during the operation that the water, which trickles down from the rubbers and carries with it some of the iron, may not collect below the columns and stain them; but this inconvenience may be wholly avoided by employing rubbers of glass.

Optical lenses are fixed on blocks by means of a cement and ground with emery by a tool of proper convexity or concavity: if they are small, a large number is fixed on the blocks at the same time. The tool is sometimes first turned around its axis by machinery, and when the lenses are to be finished, a compound motion is given to it by means of a crank; and in order to make it smoother, the wheels turn each other by brushes instead of cogs. The point of the lens where its two surfaces are parallel is determined by looking through it at a minute object while it is fixed on a wheel with a tubular axis and shifting it until the object no longer appears to move; a circle is then described, as it revolves, in order to mark its outline.

### LECTURE XIX.

Machines for trituration, by means of which larger masses of matter are crushed, broken, or ground into smaller parts, are generally categorized under the name of mills. After the pestle and mortar, the simplest machine of this kind appears to be the stamping mill; the stampers resemble the hammers of the mill employed in extracting oils from seeds, and the machine is used for reducing metal ores to powder, and sometimes also bark and linseed; the surfaces of the stampers are reinforced with iron or steel. However, bark and seeds are more usually ground by the repeated pressure of two stone wheels, rolling on an axis that is forced horizontally around a fixed point. A nobleman of distinguished rank and talent has lately employed a wheel of cast iron—formed of two portions of cones joined at their bases—as a mortar mill; after thirty revolutions, when the material is sufficiently ground, a bell rings and the horse stops.

The materials for making gunpowder are also ground by a wheel revolving in a trough. In order to <term>corn</term> <note>to form into grains</note> them, they are moistened and put into boxes with a number of holes in their bottoms; these boxes are placed side by side in a circular frame suspended by cords. The frame is agitated by a crank revolving horizontally, and the paste is shaken through the holes; the grains are then polished by causing them to revolve rapidly within a barrel.

A revolving barrel is used for forming and polishing various small round bodies, and it is often employed in agriculture as a churn for making butter. The purpose of agitation is perhaps more effectively achieved by an alternate motion, which has sometimes been produced in a barrel churn by means of a cord attached to a heavy pendulum.

Threshing machines are of two kinds; the first consists of a number of flails, beating the grain in nearly the same manner as they are used by laborers. In the other kind, which is more commonly employed in this country, the grain is drawn along by two revolving rollers and made to pass between a cylinder and its concave cover, while a number of blocks, projecting from the surface of the cylinder, beat or rub out the grains very effectively from the ears. The grain falls out at the lower part and is winnowed by a fan which the machine turns at the same time. In this manner, it is said that a horse will thresh about 100

<insert>UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</insert>

Some kinds of grain are occasionally ground in iron or steel mills, which consist of a solid cylinder or cone turning within a hollow one, with both surfaces cut obliquely into teeth. But the common mill for grinding grain is composed of two circular stones made of siliceous grit, placed horizontally. The upper stone revolves with considerable speed and is supported by an axis passing through the lower one at a distance that can be adjusted as desired. When the diameter is five feet, the stone usually makes about 90 revolutions per minute; if the speed were greater, the flour would become too hot. The grain is shaken out of a funnel, or hopper, by means of projections from the revolving axis that strike against the opening; it passes through the middle of the upper millstone and is easily admitted between the stones. The lower stone is slightly convex, and the upper one is somewhat more concave, so that the grain passes over more than half the stone's radius before it begins to be ground. After being reduced to powder, it is discharged at the circumference, its escape being aided by the convexity of the lower stone as well as by centrifugal force. The surface of the stones is cut into grooves in order to make them act more quickly and effectively on the grain. The resistance in grinding wheat has been estimated at about one-thirty-fifth of the weight of the millstone. The stones have sometimes been placed vertically, with the axis supported on friction wheels, but the horizontal position appears to be more suitable for large-scale mills. It is said that a man and a boy can grind a bushel of wheat in an hour using a hand mill. In a watermill, the grinding and processing of a bushel of wheat is equivalent to the effect of 20,160 pounds of water falling from a height of 10 feet, which is about as much work as a laborer performs in a little more than half an hour. In a windmill, when the speed is increased by the irregular action of the wind, the grain is sometimes forced rapidly through the mill without being sufficiently ground. There is an elegant method of preventing this by using the centrifugal force of two balls; these fly outward as soon as the speed increases, and as they rise in the arc of a circle, they allow one end of a lever to rise with them, while the opposite end of the lever descends with the upper millstone, bringing it a little closer to the lower one. The bran or husk is separated from the flour by sifting it in the bolting mill, which consists of a

When the flour is made into bread, the dough requires kneading. For this purpose, a machine is sometimes used in which four or more bars, parallel to the axis of motion, are turned around by means of a <term>walking wheel</term>. The dough is placed in a circular trough in which the bars revolve slightly off-center, so as to approach one of its sides during each revolution; thus, the dough is constantly compelled to change its shape.

A machine of nearly the same construction is employed for <term>levigating</term> flints after they have first been heated until they are red-hot and plunged into cold water to make them brittle. They are mixed, when necessary, with other large stones, and the water in which the process is performed carries off the powder and deposits its coarser parts in a short time, while the finer particles remain suspended much longer and are thus separated from the rest.

When a mechanical structure is to be demolished, or a natural substance is to be broken into smaller parts, we often have occasion to employ the collective force of men, the power of machinery, or the expansive force of chemical agents. Battering rams—wooden beams suspended by ropes and tipped with iron, which were used by ancient warriors when besieging a town—are now generally superseded by the introduction of artillery, although they may perhaps still offer, in some cases, a more economical and equally powerful method of operation. The same momentum and the same energy may be given to a battering ram at a lower cost than to a cannonball; but it is probable that the effectiveness of a cannonball is mainly due to its velocity increasing beyond the limit that the substance being destroyed can withstand without breaking, regardless of the mass of the striking body.

For demolishing smaller objects, pincers, hammers, and crowbars are generally sufficient; to these, more complicated instruments are sometimes added. For example, several machines have been invented for extracting ship’s bolts. A hook which grips like the common instrument for extracting teeth has been used for holding them firmly, and sometimes

<page-num>235</page-num>
# ON MODES OF CHANGING THE FORMS OF BODIES.
<meta>significant ink bleed-through from the verso page is visible in the lower half of the leaf</meta>

A screw, turned by means of wheel-work, has been used to gain a force sufficient to overcome their <term>adhesion</term>. In all such cases, however, the effect of <term>percussion</term> has a considerable advantage; and even if other means are employed, it is useful to begin by loosening the firmness of the adhesion with the blows of a hammer. In this manner, a screw may be extracted which is so firmly attached by its rust as to be immovable by other means.

The expansive force of heat is frequently of great service in dividing rocks or in destroying old buildings. This is sometimes done simply by the application of fire, as in the mine of <term>Rammelsberg</term> in the <term>Hartz</term>, where the layer containing the ore is of such a nature—partly, perhaps, because of the combustible matter that enters into its composition—that by the effect of a large quantity of fuel burned in the vast excavation of which it forms the side, it is rendered so brittle as to be worked with ease. More commonly, however, the force of <term>gunpowder</term> is employed, and rocks are generally blasted very conveniently by an explosion of this powerful agent. A hole being bored to a depth of three or four feet, the powder is placed at the bottom; a wire is then introduced, small stones and sand are rammed around it, and the wire is withdrawn, leaving a passage for firing the powder by means of a train of sufficient length to ensure the safety of the workman. It is said that the explosion is more effective when the powder does not fill the entire cavity; however, this appears to require confirmation. The chemical powers, which are the ultimate causes of the operation of gunpowder, belong to a branch of philosophy <note>science</note> which is not our task to investigate here; but the <term>elasticity</term> of the gases and vapors that are released, as modified by the heat accompanying their production, will be considered and explained in the subsequent divisions of this <term>Course of Lectures</term>.

# LECTURE XX.

## ON THE HISTORY OF MECHANICS.

The order we have followed in considering the various departments of <term>mechanical science</term> has been, to a great extent, <term>synthetical</term>. This was dictated by the plan of proceeding logically from the simplest principles to their more complicated combinations, so as to build at every step on foundations that had been firmly laid before. This method is unquestionably the best suited for the rapid progress of a student in sciences with which he is unfamiliar. But having once acquired a certain degree of knowledge, he is anxious to be informed by what steps that knowledge was originally obtained, and to which individuals humanity is indebted for each improvement that has been successively made. Therefore, although we cannot attempt to provide a complete history of mechanics, it may still be satisfying to take a short retrospect of a few of the most remarkable eras in <term>mechanical philosophy</term>, and in those parts of mathematics on which it immediately depends.

It is universally accepted that the Greeks derived the elements of mathematical, mechanical, and astronomical learning from Egypt and from the East. Diogenes Laertius, who appears very eager to claim the merit of originality for his countrymen, does not deny that Thales and Pythagoras acquired much of their knowledge during their travels. Thales of Miletus is the first who is thought to have introduced these studies into Greece. Moeris, who was probably a king of Egypt, and Theuth or Thoth, a native of the same country, are mentioned as having laid the foundations of <term>geometry</term>; but the science could scarcely have extended, in those ages, further than was barely necessary for the measurement of land—since Thales, or even a later philosopher, is said to have first discovered that two lines drawn from

Thales was one of the seven whom antiquity distinguished by the title of wise men; he flourished about 600 years before the Christian era, and he was the father of the Ionian school, whose members in later times devoted themselves more particularly to the study of moral philosophy rather than natural philosophy.

The Italian school, on the contrary, which was founded by Pythagoras, appears to have been more inclined to the study of nature and its laws. Although no branch of human knowledge was excluded from the pursuits of either of these primary divisions of the Greek sages, Socrates eventually introduced a taste for metaphysical speculation into the Ionian school, which discouraged almost all inclination to reason coolly and clearly regarding natural causes and effects. Philosophy is indebted to Pythagoras for the name it bears; his predecessors had been in the habit of calling themselves "wise," but he chose to be called only a "lover of wisdom." He had studied under Pherecydes, and Pherecydes under Pittacus; however, regarding mathematical and mechanical research, it does not appear that either of his teachers had made any improvements. Upon his return from his travels in Egypt and the East during the time of the last Tarquin, about 500 years before Christ, he found his native country of Samos under the rule of the tyrant Polycrates, and went into voluntary exile to seek a peaceful retreat in a corner of Italy. At Croto, says Ovid, he studied and taught the laws of nature.

He dealt her treasures o'er the listening land.

achievements both in mathematics and in mechanics, and in particular that he discovered the well-known relation between the hypotenuse and the sides of a right-angled triangle, and demonstrated that the square of the hypotenuse is always equal to the sum of the squares of the sides. This theorem is more essential to the perfection of geometry than any other proposition that can be named; and if we may judge by the story of his having sacrificed a hecatomb <note>A great public sacrifice, traditionally of one hundred oxen.</note> to the Muses on the occasion of the discovery, he seems to have had a foresight of the magnificence of the structure that was to be built on this foundation in later times.

Democritus of Abdera lived about a century after Pythagoras, whose works he studied and whose principles he adopted. He appears to have possessed very extensive knowledge and profound learning, but little remains of his works except for their titles. Some have attributed to him the invention of the method of arranging stones to form an arch. Seneca thinks that such a simple invention must have been practiced in earlier ages, but Mr. King has endeavored to show that its general introduction into building was of a much later date. Architecture and other mechanical arts had, however, been considerably advanced some time before this period, if it is true that Ctesiphon or Chersiphron, who built the temple of Ephesus, was a contemporary of Croesus and Thales. It is uncertain at what time stone bridges were first built, and it is doubtful whether the art of building wooden bridges was very well understood in those ages; for according to Herodotus, it was commonly believed that Thales avoided the necessity of securing a passage over the Halys for Croesus's army by encamping them on its banks and cutting a channel for the river behind them, although the historian himself is of the opinion that they passed over bridges that already existed. Curtius speaks of a stone bridge over the Euphrates at Babylon, which appears to have been built long before the time of Alexander, whose expedition he recounts; and it is scarcely probable that a stone bridge could have withstood the force of such a rapid river if it had been supported by columns alone, without arches. We are informed by Pliny that Ctesiphon lowered his large blocks of stone by placing them on heaps of sandbags and letting out the sand by degrees; it does not appear how he raised them, but the inclined plane seems to provide the simplest and most obvious method.

Archytas of Tarentum and Eudoxus of Cnidus were also Pythagoreans. They were the first who attempted to make the mathematical sciences familiar through popular illustrations; and Archytas is said by some to have invented the pulley and the screw. They lived nearly 150 years after Pythagoras, and geometry had made very rapid advances in the meantime, for the properties of the conic sections were well known to these philosophers. "The first persons," says Plutarch, "that cultivated the method of organic geometry, were of the school of Eudoxus and Archytas. These philosophers introduced elegance and variety into science by illustrations derived from sensible objects, and made use of mechanical contrivances for expediting and familiarizing the solutions of problems, which, if more mathematically treated, are complicated and difficult: each of them invented a method of determining in this manner the magnitude of two mean proportionals between two given lines, by the assistance of certain curves and sections. Plato by no means approved of their mode of proceeding, and criticized them severely for giving up and perverting the most essential advantages of geometry, and causing the science to revert from pure and incorporeal forms to the qualities of sensible bodies, subjected to narrow and servile restraints. It was for this reason that practical mechanics were separated from geometry, and were long neglected by philosophers, being considered as a department only of the art of war."

Aristotle, who was almost the last of the Ionian school, flourished a little less than half a century after Archytas; he was perhaps the author of no original discoveries relating to the principles of mechanics, but we find, in his treatise on this science, the law of the composition of motion very distinctly laid down; he makes, however, some mistakes respecting the properties of levers. His general merit in elegant literature, as well as in natural history and natural philosophy, is too well known to require praise.

The foundation of Alexandria commences a period memorable for science in general, but more particularly for mathematics and astronomy. Dinocrates was the architect whom Alexander employed in laying out and in building this celebrated city. Among those who studied in this school, the sciences are indebted to none more than to Euclid, who lived about 300 years before our era. It is uncertain how much of his *Elements* may have been derived from his own investigations; but the masterly manner in which

Epicurus was a contemporary of Euclid and is considered the last of the Pythagorean or Italian philosophers. The insight he showed in assigning the true causes to many mechanical phenomena—his explanations of which are copied by Lucretius—is sufficient to induce us to look forward with impatience to the publication of those of his works that have lately been discovered among the manuscripts of Herculaneum. Apollonius of Perga lived about half a century later; the elegance and depth of his investigations into the most complex properties of the conic sections left but little to be added to them by more modern mathematicians. The architect Philo appears to have been older than Apollonius, but he is not the Philo whose essay on machines of war is published in the collection of the Ancient Mathematicians, since that author was a pupil of Ctesibius.

For the demonstration of the fundamental properties of the lever and of the center of gravity; for the discovery of the laws of hydrostatics and of the methods for determining the specific gravity of bodies; for the construction of the first cranes and of the first planetarium; and for those improvements to the methods of mathematical investigation which have been the basis of every modern refinement in analytical calculation—for all these additions to our knowledge and our powers, we are indebted to Archimedes. On a character so prominent, we can with pleasure dwell long enough to attend to some details of his history, which are related by Plutarch in his account of the siege of Syracuse; omitting, however, such details as are clearly mythical.

> “Archimedes,” says Plutarch, “armed only with his own inventions, made light of the splendor of the Roman preparations and of the glory of the name of Marcellus.”

And these were inventions that he even considered to be of secondary value, as geometrical playthings which had been the amusements of his leisure hours. It was King Hiero who first persuaded him to transfer a portion of his science from intellectual to material objects, and to stoop in some degree to the understanding of the common people by giving a tangible form to those truths which, in their abstract state, are discoverable only by the faculty of reason. ...relative of Hiero, had asserted that any weight whatever might be moved by any given power. Relying on the validity of his arguments, he had given scope to his imagination and boasted that if he had another earth to which he could step over, he would pull the whole of the present globe out of its place. Hiero, surprised at the boldness of his assertion, requested him to give some substantial proof of its truth by moving a great weight with a small power. Upon this, Archimedes obtained a ship, which had been drawn up on the shore with great labor; after completely manning and loading her, he seated himself at a distance, and by lightly touching the starting mechanism of a machine, he pulled her along as smoothly and as safely as if she had been sailing in the deepest water. Hiero, full of astonishment and admiring the powers of mechanical art, persuaded Archimedes to construct such engines of both defense and offense as might be useful to him in case of a siege. Hiero, however, who lived a life of peace and prosperity, was not so unfortunate as to have a need for them; but they now became highly valuable to the Syracusans, and they were of even greater advantage because their inventor was present to direct their use. In fact, the whole people of Syracuse constituted but a part of Archimedes’s physical machinery, and he was the soul that moved and governed the whole. All other weapons were abandoned, and they employed his engines alone, both for their own defense and for harassing the enemy. In short, the Romans soon became so terrified that if they saw a stick or a rope upon the walls, they cried out that it was some machine of Archimedes and immediately fled; so that Marcellus at last determined to stop attempting to take the place by assault and resolved only to blockade it.

> “Archimedes, however, had such depth of intellect and such sublimity of mind that, notwithstanding he had obtained by these inventions the credit and glory of an intelligence rather divine than human, he thought it unworthy of him to leave any written treatise on the subject. He considered practical mechanics, and every art concerned with satisfying the wants of life, as ignoble and base, and rested all his hopes of fame on those works in which magnificence and elegance are exhibited, untainted by the imperfections of the material world—works that are comparable to nothing else that the mind of man has produced, and in which the subject matter only competes with the manner of treating it, while the magnitude and beauty of the one...”

We may, therefore, easily give credit to what is said of him, that being, as it were, fascinated by this domestic siren that kept him company, he often neglected his food and his clothing; that when sometimes brought by force to the baths, he used to draw his figures in the ashes of the fireplaces, and to make his calculations upon the cosmetics that were used by the attendants; deriving, like a true follower of the muses, every pleasure from an intellectual origin. Among all his beautiful discoveries, he is said to have chosen that of the proportion of the sphere and cylinder for his funeral honors; requesting of his friends that they would place on his tomb a cylinder containing a sphere, and inscribe on it the ratio which he had first determined.

Hero was of the same school, and his pursuits were similar; some of his treatises on hydraulics, pneumatics, and mechanics are published in the collection of ancient mathematicians, and some others are still extant in manuscript. We are informed by Pappus that Hero and Philo had referred the properties of the lever, the wheel and axle, the pulley, the wedge, and the screw to the same fundamental principle; so that the theory of the mechanical powers began at that time to be extremely well understood. The treatises of Hero on pneumatics and on automatons contain many very ingenious inventions, but they are designed more for amusement than for utility; among them is a cupping instrument which operates nearly in the manner of an air pump. A work by Bito on warlike machinery, addressed to King Attalus, is included in the same collection.

Vitruvius was an author of great general knowledge: he lived under one of the earliest Caesars, and the greatest part of our information respecting the mechanics of antiquity has been derived from his works. Apollodorus was employed by Trajan in building a bridge over the Danube in the year 102; he has left a treatise on besieging a town, which is to be found among the ancient mathematicians. Diophantus, Pappus, and Proclus were eminent mathematicians; Diophantus confined himself in great measure to arithmetic and pure geometry; but the last book of Pappus's collections is devoted to mechanics, and Proclus wrote a treatise on motion, which is still extant. The rudiments of algebraic notation and calculation may be found in the works of Diophantus; but the Arabians appear to have first practiced the method of denoting quantities in general by literal characters; they made, however, no considerable advances, and mathematics in general remained nearly stationary until the time of the revival of learning.

During the long interval in which learning and science were involved in the darkness of the Middle Ages, the arts that serve the convenience of life were also in great measure neglected. It is evident from many remains of antiquity that various manufactures had attained a high degree of perfection in Greece and Rome; but the invasions of the barbarians were as effective in suppressing the refinements of civilization as in checking the pursuit of literary achievements: our own country was not the earliest in recovering the arts which had been lost, but it has always received with open arms those

...who have excelled in them. The improvements made within the last few centuries in British manufacturing have earned them a reputation unrivaled by any other nation. The ancient Britons, like other Celtic nations, are believed to have made coarse wool cloths and felts, and perhaps some linen items. Their war chariots, which are mentioned by Caesar, could not have been built without some skill in the crafts of carpentry and blacksmithing. The Romans introduced a certain degree of civilization to England, but it seems to have been largely forgotten soon after they left the country. In the seventh century, several architects and craftsmen were brought from the continent by Wilfrid and Biscop. They restored the practice of building with stone, which had generally been replaced by wood, and laid the foundation for further improvements. 

In the time of King Alfred, English goldsmiths began to excel, and before the Norman Conquest, wool manufacturing had reached a high degree of perfection. The paper we use today was introduced around the year 1100; it was likely imported from the continent, since linen manufacturing was not very advanced in England until 150 years later. However, embroidery was widely practiced, even though silks were primarily woven in Sicily during the 12th century. 

Cloth manufacturing was significantly improved in the 14th century by the arrival of Kempe and other Flemish weavers in England. Many crafts benefited around the same time from the invention of the method for drawing wire, which was first introduced in Nuremberg. In the following century, the growing number of workers employed in various industries suggested to a particularly insightful mind the great principle of the division of labor. By this principle, each individual is able to achieve such a high degree of perfection in a very limited branch of a manufacture that the entire work is performed much more perfectly and quickly than if it had been started and finished by any one person, even one of greater ability and experience. 

The invention of the modern spinning wheel is attributed to Jürgen of Brunswick, and the year 1530 is assigned as its date. England soon benefited from this improvement. Many manufacturers took refuge in this country to escape the Duke of Alva’s persecutions in Flanders, and before the end of the century, a new advancement in weaving was introduced by Lee of Cambridge. He invented the stocking loom, which imitated the texture of knitted stockings that were first manufactured in Spain around the year 1550. Mills for drawing wire and

<header>ON THE HISTORY OF MECHANICS.</header>

Machines for slitting iron were also first built in the sixteenth century; according to Camden, Birmingham and Sheffield were even at that time celebrated for their manufacturing. The machinery that has since been introduced at various periods in those places provides an ease and speed that astonishes every inexperienced spectator. The names of Watt and Boulton have earned a well-deserved fame for their refined improvements; however, many other mechanics of lower rank have shown a level of ingenuity that would honor the most distinguished talents. The manufacturing in Manchester is also of considerable antiquity, but it is deeply indebted to the inventions of Arkwright and his followers, which have also been introduced in many other parts of the United Kingdom. The importance of these improvements can be judged by the quantity of cotton that is annually imported into Great Britain: in 1787, it reached 23 million pounds and employed 420,000 workers; by 1791, it had increased to 32 million pounds. About one half is used for white goods, one fourth for <term>fustians</term>, and the rest for hosiery, blended fabrics, and candle wicks. Yet the wool industry supports over a million people, who earn about nine million pounds sterling annually for their labor and use wool worth about three million pounds.

In architecture, the Anglo-Norman style prevailed in this country from the Conquest to the beginning of the thirteenth century; the arch was frequently used, and its shape was semicircular. Gothic architecture—distinguished by its pointed arches and said to have originated with the Saracens—was first introduced to England around the year 1170 and became increasingly popular for about three centuries. Among the architects of this school, two of the most famous were William of Sens and Walter of Coventry. Perhaps the most elegant example of this style is King’s College Chapel at Cambridge, which was founded by Henry VI and begun in the year 1441. Lincoln Cathedral appears to have been one of the earliest Gothic buildings; Westminster Abbey was finished around 1285, and York Minster was begun a few years later. It is difficult to decide which of these three buildings most deserves the attention of the antiquarian and the architect, or whether Canterbury Cathedral might not be equal to any of them.

<header>LECTURE XX.</header>

In the middle of an age of darkness, an isolated individual captures our attention through merits of no ordinary kind. Roger Bacon was born at Ilchester in the year 1214; it is well known that his experiments led him to a discovery of the properties of gunpowder, although he humanely concealed the nature of its composition from the public and described it only in an enigma. The extent of his optical knowledge has been variously estimated, but it was unquestionably much greater than that of the ancient philosophers. He appears, however, to have had some companions in his mechanical pursuits; he declares that he had seen chariots which could move with incredible rapidity without the help of animals; he describes a diving bell; and he says that he had been informed, on good authority, that machines had been made by which men might fly through the air. *Cimabue*, who first began to revive the long-neglected art of painting, was a contemporary of Bacon. The use of oil in painting is commonly supposed to have been introduced by *Van Eyck*, but there are traces in the records of this country of its employment as early as the year 1239.

The *clepsydrae*, or water timekeepers of the ancients, appear to have been gradually transformed, in the Middle Ages, into the clocks of the Saracens and of the Arabians; and these were introduced into Europe in the thirteenth century. About the year 1290, turret clocks were erected at Westminster and at Canterbury. The first clock of which we know the construction is that which was made by Wallingford in 1326, and which was regulated by a *fly*; and the second is that of *Defondeur*, or *Fusorius*, with a simple balance, made about 1400. But it appears that some portable watches had been constructed in the beginning of the fourteenth century; and about the year 1460, several clockmakers are said to have come to England from Flanders.

The art of engraving on metal, and of printing with the rolling press, is supposed to have been invented in the year 1423. Some attribute the art of printing with types to *Laurentius Coster* of Haarlem, who, as they say, in 1430, employed for the purpose separate blocks of wood tied together with thread. *Gensfleisch*, one of his workmen, went to Mentz and was there assisted by *Gutenberg*, who invented types of metal. But the best authors appear to disbelieve this story; and *Gutenberg*, in partnership with *Fust* and

Schaeffer is the first who is universally acknowledged to have practiced the art [of printing]. It was introduced to this country by William Caxton.

Leonardo da Vinci, the most accomplished man of his age, was born around the year 1443 and excelled not only in painting and poetry but also in architecture, mathematics, and mechanics. The state of practical mechanics in this and the subsequent centuries can be assessed from Ramelli's collection of machines, which contains several curious and useful inventions; some of them were long since forgotten and have even recently been proposed again as new.

The works of Bacon, Lord Verulam, although not immediately directed toward the advancement of mathematics or mechanics, are universally acknowledged to have contributed very significantly to the improvement of every branch of science by the introduction of a correct and conclusive method of philosophical argument and inquiry. In 1577, Guido Ubaldi published a treatise on mechanics that was not entirely free from inaccuracies, and in the following year, a valuable commentary on the works of Archimedes. Some of the properties of projectiles were, around the same time, hypothesized rather than demonstrated by Tartalea. Benedetti soon after began to reason correctly regarding the principles of mechanics; but it was left to Galileo to lay the foundations for the discoveries which have succeeded each other with increasing rapidity for more than two centuries. In the year 1589, he investigated the laws of accelerating forces and showed the nature of the curve that is described by a projectile. He inferred from observation the <term>isochronism</term> of the vibrations of a pendulum, and the principle was soon after applied by Sanctorius to the regulation of timekeepers. Stevinus, a Dutchman, was the first who clearly stated the important law by which the equilibrium of any three forces is determined; and the properties of the center of gravity were successively investigated by Lucas Valerius, Lafaille, and Guldinus, who made several additions to the elegant propositions of Archimedes relating to it.

Descartes, around the same time, was making significant additions to the science of algebra, and mathematics was soon after enriched by Cavalleri’s invention of the method of indivisibles. This method was founded on the principles introduced by Archimedes; it was further improved by Wallis and led to the even more valuable invention of fluxional analysis <note>an early form of calculus</note>.

The laws of collision were investigated at nearly the same time in England by Wren and Wallis, and in France by Huygens. After the discoveries of Archimedes and Galileo, those of Huygens hold the third place, in chronological order, among the greatest benefits that have been conferred on science. His theory of cycloidal pendulums and his doctrine of central forces were the immediate foundations for Newton’s improvements.

Hooke was as great in mechanical practice and ingenious contrivance as Huygens was in more philosophical theory. He was the first to apply the balance spring to watches, and he improved the method of using pendulums in clocks. The quadrant, the telescope, and the microscope were significantly indebted to him; he had the earliest suspicions regarding the true nature of the force that keeps the planets in their orbits; and the number of his inventions is far too great to be listed in a brief history of the progress of science.

The composition of motion, and several other mechanical and optical subjects, are elegantly treated in the lectures published by the learned Dr. Barrow. He was a professor of mathematics at Cambridge and voluntarily resigned his chair to make way for his successor—the pride of his country and an ornament to mankind. Sir Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire on Christmas Day in 1642, the year of Galileo’s death. At the age of 12, he was sent to school at Grantham, and at 18, to Cambridge. He made some important improvements in algebraic analysis and laid the foundation of his admirable method of fluxions before he was 24 years old; however, his modesty prevented him from immediately publishing any work on these subjects. His first optical experiments were also made in the year 1666, and they were communicated to the Royal Society, then in its infancy, upon his admission as a member in 1672.
