The mechanics of the universe are developed in his *Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy*, first published in 1687. The following year he was chosen as the representative of the University of Cambridge in parliament, and in 1696, he was placed, upon the recommendation of the Earl of Halifax, in a lucrative position in the Mint. From 1703 until his death in 1727, he continued as president of the Royal Society and enjoyed, until the age of 80, an uninterrupted state of good health. He was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705 and died possessing a considerable fortune. “He had the singular happiness,” says Mr. Fontenelle, “of obtaining, during his life, all the credit and consideration to which his sublime researches and his fortunate discoveries entitled him. All men of science, in a country which produces so many, placed Newton, by a kind of acclamation, at their head; they acknowledged him as their chief and their master; no opponent, nor even a cool admirer, dared to appear. His philosophy was adopted throughout England, and it is supported in the Royal Society, and in all the excellent productions of the members of that Society, with as much confidence as if it had been consecrated by the respect of a long course of ages.” A remarkable instance of the extent and refinement of Newton’s mathematical acquirements may be found in a paper by a celebrated modern mathematician on the subject of atmospheric refraction; Mr. Kramp observes, with a mixture of surprise and doubt, that Newton appears to have been acquainted with those methods of algebraic calculation which he had himself pursued; at the same time, he says that this is almost incredible, since “he must have discovered certain improvements in the higher analysis which were unknown even to Euler and to every other mathematician before Laplace.”

Although Newton was unquestionably the first inventor of the method of <term>fluxions</term> <note>the early form of calculus</note>, yet Leibniz—whether he had received any hints of Newton’s ideas, as there is some reason to suspect, or whether his investigations were wholly independent of those of Newton—was the first to publish any work on the subject; and he extended its application to many important problems, perhaps earlier than any English mathematician. James and John Bernoulli also pursued the same studies with considerable success, and the general laws of mechanics were very elegantly investigated and successfully applied by these three contemporary philosophers on the continent, while Machin, Cotes, Halley, and De Moivre were applying themselves to similar pursuits in this country. <header>LECTURE XX.</header>

The Academy of Sciences were the authors of many useful investigations relating to practical mechanics, but few of them were made public until after the year 1700. Some of their inventions appeared much later in the valuable collection of machines approved by the academy, and some of them have been inserted in the useful work published by Leupold, at Leipzig, under the title of *Theatrum Machinarum*. Throughout the last century, the transactions of various societies established for the promotion of science became more numerous every year, and the publication of the literary journals of Leipzig and Paris formed a mode of communication that was extremely useful in facilitating the spread of all new discoveries.

The philosophy of Newton also assumed a more popular and attractive form in the writings of Clarke, Pemberton, Maclaurin, and Musschenbroek, and in the lectures of S’Gravesande and Desaguliers. At the same time, more refined investigations into it were pursued with success in this country by Maclaurin and Simpson, and on the continent by Hermann, Daniel Bernoulli, Leonhard Euler, and Clairaut. Maclaurin, Bernoulli, and Euler had the honor of sharing with each other the prize proposed by the Academy of Sciences at Paris for the best essay on the intricate subject of the tides; however, a premature death prevented Maclaurin from long pursuing the career which he began so successfully. Bernoulli and Euler continued for many years to compete with each other in the elegance and extent of their research: Euler appears to have been the more profound mathematician, and Bernoulli the more accurate philosopher.

The latter half of the eighteenth century was in many respects extremely favorable to the progress of the sciences. The names of D'Alembert, Landen, Waring, Frisi, Robison, Lagrange, and Laplace deserve to be listed in the first class of mathematicians and theoretical mechanics; those of Smeaton, Wedgwood, and Watt are no less distinguished for their success in improving the practice of the useful arts and manufactures. The union of all these subjects into one system of knowledge was achieved on a magnificent scale in the *Encyclopédie*, a work which does as much honor to the labor and genius of some of its authors as it reflects disgrace on the principles and politics of others. The Society for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures, and Commerce was established in London about the same time that the Ency-

[The En]cyclopédie began to appear in Paris, and its prizes and publications have, without doubt, sparked a level of attention toward the subjects of practical mechanics and agricultural, as well as commercial, improvements, which must have been beneficial both to individuals and to the public. The Academy of Paris began to print, in 1762, a collection of descriptions of arts and trades of all kinds on an even more extensive scale than had been attempted in the *Encyclopédie*; the work was carried to a very considerable length, but it by no means includes all the articles that were intended to compose it.

The construction of watches has been so greatly improved by artists in both this country and France that they have been rendered capable of providing very essential service to navigation, especially since astronomical methods for determining a ship's position have been brought to such a degree of perfection as to greatly facilitate the frequent correction of the accidental errors of the timekeeper. The first artist to construct watches accurate enough for the determination of longitude was William Harrison, who was indebted to himself alone for his education and his inventions; in 1765, he received the promised reward of ten thousand pounds from the Board of Longitude for his labors.

There has hardly been a period in any age of the world in which the sciences, and literature in general, have been so rapidly promoted and so universally spread as within the last forty years. This advancement has been partly the cause, and partly the effect, of the great increase in scientific journals, cyclopedias, and encyclopedias, which have been annually increasing since the start of the *Journal de Physique* in 1773. These were supported by the interest they derived, in large measure, from the new and entertaining discoveries and improvements made in chemistry and natural history; some of the most extensive of these works have had a sale unprecedented even for books of more moderate length.

The charter of the Royal Institution is dated 1799; its founding will perhaps not mark an era in the history of the refinements of science, but if it is hereafter found to have given recognition to what is useful and popularity to what is elegant, the purposes of those who established it will not have been frustrated.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the progress of science, shifting focus from historical achievements to the future potential for discovery and the necessity of organized research to avoid redundancy.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XX.</header>

After all that has been achieved by the combined labors and talents of the philosophers who have been mentioned, and of many others who, though less famous, have been highly deserving, there is still ample opportunity for the employment of genius and hard work in following their footsteps. To suppose that little or nothing remains to be done reveals a lack of either knowledge or courage. The experimental research of some of the greatest philosophers has been very imperfectly conducted, and the most interesting results may be expected from repeating and varying them. Whatever progress our neighbors may have made beyond us in complex calculations and combinations, we are still able to compete with them—and shall likely long remain so—in the precision of our instruments and in the skill of using them with care and success.

When, however, we consider the astonishing size to which a collection of books in any scientific field can reach even now, and the diverse nature of the works in which many of the most valuable discussions have been shared with the public, along with the natural tendency toward laziness that a high level of civilization too often encourages, there is great reason to fear that because of the constant multiplication of new essays—which are merely repetitions of others that have been forgotten—the sciences will soon be overwhelmed by their own unmanageable size. The structure will begin to wobble under its own weight, and all the extra material we pile onto it will only serve to broaden the base without increasing the height and dignity of the building. Having been convinced of the truth of this observation through constant experience, I have spent a significant amount of time and effort to find an effective remedy for this problem; and I hope that in the future, anyone wishing to expand our knowledge in any scientific branch related to these lectures will find it easy—by consulting the authors listed in my catalog of references—to gather the necessary background on what has already been done with that same goal. For his own sake, he should learn this before beginning his pursuit, or at the very least, out of respect for the public, before he asks the world to acknowledge his improvements and discoveries.

<summary>The author encourages further scientific experimentation, noting that even established research can be improved, while warning that the growing volume of redundant publications threatens to overwhelm the sciences. To address this, he provides a catalog of references to ensure researchers build upon existing knowledge rather than repeating forgotten work.</summary>

### LECTURE XXI.
### ON HYDROSTATICS.

**THE** mechanical properties and characteristics of fluids, and the laws and phenomena of their motions, are to be the subjects of the second division of this series of lectures. Although these properties are actually derived from the same fundamental principles as the doctrines of pure mechanics, they are yet largely unable to be traced, in a clear and precise way, to the effects of simple and general causes. We are, therefore, frequently forced to rely on the help of experimental results; and for this reason, as well as others, the science of hydrodynamics may appropriately hold a middle position between mathematical mechanics and descriptive physics. In discussing the mechanics of solid bodies, we are able to begin with axioms, or self-evident truths, which are almost inseparable from the makeup of the human mind; to derive from them the general laws of motion, and to apply these laws, with little possibility of error, to every set of circumstances where we need to examine their effects; and it requires only a certain amount of attention and of mathema-

<header>LECTURE XXI.</header>

tical knowledge, to be fully convinced of the correctness of all our conclusions, without any reference to experimental proof. But here our abstract reasonings begin to fail; and whether from the imperfection of our modes of considering the mechanical actions of the particles of fluids on each other, or from the deficiencies of our analytical calculations, or, as there is more reason to suppose, from a combination of both these causes, all attempts to reduce the behaviors of fluids to a perfect mechanical theory have so far been unsuccessful. At the same time, it will appear that by a proper mixture of calculation with experiment, we may obtain sufficient foundations for all such determinations as are likely to be of any practical use.

The whole of the subjects, which will be categorized under the name <term>Hydrodynamics</term>, may be divided into three general heads: <term>Hydraulics</term>, <term>Acoustics</term>, and <term>Optics</term>; terms which are sufficiently understood as relating to the common properties of fluids, to sound, and to light, but which do not allow for a very strict definition without a still further division. The first subdivision which we shall consider will relate to the laws of the equilibrium of fluids, or of the opposition of forces acting on them without producing actual motion, comprehending <term>hydrostatics</term>, or the doctrine of the equilibrium of liquids, either within themselves or with movable bodies; and <term>pneumatostatics</term>, or the equilibrium of elastic fluids. The actual motions of fluids will be considered in the second subdivision; and the third will relate to the instruments and machines in which the principles of <term>hydrostatics</term>, <term>hydraulics</term>, and <term>pneumatics</term> are applied to the purposes of the arts or of domestic convenience. The science of hydraulics must be allowed to be of as great importance to civil life, and especially to a maritime nation, as any department of practical mechanics. Let us only reflect for a moment on what the metropolis of England would be reduced to if deprived of pipes for the conveyance of water, of pumps, and of fire engines; and how much the commerce of the whole kingdom has been facilitated by the formation of navigable canals, and we shall soon be convinced of the obligations that we owe to the art of modifying the motion of water, and to the principles of hydraulics, on which that art depends.

# ON HYDROSTATICS.

properties of fluids. In these areas, although we cannot explain with precision how every appearance is produced, we will still find a variety of very beautiful phenomena. These have often been too generally neglected and assumed to be of the most abstruse and unintelligible nature; but when carefully examined, they will appear to be much more within the reach of calculation than the simplest doctrines of hydraulics. We may also apply some of these phenomena to a very complete explanation of an extensive class of facts in optics, which, when considered in any other way, are inextricably obscure. Whether this explanation is admitted as satisfactory or not, it deserves at least a fair examination. Therefore, it would be impossible to assign the science of optics an earlier place in the order of the system, even if we agree with those who imagine that all the phenomena of light depend on causes entirely deducible from the mechanics of solid bodies.

We must begin the subject of <term>hydrostatics</term>, or the doctrine of the equilibrium of liquids, with a definition of the essential characteristics of a fluid substance. The most suitable definition appears to be that a fluid is a collection of material particles which may be considered infinitely small and as moving freely against each other in every direction without friction. Some have defined a fluid as a substance that transmits pressure equally in all directions; but this appears to be a description of a property derived from the former assumption, which is certainly simpler. Although it may be somewhat difficult to deduce it mathematically in a strictly demonstrative manner, we may still obtain a sufficient conviction of its truth from mathematical considerations without assuming it as a fundamental or axiomatic characteristic. A fluid that has no immediate tendency to expand when unrestrained is commonly considered a liquid: thus water, oil, and mercury are liquids; air and steam are fluids, but not liquids.

For the present, we shall consider a liquid as having neither compressibility nor expansibility. We must also set aside some other physical properties essential to liquids, such as cohesion and capillary attraction; although in reality, through very precise experiments, the particles of liquids are found to be subject to the same laws of elasticity that we have already examined regarding solids,

# LECTURE XXI.

...and also possess cohesive powers, which essentially distinguish them from elastic fluids, and which resist any force tending directly to separate the particles from each other, while they allow any lateral motion with perfect ease. In treating <term>hydrostatics</term>, therefore, we assume the fluids involved are of uniform density throughout; and so far as elastic fluids agree with this description, they are subject to the same laws as liquids; on the other hand, all fluids, as far as they are compressible, possess properties similar to those that will hereafter be examined when we investigate the subject of pneumatic equilibrium.

The first law of hydrostatics that catches our attention is this: the surface of every <term>homogeneous</term> gravitating fluid, when at rest, is horizontal. If any part of the surface were inclined to the horizon, the surface particles would necessarily tend toward its lowest part, in the same way as if they moved without friction on the inclined surface of a solid. And if any two portions of the surface of the fluid are separated, as in two branches of a tube or pipe, however they may be situated, the fluid cannot remain at rest unless the surfaces are in the same level plane. For if we imagine such a tube, containing water, to be made of ice, and to be immersed in a large reservoir of water, and then thawed, the water will become part of the general contents of the reservoir, and consequently will remain at rest if its surfaces are level with that of the reservoir. It is obvious that the tube has acquired no new power of supporting the water by being thawed; consequently, the water would have remained in <term>equilibrium</term> at the same height in the original state of the solid tube. The experimental proof of this proposition is easy and obvious, and the property provides one of the most common ways of determining a horizontal surface. But when we compare the heights of fluids occupying tubes of different sizes, it is necessary—if the tubes are small—to apply a slight correction on account of the actions of the tubes on the fluids they contain, which are more apparent as their diameters are smaller. The same cause also produces a <term>curvature</term> in each separate surface, which is always visible at the point of contact with the tube or vessel. (*Plate XIX. Fig 239.*)

If several separate fluids of different kinds are contained in the same vessel, they will never remain at rest unless all the surfaces intervening between

them be horizontal; and this is in fact the state of the surface of common liquids that is exposed to the pressure of the atmosphere.

The power of gravitation, strictly speaking, does not act in precisely parallel lines; thus, the surface of lakes, instead of being perfectly flat, becomes slightly convex, like the surface of the earth. It is obvious that the surface of a fluid must always be perpendicular to the direction of the combined results of all the forces acting upon it. Since the earth turns on its axis, the centrifugal force resulting from its motion is combined with that of gravity in determining the position of the general surface of the ocean.

A similar combination of centrifugal force with gravitation may be observed when a bucket is suspended by a rope and made to turn on its axis by twisting the rope: the direction of the combined forces is such that the surface must assume a parabolic form to remain perpendicular to them. Likewise, when any number of different fluids are made to revolve in the same way, or when they are enclosed in a glass globe and turned using a whirling table, the surfaces that separate them always acquire the forms of parabolic conoids when the axis remains in a vertical position. However, if the axis is in any other position, the situation of the surface will be more difficult to determine. (Plate XX. Fig. 240.)

In all these cases, the equilibrium is stable; for if any part of the fluid is raised above the surface, it will immediately tend to return to its level. But if a heavier fluid were contained in a bent tube or siphon, with its legs or branches opening downward and immersed in a lighter fluid, the equilibrium would be unstable, since once disturbed, it would never be restored. (Plate XIX. Fig 241.)

From these principles, we may infer that the pressure of a fluid on every particle of the vessel containing it—or of any other surface, real or imaginary, in contact with it—is equal to the weight of a column of the fluid whose base is equal to that particle and whose height is equal to its depth below the surface of the fluid. Thus, if we have a vessel of water one foot deep, each square foot of the bottom will sustain the pressure of a cubic foot of water,

If we have a vessel of mercury an inch deep, each square foot will sustain a pressure of one-twelfth of a cubic foot of mercury, or 1,130 ounces; the atmosphere presses on each square foot of the earth’s surface with a force of about 34,000 ounces, which is equivalent to the pressure of a column of mercury 30 inches high. The pressure of the water on a small portion of the lowest part of the side of the vessel containing it is also equal to the weight supported by an equal portion of the bottom; but we cannot estimate the force sustained by any large portion of the side without considering the different depths below the surface at which its different parts are situated.

It is obvious that if we imagine a fluid to be divided by an imaginary surface of any kind, the particles adjacent to it are pushed on either side by equal forces—the fluid below resisting them and pressing them upwards with as much force as the fluid above presses them downwards—their own weight being comparatively insignificant; for without this equality of pressures, they could not possibly remain at rest. And if we use a vessel of such a shape as to take the place of any upper portion of the fluid, the pressure against that part of the vessel which is thus substituted will be the same that previously supported the weight of the fluid removed. In order for everything to remain in equilibrium, the vessel must itself exert an equal pressure on the fluid below it, so that the pressure on the bottom will be the same as if the vessel had remained in its original state and were filled to the same height with the fluid. (Plate XIX. Fig. 242.)

To understand this more easily, we may suppose that the portion of the fluid, instead of being removed, had been solidified into a solid mass of equal density. It is obvious that this solidification of the fluid would not have altered the amount of its pressure; it would, therefore, have remained in equilibrium with the water below. The mass might also be joined with the sides of the vessel so as to form a part of it, without increasing or diminishing any of the pressures involved. We would thus obtain a vessel similar to the one under our investigation, where the pressure on the bottom is always the same as if the mass, supposed to be solidified, had remained fluid. Thus, the pressure on the base of a conical

...or pyramidal vessel, full of water, is three times as great as the weight of the water, since its volume is one-third of that of a column of the same height standing on the same base. (Plate XIX. Fig. 243.)

In this manner, the smallest given quantity of any fluid contained in a pipe can be made to produce a pressure equivalent to any given weight, however large, which rests on the cover of a closed vessel connected to the pipe. This can be done either by decreasing the diameter of the pipe and increasing its height while the weight is supported by a surface of a certain size, or by increasing the size of this surface without adding to the height of the pipe; for in either case, the total force of the fluid in supporting the weight will be equal to the weight of a column of the same height standing on the entire surface that is subjected to its action. And if the effect of the column is increased by any additional pressure, independent of its weight, that pressure can be represented by imagining the height of the column to be increased; and the effect of the additional pressure will also be increased in proportion to the size of the surface which supports the weight. It is on this principle that the pressure of water has been applied by Mr. Bramah to the construction of a very convenient press. (Plate XIX. Fig. 244.)

Although this property of fluids causes some results which would scarcely be expected by a person not accustomed to reflecting on the subject—and has, therefore, not improperly been called the hydrostatic paradox—yet it depends entirely on the general and acknowledged principles of mechanical forces. Nor can we agree with those authors who have asserted that a very small quantity of a fluid may, "without acting at any mechanical advantage" whatsoever, be made to balance a weight of any measurable size; for the immediate operation of the force very much resembles, in the most common cases, the effect of a wedge or of a movable inclined plane; thus, a wedge remains in equilibrium when the forces acting on each side are in proportion to its length, like the hydrostatic pressure on a vessel of a similar shape. The conditions of the equilibrium of fluids can also be determined, in all cases, from the general law of the descent of the center of gravity to the lowest point. Thus, it is easy to show that even when two branches of a tube are of

Consequently, the center of gravity of the entire fluid can never reach its lowest position unless both surfaces are at the same level.

Air and all other elastic fluids are subject to this general law just as liquids are. Thus, a much greater force is required to produce a blast of a specific intensity with a large pair of bellows than with a smaller pair; and for the same reason, it is much easier for a glassblower using a blowpipe to employ the muscles of his mouth and lips than those of his chest, even though the chest muscles are much more powerful. If we estimate the cross-section of the chest at one square foot, it would require a force of seventy pounds to raise a column of mercury an inch high using the muscles of respiration; however, the cross-section of the mouth is scarcely more than eight or nine square inches, and a pressure of the same intensity can be produced here with a force of about four pounds. The glassblower also gains the advantage of being able to continue breathing during the operation, as the passage from the chest to the nostrils remains open while the root of the tongue is pressed against the palate.

It is obvious that the pressure on every square inch of a vessel's side, or on every square foot of a riverbank, increases continuously as one descends toward the bottom. If we wish to determine the total pressure on all parts of the side or bank, we must use a mean depth to estimate it; this must be the depth of the point that would be the center of gravity of the surface if it had weight. Thus, if we have a hollow cube filled with water, and the center of gravity of each side is at its midpoint, the pressure on each of the upright sides would be half as great as the pressure on the bottom—that is, it would be equal to half the weight of the water contained in the cube.

only one-third of the height from the bottom. For the pressure at each point may be represented by a line equal in length to its depth below the surface, and a series of such lines may be supposed to constitute a triangle, of which the <term>centre of gravity</term> will indicate the place of the <term>centre of pressure</term> of the surface; and the height of the centre of gravity will always be one-third of the height of the triangle. It is easily inferred, from this representation, that the total pressure on the side of a vessel, or on a bank of a given length, is proportional to the square of the depth below the water to which it extends. (Plate XIX. Fig. 245.)

The magnitude of the total pressure on a concave or convex surface may also be determined by the position of its centre of gravity; but such a determination is of no practical utility, since the portions of the forces which act in different directions must always cancel each other. Thus, the perpendicular pressure on the entire internal surface of a sphere filled with a fluid is three times as great as the weight of the fluid; but the force tending to burst the sphere, at the circumference of any vertical circle, is only three-fourths of that weight.

If two fluids are of different <term>specific gravities</term>—that is, if equal volumes of them have different weights—their opposite pressures will counterbalance each other when their heights above the common surface are inversely proportional to their specific gravities; for it is obvious that the greater density of the one will precisely compensate for its deficiency in height. Thus, a column of <term>mercury</term> standing at the height of 30 inches in a tube will support the pressure of a column of water in another branch of the tube exactly 34 feet high, since the weight of 30 cubic inches of mercury is equal to that of 408 cubic inches of water. (Plate XIX. Fig. 246.)

We have hitherto considered the properties of fluids in contact with solids which are immovable and of invariable form; but it often happens that they act on substances which are moveable, and they are sometimes contained in vessels of which the form is susceptible to variation. In these cases, other considerations are necessary for determining the equilibrium of fluids and solids with each other; and, in the first place, the properties of <term>floating bodies</term> require to be investigated.

When a solid body floats in a fluid, it displaces a quantity of the fluid equal to its own weight; and every solid that is unable to do this must sink. For the solid to remain at rest, the pressure of the fluid beneath it, acting vertically, must be exactly equal to its weight. However, before the body was immersed, the same pressure was exerted on the portion of the fluid that is now displaced and was perfectly balanced by its weight; therefore, that weight was equal to the weight of the floating body.

Since the force supporting the weight of a floating body is the pressure of the fluid immediately below it, if this pressure is removed or reduced, the body may remain at rest below the surface of the fluid, even when it is specifically lighter. Thus, a piece of very smooth wood will remain in contact with the flat bottom of a container of water for some time, until the water seeps beneath it. It will also remain at the bottom of a container of mercury without any tendency to rise, since mercury does not tend to penetrate, like water, into any tiny gaps that might admit it. For a similar reason, if the pressure of the fluid above is removed from the upper surface of a solid substance completely submerged in it, the solid may remain suspended, even if it is heavier than an equal volume of the fluid. For example, if a tube or container of any kind, open at the top and bottom, has a metal base ground to fit perfectly against it without being attached, the base will appear to stick to the container when it is submerged to a sufficient depth in water, while the container remains empty.

To ensure a floating body remains in equilibrium, its <term>centre of gravity</term> must also be in the same vertical line as the <term>centre of gravity</term> of the displaced fluid; otherwise, the weight of the solid will not be completely offset by the pressure of the fluid. The nature of this equilibrium, regarding stability, is determined by the position of the <term>metacentre</term>, or <term>centre of pressure</term>, which can be considered a fixed point of suspension or support for the solid body. It is obvious that when the lower surface of the body is spherical or cylindrical, the metacentre must coincide with the centre of that shape. This is because the height of this point, as well as the shape of the displaced portion of fluid, must remain unchanged in all circumstances; the nature of the equilibrium will then depend on the distance of the

the centre of gravity above or below the centre of the sphere or cylinder. The position of the <term>metacentre</term> can always be determined from the form and extent of the surface of the displaced portion of the fluid, compared with its bulk, and with the location of its <term>centre of gravity</term>. For example, if a rectangular beam floats on its flat surface, the height of the <term>metacentre</term> above the <term>centre of gravity</term> will be to the breadth of the beam as the breadth is to twelve times the depth of the part immersed. Hence, if the beam is square, it will float securely when either the part immersed or the part above the surface is less than 21/100 of the whole; but when it is less unequally divided by the surface of the fluid, it will overset. If, however, the breadth is so increased as to be nearly one-fourth greater than the depth, it will possess a certain degree of <term>stability</term> whatever its density may be. (Plate XIX. Fig. 247.)

When the <term>equilibrium</term> of a floating body is stable, it may <term>oscillate</term> backwards and forwards in the neighborhood of its position of rest: and the <term>oscillations</term> will be more rapid in proportion as the <term>stability</term> is greater in comparison with the bulk of the body. Such <term>oscillations</term> may also be combined with others which take place in a transverse direction: a ship, for example, may roll on an axis in the direction of her length, and may heel, at the same time, upon a second axis in the direction of the beams. Besides these rotatory vibrations, a floating body which is allowed to fall into a fluid will commonly rise and sink several times by its own weight; and in all these cases, the vibrations of any one kind, when they are small, are performed in nearly equal times: but various and intricate combinations may sometimes arise from the difference of the times in which the vibrations of different kinds are performed.

When a solid body is wholly immersed in a fluid and is held in its situation by an external force, it loses as much of its weight as is equivalent to an equal bulk of the fluid. For, conceiving the fluid which is displaced by the body to have been converted into a solid by <term>congelation</term> (solidification), it is obvious that it would retain its situation, and the difference of the pressures of the fluid on its various parts would be exactly sufficient to support its weight. But these pressures will be the same if a body of any other kind is substituted for the frozen fluid; their <term>buoyant effect</term> may, therefore, be always estimated by the weight of a portion of the fluid equal in bulk to the solid.

# LECTURE XXI.

Thus, when a small figure containing a bubble of air is immersed in a jar of water that is covered by a bladder so that it may be compressed by the hand, the volume of the figure with its bubble is reduced by the pressure; it is, therefore, less supported by the water and begins to sink. When the hand is removed, it immediately rises again. (Plate XIX. Fig. 248.)

While a body is actually rising or sinking in a fluid with an accelerated motion—the force of gravity being partly used to generate <term>momentum</term> in either the fluid or the solid—the total pressure on the bottom of the vessel is necessarily somewhat reduced. Hence, the apparent weight of a jar of water will suffer a slight decrease while a bullet is descending in it, or while bubbles of air are rising in it; however, the difference can seldom be great enough to be easily perceptible to the senses.

It sometimes happens that a solid body is partly supported by a fluid and partly by another solid; of this we have an example in one of <term>Dr. Hooke’s</term> ingenious inventions for keeping a vessel always full. A half-cylinder or a hemisphere, being partly supported on an axis located in the plane of the surface of the fluid, has its weight so adjusted as to be equal to that of a portion of the fluid of half its magnitude. When the vessel is full, it is half immersed and exerts no pressure on the axis; it descends as the fluid is emptied, and its tendency to turn around its axis can only be counteracted by the pressure of the fluid on its flat side, as long as the surface of the remaining portion of the fluid retains its original level. (Plate XIX. Fig. 249.)

When a fluid is contained in a vessel of a flexible nature, the sides of the vessel will always become curved as a consequence of the pressure, and more so in proportion as the pressure is greater. The form of the curved surface will also be such that the common <term>centre of gravity</term> of the fluid and the vessel may descend to the lowest point that the circumstances of the case allow; this form is generally of too complex a nature to be determined by calculation. No mathematician has yet been able to investigate, for example, the curvature which a square or rectangular bag of leather will assume when filled with water or with corn. When, indeed, only one dimension of a vessel is considered—for instance, when the bottom of a cistern is assumed to be flexible and to be fixed at two opposite sides, while the ends are simply in

## LECTURE XXII.

### ON PNEUMATIC EQUILIBRIUM.

The laws of the pressure and equilibrium of liquids, which are the specific subjects of hydrostatics, are also applicable in general to fluids of all kinds, as far as they are compatible with the compressibility of those fluids, or with their tendency to expand.

Elastic fluids are distinguished from liquids by the absence of all cohesive force, or by their immediate tendency to expand when they are free. Such are atmospheric air, steam, and gases of various kinds; and the consideration of these fluids, in a state of rest, constitutes the doctrine of <term>pneumatostatics</term>, or of the equilibrium of elastic fluids.

That the air is a material substance, capable of resisting pressure, is easily shown by inverting an empty jar in water and by the operation of transferring air and gases from vessel to vessel in the pneumatic apparatus used by chemists. The tendency of the air to expand is shown by the experiment in which a flaccid bladder becomes distended, and shriveled fruit recovers its full size, as soon as the external pressure is removed from it by the operation of the air pump; and the magnitude of this expansive force is more distinctly seen when a portion of air is enclosed in a glass vessel, together with some mercury, in which the mouth of a tube is immersed while the other end is open and outside the vessel. Consequently, when the whole apparatus is enclosed in a very long jar and the air of the jar is exhausted, the column of mercury becomes the measure of the expansive force of the air. (Plate XIX. Fig. 251.)

If the diameter of the tube, in an apparatus of this kind, were very small in comparison with the bulk of the air confined, the column of mercury would

<summary>This page introduces the study of pneumatostatics, defining elastic fluids like air and steam by their tendency to expand. It describes experiments using an air pump and mercury to demonstrate that air is a material substance with a measurable expansive force.</summary>

<keywords>pneumatic equilibrium, hydrostatics, elastic fluids, atmospheric air, pneumatostatics, air pump, mercury, expansion, compressibility</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on pneumatostatics from page 269, specifically detailing the inverse relationship between the volume and pressure of elastic fluids.</meta>

be raised, under the ordinary conditions of the atmosphere, to a height of nearly 30 inches. But if we suppose the size of the tube to be such that the portion of air must expand to twice its natural volume before the mercury reaches a height sufficient to balance it, this height would be only 15 inches. For it appears to be a general law of all elastic fluids that their pressure on any given surface is diminished in exact proportion to the increase in their volume. Therefore, if the column of mercury in the vacuum of an air pump were 60 inches high, the air would be reduced to half its natural volume. For the same reason, the pressure of a column of 30 inches of mercury in the open air will reduce any portion of air to half its volume, since the natural pressure of the atmosphere—which is equal to about 30 inches of mercury—is doubled by adding an equal amount of pressure. Similarly, the density of the air in a diving bell is doubled at a depth of 34 feet below the water's surface, and tripled at a depth of 68 feet. This law was discovered by <term>Dr. Hooke</term>; he found, however, that when very great pressure was applied—so that the density became many times greater than in its natural state—the elasticity appeared to increase somewhat less than the density. However, this exception to the general law has not been confirmed by later and more accurate experiments.

Not only the common air of the atmosphere and other permanently elastic gases, but also steam and vapors of all kinds, appear to be equally subject to this universal law. They must, however, be examined at temperatures high enough to keep them in an elastic state. For example, if we wished to determine the force of steam twice as dense as that which is usually produced, we would be obliged to use a heat 30 or 40 degrees above that of boiling water. We would then find that steam of such density as to support the pressure of a column of 30 inches of mercury, when confined in a dry vessel, would be reduced to half its volume by the pressure of a column of 60 inches. But if we increased the pressure much beyond this, the steam would be converted into water, and the experiment would end.

That the air surrounding us is subject to the force of gravity and possesses weight can be shown by weighing a vessel that has been exhausted using an air pump, then allowing air to enter and weighing it a second time. In this manner, we may determine the

The pressure derived from the weight of the air is also the cause of the ascent of hydrogen gas, or of another portion of air that is rarefied by heat and carries with it the smoke of a fire; and this effect is made more conspicuous when either the hydrogen gas or the heated air is confined in a balloon. The reduction of the apparent weight of a body, caused by the pressure of the surrounding air, is also shown by the loss of equilibrium between two bodies of different densities upon their removal from the open air into the vacuum of an air pump. For this purpose, a light, hollow glass bulb may be exactly counterpoised in the air by a much smaller brass weight, equipped with an index that shows, on a graduated scale, the degree to which the large ball outweighs the smaller one in the receiver of the air pump due to the rarefaction of the air, which lessens the buoyant power that helps to support its weight. (Plate XIX. Fig. 252.)

From this combination of weight and elasticity in the atmosphere, it follows that its upper parts must be much thinner than those nearer to the earth, since the density is everywhere proportional to the total superincumbent weight. The weight of a column of air one foot in height is one twenty-eight thousandth of the total pressure; consequently, that pressure is increased by one twenty-eight thousandth by the addition of the weight of one foot of air, and the next foot will be denser in the same proportion, since density is always proportionate to pressure. The pressure thus increased will, therefore, still be equal to twenty-eight thousand times the weight of the next foot. This same reasoning may be continued without limit, and it can be shown that while we suppose the height to vary by uniform steps—such as distances of a foot or a mile—the pressures and densities will increase in a steady proportion. Thus, at a height of about 3,000 fathoms, the density will be about half as great as at the earth’s surface; at a height of 6,000 fathoms, one-fourth as great; and at 9,000 fathoms, one-eighth as great. From this, it is inferred that the height in fathoms may be readily found from the logarithm of the number expressing the density of the air; for the logarithm of the number 2, multiplied by 10,000, is 3,010; the logarithm of 4 is 6,020; and that of 8 is 9,031. The logarithms of numbers always increase in a steady proportion when the numbers themselves increase by equal factors. (Plate XIX. Fig. 253.)

Hence, we obtain an easy method of determining the heights of mountains with reasonable accuracy. If a bottle of air were tightly sealed on the summit of a mountain and, being brought in this state to the plain below, its mouth were inserted into a vessel of water or of mercury, a certain portion of the liquid would enter the bottle. If this liquid were weighed and found to be one-half of the quantity that the whole bottle could contain, it might be concluded that the air on the mountain possessed only half of its natural density, and that its height was 3,000 fathoms. It appears also, from this statement, that the height of a column of equal density with any part of the atmosphere, equivalent to the pressure to which that part is subjected, is everywhere equal to about 28,000 feet.

Many corrections are, however, necessary for ascertaining the heights of mountains with all the precision that the nature of this kind of measurement allows; and they involve several determinations which require a previous knowledge of the effects of heat and of the nature of the ascent of vapors, which cannot be appropriately examined at present.

We may easily ascertain, on the same principles, the height to which a balloon will ascend if we are acquainted with its bulk and its weight. For example, supposing its weight is 500 pounds and its bulk is such as to enable it to raise 300 pounds more, its specific gravity must be five-eighths as great as that of the air, and it will continue to rise until it reaches the height at which the air is of the same density. The logarithm of eight-fifths, multiplied by 10,000, is 2,040; and this is the number of fathoms contained in the height, which will, therefore, be a little more than two miles and a quarter. It may be found, by pursuing the calculation, that at the distance of the earth’s radius (nearly 4,000 miles) above its surface, the air, if it existed, would become so thin that a cubic inch would occupy a space equal to the sphere of Saturn’s orbit. On the other hand, if there were a mine about 42 miles deep, the air would become as dense as mercury at the bottom of it.

This pressure acts in all directions on every substance exposed to it; but being counterbalanced by the natural elasticity of these substances, it commonly produces no apparent effects. When, however, by means of the air pump or otherwise, the pressure of the air is removed from one side of a body while it continues to act on the other, its operation becomes extremely evident. Thus, when two hollow hemispheres in contact with each other are exhausted of air, they are made to cohere with great force. They are named Magdeburg hemispheres because Otto von Guericke <note>Original OCR: Guerike</note> of Magdeburg constructed two such hemispheres of sufficient size to withstand the pull of the emperor's six coach horses, pulling with all their force to separate them. By a similar pressure, a thin square bottle may be crushed when it is sufficiently exhausted, and a bladder may be torn with a loud noise. When the hand is placed on the mouth of a vessel connected with the air pump, it is fixed to it very forcibly when the exhaustion is performed, due to the pressure of the air on the back of the hand. The fluids also that circulate in the blood vessels of the hand are forced toward its lower surface, and the effect called suction is produced in a very striking manner. It is on the same principle that cupping glasses are employed, where a partial exhaustion is achieved by means of the flame of tow <note>Coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used as tinder</note>, which heats the air and expels a great part of it; so that the remainder, when it cools, is considerably rarefied.

It was Galileo who first explained the nature of suction from the effects of the pressure of the atmosphere, and his pupil Torricelli confirmed his doctrines by employing a column of mercury of sufficient height to overcome the whole pressure of the atmosphere and to produce a vacuum in the upper part of the tube or vessel containing it. In the operation of sucking up a fluid through a pipe, with the mouth or otherwise, the pressure of the air is only partially removed from the upper surface of the fluid, and it becomes capable of ascending to a height determined by the difference of the densities of the air within and without the cavity concerned. Thus, an exhaustion of one-fourth of the air of the cavity would enable us to raise water to the height of 8½ feet, and mercury to 7½ inches, above the level of the re-

We can draw up a much higher column of mercury by sucking with the muscles of the mouth alone than by inhaling with the chest, and the difference is much more marked than the difference in the forces with which we can blow. For in sucking, the cavity of the mouth is very much contracted by the pressure of the external air, and the same force, exerted on a smaller surface, is capable of counteracting a much greater hydrostatic or pneumatic pressure.

When a tube of glass, about three feet long, closed at one end and open at the other, is filled with mercury and then immersed in a basin of the same fluid, the pressure of the atmosphere is wholly removed from the upper surface of the mercury in the tube, while it continues to act on the mercury in the basin, and by that means on the lower surface of the column in the tube. If such a tube is placed under the receiver of an air pump, the mercury will subside in the tube as the pressure of the atmosphere is diminished; and if the exhaustion is made very complete, it will descend very nearly to the level of the open basin or reservoir. When the air is readmitted, the mercury usually rises—at sea level—to the height of about 30 inches; but as the air is lighter at some times than at others, the height varies between the limits of 27 and 31 inches. This well-known instrument, from its use in measuring the weight of the air, is called a <term>barometer</term>. In the same manner, a column of water from 30 to 35 feet in height may be sustained in the pipe of a pump; but if the pipe were longer than this, a vacuum would be produced in the upper part of it, and the pump would be incapable of acting.

In order to observe the height of the mercury in the barometer with greater convenience and accuracy, the scale has sometimes been increased by various methods: either by bending the upper part of the tube into an oblique position, as in the diagonal barometer; or by making the lower part horizontal and of much smaller diameter than the upper; or by making the whole tube straight, narrow, and slightly conical; or by placing a float on the surface of the mercury in the reservoir and causing an axis, which carries an index, to revolve by its motion. But a good simple barometer, about one-third of an inch in diameter and furnished with a <term>vernier</term>, is perhaps just as accurate as any of these more complicated instruments. The same method used to determine the relationship between the heights and densities of elastic fluids may be extended to all bodies that are compressible to any degree, and whose elasticity follows laws similar to those found in air and other gases. It is not improbable that these laws are generally applicable to all natural bodies, as far as their physical structure allows them to undergo pressure without completely losing their shape. Water, for example, was observed by <term>Canton</term> <note>John Canton (1718–1772), a British physicist known for proving the compressibility of water.</note> to be compressed by one twenty-two-thousandth of its volume by a force equal to atmospheric pressure. Consequently, this force may be represented by a column of water 750,000 feet high. The density of water at the bottom of a lake or the sea will be increased by the pressure of the fluid above it. Assuming the law of compression is similar to that of air, it can be inferred that at a depth of 100 miles, its density would be doubled, and at 200 miles, it would be quadrupled. The same measurements would also apply to the elasticity of mercury. However, there is reason to believe that in both cases, these figures are a little too small.

# LECTURE XXIII.

## ON THE THEORY OF HYDRAULICS.

Having considered the principal cases of the equilibrium of fluids, both liquid and gaseous, we proceed to examine the theory of their motions. Despite the difficulties attending the mathematical theory of hydraulics, so much has already been accomplished through practical investigations that we may generally, by comparing the results of previous experiments with our calculations, predict the effect of any proposed arrangement without an error of more than one-fifth, or perhaps one-tenth, of the whole. This degree of accuracy is fully sufficient for practice and, indeed, could scarcely have been expected given the state of the science at the beginning of the last century. Many of these improvements have been derived from an examination of the nature and magnitude of the friction of fluids. Although at first glance this friction might be supposed to be very minor, it is found to be of such importance in the application of the theory of hydraulics to practical cases—and affects the methods of calculation so significantly—that it will require to be discussed later in a separate lecture.

There is a general principle of mechanical action which was first clearly stated by Huygens, and which Daniel Bernoulli made the basis of his most elegant calculations in hydrodynamics. Assuming that no force is lost in the transfer of motion between different bodies within any system, they always acquire such velocities in descending through any space that the center of gravity of the system is capable of ascending to a height equal to that from which it descended, despite any mutual actions between the bodies. The truth of this principle may easily be inferred from the laws of collision compared with the properties of accelerating and retarding forces. Thus, if an elastic ball weighing 10 ounces and descending from a height of 1 foot is caused to act in any manner

<summary>This lecture introduces the theory of hydraulics, noting that practical experiments now allow for high accuracy in predicting fluid motion despite mathematical complexities. It also introduces the conservation of mechanical energy in a system's center of gravity as a foundational principle of hydrodynamics.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, hydrodynamics, fluid friction, Huygens, Daniel Bernoulli, center of gravity, mechanical action, equilibrium of fluids</keywords>

on a similar ball of one ounce, so as to lose the whole of its motion, the smaller ball will acquire a velocity capable of carrying it to the height of 10 feet. It is true that some other suppositions must be made in applying this law to the determination of the motions of fluids, and that in many cases it becomes necessary to suppose that a certain portion of ascending force or energy is lost as a consequence of the internal motions of the particles of the fluid. But still, with proper restrictions and corrections, the principle affords us a ready method of obtaining solutions of problems which, without some such assistance, it would be almost impossible to investigate. The principal hypothesis which is assumed by Bernoulli, without either demonstration or even the appearance of perfect accuracy, is this: that all the particles of a fluid in motion, contained in any one transverse section of the vessels or pipes through which it runs, must always move with equal velocities. Thus, if water is descending through a vessel of any form, either regular or irregular, he supposes the particles at the same height to move with the same velocity; so that the velocity of every particle in every part of a cylindrical vessel 10 inches in diameter, through which a fluid is moving, must be one-hundredth part as great as in passing through a circular orifice one inch in diameter made in its bottom. It is evident that this cannot possibly be true of the portions of the fluid nearest the bottom of the vessel, since the particles most distant from the orifice must be nearly at rest, while those which are immediately over the orifice are in rapid motion; but still, the calculations founded on the hypothesis agree tolerably well with experiments. In this case, the actual descent in any instant may be estimated by the removal of the quantity discharged from the surface of the fluid to the orifice, since the intermediate space remains always occupied. The ascending force thus obtained is to be distributed throughout the fluid according to the respective velocities of its different portions; and it may easily be shown that when the orifice is small, the part which belongs to the fluid in the vessel is wholly inconsiderable in comparison with the ascending force required for the escape of the small portion which is flowing through the orifice. The whole ascending force may, therefore, be supposed to be employed in the motion of this portion, so that it will acquire the velocity of a body falling from the whole height of the surface of the reservoir, or the velocity due to that height. It appears also that very nearly the same velocity is acquired by almost the first particles that escape from the orifice, so that no sensible time elapses before the jet flows with its utmost velocity.

In the same manner, the pressure of the atmosphere being equal to that which would be produced by a column of air of uniform density 28,000 feet high, the air would rush into a vacuum with a velocity of more than 1,300 feet in a second.

The velocity is also equal, whatever the direction of the stream may be; for since the pressure of fluids acts equally in all directions at equal depths, and the cause remains the same, the effect must also be the same. And if the motion is caused by a pressure derived from a force of any other kind, the effect may be found by calculating the height of a column of the fluid which would be capable of producing an equal pressure. When the force also arises from the difference of two pressures, the velocity may be determined in a similar manner. Thus, the pressure of a column of water 1 foot in height would force the air through a small orifice with a velocity of 230 feet in a second, corresponding to the height of 830 feet; a column of mercury 1 inch high would produce the same effect as a reservoir of water more than thirteen times as high; and the force of the air confined in a closed bottle under the receiver of the air pump will cause a jet to rise to the same height as a column of mercury which measures the difference of the elasticities of the air in the bottle and in the receiver.

A short cylindrical pipe is found to answer this purpose to some degree; but the end may be more completely obtained by a tube that is nearly conical, but with its sides a little convex inwards, so as to imitate the shape which a stream or vein of water spontaneously assumes when it runs through an orifice in a thin plate: for in such cases the

### LECTURE XXIII.

The stream contracts itself after it has passed the orifice for a distance of about half its diameter, so that at this point its thickness is only four-fifths as great as at its passage. Consequently, the quantity discharged is only five-eighths as great as that which the whole orifice would provide according to the previous calculation. Instead, therefore, of multiplying the square root of the height by 8, we may use the multiplier 5 to determine the actual discharge. However, the velocity where the stream is most contracted is only one-thirtieth less than that which is due to the total height; and when the jet is discharged in a direction nearly perpendicular, it rises almost as high as the surface of the fluid in the reservoir.

This contraction of the stream, and the resulting decrease in the discharge, is undoubtedly due to the interference between fluid particles coming from the areas on each side of the orifice and those moving directly toward it. The effect is more noticeable when the orifice is made by a pipe projecting into the reservoir, so that some of the particles approaching it must move in a path contrary to the direction of the stream. It would be possible to obtain an approximate calculation of the size of this contraction from the equilibrium that must exist between the centrifugal forces of the particles as they exit the orifice—describing various curves according to their different positions—and the pressure required for the contraction of the internal parts of the stream, which forces the particles to move more rapidly as they proceed, and which must be proportional to the height required for producing this acceleration. (Plate XX. Fig. 255.)

When a short cylindrical tube is added to the orifice, it is probable that the motion of the fluid within the tube remains somewhat similar. However, the vessel must now be considered to be extended, having a new orifice at the end of the tube where the particles cannot arrive by any side-to-side motions, and which will, therefore, not be subject to a second contraction. The discharge may, therefore, be estimated nearly according to the true measure of this orifice, as the original pressure of the fluid continues to act until the stream escapes.

The water separates from the sides of the pipe, so that it is no longer filled by the stream. Since that is the case, there is nothing to distinguish its motion from that of a stream passing through a simple orifice. However, the increase in flow is not due solely to the cohesion of the water to the sides of the pipe; for, as I have found by experiment, the effect is nearly the same in the motion of air as it is in water. The contraction caused by the motion of the water at the entrance of the short pipe may be considered simply as a contraction within the pipe itself, and the subsequent part of the pipe as either cylindrical or nearly conical. In this case, it follows from the general law on which Bernoulli’s calculations are founded that, as long as the fluid remains in one mass, the discharge will be nearly the same as if the mouth of the pipe were the only orifice, assuming that no force is lost. The exceptions that Bernoulli made to the general application of this principle in such cases—though partly supported by experiments—have been extended somewhat further, both by himself and by other authors, than those experiments have warranted. In the case of a diverging conical pipe, or a pipe with a conical end, the discharge is found to be considerably greater than what a cylindrical pipe would produce, but not quite as great as would be produced on the assumption that no force is lost. (Plate XX. Fig. 256.)

This analogy between the effects of a cylindrical and conical pipe is strongly supported by the experiments of Venturi, compared with those of Bernoulli. Bernoulli found that when a small tube was inserted into any part of a conical pipe in which the water was flowing toward the wider end, not only did none of the water escape through the tube, but the water in a vessel, placed at a considerable distance below, was drawn up by it. Venturi observed the same when the tube was inserted into the side of a cylindrical pipe near its origin; and in both cases air was absorbed as well as water, so that cohesion could not be involved in any way. But the pressure of the atmosphere is generally necessary for all effects of this kind, and both Venturi and Dr. Matthew Young have observed that a short pipe has no effect in increasing the discharge through an orifice in the vacuum of an air pump. But even if the difference were sometimes found to exist in the absence of atmospheric pressure, it might be produced by an accidental cohesion, like that which sometimes causes a column of mercury to remain suspended in similar circumstances. (Plate XX. Fig. 257.)

It references experimental work by Bernoulli, Venturi, and Dr. Matthew Young to demonstrate that cohesion alone does not account for these hydraulic phenomena.</summary>

# LECTURE XXIII.

The effect of ajutages of different kinds on the quantity of water discharged through an orifice of a given size may be most conveniently demonstrated by placing them side by side at the same height in a reservoir and allowing the water to begin to flow at the same moment through any two of them; the quantities discharged in a given time will then obviously indicate their respective velocities. If a very long pipe were used, some time would be required before the velocity became uniform; but in such cases, the slowing down arising from friction is so considerable that it causes an even greater deviation from the quantity which would be discharged by a shorter pipe in the same time.

When the aperture through which a fluid is discharged, instead of being small in every dimension, extends throughout the height of the vessel and is everywhere of equal width, the velocity must be significantly different at different points of its height; but we may find the total discharge by assuming the whole velocity is equal to two-thirds of the velocity at the lowest point. We may also find the quantity discharged by an orifice that does not extend to the surface, but is still of considerable height, by subtracting from the total discharge of an orifice that does reach the surface the amount that would have been produced by the portion of it that must be closed off to form the orifice actually existing. But in this case, the result will rarely differ significantly from that which is found by considering the pressure on the entire orifice as being derived from the height of the fluid above its center.

When a cylindrical vessel empties itself through a small orifice, the velocity of the surface—which is always in the same proportion to the velocity of the fluid in the orifice—is therefore uniformly slowed down. In its descent, it follows the same law as a heavy body thrown upward follows in its ascent; consequently, the distance actually traveled during the entire time of descent is equal to half of what would have been traveled if the initial motion had been steadily continued. Furthermore, in the time that such a vessel takes to empty itself, twice the quantity of the fluid would be discharged if it were kept full by a new supply. This may be easily shown by filling two cylindrical vessels with equal orifices in their bottoms; while one is left to empty itself, the contents of two other identical vessels are poured into the second in succession so as to keep it constantly full. It will be seen that both operations will end at the same instant.

<summary>This page explains how the size and position of an orifice affect the speed and volume of fluid discharge, particularly in cylindrical vessels. It demonstrates that a vessel kept full will discharge twice as much water as one allowed to empty itself over the same duration.</summary>

->ON THE THEORY OF HYDRAULICS.<-

A similar law may be applied to the filling of a lock from a reservoir of constant height; for in all such cases, twice as much time is required for the effect as would be necessary if the initial velocity were maintained. Immersing the orifice in a large reservoir has been found to make no difference in the volume of the discharge, so that the pressure may always be estimated by the difference in the levels of the two surfaces. Thus, when several reservoirs connect with each other through orifices of any size, the velocity of the fluid flowing through each orifice is inversely proportional to the size of the orifice. Since this velocity is produced by the difference in the heights of the fluid in the adjacent reservoirs, this difference must everywhere be proportional to the square of the corresponding velocity. But if the reservoirs were small and the orifices were opposite and near to each other, a much smaller difference in the heights of the surfaces would be sufficient to produce the required velocity. The same circumstances must be considered when determining the velocity of a fluid forced through a vessel divided by several partitions, each having an orifice. If the orifices are small in proportion to their distance from each other and are oriented in different directions, each orifice will require additional pressure equivalent to the entire velocity produced within it. However, if the partitions occupy only a small part of the vessel and are placed near to each other, the slowing of the flow will be much less significant. Cases of this kind occur very frequently in the passage of water through the pipes and valves of pumps; it is, therefore, important to avoid all unnecessary expansions as well as contractions in pipes and in canals, since force is always wasted in restoring the velocity that is lost in the wider parts.

When a siphon, or bent tube, is filled with a fluid and its ends are immersed in fluids of the same kind contained in different vessels, the whole remains at rest if both their surfaces are on the same level. If they are not, the longer column in the siphon outweighs the other, and atmospheric pressure forces the fluid up from the higher vessel until equilibrium is restored—provided, however, that this pressure is sufficiently powerful. For if the height of the tube were more than 34 feet for water, or more than 30 inches for mercury, atmospheric pressure would be incapable of forcing the fluid up to its highest part; that part would remain empty, and the fluid could no longer continue to flow. (Plate XX. Fig. 258.)

# LECTURE XXIII.

If the lower vessel is allowed to empty itself, the siphon will continue to run as long as it is supplied from the upper vessel, with a velocity nearly corresponding to the height of that portion of the fluid in the longer leg which is not counterbalanced by the fluid in the shorter leg. That is, the velocity corresponds to the height of the surface of the upper vessel above that of the lower one, or above the end of the siphon when it is no longer immersed; for the height of the pipe is in all cases to be considered as forming a part of that height which produces the pressure. Thus, the discharge of a pipe descending from the side or bottom of a vessel is nearly the same as from a similar horizontal pipe inserted into a reservoir at the total height of the descending pipe and the fluid above it. This is true even when the depth of the vessel is small in comparison with the length of the pipe, provided its capacity is sufficient to keep the pipe running full. It appears at first sight highly paradoxical that the total water discharged—where each particle is subjected to the action of gravity in a pipe 16 feet long for only half a second—should acquire a velocity of 32 feet per second, which would normally require the action of the same force of gravity for a full second. This fact may be considered as favoring the opinion of those who wish to estimate the magnitude of a force by the space through which it continues, rather than by the time during which it acts. However, if we attend to the nature of hydrostatic pressure, we shall find that the effect of the column on the atmosphere is such as to produce, or to develop, a portion of accelerating force which is actually greater than the weight of the particles immediately involved. If a doubt could be entertained regarding the truth of this theory, it might be easily removed by referring back to the general law of ascending force. It follows from that law that each particle which descends in any manner through a distance of 16 feet must acquire, either for itself or for some other particles, a power of ascending to the same height; and on the other hand, the outcome of the experiment confirms the general law. For if we fix a shallow funnel on a vertical pipe and pour water into it so as to keep it constantly full while the pipe discharges itself into a reservoir—out of which the water runs through a second pipe placed horizontally and of exactly the same dimensions as the first—the height at which the water in the reservoir becomes stationary will be very nearly equal to the height of the funnel above its surface, so that the same height produces the same velocity in both cases. (Plate XX. Fig. 259.)

<summary>This lecture explains that the velocity of fluid through a siphon or pipe is determined by the total vertical height of the fluid column. It also addresses the paradox of acceleration in pipes and confirms these hydrostatic principles through experimental comparisons of vertical and horizontal discharges.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of fluid dynamics and hydrostatic pressure, specifically explaining why the velocity of water in a descending pipe is determined by the combined effect of gravity and atmospheric pressure.</meta>

-># ON THE THEORY OF HYDRAULICS.<-

We can understand the action of the forces directly involved in this experiment by observing the mutual effects of the water and of the atmosphere. The water entering the orifice must immediately acquire a velocity equal to that of all the water in the pipe; otherwise, there would be a vacuum in the upper part of the pipe, which atmospheric pressure will not allow. This pressure, regarded as a hydrostatic force, is equal to the pressure that would be derived in any other way from a column of the same height as the pipe, since the weight of the water in the pipe is entirely employed in diminishing the counter-pressure of the atmosphere below—not only at the beginning, when it is at rest, but also while it is in motion. Because that motion is uniform throughout its descent, the power of gravitation is expended in producing pressure only; so that the pressure of the atmosphere on the water in the funnel becomes completely analogous to the pressure of a reservoir of water of the same height as the pipe. The circumstance which creates the appearance of a paradox in this experiment also exists in the simplest case of the discharge of water; for it can be shown that the portion of accelerating force actually employed in generating the velocity with which a stream is discharged through a small orifice is twice as great as the pressure of the fluid on a part of the vessel equal in size to the orifice. In the same manner, the amount of force exerted by the atmosphere on the water in the funnel, as well as the force with which the descending fluid impels the air below, is equal to twice the weight of the quantity of water existing at any time in the pipe.

There is, however, a limit which the mean velocity in such a pipe can never exceed, and which is derived from the magnitude of the pressure of the atmosphere. For the water cannot enter the pipe with a greater velocity than that with which it would enter an evacuated pipe, which is produced by the total pressure of the atmosphere. Since this pressure is equivalent to that of a column of water 34 feet high, the velocity derived from it is about 47 feet per second; so that if the vertical pipe were more than 34 feet long, there would be a vacuum in a part of it near the funnel.

Wherever a pipe of considerable length descends from a funnel, if the supply of the fluid is scanty, and especially if it approaches the orifice obliquely, the pressure of the atmosphere and the centrifugal force of the particles

In order for a <term>siphon</term> to run, it is obvious that it must first be filled; and once it is filled, it will continue to run until the <term>reservoir</term> is exhausted down to the level of its upper orifice. From this circumstance, the <term>phenomena</term> of certain <term>intermitting springs</term> have been explained; these only begin to flow when the reservoirs from which they originate have been filled by continued rains, and then they continue to exhaust them, even if the weather has become dry. By combining several such siphons and reservoirs, a great number of alternations can sometimes be produced. (Plate XX. Fig. 260.)

Since the <term>velocity</term> of a stream or <term>jet</term> issuing in any direction from a simple or converging <term>orifice</term> is nearly equal to that of a heavy body falling from the height of the reservoir, it will rise—if directed upward—to almost the same height, except for a slight difference caused by the resistance of the air and by the force lost in producing the velocity with which the particles must escape sideways before they begin to descend. The truth of this conclusion is easily confirmed by <term>experiment</term>. (Plate XX. Fig. 261.)

If a jet issues in an oblique or horizontal direction, its form will be <term>parabolic</term>, since every particle tends, as a separate <term>projectile</term>, to describe the same <term>parabola</term> in its range. It can be demonstrated that if it is emitted horizontally from any part of the side of a vessel standing on a horizontal plane, and a circle is drawn using the total height of the fluid as its diameter, the jet will reach the plane at a distance from the vessel twice as great as the distance to that point on the circle through which it would have passed if it had continued to move horizontally. And if the jet rises at any angle from the bottom of the vessel, its maximum height will be equal to that of the point where it would meet the same semicircle if it continued to move in a straight line; the horizontal range will be four times the distance measured between that same point and the side of the vessel. This law is equally true for simple projectiles, but the experiment is most conveniently demonstrated by the motion of a jet. (Plate XX. Fig. 262.)
