->ON THE THEORY OF HYDRAULICS.<-

Until now, we have considered the motions of fluids as continuing mainly in the same direction; but they are often subjected to alternating motions, which bear a significant similarity to the vibrations of <term>pendulums</term>. For example, if a long tube is immersed vertically in a fluid, and the surface of the fluid inside the tube is raised slightly by some external cause, the entire volume of the fluid will be pushed downward by a force that decreases in proportion to the elevation of the surface above the vessel's general level. When both surfaces reach the same level, the motion will continue due to the <term>inertia</term> of the fluid particles until it is stopped by the difference in <term>pressure</term>, which then begins to slow it down. This alternation will continue until the motion is stopped by <term>friction</term> and other resistances. It is also obvious that since any two vibrations—in which the forces are proportional to the distances covered—occur in equal intervals of time, these alternations will require exactly the same time to complete as the vibrations of a <term>pendulum</term> with a length equal to that of the entire tube. This is because the relative force in the tube relates to the total force of <term>gravity</term> in the same way that the elevation or depression relates to the total length of the tube. It follows, then, that if two such tubes were joined at the bottom to form a single bent tube, the vibrations could take place in the entire combined tube in the same way and in the same amount of time as in each of the separate tubes. These effects would not be significantly changed if any part of the middle of the tube was in a horizontal or an angled direction, provided that the total length remained the same. In such a tube, all vibrations, even those of considerable size, would occur in the same amount of time and would remain nearly the same size for a long while. However, in a single tube open at the bottom, the vibrations would constantly become smaller, and their duration as well as their size would change, in addition to the unavoidable resistances that would interfere with the regularity of the effects in both cases.

But it does not appear that the laws governing the vibrations of fluids in pipes will help explain the phenomena of <term>waves</term> at all. Sir Isaac Newton supposed that each wave could be compared to a fluid oscillating in a bent pipe, but the analogy is far too weak to allow us to base any proof on it. The motions of waves have been investigated in a new and improved way by Mr. Lagrange, and I have provided a concise demonstra-

This transmission would occur at a <term>velocity</term> equal to the speed a heavy body would reach when falling through half the depth of the fluid. I have reason to believe, based on observation and experiment, that when the height or depth of the surface wave is quite large compared to the depth of the fluid, the <term>velocity</term> nearly matches this determination, often being only an eighth or a tenth less than the total. In other cases, where many small waves follow one another at intervals much smaller than the depth, I have endeavored to calculate the slowing (<term>retardation</term>) that must be caused by the imperfect <term>elasticity</term> or <term>compressibility</term> of the fluid; however, it seems likely that the motion of small waves is even slower than this calculation suggests.

Regardless of any corrections these determinations of the <term>velocity</term> of waves might require, the laws governing their <term>propagation</term> can still be safely inferred from this investigation. For instance, it can be shown that if waves flow in a narrow canal of uniform depth, no matter the initial shape of the waves, every part of the fluid’s surface will successively take on that same form. The only exception is that the original elevations and depressions, by spreading their influence in both directions, will produce effects only half as large on each side; these effects will then continue until they are eliminated by various types of resistance. It can also be inferred that a fluid surface agitated by any series of impulses will receive the effects of another series in the same way a horizontal surface would. These <term>undulations</term>, crossing one another, will proceed without any interruption, as the motion of each particle is always the sum or difference of the motions belonging to the individual series.

If we suppose two equal and similar series of waves meeting each other from opposite directions in such a canal, the point where their corresponding parts meet must be free from all horizontal motion. When this reflection is sufficiently regular, it is easy to show that the combination of the direct with the reflected motions must constitute a vibration of such a nature that the whole surface is divided into portions which appear to vibrate alternately upwards and downwards, without any progressive motion, while the points separating the portions remain always at their natural level. (Plate XX, Fig. 263.)

But those series of waves that are usually observable on any broad surface, and which form a number of concentric circles, are usually reflected in such a manner as to appear to diverge, after reflection, from a center beyond the surface that reflects them. They are subject to all those laws that are more commonly noticed in the phenomena of reflected light; but as these laws are of more practical importance in their application to <term>optics</term> than to <term>hydraulics</term>, it is unnecessary at present to examine their consequences in detail. It may, however, be easily understood that a new series of waves, proceeding from a center at the same distance behind the reflecting surface as the center of the original series is before it, would produce precisely the same effect as a fixed obstacle. Consequently, the law of reflection at equal angles is a very simple inference from this mode of reasoning. (Plate XX, Fig. 264.)

When a series of waves proceeds in a uniform canal, it is obvious that the <term>center of gravity</term> of the whole fluid neither rises nor falls. From this analogy, as well as from the general application of the law of <term>ascending force</term>, it is probable that in all cases of the <term>propagation</term> of waves, the position of the center of gravity remains unaltered. Thus, when a circular wave spreads further and further from its center, its height is not diminished in the same ratio as its diameter is increased, but the square of its height alone varies in this proportion. That is, a wave that is a yard in diameter and an inch high will retain a height of half an inch when its diameter is increased to four yards.

# LECTURE XXIII.

Waves may be excited by the vibrations of an elastic rod or wire, weighted with a load, by which its motions may be made more or less rapid as desired; and the form and progress of the waves may be easily observed by placing a light under the vessel, so that their shadows may fall on a white surface, extended in an inclined position above. In this manner, the smallest ripples on the surface of the water may be made perfectly visible. (Plate XX. Fig. 265.)

By means of this apparatus, we may examine the manner in which a wave spreads out (diverges) when a portion of it has been blocked on either side or on both sides. Thus, if a wave is admitted through an opening (aperture) which is very narrow in proportion to its own width into the surface of a part of the water that is at rest, it diverges from the aperture as if from a new center; but when the aperture is considerably wider than the wave, the wave confines its motion for the most part to its original direction, with some small divergence, while it is joined on each side by fainter circular portions, spreading from the corners only. (Plate XX. Fig. 266.)

When two equal sets of circular waves, proceeding from centers near each other, begin their motions at the same time, they must cross each other in some parts of their progress so that the peaks of one set tend to fill up the troughs of the other; and this effect may be actually observed by throwing two stones of equal size into a pond at the same instant. For we may easily distinguish, in favorable circumstances, the series of points in which this effect takes place, forming continuous curves in which the water remains smooth, while it is strongly agitated in the areas between them. These curves are of the kind called <term>hyperbolas</term>, each point of the curve being so situated with respect to its <term>foci</term> as to be nearer to one than the other by a certain constant distance. (Plate XX. Fig. 267.)

The subject of waves is of less immediate importance for any practical application than some other parts of <term>hydraulics</term>; but besides being intimately connected with the phenomena of the tides, it affords an elegant subject for theoretical investigation, and provides us with sensible and undeniable evidence of the truth of certain facts which are capable of being applied to the explanation of some of the most interesting phenomena of <term>acustics</term> <note>acoustics</note> and <term>optics</term>.

<warning>Significant ink bleed-through from the reverse side of the page creates mirrored text overlays across the center and bottom of the leaf.</warning>

It may be shown, by steps nearly similar to those by which the velocity of wave motions is investigated, that a fluid contained in an elastic pipe, which receives an impulse at any part of the pipe, will transmit its effects with the same velocity as a wave would have in a reservoir of a depth that measures the elasticity of the pipe. That is, it moves with half the velocity that a body would acquire in falling from the height at which a portion of the fluid, connected with the contents of the pipe, would stand in a vertical tube. It is in this manner that the blood is transmitted through the blood vessels by means of the impulse given to it by the heart; the pulse moves forward with great rapidity, as the elastic force of the vessels is considerably assisted by the temporary actions of the muscular coats of the arteries, which cause a contraction more rapid than the dilation. While this occurs, the entire mass of the arterial blood continues to advance at the same time with a much smaller velocity—like the slow stream of a river, on the surface of which waves are continually propelled with motions independent of the river's own flow.

# LECTURE XXIV

### ON THE FRICTION OF FLUIDS.

<insert>REESE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</insert>
We have so far considered the motions of fluids independently of the resistance they undergo from the vessels containing them, and from the surfaces in contact with them, as well as from the interference of the neighboring particles with each other; there is, however, a variety of cases of very common occurrence in which these frictions most significantly affect the results of our calculations; so that before this subject was laboriously and judiciously investigated by the Chevalier de Buat, it was almost impossible to apply any part of our theoretical knowledge of hydraulics to practical purposes.

The effect of friction is particularly exemplified by the motions of rivers, in which almost the entire force of gravity is employed in overcoming it. When the inclination and the dimensions of a river continue uniform, the velocity is also everywhere equal; for otherwise the depth would become unequal: here, therefore, the force of gravitation must be an exact counterpoise to the resistance that is to be overcome, in order that the water may flow with its actual velocity; this velocity having been originally derived from the effect of a greater inclination near the origin of the river. When the river is proceeding in this way, with an even motion, it is said to be *in train*; and it is obvious that no increase of its length will produce any alteration in its velocity. There is, therefore, a very significant difference between the course of a river and the descent of a body, with an accelerated motion, along an inclined surface. For when a solid body is placed on an inclined plane, the force of friction is either great enough to overpower its relative weight and keep it at rest, or else the friction is constantly less than the gravitation, and the motion is always accelerated. But the resistance to the motions of fluids arises principally from different causes; not from the tenacity of

<meta>This page continues the discussion of fluid friction, transitioning from the general concept of resistance in rivers to the mechanical laws governing the relationship between velocity, pressure, and resistance in fluids.</meta>

### ON THE FRICTION OF FLUIDS.

the fluids, which, where it exists, is a nearly uniform force, like that of friction, but it arises principally from the irregular motions and mutual collisions of their particles; and in this case, according to the laws of mechanics, it must vary nearly in proportion to the square of the velocity. For when a body moves in a line of a certain curvature, the <term>centrifugal force</term> is always as the square of the velocity; and the particles of water in contact with the sides and bottom of a river or pipe must be deflected, as a consequence of the minute irregularities of the surfaces on which they slide, into nearly the same curvilinear paths, whatever their velocity may be, so that the resistance, which is in great measure caused by this centrifugal force, must also vary as the square of the velocity. Thus also the curvature assumed by the outline of a stream of water issuing from a simple <term>orifice</term>, which constitutes the <term>contraction</term> already described, is very nearly the same, whatever the velocity may be: nor does the friction increase with the pressure, as is demonstrated by an experiment by Professor Robison on the oscillations of a fluid through a bent tube, terminated by two bulbs, which were performed in the same time, whether the tube was in a horizontal or in a vertical position. Mr. Coulomb has also proved the same fact by experiments on the vibrations of bodies immersed in fluids, and suspended by twisted wires: he finds that precisely at the surface, the friction is somewhat greater than at any depth below it: he also considers a certain part of the friction as simply proportional to the velocity, and only a very small portion, in common fluids, as perfectly independent of it.

It is obvious that wherever the friction varies as the square of the velocity, or even when it increases in any degree with the velocity, there must always be a limit which the velocity can never exceed by means of any constant force, and this limit must be the velocity at which the resistance would become equal to the force. It is for this reason that a light body, descending through the air, soon acquires a velocity nearly uniform; and if it is caused, by any external force, to move for a time more rapidly, it will again be speedily retarded, until its velocity is restored very nearly to its original state. In the same manner the weight of the water in a river, which has once acquired a <term>stationary velocity</term>, is wholly employed in overcoming the friction produced by the bottom and the banks.

<summary>This page explains that fluid friction primarily results from particle collisions and centrifugal force caused by surface irregularities, leading to resistance that varies with the square of velocity. It also discusses how friction is independent of pressure and how constant forces eventually lead to a terminal or stationary velocity where resistance balances the driving force.</summary>

### LECTURE XXIV.

By considering the effect of the size of the surface exposed to the friction of the water, compared with the total volume contained in the river, along with the degree to which the riverbed is inclined toward the horizon, we can determine the velocity of any river for which we know the dimensions and the inclination, following the methods adopted by Mr. Buat. If we imagine the total volume of water spread over a horizontal surface equal in area to the bottom and sides of the river, the height at which it would stand is called the <term>hydraulic mean depth</term>; and it can be shown that the square of the velocity must be jointly proportional to the hydraulic mean depth and to the fall over a given length. If we measure the inclination by the fall in 2800 yards, the square of the velocity per second will be nearly equal to the product of this fall multiplied by the hydraulic mean depth. 

For example, in the Ganges and in some other great rivers, where the mean depth is about 30 feet and the fall is 4 inches per mile, the fall in 2800 yards will be about 6½ inches; this, multiplied by 360 inches, gives 2340 inches for the square of the mean velocity, and 48½ inches, or about four feet, for the mean velocity per second. This is not quite three miles an hour, which is the usual velocity of moderately rapid rivers. If, however, great precision were required in this determination, some further corrections would be necessary because of the deviation of the resistance from the exact proportion of the squares of the velocities; since friction, as we have already seen, does not increase quite as fast as this.

It is obvious that the friction of a fluid moving only on the surface of a solid would not produce any material slowing of its motion if the particles of the fluid themselves were capable of moving against each other without the least resistance; for in this case, a small portion of the fluid in immediate contact with the solid might remain at rest, and the remaining mass of the fluid might slide over this portion without any retardation. It appears, however, that the water in contact with the bottom of a river moves with a very considerable velocity, and the water just above this moves only a little faster, so that the velocity increases almost uniformly as we ascend toward the surface. It follows, therefore, that the resistance must be much greater where the particles of water slide against each other than when they glide along the surface of a solid. This internal friction operates gradually throughout the

This slowing is communicated from the bottom upward in such a manner as to be everywhere equivalent to the relative weight of the water above the section being considered. It appears from observation that once we have determined the mean velocity in English inches, we can find the surface velocity, very nearly, by adding its square root to it, and the velocity at the bottom by subtracting the same number from it: for example, since the square root of 48½ is nearly 7, the surface velocity of the Ganges will be about 55 inches, or 4 feet 7 inches per second, and the velocity at the bottom will be 41½ inches. There are, however, frequent irregularities in the proportions of the velocities at different depths; it has sometimes been observed—perhaps because of air resistance—that the velocity is slightly less right at the surface than it is a few inches below it.

For similar reasons, the velocity of a river is also generally greater in the middle than at the sides. The motion of the particles in the middle must be slowed down not only by those below them, but also by those on each side, while these, on the contrary, are pulled along by the water in the middle. The middle parts, therefore, tend to draw the sides toward them, which they cannot do without lowering the surface of the fluid next to the banks to such an extent that the difference in level acts as an equivalent to this tendency to move toward the middle. This appears to be the reason why the surface of a large river may generally be observed to be slightly convex, or a bit higher in the middle.

The course of a river is sometimes interrupted by a <term>weir</term> or a fall, whether natural or artificial; in such cases, the velocity may be calculated in the same manner as when a fluid is discharged from a reservoir through an opening of considerable height: assuming the entire section of the <term>weir</term> to be such an opening in a vessel so much higher that the velocity of a fluid issuing from the upper part of the opening would be exactly equal to the actual velocity of the river. # LECTURE XXIV.

It appears from calculations of the effects of various changes in the dimensions of rivers, as well as from immediate observation, that a considerable reduction of the breadth of a river at a particular place will often produce but a small elevation of its surface. The velocity, however, may sometimes be considerably increased by such a change, and where the bottom is of a loose nature, its particles may be carried away by means of the increased velocity, and the bed of the river may be deepened.

Where a river bends in a considerable degree, it is generally noted that the velocity of the water is greater near the concave than the convex side of the bend, that is, at the greatest distance from the center of its curvature. This effect is probably caused by the centrifugal force, which accumulates the water on that side; so that the banks are undermined, and the channel is deepened by its friction. Some authors have been led to expect that the velocity would be greater nearest to the convex bank, because the inclination of the surface must be a little greater there; but the effect of the accelerating force, in any short distance, is inconsiderable, and it is more than compensated by the lack of depth. It may easily be understood, that all angles and bends must diminish the general velocity of the river's motion, and the more so as they are more abrupt.

It has sometimes been imagined, that because the pressure of fluids is propagated equally in all directions, their motions ought also to diverge in a similar manner; but this opinion is by no means well founded, even with respect to those particles which receive their motion in an unlimited reservoir from the impulse of a stream which enters it. An experiment, which sets this fact in a clear point of view, was made long ago by Hauksbee. He produced a very rapid current of air, by means of a vessel, into which three or

From considerations similar to those used to determine the velocity of a river, we may calculate the quantity of water discharged from a pipe of any given dimensions and in any position. The same formulas will serve for estimating the magnitude of the friction in both cases; the pipe is considered as a small river, in which the mean depth is one-fourth of its diameter. However, only a part of the force of gravity is now spent in overcoming friction, with the rest being employed in producing the momentum of the water. We may obtain a sufficiently accurate determination of the velocity by assuming the height of the reservoir above the orifice of the pipe to be diminished in the same proportion as the diameter of the pipe would be increased by adding to it one-fiftieth part of its length, and then finding the total velocity corresponding to four-fifths of this height.

Thus, if the diameter of the pipe were one inch and its length 100 inches, we must suppose the effective height to be reduced to one-third by the friction, and the discharge must be calculated from a height four-fifths as great as this; this may be considered a reduction derived from the interference of the particles entering the pipe with each other's motions. If the diameter of the pipe had been two inches, the height would only have been supposed to be reduced to one-half by the friction; such a pipe would, therefore, discharge about five times as much water as the former, although it is only twice the diameter. This circumstance requires the attention of all those who are concerned in regulating the distribution of water by pipes for domestic use, or for any other purpose.

The bad effect of unnecessary expansions, as well as narrowings, in aqueducts and in pipes, may be understood from what has already been said concerning the loss of force attendant on every change of velocity; a circumstance of a similar nature sometimes happens in the animal economy <note>The functional system of a living body.</note>. When an artery is dilated so as to form an aneurysm, it has been observed that the artery is usually distended above the cavity; and this effect is easily understood from the actual increase of resistance which the aneurysm produces, combined perhaps with the previous weakness of the artery.

Mr. Gerstner has found, by some very accurate observations on the motion of water in very small pipes, that the resistance is considerably affected by the temperature at which the experiment is performed; but in the cases of rivers, and of such pipes as are commonly used in practice, no variations of temperature to which they can be liable will produce any noticeable effects. His experiments indicate a resistance, where the tubes are very small, which follows a law so different from that which is observed in more common cases, that it appears to be owing to some other cause: this cause is perhaps the capillary attraction of the open end of the tube, and it is the more probable that the resistance depends on some such circumstance, as there is reason to think that the irregularity may be in great measure removed by placing the tube wholly under water.

# LECTURE XXV.

## ON HYDRAULIC PRESSURE.

THE mutual effects of fluids and movable solids on each other depend principally on the laws of hydraulic pressure and of the resistance of fluids, which have been considered by Bernoulli as constituting a separate department of hydrodynamics, under the name of hydraulicostatics, and which are of the utmost practical importance, since the application of the powers of wind or water to the working of mills, and to the navigation of ships, are wholly dependent on them. The impulse of a fluid differs very significantly from that of a solid, for in the motions of solids, the least possible finite momentum must overpower the strongest possible pressure; but since the particles of fluids are supposed to be infinitely small, the momentum of a fluid stream may always be balanced by a certain determinate pressure, without producing motion in the solid opposed to it; so that this division of the subject of hydraulics has nothing analogous to it in simple mechanics. It is true that when a certain quantity of a fluid is made to concentrate its action almost instantaneously, its effect is nearly similar to that of a solid, for here the essential distinction, derived from the successive action of the particles, no longer exists. Thus, when a stream of fluid filling a pipe acts suddenly on an obstacle at the end of it, it requires to be resisted by a force far greater than that which originally caused its motion, unless the action of the force be continued through a considerable space: and for this reason the strength of the pipe ought to be so calculated as to be able to resist this action; its intensity may, however, be easily diminished by means of an air vessel connected with the pipe, which will allow the motion to be changed in a less abrupt manner. But in the principal cases which we are about to consider, the action of the fluid on the solid is supposed to be confined to such of its particles as are nearly in contact with the surface.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Lecture XXV on hydraulic pressure, moving from general principles to the specific relationship between fluid motion and the resulting reduction in pressure on its container.</meta>

<header>ON HYDRAULIC PRESSURE.</header>

When a part of the weight of any fluid is used to produce motion in any direction, an equal force is deducted from its pressure on the vessel in that direction. This is because the gravitational force employed in generating <term>velocity</term> cannot simultaneously cause pressure; and when the resulting motion is in any direction other than vertical, its diagonal direction must be derived immediately from the reaction of the vessel or some fixed obstacle. It is obvious that a vertical force, such as gravity, cannot produce oblique or horizontal motion by itself.

If a small stream descends from the bottom of a vessel, the weight used to produce its motion is equal to that of a column of the fluid standing on a base equal to the <term>contracted orifice</term>, and twice the height of the vessel. Thus, if the vessel is 16 feet high, the velocity of the stream will be 32 feet per second, and a column 32 feet in length will pass through the orifice each second, with the full velocity derived from its weight acting for the same amount of time. Therefore, that much of the fluid pressure in the <term>reservoir</term> must be used to produce this motion, and it must, of course, be subtracted from the total force with which the fluid acts on the bottom of the reservoir. This is the same as when two unequal weights are connected by a thread passing over a pulley; when one of them begins to descend, the pressure on the pulley is diminished by an amount that is as much less than the sum of the weights as the velocity of their common center of gravity is less than the velocity of a freely falling body. If the stream issues from the vessel in any other direction, the effect of the reduction of pressure in that direction will be nearly the same as if the vessel were subjected to an equal pressure of any other kind in the opposite direction; and if the vessel is movable, it will receive a progressive or rotatory motion in that direction. Thus, when a vessel or pipe is fixed on a center and a stream of water is discharged from it by a side orifice, the vessel turns at first with an accelerated motion. However, because of the force consumed in producing the <term>rotatory motion</term> in successive portions of the water, the velocity soon becomes nearly stationary. (Plate XXI. Fig. 272.)

From similar reasoning, it appears that the effect of a detached jet on a plane surface perpendicular to it must be equivalent to the weight of a portion of the same stream equal in length to twice the height which is capable of pro-

When a stream also acts on an obstacle in a channel sufficiently closed on all sides to prevent the escape of any considerable portion of water, its effect is nearly the same as that of a jet playing on a large surface. In such cases, the pressure is usually found to be simply equivalent to the weight of a column equal in height to the reservoir, the surface being subjected to a pressure nearly similar to that which acts on a part of the bottom of a vessel while a stream is descending through a large aperture in another part of it.

->(Plate XXI. Fig. 273.)<-

It is obvious that, in all these cases, the pressure varies as the square of the <term>velocity</term>, since the height required to produce any velocity is proportional to its square. This inference was first made in a simpler manner by comparing the <term>impulse</term> of a fluid on a solid with that of a number of separate particles striking the surface of the body; each of these would produce an effect proportional to its velocity, while the total number of particles acting in a given time would also vary in the same ratio. If the solid was in motion, and the fluid was either in motion or at rest, it is obvious that the relative velocity of the solid and the fluid, with regard to each other, would be the only cause of their mutual effects, and that the <term>hydraulic pressure</term> or resistance must be dependent on this velocity alone—except so far as the limited dimensions of the <term>reservoir</term> containing the fluid might produce a difference in the internal motions of its particles in different cases. Thus, where the fluid is so confined that the whole of the stream acts on a succession of planes, each portion into which it is divided may be considered as an <term>inelastic solid</term> striking on the surface exposed to it with a certain velocity; and in this case, the force must be considered as simply proportional to the relative velocity, and not to its square. Due to a lack of this consideration, the effects of water wheels have frequently been very erroneously stated.

# ON HYDRAULIC PRESSURE.

...the body forward in its own direction is found to be very nearly proportional to the height to which the jet would rise if it were similarly inclined to the horizon. But when a plane is situated obliquely in this way with respect to a wide stream, the force impelling it in the direction of the stream is somewhat less diminished by the obliquity, at least if we allow for its intercepting a smaller portion of the stream. Thus, if the front part of a solid is terminated by a wedge that is more or less acute, the resistance—according to the simplest theory of the resolution of forces—might be found by describing a circle on half the base of the wedge as a diameter; this would cut off a part from the oblique side of the wedge that would be the measure of the resistance, while the whole side represents the resistance to the same solid without the wedge. However, the resistance is always somewhat more than this, and the portion to be added may be found, very nearly, by adding to the fraction thus found one ten-millionth of the cube of the number of degrees contained in the external angle of the wedge. (Plate XXI. Fig. 274.)

The pressure of a fluid striking perpendicularly on a plane surface has been found to be very different at different parts of the surface, being greatest at the center and least toward the edges. Therefore, if an opening is made in the center of a circular plane covering the mouth of a bent tube, the fluid within it will rise half again as high as it would if the whole mouth were open. It is also observable that two bodies, equal and similar in the shape of the part meeting the fluid, undergo very different degrees of resistance depending on the forms of their rear terminations; for example, a thin circular plate is much more retarded than a long cylinder of the same diameter. These circumstances are utterly inexplicable according to the vague approximation that supposes resistance is produced by the immediate impulse of separate particles of the fluid on the solid. However, they are no longer surprising when we consider the true mode of action of continuous fluids, since all the motion produced by the fluid in the solid, or by the solid in the fluid, is communicated much more by means of pressure than by immediate impulse. The minute operations of this pressure are too intricate to be accurately developed, but we may observe in general that when a body moves through a resisting medium at rest, or when a stationary obstacle is opposed to a fluid in steady motion, the pressure is increased in front of the moving substance and diminished behind it, so that the surface is elevated at one part and depressed at the other,

<meta>This page continues the analysis of fluid resistance and pressure, specifically exploring how the elevation of water in front of a body and the depression behind it affect the total pressure experienced during motion.</meta>

<center>### LECTURE XXV. ###</center>

...and the more so as the velocity increases. Now it is obvious that the pressure must be greatest where the elevation is greatest; therefore, a perforation at the center of the surface indicates a greater pressure than at the circumference. Behind the body, this pressure becomes negative and has sometimes been called nonpressure. Consequently, it happens that a tube, opening in the center of the rear surface, shows the fluid within it depressed below the level of the general surface of the water. 

Thus, if we suppose the velocity of a body terminated by perpendicular surfaces to be 8 feet per second, it will require a pressure of about a foot to produce such a velocity. We may, therefore, expect an elevation of about a foot in front of the body and an equal depression behind it. Consequently, an equivalent difference must be found in the pressure of the water at any equal depths on the front and back surfaces of the body. The water elevated in front of the body escapes continually toward each side, and the deficiency behind is also filled up to some degree by the particles rushing in and following the body. However, in both cases, there is a certain quantity of water that moves forward and constitutes what is called the dead water. In front, where it is usually most observable, it forms an irregular triangle whose sides are convex inward. 

If the rear part of the body is shaped like a wedge, the water on each side will advance to fill up the vacuum even while it remains in contact with the sides, and the negative pressure will be considerably diminished. For this reason, the bottoms of ships are made to end at the rear in a shape somewhat resembling a wedge; the same design may be observed in the forms of fishes, shaped by nature for pursuing their prey with the greatest possible speed. In general, fishes, as well as ships, have a more blunt form in front than in back, but it is not certain that there would be any significant difference in resistance if they moved in the opposite direction, although some experiments seem to favor such an opinion. Perhaps if the natural form of the dead water moving before a blunt body were determined, it might suggest a solid designed to move through the water with the least resistance. Since the water must naturally assume such a form for its own motions, and because the friction of fluids on solids is less than that of fluids moving against themselves, the resistance would be diminished by substituting a solid of the same form for the fluid. (Plate XXI. Fig. 275.)

its surface, there will still be an elevation in front and a depression behind it; this elevation will be smaller in height and greater in extent as the depth at which the body is situated increases. Such an elevation appears to be somewhat analogous to the effect of a low weir placed across a river, which raises its surface and produces a swell.

If two or more differently shaped bodies—for which the resistance to motion had been determined—were moved through a fluid while in contact with each other, it is obvious that the paths taken by the particles of the fluid as they glide past them must be significantly altered by their junction. It seems natural to expect that the combined disturbance produced in the motion of the fluid, when the surfaces are joined to form a convex outline, would be somewhat less than if each surface were considered individually. Accordingly, it is found that no calculation derived from experiments on the resistance opposed to oblique plane surfaces will accurately determine the resistance to a curved surface. It appears from experiment that the resistance to the motion of a sphere is usually about two-fifths of the resistance to a flat circular object of an equal diameter. The resistance to the motion of a concave surface is greater than that of a plane. This is easily understood: since the direction in which the particles of the fluid recede from the solid must be significantly influenced by the form of the solid exposed to their action, their motion in this case must be partly retrograde as they glide toward the edges of the concave surface. Consequently, a greater amount of force must have been used than when they escape with a smaller deviation from their original direction. (Plate XXI. Fig. 276.)

For some reason that is not well understood, the hydraulic pressure of the air appears to be somewhat greater, in proportion to its density, than that of water. It has been found that the perpendicular impulse of the air on a plane surface is more than equivalent to the weight of a column of air of a height corresponding to the velocity; some say this excess amounts to one-third, while others say two-thirds of that weight. The resistance also appears to be slightly greater for a large surface than for a number of smaller ones that together have the same area.

Thus, if the velocity were 100 feet per second, the pressure on each square foot would be 20 pounds; if 1000 feet, 2000 pounds. For a sphere one foot in diameter, we may divide the square of the velocity by 1600. We may also find, in a similar manner, the maximum velocity that a given body can acquire or maintain while falling through the air; for the velocity at which the resistance equals the weight must be its limit. Thus, if a sphere one foot in diameter weighed 100 pounds, the square of its maximum velocity would be 160,000, and the velocity itself 400 feet per second; if a stone of such dimensions entered the atmosphere with a greater velocity, its motion would very soon be reduced to this limit; and a lighter or smaller body would move even more slowly. The weight of Mr. Garnerin's parachute, with its entire load, was about a quarter of a pound for each square foot; the square of its greatest velocity must, therefore, have been about 125, and the velocity 11 feet per second, which is no faster than the speed at which a person would descend when jumping from a height of two feet without bending their knees. Mr. Garnerin found the velocity even lower than this, and it is likely that the concave shape of the parachute might considerably increase the resistance. Thus, Mr. Edgeworth found that a plate 9 inches long, when bent into an arc where the chord was 7 1/4 inches, had its resistance increased by more than one-seventh. The reduction of air resistance caused by the slant of a surface is even less than that of water resistance: thus, the resistance on the slanted surfaces of a wedge is not quite as much less than the resistance on its base as its width is less than the length of those surfaces.

When the velocity of a body moving through an elastic fluid is very high, the resistance increases in a much greater proportion than the square of the velocity: thus, the slowing down of a cannonball moving with a velocity of 1000 feet per second, or slightly more, suddenly becomes much greater than the calculation suggests. The reason for this change appears to be that the compression of the air in front of the ball is necessarily confined to a smaller area, which is very intensely compressed, because the effect of the impact can only spread through the air with a certain velocity, which is not much faster than that of the ball; and this smaller portion of air must necessarily be much more compressed than a larger portion would have been. ...ball moves slowly, its effect at any instant is somewhat distributed throughout all that part of the atmosphere which the sound of the report has reached; and if the ball follows the sound very quickly, it is obvious that the portion of the air in front of the ball which is affected must be very small. Sound is observed to propagate at a velocity of about 1130 feet per second, and a cannon ball may be fired with a velocity of 2000 feet per second; however, half of this speed is very quickly lost, so that it becomes entirely useless regarding the ball's effect. If, therefore, we wish to increase the range of a cannon ball, we must increase its weight; for resistance increases only in proportion to the surface area of the ball, while the weight is determined by its volume.

It is not easy to explain in a perfectly satisfactory manner the reflection of a cannon ball, or of a stone, that strikes the surface of the sea or a body of water at an angle. We may, however, identify some causes which appear to be significantly involved in this effect. First, the surface of the water, acting for some time on the lower part of the ball, produces through its friction a degree of <term>rotatory motion</term>. By means of this motion, as the ball proceeds, it acts upon the mass of water heaped up before it and is forced by similar friction to roll upwards; thus, it rises again to a much greater height than it could possibly have reached by mere <term>hydrostatic pressure</term> of the water at such a shallow depth. But a more powerful cause than this appears to be the continuous succession of new surfaces which must be depressed, and which may be supposed to react on the ball so as to produce the same effect as a more intense pressure would have done if it had remained stationary. The mutual action of the water and the ball may be compared to the impulse of an angled stream moving with the velocity of the ball, which would propel it much more powerfully than simple <term>hydrostatic pressure</term> at a much greater depth. As in many other cases, it happens that the effects which appear most familiar to us do not by any means allow for the clearest and simplest explanation.

## LECTURE XXVI.

### ON HYDROSTATIC INSTRUMENTS, AND HYDRAULIC ARCHITECTURE.

We have now examined the fundamental laws of the principal departments of hydrodynamics, which may be considered to constitute the theory of the science; we are next to proceed to the application of this theory to a variety of practical purposes. Following the same general order we observed in mechanics, our first division will be analogous to the subject of statics and will relate to hydrostatic instruments; the second to architecture, containing some details regarding canals and embankments; the third to machinery, including the modification and application of the force of fluids considered as inelastic; the fourth and the fifth to the methods of raising and moving weights, in which the principal hydraulic and pneumatic machines will be explained respectively; and, as a part of this subject, the application of pneumatic force will also be examined.

The principles of hydrostatics are very frequently applied to determine the specific gravities of various products of nature or art. The reduction in the apparent weight of a solid body upon immersion into a fluid provides an easy method of comparing its density with that of the fluid. For, once the weight of the solid has been previously determined, if we examine how much that weight is reduced by plunging the body into pure water, we shall have the weight of an equal volume of water; and from there, we may immediately obtain the ratio of the specific gravity of the body to that of water, which is the usual standard of comparison. And if we weigh a solid of a given size—for instance, a glass ball—first in water and then in any other fluid, the amount of weight lost in each case will be in the same proportion as the specific gravities of the two fluids. A balance adapted for such examinations is called a <term>hydrostatic balance</term>; on one side, it has a scale as

Sometimes a dish is also added for holding any loose substances that will sink in water, with proper counterpoises being used as equivalents for the weight of the dish either in air or in water; and when a body lighter than water is examined, a weight of known magnitude and density is employed to sink it. (Plate XXI. Fig. 277.)

The specific gravities of any substances, and particularly those lighter than water, may also be very conveniently determined by means of a common balance, using a phial with a conical ground stopper, filling it first with water, and then either with a given fluid or with a portion of the solid whose weight has been determined, together with enough water to exclude all air.

For the speedy examination of a variety of fluids that differ only slightly in specific gravity from some known standard, a <term>hydrometer</term> may be very conveniently used. This instrument is said to have been invented by Archimedes: it consists of a hollow ball with a weight below it and a slender stem above, graduated so as to express the specific gravity of the fluid by the depth to which it sinks. Sometimes the instrument is sunk to a certain mark by means of weights placed in a dish at the end of the stem; or different weights are fixed to it below while the graduations of the scale are still observed. It may even be applied to finding the specific gravities of solids: the solid is first placed in the dish at the end of the stem, and then in a second dish that is suspended from the bulb below the water. (Plate XXI. Fig. 278.)

Another method of ascertaining the specific gravities of fluids that differ only slightly from each other in density is to have a series of glass globules, weighted so as to correspond to the specific gravities indicated by the numbers marked on them. By throwing several of them together into the fluid, one can observe which of them remains nearly stationary, without either rising to the surface or sinking. This method, though not fast, appears to be very reliable; these globules are sold under patent and are adapted for measuring the strength of spirituous liquors.

# LECTURE XXVI.

In whatever manner we compare the <term>specific gravities</term> of bodies with that of water, it is necessary for very accurate experiments either that the water be used at the temperature of the air when moderately warm, or that a proper correction should be made for its change of volume at different temperatures. <term>Platinum</term> <note>The text uses the historical term "Platina."</note>, the densest known substance, is 23 times as heavy as distilled water; gold 19 1/2, mercury 13 1/2, lead 11 1/4, silver 11, copper 9, iron and steel 7 3/4, stony substances usually about 2 1/2, rectified spirits 4/5, naphtha—the lightest liquid—7/10, cork about 1/4, common air 1/830, steam 1/2100, and pure hydrogen gas 1/12000. From this comparison, the weight of a cubic foot of any of these substances may be easily determined, since a cubic foot of water weighs nearly 1,000 ounces avoirdupois, or more nearly 998. Thus, a cubic foot of gold would weigh about 195,000 ounces and be worth above £60,000 sterling; a cubic foot of iron weighs 7,750 ounces, and a cubic foot of common stone about 2,500.

The method of measuring the volume of solid bodies by immersing them in a fluid was applied by its inventor, Archimedes, to the detection of a fraud in the composition of a mixed metal. At present, the principal use of <term>hydrometers</term> is for ascertaining, by the specific gravity of a compound of alcohol and water, the proportional quantities of its ingredients. But in all experiments of this kind, it is necessary to be aware that a considerable change of the joint volume of two substances is often produced by their mixture, and that in general their dimensions are considerably contracted. Thus, 18 gallons of water and 18 of alcohol, instead of making 36 gallons, make only 35; consequently, the specific gravity of the compound is one-thirty-fifth greater than the average of the specific gravities of the ingredients. And in some cases, the total dimensions of a single substance may even be contracted by the addition of another substance: thus iron, by the addition of one-eighth of its volume of platinum, becomes contracted by one-fortieth of that volume.

The use of the <term>spirit level</term> depends on the tendency of all fluids to maintain a horizontal surface; the freedom with which the particles of fluids move against each other renders it an instrument capable of the greatest delicacy. A tube, which is very slightly curved, being nearly filled with alcohol or ether and then perfectly closed, the bubble will always rise to the highest part of the tube, and will never be stationary at the point which is marked as its

The principles of hydrostatics have been employed in various ways for supplying lamps with oil. It is found that a lamp will burn without consuming any considerable portion of its wick as long as it is amply supplied with oil; hence it becomes desirable that the wick should always be level with the surface of the reservoir. This may be effected sufficiently well by placing the wick at the edge of a very large vessel, or at the end of a tube projecting from such a vessel, or from a vessel closed above and opening only by an orifice below, which lets in the air as the oil escapes through it. But all these methods are often attended with inconveniences of various kinds, especially where the lamp is to be used like a candle and placed on a table. A French artist has applied a little pump, which is worked by means of a spring, for raising the oil from a vessel under the lamp; but this refinement is too complicated to be practically useful. Mr. Keir's lamp contains a divided cavity, one part of which is filled with oil and the other with a saline or saccharine fluid of greater density, so that when the oil contained in the upper part of the tube is exhausted, its place is partly supplied by a fresh portion, which is forced up in consequence of the descent of the denser fluid in a much larger vessel. Still, however, the surface must be lowered by degrees; but by combining the invention with Dr. Hooke's semicylindrical counterpoise, slightly modified, the height of this fluid may be so regulated that the surface of the oil may remain almost invariable until the reservoir is quite exhausted. For this purpose, the center of gravity of the counterpoise must be a little higher than the line which bisects it, and its specific gravity must be about three-fourths as great as that of the fluid; and in this manner it may be made to raise the surface of the heavier fluid in proportion as a greater quantity of it escapes to supply the place of the oil, and to keep it always at a sufficient height above the surface which separates it from the oil, so that the wick may be amply and almost uniformly supplied. (Plate XXI. Fig. 280.)

### LECTURE XXVI.

The art of embankment is a branch of architecture entirely dependent on hydrostatic and hydraulic principles. In Holland, and in some parts of Germany, this art is indispensable to the existence of large tracts of country; and even in this island, it has been extensively useful in gaining and securing ground on the sea coast. The construction of canals, and the management of rivers and harbors, are also dependent on the same principles; and these important subjects have been discussed by various writers in many extensive treatises expressly devoted to hydraulic architecture.

When a bank or dike is to be constructed, it must be composed of materials capable of resisting, by their weight, the effort of the fluid to overturn them; by their lateral adhesion, the force tending to thrust them aside horizontally; and by their density and tenacity, the penetration of the water into their substance. If the water is in motion, they must also be able to resist its friction without being carried away by it, and they must be arranged in such a form as to be least liable to be undermined. For many of these reasons, the surface of the bank exposed to the water must be sloped toward the horizon: the line expressing the general direction of the pressure of the water ought to be confined entirely within its substance, so that no force applied in this way may be able to overturn it as a whole. This condition will always be fulfilled when the sides of the bank make an angle with each other of at least a right angle. The pressure acting on a bank sloped in this way will also tend to condense the materials and to increase their lateral adhesion, and the particles will become less liable to crumble away by their own weight than if the surface were more nearly vertical. For embankments opposed to the sea, a heavily sloped bank also has the additional advantage of breaking the force of the waves very effectively. An embankment of this kind is usually furnished with drains, formed by wooden pipes or by brickwork, closed by falling doors or valves; these allow the water to flow out at low tide, but do not permit the tide to enter. To prevent the penetration of the water, clay is often used, either mixed with gravel or sunk in a deep trench cut on each side of the canal or reservoir. (Plate XXI. Fig. 281.)

The greater or less velocity of a river must determine what substances are capable of withstanding its tendency to disturb them; some are carried away by a velocity of a few inches in a second, others remain at rest when the velocity

These are shifted slowly downwards toward the sea, being occasionally deposited in those parts where the water has the least motion, and ultimately serving to form new land, which is always advancing into the sea on each side of the mouth of a large river. It has been recommended, as a good form for a navigable river or canal, to make the width of the horizontal bottom one-fifth of that of the surface, and the depth three-tenths. (Plate XXI. If a canal or a reservoir were confined by a perpendicular surface of boards, and it were required to support it by a single prop, the prop should be placed, as we have already seen, at a distance of one-third of the total height from the bottom. However, it would always be more convenient in practice to fix the side of the reservoir at the bottom than to allow the entire pressure to be supported by the prop. It might also be strengthened by means of ribs, thicker below than above, so as to produce an equal strength throughout, wherever the prop might be placed. But if the side were formed of a single plank of uniform thickness, the strain would be most equally divided by placing the prop very near the middle of its height.

The strength of the materials employed for floodgates and sluices must be determined according to the principles that have been established in treating the passive strength of substances used for simple mechanical purposes; however, the calculations in this case become much more intricate. Thus, if we have a circular plate or plank of a uniform elastic substance, constituting the bottom of a pipe or cistern and simply supported at the circumference, a very complicated calculation is required for determining the proportion of its strength relative to that of a square plate of the same width supported only at two opposite ends. This is because at each point of the circular piece, there are two curvatures that must be considered. The square plate will support a column of fluid twice as heavy as the weight that would break it if placed at its center; and if my calculation is correct, a circular plate will support a height of water nearly sixteen-sevenths as great as a square plate. But for ordinary purposes, it will be sufficient to consider the strength as derived only from the resistance opposed to the bending in one direction, since the additional strength obtained from the lateral supports may very properly be neglected.

### LECTURE XXVI.

We may, therefore, be satisfied with determining the strain on the materials in the direction in which they provide the greatest resistance, either due to the shorter distance between the supports or by the arrangement of the fibers. It will always be most desirable to combine these circumstances so that the fibers of the wood are arranged in the direction of the shortest dimensions of the sluice. If a sluice is supported only at the top and bottom, the greatest strain will be at a distance of about three-sevenths of its height from the bottom; it is at this point that the greatest strength is required. But if the boards forming the sluice are fixed across it in horizontal directions, their strength must be greatest at the bottom. (Plate XXI. Fig. 283.)

In the construction of <term>flood gates</term>, the principles of <term>carpentry</term> must be applied in a manner very similar to those used to determine the best forms for roofs. The flood gates, if they are double without a solid obstacle between them, must meet at an angle; when this angle is very wide, the thrust against the walls or hinges must necessarily be very great. If, however, the angle were too acute, the flood gates would need to be lengthened, and in this case, their strength would be far more diminished than that of a roof with a similar elevation, since <term>hydrostatic pressure</term> always acts with full force in a perpendicular direction. The thickness required for each flood gate may be determined in the same manner as the thickness of a <term>sluice</term>.

Where a sluice board of considerable dimensions is to be raised occasionally, it may be necessary to determine the force required to overcome its friction. This <term>friction</term> is nearly proportional to the total pressure of the water and may be found, with sufficient accuracy, in pounds, by multiplying the square of the depth of the sluice in feet by 10. Thus, if the depth is 3 feet, the friction or adhesion will be about 90 pounds for each foot of the width.

# ON HYDROSTATIC INSTRUMENTS, AND HYDRAULIC ARCHITECTURE.

If the side of a canal gives way, it is sometimes important to prevent the escape of the water as much as possible. For this purpose, it is common to have doors or valves in various parts of the canal which lie nearly flat at the bottom when the water is at rest; but when the water begins to flow over them with significant velocity, they are raised by its force and stop its movement.

The usefulness of introducing canals into a commercial country can be measured, to some extent, by the results of the same labor employed in moving weights by land transport versus by water. For example, a single horse can barely pull more than a ton in weight on the best road, but on a canal, the same horse can pull a boat of 30 tons at the same speed.

The construction of piers and quays, and the management of harbors, are also important branches of hydraulic architecture. It often happens that, besides the application of the general principles of mechanics and hydrostatics to these purposes, the specific circumstances of a case may suggest to an ingenious artist <note>In this context, "artist" refers to a skilled engineer or technical designer.</note> a way to perform the required work in an effective and economical manner. We can find a good example of such an arrangement in the account given by Mr. Smeaton of the method he adopted for the improvement of the port of Ramsgate, which indeed resembles some methods that had been used before in similar cases: by creating a large excavation which is equipped with floodgates and is constantly filled at high tide, he has produced a number of artificial torrents. These escape through the sluices and become powerful agents for carrying away the material deposited by the sea, which tends to obstruct the navigation of the harbor.

# LECTURE XXVII.

## ON THE REGULATION OF HYDRAULIC FORCES.

Those modifications of the motions of fluids which are employed either for conducting them from place to place, or for applying their powers to the production of mechanical effects, may be considered as constituting a separate division of practical hydraulics, which is analogous to the subject of general machinery in practical mechanics.

A supply of water may be obtained from a reservoir, situated above the level at which it is wanted, whatever its distance may be, either by means of open canals, or aqueducts, or of closed pipes. Where an uninterrupted downward slope cannot be obtained, it is necessary to employ pipes, which may be bent upwards or downwards at pleasure, provided that no part of them is more than thirty feet above the reservoir; and when the pipe is once filled, the water will continue to flow from the lower opening. However, it is best in all such cases to avoid unnecessary angles; for when the pipe rises and falls again, a portion of the air, which is always contained in water, is frequently collected in the angle, and very materially obstructs the progress of the water through the pipe. When the bent part is wholly below the openings of the pipe, this air may be discharged by various methods. The ancients used small <term>upright pipes</term>, called <term>columnaria</term>, rising from the curve of the principal pipe to the level of the reservoir, allowing the air to escape without wasting any of the water. It may, however, frequently be inconvenient or impossible to apply a pipe of this kind; and the same purpose may be answered by fixing on the pipe a box containing a small valve, which opens downwards and is supported by a float, so as to remain shut while the box is full of water, and to fall open when any air is collected in it. (Plate XXI. Fig. 288.)

If the pipe were formed into a siphon, having its bend above both openings,

Air would collect much more abundantly because the water in the upper part of the pipe would be under less pressure, and neither of the previously mentioned methods would be useful for removing it. In such cases, it has been common to force a quantity of water violently through the pipe to carry the air out with it; but perhaps the same effect might be produced much more easily by installing a small airtight valve in the upper part of the pipe that opens outward, with a <term>stopcock</term> placed immediately before it. If the stopcock were suddenly turned as often as necessary, the <term>momentum</term> of the water in the pipe would probably carry it forward with enough force to expel the air; or, if necessary, external pressure could be added, and the air could be discharged through the valve in this manner even more readily than without it. However, it might be even simpler to have a fairly large vessel of water screwed onto the pipe, which would not fill with air for a considerable time; once full of air, it could be removed and refilled with water. (Plate XXI. Fig. 285.)

The diameter of a pipe required for conveying a specific quantity of water to a given distance can be calculated from the experiments of Mr. <term>Buat</term>, which have already been mentioned. Pipes are usually made of wood, lead, or cast iron, but most commonly of lead; and recently, tinned copper has been used with significant advantage. A lead pipe will withstand the pressure of a column of water 100 feet high if its thickness is one-hundredth of its diameter, or even less than this; but when any alternating motion is produced, a much stronger pipe is required, and it is standard practice to make leaden pipes of all kinds much thicker than this proportion.

The form and construction of stopcocks and <term>valves</term> vary greatly according to their different situations and uses. <term>Stopcocks</term> usually consist of a cylindrical or conical part, perforated in a specific direction, which can be turned within a socket formed in the pipe to open or close the passage of the fluid. Sometimes they are designed to form a connection with any one of two or more vessels as desired. A <term>valve</term> is used where the fluid is to be allowed to pass in only one direction and not return. For water, those valves are the best which obstruct the passage the least; and none appears to fulfill

A board, or a round flat piece of metal, divided unequally by an axis on which it moves, also makes a very good simple valve. Where a valve is intended to block the passage of steam, it must be made of metal; such a valve is generally a flat plate with its edge ground slightly conically, and guided in its motion by a wire or pin. For air, valves are commonly made of oiled silk supported by a perforated plate or grating. (Plate XXI. Figs. 286, 287.)

Before we consider applying the force of fluids in motion to practical purposes, we must attend to the methods of measuring the velocity of their motions. This may be done either by a comparison with linear measures or by instruments based on the laws of <term>hydraulic pressure</term>. One of the best such instruments is the tube invented by <term>Pitot</term> and improved by <term>Buat</term>. A funnel is presented to the stream, and the water in a vertical tube connected with it is raised above the level of the river, nearly to the height corresponding to the velocity. However, it is said that the result will be less liable to error if the funnel is covered by a plate with a small orifice in its center; in this case, the elevation is always one and a half times the height corresponding to the velocity. Other instruments intended for the same purpose require prior experiments to determine the degree to which they are affected by different velocities; the <term>hydrometrical fly</term> is adjusted in this manner. The impulse of the water on two inclined planes turns an axis to which they are fixed, and by its means a series of wheels with an index, which indicates the distance traveled during the time of observation. Instruments similar to these have also sometimes been employed for measuring the relative velocity with which a ship under way passes through the water; and an apparatus resembling Pitot’s has been adapted to this purpose by Captain <term>Hamilton</term>, with the addition of a tube inserted into it on a level with the surface of the water, which continually discharges a small stream into a reservoir with a velocity regulated by the pressure, and consequently equal or proportional to that of the ship itself. In this manner, he obtains an accurate record of the whole distance traveled, including the effect of all the variations of the velocity. If the orifice is small, it will be necessary to account for the temperature of the

The movements of the air may also be measured by instruments similar to those employed for determining the velocity of water streams. The direction of the wind is sometimes indicated by a wind dial, consisting simply of an index connected by wheels to a common vane or weathercock. Its velocity may be found using various wind <term>gauges</term>: these are sometimes constructed by placing a flat surface against the wind, with the pressure measured by the bending of a spring or by the winding up of a weight on a spiral barrel. Others work by receiving the stream in the mouth of a funnel to raise a column of water in a vertical tube to a height equivalent to the pressure, or to condense a quantity of air enclosed in a cavity to a degree indicated by the position of a small amount of mercury moving in a horizontal tube leading to the cavity. A small windmill, like the <term>hydrometrical fly</term>, may also be used to measure the velocity of the wind with the help of a watch.

The main methods of applying the force of fluids for useful purposes are to employ their weight, their impulse, or their pressure. The weight of water may be applied by collecting it in a reservoir that alternately ascends and descends, by causing it to act within a pipe on a movable piston, or by conducting it into the buckets of a revolving wheel. Its impulse may be directed either perpendicularly or obliquely against a movable surface, and its pressure may be obtained without any immediate impulse by causing a stream to flow horizontally out of a movable pipe that revolves around an axis. The force of the air can only be applied through its impulse, and this may be employed either perpendicularly or obliquely.

When water is collected in a single reservoir used to work a pump or raise a weight, the method of its operation may be determined by mechanical considerations alone. It is obvious that if we wish to preserve the full force of the water, we must use a second reservoir to be filled during the descent of the first, which may then descend in its turn,

The action of a column of water, enclosed in a pipe, is of a nature very similar to that of such a reservoir, except that the apparatus is more liable to friction; the arrangement of its parts is nearly similar, although in an inverted position, to that which is more commonly employed for raising water by means of pumps. But both these methods of employing the weight of water are largely confined to those cases in which it is to be procured in a small quantity and may be allowed to descend through a considerable height, and when circumstances do not allow us to employ machines which require a greater space.

We have seen that in order to determine the effect of any force employed in machinery, we must consider not only its magnitude, but also the velocity with which it can be brought into action, and we must estimate the ultimate value of the power by the joint ratio, or the product, of the force and the velocity. Thus, if we had a corn mill, for example, in which we wished the millstone to revolve with a certain velocity and to overcome a given resistance, and supposing that this effect could be obtained by means of a certain train of wheels from a given source of motion; if the velocity of the motion at its source is reduced to one half, we must double the diameter of one of the wheels by which the force is communicated in order to give the millstone the desired velocity, and thus we must introduce a mechanical disadvantage, which can only be compensated by a double intensity in the force at its origin.

If we apply this estimation of effect to the motion of an overshot wheel, we shall find that the velocity of the wheel, and consequently its breadth and the magnitude of its buckets, is completely irrelevant with respect to the value of its operation: for supposing the stream to enter the buckets with the uniform velocity of the wheel, the quantity of water in the wheel at any one time, and consequently the pressure, must be inversely proportional to the velocity, so that the product of the force and the velocity will be the same, however they may separately vary. If, however, the velocity were to become very considerable, it would be necessary to sacrifice a material part of the fall in order that the water might acquire this velocity before its arrival at the wheel; but a fall of one foot, or even less, is sufficient for producing any velocity

On the other hand, it is obvious that a certain velocity may be obtained from a wheel moving rapidly with less machinery than from another that moves more slowly. Generally, the velocity of the surface of the wheel is between two and six feet per second; and whether it is greater or smaller, the force actually applied will always be equal in effect to the weight of a portion of the stream used, equal in length to the height of the wheel. To avoid the resistance that might be caused by the stagnant water below the wheel, it is a good practice to turn the stream backward upon its nearer half, so that when the water is discharged, it may run off in the general direction of its motion. (Plate XXII. Fig. 290.)

If we allow the stream of water to acquire the maximum velocity that the entire fall can produce and strike horizontally against the floatboards of an undershot wheel, or if we wish to use the force of a river running in a nearly horizontal direction, the wheel must move at half the velocity of the stream to produce the greatest effect. Because the entire quantity of water striking the floatboards remains nearly the same regardless of the velocity—especially if the wheel is properly enclosed in a narrow channel—it is easy to calculate that the greatest possible effect will be produced when the relative velocity of the stream striking the floatboards is equal to the velocity of the wheel itself. The pressure on the floatboards is equal to that of a stream containing the same quantity of water and striking a fixed obstacle at half the velocity. This is essentially the same as the stream that escapes from the wheel, which must be twice as deep or twice as wide as the original stream since its motion is only half as rapid. As we have already seen, a column of such a stream—at twice the height relative to its velocity (which is half the height of the fall)—is the measure of hydraulic pressure. Therefore, this force will be exactly half as great as that of a similar column acting on an overshot wheel moving at the same velocity. However, the stream retarded in this way will not retain the other half of its mechanical power, since its greatest effect will be in the same proportion as an equal stream acting on an overshot wheel with one-fourth the fall of the first; the remaining fourth of the power is lost in changing the form of the water and in overcoming its friction. In whatever way we apply the force of water, we shall find that the mechanical power it possesses

Therefore, when the fall is sufficiently great, an overshot wheel is far preferable to an undershot wheel. Where the fall is too small for an overshot wheel, it is most advisable to employ a breast wheel, which shares its properties. Its floatboards consist of two portions meeting at an angle, so as to approach the nature of buckets, and the water is also somewhat confined within them by the help of a sweep or arched channel that follows the curve of the wheel, without coming into too close contact with it, which would produce unnecessary friction. When circumstances do not admit even of a breast wheel, we must be satisfied with an undershot wheel. It is recommended for such a wheel that the floatboards be placed so as to be perpendicular to the surface of the water at the moment they rise out of it; that only one-half of each should ever be below the surface; and that from three to five should be immersed at once, depending on the size of the wheel. Sometimes, however, it has been considered desirable to employ a much smaller number; for example, the water wheel that propels Mr. Symington’s steam boat has only six floatboards in its entire circumference. (Plate XXII. Fig. 291, 292.)

Since the water escaping from an undershot wheel still retains part of its velocity, it is obvious that this may be used for turning a second wheel if it is desirable to preserve as much of the force as possible. In this case, by causing the first wheel to move at two-thirds the velocity of the stream, the total effect of both will be one-third greater than that of a single wheel placed in the same stream; however, it must be considered that the expense of the machinery will also be significantly increased.
