relationship between pressure and mechanical power. It can be demonstrated that the greatest possible pressure of the wind or water on a given oblique surface at rest, tending to turn it in a direction perpendicular to that of the wind, is obtained when the surface forms an angle of about 55° with the wind. However, the mechanical power of such a pressure—which is to be estimated from a combination of its intensity with the velocity of the surface—may be increased without limit by increasing the angle of inclination, and consequently the velocity. The maximum effect that could be thus obtained would be equal to that of the same wind or stream acting on the floatboards of an undershot wheel. But since in all practical cases the velocity is limited, the effect will be somewhat smaller than this. For example, if the mean velocity of the sails or floatboards is assumed to be equal to that of the wind, the mechanical power will be more than four-fifths as great as that of an undershot wheel—that is, in the case of a windmill, more than four-fifths of the maximum effect that can be obtained from the wind. In such a case, Maclaurin has shown that the sails ought to make an angle of 74° with the direction of the wind; but in practice, it is found most advantageous to make the angle somewhat greater than this, the velocity of the tips of the sails being usually, according to Mr. Smeaton, more than twice as great as that of the wind.

It appears, therefore, that the oblique sails of the common windmill are by their nature almost as well-suited to make the best use of any hydraulic force as an undershot wheel. Since they act without interruption throughout their whole revolution, they have a decided advantage over machines that require the sails or fans to be exposed to a more limited stream of wind during only one-half of their motion. This is necessary in the horizontal windmill, where a screen is used to cover them while they are moving in a direction contrary to that of the wind; according to Smeaton, such machines are found to perform little more than one-tenth of the work of those which are more commonly employed. The sails of a common windmill are frequently made to change their position according to the direction of the wind by means of a small wheel with similar sails. This small wheel turns whenever the wind strikes either side of it and drives a pinion that turns the whole machinery. The sails are sometimes made to furl or unfurl themselves according to the velocity of the wind by means of a revolving pendulum, which rises to a greater or lesser height to prevent the damage the flour would suffer from excessive speed, or to avoid any other accidents which might happen in a mill

The tilt of a windmill's axis relative to the horizon is primarily intended to allow room for the wind's action at the lower part, where it would be weakened if the sails came too close to the building, as they would have to do if they were perfectly upright. The counter-pressure of the water, caused by the escape of a stream from a movable reservoir, was applied by Parent to the purpose of turning a millstone, and various other authors have described machines of a similar nature. They may be constructed with little or no wheelwork, and it does not seem necessary for much of the water's force to be lost in their operation; however, they have never been practically employed with success, nor have they perhaps ever had a fair trial.

The art of seamanship depends almost entirely on the management of the forces and resistances of air and water. If the laws of hydraulic pressure, regarding oblique and curved surfaces, were more completely established, we could calculate not only what a ship's motions would be under any imaginable circumstances, but we could also determine precisely what the best possible form of a ship would be, and the best arrangement for her rigging.

If we had a circular vessel or tub, with a single mast and a perfectly flat sail, and if the sail were positioned in a direction deviating only slightly from that of the wind, the tub would begin to move in a direction nearly at right angles to the wind. This is because the impulse of the wind acts almost entirely in a direction perpendicular to the sail. However, the slightest inequality in the dimensions of the sail or the force of the wind would immediately disturb the vessel's position. To avoid this inconvenience, it would be necessary to have a movable body projecting into the water to create a resistance, by means of which the vessel might be steered and the sail held in its proper place. This could be done more effectively by changing the vessel's shape from round to oval; it would then also have the advantage of moving much more easily through the water in the direction of its length than a circular vessel of equal size, and of creating even more resistance in a transverse direction. Thus, when urged by an oblique force, it would move somewhat obliquely, but always much more nearly in the direction of its length than its breadth. 

The angular deviation from the ship's track is called its lee way, and if we know the direction of the sails and the actual proportions of the resistances opposing the ship's motion in different directions, we may calculate the magnitude of the angular deviation or lee way from these resistances. Hitherto, however, such calculations have generally indicated a lee way three or four times greater than what has been observed. The use of the keel is not only to help confine the ship's motion to its proper direction, but also to diminish the tendency to vibrate from side to side, which would interfere with the effect of the sails and produce many other inconveniences. When the principal force of the wind is applied to the front part of the ship, her head would naturally turn away from the wind if the rudder were not made to project from the stern in an opposite direction. The rudder presents the surface of an inclined plane to the water gliding along the keel, preserving the ship's course—through the pressure it receives—in any direction required for her maneuvers. Commonly, however, although the sails may be arranged so that the principal force of the wind appears to be on the fore part of

When a ship is steering in this manner with a side wind, the effect of the wind has a natural tendency to overset her; and if she is too <term>crank</term>—that is, deficient in <term>stability</term>—she cannot sail well, except directly before the wind. The location of the <term>center of gravity</term>, compared with that of the <term>meta-center</term> (or imaginary center of pressure), determines the degree of stability. The most general way of increasing it is to lessen the weight of the upper part and of the rigging of the vessel, to diminish her height, or to increase her breadth, and to stow the <term>ballast</term> as low as possible in the hold. Too little attention has frequently been paid to this subject, as well as to many other departments of <term>naval architecture</term>; and although mere theoretical investigations have so far been of little service to the actual practice of <term>seamanship</term>, it cannot be doubted that an attention to what has already been discovered of the laws of <term>hydrodynamics</term>, as well as to the principles of mechanics in general, must be of great advantage to the navigator, by enabling him to derive from his own experience all the benefits which a correct mode of reasoning is capable of providing him.

## LECTURE XXVIII.

### ON HYDRAULIC MACHINES.

We shall apply the name "hydraulic machines" only to those intended for counteracting the gravity of water—that is, for raising it from a lower position to a higher one. The simplest of these are buckets, bucket wheels, and friction ropes; movable pipes are the next in order; and pumps of various kinds constitute the most extensive and the most important part of the subject. Besides these and some other similar machines, hydraulic air vessels and artificial fountains will also require to be examined.

A series of earthen pitchers, connected by ropes and turned by trundles or pinions over which they pass, has long been used in Spain under the name of <term>noria</term>; in this country, wooden buckets are sometimes employed in a similar manner. A <term>bucket wheel</term> is the reverse of an overshot <term>waterwheel</term>, and the water may be raised by buckets nearly similar to those which are designed for receiving it in its descent. Sometimes the buckets are hung on pins so as to remain full during the entire ascent, but these wheels are often liable to be out of repair. Sometimes the reverse of an undershot wheel, or rather of a breast wheel, is employed as a <term>throwing wheel</term>, either in a vertical or in an inclined position. Such wheels are frequently used for draining <term>fens</term> and are turned by windmills; the <term>floatboards</term> are not placed in the direction which would be best for an undershot wheel, but on the same principle, so as to be perpendicular to the surface when they rise out of it, in order that the water may the more easily flow off them. (Plate XXII. Fig. 296–298.)

Instead of a series of buckets connected by ropes or chains, a similar effect is sometimes produced by a simple rope, or a bundle of ropes, passing over a wheel above and a pulley below, moving with a velocity of about 8 or 10

It is probable that the water usually ascends with about half the <term>velocity</term> of the rope, and on this assumption, we might calculate its depth on the rope by comparing its relative motion with that of a small river; but the rules which serve for calculating the velocity of rivers do not perfectly agree in this case with the results of direct experiments; for the <term>friction</term> required for elevating the quantity raised by such a machine appears from calculation to correspond to a velocity about twice as great as the actual relative velocity. While the water is principally supported by the <term>friction</term> of the rope, its own <term>cohesion</term> is amply sufficient to prevent its falling completely, or being scattered by any accidental inequality of the motion. (Plate XXII. Fig. 299.)

The <term>lateral friction</term> of water has been applied in a very simple manner by Venturi to the draining of land, by means of a stream which runs through it, allowing the stream to acquire sufficient velocity to carry it over an inclined surface, and to drag with it a certain portion of water from the lowest part of this surface; but the quantity of water raised in this manner must be very inconsiderable, and the loss of force by friction very great.

A system of <term>spiral pipes</term> may be placed in the plane of a wheel, receiving the water at its circumference, and raising it by degrees, as the wheel turns, towards the axis where it is discharged; the motion of the wheel being usually derived from the same stream which supplies the pipes; but the height to which the water is raised by this machine is very small in proportion to its bulk. A single pipe wound spirally round a cylinder which revolves on an axis in an oblique situation has been denominated the <term>screw of Archimedes</term>, and is called in Germany the <term>water snail</term>. Its operation, like that of the flat spiral, may be easily conceived by imagining a flexible pipe to be laid on an inclined plane, and its lower part to be gradually elevated, so that the fluid in the angle or bend of the pipe may be forced to rise; or by supposing a tube, formed into a hoop, to be rolled up the same plane, the fluid being forced by the elevation of the tube behind it to run as it were uphill. This instrument is sometimes made by fixing a spiral partition round a cylinder and covering it with an external coating, either of wood or of metal; it should be so placed with respect to the surface

It is generally tilted from the horizontal at an angle of between 45 and 60 degrees; therefore, it is obvious that its utility is limited to those cases in which the water is only to be raised to a moderate height. The spiral is seldom single, but usually consists of three or four separate coils, forming a screw which rises slowly around the cylinder. (Plate XXII. Fig. 300, 301.)

An instrument of a similar nature is called by the Germans a <term>water screw</term>; it consists of a cylinder with its spiral projections detached from the external cylinder or coating, within which it revolves. This machine might not improperly be considered a pump, but its operation is precisely similar to that of the <term>screw of Archimedes</term>. It is evident that some loss must here be caused by the lack of perfect contact between the screw and its cover; in general, at least one-third of the water runs back, and the machine cannot be placed at an elevation greater than 30°. It is also very easily clogged by accidental impurities in the water; yet it has been found to raise more water than the <term>screw of Archimedes</term> when the lower ends of both are immersed to a considerable depth. Thus, if the height of the surface of the water to be raised were liable to any great variations, the <term>water screw</term> might be preferable to the <term>screw of Archimedes</term>. (Plate XXII. Fig. 302.)

When a <term>spiral pump</term>, consisting of many convolutions arranged either in a single plane or in a cylindrical or conical surface and revolving around a horizontal axis, is connected at one end by a watertight joint with an ascending pipe, while the other end receives nearly equal quantities of air and water during each revolution, the machine is called a <term>spiral pump</term>. It was invented about 1746 by Andrew Wirtz, a pewterer at Zurich, and it is said to have been used with great success at Florence and in Russia; it has also been employed in this country by Lord Stanhope, and I have made trial of it for raising water to a height of forty feet. The end of the pipe is furnished with a scoop, containing as much water as will fill half a coil, which enters the pipe a little before the scoop has arrived at its highest position; the other half remains full of air, which transfers the pressure of the column of water to the preceding portion, and in this manner the effect of nearly all the water in the wheel is united and becomes equivalent to that of the co-

# LECTURE XXVIII.
->VOL. I.<-

column of water, or of water mixed with air, in the ascending pipe. The air nearest the joint is compressed into a space much smaller than that which it occupied at its entrance, so that where the height is considerable, it becomes advisable to admit a larger portion of air than would naturally fill half the coil; this lessens the quantity of water raised, but it also lessens the force required to turn the machine. The joint should be conical so that it may be tightened when it becomes loose, and the pressure should be removed from it as much as possible. Assuming the machine is well-constructed, the loss of power arises only from the friction of the water in the pipe and the friction of the wheel on its axis; where a large quantity of water is to be raised to a moderate height, both of these resistances may be rendered insignificant. But when the height is very great, the length of the spiral must be much increased, so that the weight of the pipe becomes extremely cumbersome and causes great friction on the axis, as well as a strain on the machinery. For example, for a height of 40 feet, I found that the wheel required over 100 feet of pipe that was three-quarters of an inch in diameter; and since more than one-half of the pipe is always full of water, we must overcome the friction of about 80 feet of such a pipe, which will require 24 times as much excess pressure to produce a given velocity as if there were no friction. The <term>centrifugal force</term> of the water in the wheel would also significantly hinder its ascent if the velocity were considerable, since it would always be possible to turn it so rapidly as to throw the whole water back into the spoon <note>The "spoon" refers to the scoop-like intake at the start of the spiral</note>. Since the machine I had built was in disrepair, I thought it more appropriate to substitute a common <term>forcing pump</term> for it than to attempt to make any further improvements under such unfavorable circumstances. However, if the wheel and its pipes were made entirely of wood, it might in many cases succeed better; or the pipes could be made of tinned copper, or even of earthenware, which might be cheaper and lighter than lead. (Plate XXII. Fig. 303.)

The <term>centrifugal force</term>, which is an impediment to the operation of <term>Wirtz’s machines</term>, has sometimes been employed, together with the pressure of the atmosphere, as a direct agent in raising water by means of the <term>rotatory pump</term>. This machine consists of a vertical pipe, caused to revolve around its axis, and connected above with a horizontal pipe which is open at one or at both ends, the whole being furnished with proper valves to prevent the

...escape of the water when the machine is at rest. As soon as the rotation becomes sufficiently rapid, the <term>centrifugal force</term> of the water in the horizontal pipe causes it to be discharged at the end; its place is supplied by the pressure of the atmosphere on the reservoir below, which forces the water to ascend through the vertical pipe. It has also been proposed to turn a machine of this kind by the counter-pressure of another portion of water, in the manner of <term>Parent’s mill</term>, where there is enough fall to carry it off. This machine may be so arranged that, according to theory, little of the applied force is lost; but in practice, it has failed to produce a very advantageous effect. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 304.)

A <term>pump</term> is a machine so well known and so generally used that the name has not uncommonly been extended to hydraulic machines of all kinds; but the term, in its strictest sense, is to be understood as those machines in which the water is raised by the motion of one solid within another. This motion is usually alternating, but sometimes continued so as to constitute a rotation. In all the most commonly used pumps, a cavity is enlarged and contracted by turns, with the water being admitted into it through one valve and discharged through another.

One of the simplest pumps for raising a large quantity of water to a small height is made by fitting two upright beams or <term>plungers</term>, of equal thickness throughout, into cavities of nearly the same size. They are allowed only enough room to move without friction, and the plungers are connected by a horizontal beam moving on a pivot. During the ascent of each plunger, the water is admitted by a large valve in the bottom of the cavity; when the plunger descends, the water is forced to escape through a second valve in the side of the cavity and to ascend through a wide pipe to the level of the beam. The plungers should not be tapered in any way because of the great force that would be unnecessarily consumed in continually throwing out the water with great velocity as they descend from the gap formed by their elevation. This pump may be worked by a laborer walking backward and forward, either on the beam or on a board suspended below it. By means of an apparatus of this kind described by <term>Professor Robison</term>, an active man carrying a weight of thirty pounds has been able to raise 580 pounds of water every minute to a height of 11 1/4 feet for ten hours a day without fatigue. This is the greatest effect produced by a laborer that has ever been correctly stated by any author; it is equi-

# LECTURE XXVIII.

equivalent to somewhat more than 11 pounds raised through 10 feet in a second, instead of 10 pounds, which is a fair estimate of the usual force of a man, without any deduction for friction. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 305.)

It is obvious that if the <term>plungers</term> were so well-fitted to the cavity as to prevent the escape of any water between them, the ascending pipe might convey the water to any required height; the machine would then become a <term>forcing pump</term>, and the plungers might be shortened as desired, so as to take the form of a <term>piston</term> sliding within a barrel. The piston might also be situated above the level of the reservoir, and in this case the water would be forced up after it by the pressure of the atmosphere to the height of about 30 feet, but not much further: and even this height would be somewhat too great for practice, because the water might sometimes follow the piston in its ascent too slowly. Such a pump, partaking of the nature of a forcing and a sucking pump, is sometimes called a <term>mixed pump</term>. In <term>Delahire’s pump</term>, the same piston is made to serve a double purpose, the rod working in a collar of leathers, and the water being admitted and expelled in a similar manner, above and below the piston, by means of a double apparatus of valves and pipes. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 306.)

For forcing pumps of all kinds, the common piston, with a collar of loose and elastic leather, is preferable to those of a more complicated structure: the pressure of the water on the inside of the leather makes it sufficiently tight, and the friction is inconsiderable. In some pumps the leather is omitted for the sake of simplicity, the loss of water being compensated by the greater durability of the pump; and this loss will be smaller in proportion as the motion of the piston is more rapid. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 307.)

Mr. Bramah has very cleverly applied a forcing pump, by means of the well-known properties of <term>hydrostatic pressure</term>, to the construction of a convenient and powerful press. The water is forced, by a small pump, into a barrel in which it acts on a much larger piston; consequently this piston is urged by a force as much greater than that which acts on the first pump rod, as its surface is larger than that of the small one. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 308.)

In the common <term>sucking pump</term>, the valve through which the water escapes

is placed within the <term>piston</term> itself, so that the same <term>barrel</term> serves for the ascent of the water, which rises in one continuous stream while the piston is raised, and rests on the fixed <term>valve</term> while it is lowered. The velocity of the stroke should never be less than 4 inches per second, nor greater than two or three feet; the stroke should also be as long as possible in order to avoid unnecessary loss of water during the descent of the valves. The diameter of the pipe through which the water rises to the barrel should not be less than two-thirds of the diameter of the barrel itself. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 309.)

A leather bag has also been used for connecting the piston of a pump with the barrel, nearly avoiding all friction in this way; but it is probable that the lack of durability would be a major objection to such a machine. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 310.)

Where the height through which the water is to be raised is considerable, some inconvenience might arise from the length of the barrel through which the piston rod of a <term>sucking pump</term> would have to descend so that the piston might remain within the limits of <term>atmospheric pressure</term>. This may be avoided by placing the movable valve below the fixed valve and introducing the piston at the bottom of the barrel. Such a machine is called a <term>lifting pump</term>; like other <term>forcing pumps</term>, it has the disadvantage of pushing the piston ahead of the rod, which tends to bend the rod and produce unequal friction on the piston, whereas in the sucking pump, the main force always tends to straighten the rod. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 311.)

The rod of a sucking pump may also be made to work in a leather collar, and the water may be forced through a valve into an ascending pipe. By applying an <term>air vessel</term> to this or any other forcing pump, its motion may be equalized and its performance improved; for if the opening of the air vessel is large enough, the water may be forced into it during the pump's stroke at any required velocity and with little resistance from friction, whereas the loss of force from the frequent acceleration and deceleration of the entire body of water in a long pipe must always be significant. The compressed air, reacting on the water, expels it more gradually and in a continuous stream, so that the air vessel has an effect similar to that of a <term>flywheel</term> in mechanics. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 312.)

->### LECTURE XXVIII.<-

If, instead of forcing the water to a certain height through a pipe, we cause it to form a detached jet, we convert the <term>forcing pump</term> into a <term>fire engine</term>; and in general two <term>barrels</term>, acting alternately, are connected, for this purpose, with the same <term>air vessel</term>; so that the discharge is thus rendered very nearly uniform. The form of the <term>ajutage</term>, or orifice of the pipe, is by no means insignificant to the performance of the machine, since the height of the jet may be much increased by making it moderately contracted, and slightly conical rather than cylindrical. When the <term>air vessel</term> is half-filled with water, the height of such a jet will be about 30 feet; when two-thirds filled, it will be about 60 feet, as the height is always nearly proportional to the degree of compression of the air, or to the excess of its density above that of the surrounding atmosphere. Sometimes a double <term>forcing pump</term>, or <term>fire engine</term>, is formed by the alternate <term>rotary motion</term> of a flat <term>piston</term> within a cylindrical <term>barrel</term>; the axis of its motion coincides with that of the barrel, and the barrel is divided by a partition into two cavities, which are filled and emptied in the same way as the separate barrels of the common fire engine. The mechanical advantage of this machine is nearly the same as that of the more common designs, but it appears to be somewhat simpler than a standard engine of equal force. The partition may be extended across the entire diameter of the cylinder, the opposite pairs of cavities being made to communicate with each other, and thus both sides of the piston may be employed at once. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 313.)

A <term>piston</term> placed in a similar manner has sometimes been made to revolve continually and to force the water through a pipe by means of a slider or a spring, which blocks its passage in any other direction. Machines of this kind have been invented and reinvented by <term>Ramelli</term>, <term>Cavalleri</term>, <term>Amontons</term>, <term>Prince Rupert</term>, <term>Dr. Hooke</term>, <term>Mr. Bramah</term>, and <term>Mr. Gwynn</term>. <term>Mr. Gwynn’s</term> engine, which has been employed in many cases with considerable success, consists of a <term>piston</term> or roller that is nearly elliptical and well-fitted to the cylinder within which it revolves, with a <term>valve</term> pressed lightly against it by a spring, which causes a considerable part of the water contained in the cylinder to be forced into the pipe during each revolution. The whole machine is made of brass; the spring requires very little force, for the pressure of the water on the valve keeps it always close to the roller, and the friction arising from this cause is even an objection to the machine. The stream, although never

The pipes through which water is raised by pumps of any kind should be as short and as straight as possible; thus, if we had to raise water to a height of 20 feet and carry it to a horizontal distance of 100 feet by means of a <term>forcing pump</term>, it would be more advantageous to raise it vertically first into a cistern 20 feet above the reservoir and then to let it run along horizontally, or find its level in a bent pipe, than to connect the pump immediately with a single pipe carried to its destination. For the same reason, a <term>suction pump</term> should be placed as nearly over the well as possible in order to avoid a loss of force in working it. If very small pipes are used, they will greatly increase the resistance due to the friction they occasion.

Water has sometimes been raised by stuffed cushions, or by oval blocks of wood, connected with an endless rope and caused, by means of two wheels or drums, to rise in succession in the same barrel, carrying the water in a continual stream before them; but the great amount of friction from the cushions appears to be an objection to this method. From the resemblance of the apparatus to a string of beads, it has been called a <term>bead pump</term>, or a <term>paternoster work</term>. When flat boards are joined by chains and used instead of these cushions, the machine may be called a <term>cellular pump</term>; in this case, the barrel is usually square and placed in an inclined position, but there is a considerable loss from the ease with which the water runs back. The <term>chain pump</term> generally used in the navy is a pump of this kind, with an upright barrel through which leathers <note>Leather washers or discs used to create a seal.</note>, strung on a chain, are drawn in constant succession; these pumps are only used when a large quantity of water is to be raised, and they must be worked with considerable velocity in order to produce any effect at all. Mr. Cole has improved the construction of the <term>chain pump</term> so as to significantly increase the quantity of water raised by it. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 318.)

It is often necessary to produce alternating motion in pumps by means of <term>wheelwork</term>, and for this purpose, the application of a <term>crank</term> is the most common and perhaps the best method. Provided that the bar by which it acts is sufficiently long, very little force will be lost by its slanted position, and

# LECTURE XXVIII.

It is easy, by using rollers or a compound frame, to confine the head of the <term>pump rod</term> to a <term>rectilinear motion</term>. When any other method is employed, it must be remembered that the motion of the <term>pump rod</term> should always be slower at the beginning of each alternation, since a considerable part of the force is consumed in setting the water in motion, especially where the pipe is long and the velocity is high. But it may happen that, due to the nature of <term>hydraulic pressure</term> under other circumstances, the resistance may be nearly equal throughout the stroke: for example, when the motion of the <term>piston</term> is slow in comparison to that of the water in the pipe, or when the force used to produce velocity is minor in comparison with that which is required for counteracting the pressure. In such cases, it may sometimes be preferable to employ inclined surfaces of such forms as are best adapted to provide the most advantageous velocity to the <term>pump rod</term> by their pressure on a roller, which may be kept in its proper direction by the same means as when a crank is used. (Plate XIV. Fig. 184 .. 187.)

The Chinese operate their <term>cellular pumps</term>, or <term>bead pumps</term>, by walking on bars which project from the axis of the wheel or drum that drives them; and whatever objection may be made to the choice of the machine, the mode of transmitting motion to it must be allowed to be advantageous.

Pumps have sometimes been worked by means of the weight of water acting within a barrel, which resembles a second pump placed in an inverted position. The only objection to the machine appears to be the amount of friction, and even this inconvenience may perhaps be minor. The invention is by no means modern, but it is best known in Germany under the name of <term>Höll’s machine</term>, and it has been introduced into this country by Mr. Westgarth and Mr. Trevithick. A <term>chain pump</term>, or a series of buckets, may also be applied, in a nearly similar manner, to the working of machinery of any kind. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 319.)

The intervention of a portion of air is employed for raising water, not only in the <term>spiral pump</term>, but also in the <term>air vessels</term> of <term>Schemnitz</term>. A column of water, descending through a pipe into a closed reservoir full of air, forces the air to act—by means of a pipe leading from the upper part of the reservoir or <term>air vessel</term>—on the water in a second reservoir, at any distance either below or

above it, and forces this water to ascend through a third pipe to any height less than that of the first column. The air vessel is then emptied, and the second reservoir filled, and the whole operation is repeated. The air must, however, acquire a density equivalent to the pressure before it can begin to act; so that if the height of the columns were 34 feet, it must be reduced to half its dimensions before any water would be raised; and thus half of the force would be lost. In the same manner, if the height were 68 feet, two-thirds of the force would be lost. But where the height is small, the force lost in this manner is not greater than that which is usually spent in overcoming friction and other imperfections of the machinery employed; for the quantity of water actually raised by any machine is not often greater than half the power which is consumed. The force of the tide, or of a river rising and falling with the tide, might easily be applied by a machine of this kind to the purposes of irrigation. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 320, 321.)

The <term>fountain of Hero</term> precisely resembles in its operation the hydraulic vessels of <term>Schemnitz</term>, which were probably suggested to their inventor by the construction of this fountain. The first reservoir of the fountain is lower than the orifice of the jet; a pipe descends from it to the air vessel, which is at some distance below, and the pressure of the air is communicated, by an ascending tube, to a third cavity, containing the water which supplies the jet. Many other hydraulic and pneumatic instruments, intended for amusement only, and some of them of much more complicated structure, are also described in the works of <term>Hero</term>. (Plate XXIII. Fig. 322.)

The spontaneous variations of the pressure of the air, occasioned by changes in the weight and temperature of the atmosphere, have been applied, by means of a series of reservoirs equipped with proper valves, to the purpose of raising water by degrees to a moderate height. But it seldom happens that such changes are capable of producing an elevation in the water of each reservoir of more than a few inches, or at most a foot or two, in a day: and the whole quantity raised must, therefore, be very small.

The momentum of a stream of water, flowing through a long pipe, has also been employed for raising a small quantity of water to a considerable height.

# LECTURE XXVIII.

The passage of the pipe being stopped by a valve, which is raised by the stream as soon as its motion becomes sufficiently rapid, the whole column of fluid must necessarily concentrate its action almost instantaneously on the valve; and in this manner it loses—as we have before observed—the characteristic property of hydraulic pressure and acts as if it were a single solid. So, assuming the pipe to be perfectly elastic and inextensible, the impulse must overcome any pressure, however great, that might be opposed to it; and if the valve opens into a pipe leading to an air vessel, a certain quantity of the water will be forced in, so as to condense the air, more or less rapidly, to the degree that may be required for raising a portion of the water contained in it to any given height. Mr. <term>Whitehurst</term> appears to have been the first who employed this method; it was afterwards improved by Mr. <term>Boulton</term>; and the same machine has lately attracted much attention in France under the name of the <term>hydraulic ram</term> of Mr. <term>Montgolfier</term>. (Plate XXIII. Figure 323.)

## LECTURE XXIX.

### ON PNEUMATIC MACHINES.

**PNEUMATIC** machines are those that are principally dependent, in their operation, upon the properties of elastic fluids; they may be designed either for diminishing or increasing their density and pressure, such as air pumps and condensers; or for directing and applying their force, such as bellows, ventilators, steam engines, and guns.

The density and pressure of the air may be diminished, or the air may be perfectly or very nearly withdrawn from a given space, either by means of a column of mercury, or by the air pump. The ancients sometimes exhausted a vessel imperfectly by the repeated action of the mouth, and preserved the rarefaction with the assistance of a stopcock. The <term>Torricellian vacuum</term>, obtained by inverting a receiver filled with mercury, and furnished with a descending tube at least 30 inches long, is the most perfect that can be procured; but there is generally a portion of air adhering to the vessels, and mixed with the mercury, which may often be considerably diminished by agitation, but can only be completely expelled by boiling the mercury for some time in the vessel and its tube, prior to their inversion. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 324.)

The construction of an air pump greatly resembles that of a common sucking pump for raising water; but the difference in the operation to be performed requires a difference in several particular arrangements. The objectives are to rarefy or exhaust the air as completely, as expeditiously, and as easily as possible. In order for the exhaustion to be complete, it is necessary that no air remains in the barrel when the valve is opened, and that the process be continued for a very long time. For, supposing all the parts of an air pump to be perfectly well fitted, and the exhaustion to be carried on for any

<summary>This page introduces pneumatic machines, defining them as devices that manipulate the density and pressure of elastic fluids. It specifically details methods for creating a vacuum, including the Torricellian method and the fundamental principles of the air pump.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical scientific lecture on pneumatic machines, specifically detailing the mechanics and mathematical principles behind the operation of the air pump and its historical improvements.</meta>

<page-num>340</page-num>

# LECTURE XXIX.

length of time, the limit of its perfection will be a rarefaction expressed by the ratio of the air remaining in the barrel when the piston is down to the total air that the barrel is capable of containing; for such will be the rarity of the air in the barrel when the piston is raised. It becomes, therefore, important to reduce the quantity of this residual air as much as possible; and at the same time to take care that the valve may be capable of being accurately closed and easily opened, or that a stopcock may be occasionally substituted for it, which may be opened and shut by external force when the elasticity of the remaining air is too small to lift the valve. In pumping water from a well, we raise an equal quantity at each stroke, but in the air pump, we withdraw at most only equal volumes of air at different levels of rarefaction, so that the quantity extracted is continually diminished as the operation proceeds. Thus, if one-tenth of the air were exhausted by the first stroke, only nine-tenths as much—that is, one-tenth of the remainder—would be drawn out by the second; hence, in order that the process may be efficient, it is important to have the barrel as large as possible in proportion to the receiver. In cases where the presence of water vapor would be of no consequence, the exhaustion might be made very rapidly by filling the whole apparatus with water, which was the method first employed by Otto von Guericke, the inventor of the modern air pump.

In order to lessen the labor of the operation, two barrels may be employed and so connected as to work alternately; in this manner, the pressure of the atmosphere, acting on both pistons at once, opposes no resistance to their motion in either direction. In Smeaton's pump, a single barrel has nearly the same advantage: the rod of the piston works in a leather collar with oil, and the air is excluded from the upper part of the barrel by a valve through which the air passes when the piston is raised near to the top. Consequently, during the descent of the piston, there is a vacuum above it, and the air below opens the valve much earlier and passes more completely through it than in the common air pump; the piston is only exposed to the full pressure of the atmosphere during the discharge of the air through the upper valve. (*Plate XXIV. Fig. 325.*)

That the air is really removed by the operation of the air pump may be demonstrated by various experiments, which show the absence of its resistance—

(Plate XXIV. Fig. 326, 327.)

The degree of perfection of the vacuum formed by the air pump, or the rarity of the air remaining in the receiver, is measured by gauges of different kinds. The simplest <term>gauge</term> is a short tube filled with mercury and inverted in a basin of the same fluid: in this, the mercury begins to descend when the elasticity of the air becomes diminished in the proportion of the height of the gauge to that of the barometer; but on account of the <term>capillary attraction</term> of the particles of mercury for each other, there is a depression within the tube, differing in quantity according to its size, which makes it difficult to observe the exact position of the surface when the height of the column is very small, although, if that height were correctly determined, the allowance to be made for the depression might easily be calculated. It is, however, more usual to employ the long barometer gauge, in which the pressure is removed from the upper surface of the column of mercury in proportion as the exhaustion proceeds, and the height to which it is raised by the pressure of the external atmosphere is compared with that of a common barometer; the difference always indicates the density of the air left in the receiver. Sometimes a bent tube is also employed instead of the short gauge, where the difference of the height in its two branches indicates the pressure; and this instrument has the advantage of requiring no correction for capillary attraction, since the depressions of the two columns exactly counterbalance each other. But in all these cases, the mercury must be well boiled in the tubes; and in the bent tube, or <term>siphon gauge</term>, the operation is somewhat difficult.

The pressure indicated by a gauge of any kind depends on the elasticity of the whole of the fluid remaining in the receiver; but this fluid is not always atmospheric air alone. In all common temperatures, water,

Consequently, if either water or any moist substance is present under the receiver, it will be impossible to achieve a total absence of pressure; in the best pumps, the short mercurial gauge commonly stands at a height of at least half an inch. Hence, the vacuum can be made more perfect when the receiver is ground to the plate of the pump with the addition of a greasy substance, rather than when it is placed on wet leather, as was formerly the custom. The quantity of atmospheric or non-condensable air actually existing in the receiver, whether mixed with vapor or alone, is measured using Smeaton's pear gauge. This gauge is left open under the receiver during exhaustion; then, by means of a wire passing through a leather collar, its opening is plunged into a basin of mercury. Upon the readmission of air, it receives enough mercury to fill it, leaving only a small quantity of air—which had previously filled the entire cavity—in a tube rising from the neck of the gauge. By comparing the space occupied by this air with the total capacity of the gauge (using previous measurements), the degree of exhaustion of the pump with respect to air can be estimated. It is said that in an air pump of Cuthbertson’s construction, such a rarefaction has been achieved that the air sustained only one-hundredth of an inch of mercury; that is, it was expanded to nearly 3,000 times its original volume. The pear gauge often indicates a much more complete exhaustion, but this measurement relates only to the quantity of dry air present. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 328.)

A condenser is the reverse of an air pump, and sometimes the same machine is designed to serve both purposes; however, the condenser requires more strength and less delicacy than the air pump. The gauge for measuring the degree of condensation consists of a small portion of air contained in a graduated cylindrical tube, the space it occupies being indicated by a drop of mercury that confines it. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 329.)

When proper care is taken to lower the machine gradually, the diver can withstand a pressure of an atmosphere of twice or thrice the natural density. It would be advisable for every diver to be provided with a cork float, or with a hollow metal ball, which might be sufficient to raise him slowly to the surface in case of any accident happening to the bell; due to the lack of such a precaution, several lives have been lost from confusion in the signals. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 330.)

Bellows are commonly made of boards connected by leather, so as to allow the size of their cavities to be alternately increased and diminished, with the air being supplied from outside by a valve. The blast must be interrupted while the cavity is being refilled; and in order to avoid this inconvenience, a second cavity is sometimes added and loaded with a weight, which maintains the continuity of the stream. If great uniformity is required in the blast, it will be necessary to take care that the cavity is so formed as to be equally diminished while the weight descends through equal spaces; but despite this precaution, there must always be an additional velocity while the new supply of air is entering from the first cavity. Sometimes the construction of the bellows resembles that of a forcing pump; and then, if the barrel is single, a second barrel, loaded with a weight, must be provided in order to equalize the blast: or a vessel inverted in water, and either weighted or fixed, may supply the place of the second barrel. The first cavity may also be formed of a similar inverted vessel, suspended from a beam so as to be moved up and down in the water; such a machine is much used in large foundries under the name of hydraulic bellows. The quantity of water employed may be much diminished, and the operation expedited, by introducing a fixed solid or an internal inverted vessel into the center of the outer inverted vessel. This internal vessel should be capable of nearly filling up the cavity of the movable vessel when it is in its lowest position, so that the water only occupies a part of the space between the vessels. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 331.)

The gasometer differs little from the hydraulic bellows, except that it is provided with stopcocks instead of valves, and the movable cylinder is supported by a counterweight, which, in the best kind, acts on a spiral fusee,

When a shower of water, or even an irregular stream, is conveyed through a descending pipe and plunged into the water of a reservoir, a large quantity of air is carried down with the water. This air rises to the upper part of an inverted vessel that surrounds the pipe, from which it may be conveyed through another pipe in a rapid stream for any required purpose. The water then escapes at the bottom of the air vessel into the general reservoir, and runs off from its surface. The quantity of air supplied by these shower bellows is, however, small. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 333.)

The velocity of the blast produced by any pressure that forces air through a pipe of moderate dimensions can easily be determined from the height of a column of air equivalent to that pressure. For example, if the hydraulic bellows were operated with a constant pressure of 4 feet of water, the velocity would correspond to a height of about 3300 feet, and the air would move through a space of about 460 feet per second. However, in this calculation, no allowance is made for any of the factors that always diminish the discharge of fluids, and the velocity actually observed is only five-eighths as great as that which corresponds to the height. That is, in the example given here, the velocity is 285 feet per second when the air escapes through a small orifice; but when it moves through a pipe, it is about three-fourths, or 345 feet. If the pipe were of considerable length, there would also be a reduction in velocity due to friction. In some bellows actually used in practice, a pressure equivalent to 9 feet of water is applied, and in this case, the velocity must be about 500 feet per second.

Bellows may be used for the ventilation of a mine, either by forcing air into it or by drawing it out through a pipe connected to the valve. The wind may also be captured by the mouth of a slightly conical tube and made to cause a current where it is directed; such an instrument is sometimes called a *windsail* or a *horse head*. It has been proposed to draw air up through a pipe using the lateral friction of a current of air captured by such a funnel, but the effect would probably be too small to be of much practical utility.

# ON PNEUMATIC MACHINES.

A corn fan is turned by hand or by machinery; its simplest operation is to cause a portion of air to revolve with it and to create a wind in the direction of its circumference. But when a small fan is made to revolve with great rapidity, as in Papin’s Hessian bellows, centrifugal force causes the air admitted at the center to rush toward the circumference and to pass with great velocity through a pipe inserted there. The common ventilator placed in windows, which revolves in the same manner as a smoke jack due to the impulse of a current of air, serves only to slightly retard the entrance of that current, to disperse it somewhat in different directions, and to prevent any sudden increase in the intensity of the draught. However, it has little or no power to act on the air so as to prevent a decrease in the current's velocity. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 334.)

The operation of heat also provides a very effective method of ventilation. Its action on air at common temperatures causes an expansion of about 1/500 for every degree that Fahrenheit’s thermometer is raised. The air becomes lighter in the same proportion, and the fluid below it is consequently relieved of a part of its weight. Therefore, the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere outweighs it, and the lighter column is forced upward. When the shaft of a mine connects with the external air at two different heights, there is generally sufficient ventilation from the difference between the temperature of the air in the shaft and that of the surrounding atmosphere. Because the temperature of the earth is nearly constant, it causes the air in the shaft to be warmer than the external air in winter and colder in summer. Consequently, there is an upward current in winter and a downward current in summer; in more temperate seasons, these alternations take place throughout the day and night. For a similar reason, there is often a downward current in a common chimney in summer; but when a fire is burning, all the air in the chimney is heated and ascends more rapidly as the height increases. It would be easy, using the principles of hydraulics, to calculate the velocity of the draught if the height of the chimney and the average temperature of the air within it were known. For example, if the height of the chimney were 50 feet and the air inside it were 10 degrees hotter than the external air, the expansion would be one-fiftieth; with the pressure of the entire column thus reduced by one-fiftieth, the difference would be equivalent to a column one foot high,

and such a column would represent the pressure causing the draft, which might, therefore, be expected to have a velocity of 6 feet per second. If the room were perfectly closed, the air contained in it would gradually become so much lighter than the external air that it would be equivalent to one foot of the height of the column causing the pressure, and the current would then stop. If fresh air were gradually admitted through a small orifice, the current would continue, but the air in the room would always remain somewhat thinner than the external atmosphere, unless a fresh supply were admitted through large openings.

The purpose of a chimney is not so much to ventilate the room as it is to provide a sufficiently rapid supply of air for maintaining the process of combustion and to carry off the products of that process. Therefore, it is desirable to allow as little air as possible to enter the chimney without passing through the fire; this is the best general method for avoiding smoky chimneys. For wind furnaces, the flue should be as uniform as possible throughout its height—or widened rather than narrowed as it ascends—and free from any significant angles.

The ascent of a balloon is an effect of the same kind as that of air in a chimney and sometimes arises from the same cause, such as when the air within it is expanded by heat. More commonly, however, it arises from the greater lightness of hydrogen gas, with which the balloon is filled. When pure, hydrogen is only one-thirteenth as heavy as atmospheric air, but as it is commonly used, it is about one-fifth or one-sixth as heavy.

The steam engine is perhaps the most magnificent achievement of mechanical power; it has undergone successive changes and appears to have been brought very near to perfection by the improvements of Mr. Watt. The pressure of steam was first applied by the Marquis of Worcester, and afterward by Savery, to act directly on the surface of water contained in a closed vessel; this water was then forced by the elasticity of the steam to ascend through a pipe. However, a great degree of heat was required to raise water to any significant height using this machine. For steam to be capable of supporting a column of 34 feet of water in addition to atmospheric pressure, its temperature must be raised to 248° Fahrenheit.

...Fahrenheit, and for a column of 68 feet, to 271°; such a pressure, also acting on the internal surface of the vessels, made it necessary that they should be extremely strong; and the height to which water could be drawn up from below, when the steam was condensed, was limited to 33 or 34 feet. A still greater objection, however, was the great quantity of steam necessarily wasted because of its coming into contact with the cold water and the receiver, the surfaces of which had to be heated to the steam's own temperature before the water could be expelled. Hence, only a tenth or a twentieth part of the steam produced could be effective; there would likely have been an even greater loss if not for the difficulty with which heat is conducted downwards in fluids. 

These inconveniences were largely avoided in Newcomen’s engine, where the steam was gradually introduced into a cylinder and suddenly condensed by a jet of water, so that the piston was forced down with great violence by atmospheric pressure, which produced the effective stroke. This effect was, however, partly used to raise a counterweight, which descended upon the readmission of the steam and worked a forcing pump during its return when water was to be raised. Although rapid, the condensation was neither instantaneous nor complete, for the water injected into the cylinder had its temperature considerably raised by the heat emitted by the steam during its condensation. This water could only reduce the remaining steam to its own temperature, at which it might still retain a certain degree of elasticity; thus, at a temperature of 180°, steam is found to be capable of sustaining about half the pressure of the atmosphere, so that the downward movement of the piston must have been considerably retarded by the remaining elasticity of the steam when the water was much heated. 

The water from the jet was drained when the piston was at its lowest point and was afterwards pumped up to supply the boiler, as it had the advantage of being already hot. This engine, with Beighton’s apparatus for turning the valves, was until recently in general use, and it is still very frequently employed. In this, as well as in other steam engines, the boiler is equipped with a safety valve, which is raised when the force of the steam becomes slightly greater than atmospheric pressure. It is also supplied with water by means of another valve which is opened when the water level inside falls too low, triggered by the sinking of a block of stone that is partially supported by the water. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 335, 336.)

<meta>This page continues the technical history of the steam engine, moving from the inefficiencies of the Newcomen atmospheric engine discussed on the previous page to James Watt’s innovations, specifically the separate condenser and the double-acting piston.</meta>

<page-num>348</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XXIX.</header>

The cylinder of Beighton's machine is inevitably significantly cooled by the admission of the water jet and by exposure to the air. Mr. Watt has avoided this inconvenience by performing the condensation in a separate vessel, into which a small jet flows without interruption; and by introducing the steam alternately above and below the piston, the external air is completely excluded. The piston rod works through a leather collar, so that the machine has a double action, somewhat resembling that of Lahire's double pump; and as the stroke is equally effective in both directions, the same cylinder—by using an increased quantity of steam—performs twice as much work as the standard engine. We might also employ, if we thought proper, a lower temperature than that at which water usually boils, and work in this manner with a smaller quantity of steam; however, there would be some difficulty in completely preventing the infiltration of the surrounding air. On the other hand, we may increase the heat so as to produce steam at 220° or more, and thus obtain a power somewhat greater than that of atmospheric pressure; this is found to be the most advantageous mode of working the engine. However, the excess of force above atmospheric pressure cannot be greater than the pressure exerted by the column of water descending to supply the boiler, since the water could not be regularly admitted against such pressure. The steam might also be allowed to expand within the cylinder for some time after its admission, and in this manner, it appears from calculation that much more force might be obtained than if it were condensed in the usual way as soon as its admission stops. However, the force of steam expanding in this manner is greatly diminished by the cooling that always accompanies such expansion, and this method would be subject to several other practical inconveniences.

The peculiarities of Mr. Watt's construction also require other additional arrangements. For instance, it is necessary to have a pump to remove not only the water from the condenser but also the air, which is always released from the water during the boiling process. If the water used has been obtained from deep wells or mines, it contains more air than usual and ought to be exposed for some time in an open reservoir before it is used; for it appears that the quantity of air that can be contained in water is nearly proportional to the pressure to which it is subjected. The cylinder is regulated by the action of a double revolving pendulum. The piston is maintained in a position very nearly vertical by means of a movable parallelogram, fixed on the beam, which corrects its curvilinear motion with a contrary curvature. In the old engines, a chain working on an arch was sufficient because there was no upward thrust. When rotary motion is required, it may be obtained either by means of a crank or a sun and planet wheel, with the assistance of a flywheel; this machinery is generally applied to the opposite end of the beam, but it is sometimes directly connected to the piston, and the beam is not used. The cylinder is usually enclosed within a case, and the space between is filled with steam, which serves to retain the heat very effectively. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 337.)

The steam engines of Messrs. Boulton and Watt are said to save three-quarters of the fuel formerly used, and it appears that only one-quarter of the total force of the steam is wasted. Such a machine, with a thirty-inch cylinder, performs the work of 120 horses working 8 hours each per day.

When the water producing the condensation must be raised from a great depth, a considerable amount of power is sometimes lost in pumping it up. Hence, Mr. Trevithick has attempted—as Mr. Watt had indeed long before proposed—to entirely avoid the necessity of condensation by employing steam at a very high temperature and allowing it to escape when its elasticity is so reduced by expansion that it only equals that of the atmosphere. The air pump is also unnecessary in this construction, and for a small machine, it may perhaps succeed reasonably well. But there must always be a very considerable loss of steam, and although the expense for fuel may not increase in exactly the same proportion as the elasticity of the steam, the difference is likely insignificant. A great number of less essential alterations have also been made to Mr. Watt’s arrangements by various engineers, but these have generally been intended either to achieve some minor convenience or to deceive the public with a false appearance of novelty. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 338.)

The quantity of moisture, or of water of crystallization, contained in the powder, is certainly too small to furnish enough steam for so great an effect. We have no reason to suppose that the elasticity of a given quantity of any aeriform fluid or vapor is increased more than about one five-hundredth for each degree Fahrenheit that its temperature is elevated; and if we suppose the heat to be raised to more than 5,000 degrees, the force of each grain of water converted into steam will only be increased tenfold; so that if the elasticity were 40,000 times as great, the density must be 4,000 times as great as that of ordinary steam, and the whole space must be filled with an aqueous vapor almost twice as dense as water itself. It is, therefore, probable that some other parts of the materials assume, along with the water, the state of vapor and possess in this form a much greater elasticity than that of the steam; for the quantity of permanently elastic fluids that are released must be considered wholly inadequate to the effect.

The force of fired gunpowder is found to be very nearly proportional to the quantity used; consequently, if we ignore the resistance of the atmosphere, the square of the ball's velocity, the height to which it will rise, and its greatest horizontal range, must be directly proportional to the quantity of powder and inversely proportional to the weight of the ball. Count Rumford, however, found that the same quantity of powder exerted somewhat more force on a large ball than on a smaller one.

The essential properties of a gun are to confine the elastic fluid as completely as possible and to direct the motion of the bullet in a rectilinear path; and from this arises the necessity of an accurate bore. The advantage of a rifle barrel is principally derived from the more perfect contact of the bullet with its cavity; it is also supposed to produce a rotation around an axis in the direction of its motion, which makes it less liable to deviate from its path due to irregularities in air resistance. one-third. When a 24-pounder is fired with two-thirds of its weight in powder, it may be thrown almost four miles, though the resistance of the air reduces the distance to about one-fifth of that which it would cover in a vacuum.

Bullets of all kinds are usually cast in separate molds; shot are granulated by allowing the lead, melted with a little arsenic, to pass through perforations in the bottom of a vessel and to drop in a shower into water. The patent shot falls in this process through a height of 120 feet; the roundest are separated by rolling them down a slightly grooved inclined plane, while those of an irregular form fall off at the sides.

Compressed air may also be employed for propelling a bullet by means of an air gun, an instrument of considerable antiquity but of little utility. It is obvious that no human force can so far increase the density of air as to make its elasticity at all comparable to that of the fluid released by fired gunpowder; even if it were reduced to such a state, its effects would still be far inferior to those of gunpowder. This is because the maximum velocity with which it could expand itself would not exceed 1,300 feet per second; it would, therefore, be incapable of imparting to a ball a velocity even as great as this, while the vapor of gunpowder impels a heavy ball with a velocity of more than 2,000 feet per second. When, however, it is considered that by far the greatest part of such a velocity as this is used inefficiently, and that the mechanical power which is practically obtained from gunpowder is much more expensive than an equivalent exertion of any of the ordinary sources of motion, it must be admitted that the force of compressed air may possibly be applied in some cases, with advantage, as a substitute for that of gunpowder. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 339.)

## LECTURE XXX.

### ON THE HISTORY OF HYDRAULICS AND PNEUMATICS.

Despite a few observations and experiments made by Aristotle and his predecessors, the properties of fluids had rarely been the subjects of much accurate investigation before the time of Archimedes. The progress that the science of hydrostatics, in particular, made under this eminent mathematician does the highest honor to his genius and insight. His treatise on floating bodies—although the theorems it contains are not as general as they have become since recent improvements in calculation methods—still provides us with instances of very ingenious determinations of the equilibrium of floating bodies of different forms. These are grounded on the true principles of the opposition between the general directions of the body's weight and the fluid's pressure; in this manner, he has shown in what cases the equilibrium of conical and conoidal solids will be stable, and in what cases unstable. 

Archimedes was the inventor of the method of measuring the volume of a solid by immersing it in a fluid; to us, indeed, there seems to have been little difficulty in the discovery, but the ancients thought otherwise. Vitruvius observes that this invention indicates an almost incredible degree of ingenuity. The philosopher himself is said to have valued it so highly that when the idea first occurred to him in a public bath, he hastened home in an ecstasy, without remembering to clothe himself, in order to apply it to determining the specific gravity of Hiero’s crown and detecting the fraud of the maker. The goldsmith had returned the crown equal in weight to the gold that was given to him, but had adulterated it with silver; he imagined that because of the complicated form of the work, which rendered it almost impossible to determine its volume by calculation, he must certainly escape conviction. The hydrometer, which has sometimes been attributed to Hypatia, a learned Greek lady of

<header>ON THE HISTORY OF HYDRAULICS AND PNEUMATICS.</header>

Constantinople, is mentioned by Fannius, an early writer on weights and measures, and is attributed by him to Archimedes.

The forcing pump, or rather the fire engine, was the invention of Ctesibius of Alexandria, the greatest mechanic of antiquity after Archimedes. He is also said to have invented the <term>clepsydra</term>, for the hydraulic measurement of time, and Philo informs us that he constructed an air gun for propelling a stone, or rather a ball, by means of air previously compressed by a syringe. The ball was not immediately exposed to the action of the air but was impelled by the longer end of a lever, while the air acted on the shorter. Ctesibius is said to have been the son of a barber, and to have had his attention turned to mechanics and pneumatics by being employed to fit a shutter, with a counterweight sliding in a wooden pipe, for his father’s shop window.

Hero was a contemporary and a student of Ctesibius; he describes, in his treatise on pneumatics, a number of very ingenious inventions, a few of which are designed for utility, but the greater part for amusement only; they are principally siphons, hidden and combined in various ways, fountains, and water organs, besides the syringe and the fire engine. The description of this engine matches exactly the construction which is most common today; it consists of two barrels discharging the water alternately into an air vessel; and it appears from Vitruvius that this was the original form in which Ctesibius invented the pump. Hero assumes the possibility of a vacuum in the gaps between the particles of bodies, observing that without it no body could be compressible; but he imagines that a vacuum cannot exist throughout a perceptible space, and from this he derives the principle of suction. The air contained in a given cavity may be rarefied, he says, by sucking out a part of it, and he describes a cupping instrument which approaches very nearly to the nature of an imperfect air pump. (Plate XXIV. Fig. 324.)

After the time of Ctesibius and Hero, the science of hydraulics made little further progress until the revival of learning. The Romans had water mills in the time of Julius Caesar, which are described by Vitruvius; and it appears that their aqueducts were well-built, and their water pipes well

It was during the Middle Ages that navigable canals began to be considerably multiplied, first in China, and afterwards in other parts of the world. The canal from the Trent to the Witham, which is the oldest in England, is said to have been dug in 1134. The date of the earliest windmills has been traced to the year 1299. The invention of gunpowder possesses perhaps an equal claim with the art of printing to the honor of being considered the most marked feature that distinguishes the character of ancient times from that of modern times; its introduction must necessarily have tended to produce material alterations, and perhaps improvements, in the habits of nations and of individuals. It is said to have been known for a long time to the Chinese, and our countryman Roger Bacon was evidently acquainted with its properties; but it was not actually employed in Europe or in its neighborhood until about the year 1330; and the earliest artillery appears to have been that which was used by the Moors at the siege of Algeciras in 1334. King Edward had four pieces of cannon at the memorable Battle of Crécy in 1346.

About the year 1600, Galileo made the important discovery of the effects of the weight and pressure of the atmosphere in the operation of suction, and in various other phenomena. Before his time, it was generally supposed that water was raised by a suction pump because of the impossibility of the existence of a vacuum: if, however, a vacuum had been impossible in nature, the water would have followed the piston to all heights, however great. But Galileo found that the height of its ascent was limited to about 34 feet, and concluded that the weight of a column of this height was the measure of the magnitude of the atmospheric pressure. His pupil Torricelli afterwards confirmed this explanation by showing that a column of mercury was only supported when its weight was equal to that of a column of water standing on the same base; hence the vacuum obtained by means of mercury is often called the Torricellian vacuum. In 1644, Torricelli also corrected the mistake of Castelli regarding the quantities of water discharged by equal openings, at

Castelli's experiments, made about 1640, were the first of their kind, and some of them truly contributed to the improvement of the science of hydraulics, but others appeared to show that a double height of the head of water produced a double discharge. Torricelli's more accurate observations proved that a fourfold height was required in order to produce a double velocity; and his assertions were afterwards fully confirmed by Mariotte and by Guglielmini.

A little before the year 1654, Otto von Guericke of Magdeburg first constructed a machine similar to the air pump by inserting the barrel of a fire engine into a cask of water, so that when the water was drawn out by the operation of the piston, the cavity of the cask remained nearly empty of all material substance. But finding that the air rushed in between or through the staves of the cask, he enclosed a smaller cask in a larger one and made the vacuum in the internal one more complete, while the intervening space remained filled with water; yet he still found that the water was forced into the inner cask through the pores of the wood. He then obtained a sphere of copper, about two feet in diameter, and was exhausting it in the same way when the pressure of the air crushed it with a loud noise. This machine was more properly a water pump than an air pump, but the inventor soon after improved his apparatus and performed all the experiments which are to this day most commonly exhibited with the air pump, such as the apparent cohesion of two exhausted hemispheres, the operation of a jet by means of the expansion of a quantity of air enclosed in a jar, the determination of the air's weight, and others of a similar nature. He also observed that for very accurate experiments, the valve of the pump might be raised at each stroke by external force; and he particularly noticed the perpetual production of air from the water that he generally employed, which caused an imperfection in the vacuum. An account of his experiments was first published in various works by Caspar Schott, and afterwards by himself in his book entitled *Experimenta nova Magdeburgica*, printed in 1672 at Amsterdam.

The theory of pneumatics was also considerably indebted to Hooke’s important experiments on the elasticity of the air, which were afterwards confirmed and extended by Mariotte and Amontons in France, by Hales in this country, and by Richmann at St. Petersburg.

About the same time, the first steam engine was constructed by the celebrated Marquis of Worcester. Hints of the possibility of such a machine had been given a hundred years before by Matthesius, in a collection of sermons entitled *Sarepta*, and at a subsequent period by Brunau; but the Marquis of Worcester claims to have carried the project into full effect. We are informed of this by his account of what he called a "fire-water work," which is one of the entries in his *Century of Inventions*, first published in 1663, and which is described as follows:

> “I have taken a piece of a whole cannon, the end of which was burst, and filled it three-quarters full of water, stopping and screwing up the broken end, as well as the touchhole. Making a constant fire under it, within 24 hours it burst and made a great crack. Thus, having a way to make my vessels so that they are strengthened by the force within them, and having them fill one after the other, I have seen the water run like a constant fountain stream forty feet high. One vessel of water, expanded by fire, drives up forty vessels of cold water; and the man who tends the work has only to turn two cocks so that when one vessel of water is consumed, another begins to force and refill with cold water, and so on successively—the fire being tended and kept constant, which the same person can also easily perform in the time between the necessity of turning the said cocks.”

The machine, however, was not practically introduced at that time and was soon forgotten. Savery’s engines were constructed in a precisely similar manner some time before 1700, and it is uncertain whether he adopted the Marquis of Worcester’s ideas or reinvented a similar machine. As early as the year 1667, the pressure of fluids in motion, and the resistance opposed by fluids at rest to the motion of solid bodies, were experimentally examined by Huygens and some other members of the Parisian Academy. Pardies, whose works were published in 1673, attempted to determine—although upon some inaccurate suppositions—the effects of the wind on a ship’s sails under different circumstances. His principles were adopted by Renaud, who published a work on the subject in 1689; however, their imperfections were soon after pointed out by Huygens and by James Bernoulli. In 1714, John Bernoulli published an extensive treatise on the maneuvers of ships, which at last compelled Renaud to submit to so many united authorities.

It must be confessed that the labors of Newton added fewer improvements to the doctrines of hydraulics and pneumatics than to many other departments of science; yet some praise is undeniably due both to his calculations and to his experiments relating to these subjects. No person before Newton had theoretically investigated the velocity with which fluids are discharged, and although his first attempt was unsuccessful, and the method which he substituted for it in his second edition is by no means free from objections, yet either of the determinations may be considered in some cases as a convenient approximation. The observation of the contraction of a stream passing through a simple orifice, which was then new, serves to reconcile them in some measure with each other. His methods of considering the resistance of fluids are far from being perfectly accurate, yet they have led to results which, with proper corrections, are tolerably precise; and his determination of the oscillations of fluids in bent tubes was a good beginning for the investigation of their alternating motions in general.

The accurate experiments of Poleni were published in 1718: he has the merit of having first distinctly observed that the quantity of water discharged by a short pipe is greater than by a simple orifice of the same diameter;
