In 1727, Mr. Bouguer received a prize from the Academy of Paris for his essay on the masts of ships, which is said to be ingenious but by no means practically useful. He was probably encouraged by this reward to continue his application to similar studies, and about twenty years later, he published his valuable essay on the construction and maneuvers of ships, which appears to have superseded everything done before regarding the subjects of his investigation.

The first researches of Daniel Bernoulli concerning the properties and motions of fluids also date to 1727. This justly celebrated man was as successful in his application of mathematics to natural philosophy as he was ready and skillful in his calculations. The greatest part of his hydraulic theorems are founded on the principle first assumed by Huygens and called by Leibnitz the law of living or ascending force. This is admittedly only true where there is no loss of velocity due to the imperfect elasticity of the bodies concerned; for it is only with this limitation that the motions of any system of bodies are always necessarily such as to be capable of carrying the common center of gravity back to the height from which it descended while the bodies were acquiring their motions. This law of ascending force is of considerable use in facilitating the solution of a wide variety of problems. It is certain that mechanical power is always to be estimated by the product of a body's mass and the height to which it is capable of ascending. Whatever objections may have been made to using this product as the measure of the force of a body in motion—which is indeed an expression inconsistent with a correct definition of the term force—it must be confessed, on the other hand, that some of the best English mathematicians have fallen into significant errors for lack of paying sufficient attention to this general principle. Bernoulli accurately estimates in this manner the mechanical power of a variety of natural and artificial agents; among these, he examines the power of gunpowder. However, due to an accidental combination of errors, he states that the force of a pound of gunpowder is equivalent to the daily labor of 100 men, while in fact, the effect actually obtained from two tons of powder is no greater than that

His calculations of fluid motions, in some very intricate cases, are highly ingenious and satisfactory, and they are generally sufficiently confirmed by well-conceived experiments. He examines the force of the wind acting on the sails of a windmill, but due to another calculation error—which Maclaurin detected—of two angles that meet the conditions of the determination, he chose the wrong one. He assigned that sail position as the most effective, though it actually produces no effect at all.

One might object to Bernoulli's calculations on the grounds that some of the circumstances necessarily ignored in them produce a very significant effect on the results of all experiments. However, it must be acknowledged that the corrections required for these unavoidable omissions can be easily derived from simple experiments and then applied to the most complicated cases. It is, nevertheless, a more significant objection that the fundamental law of the preservation of <term>ascending force</term> can only be adopted with certain limitations. For example, when a small stream passes through a large reservoir, Bernoulli is forced to assume that the entirety of its force is consumed by the resistance it encounters. The direct manner in which the accelerating forces are supposed to act also remains entirely undetermined. It was primarily for this reason that John Bernoulli attempted to replace his son's calculations with a method of deriving the motions of fluids more directly from the gravitation of their various parts. The uniqueness of John Bernoulli's method of investigation lies in his imagining the weight of each individual particle being transferred to the surface of the fluid, creating a pressure there in the direction of gravity. He then examines how this force must operate to produce every acceleration required for the motion of fluids in vessels of all conceivable shapes.

Maclaurin, in his treatise on <term>fluxions</term> <note>an early form of calculus developed by Isaac Newton</note>, investigated several properties of fluids in his typical concise and elegant style. His remarks on the positions of windmill and ship sails are particularly interesting; he expanded significantly on what had been achieved regarding the effects of the wind and demonstrated the possibility of arranging a ship's sails in such a way as to make her advance at a greater velocity than the wind itself. A request was made to Maclaurin and, at the same time, to Desaguliers—a man of significant prominence in the mechanical sciences—regarding the quantity of water that could be transported to the city of Edinburgh through a series of pipes of certain dimensions. The project was carried out with a confidence based on their opinions, but the quantity actually obtained was only about one-sixth of Desaguliers's calculation and one-eleventh of Maclaurin's. At a still later period, the French Academicians were consulted regarding a major undertaking of a similar nature; and their report was such as to discourage the planners from making the attempt, which was consequently on the point of being abandoned, until a famous practical architect insisted—based on a rough estimate drawn from his general experience—that more than double the quantity assigned by the Academicians might be obtained. The outcome justified his assertion.

The experiments and calculations of Robins, regarding the resistance of the air and the operation of gunpowder, deserve to be mentioned with praise on account of their practical utility; but he appears to have been less successful in his theoretical investigations than Daniel Bernoulli had been several years earlier.

D'Alembert attempted, in his treatise on the motions of fluids published in 1744, to substitute a more general law for the assumptions of John Bernoulli. This law related to all changes produced in the motions of a system of bodies by their mutual actions on each other; however, his calculations are more intricate and less easily understood than some others that are capable of an equally extensive application. The late Professor Kaestner of Göttingen defended Bernoulli against D'Alembert's objections with some success and has, in many instances, facilitated and extended Bernoulli's theory. Yet, there is often a strange mixture of insight and wordiness in this author's works. Alongside an intricate and difficult <term>fluxional calculation</term>, he inserts a long string of logarithms to perform a simple multiplication; and in a work that covers the entire range of the mathematical sciences, he does not dare to determine the square root of 10 without citing an authority.

Around the same time, the profound Leonard Euler applied himself, with some success, to investigating the motion of fluids, particularly as they relate to the subjects of seamanship and naval architecture. However, Euler's investigations are generally more remarkable for their mathematical skill than for their scientific accuracy and practical application, although his calculation of air resistance on the motion of projectiles may be used with considerable advantage by the gunner.

The beginning of modern experimental improvements in hydraulics may perhaps be dated from the investigations of Smeaton regarding the effects of wind and water, which were published in the *Philosophical Transactions* for 1759. His observations are of significant importance as far as they can be immediately applied in practice, but he did little to illustrate their connection with the general principles of mechanics. It was Mr. Borda who, about ten years later, first derived from a correct theory the same results regarding the effects of undershot water wheels that Smeaton had obtained from his experiments. Before this time, the best essay on the subject of water wheels was that of Elvius, published in 1742; his calculations are accurate and extensive, but they are founded largely on the imperfect assumptions regarding the impulse of a stream of water that were generally adopted then.

Our countryman Mr. Watt obtained a patent in 1769 for his improvements to the steam engine, which include almost every essential change made since the time of Beighton. On such an important subject, it is not unnecessary to include the words of the inventor, whose admirable application of the sciences to practical purposes justly entitles him to a rank among scientific mechanics no lower than that of Ctesibius and Dr. Hooke.

> "My method of reducing the consumption of steam, and consequently fuel, in fire engines <note>early steam engines</note>," says Mr. Watt in his patent specification, "consists of the following principles. First, that vessel in which the power of steam is to be employed to work the engine—which is called the cylinder in common fire engines, and which I call the steam vessel—must, during the entire time the engine is working, be kept as hot as the steam that

First, by enclosing it in a case of wood, or any other materials that transmit heat slowly; secondly, by surrounding it with steam or other heated bodies; and thirdly, by allowing neither water nor any other substance colder than the steam to enter or touch it during that time. Secondly, in engines that are to be operated wholly or partially by the condensation of steam, the steam is to be condensed in vessels distinct from the steam vessels or cylinders, although they may occasionally communicate with them. These vessels I call condensers; and while the engines are working, these condensers ought at least to be kept as cold as the air in the vicinity of the engines through the application of water or other cold bodies. Thirdly, whatever air or other elastic vapor is not condensed by the cold of the condenser, and which may impede the working of the engine, is to be drawn out of the steam vessels or condensers by means of pumps, operated by the engines themselves or by other means. Fourthly, I intend, in many cases, to employ the expansive force of steam to press on the pistons—or whatever may be used in their place—in the same manner as the pressure of the atmosphere is currently employed in common fire engines <note>atmospheric steam engines</note>. In cases where cold water cannot be found in abundance, the engines may be operated by this force of steam alone, by discharging the steam into the open air after it has performed its function. Fifthly, where motion around an axis is required, I make the steam vessels in the form of hollow rings or circular channels, with proper inlets and outlets for the steam, mounted on horizontal axles like the wheels of a water mill. Within them are placed a number of valves that allow any object to go around the channel in only one direction. In these steam vessels are placed weights, fitted to them so as to entirely fill a part or portion of their channels, yet capable of moving freely in them by the means mentioned or specified hereafter. When the steam is admitted into these engines between the weights and the valves, it acts equally on both, so as to raise the weight to one side of the wheel and, through the reaction of the valves, successively give a circular motion to the wheel. The valves open in the direction in which the weights are pressed, but not in the opposite direction. As the steam vessel rotates, it is supplied with steam from the boiler, and the steam that has performed its function may either be discharged by means of condensers or into the open air. Sixthly, I intend, in some cases, to apply a degree of cold that is not capable of reducing the steam to water, but of contracting it considerably, so that the engines may be operated by the alternate expansion and con-

It is probable that the rotary engines described by Mr. Watt, although they appear to offer some advantage in theory, will never be generally introduced because of the difficulty of constructing steam vessels so large and of such a complicated form as would be necessary to give the machine full effect. The term of this patent was extended by an act of Parliament until the year 1799; but although the legal privilege of the original manufacturers has expired, the superiority of their workmanship still gives their engines a decided preference.

Much of the labor of later writers on hydraulics has been spent on determining the resistance of fluids to bodies of different forms moving through them—a subject that derives great importance from its immediate application to the maneuvering of ships. The most extensive experiments on these subjects were made by Bossut and some other members of the Academy of Sciences. Around the same time, Don George Juan, a gentleman who had enjoyed the best possible opportunity for actual observation and practical study while serving with Ulloa, published his *Examen Maritimo* in Madrid; it appears to be the most ingenious and useful treatise on the theory and practice of seamanship that has yet appeared. But unfortunately, his deductions, however refined and diverse, are principally founded on a mistaken theory regarding the effects of hydraulic pressure. He tacitly assumes in his fundamental proposition on the subject that a double force, acting in a given small space, will produce a double velocity, while it is well known that in such circumstances, a quadruple force would be required. From this, he derives some conclusions indicating that resistance must vary significantly at different depths below the surface of the water. In support of this assertion, he cites a few imperfect experiments by Mariotte and himself, in which some unnoticed accidental circumstances may easily have caused great irregularities. Mr. Prony, in his *Architecture Hydraulique*, appears to have followed Juan; and Professor Robison very justly observes, when speaking of this work, that if the pressure of the water alters the magnitude of the resistance at different

He claims, indeed, that the results of his calculations are in almost every instance strictly consistent with observation and experience, but it is likely that where such a coincidence really exists, it must be due to some combination of errors canceling each other out; and it is indeed very possible that his calculations, despite all their errors, may come closer to the truth than the imperfect approximations that had been used before. Juan has generally used English weights and measures because of their convenience in calculations regarding the descent of falling bodies and the impulse of water.

The works of Chapman and of Romme, on various branches of seamanship, also possess considerable merit. These authors appear to have avoided the errors of Juan, but without entering into the same level of detail regarding nautical operations as he has done.

The precise experiments of Dr. Hutton and of Count Rumford on the force of ignited gunpowder, and the resistance of the air, deserve to be mentioned as providing valuable materials for the theoretical investigator, and useful information for the practical gunner. Robins had very mistakenly assumed that all the effects of gunpowder could be derived from the expansive force of permanently elastic fluids; but Vandelli soon after maintained a contrary opinion in the *Commentaries of Bologna*, and Count Rumford has very satisfactorily shown the insufficiency of the agents considered by Robins, although he has been unsuccessful in attempting to derive the entire force from the elasticity of water vapor alone.

One of the latest inventions that must be mentioned in the history of pneumatics is the aerostatic globe, or air balloon. The suggestions of Lohmeier, Albertus, and Wilkins regarding various ways of passing through the air had long been ignored as idle speculations; and Rosnier, who in the 17th century descended at an angle over some houses using wings, was completely unable to use them for ascending. Dr. Black had demonstrated in his lectures a bladder filled with hydrogen gas, floating in the air due to its lower specific gravity, many years before Montgolfier conceived the idea of using a similar machine to lift human beings into the aerial regions. It was in 1783 that this project was first executed, and people with vivid imaginations were inclined to believe that the discovery would be of great importance to human convenience. But if we calmly consider the magnitude of the force with which the wind inevitably strikes a surface as large as a balloon, we will be convinced of the absolute impossibility of counteracting it in a way that directs the balloon in any course significantly different from that of the wind which happens to blow. With this limitation, the invention may still be useful in some cases, whenever we only wish to ascend to a great height without regarding the place where we are to land, or where we wish to reach only a height so moderate that the machine may be kept in position by ropes. In France, the balloon has recently been used with considerable success as a meteorological observatory; Mr. Biot and Mr. Gay-Lussac have ascended to a height of over four miles for the commendable purpose of determining certain facts relating to the composition of the atmosphere and to the magnetic properties of the earth.

# LECTURE XXXI.

## ON THE PROPAGATION OF SOUND.

The theory of sound, which constitutes the science of acoustics, is deserving of particular attention for many reasons; for it not only involves many interesting properties of the motions of elastic substances, but it also affords us considerable assistance in our physiological inquiries respecting the nature and operation of the senses. The subject has usually been considered as exceedingly abstruse and complex, but the difficulty has in some measure originated from the errors which were committed in the first inquiries respecting it; and many of the phenomena belonging to it are so remarkable, and so amusing, as to amply repay the labor of examining them by the entertainment that they afford. We shall consider first the nature and propagation of sound in general; secondly, the origin of particular sounds, and the effects of single sounds; thirdly, the consequences of the combinations of sounds related in various ways, constituting the doctrine of harmonics; and fourthly, the construction of musical instruments, and the history of the science of acoustics.

Sound is a motion capable of affecting the ear with the sensation peculiar to that organ. It is not simply a vibration or undulation of the air, as it is sometimes called; for there are many sounds in which the air is not involved, such as when a tuning fork or any other sounding body is held by the teeth. Nor is sound always a vibration or alternation of any kind; for every noise is a sound, and a noise, as distinguished from a continued sound, consists of a single impulse in one direction only, sometimes without any alternation; while a continued sound is a succession of such impulses, which, in the organ of hearing at least, cannot help but be alternate. If these successive impulses form a connected series, following each other too rapidly to be separately distinguished, they constitute a continued sound, like that of the voice in speak-

ing; and if they are of equal duration, they produce a musical or uniform sound, like that of a vibrating chord or string, or of the voice in singing. Thus, a quill striking against a piece of wood causes a noise, but striking against the teeth of a wheel or a comb produces a continuous sound; and if the teeth of the wheel are at equal distances and the speed of the motion is constant, it produces a musical note.

Sounds of all kinds are most usually conveyed through the medium of the air; and the necessity of the presence of air or some other material substance for its transmission is easily shown by means of the <term>air pump</term>; for the sound of a bell struck in an exhausted receiver is barely perceptible. The experiment is most conveniently performed in a movable receiver or transferrer, which may be shaken at will, while the frame that suspends the bell is supported by some very soft substance, such as cork or wool. As the air is gradually admitted, the sound becomes stronger and stronger, although it is still much weakened by the interposition of the glass: this is not because glass is in itself a bad conductor of sound, but because the change of the medium of communication—from air to glass, and again from glass to air—causes a great decrease in its intensity. It is perhaps because of the apparent ease with which sound is transmitted by air that the science of <term>acoustics</term> has been usually considered as immediately dependent on <term>pneumatics</term>, although it belongs as much to the theory of the mechanics of solid bodies as to that of <term>hydrodynamics</term>.

A certain amount of time is always required for the transmission of an impulse through a material substance, even through those substances that appear to be the hardest and the least compressible. It can be demonstrated that all minute impulses are conveyed through any homogeneous elastic medium, whether solid or fluid, with a <term>uniform velocity</term>. This velocity is always equal to the speed that a heavy body would acquire by falling through half the height of the <term>modulus of elasticity</term>—that is, in the case of air, half the height of the atmosphere, assuming it to be of uniform density. Therefore, the velocity of <term>sound propagation</term> passing through an atmosphere of a uniform elastic fluid must be the same as that of a wave moving on its surface. In order to form a distinct idea of the manner in which sound is propagated through an elastic substance, we must first consider the motion of a single particle, which, in the case of a noise, is pushed for-

We may first suppose, for the sake of simplicity, a single series of particles to be placed only in the same line as the direction of the motion. It is obvious that if these particles were absolutely incompressible or infinitely elastic, and were also held in contact with each other by an infinite force of cohesion or compression, the entire series would have to move at exactly the same time, as well as in the same manner. But in a substance that is both compressible and extensible or expansible, the motion must take a certain amount of time to be propagated to the successive particles on either side. This happens through the impulse of the first particle on those which are before it and by the reduction of its pressure on those which are behind; so that when the sound consists of a series of alternations, the motion of some of the particles will always be in a less advanced state than that of others nearer to its source. Meanwhile, at a greater distance forward, the particles will be in the opposite stage of the undulation, and still further on, they will again be moving in the same manner as the first particle, as a consequence of the effect of a previous vibration.

The position of a particle at any time may be represented by imagining it marking its path on a surface sliding uniformly along in a transverse direction. Thus, if we fix a small pencil in a vibrating rod and draw a sheet of paper along against the point of the pencil, an undulated line will be marked on the paper and will correctly represent the progress of the vibration. Whatever the nature of the sound transmitted through any medium may be, it can be shown that the path described in this way will also indicate the position of the different particles at any given time. The simplest case of the motion of the particles is that in which they follow the same law as the vibration of a pendulum, which is always found opposite a point assumed to move uniformly in a circle; in this case, the path described will be the figure called a harmonic curve. It can be demonstrated that the force driving any particle backward or forward will always be represented by the distance of the particle in front of or behind its natural place; the greatest condensation and the greatest direct velocity, as

We are inclined to imagine that very hard bodies transmit motion instantaneously, because we have no easy means of measuring the interval of time that elapses between the action of pushing the end of a rod and the protrusion of an obstacle at the other end, or between the instant of pulling a bell rope and the ringing of the bell. But it is demonstrable that in order to transmit an impulse in an infinitely small amount of time, the hardness of the substance must be infinitely great, and it must be absolutely incompressible and inextensible by any force—a property not found in any natural bodies. Even the hardest steel and the most brittle glass are very susceptible to both extension and compression.

<margin><unclear>most</unclear> 28,000</margin>

The least elastic substance that has been examined is perhaps carbonic acid gas, or fixed air, which is considerably denser than atmospheric air exposed to an equal degree of pressure. The height of the atmosphere, assuming it to be homogeneous, is in ordinary circumstances at the seaside about 28,000 feet; in falling through half this height, a heavy body would acquire a velocity of 946 feet per second. However, from a comparison of the accurate experiments of Derham, made during the day, with those of the French Academicians, made chiefly at night, it appears that the true velocity of sound is about 1,130 feet per second, which agrees very nearly with some observations made with great care by Professor Pictet. This difference between calculation and experiment has long occupied the attention of natural philosophers, but the difficulty appears to have been largely removed by the insightful suggestion of Laplace. He attributed the effect to the increase in temperature that is always found to accompany the process of condensation, and to the decrease in temperature produced by rarefaction. It is true that a greater change of temperature would be required than Mr. Dalton’s experiments on the compression of air appear to indicate, but those experiments do not perfectly agree among themselves. Furthermore, the observation made in France—that enough heat to set tow <note>coarse, broken fiber of flax or hemp</note> on fire may be produced by the operation of a condensing syringe—seems to show that Mr. Dalton’s results are somewhat below the truth. This velocity remains unchanged by any alteration of pressure indicated by the barometer, but it may be affected by a change of temperature. For when an elastic fluid is compressed, its elasticity is increased in the same ratio as its density; and the height of a homogeneous atmosphere equivalent to the pressure remains the same, consequently the velocity calculated from that height remains unaltered; but the identity of the acceleration, from the effect of heat which has been mentioned, can only be inferred from observation: this identity may, however, be satisfactorily shown by means of experiments on the sounds of organ pipes, which are intimately connected with the velocity of the transmission of sound through the air, and which are found to remain precisely the same, however the air may be rarefied or condensed. The Academicians del Cimento enclosed an organ pipe, with bellows worked by a spring, in the receiver of an air pump and of a condenser, and they found that, as long as the sound was audible, its pitch remained unchanged. Papin screwed a whistle on the orifice which admits the air into the receiver of the air pump, and I have fixed an organ pipe in the same manner; and the result agreed with the experiment of the academicians. But if the density of the air is changed, while its elasticity remains unaltered—which happens when it is expanded by heat, or condensed by cold—the height of the column, and consequently the velocity, will also be altered; so that for each degree of Fahrenheit's thermometer the velocity will vary about one part in a thousand. Bianconi has actually observed this difference of velocity according to the different heights of the thermometer, and it may be shown less directly by means of the sounds of pipes; but it has not been accurately determined whether or not the correction on account of the effect of compression in causing heat remains unaltered, although Bianconi's experiments agree very well with the supposition that no material change takes place in this respect. In pure hydrogen gas, the calculated velocity of sound should be more than three times as great as in common air, but the difference does not appear to have been so great in any experiment performed so far on the sounds of pipes in different kinds of gases. For such experiments, the comparative specific gravity of the gas may be most conveniently determined by Mr. Leslie’s method of observing the time required to empty a vessel through a small opening, by means of the pressure of an equal column of water. According to simple theory, the velocities of the gas thus discharged should be in the same proportion as the respective velocities with which sounds would be transmitted by them; and if any variation from this proportion were discovered, it must be attributed to the different degrees of heat produced by condensation in the different fluids. Steam, at the temperature of boiling water, is only one-third as heavy as common air; consequently, the velocity of sound in steam must be nearly three-fourths greater than in air.

<margin><unclear>tes : El. y air</unclear>
<unclear>vo : 1</unclear></margin>
It does not appear that any direct experiments have been made on the velocity with which an impulse is transmitted through a liquid, although it is well known that liquids are capable of conveying sound without difficulty; Professor Robison informs us, for example, that he heard the sound of a bell transmitted by water at the distance of 1,200 feet. However, it is easy to calculate the velocity with which sound must be propagated in any liquid whose compressibility has been measured. Mr. Canton has determined that the elasticity of water is about 22,000 times as great as that of air; it is, therefore, measured by the height of a column which is in the same proportion to 34 feet—that is, 750,000 feet—and the velocity corresponding to half this height is 4,900 feet in a second. In mercury, it also appears from Mr. Canton’s experiments that the velocity must be nearly the same as in water, and in spirit of wine <note>ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note> a little slower. These experiments were made by filling the bulb of a thermometer with water and observing the effects of placing it in an exhausted receiver and in condensed air, taking care to avoid changes of temperature and other sources of error.

It is also well known that solid bodies in general are good conductors of sound: thus, any vibration communicated to one end of a beam is readily conveyed to the ear applied to the other end of it. The motion of a troop of cavalry is said to be perceived at a greater distance by listening with the head in contact with the ground than by attending to the sound conveyed through the air; and we may frequently observe that some parts of the furniture of a house are a little shaken by the approach of a wagon before we hear the noise which it immediately causes. The velocity with which impulses are transmitted by solids is, in general, considerably greater than that with which they are conveyed by the air. Mr. Wunsch has confirmed this by direct observations on a series of pine rods closely joined together, which appeared to transmit a sound instantaneously, while a noticeable interval was required for it to pass through the air. I have also found that the blow of a hammer on a wall, at the upper part of a tall house, is heard as if double by a person standing near it on the ground; the first sound descends through the wall, and the second through the air. It appears from experiments on the bending of solid bodies of all kinds that their elasticity, compared with their density, is much greater than that of the air: thus, the height of the <term>modulus of elasticity</term> of fir wood is found, by means of such experiments, to be about 9,500,000 feet, from which it follows that the velocity of an impulse conveyed through it must be 17,400 feet, or more than three miles, in a second. It is obvious, therefore, that in all common experiments such a transmission must appear perfectly instantaneous. There are various methods of determining this velocity from the sounds produced under different circumstances by the substances to be examined, and Professor Chladni has in this manner compared the properties of a variety of natural and artificial materials.

We have so far considered the propagation of sound in a single straight line, or in parallel lines only; but it usually happens, at least when a sound is transmitted through a fluid, that the impulse spreads in every direction, so

<summary>This page explains that sound travels much faster through solids, such as wood or stone, than through air due to their high elasticity relative to density. It cites experiments by Mr. Wunsch and Professor Chladni to demonstrate that sound transmission in solids can seem instantaneous over short distances.</summary>

so as to occupy nearly the entire surface of a sphere at any given time. However, it is impossible for this entire surface to be affected in the same way by any sound originating from a vibration confined to a specific direction, since the particles behind the sounding body must move toward the center whenever the particles in front of it move away from the center. Consequently, in one half of the surface, the motions may be called retrograde or negative, while in the other half they are direct or positive. Therefore, at the sides where these two regions meet, the motions can be neither positive nor negative, and the particles must remain at rest; the motions must also become gradually less perceptible as they approach the boundary between the two hemispheres. This statement can be confirmed by an experiment on the vibration of a body whose motion is limited to a specific direction: the sound is scarcely audible when the ear is positioned exactly perpendicular to the direction of the vibration.

The sound diverging in this way must always spread through part of a spherical surface because its velocity must be equal in every direction; thus, the impulse will always move forward in a straight line passing through the center of the sphere or the vibrating body. However, when a hemispherical pulse reaches the surface of a flat, solid obstacle, it is reflected in exactly the same way we have already seen water waves reflect; it then takes the form of a pulse originating from a center at an equal distance on the opposite side of the surface. This reflection, when it returns directly backward, constitutes what is commonly called an echo. To hear the echo distinctly, it is necessary for the reflecting object to be at a moderate distance; otherwise, the returning sound will be confused with the original one. Additionally, it must either have a smooth surface or consist of several surfaces arranged in a suitable way. Thus, an echo can come not only from a distant wall or rock, but often from trees in a wood, and sometimes, it is said, even from a cloud.

<margin>from curved surfaces</margin>
If a sound or a wave is reflected from a curved surface, its new direction can be determined either by the condition that the velocity with which the impulse is transmitted must remain unchanged, or by the law of reflection, which requires the direction of the reflected pulse or wave to form an angle with the surface equal to that

The truth of this proposition can be easily shown by means of the apparatus already described for exhibiting the motions of the waves of water; we can also confirm it by a simple experiment on a dish of tea: the curvature of a circle differs so little from that of an ellipse of small eccentricity that, if we let a drop fall into the cup near its center, the small wave which is produced will be made to converge at a point an equal distance on the other side of the center. (Plate XXV. Fig. 340, 341.)

<margin>Speaking and hearing</margin>
If an ellipse is extended without limit, it becomes a parabola: therefore, a parabola is the proper form for the section of a tube designed to collect sound which proceeds from a great distance into a single point, or for carrying a sound in nearly parallel directions to a very distant place. It appears, therefore, that a parabolic conoid is the best form for a hearing trumpet and for a speaking trumpet; but for both purposes, the parabola should be greatly elongated and consist of a portion of the conoid far from the vertex; for to avoid confusion, it is necessary that the sound should enter the ear in directions confined within certain limits. The voice also proceeds from the mouth without any very significant divergence, so that the parts of the curve behind the focus would be completely useless in both cases. A trumpet of such a shape does not differ significantly from part of a cone; and conical instruments are found to work well enough in practice. It appears, however, unnecessary to suppose, as Mr. Lambert has done, that they differ essentially in principle from parabolic trumpets. It is not yet perfectly decided whether or not a speaking trumpet has any direct effect in strengthening the voice, independently of the reflection of sound. (Plate XXV. Fig. 342.)

When a portion of a sound pulse is separated by any means from the rest of the spherical or hemispherical surface to which it belongs, and proceeds through a wide space without being supported on either side, there is a certain degree of divergence, by means of which it sometimes becomes audible in every part of the medium transmitting it. But the sound diverging in this way is comparatively very faint, even more so than the effect of a wave of water admitted into a wide reservoir under similar circumstances, which we have already examined. Hence, in order for a speaking trumpet to produce its full effect, it must be directed in a straight line toward the hearer. Furthermore, the sound collected into the focus of a concave mirror is far more powerful than at a short distance from it; this could not happen if, as some have erroneously supposed, sound always tended to spread equally in all directions. The sounds that enter a room where there is an open window are generally heard through a mixture of this faint divergence, reflections from various parts of the window and the room, and the effect of the impulse transmitted through the walls. This diverging portion, however faint, probably assists in preserving the straight-line motion of the principal sound, and it gradually gains a little additional strength at the expense of this portion.

# LECTURE XXXII.

## ON THE SOURCES AND EFFECTS OF SOUND.

The examination of the origin of sound might naturally be considered prior to the inquiry regarding its propagation; however, it will appear that the properties of many of the most common sources of sound depend immediately on the velocity with which an impulse of any kind is transmitted through an elastic medium. It was therefore necessary to consider this velocity before the production of sound in general could be discussed.

<margin>Sound</margin>
The origin of a simple sound, without any variation, requires very little investigation: it appears that the only condition necessary for its production is a sufficient degree of velocity in the motion or impulse that causes it. A very moderate velocity must be sufficient for producing an impression on the ear; there is reason to believe that, when the sound is continuous, it may remain audible with a velocity of no more than one-hundredth of an inch per second, and perhaps even with a velocity much smaller than this. But, at its origin, it is probable that the velocity of the motion constituting a sound must always be considerably greater.

A continuous sound may be produced by a repetition of separate impulses independent of each other, such as when a wheel strikes the teeth of a pinion in rapid succession so as to force out a portion of air from between them; when a pipe, through which air is passing, is alternately opened and closed, either wholly or partially, by the revolution of a stopcock or valve; or when a number of parallel surfaces are placed at equal distances in a line nearly perpendicular to them, and a noise of any kind is reflected from each of them in succession. This is a circumstance which may often be observed when we are walking near an iron railing; a high-pitched sound is heard, which is composed of such reflections from the surfaces of the palisades.

<vocab>sound, propagation, velocity, elastic medium, impulses, pinion, stopcock, palisades</vocab>

<keywords>sound production, acoustics, impulse velocity, continuous sound, acoustic reflection, pinion, stopcock, palisades</keywords>

<margin>musical sound</margin>
Musical sounds are, however, most frequently produced by the alternating motions of substances naturally capable of isochronous vibrations, and these substances may be either fluids or solids, or instruments composed of a combination of fluids and solids.

<margin>resonance of <unclear>r</unclear></margin>
The resonance of a room or passage is one of the simplest sources of a musical sound; when the walls are parallel, the impulse is reflected backward and forward continually at equal intervals of time, so as to agree with the definition, and to produce the effect, of a musical sound.

<margin>cylindrical pipes</margin>
When we blow obliquely and uniformly into a cylindrical pipe closed at one end, it is probable that the impulse or condensation must travel to the bottom and back before the resistance is increased; the current of our breath will then be diverted from the mouth of the pipe for an equal time, which will be required for the reduction of the resistance by the discharge of the condensed air, so that the total time of a vibration will be equal to the time occupied by an impulse of any kind in passing through four times the length of the pipe. An open pipe may be considered nearly as if it consisted of two such pipes joined at their closed ends, the portions of air contained by them being agitated by opposing motions, so as to always provide each other a resistance similar to that which the bottom of the closed pipe would have provided. It is probable that when an open pipe is once filled with air that is slightly condensed, the oblique current is diverted until the effect of the discharge, beginning at the farther end, has returned to the blown orifice and allowed the current to reenter the pipe. Where the diameter of the pipe is different at different parts of its length, the investigation of the sound becomes much more intricate; but it has been pursued by Daniel Bernoulli with considerable success, although upon suppositions not strictly consistent with the actual state of the motions concerned.

In the same manner as an open pipe is divided by an imaginary base so as to produce the same sound as a closed pipe of half the length, a pipe of any kind is capable of being subdivided into any number of such pipes, supposed to meet only at each other's corresponding ends; and in general, the more violently the pipe is blown, the greater is the number of parts into which it subdivides itself, the frequency of the vibrations being always proportional to that number. Thus, an open pipe may be divided not only into two, but also into four, six, eight, or more portions, producing the same sounds as a pipe of one-half, one-third, one-fourth, or any other

Its secondary sounds are only those of a pipe whose proportion is determined by odd numbers—its length being, for example, one-third, one-fifth, or one-seventh of the original length. These secondary notes are sometimes called harmonics; they are not only produced in succession from the same pipe, but they are also often faintly heard together while the fundamental note of the pipe continues to sound. When the pipe has a large cavity connected with it, or consists principally of such a cavity with a small opening, its vibrations are usually much less frequent, and it is generally incapable of producing a regular series of harmonics.

<margin>temperature</margin>
It is obvious from this statement of the analogy between the velocity of sound and the vibrations of the air in pipes that they must be affected in a similar manner by all alterations of temperature. Thus, the frequency of the vibrations of a pipe must be increased nearly in the ratio of 33 to 34 by an elevation of 30 degrees on Fahrenheit's thermometer; and if this change is accompanied by a transition from dampness to simple moisture, the sound will be even more altered.

<margin>longitudinal vibrations of solids</margin>
Dr. Chladni has discovered that solids of all kinds, when of a proper form, are capable of longitudinal vibrations, exactly resembling in their nature those of the air in an organ pipe, and having their secondary or harmonic notes related to them in a similar manner. These vibrations are always far more frequent than those of a column of air of equal length, as the velocity with which an impulse is transmitted by a solid of any kind is usually from 5 to 16 times as great as the velocity of sound in air; so that the longitudinal sounds are always extremely high-pitched when they are produced by substances of moderate length. These sounds afford perhaps the most accurate mode of determining the velocity of the transmission of an impulse through any elastic substance, and of obtaining from that velocity the exact measure of its elasticity. They may be easily exhibited by holding a long bar or wire of iron or brass in the middle and striking it at one end with a small hammer in the direction of its length.

The vibrations by which solid bodies most usually produce sound are, however, not longitudinal, but lateral, and they are governed either by a

The vibrations of extended substances most closely resemble in their properties those of elastic fluids, and they occur most frequently in practice, although the vibrations produced by the natural elasticity of the substance may be considered the most natural.

Vibrations derived from tension are either those of chords or musical strings, or those of membranes; but the vibrations of membranes offer little variety and have not yet been very accurately investigated, the drum being almost the only instrument in which they are concerned; they do not, however, appear to differ materially in their properties from the vibrations of strings. A musical string or chord is supposed to be perfectly flexible and of uniform thickness, to be stretched between two fixed points by a force incomparably greater than its own weight, and to vibrate in a single plane through a small space on each side of its natural position. Its motions may then be traced through all their stages by comparing the chord to a portion of an elastic medium of the same length, contained between two bodies capable of reflecting any impulse at each end; for example, to a portion of air situated between two walls, or enclosed in a pipe stopped at both ends. For the vibration of such a medium will be performed in the time occupied by any impulse in traveling through twice its length; and the vibration of the chord will be performed in the same time, assuming the height or depth of the medium is equal to the length of a portion of the chord whose weight is equivalent to the force applied to stretch it, and which may be called with propriety the <term>modulus of the tension</term>. If the chord is at first bent into a figure of any kind and then released, the position of any part of it at every subsequent time will be such that it will always be in a straight line between two points moving along the figure each way with the appropriate velocity; but in order to pursue this determination, we must repeat the figure of the chord on each side of the fixed points in an inverted position, changing the ends as well as the sides. Hence it appears that, at the end of a single vibration, the whole chord will assume a similar figure on the opposite side of its natural place, but in an inverted position, and after a complete or double vibration, it will return precisely to the form which it had in the beginning. By bending any long chord near one of its ends, after first drawing a line under its natural position, it will then be evident that the chord returns in each vibration nearly to the point of inflection. At that end, it passes only a much shorter distance on the opposite side of the line, while at the other end its movements are greatest on the opposite side of the line. The result of calculating the frequency of vibration also agrees perfectly with experiment; this agreement is not materially affected by the inflexibility or elasticity of the string, by air resistance, nor by the slight increase in tension caused by the stretching of the string when it is bent. For example, if the weight or force causing the tension of a string were equal or equivalent to the weight of 200 feet of the same string—that is, if the <term>modulus of tension</term> were 200 feet long—the velocity corresponding to half this height would be 80 feet per second. Every impulse would be conveyed with this velocity from one end of the string to the other, so that if the string were 1 foot long, it would vibrate 40 times per second; if 6 inches, 80 times; and if it were 40 feet long, only once per second. Hence, it is obvious that the time of vibration of any chord is simply proportional to its length; this may be shown either by using vibrations slow enough to be counted, or by comparison with the sounds of pipes or other musical sounds. But if the tension of a chord of a given length were changed, it would need to be quadrupled in order to double the frequency of vibration. If the tension and length remained the same but the weight of the chord was varied, it would also be necessary to make the weight four times as great in order to reduce the frequency of vibration by half.

It appears from the method of tracing the progress of a vibration, which has already been established, that every chord vibrates in the same manner as if it were part of a longer chord made up of any number of such chords, continually repeated in positions that are alternately inverted. Consequently, if a long chord is initially divided into any number of such equal portions, its parts will continue to vibrate in the same manner as if they were separate chords, with the points of division alone remaining always at rest. Such subordinate sounds are called *harmonics*: they are often produced on violins by lightly touching one of the points of division with a finger when the bow is applied. In all such cases, it may be shown, by putting small

However, it is not universally true that the fundamental sound must always be accompanied by all the harmonics that the chord is capable of producing; for I have found that by bending the chord exactly at any point where it could be divided into a number of equal parts, and then allowing it to vibrate, we lose the effect of the corresponding harmonic. There is some difficulty in explaining why these sounds are produced so distinctly in cases where the theory appears to indicate only a single and simple vibration; but it seems most probable that they usually become audible because of some imperceptible irregularity in the form or weight of the chord, which is just enough to disrupt the perfect alignment of the actual motions with those predicted by theory, without producing a discordance that would offend the ear. It is easy to understand how an irregularly weighted chord might have its harmonic relationships disturbed by considering the effect of a small weight placed at one of the points of division; this will obviously slow down the principal vibration without significantly affecting the vibration of the sections bordered by it. An abrupt and irregular disturbance also seems, in many cases, to make the secondary notes more audible, while a gradual and delicate impulse, like that of the wind on the strings of an *Aeolian* harp, produces a sound almost entirely free from subordinate harmonics.

Usually, the vibration of a chord deviates from its original plane and becomes a rotation or revolution. The vibrations immediately dependent on elasticity are those of rods, plates, rings, and vessels. These admit of much greater variety and are more difficult to investigate than the vibrations of chords. A rod may be either wholly loose, or fixed at only one end, or at both; and it may be either loosely fixed, in position only, or firmly fixed, in direction as well as in position; and these conditions may be variously combined with each other; the rod may also have a variety of secondary vibrations besides the principal or fundamental sound. All these cases have been examined by various mathematicians: the subject was begun by *Daniel Bernoulli*, and much extended by *Euler*, some of whose conclusions have been corrected by *Riccati*; and *Chladni* has compared them all with experiment. The sounds produced by the same rod, either under different circumstances or as harmonics which may be heard at the same time, are scarcely ever related to each other in any simple proportion, except that when a rod is loosely fixed at both ends, the frequency of the vibrations of the subordinate notes is expressed by the series of the squares of the natural numbers, such as 1, 4, 9, and 16. But the times occupied by any similar vibrations of rods, similarly situated, are always directly proportional to the squares of their lengths, and inversely proportional to their depths. When the rod is wholly at liberty, at least two of its points must be at rest, and these are at a distance of about one-fifth of its length from either end; in the next sound of the same rod, the middle point is at rest, along with two others near the ends. vibrations of different kinds of rods as in those of chords; it can only happen in particular cases that the rod will return to its original state after a complete vibration, and these cases are probably such as seldom occur in nature.

The vibrations of plates differ from those of rods in the same way that the vibrations of membranes differ from those of chords; the vibrations which cause the plate to bend in different directions are combined with each other, and sometimes produce remarkable modifications. These vibrations may be traced through wonderful varieties by Professor Chladni's method of scattering dry sand on the plates. When they are caused to vibrate by the use of a bow, the sand is collected into lines that indicate those parts which remain either perfectly or very nearly at rest during the vibrations. Dr. Hooke had employed a similar method for showing the nature of the vibrations of a bell, and it has sometimes been common in military mining to scatter sand on a drum and to judge, by the form in which it arranges itself, from which direction the tremors produced by counter-mining proceed. (Plate XXV. Fig. 346 . . 348.)

The vibrations of rings and of vessels are closely connected with those of plates, but they are modified in a manner which has not yet been sufficiently investigated. A glass or a bell generally divides into four portions vibrating separately, and sometimes into six or eight; these may readily be distinguished by the disturbances they excite in a fluid contained within the glass. It is almost unnecessary to observe that the fluid thus applied, by adding to the mass of matter to be moved, makes the vibration slower and the sound deeper.

In some cases, the vibrations of fluids and solids are jointly involved in the production of sound. Thus, in most of the pipes of an organ called reed pipes, the length of a metal tongue is adjusted so as to be capable of vibrating at the same time as the air contained in the pipe. Sometimes, however, the air only serves to stimulate the motion of the solid, as in some other organ pipes, which are usually much shorter than would be required for producing the proper note alone, and probably in the glottis, or vocal organ, of animals. On the other hand, the alternating opening and closing—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on vibrations, specifically focusing on how sound is produced in wind instruments and how solids can be sympathetically excited by sounds through fluid mediums like air, with implications for the mechanism of hearing.</meta>

The vibrations of a solid may be excited by a wave propagated through a fluid; thus, when a loud sound strikes against a chord capable of vibrating, either accurately or very nearly with the same frequency, it causes a sympathetic tone resembling that from which it originated. The chord may produce such a sound either by vibrating as a whole or by dividing itself into any number of equal parts. Thus, if the damper is raised from any of the strings of a harpsichord, it may be made to vibrate by striking or singing any note whose sound corresponds either to that of the whole string or to that of any of its aliquot parts. Sometimes also two chords that are very nearly alike appear, when sounding together, to produce precisely the same note, which differs a little from each of those which the chords would produce separately; and a similar circumstance has been observed with respect to two organ pipes placed near each other. In these cases, the vibrating substances must affect each other through the medium of the air, in nearly the same manner as two clocks resting on the same support have been found to modify each other's motions so as to exhibit a perfect coincidence in all of them.

It is uncertain whether any fibers in the ear are thus sympathetically agitated in the process of hearing, but if there are any such vibrating fibers, their motions must necessarily be of short duration; otherwise, there would be a perpetual ringing in our ears, and we would never be able to judge accurately of the end of a sound. Besides, a sympathetic vibration may be excited not only by a sound producing vibrations of equal frequency, but also by a sound in which every alternate, or every third or fourth vibration, coincides with its motions. It would, therefore, be difficult to distinguish such sounds from each other if hearing depended simply on the excitation of sympathetic vibrations. It is true that we generally distinguish, in listening to a loud and deep sound, precisely such notes as would be produced this way; but it is only when the sounding body is capable of providing them from the nature of its vibrations, for we may listen for them in vain in the sound of a bell or of a humming top. There is, however, no doubt that the muscles with which the different parts of the ear are equipped are concerned in adjusting the tension of some of them for the better transmission of sound;

<header>ON THE SOURCES AND EFFECTS OF SOUND.</header>

And it is equally certain that their operation is not absolutely necessary in the process.

The external ear serves to some extent to collect the undulations of sounds transmitted through the air and reflect them into the auditory passage. At the bottom of this passage, they strike against the membrane of the tympanum, or drum; because it is larger and more movable than some of the subsequent parts, it is capable of transmitting a stronger impulse than they would otherwise receive. In the same way, we may often feel the tremors produced in a sheet of thick paper held in the hand by the agitation of the air from a loud sound, which would not have otherwise affected the sense of touch. The impulse received by the membrane of the tympanum is conveyed by the hammer and anvil—two small bones that together constitute a kind of bent lever—through a third minute, flattened bone to a fourth called the stirrup. This fourth bone serves merely as a handle to its base, which is a plate covering the opening of a cavity called the vestibule, and it communicates the impulse to the mucous fluid that fills this cavity. The fluid of the vestibule, thus agitated, acts immediately on the nerve endings, which form a loose membranous tissue almost floating within it. Another portion of the nerves is distributed on the surface of three semicircular tubes or canals that open at both ends into the cavity, while a third portion supplies the cochlea—a separate channel that appears to be arranged with singular skill as a micrometer of sound. It resembles the spiral coils of a snail shell and, if uncoiled, would form two long conical tubes connected at their tips. The base of one tube opens into the vestibule, while the base of the other is covered only by a membrane that separates the fluid from the air contained in the general cavity of the ear, or the tympanum. It is evident from the properties of fluids moving in conical pipes that the speed of any impulse affecting the fluid at the base of the cone must be greatly increased at its tip, while the flexibility of the membrane at the base of the second channel allows this motion to occur without difficulty. It has also been suggested that a series of fibers are arranged along the cochlea which are susceptible to sympathetic vibrations of different frequencies, depending on the nature of the sound acting on them; and, with some limitations, this opinion does not seem entirely improbable. We must, however, reason with great caution respect-

And even in the case of the human ear, many of these parts may be spared without great inconvenience; thus, we hear very perfectly by means of impressions communicated to the teeth, and through them to the large bones of the head; and even when the membrane of the tympanum and all the small bones of the ear have been destroyed by disease, the undulations of the air still continue to affect the organ in the usual manner. (*Plate XXV. Fig. 349 .. 351.*)

Such is the delicacy of the organs of hearing in their perfect state that we readily distinguish not only the frequency of the vibrations of a sound, whether constant or variable, and its loudness or softness, but also the quality of tone, depending on the law which governs each separate vibration, and which constitutes the difference between instruments of different kinds, or different instruments of the same kind, or even the same instrument differently employed. Thus, we can distinguish very accurately the voices of our friends, even when they whisper, and those modifications of the same voice which constitute the various vowels and semivowels, and which, with the initial and final noises named consonants, compose the words of a language. We judge also, without an error of many degrees, of the exact direction from which the sound approaches us; but concerning the manner in which the ear is enabled to make this discrimination, we cannot reason upon any satisfactory grounds.

# LECTURE XXXIII.

## ON HARMONICS.

The philosophical theory of harmonics, or the combinations of sounds, was considered by the ancients as offering one of the most refined applications of mathematical speculation. It has not been neglected in modern times, but it has generally been treated in either a very abstruse and confused manner, or connected entirely with the practice of music and habitually associated with ideas of mere amusement. We shall, however, find the difficulties to be by no means insurmountable, and the subject will appear worthy of attention, not only for its own sake but also for the sake of its analogy with many other departments of science.

It appears from both theory and experience that the transmission of one sound does not at all impede the passage of another through the same medium. The ear is also capable of distinguishing, without difficulty, not only two sounds at once, but also a much greater number. Since the motions produced by one series of undulations are wholly independent of the effects of another series, and each particle of the medium is necessarily moved by both sounds, its final motion must always be the result of the motions that would have been produced in it by the separate sounds, combined according to the general laws of the composition of motion, which are the foundation of the principal doctrines of mechanics. When two sounds propagated together coincide very nearly in direction, the motions belonging to each sound may be resolved into two parts: one in the common or intermediate direction, and the other transverse to it. These latter portions will obviously be very small; they will sometimes cancel each other out and can always be neglected when determining the effect of the combination, since the ear is incapable of distinguishing a difference in the directions of sounds amounting to only a few degrees.

<vocab>harmonics, mathematical speculation, undulations, composition of motion, mechanics, acoustics</vocab>

<summary>This lecture introduces the mathematical and physical study of harmonics, explaining that sound waves move through a medium independently and combine according to the laws of mechanics.</summary>
<keywords>harmonics, acoustics, wave theory, composition of motion, physics of sound, mathematical speculation</keywords>

<page-num>390</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XXXIII.</header>

only. Thus, when two equal undulations of equal frequency coincide in this manner, and when the specific motions are directed the same way at the same time, the velocities in each direction are added together, and the joint effect is doubled, or perhaps quadrupled, since it appears that the strength of sound should be estimated from the squares of the particles' velocities. But when the specific motions of the two sounds counteract each other, both their effects are completely destroyed. These combinations resemble the effects of water waves in similar circumstances, which we have already examined; they may be illustrated by drawing two curved lines representing the motions that constitute the sounds, in the same way we have already supposed them to be described by a vibrating particle on a surface moving uniformly in a transverse direction. When these figures are placed side by side, the joint effect may be represented by a third curve drawn in such a direction as to be always in the middle between the corresponding points of the first two. A similar result, but even more clearly marked, may be obtained mechanically by cutting two boards or plates of any kind into the shape of the curves, and then dividing one of them into a number of thin pieces or sliders by lines perpendicular to the general direction of the curve, or to the edge of the plate that is parallel to it. When the bottoms of these sliders are then placed on the other curve, their general outline will represent the effect of the combination. For this purpose, we may assume the form of the harmonic curve, which represents the motions of a body vibrating like a pendulum and which probably corresponds very closely to the purest and simplest sounds. (Plate XXV. Fig. 352.)

If the two undulations differ slightly from each other in frequency, they alternately tend to destroy each other and to acquire a double or perhaps a quadruple force, and the sound gradually increases and diminishes in continuous succession at equal intervals. This increase and decrease in intensity is called a **beat**, and it provides us with a very accurate way of determining the proportional frequency of vibrations when the absolute frequency of one of them is known, or the absolute frequency of both when their proportion is known. This is possible because beats are usually slow enough to be counted, even though the vibrations themselves can never be distinguished. Thus, if one sound consisted of 100 vibrations per second and produced, with another higher-pitched sound, a single

If we count the number of beats in 15 seconds, we will find the number of vibrations occurring in a single second. The easiest way to obtain two such strings or pipes in practice is to tune them by a third, so that they are respectively 4/5 and 3/4 of its length; the vibrations of the third pipe per second will also be equal to the number of beats produced by the first two in 12 seconds. (Plate XXV. Fig. 353.)

When the beats of two sounds are too frequent to be heard as distinct increases in their volume, they have the same effect as any other impulses that recur in regular succession and produce a musical note, which has been named a **grave harmonic**. Thus, two sounds in the ratio of 4 to 5 produce an audible succession of beats when they are both very low or deep; but when they are higher or sharper, they produce a grave harmonic, which an attentive ear may distinguish as a separate third sound. Those combinations of sounds that produce distinctly audible beats generally have a harsh and coarse effect and are called **discords**; however, those whose vibrations are so related that they reach a common cycle after a few alternations, and which can be observed to produce a third sound, constitute **concords**. These are more perfect as their common cycles become shorter. (Plate XXV. Fig. 353.)

The natural association of secondary sounds, which generally accompany almost all musical notes, serves to some extent as a foundation for the science of harmonics; the same sounds that are frequently connected in nature are found to be agreeable when united by art. But it seems to depend even more directly on a love of order and a preference for the regular recurrence of sensations, which is fundamentally implanted in the human mind. Therefore, when two sounds are heard together, the proportions most satisfying to the ear are those that show a more or less perfect coincidence at the shortest intervals, expressed by the smallest numbers of separate vibrations. A regular or irregular succession necessarily produces the impression of sweetness or harshness. The same sounds that form the best accompaniment for each other are also generally the most agreeable for melodies consisting of a succession of single notes; their intervals, however, are too large to be sufficient for musical purposes, and they must be mixed with other sounds related to them in a similar way.

The same constitution of the human mind that enables it to perceive harmony also appears to cause the love of rhythm—the regular succession of any impressions at equal intervals of time. Even the attachment to the people and places we are used to, and to habits of every kind, bears a significant resemblance to this same principle. The most uncivilized nations find pleasure in dancing; in this case, much of the amusement—where sentiment and grace are not involved—is derived from the recurrence of sensations and actions at regular periods of time. Thus, not only are the elementary parts of music—the single notes—more pleasing than any irregular noise, but the entire composition is governed by a rhythm, or a recurrence of periods of varying lengths. These are generally distinguished by bars, which are the constituent parts of larger periods and are themselves subdivided into smaller ones. An interruption of the rhythm is indeed occasionally introduced, but only for the sake of contrast, in much the same way that discords are occasionally mixed with concords in all modern musical pieces to achieve an agreeable variety of expression.

In a simple composition, all the intervals are referenced to a single fundamental note or keynote. Thus, any air played on a trumpet or bugle horn must consist only of the harmonics of a single sound. When an accompaniment is performed on a French horn, the length of the instrument is first adjusted to the principal note, and all the sounds it produces are selected from this natural series. However, the notes that constitute the most natural scale are not all included among the harmonics, though they are all directly dependent on a similar relationship. A sound whose vibrations are of equal frequency to those of another is called a unison; if two vibrations occur for every one of the fundamental note, the sound is called its superior octave, being the eighth of those

Because of its great resemblance to the fundamental note, it is designated by the same letter of the alphabet or by the same syllable; in this way, all audible sounds are considered repetitions of a series contained within the interval of an octave. One-third of the string or pipe gives the fifth above the octave; one-fourth gives the double octave, and one-fifth of the string gives its third. Thus we obtain the common accord or chord, or the harmonic triad, consisting of the fundamental note with its third and fifth, which produces the most perfect harmony and also contains the constituent parts of the most simple and natural melodies. But we still lack intermediate steps for the scale; these are supplied, first, by completing the triad of the fifth, which gives us the second and the seventh—where 9 and 15 vibrations correspond respectively to 8 vibrations of the fundamental—and which may also be found in the ascending series of natural harmonics. In the second place, they are supplied by adding the fourth and sixth in such proportions as to make up another perfect triad with the octave; these notes consist of 4 and 5 vibrations while the fundamental note makes 3, and they are nowhere found among the natural harmonics. The complete scale is, therefore, formed by these harmonic triads, which are contiguous to and connected with each other; the middle one is the triad of the keynote, the superior one is that of its fifth (sometimes called the dominant or governing note), and the inferior one is that of the fourth, or subdominant. This scale is derived from such simple principles that it may properly be considered a natural arrangement, and it appears to be found with little variation in uncivilized as well as in civilized countries. (Plate XXV. Fig. 354.)

A long piece would, however, be too monotonous unless the fundamental note were sometimes changed; we may, therefore, choose at will one of the auxiliary triads for the principal harmony, and we may continue the modulation or progression until every note of the scale becomes a keynote in succession. But in order to fill the intervals of these several scales in just proportion, it becomes necessary to add several new notes to the first series; for instance, if we take the seventh as a keynote, we shall need five new sounds within the octave, making twelve in total, which is the number usually employed in music. The interval between any two adjoining sounds of the twelve is called a semitone or half note; two semitones

For still further variety, we sometimes change the position of the middle note of each triad, placing the minor third (the interval expressed by the ratio of 5 to 6) below the major (which is in the ratio of 4 to 5). The scale formed in this way is called the scale of the minor mode, in contrast to the major mode, with the three principal thirds being lowered a semitone. Sometimes, however, the change is made only to the third of the keynote, especially when ascending, in order to retain the seventh of the major scale. This note leads so naturally into the octave that it is sometimes called the characteristic semitone of the key; it is for this reason that the triad containing it is called the dominant chord, which, in all regular compositions, immediately precedes the ending on the keynote.

The major and minor triads, along with the discord of the flat seventh, may be considered the foundation of all essential harmonies. The flat seventh is mainly used with the major triad during transitions from the fundamental key into its fourth, where that seventh naturally serves as a concord. It thus helps introduce the new key by clearly marking the specific note in which it differs from the old one; in such cases, the flat seventh always descends into, or is followed by, the third of the new key, and the third of the first triad ascends into the new keynote. Other discords are also sometimes introduced, but they are generally either partial continuations of a previous chord or anticipations of a following one. In regular and serious compositions, two different parts of a harmony are never allowed to accompany each other in successive octaves or fifths, since such a sequence is found to produce a disagreeable, monotonous effect—except when a series of octaves is continued for some time so as to be considered a repetition of the same part.

In some instruments they may be varied without limit at the performer's pleasure, as in the voice, in instruments with fingerboards, and in some wind instruments; but in many cases this is impractical, nor could any imaginable alteration make all the intervals perfect, unless every note were changed whenever we returned to it by steps different from those by which we had left it. The simplest way of arranging the twelve sounds is to divide the octave into twelve equal intervals, with all the notes being in the same proportion to those which immediately follow them: this is called equal temperament, because the imperfection is equal in all keys. In this system of temperament, the fifths, which consist of seven semitones, are a little too flat—that is, the interval is a little too small; the minor thirds, consisting of three semitones, are also too flat, and the major thirds are too sharp. But it has generally been considered best to preserve some keys more free from error, partly for variety and partly because some are used more frequently than others; this cannot, however, be done without making some of the scales more imperfect than in equal temperament. A good practical way of performing it is to make six perfect fifths while descending from the keynote of the natural scale, and six ascending fifths that are equally imperfect among themselves. We thus retain a slight imperfection in the scales most commonly used and make the keys which are most remote from them considerably less perfect. The fifth octave, consisting of sixteen vibrations, will be nearly the lowest audible note, and the fourteenth the highest note used in music; however, the sixteenth, consisting of over 30,000 vibrations per second, may perhaps be an audible sound. The frequency of the vibrations of other notes may easily be calculated from the known relationships they have with the note determined in this way. (Plate XXV, Fig. 355.)
