## LECTURE XXXIV.

### ON MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS.

The application of the theory of harmonics to practice depends on the construction of different kinds of musical instruments. We shall only be able to take a cursory view of these, and we shall afterwards attend to the historical order of the most remarkable steps by which both the theory and practice of music have been advanced to a high degree of refinement.

Musical instruments may be most conveniently arranged according to whether they are primarily designed for producing sound by the vibrations of strings, of membranes, of elastic plates, or of the air; or by the combined effects of the air and a solid body vibrating together. The essential varieties of stringed instruments are found in the harp, the harpsichord, the pianoforte, the clavichord, the guitar, the violin, the vielle or monochord, and the aeolian harp. In all these, the immediate power of the sound of the strings is increased by means of a sounding board, which appears to be agitated by their motion and to act more powerfully on the air than the strings could do alone.

In the harp, the sound is produced by plucking the string with the finger and allowing it to return to its place. The lyre of the ancients differed from the harp only in its form and range, except that the performer sometimes used a plectrum, which was a small instrument made of ivory or some other substance for striking the strings. Each note in the harp has a separate string; and in the Welsh harp, there are two strings to each note of the principal scale, with an intermediate row for the semitones; but in the pedal harp, the half notes are formed by pressing pins against the strings so as to shorten their effective length. Instead of this method, an attempt has lately been made to produce the semitones by changing the

In the harpsichord, and in the spinet, which is a small harpsichord, the quill acts like the finger on the harp, or the plectrum in the lyre; it is fixed to the <term>jack</term> by a joint with a spring, allowing it to pass back over the string without difficulty, which in this case is made of metal. Sometimes leather is used instead of quills, and this serves to make the tone more mellow, but less powerful. Besides two strings in unison for each note, the harpsichord generally has a third which is an octave above them. Different modifications of the tone are sometimes produced by striking the wire in different parts, by bringing soft leather loosely into contact with its fixed extremity, and by some other means. When the finger is removed from the key, a damper of cloth falls on the string and stops its motion. In all instruments of this kind, the perfection of the tone depends much on the construction and situation of the sounding board: it is usually made of thin deal wood <note>A term for fir or pine timber</note>, strengthened at different parts by thicker pieces fixed below it.

In the pianoforte, the sound is produced by the blow of a hammer, raised by a lever which is as much detached from it as possible. The dulcimer, or <term>hackbrett</term> of the Germans, is also made to sound by the percussion of hammers, but they are simply held in the hand of the performer.

The clavichord, or the <term>clavier</term> of the Germans, differs from other keyed instruments in the manner in which the length of the string is determined; it is attached at one end to a bridge, and at the other to a pin or screw as usual. However, the effective length is terminated on one side by the bridge, and on the other by a flat wire projecting from the end of the key, which strikes the string and at the same time serves as a temporary bridge as long as the sound continues. The remaining portion of the string is prevented from sounding by being in contact with a strip of cloth, which also stops the whole vibration as soon as the hammer falls. The instrument is capable of great delicacy and neatness of expression, but it is deficient in volume. The guitar is generally played with the fingers, like a harp; but each string is made to serve for several notes by means of <term>frets</term>, or cross wires, fixed to the fingerboard on which it is pressed down by the other hand. # ON MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS.

In the <term>pianoforte guitar</term>, hammers are placed between the fingers and the strings, acting like those of the pianoforte. The <term>mandolin</term> and <term>lute</term> are types of the guitar; and the <term>archlute</term> was a very powerful instrument of the same kind, formerly much used in full ensemble pieces.

In the <term>violin</term>, and in other instruments resembling it, all the strings are capable of having their length altered as desired by being pressed down on the fingerboard. The sound is produced by the friction of the bow, which is rubbed with resin. The string is carried forward by its adhesion to the bow, and when its resistance has overcome this adhesion, it begins to return in opposition to the friction; for the friction of bodies in motion is generally less than their adhesion when they are at rest with respect to each other. Furthermore, the contact of the string with the bow is usually largely interrupted by subordinate vibrations, which may be distinguished with the assistance of a microscope, in the manner already described. However, when the string changes the direction of its motion once more, it adheres again to the bow and is accelerated by it as before. The original instrument appears to have been the <term>viola</term> (or tenor), its smaller version the <term>violino</term> (violin), its larger version—expressing a greater size—the <term>violone</term> (double bass), and the smaller version of this, the <term>violoncello</term> (common bass). The <term>viola di gamba</term> had one or more long strings separate from the fingerboard, serving as an occasional accompaniment.

The <term>vielle</term>, or <term>monochord</term>, commonly called the <term>hurdy-gurdy</term>, has frets which are raised by the action of the fingers on a row of keys; and instead of a bow, the string is made to vibrate by the motion of a wooden wheel. There is a second string serving as a drone, producing always the same sound; this is furnished with a bridge loosely fixed, which strikes continually against the sounding board and produces a peculiar nasal effect. The <term>trumpet marine</term>, or <term>trumpet Marigni</term>, was a string of the same kind, which was lightly touched at specific points so as to produce harmonic notes only; it was played with a bow. The <term>Aeolian harp</term>, when moved by the wind, produces a very smooth and delicate tone, frequently changing from one harmonic of the string to another, depending on how the force of the wind varies and how it acts more or less unequally on different parts of the string. (Plate XXV. Fig. 356.)

### LECTURE XXXIV.

The human voice depends principally on the vibrations of the <term>membranes of the glottis</term>, excited by a current of air, which they alternately intercept and allow to pass; the sounds being also modified in their subsequent progress through the mouth. Perhaps the interception of the air by these membranes is only partial; or it may be more or less completely intercepted in sounds of different kinds. Indeed, the operation of the organs concerned is not perfectly understood, but from a knowledge of their structure, we may judge to some extent the manner in which they are used.

The <term>trachea</term>, or <term>windpipe</term>, conveys the air from the chest, which serves as bellows; from there, it enters the <term>larynx</term>, which is principally composed of five elastic cartilages. The lowest of these is the <term>cricoid cartilage</term>, a strong ring, which forms the basis of the rest: to this are fixed, in the front, the <term>thyroid cartilage</term>, and behind, the two <term>arytenoid cartilages</term>, composing together the cavity of the <term>glottis</term>, over which the <term>epiglottis</term> inclines backwards, as it ascends from its origin at the upper part of the <term>thyroid cartilage</term>. Within the <term>glottis</term>, its <term>ligaments</term> are extended, touching each other in the front, where they are inserted into the <term>thyroid cartilage</term>, but capable of diverging considerably behind whenever the <term>arytenoid cartilages</term> separate. These <term>ligaments</term>, as they vary their tension in consequence of the movements of the <term>arytenoid cartilages</term>, are susceptible to vibrations of various frequencies, and as they vibrate, produce a continuous sound. Strictly speaking, there are two <term>ligaments</term> on each side; but it is not fully understood how they operate; probably only one pair performs the vibrations, and the other assists, by means of the small cavity placed between them, in enabling the air to act readily upon them, and in communicating the vibrations again to the air. (*Plate XXVI. Figures 357, 358.*)

The <term>vowels</term> and <term>semivowels</term> are continuous sounds, chiefly formed by this apparatus in the <term>glottis</term>, and modified either in their origin or in their progress by the various arrangements of the different parts of the mouth. Of simple <term>vowels</term>, sixteen or eighteen may be enumerated in different languages: in the French <term>nasal vowels</term>, the sound is in part transmitted through the nostrils by the lowering of the <term>soft palate</term>: the perfect <term>semivowels</term> differ from the <term>vowels</term> only in the greater resistance which the air undergoes in its passage through the mouth; there are also nasal and semi-nasal semi-

vowels. The perfect consonants may be either explosive, susurrant <note>whispering or hissing</note>, or mute; the explosive consonants begin or end with a sound formed in the larynx; the others are either whispers or mere noises without any vocal sound. By paying attention to the various positions of the organs, and by experimenting with the effects of pipes of different forms, it is possible to construct a machine that can very accurately imitate many of the sounds of the human voice; this has indeed been actually performed by Kratzenstein and by Kempelen. (Plate XXVI. Fig. 359.)

Although the vibrating ligaments of the glottis may be anatomically called membranes, their tension is probably confined to the direction of their length; therefore, their action is the same as that of a simple string or chord. But in the case of a tambourine and a drum, the membrane is stretched in every direction, and the force of tension consequently acts in a different manner. The principal character of such instruments is their loudness—derived from the size of the surface that strikes the air—and the short duration of the sound, because of the great resistance necessarily produced by the air's reaction.

Musical instruments that produce sounds through vibrations depending on the elasticity of solid bodies are employed less frequently than others. They have a peculiar tonal character that is by no means unpleasant, but which makes them less suitable for mixing with other instruments, since their secondary harmonics are in different proportions. Such instruments include the stacada <note>a series of graduated glass or metal bars; a precursor to the xylophone or metallophone</note>—a series of glass or metal cylinders struck either directly with hammers or by means of keys—the tuning fork, the gong, the cymbal, and the bell. Bells and other similar instruments are usually made of a mixture of copper and tin, with a little brass or zinc, which is more highly elastic than any of the component parts taken separately. The harmonica consists of a series of glass vessels, either placed side by side or fixed on a common axis, and made to sound by the friction of the fingers and sometimes by cork rubbers. The vibrations of an elastic plate, agitated by a current of air which it continually admits and excludes, constitute the sound of the <term>vox humana</term> and <term>regal</term> organ pipes; these resemble the human voice as much in their effects as in the mechanism on which they depend. (Plate XXVI. Fig. 360–362.)

### LECTURE XXXIV.

Of simple wind instruments, in which the quality of the sound is determined by the vibrations of the air, the principal ones are the syrinx, the flute, the flageolet, the diapason organ pipe (whether open, stopped, or with a chimney), the humming top, and the cavity of the mouth in whistling or in playing the Jew’s harp. The pipes of the syrinx are adjusted to their respective notes by cutting them or filling them up until they are reduced to a proper length. The effective length of the flute and flageolet is altered at will by opening or shutting the holes made at specific distances along them; opening a hole at any part has the same effect as if the pipe were cut off a little beyond it, and the pitch of the tone is somewhat higher as the hole is made larger. These instruments differ little except in the mechanism by which the breath is directed to produce a sound; and the flageolet, when equipped with bellows, becomes a bagpipe. The tongue of the Jew’s harp is an elastic plate, but the sound it immediately produces serves only as a drone; its vibration, however, appears to act like the motion of a violin bow in exciting another sound. This sound, although faint, is still sufficiently musical and appears to be determined by the size of the cavity of the mouth, in much the same way as that of the humming top or the sound of the same cavity produced in whistling by a current of air forced through it. (Plate XXVI, Figs. 363–367.)

In mixed wind instruments, the vibrations or alternations of solid bodies are made to cooperate with the vibrations of a specific volume of air. Thus, in the trumpet and in horns of various kinds, the force of inflation, and perhaps the degree of tension of the lips, determines the number of parts into which the tube is divided and the harmonic that is produced. In the serpent <note>a bass wind instrument with a long, curving wooden body</note>, the lips cooperate with a tube whose effective length may be varied by opening or shutting holes, and the instrument called an "organized trumpet" appears to act in a similar manner. The trombone has a tube that slides in and out at will, changing the actual length of the whole instrument. The hautboy <note>oboe</note> and clarinet have mouthpieces of different forms made of reeds or canes; and the reed pipes of an organ, which have various constructions, are equipped with an elastic plate of metal that vibrates in unison with the column of air they contain. An organ generally consists of a number of different series of such pipes, so

The practice of music appears to have originated earlier than either its theory or any attention to the nature and general phenomena of sound. The first lyre with three strings is said to have been invented in Egypt by Hermes, during the reign of Osiris, between the years 1800 and 1500 BC. However, a tradition so remote, concerning a figure so shrouded in myth, can hardly be considered historical evidence. We cannot, therefore, expect to determine with any certainty the proportions of these strings to one another; some suppose they were successive notes of the natural scale, while others believe they contained the most perfect concords. Perhaps, in reality, each performer adjusted them in whatever way best suited his own preference. The trumpet is said to have been used around the same time; its natural harmonics might easily have provided notes to extend the scale of the lyre, but it does not appear that the ancients ever adopted this method of regulating the scale. The seven-stringed lyre is attributed to Terpander, about 700 years before our era; and two centuries later, either Pythagoras or Simonides completed the octave, which consisted of intervals differing very little from the modern scale, with the keynote being nearly in the middle of the series. In later times, the number of strings was greatly increased. The modulations and the relationships between intervals became very intricate and were greatly diversified into a variety of modes or scales. While these must have provided an inexhaustible supply of original and striking melodies, they could hardly have allowed for as many pleasing combinations as our more modern systems. Although it is certain that the ancients frequently had accompaniments in perfect harmony

The <term>tibia</term> of the ancients resembled an <term>oboe</term> or <term>clarinet</term>, for it had a reed mouthpiece, about three inches long; the same performer generally played on two of these instruments at once. There were, however, several varieties of the <term>tibia</term>; and it is not improbable that some of them may have had the simple mouthpiece of the <term>flageolet</term>.

The first philosophical observer of the phenomena of sound after Pythagoras appears to have been Aristotle. He notices a great variety of curious facts in <term>harmonics</term> among his mechanical problems, and he held a very correct idea of the true nature of the motions of the air that constitute sound. He knew that a pipe or a string of double length produced a sound whose <term>vibrations</term> occupied double the time, and that the properties of <term>concords</term> depended on the proportions of the times occupied by the vibrations of the separate sounds. It is not, indeed, improbable that at least as much as this was known to Pythagoras, since he correctly established the numerical ratios between various sounds; but so little justice has been done to his discoveries by the imperfect accounts of them which have been preserved, that we cannot expect to be able to ascertain his opinions on any subject with accuracy.

The invention of the organ by Ctesibius of Alexandria, about 2,000 years ago, marks a remarkable epoch in <term>harmonics</term>. The larger instruments of this kind were equipped with hydraulic bellows, and the smaller with bellows of leather only; and they had keys which were pressed down, like those of modern organs, by the performer's fingers, and which opened valves communicating with the pipes.

The modern system of music is one of the few sciences—if it can be called such—which owe their improvement to the Middle Ages. The old <term>ecclesiastical music</term> was probably founded in great measure on that of the Greeks; its peculiar character consisted in the adoption of any note of the scale at pleasure for a keynote, without significantly altering the other intervals; and in this manner they obtained a variety much resembling that of the <term>modes</term> or kinds of music in use among the ancients. Early in the eleventh century, Guido of Arezzo, otherwise called Aretin the monk, introduced, together with some improvements in the theory and practice of music, a new method of naming the notes by syllables.

Some curious experiments on sound may be found in the works of Bacon, but they added very little to the true theory of **acoustics**, and some of them are not perfectly accurate. Galileo rediscovered what was well known to Aristotle regarding the nature of sound; for the words of Aristotle had been so much misunderstood and misinterpreted that he could have profited but little by them. His contemporaries Mersenne and Kircher made a variety of very ingenious experiments and observations on sound and on sounding bodies, many of them unknown to authors of later date. The theory of ancient music was very accurately investigated in the middle of the 17th century by Meibomius. Our countryman Wallis, also, besides employing much learning and penetration in the illustration of ancient music, observed some isolated facts in **harmonics** which were new and interesting.

Sir Isaac Newton’s propositions respecting the velocity of the propagation of sound were the beginning of all the more accurate investigations relating to **acoustics**. It must not be denied that these propositions contain some very inconclusive reasoning respecting the nature of the motions constituting sound, by which the determination of a particular case is erroneously extended into a general solution of the problem. The velocity is, however, truly calculated, because it is in fact independent of the particular nature of the vibration, and all that is wanting to generalize the proposition is the remark, that if the velocity of sound is the same in all cases, it must be such as the calculation indicates. An error nearly similar was committed by Brook Taylor, who in the year 1714 investigated the time occupied by the vibration of a string or chord upon a particular supposition, which he considered as a necessary condition, but which in fact confined the inquiry to a limited case. It happens, however, that the same determination of the frequency of vibration is equally true in all possible cases. Sauveur obtained, about the same time

Lagrange and Euler have corrected and greatly expanded the investigations of Newton and Taylor; Bernoulli and Dalembert have also significantly contributed to the thorough examination and discussion of the subject.

Around the year 1750, Daniel Bernoulli succeeded in obtaining a solution to a problem even more difficult than those relating to the motion of strings: he determined the frequency of the vibrations of an elastic rod fixed at one end, as well as the relationships of its secondary sounds. This solution is not, in fact, absolutely universal, but it may perhaps be adapted to all possible cases by considering the effect of a combination of various sounds produced at the same time. Euler also deserves great credit for extending and simplifying the mathematical part of this investigation, although he made several mistakes regarding its mechanical application; some of these he corrected himself, and others have been noted by Riccati and Chladni.

The grave harmonics produced by the combination of two high-pitched sounds were noticed at about the same time by Romieu and by Tartini, though Romieu was first. Their existence is not only remarkable in itself, but is particularly important because it leads to some interesting conclusions regarding the nature of sound and hearing in general.

Bernoulli has also investigated, in a very ingenious manner, the sounds produced by air in pipes of various forms, although he admittedly relied on assumptions that deviated somewhat from the truth. The results of his calculations have, however, been fully confirmed by the experiments of Lambert on the sounds of flutes.

Dr. Chladni's method of examining the sounds of plates has provided a very interesting addition to our knowledge of the nature of vibrations; his discovery of the longitudinal sounds of solids is of considerable importance, and he is said to be working on an extensive study of the subject of acoustics in general. ## LECTURE XXXV.

->ON THE THEORY OF OPTICS.<-

The science of <term>optics</term> is one of the most elegant and the most important branches of <term>natural philosophy</term> and <term>mechanical philosophy</term>. It presents us with experiments that are attractive in their beauty and variety, investigations that offer an ample scope for mathematical refinements, and instruments of extensive utility both in the pursuit of other sciences and in the common employments of life. Nor is there any department in the study of nature in which an unprejudiced observer is more convincingly impressed with the characteristic marks of the perfect works of a supremely intelligent Artist.

We shall first consider the essential properties which we discover in light, and which are the basis of our calculations, together with the conclusions immediately deducible from those properties; and next, we will look at the application of these laws to practical purposes in the construction of optical instruments. We shall afterward proceed to examine the more complicated phenomena which are derived from the same laws and which are observed in natural as well as in artificial circumstances, constituting the subdivision of <term>physical optics</term>. The description of the eye and the explanation of the sense of <term>vision</term>, by means of which all these effects are connected with the human mind, is properly a continuation of the subject of physical optics: the intimate nature of light will be the next subject of investigation, and a historical sketch of the progress of the science of optics will conclude the second part of this course of lectures.

In order to avoid all hypotheses in the beginning, it will be necessary to define light from its sensible qualities. The sensation of light is sometimes produced by external pressure on the eye; we must exclude this sensation from the definition of light and must therefore call light an influence capable of entering

eye; and of affecting it with a sense of vision. A body from which this influence appears to originate is called a *luminous body*. We do not include in this definition of the term light the invisible influences that cause heat only or blacken the salts of silver, although they both appear to differ from light in no other respect than as one kind of light differs from another; they might probably have served the purpose of light if our organs had been differently constituted.

A *ray of light* is considered an infinitely narrow portion of a stream of light, and a *pencil* as a small detached stream composed of a collection of such rays accompanying each other. Just as a mathematical line is sometimes conceived to be described by the motion of a mathematical point, a ray of light may be imagined to be described by the motion of a point of light. We cannot present a single mathematical line to the senses except as the boundary of two surfaces; in the same manner, we cannot exhibit a single ray of light except as the border between light and darkness, or as the lateral limit of a pencil of light.

When light passes through a space free from all material substances, it moves with great velocity in a perfectly rectilinear direction; likewise, when it passes through a material substance perfectly uniform in its structure, it probably always moves in a similar manner. But in many cases, its motions are much interrupted. Those substances through which light passes most freely and in straight lines are called *homogeneous transparent mediums*. Perhaps no medium is, strictly speaking, absolutely transparent; for even in the air, a considerable portion of light is intercepted. It has been estimated that of the horizontal sunbeams passing through about 200 miles of air, only one two-thousandth part reaches us; and that no perceptible light can penetrate more than 700 feet deep into the sea, as a length of seven feet of water has been found to intercept one-half of the light that enters it.

It is possible that mediums, though not identical in other respects, may be homogeneous with respect to the transmission of light; for example, a glass may be filled with a fluid of such a density that the light may pass uninterruptedly through their common surface; but it generally happens that whenever the

<header>LECTURE XXXV.</header>

...nature of the medium changes, the path of light deviates from a straight line. Thus, the apparent positions of the sun and stars are changed by the effect of the atmosphere, because the light by which we judge their locations is deflected in its passage from the empty space beyond the atmosphere, first into the thinner and then into the denser air. In the same way, when we view a distant object over a fire or a chimney, it appears to dance and quiver because the rays of light by which it is seen are perpetually thrown into new positions by the various changes in the density of the air resulting from the action of heat.

When rays of light reach a surface that is the boundary between two mediums that are not uniform, they continue their progress without deviating from those planes in which their former paths lay (which are perpendicular to the surface of the mediums); however, they no longer maintain the same direction. A part of them, and sometimes nearly the whole, is reflected back from the surface, while the remaining part is transmitted and refracted, or bent. The name "refraction" is derived from the distortion it causes in the appearance of an object seen only partially by refracted light; for example, an oar partially submerged in water appears to be bent because of the refraction of the light by which its lower part is seen as it passes out of the water and into the air.

There is no instance of an abrupt change in the density of a medium without a partial reflection of the light, whether it is passing into the denser or into the thinner medium; and generally, the more obliquely the light falls on the surface, the larger the reflected portion is. No object is so black that it reflects no light at all and is perfectly invisible in a strong light, although at the surface separating two very thin substances, such as two kinds of gas, the reflection is too faint to be noticed; however, in this case, the separation is seldom perfectly abrupt.

The angles of incidence and reflection are the angles made by a ray of light, before and after its reflection, with a line perpendicular to the reflecting surface; and these angles are always equal to each other. Consequently, the inclination of the rays to the surface also remains the same. The quantity of light reflected, when other circumstances are equal, appears to

is always greatest when the difference in the optical or refractive density of the two substances is greatest. Thus, the reflection from the shared surface of glass and water is much weaker than from a surface of glass exposed to the air. Metals in general reflect a great proportion of the light falling on them, and even the reflection from the shared surface of glass and mercury appears to be only slightly weaker than the reflection from the surface of mercury immediately exposed to the air; this indicates that the optical density of metals must be exceedingly great.

It also appears that a portion of the light falling on a reflecting surface is always transmitted, at least to a certain depth, despite the apparent opacity of any large masses of the substance. Thus, if we cover a small hole in a window shutter with the thinnest gold leaf, we shall find that it transmits a greenish light. This light must have passed through the reflecting surface, but if the gold had been even one ten-thousandth of an inch in thickness, it would have been entirely intercepted, probably in much the same manner as if it had passed through 700 feet of water. In transparent substances, however, the greater part of the light penetrates to all distances with little interruption, and all rays of the same kind transmitted by the same surface form an angle of refraction with the perpendicular which is ultimately in a certain constant proportion to the angle of incidence; that is, for instance, one-half, three-fourths, or two-thirds, according to the nature of the surface. Thus, if the refractive properties of the substance were such that an incident ray, making an angle of one degree with the perpendicular, would be so refracted as to make an angle of only half a degree with the same line, another ray, incident at an angle of two degrees, would be refracted, without noticeable error, into an angle of one degree. But when the angles are larger, they vary from this ratio, with only their sines preserving the proportion with accuracy: for example, if the angle of incidence at the supposed surface were increased to 90°, the angle of refraction would be 30° only, instead of 45°. Rays of the same kind are in general distinguished by the same color, although some rays, which differ from each other in refrangibility, have scarcely a discernible difference in color; and it is possible, on the other hand, to find a surface at which the ratio of the angles is the same for rays of all kinds. (Plate XXVI. Fig. 369, 370.)

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the properties of light, specifically how the smoothness of a surface affects reflection and how refractive density relates to a substance's physical properties.</meta>

<page-num>412</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XXXV.</header>

To obtain the effects of regular reflection and transmission, we must have perfectly smooth and polished substances. All rough bodies—and sometimes even those that seem fairly smooth to the touch—have their surfaces divided into countless peaks and valleys. These constitute, in reality, many separate surfaces oriented in every imaginable direction. Because the angles of incidence and reflection are equal with respect to each of these tiny surfaces, the light is scattered in every direction, and no regularity can be observed in its path. It is true that by continuing the mechanical process of polishing, we only make these surfaces smaller and more numerous; however, when they are reduced in size so that they are not raised or lowered by more than about a millionth of an inch, they appear to become—for some physical reason—incapable of acting individually, instead working together to produce a single general effect.

In all cases of refraction, as well as reflection, if a ray of light returned directly backward along the same path to the surface, it would proceed—after a second refraction or reflection—in the direction exactly opposite to the one in which it first struck. Thus, the same lines would mark its path in both instances. For example, if we stand before a mirror with one eye shut and cover its reflection on the glass with a finger, that same finger will hide the other eye as soon as it is closed and the first eye is opened in its place. A similar effect could be observed if the glass were underwater or behind any other refracting substance. (Plate XXVI. Fig. 371.)

The medium that causes light rays to bend closest to the line perpendicular to its surface is said to have the greatest refractive density. In general, there is a significant analogy between this refractive density and the specific gravity of a substance; for example, water is more refractive than air, and glass is more refractive than water. However, flammable bodies are usually more refractive than non-flammable bodies of the same specific gravity. It is well known that, based on the high refractive power of the diamond relative to its actual density, *Sir Isaac Newton* most ingeniously conjectured that it was combustible—as more modern experiments have actually shown it to be. It is even more remarkable that he also imagined, based on the same analogy, that water consists of a combination of oily or flammable particles with others that are earthy or non-flammable. In the order of refractive

density, beginning from the lowest, or a vacuum, we have airs and gases of different rarities; water, which is the least refractive of all liquids, and which is still less refractive when frozen into ice; alcohol, oils, glass, and lastly the diamond; but probably some metallic substances are much more refractive than even the diamond.

The refractive powers of different substances are usually estimated by a comparison of the refractions produced at their surfaces in contact with the air, which, in all common experiments, has the same sensible effect as a vacuum or an empty space. The ratio of the angles of refraction and incidence, when small, and the ratio of their sines in all cases, is expressed by the ratio of 1 to a certain number, which is called the index of the refractive density of the medium. Thus, when a ray of light passes out of air into water, the sines of the angles are in the ratio of 3 to 4, or of 1 to $^4/_3$, which is, therefore, the index of the refractive density of water. In the same manner, for crown glass, the ratio is that of 2 to 3, and the index $1 \frac{1}{2}$; but for flint glass it is somewhat greater, the ratio being nearly that of 5 to 8.

It may easily be shown that a refractive substance, bounded by parallel surfaces, must transmit a ray of light—after a second refraction at its posterior surface—in a direction parallel to that in which it first passed through the air. It is also found by experiment that such a substance, placed between any two mediums of different kinds, produces no alteration in the overall angular deviation of a ray passing from one of them into the other. From this it may be inferred that the index of refraction at the common surface of any two mediums is the quotient of their respective indices. For instance, if a plate of crown glass is placed between water on one side and air on the other, it produces no change in the direction of a ray of light entering the water; and the index of refraction at the common surface of glass and water is $^9/_8$. (Plate XXVI. Figures 372, 373.)

There is one remarkable consequence of the general law by which the angles of incidence and refraction are related: when the angle of incidence exceeds a certain magnitude, the refraction may become impossible; and in this case the ray of light is wholly reflected, at an angle equal to the angle of incidence.

Consequently, when a ray passing within a dense medium falls very obliquely on its surface, it must be totally reflected; and the greater the density of the medium, the more frequently the light will be totally reflected. This reflection is more perfect than any other; the diamond owes much of its brilliance to it: the great refractive density of this substance not only gives a luster to its front surface, but also facilitates the total reflection of those rays that fall obliquely on its back surface. If we hold a prism near a window in a proper position, we may observe that its lower surface appears to be divided into two parts, one much brighter than the other; common partial reflection takes place in one, and total reflection in the other. The two surfaces are separated by a colored arch. It is colored because the total reflection begins at different angles for rays of different colors; and it is curved because the points at which the light passing to the eye forms a specific angle with the surface do not lie in a straight line. If we throw a light on a wall by a reflection of this kind, we may easily observe, as we turn the prism, the point at which the brightness of the image is very noticeably increased. (Plate XXVI. Fig. 374.)

These are the principal properties discovered in light. Before we consider their immediate application to optical instruments, we must examine the general theory of refraction and reflection at surfaces of different kinds, or the doctrines of <term>dioptrics</term> and <term>catoptrics</term>.

The rays that constitute a <term>pencil of light</term> are sometimes parallel to each other, sometimes divergent from a point, and sometimes convergent to a point. The intersection of the directions of any two or more rays of light is called their <term>focus</term>; and the focus is either actual or virtual, depending on whether the rays actually meet at that point or only appear to originate from or travel toward it. Thus, a small luminous object may represent an actual focus of diverging rays, since the light spreads from it in all directions; and the small surface into which the image of such an object, or of the sun, is collected by a lens or mirror, may represent the actual focus of converging rays. Thus, every point of an image in a mirror is perpendicularly opposite to the corresponding point of the object, and is at the same distance behind the mirror as the point of the object is in front of it. The focus into which parallel rays are collected, or from which they are made to diverge, is called the *principal focus* of a surface or substance. The principal focus of a spherical reflecting surface, whether convex or concave, is halfway between the surface and its center. If a luminous point is placed in the center of a concave mirror, the rays will all return to the same point; if the point is beyond the center, the image will be between the center and the principal focus, its distance from that focus being always inversely as that of the radiant point. Such a focus is never absolutely perfect, for the rays are never collected from the whole surface of the mirror into the same point, except when both the point and its image are in the center; but, provided that the surface is only a small portion of that of the whole sphere, the aberration will be too small to be easily observed: and the same is true of the foci produced by refracting surfaces. (Plate XXVII. Fig. 377, 378.)

When a ray of light passes through two surfaces forming an angle with each other and enclosing a denser medium, as in the case of a glass prism, it is always deflected away from the angle where the two surfaces meet. A greater number of surfaces, placed in different directions, constitute what is sometimes called a multiplying glass, each of them bending the rays of light into a different direction. (Plate XXVII. Fig. 379, 380.)

A lens is a detached portion of a transparent substance, of which the opposite sides are regular polished surfaces, of such forms as may be described by lines revolving around a common axis. These lines may be portions of circles, ellipses, hyperbolas, or any other curves, or they may be straight lines. But in general, one of the sides is a portion of a spherical surface, and the other is either a portion of a spherical surface or a plane; from which we have double convex, double concave, plano-convex, plano-concave, and meniscus lenses. The general effect of a lens may be understood by imagining its surface at any given point to coincide with that of a prism; for if the angle of the prism is *external*, as it must be when the lens is *convex*, the rays will be bent toward the *axis*; but if the base of the prism is *external* and the lens is *concave*, the rays will be deflected from the *axis*: so that a convex lens either causes all rays to *converge*, or lessens their divergence, and a concave lens either causes them to *diverge*, or lessens their *convergence*. If the radii of the surfaces are unequal, their effect will be the same as if both were equal to the harmonic mean between them, which is found by dividing the product by half the sum; or, in the case of the *meniscus*, by half the difference. Thus, if one of the radii were two inches and the other six, the effect would be the same as that of a lens with a three-inch radius; and if it were a *meniscus*, the effect would be the same as that of a lens with a six-inch radius. (Plate XXVII. Fig. 383, 384.)

The focal length of a lens made of flint glass, water, or any other substance may be found by dividing the focal length of an equivalent lens of crown glass by twice the amount the index of refraction exceeds one. Thus, since the index for water is 1⅓, we must divide the radius by ⅔, or increase it by one-half, to find the principal focal distance of a double convex or double concave lens made of water.

In order to form a picture, the rays from a great number of such points must be collected into as many distinct points of the image. Some of the rays proceeding from every radiant point must be considerably bent in order to be collected into a common focus; others remain nearly straight. If we can discover which of the rays end up either in the same line as their original direction or in a direction parallel to it, we can determine the line in which the image of the point in question is to be found. For this purpose, we use the property of the optical center, which is a point so situated that all rays passing through it, or tending toward it while they are within the lens, must ultimately acquire a direction parallel to their original direction. In some cases, the optical center may be outside the lens, but no practical inconvenience results from assuming it to be always situated within the lens, especially when its thickness is negligible. Thus, all rays passing through the middle point of the lens must proceed, without any noticeable error, in the same straight line; consequently, the image of any radiant point must be found somewhere along this line. However, in the case of a mirror, the center of its shape is also its optical center. Now, when any radiant point is moved slightly away from the axis of a lens or mirror, the distance of its image is generally slightly diminished, but the difference is too small to be observed in common cases. ## LECTURE XXXVI.

### ON OPTICAL INSTRUMENTS.

**AMONG** the great variety of instruments depending on optical principles, it is more consistent with our plan to focus first on those that may be called optical measures, which are designed either for determining the quantity or intensity of light itself, or for examining the properties of various material substances with respect to light. Reflecting quadrants and circles, which are often used in astronomical and nautical observations, although they derive their utility to some extent from optical laws, may most properly be considered as belonging to the subject of practical astronomy.

It is a frequent problem in practical investigations to compare the intensity of light provided by any two luminous objects. For this purpose, it is necessary to assume as a principle that the same quantity of light, diverging in all directions from a luminous body, remains undiminished at all distances from the center of divergence. Thus, we must suppose that the quantity of light falling on every body is the same as that which would have fallen on the area occupied by its shadow; and if there were any doubt of the truth of this supposition, it could be confirmed by some simple experiments. It follows that since the shadow of one square inch of any surface occupies, at twice the distance of the surface from the luminous point, the space of four square inches, the intensity of light diminishes as the square of the distance increases. We can judge the equality of two lights with reasonable accuracy by the judgment of the eye, but we cannot form any idea of the proportions of lights of different intensities; if, however, we move two sources of light to such distances from an object that they illuminate it to an equal degree, we may conclude that their original

Count Rumford's photometer performs this very conveniently by casting two shadows of a given object near each other on the same surface, the lights being moved to such distances that the shadows appear equally dark. (Plate XXVII, Figs. 387, 388.)

To determine the refractive density of solids, it has been customary to shape them into a prism and to measure the angular deviations they produce; and for fluids, to enclose them either in a hollow prism or between two meniscus lenses, and to measure the angular deviations produced by the prisms and the focal distances of the lenses. But in most cases, Dr. Wollaston's apparatus is far preferable to both these methods: it is designed to find the angle at which light, moving within a certain dense transparent substance, begins to be totally reflected from the common surface of that substance and the solid or fluid that is to be examined. Thus, if we first measure the angle at which light begins to be totally reflected from the back surface of a glass prism in contact with air, we may readily determine its refractive power; and then, having caused a drop of fluid to adhere to that surface, or fixed a solid to it by a small portion of some fluid denser than itself, we may observe—as we turn the prism around its axis—at what angle the drop or spot begins to disappear, and may from there calculate the refractive density of the substance. Even without actual measurement of the angle, we may readily compare the disappearance of the drop or spot with that of others placed near it, whose properties are known. Dr. Wollaston has, however, rendered the process still easier and simpler by employing a rectangular glass prism with sights fixed to a jointed frame, of such a construction as to enable him to read off, using a vernier and without any calculation, the index of the refractive power of any substance less dense than glass. (Plate XXVII, Fig. 389.)

All strictly optical instruments are employed for forming an image of an external object: the simplest are mirrors and lenses, which form a single image only, either real or virtual, and sometimes project it onto a surface designed for receiving and exhibiting it. Other instruments repeat the image once or more in several forms, generally enlarging it continu-

ally; and these are either microscopes or telescopes, which present us with great diversity in their arrangements and in the accessories that serve their purposes.

It is a general rule that when an image of an actual object is formed by any lens or speculum, if the rays converge to an actual focus, the image is inverted; but it is erect if they diverge from a virtual focus, and the object and image subtend equal angles at the center of the lens or speculum. Hence, a convex lens and a concave mirror form an inverted image, smaller than the object, whenever the object is at a greater distance than twice the principal focal length; but the image is larger when the object is within this distance. When the object is within the principal focal distance, the magnified image is virtual and erect, and may be seen by looking into the concave mirror, or by looking through the lens toward the object. But a concave lens and a convex mirror always form a virtual image of a real object, which is erect and smaller than the object. (Plate XXVII. Fig. 390 .. 394.)

When the object is precisely in the principal focus of a convex lens or a concave mirror, the virtual image becomes infinitely distant; so that from whatever point in the neighborhood of the lens it may be viewed, it must subtend the same angle, which is always equal to the angle that the object subtends at the center of the lens. Since this angle may easily be much greater than that under which the object can be conveniently viewed by the naked eye, such a lens or mirror is often used as a simple microscope; and its magnifying power may be ascertained from a comparison of the angles which the object and image subtend. Thus, if a person cannot see a minute object with the naked eye at a distance less than eight inches, a lens of half an inch focal length will represent it to him at an angle 16 times as great; but if he can see it without the lens at the distance of four inches, the lens will magnify it to his eye only eight times. Supposing, however, the eye is placed close to the lens, the object may be viewed a little within the focal distance, and its apparent angular magnitude may be increased 17 times instead of 16, and 9 times instead of 8. (Plate XXVII. Fig. 395, 396.)

Even a drop of water, placed in the perforation of a plate, makes a tolerable magnifier; and it has been proposed to substitute for water a transparent varnish, which is less liable to evaporate.

Supposing the whole light that proceeds from a distant object, and falls on a lens or speculum, to be collected in the image, its intensity must be increased in the ratio of the surface area of the lens or speculum to that of the image. The image is larger in proportion as the object is larger; consequently, the degree of condensation produced by any lens is greater as the object is smaller. Thus, if the diameter of a lens were an inch, and the image of the sun formed by it were also an inch in diameter, the density of the light would be unaltered; but the image of a star would be infinitely brighter than the direct light of the star falling on the lens. The illumination of any image formed by a lens or mirror—supposing no light is lost—is always the same as would be produced by the direct light of the surface of the lens or mirror, if it were as luminous as the surface of the object emitting the light. It may also be shown that when two lenses are of similar forms, with their focal lengths being proportional to their diameters, they must produce the same degree of illumination in the image. However, as far as the heat generated may be supposed to be a measure of the quantity of light, this conclusion is not confirmed by experiment. It is probable, however, that the greater heat produced by a larger lens is only derived from the greater extent of surface area exposed at once to the solar rays.

Lenses are most commonly made of glass, but sometimes of rock crystal, or of other transparent substances. It is difficult to find glass, especially flint glass, for large lenses that is sufficiently free from veins. It has been proposed to allow the melted glass to cool without agitation and to cut the lens out of any of its strata taken in a horizontal direction; but this method appears to be liable to several practical objections. Mirrors are made either of glass, coated with an amalgam of mercury and tin, or of metal, such as platinum, silver, or an alloy of copper and tin, to which a little arsenic and silver are sometimes added. Mirrors of metal are more perfect than those of glass because they are free from the inconvenience of a double reflection; but they

Where a large mirror is required with only a weak reflection, we may use a single surface of glass, with the back of the piece covered by a black coating of a substance that differs little from glass in its refractive density; in this way, the second reflection is avoided.

When the image formed by a lens or mirror is received on a smooth but unpolished surface capable of irregular reflection, it is visible from every direction. This type of image is shown in the camera obscura, the solar microscope, and the magic lantern (or lucernal microscope).

The general effect of the camera obscura is the same as what may often be observed in a dark room where there is a small hole in the window shutter: the large masses of light and shade in front of the windows are represented in an inverted position on the parts of the room diametrically opposite them. These areas are illuminated in different degrees, according to the amount of light that can reach them in straight lines from the external objects. A lens with a focal length somewhat smaller than the distance to the surface where the picture is projected makes the images much more distinct. However, some of them are unavoidably imperfect and ill-defined unless the objects happen to be located at the same distance from the aperture. This is because the focus of the lens can never be adjusted simultaneously for both near and more remote objects. Nor would the picture be made more natural by such an adjustment, for it would present objects to the eye with equal distinctness in a single view that could never be seen at once without some degree of confusion. Sometimes the picture is intercepted by a speculum <note>a mirror or reflector</note> placed at an angle and is thrown upward onto the surface of a plate of ground glass. Its outline may then be traced with a lead pencil, and an impression may be taken from it on moist paper, which will show the natural position of the objects without inversion. Another arrangement is to place the lens horizontally with the speculum above it, which throws the image through the lens onto a flat surface placed below. On this surface, the objects may be drawn in their natural positions, though not without some hindrance from the hand and the instrument blocking the light. To provide the most distinct image, however, such a surface should not be perfectly flat, although by using a meniscus <note>a lens that is convex on one side and concave on the other</note>

It has been common to consider the image of a very distant object, formed by a convex lens, as a portion of a spherical surface of which every part is equally distant from the center of the lens; but this estimate is extremely erroneous, for the effect of the obliquity of the different pencils of rays materially increases the curvature of the image. In fact, no pencil of rays falling obliquely on a spherical surface can be collected anywhere into a perfect focus: the image of a circle would become most distinct at one distance, and that of its diameter at another; but for both these images, the surface ought to be much more curved than what has been usually considered. The average of the curvatures required for them—which must be the best form for the ground or bottom of a <term>camera obscura</term>—is equal to that of a sphere with a radius of three-eighths of the focal distance, when a double convex lens of crown glass is employed. (Plate XXVII. Fig. 397 . . 399.)

In the solar microscope, an image is formed on a wall or screen by means of a lens of small focal length, near to which the object is placed, so that the image is very much magnified. For this purpose, the room must be darkened and the object strongly illuminated by sunlight, which is condensed by means of a large lens, and sometimes by two or more lenses placed at a distance from each other; but care must be taken to avoid burning the object by bringing it exactly into the focus; and, on the other hand, if it is much beyond the focus, the light will be thrown upon a small part of the image only. The best arrangement appears to be to bring the focus of the condensing lenses very near to the small lens; and in order to adjust the instrument in the most convenient manner, the distances of all the lenses ought to be movable at pleasure: the want of this precaution is a material defect in the usual construction of the instrument. The <term>speculum</term> which first receives the light must be capable of motion in all angular directions, in order to allow us to accommodate its position to the changing place of the sun; and the adjustment has sometimes been performed by means of a <term>heliostate</term>, an instrument calculated for turning the speculum

By night, a lamp with a large lens before it may take the place of sunlight, and the instrument will become a lucernal microscope. When painted glass slides are used as objects for the amusement of children, it is called a magic lantern. When exhibited on a larger scale and projecting an image onto a semi-transparent screen of taffeta instead of a wall, this has recently been a source of much entertainment under the name of the *phantasmagoria*—a term that implies the raising of *specters*. To favor the deception, the slides are made perfectly opaque except where the figures are introduced; the glass is covered in the light parts with a more or less transparent tint, according to the required effect. Several pieces of glass may also occasionally be placed behind each other and can be made capable of motions that nearly imitate the natural movements of the objects they represent. The figures may also be drawn with watercolors on thin paper and afterwards varnished. By moving the lantern to different distances and simultaneously altering the position of the lens more or less, the image can be made to increase or diminish and to become more or less distinct at will. Thus, to a person unaccustomed to the effects of optical instruments, the figures may appear to actually advance and retreat. In reality, however, these figures become much brighter as they are made smaller, while in nature, the imperfect transparency of the air causes them to appear fainter when they are remote than when they are near. This discrepancy could be easily remedied by placing some semi-opaque substance in between, which could be gradually made to admit more light as the figure grew larger, or by uncovering a larger or smaller portion of the lamp or its lens. In almost all <term>telescopes</term> and <term>compound microscopes</term>, the image formed by one <term>lens</term> or <term>mirror</term> acts as a new object for another. The operation of such instruments may be illustrated by placing a screen of fine gauze at the location of the image, which receives enough light to make the image visible in all directions, and yet transmits enough to form the subsequent image. The simplest of these instruments is the <term>astronomical telescope</term>. Here, the <term>object glass</term> first forms a real <term>inverted image</term>, nearly at the <term>principal focus</term> of the <term>eye glass</term>, through which this image is viewed as if by a <term>simple microscope</term>, and therefore it still remains apparently inverted. In order to find the <term>angular magnifying power</term>, we must divide the <term>focal length</term> of the <term>object glass</term> by that of the <term>eye glass</term>. This quotient consequently becomes greater as the <term>focal length</term> of the <term>object glass</term> is larger, and as that of the <term>eye glass</term> is smaller. However, the power of the instrument cannot be increased at will by reducing the <term>focal length</term> of the <term>eye glass</term>, because the <term>object glass</term> would not provide enough light to make the view distinct if the magnifying power were too great. (Plate XXVIII. Fig. 402.)

(Plate XXVIII. Fig. 405.)

Dr. Herschel's <term>reflecting telescopes</term> resemble the simple astronomical telescope in their effects; a concave <term>speculum</term>, or mirror, is substituted for the objective lens, and the <term>eyeglass</term> is placed so as to magnify the image formed by the speculum. But since the speculum, if it received the principal rays perpendicularly, would send them back in the same direction, it is necessary in this construction to have them reflected somewhat obliquely. The speculum is slightly inclined to the axis of the telescope so that the light may have free access to it. An arrangement of this kind was proposed long ago by *Maire*, but it was very little used before Dr. Herschel's time. This excellent philosopher and mechanic has carried the perfection of his telescopes to a degree far exceeding all that could have been expected from the labors of former opticians. The <term>Newtonian reflector</term> has a plane <term>speculum</term> placed in its axis, at an inclination of 45 degrees (half a right angle), which intercepts the rays about to form the image and throws them into the focus of an <term>eyeglass</term> fixed in the side of the tube. The plane <term>speculum</term> which Newton employed was the posterior surface of a rectangular prism of glass, which produces a total reflection; but Dr. Herschel has found that the sources of error are diminished by wholly omitting this <term>speculum</term>. (Plate XXVIII. Fig. 407.)

In the <term>Gregorian telescope</term>, the objective <term>speculum</term> is perforated, and the image formed by it is received into the focus of a smaller <term>concave speculum</term>, which returns it to be viewed through the aperture by the <term>eyeglasses</term>. It has been objected to this form of the reflecting telescope—which is the first that was invented—that the best part of the <term>speculum</term> is sacrificed by the perforation. But Dr. Herschel has found that the image formed by the external part of a <term>speculum</term> is in general more perfect than that which is formed by the central part. (Plate XXVIII. Fig. 408.)

For the smaller <term>concave speculum</term> of Gregory, Mr. <term>Cassegrain</term> substituted a convex one, placing it within the focal distance of the large <term>speculum</term>, so as to form the first actual image nearly in the same place as the second image of the <term>Gregorian telescope</term>; but this image is inverted. The instrument has some advantage in theory with respect to the perfection of the focus, but it is little used. (Plate XXVIII. Fig. 409.)

Dr. Smith’s <term>reflecting microscope</term> resembles <term>Cassegrain</term>’s telescope, but the rays of light are first admitted through a perforation in the small <term>speculum</term>, while that part of them which tends to fall immediately on the eye is intercepted by a screen. The convexity of the one mirror is nearly equal to the concavity of the other; and the instrument, although seldom employed, is said to succeed extremely well. (Plate XXVIII. Fig. 410.)

The <term>magnifying power</term> of a <term>refracting telescope</term> can often be measured by comparing the diameter of the <term>object glass</term> with the diameter of the narrowest space into which the beam of light contracts beyond the <term>eyepiece</term>, provided that none of the light has been intercepted in its passage through the telescope. This is because the object will be viewed through the telescope at an angle as much greater than its natural size as the diameter of the <term>object glass</term> is greater than the diameter of this contracted beam, which may be considered an image of the <term>object glass</term>. However, in the <term>Galilean telescope</term>, this method cannot be employed, since no such image is formed. The <term>field of view</term> in a simple telescope—or the angular magnitude of that part of an object which can be seen through it at once—is nearly equal to the size of the <term>eyepiece</term> as seen from the <term>object glass</term>.

If a lens is added to any <term>refracting telescope</term> at the position of the first image, it will have no effect on either the location or the magnitude of any subsequent image, but it will enlarge the <term>field of view</term> by directing more beams of light toward the original <term>eyepiece</term>. If, however, the image fell exactly on such a lens, it would be liable to be impaired by any accidental impurities within the glass or on its surface, as every opaque particle would intercept all of the light belonging to one of its points; this would not happen if the image were at a small distance from the lens. A <term>field glass</term> is, therefore, usually placed, both in telescopes and in the common <term>compound microscope</term>, a little closer to the <term>object glass</term> than the position of the first image. The curvature of the image produced by any lens has already been mentioned: it may be remedied to some extent by Mr. Ramsden’s method of placing a <term>planoconvex lens</term> a little beyond the image, with its flat side turned towards it. The <term>aberration</term> of the different parts of any single pencil of rays from the corresponding point of the image also needs to be considered in the construction of telescopes. Its magnitude is such, in the case of a double convex lens of <term>crown glass</term>, that those parts of a pencil of parallel rays which fall on it near the circumference meet each other at a point within the true focus, at a distance slightly more than one and a half times the thickness of the lens. In an image formed by a <term>concave speculum</term> of equal <term>focal length</term>, this <term>aberration</term> would be only one-fifteenth as great; it may, however, be almost entirely corrected in <term>refracting telescopes</term> by employing proper proportions in the dimensions of the various lenses. (Plate XXVIII. Figures 412, 413.)

A still more important <term>aberration</term>, from which reflecting telescopes are also wholly free, is that which arises from the different <term>refrangibilities</term> of the rays of light of different colors. These form an infinite number of images that do not perfectly agree in either position or magnitude, so that objects are rendered indistinct by the appearance of colors at their edges. This imperfection, however, Mr. Dollond has largely overcome with his <term>achromatic object glasses</term>. The construction of these depends on the important discovery that some kinds of glass separate the rays of different colors from each other much more than others, even while the total deviation produced in the pencil of light remains the same. Mr. Dollond therefore combined a concave lens of <term>flint glass</term> with a convex lens of <term>crown glass</term>, and sometimes with two such lenses. proportion to the <term>dispersive powers</term> of the respective substances when the <term>mean deviations</term> of the pencils are equal; that is, in the case of the kinds of glass commonly used, nearly in the ratio of 7 to 10. Sometimes also the <term>chromatic aberration</term>—that is, the error arising from the different <term>refrangibilities</term> of the different rays—is partially corrected in an eyepiece by placing a <term>field glass</term> in such a manner as to considerably contract the dimensions of the image formed by the least refrangible rays (which is nearest to the <term>eyeglass</term>), and to cause it to subtend an equal angle with the image formed by the most refrangible rays, this image being little affected by the glass. (Plate XXVIII. Fig. 414, 415.)

The apparent magnitude of an object viewed through a telescope may be measured with great accuracy by a scale or by wires introduced at the place of the last image, reducing afterwards the angle thus ascertained according to the magnifying power. Care must, however, be taken to avoid as much as possible the distortion which usually accompanies any curvature of the image; and the wires—one of which is sometimes made movable by means of a <term>micrometer screw</term>—must be sufficiently illuminated to be distinctly visible. Sometimes a scale is introduced which, from the apparent magnitude of a known object (such as that of a man of ordinary height, or of a portion of a wall built with bricks of the usual size), enables us at once to read off its actual distance, which is expressed on the scale in hundreds of yards. The angular magnitude of an object seen through a telescope may also be found by viewing at the same time, with the other eye, either a scale or any other object of known dimensions placed at a given distance; the <term>lucid disc micrometer</term> of <term>Dr. Herschel</term> is employed in this manner for judging of the magnitude of the <term>celestial bodies</term>. The <term>divided object glass micrometer</term> affords another mode of measurement: the object glass being divided into two semicircular portions, one of which slides on the other; each portion acts as a separate lens, and two images of every part of the object being formed, the angular distance of any two points is determined by bringing their images together and measuring the displacement of the movable portion of the object glass which is required for procuring the coincidence. Sometimes also a similar purpose is served by inserting a divided glass in the eyepiece, which acts nearly on the same

## LECTURE XXXVII.

### ON PHYSICAL OPTICS.

**H**aving examined the general theory of optics and the construction of optical instruments, we are now to consider those properties and attributes of light which belong more to its natural history than to its mechanical effects. We will trace its relationships to the specific phenomena of nature, investigate the way in which it is connected with our sensations, and inquire into the underlying mechanisms upon which the various effects of light depend. All these subjects may be properly categorized under the name of physical optics, but we shall find it convenient to reserve each of the last two for a separate examination. The sources of light, the speed of its motion, its interception and extinction, its dispersion into different colors, the way it is affected by the variable density of the atmosphere, the meteorological phenomena in which it is involved, and the unique properties of specific substances regarding it, will be the first subjects of our investigation.

The sources from which light is commonly derived are either the sun and stars, or such terrestrial bodies as are undergoing the changes that constitute combustion. The process of combustion implies a change in which a significant emission of light and heat is produced, but it is not capable of a very precise definition. In general, it requires an absorption, or at least a transfer, of a portion of oxygen; however, there appear to be some exceptions to the universality of this distinction. It has been observed that both heat and light are often produced where no transfer of oxygen takes place, and sometimes by the effect of a mixture that cannot be called combustion.

Light is also provided, without any perceptible heat, by a number of vegetable

and animal substances, which appear to be undergoing a slow decomposition, not wholly unlike combustion. Thus decayed wood and animal substances that are slightly salted often spontaneously provide a faint light without any increase in temperature; and it is not improbable that the light of the <term>ignis fatuus</term> <note>a swamp light, or will-o'-the-wisp</note> may proceed from a vapor of a similar nature.

The effects which are commonly attributed to the motions of the electrical fluid are often accompanied by the production of light; and violent or rapid friction frequently seems to be the immediate cause of its appearance. But it is difficult to determine whether friction may not be partly involved in the luminous phenomena attributed to electricity, or electricity in the apparent effects of friction. Light is sometimes produced by friction with a much lower degree of heat than is required for combustion; and even when it is accompanied by combustion, the heat produced by the combination of these causes may be very moderate. For instance, it is common in some coal mines to obtain a stream of light by the continual collision of flint and steel, produced by the machine called a fire wheel, in order to avoid setting fire to the inflammable gas emitted by the coal, which would be made to explode if it came near the flame of a candle.

There is a remarkable property which some substances possess to a high degree, and of which few substances, except metals and water, are entirely without. These substances are called <term>solar phosphori</term>; besides the light which they reflect and refract, they appear to retain a certain portion and to emit it again gradually until it is exhausted, or until its emission is interrupted by cold. The <term>Bolognan phosphorus</term> was one of the first of these substances that attracted notice; it is a sulfate of barytes, found in the state of a stone. It is prepared by exposure to heat and is afterwards made up into cakes; these, when first placed in a beam of sunlight and viewed afterwards in a dark room, have nearly the appearance of a burning coal or a red-hot iron. Burnt oyster shells and muriate of lime <note>calcium chloride</note> also have the same property, and some specimens of diamond possess it to a considerable degree. From the differing results of experiments that are apparently accurate, made by different people, there is reason to conclude that some of these phosphori emit only the same kind of light as they have received, while others exhibit the same appearance regardless of the kind of light to which they have been exposed. Sometimes it has even been found that light of a particular color has been most effica-

[effica]cious in producing in a diamond the appearance of another kind of light, which it was naturally most inclined to show. The application of heat to solar <term>phosphori</term> <note>substances that emit light after being exposed to radiation</note> generally speeds up the release of the light they have absorbed and hastens its depletion. In many substances that are not particularly known for their power to absorb light, heat also produces a temporary sparkling, or flashing, at a temperature much lower than what is needed for ignition; the most remarkable of these are powdered <term>fluor spar</term> <note>fluorite</note> and certain other crystallized substances. It appears that luminous bodies generally emit light equally in every direction—not from each individual point of their surfaces, as some have supposed, but from the entire surface as a whole. Thus, when viewed at an angle, the surface appears neither more nor less bright than when viewed directly.

However light of any kind may have first originated, there is reason to believe that the velocity at which it passes through a specific medium is always the same. It has been confirmed by the astronomical observations of Roemer and Bradley that every ray of light emitted by the sun reaches the earth in eight and one-eighth minutes, when the earth is at its average distance of about 95 million miles. Roemer calculated this velocity from observations of the eclipses of the <term>satellites of Jupiter</term>, and Bradley confirmed it through his discovery of the cause of the apparent <term>aberration</term> of the fixed stars.

This aberration is produced by the effect of the earth’s revolution in its orbit combined with the forward motion of light. Since light always travels in straight lines when its motion is perfectly uninterrupted, if a narrow tube were placed to receive a ray of light passing exactly through its center while at rest, and then—remaining pointed in the same direction—were moved sideways at a high speed, it is clear that the side of the tube would strike against the ray of light as it passed. In order to keep the light in the center, the tube would have to be tilted, just as if the light, instead of coming from its actual direction, also had a sideways motion in the opposite direction of the tube's movement. The axis of a telescope, or even the eye, may be considered similar to such a tube, as the passage of light through refracting substances does not change the necessary tilt of the axis. At various points in the earth’s orbit, the aberration
