The quantity of light reflected by a substance of any kind depends not only on the nature of the substance, but also on the obliquity <note>the angle at which light hits a surface</note> of its incidence: and it sometimes happens that a surface, which reflects a smaller portion of direct light than another, reflects a greater portion when the light falls very obliquely on its surface. Bouguer found that the surface of water reflected only one fifty-fifth part of the light falling perpendicularly on it, that of glass one-fortieth, and that of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> more than two-thirds; but when the obliquity was as great as possible, the water reflected nearly three-fourths of the incident light, and the glass only about two-thirds.

Of the light which passes by a dense substance of any kind, the greatest part continues its course undisturbed, but there is always a certain divergence, which has been called by Grimaldi <term>diffraction</term>, and by Newton <term>inflection</term>. This effect is usually accompanied by the production of colors and will, therefore, require to be more particularly considered hereafter.

<margin>
[handwritten mark]
</margin>
The separation of colors by refraction is one of the most striking of all optical phenomena. It was discovered by Newton that white light is a compound of rays of different kinds, mixed in a certain proportion; that these rays differ in color and in <term>refrangibility</term> <note>the ability to be refracted, or bent, when passing from one medium to another</note>; that they constitute a series which proceeds by gradual changes from red to violet; and that those substances which appear colored when placed in white light derive their colors only from the property of reflecting some kinds of rays most abundantly, and of transmitting or extinguishing the rest. Dr. Herschel has added to this series rays of heat less refrangible than the red, and Ritter and Dr. Wollaston have discovered, beyond the violet, other still more refrangible rays which blacken the salts of silver.

It has generally been supposed, since the time of Newton, that when the rays of light are separated as completely as possible by means of refraction, they exhibit seven varieties of color, related to each

other with respect to the space they occupy, in ratios almost identical to those of the ascending scale of the minor mode in music. The observations were, however, imperfect, and the analogy was completely imaginary. Dr. Wollaston has determined the division of the colored image, or spectrum, much more accurately than had been done before: by looking through a prism at a narrow line of light, he produces a more effective separation of the colors than can be achieved by the common method of projecting the sun's image onto a wall. The spectrum formed in this way consists of only four colors: red, green, blue, and violet. These occupy spaces in the proportions of 16, 23, 36, and 25, respectively, totaling 100 for the entire length; the red being nearly one-sixth, the green and the violet each about one-fourth, and the blue more than one-third of the length. Within their respective limits, the colors hardly differ at all in quality, but they vary in brightness; the light is most intense in the part of the green closest to the red. A narrow yellow line is usually visible at the border between the red and green, but its width barely exceeds that of the opening through which the light enters. Dr. Wollaston attributes this to the mixing of the red and green light. There are also several dark lines crossing the spectrum within and near the blue portion, where the continuity of the light seems to be interrupted. Dr. Wollaston has found this distribution of the spectrum to be the same regardless of which refracting substance was used to form it; he attributes the differences in proportions sometimes observed to accidental variations in the angle of the rays. The angular extent of the spectrum formed by a prism of crown glass is one-27th of the deviation of the red rays; with a prism of flint glass, it is one-19th. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 419.)

In light produced by the burning of terrestrial substances, the spectrum is sometimes even more interrupted. For instance, the bluish light at the base of a candle flame is separated by refraction into five distinct sections of various colors. The light from burning spirits, which looks perfectly blue, is mainly composed of green and violet rays. The light from a candle with salt thrown into it is full of a pure yellow, bordering on green, but cannot be further separated by refraction. The electric spark also provides a light that is divided differently in various circumstances. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 420.)

¶ If the width of the opening viewed through a prism is somewhat increased, the space occupied by each variety of light in the spectrum is increased in the same proportion, and each portion overlaps with the neighboring colors and is mixed with them: so that the red is followed by orange, yellow, and yellowish green, and the blue is mixed on the one side with the green and on the other with the violet; and it is in this state that the prismatic spectrum is usually shown. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 421.)

¶ When the beam of light is enlarged so much that it exceeds the angular size of the spectrum, it stays white in the center and is bordered by two different sets of colors at the different ends. These series are still divided by clearly defined lines: on the one hand, the red remains unmixed; the space belonging to the green and blue becomes a nearly uniform greenish yellow throughout, and here the appearance of color ends, with the position of the violet being hardly distinguishable from the neighboring white light; on the other hand, the space belonging to the red, green, and blue of the simple spectrum appears bluish green, becoming more and more blue until it meets the violet, which keeps its place without change. This second series is also the same one that accompanies the limit of total reflection at the back surface of a prism. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 422.)

¶ Sir Isaac Newton observed that the effect of white light on the sense of sight might be imitated by a mixture of colors taken from different parts of the spectrum, despite omitting some of the rays naturally belonging to white light. For example, if we block one half of each of the four principal portions into which the spectrum is divided, the remaining halves will still maintain the appearance of whiteness when mixed together; so it is probable that the different parts of those portions of the spectrum which appear as one color have exactly the same effect on the eye. It is certain that the perfect sensations of yellow and of blue are produced, respectively, by mixtures of red and green light, and of green and violet light, and there is reason to suspect that those sensations are always made up of separate sensations combined; at least, this theory simplifies the study of colors. It may, therefore, be adopted with advantage until it is found to be inconsistent with any of the phenomena; and we may consider white light as composed of

If we mix together, in proper proportions, any substances that exhibit these colors in their greatest purity, and place the mixture in a light sufficiently strong, we obtain the appearance of perfect whiteness; but in a fainter light, the mixture is gray, or that hue which arises from a combination of white and black—black bodies being those that reflect white light only in a very small proportion. For the same reason, green and red substances mixed together usually make a brown rather than a yellow color; and many yellow colors, when applied very thickly or mixed with black, become brown. The sensations of various kinds of light may also be combined in a still more satisfactory manner by painting the surface of a circle with different colors, in any way that may be desired, and causing it to revolve with such rapidity that the whole assumes the appearance of a single tint, or of a combination of tints resulting from the mixture of the colors. (*Plate XXIX. Fig. 423 . . 426.*)

From three simple sensations, along with their combinations, we obtain seven primitive distinctions of colors; but the different proportions in which they may be combined provide a variety of tints beyond all calculation. The three simple sensations being red, green, and violet, the three binary combinations are yellow, composed of red and green; crimson, of red and violet; and blue, of green and violet; and the seventh in order is white light, composed of all three united. However, the blue produced this way by combining all the green and violet rays is not the blue of the spectrum, for four parts of green and one of violet make a blue that differs very little from green, while the blue of the spectrum appears to contain as much violet as green. It is for this reason that red and blue usually make a purple, deriving its hue from the dominance of the violet.

It would be possible to display to the eye all at once the combinations of any three colors in every imaginable variety. Two of them could be laid down on a revolving surface in the form of triangles placed in opposite directions, and the third on projections perpendicular to the surface, which, while the eye remained at rest in any one point situated obliquely, would

The same effect may also be shown by mixing the colors in different proportions using a brush, beginning from three equidistant <margin>| ↑</margin> points as the centers of the respective colors (Plate XXIX, Fig. 427).

Ordinary atmospheric refraction cannot be determined in the usual manner from knowledge of its density and of the angular direction of the incident or refracted light. This is because the composition of the atmosphere is such that its density varies everywhere according to its height, and the curvature of the Earth's surface causes the inclination of the layers through which the ray passes to be constantly changing. The difference in temperature at different elevations also increases the difficulty of an exact calculation, and it is only very recently that Mr. Laplace, by comparing astronomical with meteorological observations, has provided a satisfactory solution to the problem in its full extent. But for practical purposes, refraction may be determined with sufficient accuracy by an approximation that is easily remembered: the deviation at all altitudes is one-sixth as great as the refraction a ray would undergo at the horizontal surface of a medium six times as dense as air. When a celestial object appears exactly on the horizon, it is actually more than half a degree below it, since the refraction amounts to 33 minutes when the barometer stands at 29.6 inches and Fahrenheit’s thermometer is at 50°.

Accidental variations in the temperature of the air in different areas, however, produce great irregularities in its refraction, especially near the horizon. The most remarkable of these is caused by the thinning of the air near the surface of water, a building, or the earth itself. As a result, a distant object appears to be lowered instead of being raised, and is sometimes seen as both lowered and raised at once, appearing double; one of the images is generally in an inverted position, as if the surface possessed a reflective power. There seems indeed to be a significant analogy between this kind of refraction and the total reflection that occurs within a denser medium. These effects are known by the names *looming*, *mirage*, and *Fata Morgana*:

they may be very completely imitated, as Dr. Wollaston has shown, by looking at a distant object along a red-hot poker, or through a saline or saccharine solution with water and spirits of wine floating on it. The effect of refraction on the apparent positions of terrestrial objects must be frequently disturbed by circumstances of this kind; but its magnitude is usually about one-tenth of the angular distance of the object, considered as a part of the earth's circumference. The atmospheric phenomena of rainbows and halos present us with examples of the spontaneous separation of colors by refraction. The rainbow is universally attributed to the refraction and reflection of the sun's rays in the minute drops of falling rain or dew, and the halos, usually appearing in frosty atmospheres, are in all probability produced by the refraction of small triangular or hexagonal crystals of snow. It is only necessary, for the formation of a rainbow, that the sun should shine on a dense cloud, or a shower of rain, in a proper situation, or even on a number of minute drops of water, scattered by a brush or by a syringe, so that the light may reach the eye after having undergone a certain angular deviation, by means of various refractions and reflections; and the drops so situated must necessarily be found somewhere on a conical surface, of which the eye is the vertex, and must present the appearance of an arch. The light which is reflected by the external surface of a sphere is scattered almost equally in all directions, setting aside the difference arising from the greater efficacy of oblique reflection; but when it first enters the drop, and is there reflected by its posterior surface, its deviation never exceeds a certain angle, which depends on the degree of <term>refrangibility</term>, and is, therefore, different for light of different colors: and the density of the light being the greatest at the angle of greatest deviation, the appearance of a luminous arch is produced by the rays of each color at its appropriate distance. The rays which never enter the drops produce no other effect than to cause a brightness or haziness around the sun, where the reflection is the most oblique: those which are once reflected within the drop exhibit the common internal or primary rainbow, at the distance of about 41 degrees from the point opposite to the sun: those which are twice reflected exhibit the external or secondary rainbow of 52°: and if the effect of the light three times reflected were sufficiently powerful, it would appear at the distance of about 42 degrees from the sun. The colors of both rainbows encroach considerably on each

There is, however, another cause for a further mixture of the colors: the arch of any single color, which belongs to any point of the sun, is accurately defined on one side only, while on the other it becomes gradually fainter, the breadth of the first minute containing about five times as much light as a minute at the distance of a quarter of a degree. The abrupt termination is on the side of the red—that is, outside the inner bow and inside the outer—so that, for this reason, the order of colors partakes, in some degree, of the nature of the red termination of a broad beam of light seen through a prism. However, it is more or less affected by this cause on account of some circumstances, which will be explained when we examine the supernumerary rainbows that sometimes accompany the bows more commonly observed. A lunar rainbow is much more rarely seen than a solar one, but its colors differ little, except in intensity, from those of the common rainbow. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 430.)

In the highest northern latitudes, where the air is commonly loaded with frozen particles, the sun and moon usually appear surrounded by <term>halos</term> or colored circles, at distances of about 22 and 46 degrees from their centers. This appearance is also frequently observed in other climates, especially in the colder months, and in the light clouds which float in the highest regions of the air. The <term>halos</term> are usually accompanied by a horizontal white circle, with brighter spots, or <term>parhelia</term>, near their intersections with this circle, and with portions of inverted arches of various curvatures. The horizontal circle also sometimes has <term>anthelia</term>, or bright spots nearly opposite to the sun. These phenomena have usually been attributed to the effect of spherical particles of hail, each having a central opaque portion of a certain magnitude, mixed with oblong particles of a specific form, floating with a certain constant obliquity to the horizon. But all these arbitrary suppositions, which were imagined by Huygens, are in themselves extremely complicated and improbable, and are wholly unauthorized by observation. A much simpler, and more natural, as well as more accurate explanation, which was suggested at an earlier period by Mariotte, had long been completely forgotten until the same idea occurred to me, without any previous knowledge of what Mariotte had done. The natural tendency of water to crystallize, in

<meta>This page continues the discussion of atmospheric optics, specifically examining how the hexagonal or triangular structure of ice crystals and their refractive properties explain the formation of various halos and parhelia.</meta>

<page-num>444</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XXXVII.</header>

Freezing at an angle of 60 degrees is sufficiently established to allow us to assume this as the constant angle of the elementary crystals of snow, which are probably either triangular or hexagonal prisms. The deviation produced by such a prism differs very little from the observed angle at which the first circle is usually seen; and all the principal phenomena that attend this circle may be explained by supposing the axes of the crystals to assume a vertical or horizontal position as a result of gravity. Thus the <term>parhelia</term>, which are sometimes a little further from the sun than the <term>halo</term>, are attributed by Mariotte to the refraction of prisms situated vertically, which produce a greater deviation because of the obliquity of the light rays relative to their axes. The horizontal circle may be deduced from the reflection, or even repeated refractions, of the vertical facets; the <term>anthelia</term> from two refractions with an intermediate reflection; and the inverted arch from the increase of deviation in light passing obliquely through prisms lying in a horizontal position. The external circle may be attributed either to two successive refractions through different prisms or, with greater probability, as Mr. Cavendish has suggested to me, to the effect of the rectangular terminations of single crystals. The appearance of colors in halos is nearly the same as in rainbows, but less distinct; the red is nearest to the luminary, and the entire halo is very poorly defined on its outer edge. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 431, 432.)

From the observed magnitude of these halos, I had concluded that the <term>refractive power</term> of ice must be significantly less than that of water, although some authors had asserted that it was greater. Dr. Wollaston later fully confirmed this conclusion using the very accurate instrument already described; his measurement agreed precisely with the average of the best observations of these halos, so that ice must be considered the least refractive of all known substances that are not <term>aeriform</term>.

Sometimes the figures of halos and <term>parhelia</term> are so extremely complicated that they defy all attempts to account for the formation of their various parts. However, if we examine the representations given by various authors of the many capricious forms frequently assumed by snowflakes, we shall see no reason to think them inadequate to produce all these appearances. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 433, 434.)

<page-num>445</page-num>
<header>ON PHYSICAL OPTICS.</header>

The most remarkable of all the phenomena of refraction is perhaps the property of certain natural substances which have a double effect on the light transmitted through them, as if two mediums of different densities freely occupied the same space—one acting only on some of the rays of light, and the other acting on the rest. These substances are usually crystalline minerals, and their refractions often have no further unusual features; however, the rhomboidal crystals of <term>calcareous spar</term>, commonly called <term>Iceland spar</term>, possess the remarkable property of separating beams of light that fall perpendicularly on them into two parts: one part is transmitted in the usual manner, while the other is deflected toward the larger angle of the crystal. It appears from the experiments of Huygens, confirmed and extended by Dr. Wollaston, that the medium causing the unusual refraction has a different refractive power depending on the direction in which the light passes through it. If an <term>oblate</term> (or flattened) spheroid is defined within a crystal—with its axis in the middle of one of the obtuse solid angles and its principal diameters in the proportion of 9 to 10—the <term>refractive power</term> for light passing in any direction will always be inversely proportional to the diameter of the spheroid parallel to that direction. Where the refractive power is greatest, it will be equal to that of the medium producing the ordinary refraction, which has an index of 5/3. A ray of light falling perpendicularly on any surface of the spar—with its point of incidence considered the center of the spheroid—will meet the surface of the spheroid at the point where it is parallel to the surface of the spar; a ray incident on the same surface in any other direction will maintain a relationship to the perpendicular ray nearly identical to that in ordinary refraction. (Plate XXIX. Fig. 435.)

It is also remarkable that the two portions of light separated in this way will not be further subdivided when passing through a second piece of spar, provided that this piece is in a position parallel to the first. However, if it is placed in a transverse direction, each of the two pencils of light will be divided into two others—a circumstance that appears to be the most incomprehensible discovery regarding the phenomena of <term>double refraction</term>.

# LECTURE XXXVIII.

## ON VISION.

The medium of communication through which we become acquainted with all the objects that we have been lately considering is the eye; an organ that exhibits, to an attentive observer, an arrangement of various substances so correctly and delicately adapted to the purposes of the sense of vision that we cannot help admiring, at every step, the wisdom by which each part is adjusted to the rest and made to contribute to effects so remote from what the mere external appearance promises. We have only been able to understand, through laborious investigation, the nature and operations of this wonderful structure, while its entire mechanism still remains far beyond any competition from human art.

The eye is an irregular spheroid, not very different from a sphere; it is principally composed of transparent substances of various refractive densities, designed to collect the rays of light—which diverge from each point of an object—to a focus on its posterior surface. This surface is capable of transmitting to the mind the impression of the color and intensity of the light, together with a distinction of the location of the focal point, as determined by the angular position of the object. (Plate XXX. Fig. 436.)

The first refraction happens at the surface of the cornea, or that transparent coat which projects forward from the eyeball; but the cornea, being of very nearly uniform thickness, has little effect by its own refractive power and serves only to give a proper form to the aqueous humor, which fills its concavity and distends it. This humor is partially divided by the uvea or iris, which is of different colors in different persons, having a perforation in its center called the pupil. Immediately behind the uvea, and closely connected to its base, are the ciliary processes, the summits of which hang,

The remaining cavity is filled by an aqueous fluid, contained within a cellular structure of extremely fine membrane, called the vitreous humor. The retina lines the entire posterior part of this cavity; it is semitransparent and is supported by the choroid (or chorioid) coat, a very opaque black or brown membrane continued from the uvea and ciliary processes. However, at the point where the retina connects with the optic nerve, the choroid is necessarily perforated; at this location, a small portion of the retina is nearly insensitive. The entire eye is surrounded by an opaque continuation of the cornea called the sclerotica.

The rays of light that enter the cornea and pass through the pupil are made even more convergent by the crystalline lens. They are collected into focal points on the retina and form an image there which, according to the standard laws of refraction, is inverted, because the central rays of each beam cross one another slightly behind the pupil. This image can easily be seen in a dissected eye by exposing the posterior surface of the retina. (Plate XXX. Fig. 437.)

By means of this arrangement of the various refracting substances, several unique advantages are obtained. If the surface of the cornea alone had been more convex, it could not have collected the lateral rays of a direct beam into a perfect focus without a different curvature near its edges; in that case, the oblique beams would have been subject to greater aberration, and they could not have been made to converge onto any focal point on the retina. A second refraction performs both these functions much more completely and also has the advantage of admitting a greater quantity of light. Additionally, if the surfaces of the interposed crystalline lens had been abrupt, there would have been a reflection at each surface, and a visible haziness would have interfered with the clear view of every luminous object. This inconvenience is avoided by the gradual increase of density toward the center, which also makes the crystalline lens equivalent to a much more refractive substance of equal size. At the same time, the lower density of the lateral parts prevents the usual aberration of spherical surfaces—caused by the excessive refraction of the side rays of direct beams—and also causes the...

Opticians have often puzzled themselves, without the least necessity, to account for our seeing objects in their natural upright position, while the image on the retina is in reality inverted. But surely the location of a focal point at the upper part of the eye could be no reason for supposing the object corresponding to it to be actually elevated. We call that the lower end of an object which is closest to the ground; and since the image of the trunk of a tree is in contact with the image of the ground on the retina, we may naturally suppose the trunk itself to be in contact with the actual ground. Because the image of the branches is more remote from that of the ground, we necessarily infer that the branches are higher and the trunk lower. It is much simpler that we should compare the image of the floor with the image of our feet, with which it is in contact, than with the actual location of our forehead, to which the image of the floor on the retina is only accidentally near, and with which indeed it would perhaps be impossible to compare it, as far as we judge by immediate sensations only.

We might indeed call in experience to our assistance and habitually correct the errors of one sense by a comparison with the perceptions of another. But it appears that some philosophers have been too hasty in supposing that the use of all our senses is derived from experience alone, and in disbelieving the existence of instinct independent of it. Without any other authority than that of their own imaginations, they have denied the observation recorded by Galen on the instincts of a kid, which is sufficiently credible to counterbalance much more than bare assertion. The instant after its birth, despite the loss of its mother, the little animal ran to some green vegetables, and having first smelled them, chewed and swallowed them. The kid could have been taught by no experience to be tempted by sight, to move with the proper muscles of locomotion, to go near and smell, and to be induced by the smell to chew, and by the taste to swallow and digest its food, if it had not been provided with some fundamental instinct by the same intelligence which so calculated the adjustments of the eye that the lens should be able to produce a perfect image of every object, and that the

The entire surface of the retina usually appears to be occupied by such an image, but it is not all of equal sensitivity; only a certain portion, near the axis, is capable of conveying distinct impressions of minute objects. However, the perfection of this limited clarity is a far greater advantage to us than a wider field of moderately accurate vision would have been; for by using the external muscles, we can easily change the position of the eye so that the image of any object before us may fall on the most sensitive part of the retina. We can readily observe the lack of sensation at the entrance of the optic nerve by placing two candles so that the distance of each from the eye is about four times their distance from each other. Then, if we direct our right eye to the left-hand candle, the right-hand candle will be lost in a confused mass of faint light, as its image on the retina falls on the point where its sensitivity is lacking.

When the attention is not directed to any specific object of sight, the refractive powers of the eye are suited to forming an image of objects at only a certain distance, which varies between individuals and also generally increases with age. Thus, if we open our eyelids suddenly without special preparation, we find that only distant objects appear as clear as we are able to make them; but by an effort of will, the eye can be adjusted to the clear perception of closer objects, though not of objects within certain limits. Between the ages of 40 and 50, the refractive powers of the eye usually begin to decrease, but it sometimes happens that where they are already too strong, the defect continues unchanged into old age. It also appears that after 50 or 60, the ability to change the eye’s focus is always greatly impaired and sometimes lost entirely.

The arguments in favor of this conclusion are of two kinds; some of them are negative, derived from the impossibility of imagining any other way of performing the <term>accommodation</term> without exceeding the limits of the actual dimensions of the eye, and from the examination of the eye in its different states by several tests capable of detecting any other changes if they had existed. For example, by the application of water to the <term>cornea</term>, which completely removes the effect of its convexity without impairing the power of altering the focus, and by holding the whole eye, when turned inward, in such a manner as to render any material alteration of its length utterly impossible.

Other arguments are deduced from positive evidence of the change of form of the crystalline, provided by the particular effects of <term>refraction</term> and <term>aberration</term> which are observable in the different states of the eye; effects which provide a direct proof that the shape of the lens must vary; its surfaces, which are nearly spherical in the resting form of the lens, assume a different determinable curvature when it is called into use. The objections which have been made to this conclusion are founded only on the appearance of a slight alteration of <term>focal length</term> in an eye from which the crystalline had been extracted; but the fact is neither sufficiently confirmed, nor was the apparent change at all significant. Even if it were proved that an eye without the lens is capable of a certain small alteration, it would by no means follow that it could undergo a change five or ten times as great.

The <term>iris</term> serves, by its variable size, to exclude more or less of the light falling on the <term>cornea</term> when its intensity would otherwise be too great; hence the <term>pupil</term> is usually smallest by day, and its increased size at night sometimes gives the eye a greater apparent luster. The <term>iris</term> also intercepts such rays as would fall on parts incapable of refracting them regularly; and by its contraction when a closer object is viewed, it lessens the confusion which would arise, in such eyes as cannot accommodate themselves sufficiently, from the size of the imperfect focal points on the <term>retina</term>. Such a contraction almost always accompanies the reduction of the <term>focal length</term>, even in a perfect eye, and it may easily be rendered visible by walking gradually up to a mirror and observing the size of the <term>pupil</term> as we approach closer and closer to our reflection. ### LECTURE XXXVIII.

...limits of perfect vision, unless we allowed for the irregularity of the form assumed by the marginal parts of the crystalline lens. The iris is also particularly useful for excluding those parts of the lateral beams of light that strike the cornea very obliquely and are refracted too much, while only a smaller beam, which enters the eye more directly, is admitted into the pupil.

The refractive powers and properties of the eye can be very conveniently determined by means of an instrument to which I have given the name <term>optometer</term>, a term first used in a nearly similar sense by Dr. Porterfield. If two or more separate groups of the rays from the same beam are admitted at different parts of the pupil, they will only be reunited on the retina when the focus is perfect. Thus, if we look through two small holes, or slits, at a tiny object that the eye is not focused on, it will appear double; and when the object is a line pointed nearly toward the eye, every point of it will appear double, except for the one at the distance of perfect vision, and an image of two lines will be seen, crossing each other at this point. In this way, the measurement of the focal length of the eye is performed directly by looking at the optometer. The scale can be extended by adding a lens, which allows us to produce the effect of a longer line while the instrument remains portable.

When the eye possesses too much refractive power to clearly perceive distant objects, the pupil is generally large, so that the blurring of the image is somewhat reduced by partially closing the eyelids; from this habit, an eye formed in this way is called <term>myopic</term>. In such cases, with the help of a concave lens, the divergence of the light rays can be increased, and a virtual image can be formed at a distance much closer than that of the object, providing perfect vision. For a far-sighted or <term>presbyopic</term> eye, on the contrary, a convex lens is required in order to obtain a virtual image at a greater distance than the object; it often happens that the rays must be made not only to diverge less than before, but even to converge toward a focus behind such an eye, in order to make its vision clear. Presbyopic people generally have a small pupil and, therefore, rarely develop the habit of covering any part of it with their eyelids.

# ON VISION.

When the images of the same object fall on certain corresponding points of the retina in each eye, they appear to the senses as only one; but if they fall on parts that do not correspond, the object appears double. In general, all objects at the same distance, in any one position of the eyes, appear alike—either double or single. The <term>optical axes</term>, or the directions of the rays falling on the points of most perfect vision, naturally meet at a great distance; that is, they are nearly parallel to each other. In looking at a nearer object, we make them converge toward it, wherever it may be situated, by means of the external muscles of the eye. While in eyes with perfect vision, the refractive powers are altered at the same time by an involuntary coordination, so as to form a distinct image of an object at the given distance. This correspondence between the position of the axes and the focal length is, in most cases, unalterable; however, some people perhaps have the power of altering it to a slight degree, and in others, the adjustment is imperfect. But the eyes seem to be, in most persons, inseparably connected regarding the changes that their refractive powers undergo, although it sometimes happens that those powers are originally very different in each eye.

These motions enable us to judge the distance of an object quite accurately within certain limits; and beyond these limits, the degree of distinctness or blurriness of the image continues to assist our judgment. We estimate distances much less accurately with one eye than with both, since we are deprived of the assistance usually provided by the relative position of the optical axes; thus, we seldom succeed on the first try when attempting to pass a finger or a hooked rod sideways through a ring with one eye closed. Our idea of distance is also usually regulated by a knowledge of the real size of an object while we observe its <term>angular magnitude</term>; on the other hand, knowledge of the real or imaginary distance of the object often directs our judgment of its actual size. The quantity of light intercepted by the intervening air, and the intensity of the blue tint which it causes, are also elements of our involuntary calculation; hence, in a mist, the obscurity increases the apparent distance and, consequently, the supposed size of an unknown object. In estimating a distance, we naturally observe the number and extent of the intervening objects; so a distant church in a wooded and hilly landscape appears more remote than if it were situated on a plain. For a similar reason, the apparent distance of an object seen

The sun, moon, and stars are much less luminous when they are near the <term>horizon</term> than when they are more elevated, because a greater quantity of their light is intercepted during its longer passage through the <term>atmosphere</term>. We also observe a much greater variety of closer objects in nearly the same direction; we cannot, therefore, help imagining them to be more distant when they rise or set than at other times. Since they subtend the same angle, they appear to be actually larger. For similar reasons, the apparent shape of the <term>starry heavens</term>, even when free from clouds, is that of a <term>flattened vault</term>; its summit appears to be much closer to us than its horizontal parts, and any of the <term>constellations</term> seem to be considerably larger when near the horizon than when at the <term>zenith</term>. (Plate XXX. Fig. 438.)

The faculty of judging the actual distance of objects is an impediment to the deception that it is partly the business of a <term>painter</term> to produce. Some of the effects of objects at different distances may, however, be imitated when painting on a flat surface. Thus, assuming the eye is adjusted to a given distance, objects at all other distances may be represented with a certain indistinctness of outline, which would naturally accompany the images of the objects themselves on the <term>retina</term>. This indistinctness is so generally necessary that its absence creates the disagreeable effect called <term>hardness</term>. The apparent magnitude of the subjects in our design, and the relative positions of the intervening objects, may be imitated by the rules of <term>geometrical perspective</term> so as to agree perfectly with nature. We may still further improve the representation of distance by attending to the art of <term>aerial perspective</term>, which consists of a proper observation of the loss of light and the bluish tinge caused by the presence of a greater or lesser depth of air between us and the different parts of the scenery.

In the panorama, which has recently been exhibited in many parts of Europe, the effects of natural scenery are very closely imitated: the deception is favored by the absence of all other visible objects, and by the faintness of the light, which assists in concealing the defects of the representation, and for which the eye is usually prepared by being long detained in the dark winding passages that lead to the place of exhibition.

The impressions of light on the retina appear to be always permanent to a certain degree, and more so as the light is stronger; but it is uncertain whether the retina possesses this property merely as a solar phosphorus, or in consequence of its peculiar organization. The duration of the impression is generally from one-hundredth of a second to half a second, or more; hence, a luminous object revolving in a circle makes a bright ring, and a shooting star leaves a train of light behind it, which is not always real. If the object is painfully bright, it generally produces a permanent spot, which continues to pass through various changes of color for some time, without much regularity, and gradually vanishes: this may, however, be considered a morbid effect.

<margin>V</margin>
When the eye has been fixed on a small object of a bright color, and is then turned away to a white surface, a faint spot, resembling in form and size the object first viewed, appears on the surface, of a color opposite to the first—that is, of such a color as would be produced by withdrawing it from white light; thus, a red object produces a bluish-green spot, and a bluish-green object a red spot. The reason for this appearance is probably that the portion of the retina, or of the sensorium, that is affected has lost a part of its sensibility to the light of that color with which it has been impressed, and is more strongly affected by the other constituent parts of the white light. A similar effect is also often produced when a white or gray object is viewed on a colored ground, even without altering the position of the eye: the whole retina being affected by sympathy in nearly the same manner as a part of it was affected in the former case. ## LECTURE XXXIX.

### ON THE NATURE OF LIGHT AND COLOURS.

The nature of light is a subject of no significant importance to the concerns of daily life or to the practice of the arts, but it is in many other respects extremely interesting, especially as it tends to assist our views both of the nature of our sensations and of the constitution of the universe at large. The examination of the production of colors, in a variety of circumstances, is closely connected with the theory of their essential properties and their causes; and we shall find that many of these phenomena will afford us considerable assistance in forming our opinion respecting the nature and origin of light in general.

It is generally agreed that light either consists of the emission of very minute particles from luminous substances, which are actually projected and continue to move with the velocity commonly attributed to light, or in the excitation of an undulatory motion, analogous to that which constitutes sound, in a highly light and elastic medium pervading the universe; but the judgments of philosophers of all ages have been much divided with respect to the preference of one or the other of these opinions. There are also some circumstances which lead those who entertain the first hypothesis either to believe, with Newton, that the emission of the particles of light is always attended by the undulations of an ethereal medium, accompanying it in its passage, or to suppose, with Boscovich, that the minute particles of light themselves receive, at the time of their emission, certain rotational and vibrational motions, which they retain as long as their projectile motion continues. These additional suppositions, however necessary they may have been thought for explaining some particular phenomena, have never been very generally understood or admitted, although no attempt has been made to adapt the theory in any other manner to those phenomena.

<summary>This lecture introduces the theoretical nature of light, weighing the two primary scientific hypotheses: the emission of particles (corpuscular theory) versus undulatory motion (wave theory). It mentions that while proponents of the particle theory, like Newton and Boscovich, added complex suppositions to explain certain phenomena, these ideas were not universally accepted.</summary>

<keywords>nature of light, colours, emission theory, undulatory motion, Newton, Boscovich, ethereal medium, luminous substances, physics history</keywords>

--- Page 488 ---
<meta>This page continues Lecture XXXIX, transitioning from the introductory definitions of the emission and undulatory theories of light to a detailed comparison of how each theory explains the physical behavior of light, specifically its propagation and diffraction.</meta>

<page-num>458</page-num>
# LECTURE XXXIX.

We shall proceed to examine in detail the manner in which the two principal hypotheses regarding light may be applied to its various properties and characteristics; and in the first place, to the simple propagation of light in straight lines through a vacuum, or a very rare, uniform medium. In this circumstance, there is nothing inconsistent with either hypothesis; but it undergoes some modifications, which require to be noticed, when a portion of light is admitted through an opening and spreads itself in a slight degree in every direction. In this case, it is maintained by Newton that the edge of the opening possesses an attractive force which is capable of inflecting <note>bending or diffracting</note> the rays. However, there is some improbability in supposing that bodies of different forms and of various refractive powers should possess an equal force of inflection, as they appear to do in the production of these effects. Furthermore, there is reason to conclude from experiments that such a force, if it existed, must extend to a very considerable distance from the surfaces concerned—at least a quarter of an inch, and perhaps much more—which is a condition not easily reconciled with other phenomena. In the Huygenian system of undulation, this divergence or <term>diffraction</term> is illustrated by a comparison with the motions of waves of water and of sound, both of which diverge when they are admitted into a wide space through an opening; indeed, it has so much divergence that it has usually been considered an objection to this opinion that the rays of light do not diverge to the degree that would be expected if they were analogous to the waves of water. But as it has been remarked by Newton that the pulses of sound diverge less than the waves of water, so it may fairly be inferred that in an even more highly elastic medium, the undulations constituting light must diverge much less considerably than either. (Plate XX. Fig. 266.)

With respect, however, to the transmission of light through perfectly transparent mediums of considerable density, the system of <term>emanation</term> <note>the particle or emission theory</note> faces some difficulties. It is not to be supposed that the particles of light can freely pass through the ultimate atoms of matter which compose a substance of any kind; they must, therefore, be admitted in all directions through the pores or interstices of those atoms. For if we allow such suppositions as Boscovich’s—that matter itself is penetrable, that is, immaterial—it is almost useless to argue the question further. It is certain that some substances retain all their properties when they are reduced to the thickness of one ten-millionth of an inch at most, and we cannot therefore suppose the distances

Now, if ten feet of the most transparent water transmits, without interruption, one half of the light that enters it, each section or layer the thickness of one of these pores of matter must intercept only about one twenty-thousand-millionth part. Consequently, the space or area occupied by the particles must be that much smaller than the gaps between them, and the diameter of each atom must be less than the 140,000th part of its distance from neighboring particles. Thus, the total space occupied by the substance would be as sparsely filled as the whole of England would be by a hundred men placed at a distance of about thirty miles from each other. This astonishing degree of porosity is not, indeed, absolutely impossible, and there are many reasons for believing this description agrees somewhat with the actual makeup of material substances; however, the <term>Huygenian hypothesis</term> does not require the disproportion to be nearly so great. In that system, the general direction and even the intensity of an <term>undulation</term> would be very little affected by the interference of atoms of matter, while these atoms may simultaneously be supposed to assist in transmitting the impulse by propagating it through their own substance. Euler, indeed, imagined that the waves of light might be transmitted through the solid substance of material bodies alone, in exactly the same way that sound is propagated; but this theory is unacceptable for many reasons.

A very striking fact regarding the movement of light is the uniformity of its velocity in the same medium. According to the <term>projectile hypothesis</term>, the force required for the free emission of light must be about a million million times as great as the force of gravity at the earth’s surface. This force must either act with equal intensity on all particles of light, or it must push some of them through a greater space than others if its action is less powerful, since the velocity is the same in all cases. For example, if the projectile force is weaker regarding red light than regarding violet light, it must continue its action on the red rays for a greater distance than on the violet rays. There is no other instance in nature of a simple projectile moving with a velocity that is uniform in all cases, regardless of its cause, and it is extremely difficult to imagine that such an immense force of repulsion can exist in all substances capable of

Another cause would also naturally interfere with the uniformity of the velocity of light if it consisted merely of the motion of projected <term>corpuscles</term> of matter. Mr. Laplace has calculated that if any of the stars were 250 times as large in diameter as the sun, its attraction would be so strong that it would destroy the entire momentum of the light corpuscles proceeding from it, rendering the star invisible at a great distance. Although there is no reason to imagine that any of the stars are actually of this magnitude, some of them are probably many times larger than our sun, and therefore large enough to produce such a slowdown in the motion of their light that it would materially alter its effects. It is almost unnecessary to observe that the uniformity of the velocity of *light* in those spaces free from all material substances is a necessary consequence of the <term>Huygenian hypothesis</term>, since the <term>undulations</term> of every homogeneous elastic medium are always propagated, like those of sound, with the same velocity as long as the medium remains unchanged.

Under either theory, there is no difficulty in explaining why the angles of incidence and reflection are equal. These angles are equal both in the collision of common elastic bodies with others incomparably larger, and in the reflections of water waves and the vibrations of sound. It is equally easy to demonstrate that the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction must always be in the same proportion at the same surface, whether the surface is supposed to possess an attractive force capable of acting on the particles of light, or to be the boundary of a medium through which the undulations are propagated at a slower speed. There are, however, some cases of the production of colors which lead us to suppose that the velocity of light must be lower in a denser medium than in a thinner one. If this fact were fully established, the existence of such an attractive force could no longer be accepted, nor could the system of emanation be maintained by anyone.

by undulations, propagated in all cases through an ethereal medium. The mechanism of these supposed undulations is so complicated and accompanied by so many difficulties that the few who have examined them have generally been entirely dissatisfied with them; the internal vibrations of the light particles themselves, which Boscovich has imagined, seem hardly to require a serious discussion. It may, therefore, safely be asserted that in the projectile hypothesis, this separation of the rays of light of the same kind—by a partial reflection at every refracting surface—remains completely unexplained. In the undulatory system, on the contrary, this separation follows as a necessary consequence. It is simplest to consider the ethereal medium that pervades any transparent substance, together with the material atoms of the substance, as together constituting a compound medium that is denser than pure ether but not more elastic. By comparing the adjacent particles of the thinner and denser mediums with common elastic bodies of different sizes, we can easily determine not only how, but almost to what degree, this reflection must occur in different circumstances. Thus, if one of two equal bodies strikes the other, it communicates its entire motion to it without any reflection. However, a smaller body striking a larger one is reflected, with more force as the difference in their size increases. A larger body striking a smaller one continues forward with a reduced velocity; the remaining motion—in the case of an undulation falling on a thinner medium—constitutes part of a new series of motions that necessarily returns backward at the appropriate velocity. We may observe a circumstance very similar to this last one in a portion of mercury spread out on a horizontal table; if a wave is created at any part, it will be reflected from the edge of the mercury almost in the same manner as from a solid obstacle.

The total reflection of light falling with a certain angle on the surface of a thinner medium becomes, under both theories, a specific case of refraction. In the undulatory system, it is convenient to suppose that the two mediums are separated by a small space in which their densities gradually approach one another, so that the undulation may be turned around gradually to be reflected at an equal angle. However, this supposition is not strictly necessary, and the same effects can be expected at the surface of two mediums separated by an abrupt boundary.

<summary>The author argues that the undulatory theory explains partial and total reflection more effectively than the projectile theory by likening the interaction of light waves with different mediums to the collision of elastic bodies. This model accounts for the return of motion (reflection) when waves move between mediums of different densities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the corpuscular (emanation) and undulatory theories of light, examining how each accounts for phenomena like combustion, friction, solar phosphori, aberration, and the double refraction of Iceland spar.</meta>

<page-num>462</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XXXIX.</header>

The chemical process of combustion can easily be imagined either to release the particles of light from their various combinations or to agitate the elastic medium through the internal motions accompanying it. However, the effects of friction on substances incapable of undergoing chemical changes, as well as the movement of the electric fluid through imperfect conductors, provide examples of the production of light where there seems to be no easy way to assume a decomposition of any kind. The phenomena of solar phosphori appear to closely resemble the sympathetic sounds of musical instruments, which are vibrated by other sounds carried to them through the air. It is difficult to understand in what state the corpuscles of light could be held by these substances so as to be re-emitted after a short period of time; and if it is true that diamonds are often found which exhibit a red light after having received only violet light, it seems impossible to explain this property based on the assumption that the same corpuscles are retained and subsequently emitted.

The phenomena of the aberration of light agree perfectly well with the system of emanation; and if the ethereal medium, supposed to pervade the earth and its atmosphere, were carried along with it and shared significantly in its motions, these phenomena could not easily be reconciled with the theory of undulation. But there is no necessity for such an assumption: advocates of the Newtonian view will not deny that all material bodies are sufficiently porous to allow a medium pervading them to remain almost absolutely at rest; and if this is granted, the effects of aberration will appear to be precisely the same in either hypothesis.

The unusual refraction of Iceland spar has been most accurately and satisfactorily explained by Huygens, based on the simple assumption that this crystal possesses the property of transmitting an impulse more rapidly in one direction than in another. From this, he infers that the undulations constituting light must assume a spheroidal instead of a spherical form, and he establishes laws for the direction of its motion that are incomparably more consistent with experiment than any attempts made to adapt the phenomena to other principles. It is true that nothing has yet been done to help us understand the effects of a subsequent refraction by a second crystal, unless one can be satisfied with the mere name of polarity.

...assigned by Newton to a property which he attributes to the particles of light, and which he supposes directs them in the specific type of refraction they are to undergo. But under any hypothesis, until we discover the reason why a part of the light is at first refracted in the usual manner and another part in the unusual manner, we have no right to expect that we should understand how these dispositions are continued or modified when the process is repeated.

In order to explain, within the system of emanation, the dispersion of rays of different colors by means of refraction, it is necessary to suppose that all refractive mediums have an elective attraction that acts more powerfully on the violet rays, in proportion to their mass, than on the red. But an elective attraction of this kind is a property foreign to mechanical physics; when we use the term in chemistry, we only admit our inability to assign a mechanical cause for the effect and refer to an analogy with other facts whose intimate nature is perfectly unknown to us. It is indeed not very easy to give a demonstrative theory for the dispersion of colored light based on the assumption of undulatory motion; but we may derive a very satisfactory illustration from the well-known effects of waves of different widths. A simple calculation of the velocity of waves propagated in a liquid that is perfectly elastic, or incompressible, and free from friction, assigns to all of them precisely the same velocity, whatever their width may be. The compressibility of actual fluids, however, introduces a necessity for a correction according to the width of the wave; and it is very easy to observe, in a river or a pond of considerable depth, that wider waves proceed much more rapidly than narrower ones. We may, therefore, consider the pure ethereal medium as analogous to an infinitely elastic fluid in which undulations of all kinds move with equal velocity; material transparent substances, on the contrary, resemble those fluids in which we see the large waves advance beyond the smaller ones. By supposing the red light to consist of larger or wider undulations and the violet of smaller ones, we may sufficiently clarify the greater refrangibility of the red than of the violet light.

It is not, however, merely on the ground of this analogy that we may be induced to suppose the undulations constituting red light to be larger than those of violet light; a very extensive class of phenomena leads us still further...

Assuming that light of any given color consists of undulations of a specific width, or of a given frequency, it follows that these undulations must be subject to those effects which we have already examined in the case of water waves and sound pulses. It has been shown that two equal series of waves, proceeding from centers near each other, may be seen to destroy each other's effects at certain points, and at other points to double them; and the beating of two sounds has been explained by a similar interference. We are now to apply the same principles to the alternate union and extinction of colors. (Plate XX. Fig. 267.)

In order for the effects of two portions of light to be combined in this way, it is necessary that they be derived from the same source and that they arrive at the same point by different paths, in directions that do not deviate much from each other. This deviation may be produced in one or both of the portions by diffraction, by reflection, by refraction, or by any of these effects combined; but the simplest case appears to be when a beam of <term>homogeneous light</term> falls on a screen in which there are two very small holes or slits, which may be considered as centers of divergence from which the light is diffracted in every direction. In this case, when the two newly formed beams are received on a surface placed so as to intercept them, their light is divided by dark stripes into nearly equal portions, but becoming wider as the surface is further from the <term>apertures</term>, so as to subtend nearly equal angles from the apertures at all distances, and also wider in the same proportion as the apertures are closer to each other. It sometimes happens that an object, by which a shadow is formed in a beam of light admitted through a small aperture, does not have parallel sides. Thus, the two portions of light that are diffracted from two sides of an object at right angles with each other frequently form a short series of curved fringes within the shadow, situated on each side of the diagonal. These were first observed by Grimaldi and are completely explained by the general principle of the interference of the two portions encroaching perpendicularly on the shadow. (Plate XXX. Fig. 445.)

But the most obvious of all the appearances of this kind is that of the fringes which are usually seen beyond the edge of any shadow formed in a beam of light admitted through a small aperture. In white light, three of these fringes are usually visible, and sometimes four; but in light of only one color, their number is greater, and they are always much narrower as they are further from the shadow. Their origin is easily deduced from the interference of the direct light with a portion of light reflected from the edge of the object that produces them; the angle of its incidence causes a reflection so abundant as to show a visible effect, however narrow that edge may be. The fringes are, however, made more obvious as the quantity of this reflected light increases. According to this theory, it follows that the distance of the first dark fringe from the shadow should be half as great as that of the fourth, as the difference of the lengths of the different paths of the light is proportional to the squares of those distances. The experiment precisely confirms this calculation, with only the same slight correction required in all other cases: the distances of the first fringes are always slightly increased. It may also be observed that the extent of the shadow itself is always increased, and in nearly an equal degree with that of the fringes: the

# LECTURE XXXIX.

The reason for this circumstance appears to be the gradual loss of light at the edges of every separate beam, which is so strongly analogous to the phenomena seen in water waves. This same cause may also perhaps have some effect in producing the general modification or correction of the position of the first fringes, although it appears to be scarcely sufficient to explain all of it. (Plate XXX. Fig. 446.)

A still more common and convenient method of demonstrating the effects of the mutual interference of light is provided to us by the colors of the thin plates of transparent substances. The lights here are derived from the successive partial reflections produced by the upper and lower surfaces of the plate; or, when the plate is viewed by transmitted light, from the direct beam which is simply refracted and that portion of it which is twice reflected within the plate. The appearance in the latter case is much less striking than in the former because the light affected in this way is only a small portion of the whole beam with which it is mixed. In the former case, the two reflected portions are of nearly equal intensity and may be separated from all other light tending to overpower them. In both cases, when the plate is gradually reduced in thickness to an extremely thin edge, the order of colors may be exactly the same as in the stripes and coronae already described; their distance only varies when the surfaces of the plate, instead of being flat, are concave, as frequently happens in such experiments. The scale of an oxide, which is often formed by the effect of heat on the surface of a metal—particularly iron—provides us with an example of such a series formed in reflected light. This scale is at first inconceivably thin and destroys none of the reflected light; it soon, however, begins to be a dull yellow, which changes to red, and then to crimson and blue, after which the effect is destroyed by the opacity that the oxide acquires. Usually, however, the series of colors produced in reflected light follows a somewhat different order: the scale of oxide is denser than the air, and the iron below is denser than the oxide. But where the media above and below the plate are either both less dense or both denser than the plate itself, the different natures of the reflections at its different surfaces appear to produce a modification in the state of the undulations, and the infinitely thin edge of the plate becomes black instead of white, with one of the portions of light immediately destroying the other instead of reinforcing it. Thus, when a film of soapy water is stretched over a

When two glasses, one of which is slightly convex, are pressed together with some force, the layer of air between them shows the appearance of colored rings. These begin from a black spot at the center and become narrower and narrower as the curved shape of the glass causes the thickness of the layer of air to increase more and more rapidly. The black is followed by a violet so faint as to be barely perceptible; next to this is an orange-yellow, and then crimson and blue. When water, or any other fluid, is substituted for the air between the glasses, the rings appear where the thickness is smaller than that of the air layer in the same proportion that the refractive density of the fluid is greater. This is a result which necessarily follows from the ratio of the velocities with which light must—according to the Huygenian hypothesis—be supposed to move in different media. It is also an equally necessary consequence of this theory, and one equally inconsistent with all others, that when the direction of the light is oblique, the effect of a thicker plate must be the same as that of a thinner plate when the light falls perpendicularly upon it; the difference in the paths taken by the different portions of light corresponds precisely with the observed phenomena. (Plate XXX. Fig. 447–449.)

Sir Isaac Newton suggests that the colors of natural bodies in general are similar to these colors of thin plates and are determined by the size of their particles. If this opinion were universally true, we could always separate the colors of natural bodies through refraction into a number of different portions with dark spaces in between; this is because every part of a thin plate that shows color produces such a divided spectrum when viewed through a prism. Accordingly, there are many natural colors in which such a separation can be observed; one of the most remarkable of these is blue glass, likely colored with cobalt, which becomes divided into seven distinct portions. It seems, however, impossible to assume that the production of natural colors is perfectly identical to those of thin plates because of the known smallness of the particles of coloring bodies—unless the refractive density of these particles is at least 20 or 30 times as great as that of glass or water. This is, in fact, not at all improbable regarding the fundamental atoms of matter,

The colors of <term>mixed plates</term> constitute a distinct variety of the <term>colors of thin plates</term>, which has not been commonly observed. They appear when the gap between two glasses, nearly in contact, is filled with a great number of tiny portions of two different substances, such as water and air, oil and air, or oil and water. The light which passes through one of the <term>media</term>, moving with a greater <term>velocity</term>, arrives before the light passing through the other. As their effects on the eye are mixed and combined, their <term>interference</term> produces an appearance of colors very similar to the colors of simple thin plates seen by transmission, but at much greater thicknesses, depending on the difference of the <term>refractive densities</term> of the substances used. The effect is observed by holding the glasses between the eye and the edge of a bright object, and it is most conspicuous in the portion seen against the dark area beyond the object, being produced by the light scattered irregularly from the surfaces of the fluid. Here, however, the effects are inverted, with the colors resembling those of common thin plates seen by reflection; and the same considerations regarding the nature of the reflections are applicable to both cases. (Plate XXX. Fig. 450.)

The production of <term>supernumerary rainbows</term>, which are sometimes seen inside the primary and outside the secondary bow, appears to be intimately connected with the colors of thin plates. We have already seen that the light producing the ordinary rainbow is double; its intensity is greatest only at its edge, where the common bow appears, while the entire light is extended much more widely. The two portions involved in its production must divide this light into <term>fringes</term>; but unless almost all the drops of a shower happen to be of the same size, the effects of these fringes must be blurred and destroyed. In general, however, they must at least cooperate more or less in producing one dark fringe, which must cut off the common rainbow much more abruptly than it would otherwise have been terminated, and consequently improve the distinctness of its colors. The size of the raindrops required for producing those rainbows that are usually observed is between the 50th and the 100th of an inch; they become gradually narrower as they are farther from the common

The last species of the colors of double lights, which it will be necessary to notice, consists of those which have been named, from Newton’s experiments, the colors of thick plates, but which may be called, more appropriately, the colors of concave mirrors. The front surface of a glass mirror, or any other transparent surface placed before a <term>speculum</term> of metal, scatters irregularly in every direction two portions of light: one before, and the other after its reflection. When the light falls obliquely on the mirror, being admitted through an aperture near the center of its curvature, it is easy to show, from the laws of reflection, that the two portions thus scattered will combine in their effects throughout the circumference of a circle passing through the aperture; this circle will consequently be white, and it will be surrounded with circles of colors at nearly equal distances, resembling the stripes produced by diffraction. The analogy between these colors and those of thin plates is by no means as close as Newton supposed it, since the effect of a plate of any considerable thickness must be absolutely lost in white light after ten or twelve alternations of colors at most, while these effects would require the whole process to remain unaltered—or rather to be renewed—after many thousands or millions of changes. (Plate XXX. Fig. 452.)

It is presumed that the accuracy with which the general law of the interference of light has been shown to be applicable to such a great variety of facts, in circumstances the most dissimilar, will be allowed to establish its validity in the most satisfactory manner. The full confirmation or decided rejection of the theory by which this law was first suggested can be expected from time and experience alone; if it is disproven, our prospects will again be confined within their ancient limits, but if it is fully established, we may expect an ample extension of our views of the operations of nature, by means of our acquaintance with a medium so powerful and so universal as that to which the propagation of light must be attributed.

## LECTURE XL

### ON THE HISTORY OF OPTICS.

The science of optics is not one of those that the philosophers of antiquity cultivated with the greatest diligence and success; almost every refinement relating to it has originated over the course of about two centuries, and some of its greatest improvements have been made within the last fifty years. The reflection of light rays is indeed an occurrence too frequent and too obvious to have escaped the notice of even the earliest observers: a river or a fountain was the first mirror; its effect was easily imitated by mirrors made of metal. As soon as any philosophical attention was paid to the phenomenon, it was easy to determine the equality of the angles of incidence and reflection; but although it was well known that an oar, partially immersed in water, no longer appeared straight, it was a long time before any attempts were made to determine the relationship between the angles of incidence and refraction. The Greeks were, however, acquainted with the properties of the burning glass, which was sold as a curiosity in toy shops; for it is well known that one of the characters introduced by Aristophanes proposes to destroy his adversary's papers with the help of this instrument. The magnifying powers of lenses were, however, but little understood, although it is hardly believable that they could have escaped the notice of a person in possession of a burning glass; it appears from Seneca that the Romans at least were informed of the effects of spherical refracting substances, and it is not improbable that they were occasionally used in the arts.

Empedocles is perhaps the first person on record who wrote systematically on light. He maintained that it consisted of particles projected from luminous bodies, and that vision was performed both by the effect of these particles on the eye and by means of a visual influence emitted by the eye

Aristotle combated both of these doctrines; he thought it absurd to suppose that a visual influence was emitted by the eye, and that it should not enable us to see in the dark; and he considered it more probable that light consisted of an impulse, propagated through a continuous medium, than of an emanation of distinct particles. Light, he says, is the action of a transparent substance; and if there were absolutely no medium between the eye and any visible object, it would be absolutely impossible for us to see it.

It is said that Archimedes made a compound burning mirror of sufficient power to set the Roman ships on fire: in this form, the story is hardly probable, although the possibility of burning an object at a great distance by a collection of plane mirrors has been sufficiently shown by the experiments of Buffon. It is, however, not unlikely that Archimedes was acquainted with the properties of reflecting surfaces, and that he confirmed his theories by some experimental investigations. The work on <term>catoptrics</term>, attributed to Euclid, contains the determination of the effects of reflecting surfaces of different forms; but it is not thought to be genuine. The existence and the magnitude of atmospheric refraction were well known to Ptolemy, and a treatise by this astronomer on the subject is still extant in manuscript.

The mathematical theory of optics, or the science of <term>dioptrics</term> and <term>catoptrics</term>, made some advances in the Middle Ages from the work of Alhazen and Vitellio. Alhazen was mistaken in some of his propositions regarding refraction; Vitellio, a native of Poland, gave a more correct theory of this subject and constructed a table of refractive densities, showing the supposed proportions of the angles of incidence and refraction in the respective media.

The invention of the <term>magic lantern</term> is attributed to Roger Bacon, and the <term>lens</term> was soon afterward commonly applied to the assistance of defective sight. It has been much disputed whether or not Bacon was acquainted with <term>telescopes</term>; the prevailing opinion is that the passages which have been alleged to prove it are insufficient for the purpose; but there is reason to suspect, from the testimony of Recorde, who wrote in 1551, not only that Bacon had
