Digges also, in a work published in 1571, has a passage of a similar nature, and from Bacon's own words it has been conjectured that an instrument resembling a telescope was of even much higher antiquity. But the first person who is certainly known to have made a telescope is Janson, a Dutchman, whose son, by accident, placing a concave and a convex spectacle glass at a little distance from each other, observed the increased apparent magnitude of an object seen through them; based on this, the father fixed two such glasses in a tube a few inches long and sold the instrument in this form. He also made some telescopes of greater powers, and one of his family discovered a satellite of Jupiter with them. Galileo had heard of the instrument but had not been informed of the details of its construction; he reinvented it in 1609, and the following year, he also rediscovered the satellite which Janson had seen a little earlier.

It was Kepler, however, who first reduced the theory of the telescope to its true principles; he laid down the common rules for finding the focal lengths of simple glass lenses; he showed how to determine the magnifying power of the telescope and pointed out the construction of the simple astronomical telescope, which is more convenient for accurate observations than the Galilean telescope, since the micrometer may be more easily applied to it. A third glass, for restoring the erect position of the object, was later added by Scheiner, and a fourth, for increasing the field of view, by Rheita. Kepler also performed some good experiments on the nature of colored bodies and showed the inverted position of the image formed on the retina of the eye. Maurolycus of Messina had demonstrated, in 1575, that the pencils of light are brought to focal points on the retina; Kepler's observations occurred thirty or forty years later.

The next great step in optics was made by De Dominis, who in 1611 first explained the cause of the interior or primary rainbow, and this was soon followed by a still more important discovery respecting the nature of refraction, first made by Snellius, who ascertained, around 1621, that the sines of the angles of incidence and refraction are always in the same proportion to each other at the same surface; however, he died in 1626 without having made his discovery public. Descartes also explained the formation of the secondary rainbow and accurately determined the angular magnitude of both bows from mathematical principles; he did not, however, give a sufficient reason for the production of colors in either case. Descartes imagined light to consist of motion, or rather pressure, transmitted instantaneously through an infinitely elastic medium, and he attributed colors to a rotatory motion of the particles of this medium. He supposed that light passed more rapidly through a denser medium than through a rarer one; other philosophers about the same time maintained a contrary opinion, without deciding with respect to any general theory of light. Thus, Fermat and Leibnitz deduced, on this supposition, the path of refracted light from the natural tendency of every body to reach its goal by the shortest possible way; and Barrow derived the same law, in a more geometrical manner, from a similar hypothesis respecting the velocity of light, by considering a pencil of light as a collection of parallel rays influencing each other's motions. We are indebted to this learned mathematician for the first accurate investigation of the properties of refracting and reflecting surfaces, and for the most general determination of the positions of focal points.

The industrious Mr. Boyle had noticed with attention the phosphorescence of diamonds, the colors produced by the effect of scratches on the surfaces of polished metals, and the diversified tints which a bubble or a film of soapy water usually assumes. His assistant, Dr. Hooke, investigated these and other similar appearances with still greater accuracy and proposed, in his *Micrographia*, which was published in 1665, a theory of light considerably resembling that of Descartes. He supposes that light is an impulse propagated through a medium that is highly, but not infinitely, elastic; that refraction is produced by the easier transmission of light through the denser medium; and that the difference of color consists in the different law of the particular impulse constituting colored light, so that red and blue differ from each other in the same manner as the sound of a violin and of a flute. He explained the colors of thin plates from the interference of two such pulses partially reflected from the upper and under surface; but the hypothesis which he assumed, respecting the nature of colors, renders this explanation wholly

It was still believed that every refraction actually produces color, instead of separating the colors already existing in white light; but in the year 1666, Newton first made the important discovery of the actual existence of colors of all kinds in white light, which he showed to be nothing other than a compound of all possible colors, mixed in certain proportions with each other, and capable of being separated by refraction of any kind.

About the same time that Newton was making his earliest experiments on <term>refraction</term>, Grimaldi's treatise on light appeared; it contained many interesting experiments and ingenious remarks on the effects of <term>diffraction</term>, which is the name that he gave to the spreading of light in every direction upon its admission into a dark chamber, and on the colors which usually accompany these effects. He had even observed that in some instances the light of one <term>pencil</term> tended to extinguish that of another, but he had not inquired in what cases and according to what laws such an <term>interference</term> must be expected.

The discoveries of Newton were not received without some controversy either at home or abroad; the essential points of his theory were, however, soon established, but Dr. Hooke very warmly opposed the hypothesis which Newton had suggested respecting the nature and propagation of light. On this subject Newton professed himself by no means tenacious; he was not, however, convinced by Dr. Hooke, and disliked the dispute so much, that he deferred the publication of his treatise on <term>optics</term> till after Hooke's death in 1703. Very soon after his first communication to the Royal Society, in 1672, he had sent them a description of his <term>reflecting telescope</term>, which was perhaps the first that had been constructed with success, although Gregory had invented his instrument some years before, and a plan of a similar kind had been suggested by Eskinard <note>Possibly Francesco Eschinardi (1623–1703).</note> as early as 1615. With respect to the nature of light, the theory which <term>Newton</term> adopted was materially different from the opinions of most of his predecessors. He considered indeed the operation of an <term>ethereal medium</term> as absolutely necessary to the production of the most remarkable effects of light, but he denied that the motions of such a medium actually constituted light; he asserted, on the contrary, that the essence of light consisted in the projection of minute particles of matter from the luminous body, and maintained that this projection was only accompanied by the vibration of a medium as an accidental circumstance, which was also renewed at the surface of every refractive or reflective substance.

In the meantime, <term>Bartholin</term> had called the attention of naturalists and opticians to the singular properties of the <term>Iceland crystal</term>, and had hastily examined the laws of its unusual refraction. On this subject <term>Huygens</term> had been much more successful: his analysis of the phenomena of the <term>double refraction</term> is a happy combination of accurate experiment with elegant theory; it was published in 1690, making a part of his treatise on light, the fundamental doctrines of which he had communicated to the Academy of Paris in 1678. They scarcely differ in their essential parts from those of our countryman <term>Dr. Hooke</term>, but Huygens has left the subject of colors wholly untouched. <term>Roemer</term> had then lately made the discovery of the immense <term>velocity of light</term> with which light passes through the celestial regions, by observing the apparent irregularities of the eclipses of <term>Jupiter’s satellites</term>; and Huygens readily admitted this property into his system; although Hooke, by a singular caprice, professed himself more ready to believe that the propagation of light might be absolutely instantaneous, than that its motion could be successive, and yet so inconceivably rapid. The merits of Huygens in the mathematical theory of optics were no less considerable than in the investigation of the nature of light; his determinations of the <term>aberrations of lenses</term> were the first refinement on the construction of <term>telescopes</term>.

The optics of Bouguer were first published in 1729, and an improved edition appeared thirty years later; this author's merits in examining the properties of various substances regarding the transmission and reflection of light under different circumstances, and in comparing different kinds of light, deserve the highest praise. Dr. Porterfield’s investigations into the functions of the eye greatly helped to illustrate the workings of this admirable organ, and some valuable remarks by Dr. Jurin on the same subject were published soon after in Dr. Smith’s elaborate treatise on optics, which contains everything that had been achieved at that time regarding the mathematical aspects of the science.

The invention of achromatic telescopes is justly and universally attributed to our countryman Mr. Dollond, but there is reason to believe that he was not the very first person to make this improvement. Mr. Hall, a gentleman from Worcestershire, is said to have discovered, around 1729, Sir Isaac Newton’s mistake in assuming that rays of different colors must necessarily be separated equally by all surfaces that produce the same average refraction. By combining the different dispersive properties of various types of glass, he constructed several compound objective lenses in 1733; these were designed not only to eliminate all appearance of color but also to correct the imperfect refractions caused by the spherical surfaces of the individual lenses. <page-num>479</page-num>
<header>ON THE HISTORY OF OPTICS.</header>

It was as a result of a discussion with Euler, Klingenstierna, and some other mathematicians that Mr. Dollond was led to conduct experiments on the refraction of different kinds of glass; these gentlemen had not questioned the general truth of Newton's opinion regarding the dispersion of different colors, but Euler had asserted that the eye itself produced a refraction free from the appearance of color, and Klingenstierna had shown the possibility of producing a deviation by refraction without a separation of color, according to the laws of refraction laid down by Newton himself. Once Dollond had discovered the significant difference which exists between the dispersive properties of flint glass and crown glass, it was easy to produce the required combination; but this ingenious artist was not satisfied with the advantage of being free from colors alone; he adjusted the forms and apertures of his lenses in the most skillful manner to correct various kinds of aberrations, and he was also particularly fortunate to be able to obtain, around the time of his discovery, a glass of a quality superior to any that has been manufactured since.

This opinion of Euler's regarding the eye was, however, by no means well-founded, for the eye acts very differently on rays of different colors, as we may easily observe by viewing a minute object in different parts of a beam of light transmitted through a prism. It must be admitted that this great mathematician was less fortunate in his optical theories than in many other departments of science; his mathematical investigations into the effects of lenses are much more intricate and verbose than the subject actually requires, and regarding the nature and propagation of light, he adopted several paradoxical opinions. Assuming the theory of Huygens, along with the additional hypothesis regarding the nature of colors—which had been suggested by Newton and maintained by Pardies and Malebranche—namely, that the difference in colors, like that of tones in music, depends on the different frequency of the vibrations constituting light; he imagined that opaque bodies are not seen by reflected light, but that their particles are agitated by the impact of the light which falls on them, and that the vibrations of these particles make the bodies visible again in every direction; he also conceived that the undulations of light are simply propagated through the solid substances of transparent media, in the same way as sound travels through the air. But on these suppositions, all bodies would have the properties of solar

<page-num>480</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XL.</header>

...and the refraction of the rarest natural bodies would be incomparably greater than that which is actually found in the densest bodies. On the whole, although Euler's character has been so highly and deservedly respected that a certain degree of authority is attached to all his opinions—to the point that, in this instance, the name of Huygens has been almost superseded by that of Euler—yet in fact he has added no supporting evidence at all to the theory. Instead, through inaccurate and injudicious reasoning, he has done real harm to the cause he sought to support.

Lambert's research may be considered a continuation of Bouguer's; it presents us with many interesting observations on the natural history of light and the properties of various bodies regarding it. Mr. Lambert first determined that a luminous surface emits its light with nearly equal intensity in all directions, so that any part of it appears almost equally brilliant to an eye placed in any direction, while the light thrown by each square inch or square foot of the surface in any direction differs according to the obliquity of that direction. The mathematical theory of optics is significantly indebted to the work of Clairaut, D'Alembert, and Boscovich; Jeaurat, Beguelin, Redern, and Klügel have also continued the investigation. Their calculations may be of considerable utility to the practical optician, but it requires the ingenuity of a Dollond or a Ramsden to apply all the results to any useful purposes.

Mazéas's experiments on the colors of thin plates are merely repetitions of Newton's under less favorable conditions. Mr. Dutour has, however, considerably varied and extended these experiments, as well as those on the colors produced in diffracted light, though without achieving any significant general results. Comparetti's experiments on inflection seem accurate, but they are far too complex to be easily compared with each other or with the observations of previous researchers.

The late Dr. Priestley provided an essential service to the science of optics—viewed as a subject for the interest of the general reader—by providing an elegant and well-written account of the main experiments and theories published before the year 1770. But this work is very deficient...

<meta>This page continues the evaluation of 18th-century optical researchers, moving from the shortcomings of certain mathematical works to the experimental successes of Delaval, Darwin, Wollaston, and Herschel.</meta>

<page-num>481</page-num>
-><header>ON THE HISTORY OF OPTICS.</header><-

...deficient in mathematical accuracy, and the author was not enough of a master of the science to distinguish the good from the mediocre.

Mr. Delaval’s experiments on colors appear to show very satisfactorily that all coloring substances in common use owe their tints to rays that are separated from white light during its passage through them, and not, as Newton supposed, to the reflection of a particular color from the first surface. It has been observed that Kepler and Zucchius had long ago performed experiments nearly similar to those of Mr. Delaval. Dr. Robert Darwin’s investigation into the effects of strong lights on the eye appears to encompass almost all possible varieties of these ocular spectra, but it does not lead to any fundamental analogy capable of explaining the most intricate of them.

The phenomena of unusual atmospheric refraction, which frequently produces double or triple images of objects seen near a heated surface, have been successively illustrated by Mr. Huddart, Mr. Vince, and Dr. Wollaston, so that at present there appears to be little doubt remaining regarding their origin. Dr. Wollaston’s instrument for measuring refractive densities greatly facilitates the examination of the optical properties of various kinds of substances. He has applied it very successfully to the confirmation of Huygens’s theory of double refraction; he has corrected the common opinion regarding the division of the prismatic spectrum; he discovered, without being acquainted with Ritter’s observations, the dark rays that blacken silver salts; and he has noted a singular property in some natural as well as artificial crystals, which appear to be one color when viewed along the axis and another color when viewed in a transverse direction.

The sciences of optics and astronomy are equally indebted to Dr. Herschel. He has brought the construction of the reflecting telescope to a degree of perfection far exceeding all that had been previously attempted, and the well-known improvements that astronomy has derived from his observations are numerous and important. In the course of his research to achieve his more immediate goals, he also had the good fortune to discover the separation of heat rays from light rays by means of refraction—a fact that has been sufficiently established by the experiments of several other people.

<page-num>482</page-num>
### LECTURE XL.

The investigations of Mr. Laplace, relating to atmospheric refraction, may be considered the latest application of refined mathematics to the purposes of optics and astronomy. I have myself attempted to attain a degree of certainty in attributing the changes of the refractive powers of the eye to a variation in the form of the crystalline lens; I have discovered a general law of the mutual action of two portions of light interfering with each other, for which no exception has yet been shown; and by reviving a theory of light similar to that of Hooke and Huygens, with an improvement originally suggested by Newton regarding the nature of colors, I have endeavored to obtain a satisfactory explanation of many circumstances which appear, upon a minute examination, to be absolutely insuperable difficulties in every other hypothesis. It cannot be expected that all objections to such a system will be silenced at once, but if even just a full and candid discussion of the facts I have advanced is encouraged, I trust that the science of optics will be essentially benefited, even if the theory should ultimately be refuted.

He advocates for a wave-based theory of light and invites scientific debate to further the field of optics.</summary>

## LECTURE XLI.

### ON THE FIXED STARS.

**THE** branches of natural philosophy, which are to be the subjects of the third and last division of these lectures, are included in the description implied by the term <term>*physics*</term>, or the history of the specific phenomena of nature; and the account which will be given of these phenomena will be accompanied by as much mechanical theory and analogical reasoning as can be applied to them with sufficient certainty, and without too much intricate calculation.

The science of astronomy might, without much impropriety, have been considered a part of mechanics; but there are circumstances intimately connected with it for which a knowledge of the motions of fluids in general, and also of <term>*optics*</term>, is absolutely necessary for a complete investigation. It could not, therefore, hold any other place in a strict order of arrangement than that which is assigned to it here; and, since it will not be in our power

Although we shall be able to pursue the details of the most remarkable appearances which they exhibit, for this reason we may more properly consider such a view of astronomy as belonging to descriptive rather than theoretical philosophy. This method of treating the subject is sometimes called plain astronomy, in contrast to the mechanical theory of the science, which is called physical astronomy. However, it is obvious that in the sense which we are currently applying to the word physics, what is commonly called plain astronomy must be termed physical or descriptive, and what is usually called physical must be named mathematical astronomy. We shall, therefore, largely confine ourselves to descriptive astronomy, and shall take only a general view of the laws of gravitation as an illustration of the phenomena previously described. After having considered the magnificent objects of astronomy, which are scattered throughout the universe, we descend to geography, or the specific history of the terraqueous globe <note>The globe consisting of both land and water.</note>, and to the tides, produced by the influence of the celestial bodies on the ocean. Then, leaving the characteristics of the larger features of the matter that constitutes the earth, we come naturally to the properties and powers of its individual particles, and to the phenomena of heat, electricity, and magnetism. These are either qualities of matter or are dependent on substances differing in some respects from common matter. In the next place, we proceed to the combination of all these substances and actions in meteorology, and in the phenomena of vegetable and animal life; a general view of these will complete our discussions on the subject of physics. The science of chemistry, or the study of the qualities of particular kinds of matter, might be said to belong to the investigation of the properties of matter in general; but this science is of too great extent and importance to occupy a subordinate place in a system of natural philosophy, and must, therefore, be considered as requiring a separate course of study.

In our astronomical inquiries, we shall first examine the phenomena of the heavens and earth in their simplest form, not as they immediately appear to our observation, but as they are shown by undeniable proofs to be naturally arranged. The stars and sun, the planets and their satellites, and lastly the comets, will be individually described; the causes of the motions of

# ON THE FIXED STARS.

these bodies will be briefly indicated; their perceptible effects with respect to the inhabitants of the earth will be shown, and the practical methods of determining their locations and orbits will be explained.

When we begin to consider, on a large scale, the properties of matter and of space, we are impressed at first sight with the unimaginable disproportion between the magnitude of space and of perceptible matter. We are naturally led to inquire if the seemingly empty expanse of the universe is entirely without any matter or substance. Indeed, the atmospheres of the planets cannot be said to end absolutely at any specific point, but they must become unimaginably thin at a very moderate distance. However, the substance that produces the sensation of light must be found everywhere, at least without any perceptible gap; for if an eye were placed at any point in the regions of unbounded space, wherever human investigation or imagination can penetrate them, some luminous object would be visible to it at every moment, and, in general, countless objects might be seen in every direction. 

Light, therefore, must be present everywhere, whether we suppose it to consist of distinct projected particles, or to be a condition of a highly elastic ether that fills the universe in a state so thin that, although it forms a continuous medium, it allows all bodies to move through it without noticeable resistance and is even admitted into their pores with complete freedom. If we follow Newton's opinion on the nature of light, we must assume that both such an ethereal medium, nearly at rest, and the particles of light moving swiftly through it, exist together in all places—not to mention the possibility of the coexistence of a thousand other unseen and unknown substances, essences, and influences in the same specific location, which may forever defy the pride of an arrogant philosophy that would aspire to comprehend the entire extent of the mighty work of creation within its own limited sphere.

The expanse of the universe is scattered at immense distances with separate portions of a substance which we assume to be matter, constituting stars (or suns), planets, and comets—bodies which certainly share the ability to emit or reflect light and which, in all probability, have many other properties in common. Those that emit their own light are

<meta>This page continues the discussion on descriptive astronomy, transitioning from the nature of light and ethereal mediums to the specific properties of the celestial bodies known as fixed stars, including their light, composition, and distribution.</meta>

<header>LECTURE XLI.</header>

...called *fixed* stars; and this appears to be the only criterion that we can apply to a star: for the word *fixed* is only to be understood in a comparative sense.

The stars must necessarily shine by their own light; for if we grant that they consist of gravitating matter, it must be allowed that no star could be near enough to another to be seen by reflected light without a very noticeable change in the positions of both as a consequence of their mutual gravitation. Nor would it be possible, on account of their immense distance from us, to distinguish two such bodies from each other. It follows also, on the same supposition of the universality of the force of gravity, that the form of the stars must be nearly spherical.

The light of the stars appears to the naked eye to be generally white, being too faint to excite the idea of a particular color; but when it is concentrated by Dr. Herschel's large speculums, it displays various hues in various stars; and indeed, to the naked eye, some of the stars appear a little redder and others a little bluer. The cause of the twinkling of the stars is not fully determined, but it is attributed, with some probability, to changes which are constantly taking place in the atmosphere and which affect its refractive density. It is said that in some climates, where the air is remarkably serene, the stars hardly appear to twinkle at all.

Over two thousand stars are visible to the naked eye; and when a telescope is used, their number appears to increase with no other limit than the imperfection of the instrument. Dr. Herschel has observed in the Milky Way more than ten thousand stars in the space of a square degree. Lucretius and Dr. Halley have argued that their number must be absolutely infinite so that all of them may remain at rest by the opposition of attractions acting in every possible direction; but we are by no means certain that they do remain in perfect equilibrium.

We can give no exact account of the actual magnitude of the stars, but they are divided into seven or more orders according to their degrees of apparent brightness. There is, however, reason to suppose, from the quantity of light emitted by the brightest stars, that some of them are much

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the nature of fixed stars, specifically addressing their dimensions and the immense distances between them and the Earth.</meta>

<page-num>491</page-num>
<header>ON THE FIXED STARS.</header>

...larger than the sun. Those stars which are below the sixth magnitude are scarcely visible without the help of telescopes. The distances of all the stars from us and from one another are so great that they cannot be immediately compared with their diameters; for no star subtends an angle large enough to be determined by direct observation. The more perfect the instruments that we employ, the smaller the apparent diameters of the fixed stars appear. Dr. Herschel found that one of the stars of the first magnitude, when viewed in his best telescopes, appeared to be about one-third of a second in diameter. But there is always a limit to the perfection of the focus of the telescope and of the eye, and, however accurate both may be, the image of every radiant point will occupy a space of a certain size on the retina, which does not depend on the size of the object. Thus, it will perhaps be forever impossible to measure any angle which is only a very small fraction of a second. (Plate XXXI. Fig. 453, 454.)

There is, however, reason to suppose that the angle subtended by the nearest stars is in reality more than a hundred times smaller than the angle measured by Dr. Herschel; for it may be conjectured that our distance from the nearest stars is about one hundred trillion miles <note>The original text uses "a hundred million million miles."</note>, taking about one-third of a second for the annual parallax of the earth—that is, for the change in the apparent positions of some of the fixed stars resulting from the earth’s annual motion. This seems to be nearly the maximum amount of an annual parallax that could have completely escaped observation; for Dr. Herschel supposes that, by means of double stars, a parallax of only one-tenth of a second might become detectable, and even this has never yet been discovered. On the other hand, if the parallax were really much smaller than this, it would be necessary to suppose the actual size or brightness of the brightest stars to be incomparably greater than that of the sun; for at the distance of a hundred trillion miles, our sun would appear, according to Lambert’s calculations, only about one-fourth as bright as Saturn, or like a star of only the second or third magnitude. Perhaps, indeed, the stars may differ as much from each other in magnitude as the planetary bodies do, but it is somewhat more natural to imagine them more nearly equal until we have some reason for suspecting any significant inequality in their dimensions. At any rate, there is little doubt that the diversity of their apparent magnitudes is principally due to their different distances; perhaps none of them are

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of the distances and physical dimensions of stars, as well as the observation and cataloging of nebulae.</meta>
<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>492</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XLI.</header>
<sig>3</sig>
<meta>bleed-through from reverse page</meta>

much nearer to each other than the nearest are to us; and there may still be a very great variety in their actual dimensions. There can be only twelve points on the surface of a sphere that are as far from each other as they are from the center; in a sphere of twice the radius, there may be about 50 points at the same distance; in a sphere of three times the radius, more than 100. It has been observed that these numbers do not differ greatly from the actual numbers of the stars of the first, second, and third magnitudes, although it is true that they are not by any means placed at equal angular distances from each other. 

But, from a comparison of the light of different stars, we may infer that if their real magnitudes are nearly equal, their distances must increase much faster than in this arithmetical progression; that is, that the stars of the second magnitude are more than twice as remote as those of the first, and those of the third are more than three times as remote. Mr. Michell found the light of Sirius to be between 400 and 1000 times as great as that of a star of the sixth magnitude; consequently, supposing these stars are actually equal, their distances must differ in the ratio of 1 to 20 or 30, since light always diminishes in proportion to the square of the distance of the luminous object. 

The light of stars of different magnitudes, situated near each other, may be compared by viewing them through two apertures of different sizes cut in cards, with one held before each eye. The apertures are reduced to such sizes that the stars may appear equally bright, and the comparison may be extended to the light of the sun by finding a star and a planet of equal brightness and calculating what proportion of the sun's light must be reflected by the planet, based on the most probable assumption regarding the nature of its surface to reflect more or less of the light which falls on it.

The stars are generally dispersed without any regular order, but we may observe in many parts of the heavens that a number of them are so much nearer together than to the rest that they form a cluster or nebula. The ancients had noticed some of the most conspicuous nebulae, but Huygens first directed the attention of modern astronomers to the large one situated in the constellation Orion. Herschel has now given us catalogs of 2500 nebulae: many of them can be resolved by very high magnifying powers into separate stars, but others appear to consist of a luminous matter spread uniformly in the neighborhood of the several stars to which they seem to belong. (Plate XXI. Fig. 455 . . 463.)

<page-num>493</page-num>
<header>ON THE FIXED STARS. 493</header>

It has been conjectured that all stars are arranged in nebulae, and that those which appear to us to be more widely separated are individual stars of that particular nebula in which we are placed. The marginal parts of this nebula may be observed in the form of a glowing zone called the Milky Way, which is too distant to allow its individual stars to be perceived by the naked eye. This opinion was first suggested by Professor Kant, the author of the system of metaphysics called critical philosophy. The idea was adopted by Lambert, who considers the largest stars as constituting a distinct nebula placed among a multitude of others, which together produce the appearance of a continuous zone; and Dr. Herschel has investigated very particularly the shape of a single nebula that would be capable of being projected into the form of the Milky Way. We must not, however, suppose that each of Dr. Herschel's 2,500 nebulae can be at all comparable in size to this supposed nebula, since many of them are almost as much resolved by the telescope into single stars as the Milky Way itself; this would be utterly impossible if the stars they contain were as numerous as those of the nebula to which the Milky Way belongs. Supposing all the stars of this nebula to be as remote from each other as the nearest of them are from the sun, it may be calculated that the most distant are about 500 times as far from us as the nearest, and that light, which is probably 15 or 20 years in traveling to us from Sirius, would be nearly twenty thousand years in passing through the whole diameter of the Milky Way. A nebula of the same size as this, appearing like a diffused light of one degree in diameter, must be at such a distance that its light would require a million years to reach us. (Plate XXXI. Fig. 464.)

The stars are not, properly speaking, absolutely fixed with respect to each other, for several of them have specific motions, which have been discovered by a comparison of accurate observations made at very distant times. Arcturus, for instance, has a progressive motion amounting to more than two seconds annually. Dr. Maskelyne found that out of 36 stars whose positions he ascertained with great precision, 35 had a <term>proper motion</term>. Mr. Michell and Dr. Herschel have conjectured that some of the stars revolve around others which are apparently situated very near them; and perhaps even all the stars may in reality change their places more or less, although their re-

<meta>This page continues the discussion of star systems and nebulae, transitioning from the distance of the Milky Way to Dr. Herschel's specific classifications of various celestial bodies based on their gravitational interactions and appearances.</meta>

<page-num>494</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XLI.</header>

relative positions, and the directions of their paths may often render their motions imperceptible to us.

Regarding all these arrangements of stars into different systems, Dr. Herschel has recently entered into a very extensive field of observation and speculation, and has divided them into a number of classes, to each of which he has assigned a distinct character. He supposes some, like our sun, to be isolated stars, beyond the reach of any significant influence from the gravitation of others; and he conceives that planets and comets revolve around these alone. He imagines double stars, in general, to be much closer to each other, so as to be materially affected by their mutual gravitation, and to preserve their distance only by means of the centrifugal force derived from a revolution around their common center of inertia; an opinion which, he thinks, is strongly supported by his own observations of certain changes in the positions of double stars. He supposes others, again, to be united in triple, quadruple, and even more complex systems. A fourth class consists of nebulae like the Milky Way, where the clusters of stars are rounded and appear brightest in the middle. Dr. Herschel distinguishes groups of stars from these by a lack of apparent condensation around a center of attraction, and clusters by an even greater central compression. A seventh class includes such nebulae as have not yet been resolved into stars, some of which Dr. Herschel supposes to be so remote that the light emitted by them must actually have been two million years in traveling to our system. The nebulae of another description resemble stars surrounded by a blur, or a faint disc of light. A diffused milky nebulosity, apparently produced by some cause distinct from the direct light of any stars, is the next in order; and Dr. Herschel has distinguished other more contracted nebulous appearances, in different states of condensation, into the classes of nebulous stars and planetary nebulae, both with and without bright central points. Many of these distinctions are perhaps too subtle to be verified by common observers; but the discovery of the existence of double and triple stars, revolving around a common center, will, if it is confirmed, add one more to the list of Dr. Herschel's important improvements.

It is, however, fully established that some of the stars have periodic

For instance, the star *Algol*, which is usually of the second magnitude, drops to the fourth magnitude at intervals of 2 days and 21 hours, taking 7 hours for the gradual decrease and recovery of its light. A less likely theory regarding this change in brightness was proposed by *Maupertuis*, who imagined that the disc of the star might be significantly flattened by a rapid rotation, and its edge occasionally presented to us as a result of the disturbances produced by the attraction of planets revolving around the star. Other irregular variations might possibly be caused by the appearance and disappearance of spots, occurring like sunspots without any fixed order or known cause; and over the course of centuries, many stars have completely disappeared and sometimes been recovered again; others have appeared for a short time where no star had been seen before. Such a temporary star was observed by *Hipparchus* 120 years before our *era*, and this event suggested to him the usefulness of creating an accurate catalog of all the stars and their respective positions; this catalog still exists, having been preserved by *Ptolemy*, who added 4 stars to the 1022 it originally contained. In 1572, *Cornelius Gemma* discovered a new star in *Cassiopeia* that was bright enough to be seen during the day and gradually disappeared over sixteen months. *Kepler*, in 1604, observed a new star in *Serpentarius* that was more brilliant than any other star or planet and constantly changed into all the colors of the rainbow, except when it was near the horizon; it remained visible for about a year. Many other new stars have also been observed at different times.

To describe specific fixed stars according to their relative positions, it is necessary to consider them as they appear to the inhabitants of the earth. For the sake of convenience, they have been divided into groups that form imaginary shapes called constellations. This division dates back to very ancient times, and although it may be useless, and sometimes even inconvenient, for the purposes of precise observation, these arbitrary names and associations greatly assist the memory in recalling the major features of the heavens. ->### LECTURE XLI.<-

It is usual to describe particular stars by their position with respect to the imaginary figure to which they belong, or, more commonly at present, by the letters of the Greek alphabet, which were first applied by Bayer in 1603; in addition to these, they are identified by Roman letters and by the numbers of particular catalogs.

There are two principal methods of representing the stars: the one is by depicting them on a globe, where each star occupies the spot in which it would appear to an eye placed in the center of the globe, and where the positions are consequently reversed when we look at them from the outside, in the same manner as a word appears reversed when seen through the back of the paper. The other method is by charts, which are generally so arranged as to represent the stars in positions similar to their natural ones, or as they would appear on the internal concave surface of the globe. Sometimes also the stars have been depicted as they would be projected onto imaginary surfaces without any reference to a globe; for instance, on the surfaces of transparent cones or cylinders. The art of constructing all such projections belongs to the subject of perspective.

In describing the particular stars, it will be most convenient to begin with those that never set in our climates, and we may then relate the positions of others to their locations with respect to these.

The Great Bear is the most conspicuous of the constellations which never set; it consists of seven stars, arranged like the four wheels of a wagon and its three horses, except that the horses are attached to one of the wheels. The two hind wheels are the "pointers," which direct us to the pole star at the extremity of the tail of the Little Bear; and further on, to the constellation Cassiopeia, which is situated in the Milky Way where it is nearest to the pole, and which consists of several stars nearly in the form of the letter W. The two northernmost wheels of the Great Bear, or wain, point at the bright star Capella, the goat, in Auriga. Descending along the Milky Way from Cassiopeia, if we go toward Capella, we come to Algenib in Perseus; and a little further from the pole, we find Algol, or Medusa's head; but if we take the opposite direction, we arrive at Cygnus, the swan; and beyond it, a little out of the Milky Way, is the bright star Lyra. ## LECTURE XLII.

### ON THE SOLAR SYSTEM.

<insert>REESE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</insert>

**THE** most conspicuous of all the celestial bodies that we have been examining is the sun, that magnificent luminary which occupies the center of the system that includes our earth, together with a variety of other primary and secondary planets, and a still greater number of comets.

The sun agrees with the fixed stars in the property of emitting light continually, and in constantly retaining its relative situation with very little variation; it is probable also that these bodies have many other properties in common. The sun is, therefore, considered as a fixed star comparatively near us; and the stars as suns at immense distances from us: and we infer from the same analogy, that the stars possess gravitation and the other general properties of matter; they are supposed to emit heat as well as light; and it has with reason been conjectured that they serve to nurture the inhabitants of a multitude of planetary bodies revolving around them.

The sun, like many other stars, probably has a progressive motion, which is supposed, from a comparison of the apparent motions of a great number of the stars, to be directed toward the constellation Hercules. It is beyond all question that many of the stars have motions peculiar to themselves, and it is not certain that any of them are without such motions: it is, therefore, in itself highly probable that the sun may have such a motion. But Dr. Herschel has confirmed this conjecture by arguments almost demonstrative. He observes that the apparent proper motions of 44 stars out of 56 are very nearly in the direction which would be the result of such a real motion of the solar system: and that the bright stars Arcturus and Sirius, which are probably the nearest to us, have, as they ought to have, the

Furthermore, the star Castor appears, when viewed with a telescope, to consist of two stars of nearly equal magnitude; and although they both have a considerable apparent motion, they have never been found to change their distance from each other by even a single second. This circumstance is easily understood if both their apparent motions are assumed to arise from a real motion of the sun, but it is much less probable if one supposes two separate and independent motions.

In addition to this progressive motion, the sun is subject to some small change of position depending on the locations of the planetary bodies. This was long inferred from theory alone, but has been actually demonstrated by modern observations. Assuming all the planets were in conjunction, or nearly in the same direction from the sun, the common center of inertia <note>center of mass</note> of the system is at a distance of about one solar diameter from the sun's center. And since the center of inertia of the whole system must be undisturbed by any reciprocal actions or revolutions of the bodies composing it, the sun must describe an irregular orbit around this center, with its greatest distance from it being equal to its own diameter. We may form an idea of the magnitude of this orbit by comparing it with the orbit of the moon: a body revolving around the sun while in contact with its surface would be nearly twice as far from the sun's center as the moon is from the earth. Therefore, the sun's revolution around the common center of gravity of the system must be, at its most remote point, four times the distance of the moon from the earth.

The sun revolves on its axis in 25 days and 10 hours with respect to the fixed stars. This axis is directed toward a point about halfway between the pole star and Lyra, with the plane of rotation being inclined a little more than 7° to the plane in which the earth revolves. The direction of this motion is from west to east—terms which we can only define based on our prior knowledge of the stars—by saying that the motion is such that a point on the sun's surface, initially opposite Aries, moves toward Taurus. Nor do we have any better way of describing north and south, or right and left; we can only say, by comparison, that if we are positioned with our heads toward the north and looking toward the center, our right hands will be to the east and our left hands to the west. All the rotations of the various bodies that compose the solar system, as far as they have been determined, are in the same direction, and all their

The time and direction of the sun's rotation are determined by the changing position of the spots which are usually visible on its disc, and which some astronomers suppose to be elevations; however, others—apparently with better evidence—consider them to be excavations or gaps in the luminous matter covering the sun's surface. These spots are frequently observed to appear and disappear, and in the meantime they are subject to great variations, but they are generally found around the same points of the sun's surface. Lalande imagines that they are parts of the sun's solid body which, by some agitations of the luminous ocean with which he believes the sun to be surrounded, are left nearly or entirely bare. Dr. Wilson and Dr. Herschel are inclined to consider this ocean as consisting of a flame rather than a liquid substance, and Dr. Herschel attributes the spots to the emission of a gaseous fluid, not yet in combustion, which displaces the general luminous atmosphere and is afterward to serve as fuel for supporting the process. Consequently, he supposes the appearance of many spots to be indicative of the approach of warm seasons on the surface of the earth, and he has attempted to maintain this opinion with historical evidence. The exterior luminous atmosphere has a somewhat mottled appearance; some parts of it, appearing brighter than others, have generally been called *faculae*, but Dr. Herschel distinguishes them by the names of *ridges* and *nodules*. The spots are usually surrounded by margins less dark than themselves, which Dr. Herschel calls *shallows*, and which he considers as parts of an inferior layer consisting of opaque clouds, capable of protecting the immediate surface of the sun from the excessive heat produced by combustion in the superior layer, and perhaps of making it habitable for living beings. (Plate XXXI. Fig. 465 .. 469.)

At its surface, a heavy object would fall through no less than 450 feet in a single second; therefore, if every other circumstance allowed human beings to live on it, their own weight would present an insurmountable difficulty. Their weight would become nearly thirty times greater than it is on the surface of the earth, and a man of moderate size would weigh more than two tons. Some of the most famous astronomers have imagined—based on the relative light of different parts of the sun’s disc, or visible surface—that it is surrounded by a very dense and vast atmosphere that is not perfectly transparent. They believed that without such an atmosphere, the edges (which are seen at the sharpest angles) would necessarily appear much brighter. However, this opinion is entirely wrong, and the conclusions drawn from it regarding the sun’s atmosphere are therefore baseless.

We are, however, certain through direct observation that some gaseous substance exists in the sun’s vicinity, creating the phenomenon known as the zodiacal light. This is sometimes seen extending beyond the orbit of Mercury, nearly in the plane of the sun’s rotation on its axis. It is said to have been first clearly described in Childrey’s *Britannia Baconica*, a work published in 1661, and it was later observed in greater detail by Cassini, Mairan, and others. In the tropical zone, it is visible almost constantly; and in these climates, it can often be seen in early March after the end of twilight. It appears as a narrow triangle, somewhat rounded off, with a whiteness resembling the Milky Way. It rises from the sun as its base, like the projection or cross-section of a very flat spheroid, and extends to a distance of more than 50° from the sun. The entire orbit of Venus never spans an angle larger than 96° from the earth; consequently, this substance must occasionally surround both Mercury and Venus. If it were not extremely thin, it would cause some disturbance in their movements; however, in reality, it does not seem to hinder even the progress of the tails of comets, which are likely themselves of very low density. Some persons have attributed the appearance to the refraction of the earth's atmosphere alone; but if it arose from any such cause as this, its direction could hardly be oblique with respect to the horizon, and it is highly improbable that it should always happen to coincide with the plane of the sun's rotation. (Plate XXXI. Fig. 470.)

The sun is accompanied in its progressive motion among the fixed stars by ten planetary bodies of different magnitudes, revolving around it from west to east in orbits approaching circles, and visible to us by means of the light which they receive from it. These are Mercury, Venus, the Earth, Mars, Juno, Pallas, Ceres, Jupiter, Saturn, and the <term>Georgian planet</term>. It is unnecessary to present any arguments at this time to prove the actual existence or direction of any of these motions; their complete agreement with the visible phenomena of the heavens and with the laws of gravitation will hereafter be shown to afford sufficient evidence of the accuracy of the accepted theory of the arrangement of the solar system. The motion of the earth is most indisputably proved by the apparent <term>aberration of the fixed stars</term>, derived from the different directions of this motion at different times, and corresponding precisely with the known velocity of light, deduced from observations of a very different kind. That the planets receive their light from the sun is undeniably shown by the appearance of the discs of many of them when viewed through a telescope, as only those parts of their surfaces are luminous on which the sun shines at the time of observation.

These planets are neither all in one plane, nor does any one of them remain precisely in the same plane at all times; but their deviations from their respective planes are inconsiderable, and they are commonly represented by assuming that each planet revolves in a plane passing through the sun, and that the position of this plane is liable to slight variations. There is, however, a certain imaginary plane, determinable from the positions, the velocities, and the masses of the planets, which—like the center of inertia—never changes its position because of any mutual actions of the bodies of the system; this plane of inertia is called the <term>fixed ecliptic</term>. Its position is nearly halfway between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn, and it is inclined at only a small angle to the plane of the earth's orbit, which is called the <term>earth's ecliptic</term>, or simply the <term>ecliptic</term>.

<header>LECTURE XLII.</header>

The ecliptic passes through the constellations called the signs of the zodiac, between Aries, the Pleiades, Gemini, and Regulus to the north, and Aldebaran, Spica, and Antares to the south. Its position has shifted slowly over many ages, so that its northernmost point is now more than one-third of a degree further from the pole star than it was in the time of Eratosthenes, who observed its position 230 years before the birth of Christ. It appears from Lagrange’s calculations that the limit of its greatest possible variation is about 10 or 11 degrees. The ecliptic is supposed to be divided into twelve angular parts, or *signs*, each containing thirty degrees; they are named Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricornus, Aquarius, and Pisces. Those who prefer the rhythm of a Latin couplet to help the memory may repeat them like this:

->Sunt Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo,<-
->Libraque, Scorpius, Arcitenens, Caper, Amphora, Pisces.<-

The planes of the orbits of the other primary planets—excepting the three tiny planets recently discovered—intersect the ecliptic at small angles, and the lines of intersection are called *lines of the nodes*. The nodes of all the planets move very slowly, though not quite uniformly, from east to west; that is, in relation to the fixed stars. At present, the inclinations of all the orbits appear to be decreasing slightly: that of Jupiter’s orbit is 6 minutes less than it was in the time of Ptolemy.

The orbit of each planet is very nearly an ellipse, one focus of which coincides with the sun—or rather, with the common center of inertia of the sun and the planet. The ends of the major axis, where the orbit is furthest from and nearest to the sun, are called the *upper* and the *lower* <term>apsis</term>, or the *aphelion* and *perihelion*; the mean distance is at either end of the minor axis, and the distance from the center of the ellipse to the sun is called the *eccentricity*. The slight deviations of the planets from these elliptical paths are accounted for by considering the apsides as moving, and this motion is *direct*—that is, from west to east—in the case of all the planets except Venus, whose aphelion has a *retrograde* motion relative to the fixed stars.

The elliptical motion of the planets was first discovered by Kepler; and

The observations on which Kepler based these important laws were made principally on the planet Mars. He determined by calculation—based on the then generally adopted theory of motion in an eccentric circle—what the approximate position of the planet must be with respect to the sun (that is, its heliocentric position); then, by observing its geocentric position with respect to the earth, he was able to construct a triangle representing the positions of the three bodies. By repeating this operation in various parts of the orbit, he discovered its form; having done this, the velocity of the motion in different parts of the orbit was easily determined from the apparent change of position in a given time. (Plate XXXII. Fig. 471.)

The same astronomer also determined that the squares of the orbital periods of the different planets are proportional to the cubes of their mean distances from the sun. For example, if one planet were four times as distant as another, it would revolve in a period eight times as long, since the cube of 4 is equal to the square of 8; thus Mars is nearly four times as remote from the sun as Mercury, and the Georgian planet <note>The "Georgian planet" refers to Uranus, named by its discoverer William Herschel in honor of King George III.</note> is four times as remote as Jupiter, and their periods are each nearly eight times as long as those of their respective counterparts.

It is probable that all the planets have a rotational motion from west to east, which is either perfectly or very nearly uniform. This motion has been observed in Venus, the Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn; and from certain phenomena regarding the satellites of the Georgian planet, Mr. Laplace thinks it may also be assumed as nearly certain that this planet has a rotational motion as well. The shape of the planets is spheroidal; they are more or less flattened at the poles, depending on how rapidly they revolve on their axes. These axes remain, with very slight deviation, in a position that is always parallel in every part of the orbits.

But, over time, the gradual change of the position of the axis produces a noticeable effect. In the case of the earth, this effect is called the precession of the equinoxes. The equinoctial points are the intersections of the apparent ecliptic—the path of the sun in the heavens—

Consequently, it happens that the constellations known as the signs of the zodiac are now at a considerable distance from those divisions of the ecliptic that bear the same names.

The earth’s axis also undergoes a small periodic change of inclination, or a nutation, which occurs over about 19 years and amounts in total to only 18 seconds. Its existence was determined by Newton from theory, although he failed in his attempt to calculate its exact quantity with accuracy; it was first actually observed by Dr. Bradley around the year 1747. The absolute direction of the axis in the heavens is also subject to some variation over the course of many ages, but this change has not always been sufficiently distinguished from the change in the position of the ecliptic. The inclination of the equator to the ecliptic is now very nearly 23° 28'.

To help remember a general idea of the proportional distances of the primary planets from the sun, we may set the distance of the Earth at 10 and that of Saturn at 100; the distance of Mercury will then be 4, to which we must add 3 for Venus, making 7; twice 3 (or 6) for the Earth, making 10; twice 6 (or 12) for Mars, making 16; twice 12 (or 24), making 28, for the three small planets—Juno, Pallas, and Ceres; twice 24 (or 48), making 52, for Jupiter; twice 48 (or 96) for Saturn, making 100; and twice 96 (or 192), making 196, for the Georgian planet <note>The "Georgian planet" refers to Uranus.</note>; and these sums will represent the distances in the nearest whole numbers, without any significant exception.

The planet Mercury is little more than one-third as large as the Earth in diameter. It completes its revolution in slightly less than three months, at about two-fifths of the Earth's distance. Its orbit is more eccentric, and more inclined to the ecliptic, than those of any of the planets ex-

Venus is very nearly as large as the Earth; Dr. Herschel even considers it to be slightly larger. Its density has been estimated from the perturbations in the motions of the other planets caused by its attraction, and it has been supposed to be a little less than that of the Earth.

The distance of the Earth from the sun is about 95 million English miles; and this measurement is generally supposed to be accurate enough that there is no probability of an error of more than a million or two at most, although some authors are still inclined to believe that the distance may be even greater than a hundred million. The period of its revolution—with respect to the equinoctial points, which are the usual standard of comparison because their position determines the annual return of the seasons—is 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 48 seconds; and this is called its tropical revolution. That of its absolute or sidereal revolution is 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 8 seconds; the difference, which is 20 minutes and 20 seconds, is the time taken to pass over the space through which the equinoctial points have receded in the course of the tropical year. By a "day," we always understand the time that elapses during the rotation of the Earth with respect to the sun; a sidereal day is about four minutes shorter.

At a distance from the sun exceeding that of the Earth by one-half, the planet Mars revolves in about one and seven-eighths years. It has half the Earth’s linear dimensions; it has spots that change their form and, therefore, probably has an atmosphere. Jupiter is the largest of all the planets, its diameter being 11 times as great as that of the Earth, and the force of gravitation at its surface being triple the terrestrial gravitation. It revolves in about 12 years, at a little more than five times the Earth's distance from the sun. Its rotation is performed in less than ten hours, its equator being inclined about three degrees to its ecliptic, which makes an angle of 1° 19' with ours. Its belts are supposed by many to be clouds in its atmosphere; they seem to have a rotation somewhat slower than that of the planet.

The diameter of Saturn is ten times as great as that of the Earth, but, on account of the lower density of its substance, the force of gravity at its surface scarcely exceeds its force at the surface of the Earth. It revolves in 29 and a half years, in an orbit inclined 2 1/2° to the ecliptic, at the distance of 9 1/2 semidiameters of the Earth's orbit; its rotation occupies only 10 1/4 hours, and its equator is inclined about 30° to our ecliptic. These ten planetary bodies are the only ones discovered so far that have any claim to be considered <term>primary planets</term>—that is, as bodies revolving around the sun in orbits so nearly circular that they always remain within the reach of our observation. It has been speculated that the number of planets may in reality be much greater; not only might many small and perhaps invisible bodies be revolving in the gaps between the planets we know, but larger bodies might also belong to our system that never approach close enough to be seen by us. Some have even given names borrowed from ancient mythology to these imaginary planets, but the idea of such an assignment of names is to be regarded as belonging more to the realm of poetic fiction than to that of solid science.

The largest and most remote of the primary planets have their attendant <term>satellites</term>, or <term>secondary planets</term>, accompanying them in their respective revolutions around the sun and moving, at the same time, in subordinate orbits around the primary planets. The orbits of the satellites of the <term>Georgian planet</term> <note>The planet Uranus</note> are nearly perpendicular to the <term>ecliptic</term>; and some of their revolutions are supposed to be rather <term>retrograde</term> than direct.

Besides the bodies that revolve completely around the sun within the limits of our observation, there are others for which we only conclude from analogy that they perform such revolutions. These are the <term>comets</term>; they generally appear attended by a nebulous light, either surrounding them as a <term>coma</term> or stretched out to a considerable length as a tail; and they sometimes seem to consist of such light only. Their orbits are so eccentric that in their more remote positions, the <term>comets</term> are no longer visible to us, although at other times they approach much nearer to the sun than any of the planets; for the comet of 1680, when in its <term>perihelion</term>, was at a distance of only one-sixth of the sun's diameter from its surface. Their tails are often of great extent, appearing as a faint light directed always toward a point nearly opposite to the sun. It is quite uncertain what substance they consist of, and it is difficult to determine which of the conjectures respecting them can be considered the least improbable. It is possible that, on account of the intense cold to which the <term>comets</term> are subjected during the greatest part of their revolutions, some substances lighter than anything we can imagine on Earth may be retained by them in a liquid or even in a solid form until they are released by the effect of the sun's heat. However, we are still equally at a loss to explain the rapidity of their ascent, for the buoyancy of the sun's atmosphere cannot possibly be supposed to be adequate for the effect; and on the whole, there is perhaps reason to believe that these appearances are derived from some cause bearing a considerable analogy to the fluid supposed to be involved in the effects of <term>electricity</term>. It is probable that the density of the <term>nucleus</term>, or the body of the comet itself, is comparatively small, and its attraction for the tail consequently weak, so that it has little tendency to reduce the tail—even if it consists of a material substance—to a spherical form. Since some <term>comets</term> have no visible <term>nucleus</term> at all, there is no difficulty in supposing the <term>nucleus</term>, when present, to be of very moderate density, and perhaps to consist of the same kind of substance that constitutes the tail or <term>coma</term>, in a state of somewhat greater condensation. Nearly 500 comets are recorded to have been seen at different times, and the orbits of about a hundred have been correctly ascertained; but we have no opportunity of observing a sufficient portion of the orbit of any comet to determine the whole of its form as an ellipse with accuracy, since the part which is within the limits of our observation does not noticeably differ from a parabola, which would be the result of an ellipse prolonged without end.

Two comets at least, or perhaps three, have been recognized in their return. A comet appeared in 1770 which Prosperin suspected moved in an orbit materially different from a parabola; Mr. Lexell determined its period to be 5 years and 7 months, and its extreme distances to be between the orbits of Jupiter and Mercury; but it does not appear that any subsequent observations have confirmed his theory. It has, however, been calculated that, assuming the theory is correct, it must afterward have approached so near to Jupiter as to have the form of its orbit entirely changed.

Dr. Halley foretold the return of a comet around 1758, which had appeared in 1531, 1607, and 1682, at intervals of about 75 years; and with Clairaut's further correction for the perturbations of Jupiter and Saturn, the time agreed within about a month. The mean distance of this comet from the sun must be less than that of the <term>Georgian planet</term> <note>The planet Uranus</note>; so that by improving our telescopes even further, we may, perhaps, hereafter be able to consider some of the comets as planets, insofar as their remaining always visible would entitle them to that name. ## LECTURE XLIII.

### ON THE LAWS OF GRAVITATION.

Sir Isaac Newton first systematically demonstrated that all the motions of the heavenly bodies, which have been described, may be deduced from the effects of the same force of gravitation that causes a heavy body to fall to the earth; he showed that, as a result of this universal property of matter, all bodies attract each other with forces that decrease as the squares of the distances increase; and in recent years, the same theory has been still more accurately applied to the most complicated phenomena. We are now to take a general view of how this law operates, in the same order in which the characteristics of the celestial bodies have been listed. It will not be possible to investigate mathematically the effects of gravity in each particular motion, but we may to some extent illustrate the subject by considering how astronomers have proceeded in their explanations and calculations, and we may enter sufficiently into the principles of the theory to understand the possibility of its applications.

The bodies that exist in nature are never single gravitating points; and in order to determine the effects of their attraction, we must suppose the actions of an infinite number of such points to be combined. Newton showed that all the matter of a spherical body, or of a spherical surface, may be considered—when estimating its attractive force on other matter—as collected in the center of the sphere. The steps of the demonstration are these: a particle of matter, placed at the summit of a given cone or pyramid, is attracted by a thin surface, also composed of attractive matter, occupying the base of the cone, with equal force, regardless of the length of the cone, provided that its angular position remains unchanged: hence it is easily inferred that if a gravitating point is placed anywhere within a hollow sphere, it will remain in equilibrium, as a result of the opposite and

equal actions of the infinite number of minute surfaces, terminating the opposite pyramids into which the sphere may be divided. It is also demonstrable, with the help of a <term>fluxional calculation</term> <note>calculus</note>, that a point placed outside the surface is attracted by it in exactly the same way as if all the matter it contains were collected in the center. Consequently, the same is true of a <term>solid sphere</term>, which may be assumed to consist of an infinite number of such hollow spheres. If, however, the point were placed within a solid sphere, it would be pulled toward the center by a force that is simply proportional to its distance from that center. This proposition helps greatly to simplify all calculations of the attractions of the <term>celestial bodies</term>, since all of them are so nearly spherical that their action on any distant bodies is the same as if all the matter of which they consist were condensed into their respective centers. But if the force of <term>gravitation</term> varied according to any law other than the one found to prevail, this simplification would no longer be allowed, even regarding a sphere.

It can scarcely be doubted that the power of gravitation extends from one fixed star to another, although its effects in this case may be much too small to be perceived by us. It may possibly influence the progressive motions of some of the stars; and if, as <term>Dr. Herschel</term> supposes, there are double and triple stars revolving around a common center, they must be held in their orbits by the force of gravity. Dr. Herschel also imagines that the motion of our sun is in some measure derived from the same cause, being directed nearly toward a point where two layers of the <term>milky way</term> meet. The attraction of the stars, all else being equal, must, however, be proportional to their brightness; yet that part of the heavens toward which the sun is probably moving appears to give less light than almost any other part, nor does the hemisphere of which it is the center contain as many bright stars as the opposite hemisphere. If <term>Sirius</term> is a million times as far from the sun as the earth is, and if it should descend toward the sun by means of their mutual gravitation only, it would move, by a rough estimate, only about 40 feet in the first year, and in 1,000 years only 8,000 miles. It has been conjectured that the mutual gravitation of the stars of a <term>nebula</term> is sometimes the cause of the peculiar form of the cluster, which somewhat resembles that of a drop of liquid held together by its cohesion; but

...unless the form of the nebula was originally spherical, it could scarcely have acquired that form from the operation of gravity, since the spherical form of a drop is due as much to elasticity as to the attractive force of the particles of water; and it would be necessary, in order to preserve the analogy, that the stars should also be floating in an incompressible fluid.

The sun’s change of position, dependent on the relative situation of the planets, is so slight that it escaped observation until its existence had been deduced from theory. It is not that this change would be unnoticeable if we had any means of detecting it, since it may amount in total to a distance equal to twice the sun’s diameter, or seven times the distance of the moon from the earth; and this change is easily deduced from the general and unquestionable law of mechanics: that the position of the <term>center of inertia</term> of a system cannot be changed by any reciprocal or mutual action of the bodies composing it, the action of gravity being found to be perfectly reciprocal. But the earth accompanies the sun to a great extent in this movement, and the other planets are also more or less affected by similar motions; so the relative positions are much less disturbed than if the sun followed this irregular orbit due to a cause outside the rest of the system.

The simple revolution of a body in a given plane indicates, at first sight, the existence of an attractive force directed to some point within the orbit; and the <term>Keplerian law</term> of the equality of the areas covered in equal times, by a line drawn from each planet to the sun, agrees precisely with what can be demonstrated regarding the effects of <term>central forces</term>, and points at once to the sun as the center of attraction of the system. And since the orbits of the planets are elliptical, and the sun is placed in one of the foci of each, it may be mathematically proved that the force directed to the sun must increase in proportion as the square of the distance decreases.

The times of the revolutions of the planets are also in perfect conformity with the laws of gravitation; that is, the squares of the times are proportional to the cubes of the distances from the sun. It was easy to infer, from what <term>Huygens</term> had already demonstrated regarding <term>centrifugal forces</term>, that this <term>Keplerian law</term> must be true of bodies revolving in circles by the force of gravitation;

...but Newton first demonstrated the same proportion with respect to <term>elliptical orbits</term>, and showed that the time of revolution in an <term>ellipse</term> is equal to the time of revolution in a circle whose diameter is equal to the major axis of the ellipse, or whose semidiameter is equal to the mean distance of the planet.

The universality of the laws of gravitation, as applied to the different planets, also shows that the matter they are composed of is equally subject to its power; for if any of the planets contained a portion of an inert substance that required a force to set it in motion, yet was not subject to the force of gravitation, the motion of that planet would be significantly different from that of any other planet in a similar position.

The deviations of each planet from the plane of its orbit, and the motions of its <term>nodes</term> (the points where the orbit intersects the plane of the ecliptic), as well as the motions of the <term>aphelion</term> (the point where the orbit is furthest from the sun), have also been deduced from the attractions of other planetary bodies; however, the calculations of the exact quantities of these <term>perturbations</term> are extremely complex. In general, each of the disturbing forces causes the nodes to have a slight degree of <term>retrograde motion</term>; but on account of the peculiar situation of the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn, it happens that the retrograde motion of Jupiter’s node, on the plane of the orbit of Saturn, produces a direct motion on the ecliptic. Thus, the action of Saturn tends to reduce the effect of the other planets in causing a retrograde motion of Jupiter’s nodes on the ecliptic.

The <term>secular diminution</term> of the <term>obliquity of the ecliptic</term>—that slow variation of its position which is only discovered by comparing very distant observations—is caused by the change of position of the Earth’s orbit resulting from the attractions of the other planets, especially Jupiter. It has been calculated that this change may amount, over the course of many ages, to 10° or 11° with respect to the fixed stars; however, the obliquity of the ecliptic relative to the equator can never vary more than two or three degrees, since the equator will follow, to some extent, the motion of the ecliptic.
