But since the attractive force of a sphere on particles at an equal distance from its center is everywhere equal, the equatorial parts would necessarily recede from the axis until the greater number of particles, acting in the same column, compensated for the greater effect of the <term>centrifugal force</term>. The form would thus be changed from a sphere to an <term>oblate</term> or <term>flattened spheroid</term>; and the surface of a fluid, either wholly or partially covering a solid body, must assume the same figure so that it may remain at rest. The surface of the sea is therefore <term>spheroidical</term>, and that of the earth deviates from a spheroidical figure only as far as it is above or below the general level of the sea. (Plate XXXIV. Fig. 486.)

The actions of the sun and moon on the prominent parts around the earth's equator produce a slight change in the position of its axis, in the same manner as the attractions of the other planets cause a deviation from the plane of its orbit. From this arises the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term>, or the retrograde motion of the <term>equinoctial points</term>, amounting annually to about 50 seconds. The <term>nutation</term> of the earth's orbit is a small periodic change of the same kind, depending on the position of the moon's nodes. In consequence of this, according to Dr. Bradley's original observations, the pole of the equator describes a small ellipse in the heavens, the diameters of which are 16 and 20 seconds. The same cause is also involved in modifying the <term>secular variation</term> of the <term>obliquity of the ecliptic</term>; and on the other hand, this variation has a considerable effect on the apparent precession of the equinoxes. Because of the different amount of precession at different times, the actual length of the <term>tropical year</term> is subject to a slight variation; it is now 4 or 5 seconds shorter than it was in the time of Hipparchus. The maximum change that can occur from this cause amounts to 43 seconds.

The secular acceleration of the moon's mean motion, which had long presented a difficulty amounting almost to an exception against the sufficiency of the theory of gravitation, has at last been satisfactorily deduced by Mr. Laplace from the effect of the gradual change of the eccentricity of the earth's orbit, which is subject to a very slow periodical variation, and which causes a difference in the magnitude of the sun's action on the lunar revolution.

The perfect coincidence of the period of the moon's rotation with that of its mean revolution has been supposed to be, in some degree, an effect of the attraction exerted by the earth on a prominent part of its surface; there are, however, many reasons to doubt the sufficiency of this explanation. If the periods had originally been very nearly equal, we might imagine that the motion of the earth would have produced a libration or oscillation in the position of the moon, retaining it always within certain limits with respect to the earth: no libration is, however, observed that can be derived from any inequality in the moon's rotation; and it has very properly been suggested that the same attraction toward the earth ought to have made the moon's axis precisely perpendicular to the plane of its orbit, instead of being a little inclined to it. At the same time, the appearance of a similar coincidence in the periods of the rotation and revolution of many other satellites makes it probable that some general cause must have existed which has produced the same effect in so many different cases.

The velocity of a comet in its perihelion is such that its square is twice as great as the square of the velocity of a body revolving in a circle at the same distance. It was determined by Halley and Clairaut that the attractions of Jupiter and Saturn would delay the return of the comet of 1759 by about 618 days; and the prediction was fulfilled within the probable limits that they had assigned for the error of the calculation. The labors of Clairaut have indeed in many respects improved the science of mathematical astronomy; he was the first who obtained a complete determination of the effects of the mutual actions of three gravitating bodies disturbing each other's motions; and his investigations, which were founded on those of Newton, led the way to still further improvements and refinements, which have been since made in succession by Euler, Lagrange, and Laplace.

<header>LECTURE XLIV. ON THE APPEARANCES OF THE CELESTIAL BODIES.</header>

# LECTURE XLIV.
## ON THE APPEARANCES OF THE CELESTIAL BODIES.

We will next proceed to examine the observable effects produced by those motions which we first considered in their simplest state, and later in regard to their causes and their laws. Many authors have chosen instead to pursue a contrary method, and have attempted to imitate the original and gradual development of the fundamental motions from their apparent effects. But no understanding is sufficiently clear, and no memory strong enough, to comprehend and retain all these varied appearances with accuracy and ease, unless assisted by some previous idea of the real changes that produce them, or by some temporary hypothesis regarding them. Such a hypothesis may have been useful in its time for the better connection of the phenomena, even though it does not currently deserve to be used for a similar purpose in preference to simpler and better theories which happen to be historically of a later date.

The proper motions of the fixed stars, as they are subjected to our observation, undergo two modifications: one from the relative direction of the motion, by which it may be more or less hidden from our view; the other from the proper motion of the sun and the planets accompanying him. This motion has indeed only been inferred from the apparent motions of a great number of stars, which are either partly or totally attributable to it, and which could scarcely have coincided as accurately as they do if they had arisen from the real and separate motion of each individual star.

Among the motions of the primary planets, that of the earth itself requires a principal share of our attention. The apparent positions of the fixed stars are not noticeably affected by the earth's annual revolution; if any of them were considerably less distant than they are, it is probable that this motion would

Dr. Hooke once supposed that he had discovered such a parallax, but later observations have not confirmed those of Dr. Hooke. The stars do, however, show a small aberration as a consequence of the progressive motion of the Earth in its orbit, combined with the finite velocity of light; and since the standard of comparison is the Earth’s axis, its nutation must also, to some degree, affect the apparent positions of the stars. It was while endeavoring to determine the annual parallax that Dr. Bradley discovered both the aberration of light and the nutation of the Earth’s axis.

The revolution of the Earth in its orbit around the Sun produces the apparent motion of the Sun among the stars, by which it traces its annual path in the ecliptic with an apparent angular velocity equal to the angular velocity of the Earth, which varies considerably at different times. It took some investigation into the sizes and distances of the heavenly bodies to be convinced that the Sun and stars did not actually possess the motion that a superficial inspection of the heavens would naturally lead a spectator to attribute to them; but it is currently completely unnecessary to provide arguments to prove that the true cause of these apparent motions is the real motion of the Earth. The effect of the Earth’s annual revolution is the change of position of the Sun among the fixed stars: it is obvious that the Sun will always appear, when viewed from the Earth, in a place diametrically opposite to that in which the Earth would appear if seen from the Sun. Consequently, since the Earth and Sun remain in the same plane, the apparent path of the Sun will mark the same circle among the stars as the Earth would appear to describe if viewed from the Sun—that is, the ecliptic. If the light of the stars were much stronger, or that of the Sun much weaker, we might see it pass by the stars in every part of the ecliptic, just as we see the moon; but we are now obliged to observe which stars are in turn diametrically opposite to the Sun, or at certain distances from it, and thus we obtain an accurate knowledge of its path.

The sun's apparent diameter is larger by one-thirtieth in January than in June; consequently, the earth is that much closer to the sun in winter than in summer. Since the revolving radius of the earth's orbit covers equal areas in equal amounts of time, the angular motion must increase as the square of the distance decreases, or about twice as fast as the distance itself decreases. Therefore, the total variation of the sun's apparent daily motion is one-fifteenth of its average motion; hence, the sun passes through the winter half of the ecliptic in a period seven or eight days shorter than the summer half. Depending on the earth's various positions relative to the plane of the sun's equator, the sun's rotation on its axis causes the paths of its spots to take on different shapes; when the earth is in that plane, the paths appear straight, but in all other positions, they appear elliptical.

The rotation of the earth on its axis produces the even more obvious cycles of day and night and, combined with its annual motion, causes the change of seasons. Since the axis always remains parallel to itself and is tilted toward the plane of the ecliptic at an angle of about 66½°, the plane of the equator—which is perpendicular to the axis—must pass through the sun twice a year. When this occurs, the limit of illumination (the circle that separates the dark portion of the earth from the illuminated part) passes through the poles. As the earth turns on its axis, every point on its surface must remain in light and in darkness for an equal length of time. Therefore, the points on the ecliptic where the sun is located at these times are called the equinoctial points. At all other times, one of the earth's poles is in the light while the other is in the shadow; all points on the earth nearest to the illuminated pole have days longer than their nights, while the regions on the opposite side of the equator—which are consequently nearer to the unilluminated pole—have shorter days. The regions nearest the poles also have one of their days and one of their nights extended to a period of several ordinary days, or even months, whenever they revolve entirely within the limit of illumination. (Plate XXXIV. Fig. 489.)

The sun appears to trace a circle in the heavens every day that is more or less distant from the plane of the equator, depending on the current position of the earth's axis. This distance is always the same as the distance of the poles from the limit of illumination and never exceeds 23½°; so that by determining the

More correctly speaking, however, the sun's apparent path is a spiral, formed by the continuation of these supposed circles into each other.

The effect of the centrifugal force, derived from the earth's rotation, is perceptible at the equator in the slowing of the vibrations of pendulums. The total centrifugal force at the equator is found, by calculation, to be $\frac{1}{289}$ of the force of gravity; but the decrease of the force of gravitation appears, by experiments on pendulums, to be $\frac{1}{179}$. This reduction is the sum of the centrifugal force and the decrease of gravity caused by the oblate shape of the earth, as the equatorial parts are further removed from its center, and the force of gravity is less powerful there. The changes of inclination in the earth's axis are observable in the positions of the equinoctial points and in the situation of the plane of the earth's equator with respect to the fixed stars; and the long-term decrease of the tilt of the ecliptic is discoverable by a comparison of distant observations of the sun's apparent motion and the positions of the fixed stars with respect to the ecliptic.

For the phenomena of twilight, we are principally indebted to the light reflected by the atmosphere: when the sun is only a certain distance below the horizon, it shines on some part of the air immediately visible to us, which provides us with a portion of reflected light. The distance at which this may happen has been variously estimated, and it is perhaps actually different in different climates, being a little greater in countries near the poles than in those which are nearer the equator. There is also sometimes a secondary twilight, when the parts of the atmosphere which reflect a faint light on the earth are themselves receiving this light from an earlier reflection. Some have assigned 18° as the limit of twilight, and on this supposition, allowing for refraction, the atmosphere must be capable of reflecting detectable light at a height of about 40 miles. Mr. Lambert <note>Johann Heinrich Lambert (1728–1777), a Swiss polymath who made significant contributions to physics and astronomy.</note>, on the contrary, makes the limit only about 6$\frac{1}{2}$°. The revolutions of the <term>primary planets</term>, combined with that of the Earth, necessarily produce the various relations in which they are in either <term>opposition</term> or <term>conjunction</term> with respect to each other or to the sun, and in which the apparent motion is <term>direct</term> or <term>retrograde</term>, or the planet is <term>stationary</term>, according to the directions and the relative velocities of their real motions. If the Earth were at rest, the inferior planets would appear to be stationary when they are at their greatest <term>elongation</term> or angular distance from the sun; but because of the effect of the Earth’s motion, <term>Venus</term> is stationary at an elongation of about 29°, while its greatest elongation is between 45° and 48°. The greatest elongation of <term>Mercury</term>, in each revolution, is from 28 1/3° to 17 1/2°, according to the position of its orbit, which is very eccentric. All these appearances are exactly the same as if the sun actually revolved around the Earth and the planets accompanied it in its orbit, performing their several revolutions around it at the same time; the path that would thus be described in the heavens, which is of a <term>cycloidal</term> nature, correctly represents the true positions of the planets with respect to the Earth. The apparent angular deviation from the <term>ecliptic</term>, or the <term>latitude</term> of the planet, is also greater or less depending on whether the Earth is closer to or farther from the planet, as well as according to the inclination of its orbit and its distance from the <term>node</term>. (Plate XXXIV, Figures 492 to 494.)

The various appearances of the illuminated disks, especially those of the inferior planets, and the <term>transits</term> of these planets across the sun, depend on their positions in their orbits and on the locations of the nodes with respect to the Earth. <term>Jupiter</term>, <term>Saturn</term>, and the <term>Georgian planet</term> <note>A former name for the planet Uranus.</note> are so remote compared to the Earth’s distance from the sun that they always appear fully illuminated. Venus is brightest at an elongation of about 40° from the sun, in that part of its orbit which is nearest to the Earth; it then appears like the moon when it is five days old, with one-fourth of its disk being illuminated. It casts a shadow and may even be seen during the daytime in our climates if it happens to be far enough north—a circumstance that occurs once about every eight years. In order for there to be a transit of Venus across the sun, it must be within the distance of 1 1/4° of its node at the time of conjunction,

otherwise she will pass either to the north or to the south of the sun, instead of being positioned directly between the sun and the earth.

The phases and eclipses of the moon are very obviously due to the same causes; only the part of the moon on which the sun shines is strongly illuminated, although the remaining part is faintly visible because of the light reflected onto it from the earth. It is, therefore, most easily seen near the time of the new moon, when the greatest part of the earth's surface facing the moon is illuminated. The parts of the moon which are directly facing the earth appear to undergo a libration, or change of position, of two kinds, each amounting to about 7 degrees: the one arising from the unevenness of the moon's velocity in her orbit at different times, and the other from the inclination of the axis of her rotation to her orbit. Besides these changes, the daily rotation of the earth may produce, for a spectator situated on some parts of it, a third kind of libration, or a change of almost two degrees in the appearance of the moon at her rising and setting. (Plate XXXIV. Fig. 495.)

When the moon passes the conjunction, or becomes new, near a node, she eclipses the sun; and when she is full, or in opposition, under similar circumstances, she enters the earth's shadow. The earth's shadow consists of two parts: the true shadow, within which none of the sun's surface is visible, and the penumbra, which is deprived of only a portion of the sun's light. The true shadow forms a cone ending in a point at a little more than 3½ times the average distance of the moon; the penumbra, on the contrary, constitutes, together with the shadow, a portion of a cone widening from the earth without limit. However, the only effect of this imperfect shadow is that it makes the beginning of a lunar eclipse impossible to determine very precisely; for the edge of the darkened part of the moon, as it appears in the progress of the eclipse, is that of the true shadow, only slightly enlarged by the penumbra. The true shadow, where the moon crosses it, is about 80 minutes in diameter as seen from the earth, while the moon itself is only 30. This shadow is not, however, wholly deprived of the sun's light; for atmospheric refraction bends the light passing nearest to the earth at an angle of 66 minutes, and causes a great part of the shadow to be filled with light of a reddish hue, by which the moon remains still visible to us.

When the sun is eclipsed, it depends on the positions of the earth and moon in their orbits whether the sun or moon subtends the greatest angle as seen from the earth; since at their average distances, their apparent diameters are each about half a degree. If the sun's apparent diameter is the greater, the eclipse, when the centers coincide, must be annular, with the margin of the sun's disk being still visible in the form of a ring. When the moon's apparent diameter is greater than the sun's, the eclipse, if central, becomes total; but a ring of pale light is still seen around the disk, which has been attributed to the effect of the sun's atmosphere, since that of the moon is probably too insignificant to produce the appearance. A red streak is also sometimes observed at the margin before the actual emersion of the sun. The degree of darkness depends on the location of the place of observation within the shadow, due to the greater or lesser illumination of the atmosphere within view; sometimes a considerable number of stars may be seen during a total eclipse of the sun.

It is obvious that, since the earth is much larger than the moon, the whole shadow of the moon will only pass over a part of the earth's surface; and that no solar eclipse can be visible across the entire hemisphere turned toward the sun. Lunar eclipses, on the contrary, present the same appearance wherever the moon is visible. In the same manner, to a spectator on the moon, an eclipse of the earth, or a transit of the moon's shadow over the earth's disk, would have nearly the same appearance wherever he might be positioned; but an eclipse of the sun by the earth would be total only for that part of the moon's surface which appears dark to us at the same time. (Plate XXXIV. Fig. 497–499.)

The moon's nodes arrive at very nearly the same position with respect to the earth after 223 lunations, or revolutions of the moon, which are completed in 18 years (of 365 days each), 15 days, 7 hours, and 43¾ minutes. Thus, after a period of about 18 years, the series of eclipses recommences in nearly the same order. This circumstance was observed by the ancients, and is

When the full moon happens within 7½° of the <term>node</term>, there must be a lunar eclipse; and there may be an eclipse at a distance of 13° from the <term>node</term>. An eclipse of the sun may happen when the moon changes, or comes into conjunction with the sun, at any distance within 17½° of the <term>node</term>. The average number of eclipses which occur in a year is about 4, and there are sometimes as many as 7: there must necessarily be two solar eclipses, but it is possible that there may not be even one lunar eclipse. In speaking of the magnitude of the part of the sun or moon eclipsed, it is usual to consider the whole diameter as divided into 12 parts, called <term>digits</term>, each of which contains 30 minutes: thus, if one-fifth part of the diameter were dark, the extent of the eclipse would be called 2 <term>digits</term> 12 minutes.

The moon travels through the heavens with a motion contrary to their apparent <term>diurnal revolution</term>. Hence it rises and sets, on average, about three-quarters of an hour later every day. The least possible difference between the time of the moon's rising on two successive days is 17 minutes in London; and this circumstance occurs once in about 19 years, which is nearly the period of the moon's <term>nodes</term> with respect to the heavens: the greatest possible difference is 1 hour 17 minutes. But it happens every month that the difference becomes greater and less by turns, and when the least difference is at the time of the full moon, it is usually called the <term>harvest moon</term>. In parts nearer to the poles, the moon often rises at the same hour on two successive days.

The eclipses of the <term>satellites</term> of Jupiter exhibit appearances extremely interesting for their utility in identifying the same instant of time in different places. On account of the small inclination of their orbits to the plane of Jupiter's orbit, the first three never pass the shadow without being plunged into it, and the fourth but seldom; while those of Saturn are much less frequently liable to be eclipsed, on account of their greater deviation from the plane of its <term>ecliptic</term>. These satellites are also frequently hidden behind the body of the planet, and this circumstance constitutes an <term>occultation</term>: hence it happens that we can never see both the <term>immersion</term> of the first satellite into the shadow of Jupiter and its <term>emersion</term> from it; but both the <term>immersion</term> and <term>emersion</term> of the three outer satellites are sometimes observable. Saturn exhibits a variety of forms according to its angular position: it disappears to common observation when either its edge or its dark side is presented to us; but to Dr. Herschel's telescopes, it never becomes invisible. The light reflected from the planet is probably sufficient for illuminating, in some measure, the side not exposed to the sun's direct rays.

The comets are seen for a short time and are then lost to our view; their tails are generally situated in the planes of their orbits, following them in their descent toward the sun and preceding them in their ascent, with a slight degree of curvature in their forms. They must also appear more or less arched to us, and of different lengths, according to their distances and the angular position of their orbits with respect to the ecliptic.

The proportion of the light provided by the different heavenly bodies has been variously estimated by different authors; but there is little reason to question the accuracy of the experiments and calculations of Mr. Bouguer. He states the intensity of the moon's light as only one three-hundred-thousandth of that of the sun. These calculations have been extended by Euler and by Lambert. Euler considers the direct light of the sun as equal to that of 6,560 candles of a moderate size, supposed to be placed at the distance of 1 foot from the object; he calculates that of the moon as equal to the effect of 1 candle at the distance of 7½ feet; the light of Venus to a candle at 421 feet; and the light of Jupiter to a candle at 1,620 feet. Consequently, the sun would appear only as bright as Jupiter if it were removed to a distance 131,000 times as great as its present distance. (Plate XXXIV. Fig. 500.)

When we reflect on the magnificence of the great picture of the universe, the outlines of which we have been considering, we are lost in the contemplation of the immensity of the prospect; and returning to the comparatively diminutive proportions of our individual persons, and of all the objects with which we are most immediately connected, we cannot help feeling our own insignificance in the material world. The mind, notwithstanding, endeavors to raise itself above the restraints which nature has imposed on the body and to penetrate the abyss of space in search of congenial existences. # LECTURE XLIV.

A poet has few facts to communicate, and these he wishes to expand and diversify; he dwells on a favorite idea and repeats it in a thousand symbolic forms; his object is to say a little, very elegantly, in very indirect and somewhat obscure terms. But the information which the <term>natural philosopher</term> has to impart is too extensive to allow for wordiness in its detail; his subjects are too intricate to be compatible with digressions for amusement, which, besides interrupting, are too likely to weaken the mind; and if he is ever fortunate enough to entertain, it must be by gratifying the love of truth and satisfying the thirst for knowledge. We have, however, a favorable specimen of highly ornamented philosophy in Fontenelle's *Plurality of Worlds*; a work which must be acknowledged to convey much information in a very interesting form, although somewhat tinged with a certain frivolity which is not always agreeable. We need not attempt to follow all the flights of Fontenelle's imagination; it will be sufficient for our purpose to pursue his ideas in a simple list of the most remarkable phenomena that would occur to a spectator placed on each of the planets.

Of Mercury we know little except the length of its year, which is shorter than three of our months. Supposing all our heat to come from the sun, it is probable that the average heat on Mercury is above that of boiling <term>quicksilver</term>; and it is scarcely possible that there should be any point about its poles where water would not boil. The sun's diameter would appear, if viewed from Mercury, more than twice as great as it does to us on the earth.

The inhabitants of the moon, if the moon is inhabited, must be capable of living with very little air and less water. There is reason to think their atmosphere is less than a mile high and is never cloudy; so the sun must shine without interruption for a whole fortnight on the same spot, without having its heat moderated by the presence of air or by the evaporation of moisture. The lack of water on the moon is not, as some have supposed, the necessary consequence of the lack of an atmosphere; rather, it is inferred partly from the total absence of clouds, and partly from the irregular appearance of the edge of the moon as seen during a solar eclipse. No part of it is defined by a line regular enough to allow us to suppose it is the surface of a liquid. The continents and seas come gradually and regularly into view, offering a variety that is equally pleasing and useful. To us, such a timepiece would be of inestimable value, as it would offer us an easy method of discovering the longitude of a place by comparing its motion with solar time. But on the moon, the relative position of the Earth and sun, or of the Earth and stars alone, would be sufficient for determining the location of any place in sight of the Earth; however, if there are no seas and no navigation, astronomical observations of this kind would be of very little use. The assistance of the Earth's phases in the measurement of time might, however, still be very useful for many purposes to the inhabitants of the closer half of the moon. Probably the more distant part is largely deserted, for in their long night of half a month, they must be in extreme need of the light reflected from the Earth, unless the inhabitants have the ability to sleep through the entire dark fortnight. The surface of the moon appears to be very rocky and barren, and prone to frequent disturbances from volcanoes. It appears to be doubtful whether either of the three little planets newly discovered <note>the asteroids Ceres, Pallas, and Juno</note> can be sufficiently solid to give a firm footing to any material beings; we should probably weigh only a few pounds each if transported there. The light reflected from Ceres is of a more ruddy hue than that of Pallas; both of these planets are attended by more or less of a nebulosity <note>a cloudy or hazy quality</note>, proceeding, perhaps, from copious atmospheres; and in this respect, as well as in the great inclination of their orbits, they appear to have some affinity to comets. It is tolerably certain that neither of them is 200 miles in diameter; and Juno is also probably about the same size.

On the whole, we are tempted, by an almost irresistible analogy, to conclude that the planets are all in some manner or other inhabited; but at the same time, we can scarcely imagine that a single species of terrestrial animal, or even plant, could exist on any of them. Their minerals may, perhaps, resemble ours, and if the stones which Mr. Howard <note>Edward Howard, who published a chemical analysis of meteorites in 1802</note> has analyzed are truly lunar products, we have proof that the moon at least contains some substances resembling those which compose the earth. However, the seas and rivers of the other planets must consist of some fluid unknown to us, since almost all our liquids would either be frozen or converted into vapor on any of them.

## LECTURE XLV.

### ON PRACTICAL ASTRONOMY.

It is generally most convenient in practical astronomy to ignore the real motions and to consider only the apparent motions of the sun, the stars, and planets; for the visible effects must be precisely the same whether the sun or the earth performs a revolution in the plane of the ecliptic, and whether the earth actually moves on its axis, or all the celestial bodies move around it in a day. We may, therefore, suppose the sun moves, as it appears to do, from west to east in the ecliptic, so as to advance almost a degree in 24 hours, and from east to west, together with all the stars and planets, so as to perform a full revolution in a day. To speak more accurately, the sun appears to describe a spiral in every sidereal day, which differs a little from a circle and is also about a degree shorter, so that about four minutes more are required for the sun to return to the same part of the heavens and complete a solar day.

In order to determine the position of any point in the heavens, it is customary to compare its situation either with the plane of the earth's equator or with the ecliptic. Its angular distance from the equator is called its declination, and from the ecliptic, its latitude. These distances must be measured in planes perpendicular to those of the equator or ecliptic, and the distances of these planes from their intersection, or from the equinoctial point in Aries, are called respectively the right ascension and the longitude of the point being described. For the stars, the declination and right ascension are most usually recorded; but with respect to the sun and the planets, which perform their revolutions in or near the ecliptic, it is most convenient to calculate their latitude and longitude.

The plane passing through the earth's axis and the location of a spectator is

...the plane of the meridian of that place; and a plane touching the earth at any point is its horizon. With respect to the appearances of the fixed stars, this plane may be considered as passing through the earth’s center in the same direction: and the difference is scarcely perceptible with respect to the sun and the primary planets; but in observations of the moon’s position, these planes must be carefully distinguished. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 502.)

The instruments required for astronomical observations are mainly related to geometrical or optical apparatus, or to the measurement of time. Specific constructions and combinations are, however, necessary to adapt quadrants, graduated circles, telescopes, and transit instruments for use in observatories; and astronomical observations are as necessary for the correct determination of time as artificial timekeepers are useful for other astronomical purposes.

The most accurate standard of time is the daily rotation of the earth on its axis, as determined by its position with respect to the fixed stars. The time passing between two successive crossings of any star over the same meridian, which constitutes a <term>sidereal day</term>, may be measured with great precision; and for this purpose, the star may be observed with almost equal accuracy in any other position, and sometimes with greater convenience. The length of the sidereal day may be considered perfectly constant, as the inequalities arising from the <term>aberration of light</term> and the <term>nutation</term> of the earth’s axis are too small to be easily detected; however, the correction for aberration may be applied when necessary. For observations of this kind, it is common to have a clock adjusted to sidereal time, which not only allows for an easier comparison with the transits or passages of any star over the meridian but also, by the difference in time between any two transits, shows at once the difference of <term>right ascension</term> of the stars or planets, expressed in time instead of degrees.

Solar days are not only about four minutes longer than sidereal days, but they are also unequal among themselves; and this inequality arises from two causes. The first is that even if the sun’s motion in the <term>ecliptic</term> were uniform, his daily changes of right ascension would be different at different times, and the difference between his path in every sidereal day, and

a whole circle, depending on this change, would also vary; the other being that the sun's motion in the ecliptic is actually variable, and consequently the daily change of right ascension is subject to a double inequality. Because of this, solar time matches mean time at only four moments in the year; mean time is derived by assuming the entire 365 days are divided into as many equal parts. This difference is called the equation of time, and it sometimes amounts to as much as 16 minutes. The term "equation" is commonly applied in astronomy to any small quantity which is to be added to or subtracted from another quantity. Thus, in calculating the position of a planet, it is usual to find its mean position from the tables of its motion—where it would be found if its orbit were circular—and then to derive the true position by means of various corrections called equations. In France, solar time is considered the true time and is used for all civil purposes, so that clocks there are sometimes equipped with a complicated apparatus designed to mimic the inequalities of the sun's actual apparent motion. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 503.)

The art of dialling primarily consists of projecting, on a given surface, such lines as will align with the shadow of an index or gnomon parallel to the earth's axis, at intervals corresponding to the different hours of the day. Therefore, nothing more is necessary for the construction of a dial than to determine the intersections of the surface on which the dial is to be built with planes passing through the edge of the gnomon and situated at equal angular distances from each other. For example, if we suppose the plane of the dial is perpendicular to the gnomon and parallel to the equinoctial, the hour lines of the dial will be at equal distances from each other; but in other cases, their distances will be unequal and must be determined either by calculation or by construction. A point may also be used as a gnomon, as well as a line; but in this case, the hour lines must cover a larger portion of the surface so that the shadow of the point always falls among them. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 504 . . 506.)

The changes of the seasons depend on the return of the sun to the same position with respect to the equator, or on the length of the tropical year—so called from the tropics, which are circles supposed to be parallel to the equator, and between which the sun travels continually backwards and forwards, appearing to remain for some time, when he is near them, with

<page-num>539</page-num>
<header>ON PRACTICAL ASTRONOMY.</header>

very little change in declination; for this reason, the time when the sun touches either tropic is called the solstice. Since the variations of light and darkness also depend on the solar day, it is necessary, for the regulation of the civil calendar, to establish the relationship between the periods of the solar day and the tropical year. Because the tropical year exceeds the length of 365 days by 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 48 seconds, it is common to add an intercalary day to the ordinary year once roughly every four years. The ancient Egyptians counted only 365 days in a year, and their official new year arrived progressively earlier and earlier; thus, after 1,507 of their years, it would have occurred successively on each of the 365 days before returning to its original position. The same method of calculation was also adopted by the Greek astronomers. The Romans inserted intercalary days—at first without much regularity, according to the direction of their augurs—until the time of Julius Caesar. Observing that the year was almost six hours longer than 365 days, he added a day to the calendar every fourth year by counting twice the day in February called *sexto calendas Martias*; consequently, this year of 366 days was called a bissextile year. The new moon immediately following the winter solstice in the 707th year of Rome was established as the first of January of the first year of Caesar's calendar. The 25th of December in his 45th year is considered the date of the Nativity of Christ, and Caesar's 46th year is counted as the first year of our era. The preceding year is commonly called year 0 by astronomers, but year 1 <insert><image-desc>Circular library stamp of the Reese Library, University of California</image-desc> REESE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</insert> before Christ by chronologists. However, the correction introduced by Caesar was too large, the error being exactly 7 days every 900 years; thus, by 1582, it amounted to about 12 days. This error was not entirely removed by Pope Gregory when he reformed the calendar; he omitted only 10 days from the usual count to return the schedule of movable feasts to the same state in which they had been established by the Council of Nicaea in the fourth century. He decided at the same time that the final year of every century should pass without an intercalary day, except for every fourth century, which was still to be a bissextile year. Thus, every year divisible by four without a remainder is generally a bissextile or leap year, but the last year of every century must be a common year unless the century number is divisible by 4; for instance, the year 1800 was a common year, while 2000 was a bissextile year. In this manner, 27 Julian bissextile years are omitted every 3,600 years, whereas the true length of the year would require the omission of 28; but so

<meta>This page continues the discussion of calendar history and the measurement of time, specifically comparing the Gregorian calendar to the Persian and French Republican systems, and introducing the Metonic cycle.</meta>

<page-num>540</page-num>
<header>LECTURE XLIV.</header>

Such a small difference can be of no significant consequence. The Persians had introduced into their calendar, in the 11th century, a method of intercalation that was even more accurate; they designate only 8 years as leap years every 33 years, counting four common years together instead of three at the end of this period, so that in 132 years they have 32 leap years instead of 33; and the error is only one day in about five thousand years. If any change to the Gregorian calendar were considered necessary, it would be easy to make the final year of every fourth and fifth century alternately a leap year, and this correction would be as accurate as it is possible for our calculations to render it. The adoption of the Gregorian calendar in this country was delayed for some time by religious prejudices; one of the most valid objections to it was that 2 days of the actual error remained uncorrected; but better arguments finally overcame these difficulties, and the "New Style" was introduced on September 14, 1752, which would have been called the 3rd according to the "Old Style."

Once generally established, any reasonable approximation of this kind seems more suitable than the method that was recently adopted in France, where the Republican year began at the exact moment of midnight preceding the sun’s arrival at the autumnal equinox. Mr. Lalande very wisely observes that there are several years in which the sun will pass the equinox so close to midnight that current calculations cannot determine on which day the Republican year should begin; perhaps these arguments, along with others, helped facilitate the restoration of the ancient calendar.

The cycles of the sun and moon are not very obviously commensurable, as the solar year contains 12 lunar months and nearly 11 days; but Meto discovered, more than 2,000 years ago, that 19 solar years contain exactly 235 lunar months. This determination is so accurate that it makes the lunar month only about half a minute too long. Because of this, it happens that in every 19-year period, the moon’s age is the same on the same day of the year. The year's number within the Metonic cycle is called the Golden Number, because Meto’s calendar was ordered to be engraved in gold letters on a marble pillar during the celebration of the Olympic Games. Currently, if we add 1 to the year and divide it by 19, the remainder will be the Golden Number; thus, for 1806, the Golden Number is 2.

If we subtract 1 from the golden number, then multiply by 11, and divide by 30, the remainder will be the epact, which is the moon’s age on the first of January, without any significant error; thus, for 1806, the epact is 11, and the moon is actually 11 days old on the first of January.

From a combination of various kinds of chronological periods, Scaliger conceived of the Julian period as an epoch to which all past events might be conveniently referenced, beginning 4713 years before the birth of Christ. Laplace proposes, as a universal epoch, the time when the earth’s apogee was at right angles with its nodes, in the year 1250, calling the vernal equinox of that year the first day of the first year. However, the fewer changes of this kind that we make, the less confusion we introduce into our chronology. The astronomical year begins at noon on the 31st of December, and the date of an observation expresses the days and hours actually elapsed from that time. Thus, the first of January 1806, at 10 in the morning, would be called, in astronomical language, 1805 December 31 days 22 hours, or more properly 1806 January 0 day 22 hours.

For determining the position of any of the celestial bodies by direct measurement, it is usual to determine its meridian altitude using quadrants, and the time of its passing the meridian using transit instruments. The large quadrants generally used for this purpose in observatories are fixed to vertical walls to give them greater stability, and are therefore called mural quadrants; sometimes only a smaller portion of an arc is adapted for observations near the zenith, under the name of a zenith sector. A transit instrument is a telescope so fixed on an axis that it always remains in the plane of the meridian; the axis is perpendicular to this plane and is consequently in a horizontal position, directed east and west. Those who are in the constant habit of careful observation can, in this manner, estimate the precise time of a celestial object passing over the meridian without an error of even a tenth of a second, so that its angular right ascension may be determined within about a second of the truth. A very convenient way to adjust a transit instrument is to direct it to the north polar star at the same time that the last of the three horses in the wain <note>The "wain" refers to the constellation Ursa Major, specifically the Big Dipper.</note> is perpendicularly above or below it: this process, in 1751, gave the true meridian precisely; but since that time,

The precession of the equinoxes, which produces a slight change in the positions of the stars, has made it necessary to wait 1 minute 13$\frac{1}{2}$ seconds for every ten years that have elapsed. Thus, in 1806, if we wait 6$\frac{1}{2}$ minutes, the pole star will then be precisely in the meridian and will serve for the correct adjustment of the instrument. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 507 .. 510.)

The quadrant in most common use, especially for nautical observations, was first proposed by Newton, but improved, or perhaps reinvented, by Hadley. Its operation depends on the effect of two mirrors which bring both objects—the angular distance of which is to be measured—simultaneously into the field of view; the inclination of the <term>speculums</term> <note>mirrors, typically made of polished metal</note> by which this is performed serves to determine the angle. The ray proceeding from one of the objects is made to coincide, after two reflections, with the ray coming immediately from the other; since the inclination of the reflecting surfaces is then half the angular distance of the objects, this inclination is read off on a scale in which every actual degree represents two degrees of angular distance and is marked accordingly. There is also a second fixed speculum, placed at right angles to the movable one when it is in its furthest position, which then produces a deviation of two right angles in the apparent position of one of the objects; this enables us, by moving the index, to measure any angle between 180° and 90°. This operation is called the back observation; it is, however, seldom employed because of the difficulty of adjusting the speculum for it with accuracy. The reflecting instrument originally invented by Hooke was arranged in a somewhat different manner. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 511.)

From the meridian altitude of any point, it is easy, when the elevation of the pole is known, to deduce its declination; and its right ascension may be found from the time of its passage over the meridian after that of the equinoctial point, allowing 15 degrees for each sidereal hour. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 512.)

This is equal to the angle subtended at the center of the celestial body by the semidiameter of the earth passing through the place of observation, since all calculations of the geocentric positions of the heavenly bodies are referred to the earth's center. This angle, which must be added to the apparent altitude, sometimes amounts to more than a degree in the case of the moon when it is near the horizon. Refraction, which acts in the opposite direction and must be subtracted from the altitude, is about 33 minutes at the horizon. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 513.)

The most important applications of practical astronomy are the determination of the latitudes and longitudes of places on the earth's surface. Latitude—which is the angular distance of a place from the equator, or the angle formed by the plane of its horizon with the earth's axis—is easily determined by finding the meridian altitude of a body with a known declination. By subtracting or adding the declination, we immediately have the elevation of the equinoctial (or the plane of the equator) above the horizon; subtracting this from a right angle gives us the elevation of the pole, which is the latitude. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 512.)

It is also common to determine the latitude of a place using two altitudes observed at different times on the same day, while accurately noting the interval of time that passes between the observations. This method has a great advantage in cloudy weather, when it is not possible to ensure the observation of a meridian altitude.

The longitude of a place, or the relative position of its meridian, is not nearly as easily determined. For this purpose, it is necessary to determine the time that passes between a given point in the heavens passing over its meridian and some other meridian that serves as a standard of comparison. Thus, if the sun arrives at the meridian of any place three hours later than at the meridian of London, that place must necessarily be 45 degrees west of London, or at 45° west longitude. If we know that when it is noon at a given place, it is three o'clock in the afternoon at Greenwich, we can be certain that we are somewhere on a meridian 45° west of Greenwich. If we had perfect timekeepers, we could easily adjust them

The timekeepers we have are indeed accurate enough to be of considerable use, but it is necessary to compare them frequently with astronomical observations of phenomena that occur at times which can be correctly calculated. Sometimes the transits of Mercury and Venus, or lunar eclipses, are used for this purpose, but more commonly the eclipses of the satellites of Jupiter are used. These, however, cannot be easily observed without a more powerful telescope than can be used at sea. Furthermore, the theory of the moon’s motion has been so much improved in recent years that its distance from the sun or from a fixed star can be calculated accurately enough to determine the time in London or Paris without an error of more than one-third of a minute. Thus, assuming the observation could be made perfectly correctly, the longitude could be determined within about one-twelfth of a degree, or at most five nautical miles.

The observed parallax of the sun and moon may be used to determine their distances from the earth; but for the sun, a simple comparison of its calculated altitude with its apparent altitude is not enough to accurately determine the magnitude of the parallax. Sometimes the parallax of Mars, which is considerably greater than the sun’s, has been measured directly. However, the most accurate way to determine the actual dimensions of the solar system is to observe a transit of Venus across the sun’s disk from two places situated on opposite parts of the earth’s surface. This is because the diurnal motion of some parts of the earth is in the same direction as the motion of Venus in its orbit, while in other parts it is in the opposite direction. The different effects of these motions provide a way to compare the rotational velocity of the earth with the progressive velocity of Venus. Consequently, from the known velocity at which the earth's surface rotates, we can infer the actual velocity of Venus and its distance from the sun. From this, the distances of all the other planets can be easily deduced. (Plate XXXV. Fig. 514.)

The most advantageous places for the experiment are those that differ most in longitude and are most remote from each other. Consequently, Captain Cook was sent by the British government to the South Seas in the years 1761 and 1769 in order to observe the transits of Venus from the island of Otaheite. These observations were compared with those made at Wardhuys in Danish Lapland. The difference in the time occupied by the transit at these places was found to be 23 minutes and 10 seconds, and from this comparison, corrected by a number of related observations, the sun’s mean parallax was found to be 8 and two-thirds seconds, or perhaps 8 3/4; for it does not appear that we are certain of having avoided even an error of one-fortieth part of the whole. However, Mr. Laplace’s determination of the sun’s distance from the lunar motions agrees very well with the result usually considered to be the outcome of the observations of the transit of Venus.

The relative densities of the sun and of those planets that have satellites may be calculated from the periods and distances of the bodies revolving around them. The densities of the other planets have sometimes been assigned based on conjecture alone, but in recent years, the mathematical theory of planetary perturbations has been made so perfect that some reliance may perhaps be placed on the density assigned to them from calculations of this kind. It was formerly supposed that the densities of the planets were consistently greater the nearer they were to the sun; but it is now certain that the <term>Georgian planet</term> is denser than Saturn, and it is probable that Venus is somewhat less dense than the earth. The mass of the moon is deduced from a comparison of the effects of her attraction on the earth and sea with those of the sun’s attraction.

The artificial globe serves as a useful instrument for determining, in a rough manner and without calculation, the positions and movements of the heavenly bodies at particular times; their locations being first ascertained from tables, or, in the case of the sun, merely from a scale on the globe’s horizon or on its surface. By means of the celestial globe, the apparent motions of the fixed stars may be represented in a nearly similar manner, provided proper attention is paid to the position of the sun in the ecliptic to determine the corresponding time.

Many of these operations may also be performed with equal convenience using a planisphere, which is a stereographic projection of the globe on a plane surface. Professor Bode’s planisphere includes in one view all the stars that are ever visible at Berlin; he has added to it a movable circle representing the horizon of that place, which carries with it the circles of altitude and azimuth drawn on transparent paper. This is adjusted, by graduations at the edge of the chart, to the day and hour for which we wish to ascertain the apparent positions of the heavenly bodies. Any other chart of the stars with the pole at its center may be used for a similar purpose by cutting out a circle, or part of a circle, to represent the horizon of a place for which the latitude is given; and if the stars are projected, as is usual, on two equal charts, they must have two equal arcs to represent the respective parts of the horizon belonging to them. To represent both the real and the apparent motions of the different parts of the solar system, planetariums or orreries have sometimes been used. In these, the relative periods of the revolutions are expressed by various combinations of wheelwork. Archimedes was the original inventor of these instruments, and Huygens revived them with many improvements in more recent times. The construction of the large planetarium, which was built in the building of the Royal Institution, was primarily directed by Mr. Pearson. I suggested to him that the instrument could be placed in a vertical position, and that the eccentricities of the planetary orbits could be shown by the revolution of short arms, held in place by weights. Their deviation from the plane of the ecliptic could be shown by inclining the axes of these arms at an appropriate angle to the plane of the instrument. The other parts of the arrangement that are novel were entirely Mr. Pearson's invention; he seems to have made the instrument more accurate in many respects than any other planetarium ever built.

# LECTURE XLVI.

## ON GEOGRAPHY.

From the consideration of the stars, the sun, and the planets in general, we are now to descend to that of the Earth—the particular planet which we inhabit, and which we can examine more minutely than the other parts of the solar system. Its external form, its divisions (whether astronomical or natural), its most remarkable features, and its internal structure will require separate investigation.

The general curvature of the Earth’s surface is easily observable in the disappearance of distant objects; in particular, when the view is limited by the sea—the surface of which, due to the common property of a fluid, naturally becomes smooth and horizontal. For it is well known that the sails and rigging of a ship come into view long before her hull, and that each part is seen sooner as the eye is more elevated. On shore, the frequent inequalities of the solid parts of the Earth usually cause the prospect to be bounded by some irregular prominence, such as a hill, a tree, or a building, so that the general curvature is less observable.

The surface of a lake or sea must always be perpendicular to the direction of a plumb line, which may be considered the direction of the force of gravity. By means of either a plumb line or a spirit level, we may ascertain the angular position of any part of the Earth’s surface with respect to a fixed star passing the meridian. By going a little further north or south and repeating the observation on the star, we may find the difference in the inclination of the surfaces at both points. Naturally, assuming the Earth is a sphere, this difference in latitude will be the angle subtended at its center by the given portion of the surface, from which the whole circumference may be determined; the earliest measurements of the Earth were conducted on these principles.

were conducted. The first of these that can be considered accurate was performed by Picart in France toward the end of the seventeenth century.

However, the spherical form is only an approximation of the truth. Newton calculated, and the French Academicians (sent to the equator and the polar circle) confirmed experimentally, that to accurately represent the Earth, the sphere must be flattened at the poles and bulge at the equator. We may therefore consider the Earth as an oblate elliptic spheroid; its curvature is greater—and consequently each degree is shorter—at the equator than it is nearer the poles. If the density of the Earth were uniform throughout, its ellipticity (the difference in the length of its diameters) would be <gloss>1/230</gloss> of the whole. On the other hand, if it consisted of matter with negligible density attracted by an infinite force at the center, the ellipticity would be only <gloss>1/577</gloss>. Whatever the internal structure of the Earth may be, its form must fall between these limits, since its internal parts must necessarily be denser than the parts nearer the surface. Indeed, if the Earth consisted of water or ice as compressible as common water or ice, and followed the same laws of compression as elastic fluids, its density at the center would be several thousand times greater than at the surface. Even steel would be compressed to one-fourth of its bulk, and stone to one-eighth, if it extended to the Earth’s center; thus, there can be no doubt that the central parts of the Earth must be much denser than the surface. Whatever this difference may be, Clairaut demonstrated that the fractions expressing the ellipticity and the apparent reduction of gravity at the equator must always add up to <gloss>5/576</gloss>. It has been found, through the most accurate observations of pendulum lengths at different latitudes, that the force of gravity is <gloss>1/180</gloss> less powerful at the equator than at the pole. From this, the ellipticity is calculated to be <gloss>1/320</gloss> of the equatorial diameter—the same form that would be produced if about three-eighths of the total force of gravity were directed toward a central particle while the density of the rest of the Earth remained uniform.

This method of determining the Earth's general form is much less prone to error and irregularity than measuring the lengths of degrees in various locations, as accidental variations in curvature caused by local differences in density, or even surface elevations, may often

For example, a degree measured at the Cape of Good Hope, at latitude 33° south, was found to be longer than a degree in France, at latitude 46° north; and the measurements in Austria, North America, and England have all shown signs of similar irregularities. There also appears to be some difference in the length of degrees at the same latitude but in different longitudes. We may, however, imagine a regular elliptical spheroid to coincide very closely with any small portion of the earth's surface, although its form must be somewhat different for different parts. Thus, for the greater part of Europe—that is, for England, France, Italy, and Austria—if the measurements have been correct, this osculating spheroid must have an ellipticity of $\frac{1}{150}$.

The earth is astronomically divided into zones and into climates. The torrid zone is bounded by the tropics, at a distance of 23° 28' on each side of the equator, containing all those places where the sun is sometimes vertical, or directly overhead. The frigid zones are within the polar circles, at the same distance from the poles, including all places that remain annually within the limit of light and darkness for a full diurnal rotation of the earth, or longer. The temperate zones, situated between these, have an uninterrupted alternation of day and night but are never subjected to the sun's vertical rays. At the equator, therefore, the sun is vertical at the equinoxes; its lowest meridian altitude occurs at the solstices, when it is 66° 32'—which is more than it is for us at midsummer—and this happens once on the north and once on the south side of the hemisphere. Between the equator and the tropics, the sun is vertical twice a year, when its declination is equal to the latitude of the place; its lowest meridian altitudes, which are unequal to each other, occur at the solstices. At the tropics, the meridian sun is vertical only once a year, and at the opposite solstice, or midwinter, its meridian altitude is 43° 4', just as it is for us in April and the beginning of September. At the polar circles, the sun describes a complete circle on midsummer day, touching the northern or southern point of the horizon; and in midwinter, it shows only half its disc above the horizon for a few minutes at the opposite point—neglecting the elevation caused by refraction, which, in these climates especially, is by no means insignificant. The climates, in the astronomical sense of the word, are determined by the duration of the longest day in different parts of the earth’s surface; but this division is of no practical use, nor does it provide any standard for judging the climate in a meteorological sense.

The natural division of the surface of the globe is into sea and land: about three-fourths of the whole is occupied by water, although it is probably nowhere at a depth that is comparatively very great—at most a few miles on average. The remaining fourth consists of land, elevated more or less above sea level, interspersed in some parts with smaller bodies of water at various heights, and, in a few instances, somewhat lower than the general surface of the main ocean. For example, the Caspian Sea is said to be about 300 feet lower than the ocean, and in the interior of Africa, there is probably a lake that is equally low.

We cannot observe any general symmetry in this distribution of the earth’s surface, except that the two large continents of Africa and South America have a slight resemblance in their forms, and each of them ends to the east with a collection of numerous islands. The large capes projecting to the south also share a similarity in their form and the islands near them: to the west, the continents are carved into large bays, and the islands are to the east. Thus, Cape Horn has the Falkland Islands, the Cape of Good Hope has Madagascar, and Cape Comorin has Ceylon to the east. (Plate XLII, XLIII.)

The great continent, composed of Europe, Asia, and Africa, makes up about a seventh of the whole surface of the earth, America about a sixteenth, and Australasia or New South Wales about a fiftieth; or, expressed in hundredth parts of the whole: Europe contains 2, Asia 7, Africa 6, America 6, and Australasia 2, with the remaining 77 being sea (although some authors assign only 72 parts out of 100 to the sea and 28 to the land). Mount Sinai in Japan <note>Possibly a reference to a mountain in Japan known to the author by this name, or a geographical error</note>, Mount Caucasus, Etna, the Southern Pyrenees, St. George among the Azores, Mount Adam in Ceylon <note>Sri Lanka</note>, Atlas, Olympus, and Taurus are also high mountains; and there are some very considerable elevations in the island of Hawaii <note>Owhyhee</note>. Ben Nevis, in Scotland, is the loftiest of the British hills, but its height is considerably less than a mile. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 519.)

The most elevated mountains, except for the summits of volcanoes, consist of rocks, more or less mixed, without regular order, and commonly of granite or porphyry. These are called primary mountains; they run generally from east to west in the Old World, and from north to south in the New; and many of them are observed to have an easier ascent on the east than on the west side. The secondary mountains accompany them in the same direction; they consist of strata, mostly calcareous and argillaceous—that is, of the nature of limestone and clay—with a few animal and vegetable remains in an obscure form, together with salt, coal, and sulfur. The tertiary mountains are even smaller; and in these, animal and vegetable remains are very abundant; they consist chiefly of limestone, marble, alabaster, building stone, millstone, and chalk, with beds of flint. Where the secondary and tertiary mountains are intersected by valleys, the opposite strata often correspond at equal heights, as if the valleys had been cut or washed from between them; but sometimes the mountains have their strata disposed as if they had been elevated by an internal force and their summits had afterwards crumbled away, the strata which are lowest in the plains being highest in the mountains. The strata of these mountains are often intermixed with veins of metal, running in all possible directions and occupying vacuities <note>empty spaces or voids</note> which appear to be of somewhat later date than the original formation of the mountains. The volcanic mountains interrupt those of every other description without any regularity, as if their origin were totally independent of that of all the rest.

The internal constitution of the earth is little known from actual observation, for the depths to which we have penetrated are comparatively very inconsiderable, the deepest mine scarcely descending half a mile perpendicularly.

<header>ON GEOGRAPHY.</header>

It appears that the strata are more commonly in a nearly horizontal direction than in any other; and their thickness is usually almost uniform for some distance. However, they are not arranged in the order of their specific gravity, and the opinion that they follow one another in a similar series throughout the greater part of the globe appears to rest on very slight foundations.

From observations on the attraction of the mountain Schiehallion <note>The mountain is now usually spelled Schiehallion; it was spelled "Shehallion" in the original text</note>, Dr. Maskelyne inferred the actual mean density of the Earth to be 4.5 times that of water, judging from the probable density of the internal substance of the mountain, which he supposed to be solid rock. Mr. Cavendish has concluded more directly, from experiments on a mass of lead, that the mean density of the Earth is 5.48 times that of water. Mr. Cavendish’s experiments, which were performed with the apparatus invented and procured by the late Mr. Michell, appear to have been conducted with all possible accuracy, and must undoubtedly be preferred to conclusions drawn from the attraction of a mountain, whose internal parts are perfectly unknown to us, except by conjectures founded on its external appearance. Supposing both series of experiments and calculations to be free from error, it would only follow that the internal parts of Schiehallion are denser, and perhaps more metallic, than was previously imagined. The density assigned by Mr. Cavendish is not at all greater than might be conjectured from observations on the vibrations of pendulums; Newton had long ago proposed it as a probable supposition that the mean density of the Earth might be about 5 or 6 times as great as that of water, and the perfect agreement of the results of many modern experiments with this conjecture affords us a new proof, in addition to many others, of the accuracy and insight of that illustrious philosopher.

## LECTURE XLVII.

### ON THE TIDES.

The form and structure of the solid parts of the globe have offered few remarkable features capable of capturing our attention, except for the general distribution of land and water and the permanent differences in elevation across various parts of the earth. But the sea exhibits a series of phenomena far more interesting to the mathematical philosopher, because they allow for a methodical investigation and a deduction from general causes, the actions of which can be traced in detail. For the height of the sea's surface at any given place is observed to be subject to periodic variations, which are found to depend on the relative position of the moon, combined in some measure with that of the sun. These variations are called tides; they were too obvious to escape the observation even of the ancients, who inhabited countries where they are least noticeable. For Aristotle mentions the tides of the northern seas and remarks that they vary with the moon and are less noticeable in small seas than in the ocean; Caesar, Strabo, Pliny, Seneca, and Macrobius also give reasonably accurate accounts of them.

There are in the tides three orders of phenomena that are separately distinguishable: the first kind occurs twice a day, the second twice a month, and the third twice a year. Every day, around the time the moon passes over the meridian, or a certain number of hours later, the sea rises above its average height, and at this time it is called high water. The elevation gradually subsides, and in about six hours it is low water, with the sea having reached its lowest point; after this, it rises again when the moon passes the meridian below the horizon, so that the ebb and flood occur twice a day, but they become later every day by about 50 1/2 minutes, which is the amount by which a lunar day exceeds a solar one, since 28 1/2 lunar days are nearly equal to 29 1/2 solar days.

<page-num>577</page-num>

### ON THE TIDES.

The second phenomenon is that the tides are noticeably increased at the time of the new and full moon; this increase and decrease constitute the spring and neap tides. The increase also becomes even more observable when the moon is in its perigee, or nearest to the earth. The lowest as well as the highest water occurs at the time of the spring tides; the neap tides neither rise so high nor fall so low.

The third phenomenon of the tides is the increase which occurs at the time of the equinoxes: so that the greatest tides occur when a new or full moon happens near the equinox while the moon is in its perigee. The effects of these tides are often further increased by the equinoctial winds, which are sometimes so powerful as to produce a greater tide before or after the equinox than that which happens in the usual course at the time of the equinox itself.

These simple facts are amply sufficient to establish the dependence of the tides on the moon; they were first correctly explained by Newton as the necessary consequences of the laws of gravitation, but the theory has been further improved by the work of later mathematicians. The entire investigation has been considered the most difficult of all astronomical problems; some of the circumstances depend on causes which must probably remain forever unknown to us; and unless we could everywhere measure the depth of the sea, it would be impossible to apply a theory, even if absolutely perfect, to the solution of every difficulty that might occur. A very unwise attempt has been made to attribute the phenomena of the tides to causes totally different from these, and depending on the annual melting of the polar ice: the reputation of its author is the only claim it has even to be mentioned; and a serious refutation of such a groundless opinion would be perfectly unnecessary.

A detached portion of a fluid would naturally assume a spherical form through its mutual gravitation, but if it gravitates toward another body at a distance, it will become an oblong spheroid whose axis will point toward the attracting body; for the difference of the attraction of this body on its different parts will tend to separate them from each other in the greatest part of the sphere, that is, at all places within the angular distance of 79½° from

# LECTURE XLVII.

the line passing through the attracting body, either in the nearer or in the remoter hemisphere; but to urge them towards the center, although with a smaller force, in the remaining part. Hence, in order for there to be an equilibrium, the depth of the fluid must be greatest where its gravitation, thus composed, is least; that is, in the line directed towards the attracting body, and it can be shown that it must assume the form of an oblong elliptic spheroid.

If the earth were entirely fluid, and the same part of its surface were always turned towards the moon—with the pole of the spheroid being directly beneath the moon—the lunar tide would remain stationary. The greatest elevation would be at the points nearest to the moon and furthest from it, and the greatest depression would be in the circle equidistant from these points; however, due to the smaller surface area to which it is confined, the elevation would be twice as great as the depression. The actual height of this elevation would probably be about 40 inches, and the depression 20, making a total tide of 5 feet. Also, if the waters were capable of instantly assuming the form required by equilibrium, the summit of an equally elevated spheroid would still be directed towards the moon, despite the earth's rotation. This may be called the primitive tide of the ocean; but because of the continuous change of position required to adjust the surface to a similar position relative to the moon as the earth revolves, the form must be materially different from that of such a spheroid of equilibrium. The force employed in producing this adjustment may be estimated by considering the actual surface of the sea as that of a wave moving on the spheroid of equilibrium, and producing a sufficient velocity in the water to preserve its actual form. From this way of considering the subject, we can derive a theory of the tides that appears simpler and more satisfactory than any published so far; and by comparing the tides of narrower seas and lakes with the motions of pendulums suspended on vibrating centers, we may extend the theory to all possible cases.

If the center of a pendulum is made to vibrate, the vibrations of the pendulum itself, once they have reached a steady state, will occur in the same time as those of the center; but the motion of the pendulum will be either in the same direction as that of the center, or in the opposite direction, depending on whether the time of this forced vibration is longer or shorter.

In order for the <term>lunar tides</term> of an <term>open ocean</term> to be direct, or synchronous, its <term>depth</term> must be greater than 13 <term>miles</term>, and for the <term>solar tides</term>, greater than 14. The less the depth exceeded these limits, the greater the <term>tides</term> would be, and in all cases they would be greater than the <term>primitive tides</term>. But in fact, the height of the <term>tides</term> in the <term>open ocean</term> is always far less than what would be produced in this manner; it is therefore improbable that the <term>tides</term> are ever direct in the <term>open ocean</term>, or that the depth of the sea is as great as 13 <term>miles</term>.

In order for the height of the <term>inverted or remote lunar tides</term> to be five <term>feet</term>, or equal to that of the <term>primitive tides</term>, the <term>depth</term> of the <term>open sea</term> must be 6½ <term>miles</term>; and if the height is only two <term>feet</term>, which is perhaps not far from the truth, the <term>depth</term> must be 3 <term>miles</term> and five-sevenths.

The <term>tides</term> of a <term>lake</term> or <term>narrow sea</term> differ materially from those of the <term>open ocean</term>, since the height of the water hardly undergoes any variation in the middle of the <term>lake</term>; it must always be <term>high water</term> at the <term>eastern extremity</term> when it is <term>low water</term> at the <term>western</term>: and this must happen at the time when the places of <term>high and low water</term>, with respect to the <term>primitive tides</term>, are equally distant from the middle of the <term>lake</term>. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 520.)

The <term>tides</term> may be direct in a <term>lake</term> 100 <term>fathoms</term> deep and less than 8 <term>degrees</term> wide; but if it is much wider, they must be inverted. Supposing the depth is a <term>mile</term>, they will be direct when the breadth is less than 25°; but if a <term>sea</term>, like the <term>Atlantic</term>, were 50 or 60 <term>degrees</term> wide, it must be at least four <term>miles</term>
