So far, we have considered the motion of the water as being free from all <term>resistance</term>; but where the <term>tides</term> are <term>direct</term>, they must be slowed down by the effect of any kind of <term>resistance</term>; and where they are <term>inverted</term>, they must be accelerated. In both cases, a small amount of <term>resistance</term> produces a significant difference in the time of <term>high water</term>.

Where a significant <term>tide</term> is observed in the middle of a limited portion of the sea, it must be derived from the effect of the elevation or depression of the ocean in its neighborhood. Such <term>derivative tides</term> are probably combined in almost all cases with the <term>oscillations</term> belonging to each particular branch of the sea. Mr. Laplace supposes that the <term>tides</term> observed in the most exposed European harbors are produced almost entirely by the transmission of the effect of the <term>main ocean</term> over about a day and a half; but this opinion does not appear to be justified by observation. For the interval between the times of <term>high water</term> belonging to the same <term>tide</term>, in any two places between Brest and the Cape of Good Hope, has not been observed to exceed about twelve hours at most. Nor can we find a greater difference by comparing the state of the <term>tides</term> at more exposed locations such as St. Helena, the Cape Verde Islands, the Canaries, the Madeiras, and the Azores, which form such a succession as might be expected to have indicated the progress of the principal <term>tide</term>, if it were as Mr. Laplace supposes. The only part of the ocean that we can consider as completely open lies to the south of the two great continents, primarily between the latitudes 30° and 70° South. The original <term>tide</term>—which occurs in this widely extended ocean where its depth is sufficiently uniform—must take place, according to the theory that has been proposed, at some time before the sixth <term>lunar hour</term>. It sends a wave into the Atlantic, which takes perhaps 12 or 13 hours in its passage to the coast of France, but certainly no more. This <term>tide</term>, which would happen at the sixth <term>lunar hour</term> after the <term>moon's transit</term> if there were no <term>resistance</term>, is probably so hindered by <term>resistance</term> that the water begins to recede around the fourth hour, and in some seas even slightly earlier, though in others it may follow its natural course more closely. The tide entering the Atlantic appears to advance northwards at the rate of about 500 miles an hour, which corresponds to a depth of about 3 miles, reaching <term>Sierra Leone</term> at the 8th hour after the moon's southing. This part of <term>Africa</term> is not very far from the meridian of the middle of the south <term>Atlantic ocean</term> and has little share in the primitive tides of that ocean. The southern tide then seems to pass by <term>Cape Blanco</term> and <term>Cape Bojador</term>, arriving at <term>Gibraltar</term> at the 13th hour, and uniting its effects with those of other tides at various parts of the coast of <term>Europe</term>.

We may therefore consider the <term>Atlantic</term> as a detached sea about 3,500 miles wide and 3 miles deep; a sea of these dimensions is capable of tides considerably larger than those of the open ocean, though we cannot determine exactly how much larger without more accurate measurements. These tides would occur on the <term>European coasts</term>, if there were no resistance, a little less than 5 hours after the moon's southing, and on the coast of <term>America</term>, a little more than seven hours after. However, the resistance opposed to the motion of the sea may easily accelerate the time of high water in both cases by about two hours; so it may occur a little before the third hour on the western coasts of <term>Europe</term> and <term>Africa</term>, and before the fifth on the most exposed parts of the eastern coast of <term>America</term>. Throughout the <term>Atlantic</term>, this tide may be combined more or less with both the general southern tide and the partial effects of local elevations or depressions in the sea floor, which may cause various kinds of irregularities. The southern tide is, however, probably less significant than has sometimes been supposed; for, in the latitudes where it must originate, the extent of the elevation can only be half as great as at the <term>equator</term>. Furthermore, the <term>Islands of Kergulen's Land</term> <note>Modern Kerguelen Islands</note> and <term>South Georgia</term>, in latitudes of about 50° and 55°, have their tides delayed until the 10th and 11th hours, apparently because they receive them principally from distant parts of the ocean that are nearer to the <term>equator</term>.

Thus the tide is an hour or two later at the <term>Scilly Islands</term> than in the <term>Atlantic</term>; at <term>Plymouth</term> it is three hours later; at <term>Cork</term>, <term>Bristol</term>, and <term>Weymouth</term> it is four; at <term>Caen</term> and <term>Havre</term> it is six; at <term>Dublin</term> and <term>Brighthelmstone</term> <note>Brighton</note> it is seven; at <term>Boulogne</term> and <term>Liverpool</term> it is eight; at <term>Dover</term> it is near nine; at the <term>Nore</term> it is eleven; and at <term>London Bridge</term> it is twelve and a half. Another portion appears to proceed around <term>Ireland</term> and <term>Scotland</term> into the <term>North Sea</term>; it arrives from the <term>Atlantic</term> at <term>Londonderry</term> in about three hours, at the <term>Orkneys</term> in six, at <term>Aberdeen</term> in eleven, at <term>Leith</term> in fourteen, at <term>Leostoffe</term> <note>Lowestoft</note> in twenty, and at the <term>Nore</term> in about twenty-four hours, so as to meet there the subsequent tide coming from the south. From the time taken by the tide in traveling from the mouth of the <term>English Channel</term> to <term>Boulogne</term>, at the rate of about 50 miles an hour, we may calculate that the mean depth of the channel is about 28 <term>fathoms</term>, regardless of the magnitude of the resistances of various kinds to be overcome, which require us to suppose the depth is from 30 to 40 <term>fathoms</term>. In the great river of <term>Amazons</term>, the effects of the tides are still perceptible at the <term>straits of Pauxis</term>, 500 miles from the sea, after an interval of several days spent in their passage upstream; for the slower forward motion of the water no more hinders the progress of a wave against the stream than the velocity of the wind prevents the transmission of sound in an opposite direction. <page-num>583</page-num>
<header>ON THE TIDES.</header>

These are the general outlines of the lunar tides; they are, however, subject to a great variety of modifications, in addition to their combination with the tides produced by the sun. When the moon is exactly over the equator, the highest part of the remoter, or inferior, as well as of the nearer or superior tides, also passes over the equator, and the effect of the tide in various latitudes decreases gradually from the equator to the pole, where it disappears. But when the moon has north or south declination, the two opposite summits of the spheroid describe parallels of latitude, remaining always diametrically opposite to each other. Consequently, the two successive tides must be unequal at every place except the equator, with the larger tide occurring when the nearer elevation passes its meridian; and the average between both is somewhat smaller than the equal tides which happen when the moon passes the equator.

This inequality is, however, much less significant than it would be if the sea immediately assumed the form of the <term>spheroid of equilibrium</term>; and the most probable reasons for this circumstance are: first, that our tides are partly derived from the equatorial seas; second, that the effects of a preceding tide are to some extent continued so as to influence the height of a succeeding one; and, third, that the tides of a narrow sea are less affected by its latitude than those of a wide ocean. The height of the sea at low water is the same regardless of what the moon's declination may be. There is also a slight difference in the tides according to the position of the moon's <term>nodes</term>, which allows her declination to be greater or less; this difference is most observable in high latitudes—for instance, in <term>Iceland</term>—since, in the neighborhood of the poles, the tides depend almost entirely on the declination.

In all these cases, the law of the elevation and depression of each tide may be derived, like that of the vibrations of a <term>pendulum</term> and of a balance, from the uniform motion of a point in a circle. Thus, if we imagine a circle to be placed in a vertical plane, having its diameter equal to the total magnitude of the tide and touching the surface of the sea at low water, the point in which the surface meets the circumference of the circle will advance with a uniform motion; so that if the circle is divided into 12 parts, the point will pass over each of these parts in one <term>lunar hour</term>. It sometimes happens, however, in confined situations, that the rise and fall of the water deviates considerably from this law, and the tide rises somewhat more rapidly than it falls; and in rivers, for example in the <term>Severn</term>, the tide frequently advances

The actual progress of the tides may be most conveniently observed by means of a pipe descending some distance below the surface, so as to be beyond the reach of surface disturbances, and having a float inside it carrying a wire that indicates the height of the water on a properly graduated scale.

We have so far considered the tides only as they are caused by the moon; but in fact, the tides as they actually exist also depend on the action of the sun, which produces a series of effects precisely similar to those of the moon, although much less noticeable because of the sun's greater distance; the solar tide is only about two-fifths as large as the lunar tide. These tides occur independently of each other, nearly to the same degree as if both were single; and the combination resulting from them is alternately increased and diminished according to whether they agree or disagree regarding the time of high water at a given place. This is similar to how a periodic increase and decrease of the combined effect is produced if two series of waves (each equal in height, with widths in a ratio of 29 to 30) are supposed to pass in the same direction over the surface of a fluid, or if two similarly related sounds are heard at the same time. From this are derived the spring and neap tides: the effects of the sun and moon are united at the times of <term>conjunction</term> and <term>opposition</term> (at the new and full moon) and are opposed at the <term>quadratures</term> (the first and last quarters). The high tides at the times of the <term>equinoxes</term> are produced by the joint operation of the sun and moon, when both of them are situated so as to act more powerfully than at other times.

The lunar tide, being much larger than the solar tide, must always determine the time of high and low water; during the spring and neap tides, this timing remains unaltered by the effect of the sun. Thus, in the neap tides, the actual time of low water is the same as the solar high water; but at intermediate times, the lunar high water is more or less accelerated or retarded. The progress of this alteration may easily be traced by means of a simple

If we construct a triangle where two of the sides are two feet and five feet in length, and the external angle they form is equal to twice the distance between the luminaries <note>the sun and the moon</note>, the third side will show precisely the magnitude of the combined tide. The halves of the two angles opposite the first two sides will show the acceleration, or retardation, of the times of high water belonging to the separate tides respectively. From this, it appears that the greatest deviation of the joint tide from the lunar tide amounts to 11° 48′ in longitude, and the corresponding time to 47 minutes, assuming the proportion of the forces remains always the same. However, in fact, the forces increase in proportion as the cubes of the distances of their respective luminaries diminish, as well as from other causes; in order to determine their joint effects, the lengths of the sides of the triangle must be varied accordingly. In some ports, due to a combination of circumstances in the channel through which the tides reach them, or in the seas where they originate, the influence of the sun and moon may acquire a proportion somewhat different from that which naturally belongs to them. For example, at Brest, the influence of the moon appears to be three times as great as that of the sun, whereas it is usually only two and a half times as great. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 522.)

The greatest and least tides do not happen immediately at the times of the new and full moon, but at least two, and commonly three tides after, even at those places which are most directly exposed to the effects of the general tide of the ocean. The theory that has been proposed will provide us with a very satisfactory reason for this circumstance: the resistance of fluids in general is proportional to the square of the velocity; consequently, it must be much greater for the lunar than for the solar tide, in proportion to the magnitude of the force. Therefore, the acceleration of the lunar tide produced by this cause must be greater than that of the solar tide. Thus, it may happen that when the lunar tide occurs two or three hours after the transit of the moon, the solar tide may occur three or four hours after that of the sun, making it about an hour later at the times of conjunction and opposition. The tides will be highest when the moon passes the meridian about an hour after the sun; while at the precise time of the new and full moon, the lunar tide will be retarded about a quarter of an hour by the effect of the solar tide.

<header>LECTURE XLVII.</header>

The specific shapes of the channels through which the tides reach different places produce many local variations. The most common of these is that, because the shores of the channels converge, the tides rise much higher than they do in the open sea. Thus, at Brest, the height of the tides is about 20 feet; at Bristol, 30; at Chepstow, 40; at St. Malo, 50; and at Annapolis Royal, in the Bay of Fundy, sometimes as much as 100 feet. However, in some of these cases, a partial oscillation of a limited portion of the sea may be a direct result of the attraction of the luminary <note>the sun or the moon</note>. In the Mediterranean, the tides are generally insignificant, yet they are still noticeable; at Naples, they sometimes reach a foot, at Venice, more than two feet, and in the Euripus <note>the strait between Euboea and Boeotia</note>, for a certain number of days in each lunar month, they are very clearly observable due to the currents they cause. In the West Indies and the Gulf of Mexico, the tides are also less pronounced than in neighboring seas, perhaps because of certain combinations resulting from variations in the depth of the ocean and the different channels through which the tides travel.

To more easily understand the effects of such combinations, we might imagine a canal as large as the Amazon River that connects to the ocean at both ends, so that it receives an equal series of tides at each end, which then travel toward the opposite end. If we assume the tides enter both ends at the same moment, they will meet in the middle and continue their progress without interruption. Exactly in the middle, the times of high and low water for each series will always coincide, and the effects will be doubled. The same will happen at points where a tide arrives from one end at the same moment that an earlier or later tide arrives from the other. However, at the intermediate points, the effects will be diminished, and at some they will be completely canceled out where the high water of one tide coincides with the low water of another. Isaac Newton explained the tides at the port of Batsha in Tonkin <note>in modern-day Vietnam</note> using these types of considerations. In this port, there is only one tide per day; high water occurs at the sixth lunar hour, or at the moon's setting, when the moon has a northern declination, and at its rising when it has a southern declination. When the moon has no declination, there is no tide. To explain this circumstance, we can represent the two unequal tides that occur in succession every day by combining two equal tides with another tide, in-

Their joint result will be a tide as much greater than either as the diagonal of a square is greater than its side; the times of high and low water being intermediate between those belonging to the diurnal tides considered separately. Thus, in the port of Batsha, the larger tide probably arrives at the third lunar hour directly from the Pacific Ocean, and at the ninth hour from the Gulf of Siam, having passed between Sumatra and Borneo; so the actual time of high water is at the sixth lunar hour. The magnitude of this compound tide is by no means inconsiderable; it sometimes amounts to as much as 13 feet. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 523, 524.)

Besides the variations in the height of the sea which constitute the tides, the attractions of the sun and moon are also supposed to cause a slowing of its rotational motion. As a result, the water is left a little behind the solid parts of the earth, and a current is produced whose general direction is from east to west. This current comes from the Pacific and Indian oceans, around the Cape of Good Hope, along the coast of Africa, then crosses to America. There it is divided and reflected southward toward Brazil and northward into the Gulf Stream, which travels around the Gulf of Mexico and proceeds northeastward into the vicinity of Newfoundland, and then probably eastward and southeastward once more across the Atlantic. It is perhaps because of these currents that the Red Sea is found to be about 25 feet higher than the Mediterranean. Their direction may possibly have changed over the course of many ages, and with it the level of the Mediterranean also; since the floor of the cathedral at Ravenna is now several feet lower with respect to the sea than it is supposed to have been formerly, and some steps have been found in the rock of Malta, apparently intended for climbing it, which are currently underwater.

The atmosphere is also liable to elevations and depressions analogous to those of the sea, and perhaps these changes may have some small effect on the winds and on the weather; but their influence must be very inconsiderable—

The height of an atmospheric tide must be very nearly the same as the observed height of the principal tides of the sea; and the variation of atmospheric pressure, which is measured by the difference between the actual form and the <term>spheroid of equilibrium</term>, must be equivalent to the weight of a column of about 10 feet of air, or only 1/100 of an inch of mercury. A periodic variation five times as great as this has indeed been observed near the equator, where the state of the atmosphere is least liable to accidental disturbances; but this change cannot in any degree be attributed to the effect of the moon’s action, since it always happens at about the same hour of the day or night. The atmosphere is also affected by a general current from east to west, like that of the sea, and there is reason, based on astronomical observations, to suppose that a similar circumstance happens in the atmosphere of Jupiter, on account of the actions of its satellites, which must be considerably more powerful than that of the moon.

## LECTURE XLVIII.

### ON THE HISTORY OF ASTRONOMY.

We have now taken a general view of the most striking phenomena of the universe at large, of the great features of the solar system, and of the peculiarities of the planet which we inhabit, with respect both to its solid and to its fluid parts. All these are departments of astronomy, and we shall conclude our examination of the subject with a summary of the history of the science, principally extracted and abridged from Laplace’s *Exposition du systême du monde*.

In all probability, the astronomy of the earliest ages was confined to observations of the obvious motions and eclipses of the sun and moon, the rising, setting, and occultations of the principal stars, and the apparent motions of the planets. The progress of the sun was followed by observing the stars as they were lost in the twilight, and perhaps also by the variation of the length of the shadow of a detached object, observed at the time of the day when it was shortest. In order to recognize the fixed stars and their different motions, the heavens were divided into constellations; and twelve of these occupied the zone called the zodiac, within the limits of which the sun and planets were always found.

The entry of the sun into the constellation Aries, or the Ram, signaled the beginning of spring in the time of Hipparchus. As the season advanced, the sun continued its progress through the Bull, the Twins, and the other signs in order. Some of these appear to have been named for their relation to the agriculture and to the climates of the countries in which they were conceived, and others from the celestial phenomena attending the sun’s passage through them; the Crab, for example, representing its retrograde motion after the time of the solstice, and the Balance representing the equality of day and night.

# LECTURE XLVIII.

But because the motion of the equinoctial points has changed the course of the seasons somewhat in relation to the stars, the signs of the ecliptic—by which the positions of the sun and planets are described—no longer coincide precisely with the constellations of the zodiac from which they derive their names.

The most ancient observations in our possession that are accurate enough to be used in astronomical calculations are those of three lunar eclipses made at Babylon in the years 719 and 720 before the Christian era. Ptolemy, who has passed these records down to us, used them to determine the period of the moon's mean motion; therefore, he likely had no older records upon which he could depend. The Chaldeans, however, must have conducted a long series of observations before they could discover their <term>Saros</term>, or lunar period of 6,585⅓ days (about 18 years). They had learned at a very early date that during this period, the position of the moon, its node, and its apogee return nearly to the same situation relative to the earth and sun; consequently, a series of nearly similar eclipses recurs. The observations attributed to Hermes suggest a date seven hundred years earlier than those of the Babylonians, but their authenticity appears to be extremely doubtful.

The Egyptians were acquainted very early with the length of the year as consisting of nearly 365 and a quarter days, and from this they derived their Sothic period of 1,460 years (consisting of 365 days each). The accurate alignment of the faces of their pyramids with the points of the compass is considered proof of the precision of their observations. However, their greatest achievement was the discovery that Mercury and Venus revolve around the sun, rather than around the earth as had probably been believed previously; they did not, however, assume the same for the superior planets. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 525, 526.)

In Persia and in India, the origins of astronomy are lost in the darkness that shrouds the early history of those countries. We find the annals of no country to be as ancient and as well-authenticated as those of China, which are confirmed by an indisputable series of historical monuments. The regulation of the calendar and the prediction of eclipses were regarded in China as important objectives, for which a mathematical tribunal was established at a very early period. The Indian tables indicate a much higher degree of perfection in the early state of the science than what had been achieved in China; however, we have every reason to believe that they are not from a very remote antiquity. “Here,” says Mr. Laplace—who must be recognized as being free from prejudices in favor of established opinions—“I am sorry to be forced to differ from an illustrious philosopher, Mr. Bailly. After distinguishing his career with a variety of works useful to the sciences and to humanity at large, he fell victim to the most bloodthirsty tyranny that ever disgraced a civilized nation. The Indian tables refer to two principal eras, one placed at 3102 years before Christ, and the other at 1491. These are connected by the mean motions, rather than the true motions, of the sun, moon, and planets; therefore, one of these eras must necessarily be fictional. The celebrated author previously mentioned sought to establish in his treatise on Indian astronomy that the earlier of these eras was based on observation. But if we calculate from our own improved tables, we find that the general conjunction of the sun, moon, and planets supposed by the Indian tables never actually happened, even though it can be calculated according to those tables by working backward from the later series. The equation of the sun’s center, which depends on the eccentricity of the earth’s orbit, does indeed seem to indicate an even greater antiquity; however, its magnitude, as derived from eclipses, must have been affected by a corresponding error regarding the moon's position. Furthermore, the determination of the moon's mean motion suggests it is likely that these tables date from even later than Ptolemy.”

In astronomy, as in other sciences, the Greeks were the students of the Egyptians; they appear to have divided the stars into constellations 1,300 or 1,400 years before Christ. Newton attributes this arrangement to Chiron, and he assumes that Chiron made the middle of the constellations correspond to the beginning of their respective signs. But until the founding of the School of Alexandria, the Greeks treated astronomy as a purely speculative science and indulged in the most trivial conjectures regarding it. Thales of Miletus, who was born in the year 640 before Christ, having traveled and studied in Egypt, founded the Ionian school of philosophy upon his return. In this school, he taught the sphericity of the earth and the obliquity of the <term>ecliptic</term> with respect to the equator. He also explained the true causes of eclipses, which he was even able to foretell—unquestionably by using the information he had obtained from the Egyptian priests.

Pythagoras of Samos was born 590 years before Christ; he probably benefited from the information that Thales had acquired and also traveled to Egypt for his further improvement. It is conjectured that he was acquainted with the daily and annual motions of the earth, but he did not publicly profess the true system of the world. This was taught after his death by his disciple Philolaus, around the year 450, as well as by Nicetas and others of the school. They considered all the planets to be revolving around the sun and as inhabited globes, and they understood that comets were only eccentric planets. Some time after this, the lunar period of Meto was publicly made known at the Olympic games and was universally adopted as the basis of the calendar. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 527.)

The next occurrence regarding astronomy that deserves to be noticed is the foundation of the school of Alexandria, which was the first source of accurate and continuous observations. Upon the death of Alexander and the subsequent division of his empire, the province of Egypt fell to the lot of Ptolemy Soter—a prince whose love of science and whose generosity toward its professors attracted a great number of learned men from various parts of Greece to his capital. His son, Ptolemy Philadelphus, continued and increased the benefits his father had conferred on them, and he built the magnificent edifice that contained both the celebrated library collected by Demetrius Phalereus and an observatory furnished with the necessary books and instruments. The first astronomers appointed to occupy this building were Aristyllus and Timocharis; they flourished about 300 years before Christ and accurately observed the positions of the principal stars of

Aristarchus of Samos was the next; he devised a method of finding the sun's distance by observing the portion of the moon's disc that is illuminated when she is precisely in the <term>quadrature</term>, or 90° distant from the sun. Although he failed in his attempt to determine the sun's distance with accuracy, he nevertheless showed that it was much greater than could have been imagined at that time; he also asserted that the earth was but as a point in comparison with the magnitude of the universe. His estimate of the distance of the sun was made by Archimedes the basis of a calculation of the number of grains of sand that would be contained in the whole heavenly sphere, intended as an illustration of the powers of numerical calculation and of the utility of a decimal system of notation, which was the foundation of modern arithmetic.

Eratosthenes, the successor of Aristarchus, is known for his observation of the <term>obliquity of the ecliptic</term> and his measurement of a certain portion of the earth's circumference. He determined the whole circumference to be 250,000 <term>stadia</term>, but the length of his stadium is uncertain. Ptolemy, calculating perhaps from the same measures or from others still more ancient, calls it 180,000; which, if the stadium is determined from the <term>Nilometer</term> at Cairo and from the base of the pyramid, is within one-thousandth of the truth, the length of the base of the pyramid being equal to 400 Egyptian cubits, or to 729 feet 10 inches English.

Hipparchus <note>The OCR text reads "Hipparchsu".</note> of Bithynia flourished at Alexandria about the year 140 before Christ. Employing the observations of Timocharis and comparing them with his own, he discovered the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term>. He also observed that the summer was 9 days longer than the winter, and that the solstices divided each of these seasons slightly unequally. In order to explain this, Hipparchus supposed the sun to move uniformly in an eccentric circle, with the distance of its center from that of the earth being 1/24 of the radius, and he placed the <term>apogee</term> in the sixth degree of Gemini. Probably the annual equation of the moon, which has some influence on the timing of eclipses, was the cause of his making the <term>eccentricity</term> too great; had he assumed it to be just one-fifth less, the supposition would have represented the sun's place with tolerable accuracy. The three-century interval that passed between Hipparchus and Ptolemy offers us little that is remarkable in the progress of astronomy, except for the reformation of the calendar by Julius Caesar. Caesar was assisted in making this arrangement by Sosigenes, an astronomer from the same school that gave birth to all the preceding discoveries as well as to the improvements made by Ptolemy. This great astronomer was born at Ptolemais in Egypt and was active around the year 140 of our era. He continued the vast project, begun by Hipparchus, of reforming the entire science that he studied. He discovered the <term>evection</term> of the moon, or the change in her velocity caused by the position of the <term>apogee</term> with respect to the sun; he determined the value of this <term>equation</term> with great precision. In order to represent it, he supposed the moon to perform a subordinate revolution in an <term>epicycle</term>, or a smaller circle, the center of which was carried around in the line of the general orbit, which he considered to be an <term>eccentric circle</term>. This mode of approximation is exceedingly ingenious; it is said to have been the invention of <term>Apollonius of Perga</term>, the mathematician, and although it sometimes becomes complicated, it is very convenient for calculation; and it may be used effectively in the representation of the planetary motions by machinery.

Ptolemy adopted the most ancient opinion regarding the <term>solar system</term>, verticalizing the belief that all the heavenly bodies revolve around the earth; the moon being nearest, then Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. This opinion had long been the most common, although some astronomers had placed Mercury and Venus at greater distances than the sun, and some attributed only a daily motion to the earth; but the doctrine of the <term>Pythagoreans</term> appears to have been completely discredited or forgotten. Ptolemy determined the amount of the <term>precession of the equinoxes</term> from a comparison of his own observations with those of Hipparchus; but he made it smaller than the truth; and he probably formed his table of the positions of the stars by applying this erroneous correction to the tables of Hipparchus in order to accommodate them to his own time. Both these errors may, however, be explained in other ways, by supposing him to have followed Hipparchus in the length of the <term>tropical year</term>, which, being somewhat too long, caused an error

Ptolemy's principal work is his mathematical system of astronomy, which was afterwards called the <term>Great Syntaxis</term> or body of astronomy, and is at present frequently quoted by the Arabic name <term>Almagest</term>. Ptolemy was the last as well as the greatest of the Alexandrian astronomers, and the science made no further progress until the time of the Arabians. The first of these was Almamoun, who was the son of the celebrated Aaron Reschid; he reigned at Bagdad in 814, and having conquered the Greek emperor, Michael the Third, he made it a condition of peace that a copy of the works of each of the best Greek authors should be delivered to him. Among them were the works of Ptolemy, of which he procured an Arabic translation. Almamoun also observed the <term>obliquity of the ecliptic</term> and measured the length of a degree on the plains of Mesopotamia.

Among the astronomers protected by this prince and his successors, Albategni was the most eminent. He ascertained with great accuracy, in 880, the <term>eccentricity</term> of the solar motion, and discovered the change of the place of the sun's <term>apogee</term>, or of the earth's <term>aphelion</term>.

Ibn Junis made his observations at Cairo, about the year 1000; he was a very assiduous astronomer, and determined the length of the year to within 2 seconds of the truth. At this time the Arabians were in the habit of employing, in their observations, the vibrations of a pendulum.

The Persians soon after applied themselves to astronomy; and in the eleventh century they invented the approximation of reckoning 8 <term>bissextiles</term> <note>leap years</note> in 33 years, which was afterwards proposed by Dominic Cassini as an improvement of the Gregorian calendar. It was not long after the time of Ulugh Beigh that Copernicus laid the foundation for the more accurate theories that modern improvements have introduced into astronomy. Dissatisfied with the complicated hypotheses of the Ptolemaic system, he examined the works of the ancients in search of more probable opinions. He found from Cicero that Nicetas and other Pythagoreans had maintained that the sun is placed in the center of the system, and that the earth moves around it along with the other planets. He applied this idea to the numerous observations which the diligence of astronomers had accumulated, and he had the satisfaction of finding them all in perfect conformity with this theory. He quickly discarded the Ptolemaic epicycles, which had been devised to explain the alternations of the direct and retrograde motions of the planets. In these remarkable phenomena, Copernicus saw nothing but the necessary consequences produced by the combination of the motions of the earth and planets around the sun; and from a minute examination of these circumstances, he calculated the relative distances of the planets from the sun, which until then had remained unknown. In this system, everything bore the marks of that beautiful simplicity which pervades all the works of nature and which, once understood, carries within itself sufficient evidence of its truth. Copernicus was born at Thorn, in Polish Prussia, in 1473; he studied in Italy and taught mathematics at Rome, and later settled into a canonicate at Frauenberg. There, in thirty-six years of retirement and meditation, he completed his work on the celestial revolutions, which had scarcely been published when he died.

About this time, William IV, Landgrave of Hesse-Cassel, not only enriched astronomy with his own observations but also used his influence with Frederick, King of Denmark, to obtain patronage for the celebrated Tycho Brahe. Frederick agreed to give him the small island of Huen, at the entrance of the Baltic, where Tycho built his observatory of Uraniburg and, over a period of twenty-one years, made a prodigious collection of accurate observations. After the death of his patron, his progress was hindered, and he sought a position at Prague under the Emperor Rudolph. Here he

<meta>This page concludes the biographical details of Copernicus and transitions into the life and work of Tycho Brahe. It specifically details the Tychonic system—a hybrid of geocentrism and heliocentrism—and introduces Johannes Kepler’s work on elliptical orbits and planetary laws.</meta>

<header>ON THE HISTORY OF ASTRONOMY.</header>

He died soon after, at the age of 55. Struck by the objections made to the system of Copernicus—principally those deduced from a misinterpretation of the scriptures—he imagined a new theory which, although mechanically absurd, is still astronomically correct. For he supposed the earth to remain at rest in the center, and the stars to revolve around it, together with the sun and all the planets, in a <term>sidereal day</term>; he also supposed the sun to have an annual motion, carrying the planets with it in their orbits. Here, the apparent or relative motions are precisely the same as in the Copernican system. The argument that Tycho Brahe drew from the scriptures in favor of his theory was, therefore, in every way injudicious; for it is not to be imagined that anything but relative motion or rest could be intended in the scriptures when the sun is said to move or to stand still. 

But in the Copernican system, there was an evident regularity in the periods of all the planets: that of the earth being longer than that of Venus and shorter than that of Mars, which were the neighboring planets on each side. When Tycho imagined the sun to move around the earth, this analogy was entirely lost. Tycho Brahe was the discoverer of the <term>variation</term> and of the <term>annual equation</term> of the moon; the first being an irregularity in its velocity that depends on its position with respect to the sun, and the other being a change in the magnitude of all the perturbations produced by the sun, which depends on its distance from the earth. (Plate XXXVIII. Fig. 529.)

Kepler was the pupil and assistant of Tycho, whose observations were the basis of his important discoveries: he succeeded him in his appointments at Prague and enjoyed the title of Imperial Mathematician. Adopting the Copernican system, which was then becoming popular, he proceeded to examine the distances of the celestial bodies from each other at various times. After many fruitless attempts to reconcile the positions of the planets with the supposition of revolutions in eccentric circles, he at last discovered that their orbits are <term>ellipses</term>. He demonstrated, chiefly from his observations on the planet Mars, that the revolving radius—or the line drawn from the sun to the planet—always describes equal areas in equal times. By comparing the periods and the mean distances of the different planets with each other, he found, after 17 years of calculation, that the squares of the times of revolution are always proportional to the cubes of the mean distances from the sun.

Kepler died in 1630; before his death, he had the satisfaction of applying his theory to the motions of Jupiter's satellites. These, along with the phases of Venus and the spots on the sun, had recently been discovered in Italy through the telescopic observations of Galileo. This great man—celebrated both for his theory of projectiles and for his zealous defense of the Copernican system—was born at Pisa in 1564 and lived to the age of 78. He was full of an enthusiasm that led him to despise the threats of the Inquisition and submit patiently to its persecutions. He died in 1642, the year in which Newton was born.

The invention of logarithms by Baron Napier must be noted for its importance to practical astronomy, and the laborious observations of Hevelius also deserve to be mentioned with praise. The discoveries of the shape of Saturn's ring and one of its satellites by Huygens—as well as four more satellites, along with the belts and rotation of Jupiter by Dominic Cassini—were among the early improvements resulting from the introduction of the telescope. But without dwelling on any of these subjects, we move quickly to the establishment of the system of gravitation, which has immortalized the name of Newton and brought unrivaled honor to the country of his birth.

The mutual attraction of all matter seems to have been suspected by the Epicureans, but Lucretius never speaks of it in terms sufficient to convey a clear idea of a reciprocal force. Gregory, in the preface to his *Astronomy*, has endeavored to prove that Pythagoras must have been acquainted even with the law of the decrease of gravitation, and Lalande appears to agree with his arguments. However, these arguments rest only on the bare possibility that Pythagoras might have deduced an analogy from the tension of chords—which we have no reason to suppose he even completely understood—simply because he fancifully imagined a correspondence between the planets and the strings of a lyre. But the nature of gravitation had long been suspected to some extent; Plutarch had asserted that the moon is held in its orbit by it, like a stone in a sling, and Bacon, Copernicus, Kepler, Fermat, and Roberval were aware of its effectiveness. Bacon, in his *Novum Organum*, calls the descent of heavy bodies the motion

Kepler also mentions the perfect reciprocity of the action of gravitation, and considers the lunar irregularities as produced by the attraction of the sun. But our most ingenious countryman, Dr. Hooke, was still more decisive in attributing the revolutions of the planets to the combination of a projectile motion with a centripetal force; he expresses his sentiments on the subject very clearly in his *Attempt to prove the motion of the earth*, published in 1674, and had his skill in mathematics been equal to his practical sagacity, he would probably have completed, or at least have published, the discovery before his great contemporary.

It must be confessed that Newton’s good fortune was equal to his talents and his application; for had he lived earlier, he might probably have confined his genius to speculations purely mathematical; had he lived later, his discoveries in natural philosophy might have been anticipated by others; and yet Newton would perhaps have improved still more on their labors than they have done on his. It was in 1676, when he was 34 years old, that he first demonstrated the necessary connection of the planetary revolutions in elliptic orbits with an attractive force varying inversely as the square of the distance. But he had collected the law of the force from the discoveries of Kepler respecting the periods of the different planets some time before 1671, as he asserts to Dr. Halley, and, to the best of his recollection, about 1668, although in his *Principia* he allows, with the most laudable candor, to Wren, Hooke, and Halley, the merit of having made the same discovery, without any connection with each other’s investigations or with his own. The manner in which Newton was led to attend particularly to the subject is thus related by Pemberton, in the preface to his *View of Sir Isaac Newton’s philosophy*.

> “The first thoughts,” says Pemberton, “which gave rise to his *Principia*, he had when he retired from Cambridge in 1666, on account of the plague. As he sat alone in a garden, he fell into a speculation on the power of gravity: that as this power is not found perceptibly diminished at the remotest distance from the center of the earth to which we can rise, neither at the tops of the loftiest buildings, nor even on the summits of the highest mountains; it appeared to him reasonable to conclude that this power must extend much further than was usually thought; why not as high as the moon?

He said to himself; and if so, its motion must be influenced by it; perhaps it is held in its orbit by that force. However, although the power of gravity is not noticeably weakened by the small change in distance at which we can place ourselves from the center of the earth, it is very possible that, as high up as the moon, this power may differ greatly in strength from what it is here. To estimate what the degree of this decrease might be, he considered that if the moon is held in its orbit by the force of gravity, no doubt the primary planets are carried around the sun by a similar power. And by comparing the periods of the several planets with their distances from the sun, he found that if any power like gravity held them in their courses, its strength must decrease in the duplicate proportion of the increase of distance. He concluded this by supposing them to move in perfect circles concentric to the sun, from which the orbits of most of them do not differ much. Supposing, therefore, that the power of gravity decreased in the same manner when extended to the moon, he calculated whether that force would be sufficient to keep the moon in its orbit. In this calculation, being away from his books, he used the common estimate used by geographers and our seamen before Norwood had measured the earth—that 60 English miles were contained in one degree of latitude on the surface of the earth. But as this is a very faulty assumption—each degree actually containing about 69 1/2 of our miles—his calculation did not meet expectations; because of this, he concluded that some other cause must at least combine with the action of the power of gravity on the moon. For this reason, he set aside any further thoughts on the matter for a time. But some years later, a letter he received from Dr. Hooke prompted him to inquire into the real path in which a body dropped from any high place descends, taking the rotation of the earth around its axis into consideration. Such a body, having the same motion that the place it falls from has due to the rotation of the earth, is to be considered as projected forward and, at the same time, drawn down toward the center of the earth. This gave him the occasion to resume his former thoughts concerning the moon; and since Picart in France had recently measured the earth, by using Picart's measurements, the moon appeared to be kept in its orbit purely by the power of gravity; and consequently, that this power decreases as you move away from the center of the earth, in the manner our author had previously conjectured. Based on this principle, he found the line described by a falling body to be an ellipse, the center

The astronomers of Great Britain have been no less diligent in the practical part of the science than they have been successful in the theoretical part. The foundation of the observatory at Greenwich was laid in 1675, some years before the completion and publication of Newton’s discoveries. It is with the building of this structure that modern refinements in practical astronomy may be said to have begun; its immediate object was to assist in perfecting the science of navigation, and the series of observations made there has provided an invaluable wealth of materials to astronomers of every country. A reward had been proposed, more than half a century earlier, by Philip III of Spain for discovering a way to determine the longitude of a ship at sea, and the states of Holland had followed his example; a large reward was also offered by the French government during the minority of Louis XV. In 1674, Mr. St. Pierre, a Frenchman, had undertaken to determine the longitude of a place based on observations of the moon’s altitude, and King Charles II was persuaded to appoint a commission to examine his proposals. Mr. Flamsteed was consulted by the commissioners and was added to their number; he demonstrated the disadvantages of the method proposed by Mr. St. Pierre and the inaccuracy of the existing tables of lunar motions, as well as the catalogs of the positions of the stars. However, he expressed his opinion that if the tables were improved, it would be possible to determine the longitudes of places with sufficient accuracy through lunar observations. In the year 1714, the British Parliament offered £20,000 for a determination of the longitude of a ship at sea within an error of 30 miles, and a smaller sum for a less accurate method, appointing at the same time a Board of Longitude for the examination of the methods which might be proposed. Under this act, several rewards were assigned, and in 1774, it was superseded by another, which offers £5,000 for the invention of any timekeeper or other method capable of determining the longitude of a place within 1 degree, and £10,000 if within 30 miles; and a reward of £5,000 to the author of any lunar tables which should be found within 15 seconds of the truth, allowing the Board also the power of granting smaller sums at their discretion. Timekeepers are at present very commonly employed in the British Navy, and some of them have been capable of determining the longitude within half a degree after having been two or three months at sea. The lunar tables which have been employed for the Nautical Almanacs are those of Professor Mayer, who adopted the methods of calculation invented by Leonard Euler; but the tables of Mr. Burg of Vienna are still more accurate and are said to be always within about ten seconds of the truth.

The progress of astronomy since the death of Newton in 1727 has been fully equal to what its most optimistic followers could have hoped. The great discoveries of the aberration of the fixed stars and of the nutation of the Earth's axis were made by our countryman Bradley, with the assistance of the instruments for which he was indebted to the delicate workmanship of our artists. Among these, the names of Bird, Short, Sisson, Graham, Dollond, Harrison, and Ramsden have long been celebrated throughout Europe. The astronomers of Sicily and Germany have, however, the honor of the first discovery of the three humbler members of the solar system which have been last introduced to our acquaintance: Ceres by Piazzi, Pallas by Olbers, and Juno by Harding. And the mathematicians of France have excelled all their predecessors in the elaborate and refined application of the theory of gravitation to the investigation of the most minute and intricate details of the celestial motions.

## LECTURE XLIX.

### ON THE ESSENTIAL PROPERTIES OF MATTER.

The objects that have lately occupied our inquiries are the most sublime and magnificent that nature anywhere displays to us, and the contemplation of them naturally excites, even in an uncultivated mind, an admiration of their dignity and grandeur. But all magnitude is relative; and if we examine with more calm attention, we shall find still greater scope for our investigation and curiosity in the microscopic world than in the telescopic one. Pliny has very justly observed that nature nowhere displays all her powers with greater activity than in the smallest objects perceptible to our senses; and we may judge how wide a field of research the corpuscular properties of matter afford from the relatively small progress that has been made in cultivating it so far. For while the motions of the vast bodies that roll through the heavens have been completely subjected to the most rigorous calculations, we know nothing, except from experience alone, of the analogies by which the minute actions of the particles of matter are regulated. It is probable, however, that they all depend ultimately on the same mechanical principles. We have seen, for example, that the widely extended elevations and depressions of the ocean, which are raised by the attractive powers of the two great luminaries and cover half the globe at once, are governed and combined according to the same laws that determine the motions of the smaller waves excited by different causes in a canal, the rapid vibrations of a medium transmitting sound, or the inconceivably small undulations which are capable of accounting for the phenomena of light, and which must be exerted in spaces as much smaller than those of sound as a grain of sand is smaller than a mountain. Thus, the elimination of the effects of the semidiurnal changes of the tide, and the preservation of the diurnal change in the harbor of Batsha, may be explained precisely in the same manner as the reflection of red light from a transparent substance of such a

We are now to descend from the properties of the large masses of matter, which form the great features of the universe, to the specific properties of the matter that constitutes them, as far as they are common to all matter in general; but those properties which are unique to certain kinds of matter only—being the subjects of chemical science—are not to be included in the discussion. If we are asked for a definition of matter, it will be somewhat difficult to avoid all circular expressions. We may use gravitation as a test of matter, but then we must say that whatever is attracted by other matter is also to be called matter, and this assumes the subject of our definition is already known. Furthermore, the property of attraction may also possibly belong to substances that are not simply material; for the electrical fluid, if such a fluid exists, is probably attracted by matter, and yet it seems to be different in most respects from any form of common matter. A similar difficulty would occur if we attempted to define matter by its impenetrability or mutual repulsion, or if we considered everything material that is capable of affecting the senses. We must, therefore, take it for granted that matter is understood without a definition, and we may describe it as a substance occupying space, or as a gravitating or ponderable substance.

It cannot be determined with certainty whether matter is originally of one kind, owing its different appearances only to the form and arrangement of its parts, or whether there are various kinds of simple matter, essentially distinct from each other; however, the probability appears to favor the former supposition. However this may be, the properties of matter are by no means as simple in their nature, nor as easily reduced to general laws, as the more mathematical doctrines of space and motion. Since our knowledge of them depends more on experience than on abstract principles, they may properly be considered as belonging to specific physics. We have found no inconvenience from omitting the doctrine of matter as a part of the subject of mechanics; although, in treating the strength of materials as secondary to practical mechanics, it was necessary to consider the effects of some of these properties as deduced from experiment, it will appear that it was impossible to examine their origin and mutual connection without

We may distinguish the general properties of matter into two principal classes: those which appear to be inseparable from its constitution, and those which are only accidental, or which are not always attached to matter of all kinds. The essential properties are chiefly extension and divisibility, density, repulsion (or impenetrability), inertia, and gravitation; the accidental properties are in large measure dependent on cohesion, such as liquidity, solidity, symmetry of arrangement, cohesive elasticity, stiffness, toughness, strength, and resilience.

The extension of matter can scarcely be considered a property separate from its impenetrability, unless we conceive that it can occupy space without excluding other bodies from it. This opinion has indeed been maintained by some philosophers, who have imagined that the minute particles which they suppose to constitute light may penetrate the ultimate atoms of other matter without annihilating or displacing them; and if this hypothesis were admitted, it would be necessary to consider each particle of matter as a sphere of repulsion, extended without being impenetrable.

The divisibility of matter is great beyond the power of imagination, but we have no reason for asserting that it is infinite; for the demonstrations which have sometimes been cited in favor of this opinion are obviously applicable to space only. The infinite divisibility of space seems to be essential to the conception that we have of its nature; and it may be strictly demonstrated that it is mathematically possible to draw an infinite number of circles between any given circle and its tangent, none of which shall touch either of them except at the general point of contact; and that a ship, following always the same oblique course with respect to the meridian—for example, sailing northeast—would continue perpetually to approach the pole without ever completely reaching it. But when we inquire into the truth of the old maxim of the schools, that all matter is infinitely divisible, we are by no means able to decide so positively. Newton observes that it is doubtful whether any human means may be sufficient to separate the particles of matter beyond a certain limit; and it is not impossible that some such limit exists.

Even if there are, it is almost certain that matter is never annihilated in this way in the common course of nature.

It remains to be examined how far we have any experience of the actual extent of the divisibility of matter, and we shall find no appearance of anything like a limit to this property. The smallest spherical object visible to a good eye is about 1/2000 of an inch in diameter; with the assistance of a microscope, we may perhaps distinguish a body one-hundredth part as large, or 1/200,000 of an inch in diameter. The thickness of gold leaf is less than this, and the gilding of lace is still thinner, probably in some cases no more than one ten-millionth of an inch; so that 1/2000 of a grain would cover a square inch, and a portion barely large enough to be visible by a microscope might weigh only the 80 million-millionth part of a grain. A grain of musk is said to be divisible into 320 quadrillion parts, each of which is capable of affecting the olfactory nerves. There are even living beings visible to the microscope of which a million million would not make up the bulk of a common grain of sand. But it is even more remarkable that, as far as we can discover, many of these animalcules <note>microscopic organisms</note> are as complicated in their structure as an elephant or a whale. It is true that the physiology of the various classes of animals is somewhat simpler as they deviate more from the form of quadrupeds and from that of the human species; the solid particles of the blood do not vary in their magnitude at the same ratio as the bulk of the animal, and some of the lower classes appear to approximate very closely the nature of the vegetable world. But there are single instances that seem to destroy this gradation entirely: Lyonnet <note>Pierre Lyonet, an 18th-century naturalist known for his detailed dissections of insects</note> has discovered a far greater variety of parts in the caterpillar of the willow butterfly than we can observe in many animals of the largest dimensions. Among microscopic insects in particular, we see an abundance of machinery subservient to the various purposes of the limited life of the little animal; in their structure, nature appears ostentatious of her power to give perfection to her minutest works.

<term>Impenetrability</term> is usually attributed to matter based on the common observation that two bodies cannot occupy the same place at once. It is in this way that we distinguish matter from space; for example, when we dip an inverted jar into mercury, the air contained in the jar pushes down the surface of the mercury and prevents it from occupying the space within the jar. But if the jar had been empty of matter, like the vacuum above the mercury in a <term>barometer</term>, nothing would have prevented it from being filled by the mercury as soon as either its weight or the pressure of the atmosphere forced it to enter the jar.

But it does not appear that our senses are fully capable of extending this proposition to all substances, whether material or not. We cannot prove experimentally that the influence of <term>gravitation</term> is incapable of pervading even the ultimate particles of solid matter, for this power appears to suffer no reduction or change when a third body is placed between the two gravitating masses. In the same manner, a magnet acts as quickly on a needle through a plate of glass or gold, whatever its thickness may be, as if only a vacuum stood between them. One may, however, ask if the gold or the glass has certain passages or <term>pores</term> through which the influence may be transmitted. It can be shown, in many instances, that substances which are apparently solid have many orifices into which other substances may enter; thus, mercury may easily be made to pass through leather or through wood by the pressure of the atmosphere or by any other equal force. It may be observed that it requires only a more or less minute division of <term>matter</term> to reduce the magnitude of the <term>interstices</term> <note>gaps</note> between neighboring particles to within any given dimensions. Thus, <term>platina</term> <note>platinum</note> contains, in a cubic inch, more than 200,000 times as many <term>gravitating atoms</term> as pure <term>hydrogen gas</term>, yet both of these <term>mediums</term> are free from perceptible <term>interstices</term> and appear to be equally continuous. There may possibly be other substances in nature that contain, in a given space, 200,000 times as many atoms as <term>platina</term>; although this supposition is not entirely probable in its full extent. For the earth is the densest of any of the <term>celestial bodies</term> with which we are fully acquainted, and the earth is only one-fourth as dense as it would be if it were composed entirely of <term>platina</term>; so we have no reason to believe that there exists in the <term>solar system</term> any considerable quantity of a substance even as dense as <term>platina</term>.

Besides this <term>porosity</term>, there is still room to suppose that even the ultimate particles of <term>matter</term> may be permeable to the causes of <term>attractions</term> of various kinds, especially if those causes are immaterial. Nor is there anything in the impartial study of <term>physical philosophy</term> that can lead us to doubt the existence of <term>immaterial substances</term>; on the contrary, we see analogies that lead us almost directly to such an opinion. The <term>electrical fluid</term> is supposed to be essentially different from common <term>matter</term>; the general medium of <term>light</term> and <term>heat</term>, according to some, or the principle of <term>caloric</term>, according to others, is equally distinct from it. We see forms of <term>matter</term> differing in <term>subtility</term> <note>fineness</note> and <term>mobility</term>, under the names of <term>solids</term>, <term>liquids</term>, and <term>gases</term>. Above these are the <term>semimaterial existences</term> which produce the phenomena of <term>electricity</term> and <term>magnetism</term>, and either <term>caloric</term> or a <term>universal ether</term>; and higher still, perhaps, are the causes of <term>gravitation</term> and the immediate agents in <term>attractions</term> of all kinds, which exhibit some phenomena apparently even more remote from all that is compatible with <term>material bodies</term>. Of these different orders of beings, the more refined and immaterial appear to freely pervade the grosser. It seems, therefore, natural to believe that the analogy may be continued even further, until it rises into existences that are absolutely immaterial and spiritual. We do not know but that thousands of <term>spiritual worlds</term> may exist, forever unseen by human eyes; nor do we have any reason to suppose that even the presence of <term>matter</term> in a given spot necessarily excludes these existences from it. life, wherever living beings can be situated, may therefore speculate freely on the possibility of independent worlds; some existing in different parts of space, others pervading each other, unseen and unknown, in the same space, and others again to which space may not be a necessary mode of existence.

Whatever opinion we may hold regarding the ultimate <term>impenetrability</term> of <term>matter</term> in this sense, it is probable that the particles of <term>matter</term> are absolutely impenetrable to each other. This <term>impenetrability</term>, however, is not commonly brought into effect in cases of apparent contact. If the particles of <term>matter</term> making up water and steam, or any other gas, are of the same nature, those of the gas cannot be in perfect contact; and when water is contracted by the effect of cold, or when two fluids have their joint volume diminished by mixture—as in the case of alcohol or <term>sulfuric acid</term> and water—the particles cannot have been in absolute contact before, even though they would have resisted any attempt to compress them with great force. Metals of all kinds that have been melted also become permanently denser when they are hammered and <term>laminated</term> <note>pressed into thin layers</note>. A still more striking and elegant illustration of the nature of <term>repulsive force</term> is shown in the contact of two pieces of polished glass. The colors of thin plates provide us, by comparison with the observations of <term>Newton</term>, the most delicate <term>micrometer</term> that can be desired for measuring any distances less than the ten-thousandth of an inch. It was remarked by <term>Newton</term> himself that when two plates of glass are within about this distance of each other, or somewhat closer, they support each other’s weight just as if they were in actual contact, and that some additional force is required to make them approach still nearer. Nor does it seem probable that the contact is ever perfect; otherwise, they might be expected to <term>cohere</term> <note>stick together</note> in such a way as to become a single mass. <term>Professor Robison</term> has determined by experiment the force necessary to produce the greatest possible degree of contact, and finds it equivalent to a pressure of about a thousand pounds for every square inch of glass. It is therefore obvious that in all common cases of contact between two distinct bodies, it must be this <term>repulsive force</term> that keeps them in their positions. I have found that glass placed on a metal surface exhibits this force to nearly the same degree as if placed on another piece of glass; it is also independent of the presence of air, but under water, it disappears.

<page-num>612</page-num>
### LECTURE XLIX.

The existence of a <term>repulsive force</term>, extending beyond the actual surface of a <term>material substance</term>, having been proved, some have conjectured that such a force, unconnected with any <term>central atom</term>, may be sufficient for producing all the <term>phenomena of matter</term>. This representation may be admitted without much difficulty, provided it is allowed that the force becomes infinite at or near the center; but it has sometimes been supposed that it is everywhere less than infinite, and consequently that matter is not absolutely impenetrable. However, such a supposition appears to lead to the necessity of believing that the <term>particles</term> of matter must sometimes be annihilated, which is not a very probable opinion.

The magnitude of the <term>repulsive force</term>, by which the <term>particles</term> of any single body are enabled to resist <term>compression</term>, increases nearly in proportion to the degree of <term>compression</term>, or to the decrease of the distances between the <term>particles</term>. This is almost a necessary consequence of any primary law that can be imagined for the immediate actions of the <term>particles</term>: for instance, if the repulsion increased either as the square or as the cube of the distance diminished, the effect of a double change of dimensions would always be nearly a double change of the <term>repulsive force</term>; that is, if an <term>elastic substance</term> were compressed by one-thousandth part of its volume, it would in either case resist twice as much as if it were only compressed by one two-thousandth.

It is obvious that if the <term>particles</term> of matter possess a <term>repulsive force</term> decreasing in any regular proportion with the increase of distance, they can never remain at rest without the operation of some external pressure, but will always retain a tendency to expand. This is the case for all <term>elastic fluids</term>, the <term>density</term> of which is found to vary exactly as the compressing force; from which it may be demonstrated that the primary <term>repulsive force</term> of the <term>particles</term> must increase in the same proportion as the distance decreases. It follows also that this force can only be exerted between such <term>particles</term> as are either actually or very nearly in contact with each other; since it requires no greater pressure, acting on a given surface, to retain a gallon of air in the space of half a gallon than to retain a pint in the space of half a pint; this could not be the case if the <term>particles</term> exercised a <term>mutual repulsion</term> at all possible distances.

<summary>This page discusses the theory of repulsive forces between particles as the primary cause of the properties of matter and its resistance to compression. It explains that in elastic fluids, such as air, these forces only act at very short distances, with density varying in direct proportion to the compressing force.</summary>

<keywords>repulsive force, material substance, central atom, phenomena of matter, particles, compression, elastic substance, elastic fluids, density, mutual repulsion, physics, matter theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the repulsive forces between particles, specifically critiquing contemporary theories regarding the interaction of different gases and how these forces persist in liquid and solid states.</meta>

<page-num>613</page-num>
<header>ON THE ESSENTIAL PROPERTIES OF MATTER.</header>

Mr. Dalton has proposed a unique theory respecting the constitution and mutual repulsion of <term>elastic fluids</term>; he imagines that when any two <term>gases</term> of different types are mixed, the particles of each gas repel only the similar particles of the same gas, without exerting any action on those of the other gas, except when the ultimate solid atoms happen to interfere. The idea is ingenious and original, and may perhaps be of use in connecting some facts together, or in leading to some other less improbable suppositions; but it may easily be shown that Mr. Dalton's hypothesis cannot possibly be true in its full extent. It would follow from it that two portions of gases of different types could not exist for a noticeable time in the same vessel without being uniformly diffused throughout it, while the fact is clearly otherwise. For <term>hydrogen gas</term> remains, when left completely at rest, for a very considerable time above, and <term>carbonic acid gas</term> below, a portion of <term>common air</term> with which it is in contact; nor is there any circumstance involving the mixture of gases that may not be explained without adopting such a paradoxical opinion. Mr. Dalton thinks that, according to the laws of <term>hydrostatics</term>, no two gases that are not chemically united could remain mixed if their particles acted mutually on each other; but the laws of <term>hydrostatics</term> do not apply to the mixture of single particles of fluids of different types, since they are only derived from the assumption of a collection of particles of the same type.

In liquids and in solids, this <term>repulsive force</term> appears at first sight to be missing; but when we consider that the particles of both liquids and solids are influenced by the attractive force of <term>cohesion</term>, we shall see the necessity for the presence of a <term>repulsive force</term> in order to balance it. It is, therefore, probable that the particles of <term>aeriform fluids</term> still retain their original repulsive powers when they are reduced to a state of liquidity or solidity by being subjected to the action of a second force, which causes them to cohere.

The mutual <term>repulsion</term> of the particles of matter is a reciprocal force, acting equally in opposite directions on each of the bodies concerned. It scarcely requires either experiment or argument to show that if two bodies repel each other, neither of them will remain at rest, but both will move with equal amounts of <term>motion</term>. Thus, if a portion of <term>condensed air</term> is made to act upon the bullet of an air gun, it will force the gun backwards with as much <term>momentum</term> as it impels the bullet forwards.

### LECTURE XLIX.

<term>Inertia</term> is that property of <term>matter</term> by which it retains its state of rest or of uniform motion, in relation to a stationary space, as long as no external cause occurs to change that state. This property depends on the internal constitution of <term>matter</term>; it is generally exhibited by means of the <term>force</term> of <term>repulsion</term>, which enables a body in motion to displace another in order to continue its motion, or by means of some <term>attractive force</term>, which causes two bodies to approach their common centre of <term>inertia</term> with equal <term>momenta</term>.

Another universal property of <term>matter</term> is reciprocal <term>gravitation</term>, of which the <term>force</term> is directly in the combined proportion of the quantities of <term>matter</term> attracting each other, and inversely as the square of their distance. In order to prove that the <term>gravitation</term> towards a given substance—for instance, the weight of a body, or its <term>gravitation</term> towards the earth—is precisely in proportion to the <term>mass</term> or <term>inertia</term> of the movable <term>matter</term> of which it consists, Sir Isaac <term>Newton</term> made two equal <term>pendulums</term> with hollow balls of equal size. In order that the resistance of the air might be the same with respect to both, he placed various different substances successively within the balls and found that the time of vibration remained always the same; from this, he inferred that the attraction was proportional in all cases to the quantity of <term>matter</term> possessing <term>inertia</term>. For if any of these substances had contained particles capable of receiving and communicating motion, yet without being subject to <term>gravitation</term>, they would have slowed the vibrations of the <term>pendulum</term> by adding to the quantity of <term>matter</term> to be moved without increasing the moving <term>force</term>. The law of <term>gravitation</term>, which indicates the rate of its increase as the distance decreases, is principally deduced from astronomical observations and calculations; it is the simplest that can be conceived for any influence that either spreads from a center or converges toward a center, for it supposes the <term>force</term> acting on the same substance to be always proportional to the angular space that it occupies.

<term>Newton</term> appears to have considered these laws of <term>gravitation</term>, which he first discovered, rather as derivative than as original properties of <term>matter</term>; and although it has often been asserted that we gain nothing by referring them to pressure or to impulse, yet it is undoubtedly advancing a step in the explanation of natural phenomena to lessen the number of general principles; and if it were possible to refer either all attraction to a modification of re-

It also notes that Newton viewed the laws of gravitation as derivative properties rather than primary ones.</summary>

Lately, it has been very common to consider all the phenomena of nature as derived from the motions of the corpuscles of matter, agitated by forces varying according to certain intricate laws. These laws are supposed to be primary qualities, and it is considered a kind of sacrilege to attempt to assign any further cause for them. This theory was chiefly introduced by Boscovich, and it has prevailed very widely among algebraic philosophers, who have been in the habit of deducing all their quantities from each other by mathematical relations—making, for example, the force a certain function or power of the distance, and then imagining that its origin is sufficiently explained. When a geometrician has translated this language into his own and converted the formula into a curve, with as many bends and reflections as the labyrinth of Daedalus, he imagines that he has depicted the whole procedure of nature to the senses. Such methods may often be of temporary advantage, as long as we are content to consider them only as approximations or as classifications of phenomena; but the grand scheme of the universe must surely, amidst all the stupendous diversity of parts, preserve a more dignified simplicity of plan and of principles than is compatible with these complicated suppositions.

"To show," says Newton in the preface to the second edition of his *Optics*, "that I do not take gravity for an essential property of bodies, I have added one question concerning its cause, choosing to propose it by way of a question because I am not yet satisfied about it for want of experiments." In the query mentioned here, he proceeds from the supposition of an elastic medium pervading all space—a supposition which he advances with considerable confidence and which he supports by very strong arguments deduced from the phenomena of light and heat, as well as from the analogy of electrical and magnetic influences. This medium he supposes to be much rarer within the dense bodies of the sun, the stars, the planets, and the comets than in
