The effects of gravitation might be produced by a medium constituted in this way, if its particles were repelled by all material substances with a force decreasing—like other repulsive forces—simply as the distances increase. Its density would then be everywhere such as to produce the appearance of an attraction varying like that of gravitation. Such an ethereal medium would therefore have the advantage of simplicity in the original law of its action, since the repulsive force known to belong to all matter would be sufficient, when modified in this way, to account for the principal phenomena of attraction.

It may be questioned whether a medium capable of producing the effects of gravitation in this manner would also be equally susceptible to those modifications we have supposed necessary for the transmission of light. In either case, it must be assumed to pass through the apparent substance of all material bodies with perfect freedom; there would, therefore, be no reason to fear any difficulty from a slowing down of celestial motions. The ultimate, impenetrable particles of matter are perhaps scattered as thinly through their external forms as the stars are scattered in a nebula, which still has the distant appearance of a uniform light and a continuous surface. There seems no reason to doubt the possibility of the propagation of an undulation through the Newtonian medium with the actual velocity of light. It must be remembered that the difference in its pressure is not to be estimated from the actual bulk of the earth or any other planet alone, but from the effect of the sphere of repulsion of which that planet is the center; we may then deduce the force of gravitation from a medium of no very enormous elasticity.

We shall later find that a similar combination of simple pressure with a variable repulsion is also observable in the force of cohesion. Supposing two particles of matter—floating in such an elastic medium capable of producing gravitation—approach each other, their mutual attraction would at once be changed from gravitation to cohesion upon the exclusion of the portion of the medium intervening between them. # LECTURE L.

## ON COHESION.

Those properties of matter, which we have recently examined, if they are not absolutely inseparable from its constitution, are, at least, always found attached to such matter as we are able to submit to our experiments. There are, however, many other general properties, to which all matter appears to be liable, although none is perpetually subjected to them, and these are principally, if not entirely, dependent on the force of cohesion.

In order that any two particles of matter may cohere, it is necessary that they be within a very small distance of each other, and the density of any substance, composed of cohesive particles, must probably always be more than half as great as that of water. There are indeed some solids apparently a little lighter than this, but they appear to be extremely porous; and perhaps the solid substances of some of the celestial bodies may also be a little less dense. It frequently happens, that the compression of an elastic fluid alone is sufficient to cause the force of cohesion to take place between its particles; thus, if common steam be exposed, in a closed vessel, to a pressure greater than that of the atmosphere, it will be wholly condensed into water, provided that no elevation of temperature be allowed; and the same has been experimentally shown of many other aeriform fluids, which may be reduced to liquids by pressure; but others of these fluids retain their elasticity, notwithstanding any force which human art can apply to them.

It is probable that as soon as the particles of any elastic fluid are brought within the reach of the force of cohesion, it commences at once in its full extent, so as to cause them to rush together, until it is balanced by that of repulsion, which continually increases as the particles approach nearer to each other; they must then remain, perhaps after some vibrations, in a state of

The author also notes the balance between the attractive force of cohesion and the counteracting force of repulsion between particles.</summary>

<keywords>cohesion, matter, particles, density, elastic fluid, steam, aeriform fluids, repulsion, condensation, physics</keywords>

The distance at which the force of cohesion begins is not the same for all kinds of matter, nor even for the same substance at different temperatures; it is smaller for all kinds of vapors as their temperature rises, with the cohesion itself also being smaller. If the experiments on the density of steam have been correct, it follows that the force of repulsion must increase more rapidly than the distances decrease; for the elasticity of water is nearly ten times as great as what would be inferred from the compression of steam into a substance of equal density. This supposition also agrees with experiments on the mean density of the earth, which is probably not as great as it would be if the force of repulsion increased in the simple ratio of the density. The law of repulsion also appears to be modified to some degree by the effect of heat, which increases its force more considerably at greater distances than at smaller ones. It appears indeed, from the decrease in a spring’s elasticity when heated, that the repulsive force of the particles of bodies at very small distances is even diminished by heat, unless the force is again supposed to decrease much more rapidly than the distance diminishes. For example, the decrease in the elasticity of iron caused by heat is about thirty times as great as the increase in the distance between its particles; so the original repulsive force must probably be somewhat diminished, although less than the cohesive force. At greater distances, however, the force of repulsion is certainly increased; for the elasticity of vapors and gases of all kinds is evidently greater as the temperature rises. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 530.)

The cohesion of two or more particles of matter to each other does not interfere with their power to repel other particles situated in a different direction. For instance, two pieces of glass must be brought together with considerable force, and generally with some friction, before they can begin to cohere; and a small drop of water, falling lightly on the surface of a pond, may remain for some moments without coming into perfect contact with it. The same circumstance is even more observable in slightly warmed spirit of wine <note>an old term for ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note>.

The first and simplest effect of cohesion is to produce liquidity. That all liquids possess some cohesion is very obvious from their tendency to assume a spherical form when they are sufficiently detached from other sub-

Without cohesion, indeed, a liquid would only be a very fine powder, except that the particles of powders do not have the power of moving with perfect freedom against each other, which is what constitutes fluidity. The apparent weakness of the cohesion of liquids is entirely due to this mobility, since their form may be changed to any degree without significantly increasing the distances between their particles; it is only under particular circumstances that the effects of their cohesion can become noticeable.

When a liquid is considered to be unlimited in its extent, the repulsion of its particles, situated in all possible directions with regard to each other, may be assumed in all cases to precisely balance the cohesion derived from the actions of particles situated in a similar way. This must also be the state of the internal parts of every detached portion of a liquid, where they are so far from the surface as to be beyond the minute distance that is the limit of the action of these forces. But the external parts of the drop will not remain in the same kind of equilibrium: they may be considered as a thin coating of a liquid surrounding a substance that resists only in a direction perpendicular to its surface and does not interfere with the mutual actions of the particles of the liquid. Now, since the repulsive force increases as the distance decreases, it must be exerted more powerfully by the nearest particles, while the cohesion is directed equally toward all the particles within a certain distance. Wherever the surface is curved, the combined cohesive force will be directed toward a more remote part of the curve than the repulsive force opposing it, so that each particle will be driven, by the combination of these forces, toward the concave side of the curve, and more so as the curvature is greater. Therefore, the coating of the liquid, constituted in this way, must exert a force on the parts in contact with it that is precisely similar to that of a flexible surface which is stretched everywhere by an equal force. From this simple principle, we may derive all the effects produced by a cohesion of this kind, which, because it is most commonly observed in the ascent of water in capillary tubes, has been called capillary attraction. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 531.)

It may also be shown that if the attractive power of the solid is equal to that of the liquid, or even greater, it will be wetted by the liquid, which will rise until its surface acquires the same direction as that of the solid; and in other cases, the angle of contact will be greater in proportion as the solid is less attractive. These conclusions are obtained by comparing the common surface of the liquid and solid with the surface of a single liquid whose attractive power is equal only to the difference of the respective powers of the substances concerned; and the comparison is equally applicable to the contact of two liquids of different densities.

The magnitude of the superficial cohesion or contractility of a liquid may be expressed, to a certain extent, by a certain weight; thus, every inch of the surface of water is stretched each way by a force equal to the weight of the hundredth part of a cubic inch of water, or to two and a half grains: and for each inch of the surface of mercury, the force is equivalent to 17 grains, which is the weight of $\frac{1}{200}$ of a cubic inch of mercury. Thus, if a solid of any form whose surfaces are vertical, and which is capable of being wetted by either of these fluids, is immersed into a reservoir containing it, the fluid will be elevated around it to such a height that 2$\frac{1}{2}$ or 17 grains, for each inch of the circumference of the solid, will remain above the general level of the reservoir, the surface assuming nearly the same form as a very long and slender elastic rod, fixed horizontally at one end and bearing a large weight at the other. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 534.)

The elevation of the summit of an extended surface of water, in contact with the flat and upright surface of a solid which is wetted by it, is one-seventh of an inch: but when two such surfaces—for instance, two plates of glass—are brought near to each other, the elevation of the water between them must be greater than this, so that each inch of the line of contact may support its proper weight: thus, if the distance were one-fiftieth of an inch,

It is obvious that if the lower part of the tube is either narrowed or widened, the height of the fluid will remain unchanged, while its weight may be varied without limit; for the hydrostatic pressure on the surface is the same, in both these cases, as if the diameter of the tube were uniform throughout its length. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 536.)

The attractive force of glass for mercury is less than half as strong as the mutual attraction between the particles of mercury, and the surface of mercury in a dense glass vessel becomes, therefore, convex and depressed; the angle of contact being about 140°, and the depression one-seventeenth of an inch. Between two plates of glass, the depression of mercury is an inch when their distance is 1/133 of an inch, and in a tube when its diameter is 1/67 of an inch. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 537, 538.)

A liquid may also adhere to a horizontal surface which is gradually raised from it, until the hydrostatic pressure becomes sufficient to overcome the cohesion of its surface parts; the internal part of the fluid being usually raised, not directly by the force of cohesion, but by the pressure of the atmosphere. The solid bears the entire weight of the liquid which is elevated above the surface; and when the surface is perfectly wetted, this weight is equal, at the moment of separation, to the hydrostatic pressure, or rather the suction, corresponding to the height; but in other cases the weight may be somewhat greater than the hydrostatic pressure on the surface of the solid, due to the elevation that surrounds the body, which is not offset by the depression immediately beneath it. If the drop is very small, its shape may be nearly spherical; but when its size becomes significant, its height must always be less than the height at which the liquid would separate from a horizontal surface. It will approach this limit more closely as its attraction to the surface on which it stands becomes weaker. Thus, a wide portion of mercury stands on glass at a height of 2/15 of an inch, and on paper at nearly 1/7 of an inch; and a portion of water will stand on a cabbage leaf, or on a table strewn with the seeds of <term>lycopodium</term>, at nearly the height of one-fifth of an inch. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 541.)

For the operation of a powder like <term>lycopodium</term>, it appears to be only necessary that it should possess a weaker power of attraction than water and should, therefore, be incapable of being easily wetted by it. Each particle of the powder, being then only partially in contact with the water, will project beyond its surface and prevent the water from coming into contact with any of the surrounding bodies, while the surface takes on such a curvature as is sufficient to withstand the pressure of the internal parts. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 542.)

When any kind of dry and light substance is placed on the surface of water, its weight is not enough to bring it within the distance at which <term>cohesion</term> begins, and it floats, surrounded by a slight depression. Any substance of this kind, or any other substance surrounded by a depression—such as a ball of glass or iron floating on mercury—appears to be attracted by another similar substance nearby; for the depression between the two substances is increased, and the pressure of the fluid on that side is consequently reduced, so that they are pushed together by a force that varies inversely as the square of the distance. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 543.)

If two smooth plates of any kind are perfectly wetted by a fluid and brought into contact, they exhibit an appearance of cohesion that is greater as the quantity of fluid is smaller. If we attempt to separate them, the fluid is drawn inwards so as to make its surface concave, and it resists the separation of the plates with a certain force. This force acts with *a hydrostatic advantage* that becomes greater as their distance is smaller, and it thus produces the appearance of a cohesion varying in proportion to the distance. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 544.)

Supposing the two plates are separated at one end and the fluid between them takes the form of a drop, one of the marginal surfaces of the drop, being narrower than the other, will act with a greater advantage, like a tube of smaller diameter, and will tend to draw the drop towards it. The apparent attraction toward the line where the glasses contact will increase in proportion as the square of the distance decreases. This result was experimentally observed almost a century ago, but it has usually been explained on mistaken grounds. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 545.)

The attractive power of water is greater than that of oils; therefore, a small portion of oil thrown on water is caused to spread on it with great rapidity by means of the force of cohesion. It does not appear that any lack of chemical affinity between the substances concerned diminishes their cohesive power; water readily adheres to solid tallow, and essential oils would probably adhere still more readily to ice. There is, however, some difficulty in understanding how these oils can so suddenly come within the limit of the cohesive force of water, while the drops of water themselves sometimes remain for a few seconds beyond it.

The magnitude of the cohesion between fluids and solids, as well as between the particles of fluids themselves, is shown more directly by an experiment on the maintenance of a column of mercury in a barometer tube at a height considerably greater than that at which it usually stands due to atmospheric pressure. If the mercury has been well boiled in the tube, it can be made to remain in contact with the closed end at a height of 70 inches or more; and by agitation alone, it can be made to cohere so strongly that it occupies the entire length of a common barometer tube, which is several inches higher than the height at which atmospheric pressure sustains it. A small siphon may also convey mercury from one vessel to another in the vacuum of an air pump; in both these cases, it is obvious that no force other than cohesion can hold the upper surface of the mercury in contact with the glass, or its internal parts in contact with each other.

The force of cohesion may also be exerted by solid substances on other solids, whether of the same kind or of different kinds. Thus, two masses of lead, once united by pressure and a little friction, require a very significant force to separate them. It can be shown, either by measuring this force or by suspending the lead in the vacuum of an air pump, that atmospheric pressure is not significantly involved in producing this appearance of cohesion, since its strength far exceeds that of the atmospheric pressure. Cohesion of this kind is sometimes practically useful in the arts; small ornaments of laminated silver remain attached to iron or steel, with which they have been made to cohere by the powerful pressure of a blow, so as to form a single mass with it.

Harder substances, such as marble or glass, cohere only weakly, perhaps because their surfaces are never so perfectly adjusted to each other that they touch throughout. The placement of a fluid between them usually increases the apparent attraction of such substances, but this circumstance has already been explained by the effect of the capillary contraction of its surface; and when the substances are completely immersed in a fluid, the cohesion is increased little, if at all.

The immediate cause of solidity, as distinguished from liquidity, is the lateral adhesion of the particles to each other, to which the degree of hardness or solidity is always proportional. This adhesion prevents any change in the relative position of the particles, so that they cannot be moved from their places without experiencing considerable resistance from the force of cohesion, while the particles of liquids may remain equally in contact with their neighboring particles despite their change of form. When a perfect solid is stretched or compressed, the particles—being held in their positions by the force of lateral adhesion—can only move directly toward or away from each other. The resistance is nearly the same as if the same substance, in a fluid state, were enclosed in an unalterable vessel and forcibly compressed or dilated. Thus, experiments show that the resistance of ice to extension or compression differs very little from that of water contained in a vessel; and the same effect may be produced even when the solidity is not the most perfect the substance allows; for the immediate resistance of iron or steel to flexure is the same whether it is harder or softer. It often happens, however, that the magnitude of the lateral adhesion is limited enough to allow for easier extension or compression, yet it may still retain the power to restore the bodies to their original form through its reaction. This force may even be the principal, or perhaps the only, source of a body's elasticity. Thus, when a piece of elastic gum <note>natural rubber</note> is stretched, the average distance between its particles is not significantly increased, for it is said to become more dense, rather than less, during its extension; consequently, the change of form is to be attributed to a displacement of the particles rather than to their separation to a greater

Some other substances also, approaching more nearly to the nature of liquids, may be extended to many times their original length with a resistance continually increasing; in such cases, there can scarcely be any material change of the specific gravity of these substances. Professor Robison has mentioned the juice of bryony as providing a remarkable instance of such viscidity.

It is probable that the immediate cause of the lateral adhesion of solids is a symmetrical arrangement of their constituent parts. It is certain that almost all bodies, in becoming solid, tend to assume the form of crystals, which clearly indicates the existence of such an arrangement; and all the hardest bodies in nature are of a crystalline form. It appears, therefore, consistent both with reason and with experience to suppose that a crystallization, more or less perfect, is the universal cause of solidity. We may imagine that when the particles of matter are arranged without any order, they can offer no strong resistance to a motion in any direction; but when they are regularly placed in certain positions with respect to each other, any change of form must displace them in such a manner as to increase the distance of an entire row at once; and hence they may be enabled to cooperate in resisting such a change. Any inequality of tension in a particular part of a solid is also probably a cause of hardness, insofar as it tends to increase the strength of union of any part of a series of particles which must be displaced by a change of form.

The immediate resistance of a solid to extension or compression is most properly called its elasticity, although this term has sometimes been used to denote a facility of extension or compression arising from the weakness of this resistance. A practical mode of estimating the force of elasticity has already been explained, and according to the simplest statement of the nature of cohesion and repulsion, the weight of the modulus of elasticity is the measure of the actual magnitude of each of these forces. It follows that an additional pressure, equal to that of the modulus, would double the force of cohesion and require the particles to be reduced to half their distance in order for the repulsion to balance it; and in the same manner, an extending force equal to the weight of half the modulus would reduce the force of cohesion to one half and extend the substance to twice its dimensions. There is some reason to suppose that if the mutual repulsion of the particles of solids varies a little more rapidly than their distance, the <term>modulus of elasticity</term> will be a little greater than the true measure of the total cohesive and repulsive force: this difference will not, however, affect the accuracy of our calculations regarding the properties of elastic bodies, which are based on the magnitude of the modulus as already determined.

The stiffness of a solid is measured by its immediate resistance to any force tending to change its form; in this sense, if the force is applied so as to extend or to compress it, or to overcome its lateral adhesion by the effect which we have previously called <term>detrusion</term>, the primitive elasticity and rigidity of the substance, together with its size, will determine its stiffness. But if the force is applied otherwise, so as to produce <term>flexure</term> or <term>torsion</term>, the form of the body must also be taken into the calculation, in the manner which has already been explained in the lecture on <term>passive strength</term>. The stiffness of a body with respect to any longitudinal force is directly proportional to its transverse section, and inversely proportional to its length; for the same force that will compress or extend a rod 100 yards long enough to change its length by an inch, will produce a change of only half an inch in a rod 50 yards long. We have seen that the distance through which a body may be extended or compressed without any permanent alteration of form constitutes its <term>toughness</term>; that its strength, or the ultimate resistance which it provides, depends on the combined magnitude of its toughness and elasticity or stiffness; and that its <term>resilience</term>, or the power of overcoming the energy or impetus of a body in motion, is proportional to the strength and toughness combined.

Softness, or lack of solidity, is generally accompanied by a proportional susceptibility to permanent alteration of form without breaking; sometimes, however, due to a lack of cohesion, a soft body is simultaneously brittle. Soft substances which are capable of significant direct extension are called <term>viscous</term> or <term>tenacious</term>; of these, birdlime, sealing wax, and sufficiently heated glass are some of the most remarkable. Harder substances which have the same property are called <term>ductile</term>, and when the alteration is made by striking and compression, they are termed <term>malleable</term>. Of all substances gold is perhaps the most ductile; the thinness of leaf gold and of the gilding of silver wire has already been mentioned; and it is said that

The ductility or tenacity of a spider's web is of a different kind; it is particularly shown by its capability of being twisted, almost without limit, and of accommodating itself to its new position without any effort to untwist.

With respect to the ultimate agent by which the effects of cohesion are produced—if it is allowable to seek for any other agent than a fundamental property of matter—it has already been observed that appearances extremely similar might be derived from the pressure of a universal medium of great elasticity. We see some effects so nearly resembling them, which are unquestionably produced by the pressure of the atmosphere, that one can scarcely avoid suspecting that there must be some analogy in the causes. Two plates of metal, which cohere enough to support each other in the open air, will often separate in a vacuum; when a boy draws a stone along by a piece of wet leather, the pressure of the atmosphere appears to be materially involved. The well-known experiment of the two exhausted hemispheres of <term>Magdeburg</term> affords a still more striking instance of apparent cohesion derived from atmospheric pressure. If we place between them a thick ring of elastic gum, we may represent the natural equilibrium between the forces of cohesion and of repulsion; for the ring would resist any small additional pressure with the same force as would be required for separating the hemispheres so far as to allow it to expand in an equal degree. At a certain point, the ring would expand no more; the air would be admitted, and the cohesion destroyed, in the same manner as when a solid of any kind is torn asunder. But all suppositions founded on these analogies must be considered as merely conjectural; and our knowledge of everything which relates to the intimate constitution of matter—partly from the intricacy of the subject and partly for want of sufficient experiments—is at present in a state of great uncertainty and imperfection. One of the most powerful agents in changing and modifying the forms of matter is the operation of heat, by which the states of solidity, liquidity, and elastic fluidity are often produced in succession; and the investigation of the nature and effects of heat will constitute the subject of the next two lectures.

## LECTURE LI.

### ON THE SOURCES AND EFFECTS OF HEAT.

IT may seem doubtful to some whether the subject of heat belongs most properly to mechanical or to chemical philosophy. Its influence in chemistry is unquestionable and essential; but its mechanical effects are no less remarkable. It could not, therefore, properly be omitted from either a course of chemical or physical lectures, especially by those who are convinced that what we call heat is, in its essential nature, a mechanical state of matter rather than a specific substance. We shall first investigate the nature of the primary sources of heat, and then the manner of its transmission and its most common effects, whether temporary or permanent. The methods of measuring heat and the most probable opinions regarding its nature will afterward be considered separately.

Heat is an influence capable of affecting our nerves in general with the specific sensation that bears its name; the reduction of this produces the sensation called cold. Any significant increase in heat gives us the idea of positive warmth or hotness, and its reduction triggers the idea of positive cold. Both these ideas are simple, and each of them might be derived from either an increase or a decrease of a positive quality. However, there are many reasons for supposing heat to be the positive quality, and cold the reduction or absence of that quality—although we have no more experience with the total absence of heat than we do with its greatest possible accumulation, which might be called the total absence of cold. In some cases, our organs provide us with very delicate tests of any increase or decrease in heat, but it is more commonly recognized by the expansion in size generally produced in those bodies to which heat is added in an increased quantity, and the contraction of those from which it is removed.

<summary>This lecture introduces the study of heat as both a mechanical and chemical phenomenon, arguing that heat is a mechanical state of matter rather than a substance. It defines heat and cold as relative sensations and identifies expansion and contraction as the primary physical indicators of temperature changes.</summary>
<keywords>heat, cold, mechanical philosophy, chemical philosophy, sensation, expansion, contraction, thermodynamics, temperature measurement</keywords>

--- Page 642 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of heat, moving from the definition of heat and cold to the specific methods by which heat is generated, such as compression, friction, and chemical reactions.</meta>

### LECTURE LI.

The simplest ways of generating heat appear to be the compression of elastic fluids and the collision or friction of solid bodies; although a more common and more powerful source of heat is found in various chemical combinations and decompositions. These are produced by the peculiar <term>elective attractions</term> of different substances for each other, or from the influence of the solar rays, which are probably emitted as a result of the chemical processes that continually take place at the surface of the sun.

The effects of the condensation and rarefaction of elastic fluids are shown by the condenser and the air pump; when an exhaustion is made with rapidity, the thermometer, placed in the receiver of the air pump, usually sinks a degree or two; and when the air is readmitted abruptly into a partial vacuum, the sudden condensation of the rarefied air raises the mercury; and a similar rise in temperature is produced by the operation of the condenser. Much of this heat is soon dissipated, but by observing the speed with which the thermometer rises, Mr. Dalton has estimated that air, compressed to half its volume, has its temperature raised about 50 degrees Fahrenheit; and some of his experiments indicate, when accurately examined, an even greater change. For the present, we may define the meaning of the term degree, on Fahrenheit’s scale, as corresponding to an expansion of a portion of mercury amounting to one ten-thousandth part of its volume; and a degree of Réaumur originally corresponded to an expansion of a weak spirit of wine, amounting to one-thousandth part of its volume. It may be inferred from the velocity of sound—supposing that the excess of its velocity, above the common calculation, is entirely derived from the heat and cold produced by condensation and expansion—that a condensation amounting to 1/180 of the volume of any portion of air will raise its temperature one degree Fahrenheit. When air is very rapidly compressed in the condenser of an air gun, it is sometimes so much heated as actually to set fire to a small portion of tow <note>coarse, broken fiber of flax, hemp, or jute</note>, placed near the end of the barrel.

The production of heat by friction is too well known to require experimental proof; but Count Rumford has taken particular care to determine every circumstance which can be supposed to be involved in the operation of this cause; and the results of his experiments are so striking, that they de-

deserve to be briefly related. He took a cannon that had not yet been bored, which had a projection of two feet beyond its muzzle—a part that is usually cast with the piece in order to ensure the solidity of the metal throughout, due to the pressure caused by its weight. This piece was reduced to the shape of a cylinder and joined to the cannon by a smaller neck, and a large hole was bored into it. The entire cannon was then made to revolve on its axis using horse power, while a blunt steel borer was pressed against the bottom of the hollow cylinder with a force equal to about 10,000 pounds <term>avoirdupois</term>; the contact surface of the borer with the bottom of the cylinder was about two square inches. This apparatus was wrapped in flannel when its temperature was about 60°. In half an hour, after the cylinder had made 960 turns and the horses were stopped, a mercury thermometer was introduced into a hole in the bottom of the cylinder, extending from the side to the axis; it stood at 130°, which Count Rumford considers to be very nearly the average temperature of the cylinder. The dust or metal shavings worn away by the borer weighed only 837 grains, or about 1/950th of the total weight of the cylinder. In another experiment, the cylinder was surrounded by a tight pine box fitted with leather collars to allow it to revolve freely, and the space between the cylinder and the box was filled with 19 pounds of cold water. This water was kept out of the cylinder's bore by oiled leathers fixed on the borer; after two and a half hours, the water was made to boil. From this, Count Rumford calculates that the heat produced in this manner by friction was equal to that of nine wax candles, each three-quarters of an inch in diameter, burning for the same amount of time.

An even more rapid increase in temperature can be obtained where the relative velocity of the bodies is greater, or where they strike each other with violence. Thus, a soft nail can be so heated by three or four blows of a hammer that one may light a match with it; and by continuing the action, it can be made red hot. Two pieces of wood can also be set on fire using a lathe. When a wagon takes fire because its wheels have not been properly greased, the friction is likely increased by the stickiness of the hardened tar, which perhaps becomes more combustible as it dries.

### LECTURE LI.

One of the most remarkable circumstances attending the production of heat by friction is the discovery of Professor Pictet that it is often much more powerfully excited by soft substances than by harder ones. In making some experiments in a vacuum to examine how far the presence of air might be involved in the effects of friction, he accidentally placed some cotton between the bulb of his thermometer and the cup, which was subjected to the friction of various substances as it revolved; he found that the soft filaments of the cotton excited much more heat than any of the other substances used.

The chemical production of heat is of greater practical importance than its mechanical excitation; however, we cannot attempt to determine by what means chemical changes operate in exciting heat. There is certainly no general law of composition or decomposition that can be applied to all such cases: most commonly, heat is produced when oxygen exchanges a gaseous for a solid state, or enters into a new combination and still remains gaseous; but in the case of gunpowder, heat is released while a gas is produced from a solid; and in some other cases, the <term>oxygenous principle</term> is completely uninvolved. It appears on the whole that, however heat may be excited, the <term>corpuscular powers</term> of cohesion and repulsion are always disturbed and called into action, their equilibrium being destroyed and again restored, whether by mechanical or chemical means. A wax candle, 3/4 of an inch in diameter, loses a grain of its weight in 37 seconds and consumes about three grains, or 9 cubic inches, of oxygen gas, producing enough heat to raise the temperature of about 15,000 grains of water by a single degree. According to the experiments of Mr. Lavoisier and Mr. Laplace, the combustion of ten grains of phosphorus requires the consumption of 15 grains of oxygen, the combustion of ten grains of charcoal 26, and of hydrogen gas 56. By the heat produced during the combustion of a pound of phosphorus, 100 pounds of ice may be melted; during that of a pound of charcoal 96 1/2, of hydrogen gas 295 1/2, of wax 133, and of olive oil 149; and during the <term>deflagration</term> of a pound of <term>nitre</term> with about one-sixth part of its weight of charcoal, twelve pounds of ice may be melted.

The manner in which heat, when excited or released by any of these means, passes from one body to another, requires to be very particularly exa-

# ON THE SOURCES AND EFFECTS OF HEAT.

...determined. We shall find that this communication happens in one or both of two ways: by contact or by radiation. We shall also find that it may differ both with respect to the quantity of heat involved and the time the process takes. Whatever heat may be, we may safely conclude that in substances of the same kind—at the same temperature or apparent degree of warmth or coldness—its quantity must be proportional to the mass or weight. For instance, a quart of water from a given cistern contains twice as much heat as a pint; and where this is true of the different parts of any substance, they must remain in equilibrium with respect to heat. 

But if two equal portions of the same substance, containing different quantities of heat, are in contact, they will affect each other in such a manner as to have their temperatures equalized—and they will do so more rapidly as the contact is more perfect. Thus, if two portions of a fluid at different temperatures are mixed together, they will immediately acquire an intermediate temperature. When two solids are in contact, the quantity of heat communicated by the hotter to the colder in a given time is nearly proportional to the difference in their temperatures. From this, it would follow that they could never reach precisely the same temperature in any finite amount of time; but in fact, the difference in temperature is rendered too small to be perceptible within a moderate amount of time. 

The nature of the substances involved also has a significant effect on the speed with which heat is communicated through their internal parts. Metallic bodies generally conduct it most readily, while earthy and vitreous <note>glassy</note> bodies conduct it the least. However, the various metals possess this power in different degrees: silver and copper conduct heat more rapidly than iron, and platinum <note>originally "platina"</note> transmits it only very slowly. Professor Pictet supposes that heat ascends within solid bodies more readily than it descends; but the effect of the air remaining in the imperfect vacuum of the air pump may be sufficient to explain his experiments. The difference in temperature produces an ascending current in the vicinity of the heated body, by which means the cold air continually approaches its lower parts and carries the heat upwards. It has also been found that the rarefaction of air does not at all diminish its power of conducting heat in proportion to the decrease in its density.

Count Rumford's experiments have shown that all fluids are very imperfect conductors of heat through immediate contact, although it is scarcely believable that they can be absolute non-conductors; but heat is usually communicated

### LECTURE LI.

Consequently, a fluid heated on its surface transmits heat very slowly downwards, since the parts that are first heated, being made specifically lighter, retain their position above the colder and heavier parts. Conversely, any cause of heat applied at the bottom of a vessel very soon reduces all its contents to a uniform temperature. It also appears, from some recent experiments, that the immediate transmission of heat within the internal parts of solids is much slower than has commonly been supposed; indeed, it has been found almost impossible to keep a thermometer at the center of a large, solid globe of metal at the same temperature as that of its outer surfaces.

Besides the communication of heat by contact, it is usually, if not always, emitted from the surfaces of bodies in the form of **radiant heat**. This is thrown off in all directions, wherever it meets no obstacle from a substance impenetrable to it, and is propagated in nearly the same manner as light—and probably with the same velocity—without producing any permanent effect on the temperature of the medium transmitting it. Thus, a thermometer suspended by a fine thread under the receiver of an air pump, or in the *Torricellian vacuum* <note>A vacuum created by filling a tube with mercury and inverting it into a basin, named after Evangelista Torricelli.</note>, will continue to change its temperature along with that of the surrounding bodies; in this case, the entirety of the heat must be communicated by radiation. Mr. Leslie has discovered that the quantity of heat thus emitted depends not only on the temperature, but also on the nature of the surface involved; a polished surface of tin emits only $\frac{12}{100}$, or less than one-eighth as much, as the same surface would if it were blackened. A surface of tin scraped with a file in one direction has its powers of radiation more than doubled; but by crossing the scratches, they are reduced nearly to their original state. A coating of isinglass <note>A form of gelatin obtained from fish</note>, resin, or writing paper, or a glossy surface of any kind, produces an effect nearly approaching that of black paint. This radiation from a heated surface, like that of light, takes place in almost equal degrees in every direction; and its magnitude is nearly independent of the nature of the fluid in contact with the surface, provided however that it is an elastic fluid <note>A gas, such as air</note>; for water does not seem to transmit every kind of radiant heat freely. It appears that the radiant heat emitted by a surface of glass, or of black paint, is about one-third greater than that which is at the same time carried off by the atmospheric air; but that the radiation from a metallic sur—

Solar heat radiates freely through air, glass, water, ice, and many other transparent media without producing any noticeable effect on their temperatures; even when it is concentrated by the effect of a burning mirror, it scarcely affects the air through which it passes, and other transparent media only slightly. But the heat of a fire warms a piece of common glass very rapidly, and its further progress is almost entirely blocked by the glass, although a certain portion probably still continues to accompany the light in all cases. Hence, a glass screen is sometimes practically convenient for allowing us to see a fire while protecting us at the same time from its excessive heat. Mr. Lambert showed that <term>culinary heat</term> was much more strongly reflected by metal mirrors than by glass ones, although little difference was observable in the quantity of light; he very justly attributed this difference to the glass intercepting a part of the heat, acting like an opaque substance toward it, even though it transmitted the light freely. Opaque substances in general appear to be wholly impervious to <term>radiating heat</term> of all kinds; but Dr. Herschel has found that dark red glass, which transmits only a very small portion of light, allows some kinds of <term>radiant heat</term> to pass through it with very little interruption.

In other respects, <term>radiating heat</term> is subject, in all cases, to the optical laws which govern the <term>reflection</term> and <term>refraction</term> of light. Dr. Hoffmann appears to have been the first to collect the invisible heat of a stove into a focus by the reflection of one or more concave mirrors. Buffon, Saussure, Pictet, and Mr. King afterwards performed similar experiments on the heat from a plate of iron and a vessel of boiling water. Mr. Pictet, as well as Hoffmann, employed two mirrors facing each other; by means of this arrangement, the experiment may be performed when the thermometer is placed at a considerable distance from the heated body.

<page-num>638</page-num>

# LECTURE LI.

Heat may flow in different directions through the same medium without being interrupted. There seems to be no more reason for a hot body to stop emitting heat while it is receiving heat from another body than there is for a luminous body to stop giving off light when another body shines on it. This continual interchange of heat, which in common cases constitutes a kind of equilibrium of motion, appears to have been first suggested by Mr. Prévost as an explanation for an experiment on the "reflection of cold." This experiment was revived by Mr. Pictet but was originally conducted some centuries earlier by Plempius and by the Academicians del Cimento. 

A thermometer, for example, must be assumed to maintain its temperature by continuously receiving radiant heat from surrounding bodies, which replaces the heat it constantly radiates in all directions toward those bodies. Suppose a thermometer is placed near the focus of a metallic <term>speculum</term> (mirror) that is nearly hemispherical. About half of the heat the thermometer would otherwise have received from its surroundings must be blocked by the mirror. Because the mirror is metallic, it emits very little radiant heat itself; however, it reflects an equal amount of heat from objects on the opposite side, so the temperature of the thermometer remains unchanged. 

But all the heat that reaches the thermometer from the mirror must have passed through the <term>conjugate</term> (or corresponding) focus. If a body at the same temperature is placed in that focus, the radiation will remain the same. However, if a substance that is absolutely cold were placed there, all the heat previously reflected by the mirror would be blocked—that is, almost half of the heat received by the thermometer from its surroundings. If a piece of ice is placed in the conjugate focus, a sensitive thermometer will instantly show a drop in temperature, as if the cold were being reflected in the same manner as heat or light.

Dr. Herschel's experiments have shown that radiant heat consists of various parts that are differently <term>refrangible</term> (capable of being refracted), and that, in general, invisible heat is less refrangible than light. This discovery must be recognized as one of the greatest made since the time of Newton, even though the theories of some speculative philosophers might have suggested it a few years earlier. Dr. Herschel was occupied with determining the properties of various kinds of colored glass to see which were best suited for allowing the eye to view the sun through a telescope. Sir Henry Englefield has repeated these experiments with many additional precautions, and Mr. Davy witnessed their perfect accuracy. The excess of heat beyond the spectrum was even significant enough to be determined by the sense of warmth felt by directing it onto the hand. Compared with a thermometer, the skin appears to have a sensitivity better adapted to the perception of radiant heat than to that of heat transferred by contact. This is perhaps because a much smaller quantity of heat is sufficient to raise the temperature of the thin <term>cuticle</term> (outer skin layer) very considerably, compared to what would be required to affect any thermometer to the same degree.

It was first observed in Germany by Ritter, and soon afterward in England by Dr. Wollaston, that <term>muriate of silver</term> (silver chloride) is blackened by invisible rays which extend beyond the prismatic spectrum on the violet side. It is therefore probable that these "black" or invisible rays—along with the violet, blue, green, perhaps the yellow, and the red rays of light, and the rays of invisible heat—constitute seven different degrees of the same scale. These are distinguished from each other into this limited number not by natural divisions, but by their effects on our senses; and we may also conclude that there is some similar relationship between heated and luminous bodies of different kinds.

The effects of heat, originating and communicated in this way, may be divided into those which are only temporary and those which are permanent. The permanent effects are principally confined to solids, but the temporary effects differ regarding substances in different states of <term>aggregation</term> (matter), and they also frequently involve a change from one of these states to another. The effect of heat on an <term>elastic fluid</term> (gas) is the simplest of all these, being merely an expansion of about one five-hundredth of its volume for each degree Fahrenheit that the temperature is raised; or an equivalent increase—

This expansion is very nearly the same for all gases and vapors, amounting to 1/500 for each degree at the common temperature of 56° Fahrenheit; but at higher temperatures, it is less than 1/500 of the bulk of the gas, and at lower temperatures somewhat more, being nearly the same in quantity for the same portion of the fluid at all temperatures.

When an <term>elastic fluid</term> <note>a gas or vapor</note> is contracted by cold within certain limits—determined by the degree of pressure to which it is exposed, as well as by the nature of the fluid—its particles become subject to the force of cohesion; they rush even closer together and form a liquid. Thus, when steam, under common atmospheric pressure, is cooled below the temperature of boiling water, it is instantly condensed and becomes water; but with a pressure of two atmospheres, it would be condensed at a temperature 36° higher; and with the pressure of only half our atmosphere, it might be cooled 33° lower than the common temperature of boiling water without condensation. Similar effects take place in vapors of other kinds at higher or lower temperatures, as a double pressure produces, in all cases, an equal disposition toward condensation when accompanied by a decrease in temperature of between 20 and 40 degrees—most commonly of about 35° Fahrenheit. Thus, the vapor of spirit of wine <note>ethanol</note> is usually condensed at 175° Fahrenheit; but with double the pressure, it is condensed at a temperature 39° higher; and with the pressure of half an atmosphere, at a temperature 35° lower. The vapor of ether, which is commonly condensed at 102°, requires a temperature 38° higher with a double pressure, or just as much lower with half the usual pressure. If the temperature is below the freezing point of the liquid and the pressure is sufficiently reduced, the vapor may still retain its elasticity, but a further reduction of temperature or increase of pressure will convert it immediately into a solid.

The expansion of liquids by the effect of heat is much less uniform and regular than that of <term>elastic fluids</term>, since it varies considerably, not only in different liquids, but also in the same liquid at different temperatures. It is generally greater as the temperature becomes more elevated, and is sometimes almost in proportion to how much the temperature exceeds a certain point at which expansion begins. This variation appears to be the least significant in mercury, although even this fluid expands a little more rapidly as it becomes more heated; but the expansion is always very nearly one ten-thousandth for each

When the temperature of a liquid is elevated enough to become equal to that of its vapor in a state capable of sustaining atmospheric pressure, or any other pressure which may be substituted for it, a certain portion of the liquid is converted into vapor; and the heat being generally applied at the bottom of the vessel, the vapor rises up in bubbles, and the effect is called boiling. The entire liquid is not converted at once into vapor, because a certain quantity of heat appears to be consumed by the change, and a constant supply of heat is necessary in order for the operation to continue.

It is not, however, only at the boiling point that a fluid begins to be converted into vapor: the pressure of the atmosphere is not sufficient to completely prevent the detachment of a certain quantity of vapor from its surface at a temperature which is incapable of supporting it separately in the form of steam in the open air, and it may be thus suspended when mixed either with common air or with any other elastic fluid <note>gas</note> at the ordinary temperature of the atmosphere. There is perhaps no liquid absolutely free from a disposition to evaporate: even mercury rises in the vacuum of the barometer and lines the cavity with small globules; and it is said that the effect of light is favorable to this slow evaporation. At whatever temperature evaporation takes place, it is always accompanied by the production of cold; hence it is usual in warm climates to employ various methods of promoting evaporation in order to lower the temperature of the air, to cool liquids for drinking, or even to procure ice for domestic uses.

It appears that all aqueous <note>water-based</note> fluids contract by cold until we arrive at a certain point, which is generally about 7 or 8 degrees higher than their freezing point: they then expand again almost in an equal degree as they are still further cooled; and provided that they are free from agitation, they may remain liquid at a temperature considerably below the point at which they usually freeze and at which their ice always melts. Water may be cooled in this manner to about 10° Fahrenheit, and if it is then agitated, or especially if a small particle of ice or snow is thrown into it, a certain part of it will instantly freeze, and its temperature will be raised at once to 32°, in consequence of the heat which is always produced or released during the act of freezing. In most cases, although not in all, the solid occupies more space than the fluid; thus, it is probable that ice, when perfectly free from air bubbles, is at least one-sixteenth lighter than water at the same temperature. A saturated solution of Glauber's salts <note>sodium sulfate</note>, or sulfate of soda, in hot water, may be cooled slowly to the temperature of the atmosphere when the pressure of the air is excluded, and may be made to crystallize by admitting air suddenly, the liquor becoming at the same time warm in consequence of the heat which is released; and there is no doubt but that the freezing of water, and perhaps of all other substances, is a crystallization of the same kind.

The melting of solids, and their conversion into fluids by the action of heat, is subject to fewer irregularities than any of its other effects; the change depends only on the temperature and is not accelerated or delayed by any accidental circumstances. When the temperature is too low, or the pressure too small, for the substance to exist in a liquid form, it may still be converted into vapor, either mixed with air or in a separate state. The effects of the expansion of bodies by heat, and of their contraction by cold, are observed in the frequent accidents which happen to glass and to porcelain from a sudden change of temperature. Glass conducts heat so slowly that one side of a vessel may become much heated, and consequently expanded, while the other remains much colder. If the vessel cannot readily adapt its form to this change of proportions, it will most commonly crack, as the colder parts divide because they are being stretched too much by the adjoining hotter parts. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the thermal properties of materials. While the previous page addressed the expansion of various solids and the conversion of matter between states, this page focuses on the internal stresses created during the cooling of glass and metals, explaining the necessity of annealing and tempering.</meta>

<meta>Considerable show-through/ghosting from the reverse side of the page is visible in the background.</meta>

the less liable it is to crack from any sudden expansion; and if it is very thick, however simple its form may be, it will still crack; for no flexing that it can undergo can be sufficient for the equilibrium of the external parts without being too great for the parts near the middle.

When molten glass is very suddenly cooled, its external parts become solid first and determine the size of the whole piece, while it still remains fluid inside. The internal part, as it cools, tends to contract still further, but its contraction is prevented by the resistance of the external parts, which form an arch or vault around it, so that the whole is left in a state of stress; and as soon as the equilibrium is disturbed in any one part, the entire structure is destroyed. Hence it becomes necessary to anneal all glass by placing it in an oven where it is left to cool slowly; for, without this precaution, a very slight cause would destroy it. The Bologna jars, sometimes called proofs, are small, thick vessels made for the purpose of demonstrating this effect; they are usually destroyed by the impact of a small, sharp object—for instance, a single grain of sand dropped into them. A small object often appears to be more effective than a larger one, perhaps because the larger one is more likely to strike the glass with a blunt part of its surface. In the same manner, glass drops—sometimes called Prince Rupert's drops—which are formed by allowing a portion of molten green glass to fall into water, remain in equilibrium while they are whole. But when the small projecting tail is broken off, the entire piece rushes together with great force and, rebounding by its elasticity, creates the effect of an explosion. The ends of these drops can sometimes, but not always, be gradually ground off without destroying them, so the shock produced by breaking the drop seems to be involved in the destruction of the equilibrium.

The tempering of metals appears to have a significant analogy to the annealing of glass; when they are made red hot and suddenly cooled, they acquire a great degree of hardness, which makes them suitable for some purposes, while the brittleness that accompanies it would be inconvenient for others. By heating them again to a more moderate temperature and allowing them to cool more gradually, they are rendered softer and more flexible—and even more so as the heat applied in this way is increased.

However, in the current state of our knowledge, it is safer to be content with tracing the analogy between these effects in different kinds of substances and under various circumstances, without attempting to completely understand the immediate operation of the forces involved.

## LECTURE LII.

### ON THE MEASURES AND THE NATURE OF HEAT.

The principal details concerning the origin, progress, and effects of heat having been noted in the last lecture, we now proceed to examine the most common ways of measuring its degrees and quantity, and to inquire into the most probable opinions regarding its inner nature and immediate operation.

The expansion of solids is measured by a <term>pyrometer</term>, which is designed to make the smallest change in dimensions perceptible either by mechanical or optical means. The first of these methods was adopted by those who first investigated these effects; a bar of metal was placed in a vessel of water or oil, which was heated by lamps, while the ends of the bar were in contact with a fixed point on one side and a series of levers on the other. These levers multiplied the expansions to make them easily observable by using the end of the last lever as an index. But it is obvious that the expansion of the fixed part of the instrument, and the irregular changes in the temperature of the levers themselves, must significantly interfere with the accuracy of such an instrument. A much more accurate method of determination is to use two microscopes fixed to an apparatus that is kept at a constant temperature by means of ice, and to observe the change of position of either end of the heated bar with a <term>micrometer</term>.

For such purposes, the degrees of heat may be determined by the natural measurements of the freezing and boiling points of certain liquids, and of water in particular; however, for subdividing the intervals between these points, other means must be used. The most natural way of determining the intermediate degrees of heat, which must be considered the standard for the

If we mix together equal quantities of the same liquid at two different temperatures, they will obviously reach an intermediate temperature, which is the natural mean between the separate temperatures—provided that no heat is lost or gained during the process, and provided that no irregularity is produced by the liquid approaching a state of congelation <note>freezing</note>, the existence of which might be detected by comparing experiments on various liquids at the same temperatures. By repeating the operation, we may subdivide the intervals as often as we please, or we may mix the liquids in any other proportion to obtain any other point of the scale at once, which may afterwards be identified by a thermometer of any description.

There is also another method of comparing the divisions of a thermometer with those of the natural scale, but it is not wholly free from objections; the instrument being placed in a cone of the sun's rays, made to converge by means of a lens or mirror, the quantity of heat falling on it must be nearly in the inverse proportion of the square of its distance from the focus; and the elevation of a common thermometer appears to be nearly proportional to the heat that is thrown on it in this manner.

The expansion of solids probably comes the closest to the steps of the natural scale, although even in this there seems to be some inequality; but the expansion of mercury is scarcely less regular, and a portion of mercury enclosed in a glass bulb, having a fine tube connected with it, forms a thermometer that is the most convenient, and most probably the most accurate, of any for common use. Its degrees correspond very nearly with those of the natural scale, although, according to the most accurate experiments, they appear to indicate a temperature 2 or 3 degrees too low toward the middle of the common Fahrenheit scale. There is an inequality of the same kind, but still greater, in the degrees of the spirit thermometer; and this instrument also has the disadvantage of being liable to burst in a heat below that of boiling water. However, it is well calculated for the measurement of very low temperatures, since pure alcohol has never yet been frozen, while mercury has been reduced to a solid by the cold of Siberia and of Hudson's Bay; but both mercury and linseed oil support a heat of between 500 and 600° without ebullition <note>boiling</note>. Mr. Wedgwood's thermometer derives its properties from the contraction of a small brick of prepared clay, which contracts more as the heat to which it is exposed increases. It is hardly believable that the operation of any kind of furnace can produce a heat of so many thousand degrees on a natural scale, as Mr. Wedgwood's experiments led him to suppose, nor is this assumption consistent with the observations of other scientists.

Mercury thermometers are generally hermetically sealed, with the tube being perfectly closed at the end to exclude dust and prevent the evaporation of the mercury. When a standard thermometer is to be calibrated, its freezing point is easily fixed by immersing it completely in melting snow or crushed ice. However, some further precautions are required for the boiling point. The easiest method seems to be immersing its bulb in an open vessel of boiling water, covering it with several folds of cloth, and pouring hot water over it continually; for if it were immersed to a significant depth, the pressure would raise the temperature of the boiling point, and if it were not covered, the mercury in the tube would be too cold. Attention must also be paid to the state of the barometer. It must either stand at 30 inches, or the position of the boiling point must be raised when the barometer is lower than 30, and lowered when it is higher; a difference of nine-tenths of an inch in either direction requires an adjustment equal to <gloss>1/100</gloss> <note>Small vertical fraction in original text.</note> of the interval between freezing and boiling. When making these subdivisions, care must be taken to examine the uniformity of the tube's bore throughout by observing the length occupied by a detached portion of mercury, and to allow for any irregularities that may have been detected. The expansion, which is observed in a mercurial thermometer, is in reality only the difference between the expansions of mercury and of glass; however, this circumstance produces no difference in the accuracy of the results. The separate effects of the expansion of glass are sometimes perceptible; for example, when a thermometer is plunged suddenly into hot water, the glass, being heated first, expands more rapidly than the mercury, and the thermometer falls for a moment. This circumstance would perhaps be even more observable in a thermometer filled with alcohol or water; for an equal volume of these liquids would take much longer to acquire the temperature of the surrounding medium than a mercurial thermometer would.

The expansion of elastic fluids provides, in some cases, a test of heat that is very convenient due to its great sensitivity, and because a very small quantity of heat is sufficient to raise their temperature considerably. The thermometer first invented by *Drebel* was an air thermometer; but instruments of this kind, when they are subject to the variations of atmospheric pressure as well as to those of its temperature, are properly called manometers. To enable us to employ them as thermometers, they require a comparison with a barometer; while, on the other hand, they may be used as barometers if the temperature is otherwise determined. They are, however, very useful even without this comparison in delicate experiments of short duration, since changes in the barometer are seldom very rapid; and they may also be completely freed from the effects of atmospheric pressure in various ways. *Bernoulli’s* method consists of closing the bulb of a common barometer so as to leave the column of mercury in equilibrium with the air contained in the bulb at its current temperature. This is capable of indicating—by the changes in its height and pressure—any subsequent changes in the temperature of the air, which must affect both its volume and its elasticity. *Mr. Leslie’s photometer*, or *differential thermometer*, has some advantages over this instrument, but it can only be employed where the changes of temperature can be confined to only a part of the instrument. The elasticity of the air contained in the bulb is here counteracted not by the pressure of a column of mercury, but by the elasticity of another portion of air

The degree of heat, as determined by a thermometer, is only to be considered as a relation to the surrounding bodies, by virtue of which a body maintains the equilibrium of temperature when it is in the vicinity of bodies equally heated. Thus, if a thermometer stands at 60°, both in a vessel of water and in another of mercury, we may infer that the water and the mercury may be mixed without any change in their temperature; but the absolute quantity of heat contained in equal weights, or in equal volumes, of any two bodies at the same temperature, is by no means the same. Thus, in order to raise the temperature of a pound of water from 50° to 60°, we need only to add to it another pound of water at 70°, which, while it loses 10° of its own heat, will communicate 10° to the first pound; but the temperature of a pound of mercury at 50° may be raised 10° by means of the heat imparted to it by mixing with it one-thirtieth part of a pound of water at the same temperature of 70°. Hence we derive the idea of the capacities of different bodies for heat, which was first suggested by Dr. Irvine, the capacity of mercury being only about one-thirtieth part as great as that of water. And by similar experiments it has been established that the capacity of iron is one-eighth of that of water, the capacity of silver one-twelfth, and that of lead one-twenty-fourth. But for equal volumes of these different substances, the disproportion is not quite so great; thus, copper contains nearly the same quantity of heat in a given volume as water; iron, brass, and gold contain a little less, silver 5/9 as much, but lead and glass each contain about one-half only.

It is obvious that if the capacity of a body for heat, in this sense of the word, were suddenly changed, it would immediately become hotter or colder, according to the nature of the change—a decrease in the capacity producing heat, and an increase producing cold. Such a change of capacity is often a convenient mode of representation for some of the sources of heat and cold. Thus, when heat is produced by the condensation of a vapor, or by the freezing of a liquid, we may imagine that the capacity of the substance is diminished, and that it overflows, as a vessel would do if its dimensions were contracted. Experiments show, in some such cases, that the capacity of the same substance is actually greater in a liquid state than in a solid state, and greater in a state of vapor than in either; and both **Dr. Irvine** and **Dr. Crawford** have attempted to deduce, from a comparison of the proportional capacities of water and ice with the quantity of heat released during freezing, a measure of the total heat contained in these substances, and an estimation of where the absolute lack of heat, or the <term>natural zero</term>, should be located on the thermometer scale. Thus, when a pound of ice at 32° is mixed with a pound of water at 172° Fahrenheit, the entire excess of 140° is absorbed in the conversion of the ice into water, and the mixture is reduced to the temperature of 32°; and, on the other hand, when a pound of ice freezes, a certain quantity of heat is released which is probably capable of raising the temperature of a pound of water by 140°, or that of 140 pounds by a single degree. **Dr. Crawford** found, by means of other experiments, that a quantity of heat capable of raising the temperature of water by 9° would raise that of ice by as much as 10°; hence he inferred that the capacity of ice was 9/10 as great as that of water, and that if this capacity, instead of being reduced to 9/10, had been entirely destroyed, the quantity of heat released would have been 10 times as great, or about 1400°. This has, therefore, been considered as the total quantity of heat contained in a pound of water at 32°, and the beginning of the natural scale has been placed about 1368° below the zero point of Fahrenheit. **Dr. Irvine** makes the capacity of ice even less significant and places the natural zero about 900 degrees below that of Fahrenheit.

If direct experiments on the quantities of heat required to produce certain increases in temperature in different states of the same substance—when compared in this way with the release or absorption of heat that occurs while those changes are performed—agreed with similar experiments made on different substances, there would be no objection to this way of representing it. But if it should appear that such comparisons frequently present us with contradictory results, we could no longer consider the theory of heat capacities sufficient to explain these phenomena. Regarding the simple changes involving freezing and melting, condensation and evaporation, and compression and expansion, there appears to be at present no evidence that this theory is insufficient; however, it has perhaps not yet been shown that the heat absorbed in any one change is always precisely equal to the heat that is released.

If, however, we attempt to derive the heat produced by friction and by combustion from changes in the capacities of bodies estimated this way, we shall find that comparing even a few facts is enough to demonstrate the flaws in such a theory. **Count Rumford** found no noticeable difference between the capacities of solid iron and its chips; but if we even suppose, for the sake of the argument, that the pressure and friction of the drill had reduced the capacity of the iron by one-twelfth, making it no greater than that of copper, we would then find that one-twelfth of the absolute heat of the chips ground off this way must have amounted to over 60,000 degrees **Fahrenheit**. Consequently, the <term>natural zero</term> would have to be placed over 700,000 degrees below the freezing point, instead of only 1,400 or 1,500. It is, therefore, impossible to suppose that any change in capacities can account for the production of heat by friction. Nor is it any easier to apply this theory correctly to the phenomena of combustion. A pound of <term>nitre</term> <note>potassium nitrate or saltpeter</note> contains about half its weight of dry acid, and the capacity of the acid, when diluted, is little more than half as great as that of water. The acid of a pound of nitre must, therefore, contain less heat than a quarter pound of water. But **Lavoisier** and **Laplace** have found that the <term>deflagration</term> <note>intense, rapid combustion</note> of a pound of nitre produces enough heat to melt twelve pounds of ice; consequently, the heat released by the decomposition of a pound of dry nitrous acid must be enough to melt 24 pounds of ice. Even assuming the gases released during the combustion absorb no more heat than the charcoal contained—which is highly improbable for several reasons—it follows that a pound of water ought to contain at least as much heat as would be enough to melt 48 pounds of ice, which is about 6,720 degrees Fahrenheit.

In short, the further we pursue such calculations, the more we shall be convinced of the impossibility of applying them to these phenomena. substance, without being included in the quantity required for maintaining its actual temperature. But even this hypothesis is wholly inapplicable to the release of heat by friction, where all the qualities of the substances concerned remain precisely the same after the operation as they were before it. If any further argument were required to disprove the opinion that the heat generated by friction is derived from a change of capacity, it could be obtained from Mr. Davy’s experiment on the mutual friction of two pieces of ice, which converted them into water in a room at the freezing point temperature. For in this case, it is undeniable that the capacity of the water must have been increased during the operation; therefore, the heat produced could not have been caused by the decrease of the capacity of the ice.

This discussion naturally leads us to an examination of the various theories which have been formed respecting the internal nature of heat; a subject upon which popular opinion seems to have been lately led away by very superficial considerations. The ease with which the mind imagines the existence of an independent substance, subject to no significant variations except those of its quantity and distribution—especially when an appropriate name and a place in the order of the simplest elements has been bestowed on it—appears to have caused the most eminent chemical philosophers to overlook some insurmountable difficulties attending the hypothesis of caloric. *Caloric* has been considered a peculiar elastic or ethereal fluid, pervading the substance or the pores of all bodies in different quantities, according to their different capacities for heat and according to their actual temperatures. It is seen as being transferred from one body to another upon any change of capacity, or upon any other disturbance of the equilibrium of temperature. It has also been commonly supposed to be the general principle or cause of repulsion; and in its passage from one body to another by radiation, it has been imagined by some to flow in a continuous stream, and by others in the form of separate particles moving with inconceivable velocity at great distances from each other.
