If the heat is neither received from the surrounding bodies—which it cannot be without a drop in their temperature—nor derived from the quantity already accumulated in the bodies themselves—which it could not be, even if their capacities were reduced to any imaginable extent—there is no alternative but to admit that heat must be actually generated by friction. And if it is generated out of nothing, it cannot be matter, nor even an immaterial or semi-material substance. The related parts of the theory also have their separate difficulties: for example, if heat were the general principle of repulsion, its increase could not diminish the elasticity of solids and of fluids; if it consisted of a continuous fluid, it could not radiate freely through the same space in different directions; and if its repulsive particles followed each other at a distance, they would still approach near enough to each other, in the focus of a burning glass, to have their motions deflected from a straight-line direction.

If heat is not a substance, it must be a quality; and this quality can only be motion. It was Newton’s opinion that heat consists in a tiny vibratory motion of the particles of bodies, and that this motion is communicated through a vacuum by the waves of an elastic medium, which is also involved in the phenomena of light. If the arguments which have been lately advanced in favor of the undulatory nature of light are considered valid, there will be still stronger reasons for admitting this doctrine regarding heat. It will only be necessary to suppose the vibrations and waves that principally constitute it to be larger and stronger than those of light. At the same time, the smaller vibrations of light, and even the blackening rays <note>Early scientific term for ultraviolet rays, known for their chemical effects such as darkening silver salts.</note>—derived from even more tiny vibrations—may, perhaps, when sufficiently condensed, work together in producing the effects of heat. These effects, beginning from the blackening rays, which are invisible, are a little more perceptible in the violet, which still possesses only a faint power of illumination; the yellow-green afford the most light; the red give less light but much more heat, while the still larger and less frequent vibrations, which have no effect on the sense of sight, may be supposed to give rise to the least refrangible rays and to constitute invisible heat.

The effects of heat on the cohesive and repulsive powers of bodies have sometimes been attributed to the centrifugal forces and mutual collisions of the revolving and vibrating particles; and the increase of the elasticity of <term>aeriform</term> fluids has been very minutely compared with the force that would be derived from an acceleration of these internal motions. In solids and in liquids, however, this increase of elasticity is not observable, and the immediate effect of heat diminishes not only the force of cohesion, but also in some degree that of repulsion; so that these vibrations, if they exist, must derive their effect on the <term>corpuscular</term> forces from the alterations they produce in the positions of the particles, with respect to the causes of these forces.

The different chemical effects of heat and light are far from providing any objection to this system; it is extremely easy to imagine the attraction between two or three bodies being modified by the agitations into which their particles are thrown. If certain undulations are capable of affecting only one of the three bodies, its cohesion with both the others may be weakened, and hence their mutual attraction may be comparatively increased; and from various combinations of such differences in the operation of different kinds of heat and light, a great diversity of effects of a similar kind may be derived.

# LECTURE LII.

The air, or any other medium that transmits sound, conveys its undulations to distant parts by means of its elasticity. And we shall find that the principal phenomena of heat may actually be illustrated by a comparison with those of sound. The excitation of heat and sound are not only similar, but often identical, as seen in the processes of friction and percussion. They are both communicated sometimes by contact and sometimes by radiation; for besides the common radiation of sound through the air, its effects are communicated by contact when the end of a tuning fork is placed on a table, or on the sounding board of an instrument, which receives an impression from the fork that is afterwards propagated as a distinct sound.

The effect of radiant heat in raising the temperature of a body upon which it falls resembles the sympathetic vibration of a string when the sound of another string in unison with it is transmitted to it through the air. The water that is splashed about by the vibrating ends of a tuning fork dipped into it may represent the way in which particles at the surface of a liquid are thrown beyond the reach of the force of cohesion and converted into vapor. The release of heat resulting from condensation may be compared to the increase of sound produced by lightly touching a long string that is slowly vibrating, or revolving in such a way that it emits little or no audible sound. Meanwhile, the reduction of heat by expansion, and the increase of a substance’s capacity for heat, may be attributed to the greater space afforded to each particle, allowing it to be equally agitated with a less perceptible effect on the neighboring particles.

In some cases, indeed, heat and sound not only resemble each other in their operations but produce precisely the same effects. For example, an artificial magnet, whose force is quickly destroyed by heat, is affected more slowly in a similar way when made to ring for a considerable amount of time. Furthermore, an electrical jar <note>Specifically a Leyden jar, an early device for storing static electricity.</note> may be discharged either by heating it or by causing it to sound through the friction of a finger.

All these analogies are certainly favorable to the opinion that heat is vibratory in nature, an idea that has been sufficiently sanctioned by the authority of the greatest philosophers of the past and the most sensible thinkers of the present. Those, however, who look up with unqualified reverence to the dogmas of the modern schools of chemistry will probably long retain a

<summary>This page draws extensive parallels between the behavior of sound and heat to argue that heat is a form of vibration rather than a material substance. It explains phenomena like radiation, evaporation, and magnetic loss as mechanical effects comparable to acoustic resonance and vibration.</summary>

## LECTURE LIII.

### ON ELECTRICITY IN EQUILIBRIUM.

The phenomena of electricity are as amusing and popular in their external form as they are intricate and complex in their internal nature. In examining these phenomena, a philosophical observer will not be content with such exhibitions as dazzle the eye for a moment without leaving any impression that can be instructive to the mind; rather, he will be anxious to trace the connection of the facts with their general causes, and to compare them with the theories which have been proposed concerning them. Although the doctrine of electricity is in many respects still in its infancy, we shall find that some hypotheses may be assumed which are capable of explaining the principal circumstances in a simple and satisfactory manner, and which are extremely useful in connecting a multitude of detached facts into an intelligible system. These hypotheses, founded on the discoveries of Franklin, have been gradually formed into a theory by the investigations of Aepinus and Mr. Cavendish, combined with the experiments and inferences of Lord Stanhope, Coulomb, and Robison.

We shall first consider the fundamental hypotheses on which this system depends, and secondly the conditions of equilibrium of the substances concerned in it; determining the mode of distribution of the electric fluid, and the forces or pressures derived from its action when at rest. All of these will be found to be deduced from the theory precisely as they are experimentally observable. The motions of the electric fluid will next be noticed, as far as we can form any general conclusions respecting them; and the manner in which the equilibrium of electricity is disturbed, or the excitation of electricity, will also be considered; and, in the last place, it will be necessary to take a view of the mechanism or the

The author plans to discuss the distribution of the electric fluid at rest, its forces, and the nature of electrical excitation.</summary>

<keywords>electricity, equilibrium, electric fluid, Franklin, Aepinus, Cavendish, Stanhope, Coulomb, Robison, electrostatics</keywords>

<page-num>659</page-num>
<header>ON ELECTRICITY IN EQUILIBRIUM.</header>

practical part of electricity, and to examine the natural and artificial apparatus concerned in electrical phenomena, as well as in those effects, which have been called galvanic.

It is assumed that a unique ethereal fluid permeates the pores, if not the actual substance, of the earth and of all other material bodies, passing through them with more or less ease, according to their different powers of conducting it: that the particles of this fluid repel each other, and are attracted by the particles of ordinary matter; that the particles of ordinary matter also repel each other; and that these attractions and repulsions are equal among themselves, and vary inversely as the squares of the distances of the particles.

The effects of this fluid are distinguished from those of all other substances by an attractive or repulsive quality, which it appears to impart to different bodies. This quality differs in general from other attractions and repulsions by its immediate decrease or cessation when the bodies, acting on each other, come into contact, or when they are touched by other bodies. The name electricity is derived from electrum, amber; for it was observed long ago that amber, when rubbed, continues for some time to attract small bodies; but at present electricity is usually generated by other means. In general, a body is said to be electrified when it contains—either as a whole, or in any of its parts—more or less of the electric fluid than is natural to it; and it is assumed that what is called positive electricity depends on an excess, and negative electricity on a deficiency of the fluid.

These repulsions and attractions are assumed to act, not only between two particles which are either perfectly or very nearly in contact with each other, but also between all other particles at all distances, whatever obstacles may be placed between them. Thus, if two electrified balls repel each other, the effect is not hindered by the placement of a plate of glass between them: and if any other substance placed between them appears to interfere with their mutual action, it is in consequence of its own electrical properties. In these respects, as well as in the law of their variation, the electrical forces differ from the common repulsion which operates between the particles of elastic fluids, and resemble more nearly that of gravitation. Their intensity, when separately considered, is much greater than that of gravitation, and they might be supposed

to be materially involved in the great phenomena of the universe; but in the common neutral state of all bodies, the electrical fluid, which is everywhere present, is distributed in such a way that the various forces hold each other exactly in equilibrium, and the separate results are canceled; unless we choose to consider gravitation itself as arising from a relatively small inequality between the electrical attractions and repulsions.

The attraction of the electric fluid to ordinary matter is shown by its transfer from one body to another which is less abundantly supplied with it, as well as by many other phenomena. This attraction of the fluid of the first body to the matter of the second is precisely equal to its repulsion for the quantity of fluid that naturally belongs to the second, which is required to saturate its matter. For the excess or deficiency of the fluid in the first body does not immediately produce either attraction or repulsion, as long as the natural distribution of the fluid in the second body remains unaltered.

Since two neutral bodies, the matter of which is saturated by the electric fluid, show no attraction for each other, the matter in the first must be repelled by the matter in the second; otherwise, its attraction for the fluid of the second would remain uncompensated. We are, however, scarcely justified in classifying this mutual repulsion among the fundamental properties of matter; for useful as these laws are in explaining electrical appearances, they seem to deviate too far from the magnificent simplicity of nature's works to be admitted as primary consequences of the constitution of matter. They may, however, be considered as modifications of some other more general laws, which are yet wholly unknown to us.

When the equilibrium of these forces is destroyed, the electric fluid is put in motion. Those bodies which allow the fluid a free passage are called perfect conductors; but those which impede its motion, more or less, are nonconductors, or imperfect conductors. If a person, connected with the conductor, is placed on a stool with glass legs, the electricity will no longer pass through him to the earth, but may be so accumulated as to make its way to any neighboring substance which is capable of receiving it, exhibiting a luminous appearance called a spark; and a person or a substance, so placed as to be in contact with nonconductors only, is said to be insulated. When electricity is subtracted from the substance thus insulated, it is said to be negatively electrified, but the sensible effects are nearly the same, except that in some cases the form of the spark is a little different.

Perfect conductors, when electrified, are in general either overcharged or undercharged with electricity in their most distant parts at the same time; but nonconductors, although they have an equal attraction for the electric fluid, are often differently affected in different parts of their substance, even when those parts are similarly situated in every respect, except that some of them have had their electricity increased or diminished by an external cause. This property of nonconductors may be illustrated by means of a cake of resin, or a plate of glass, to which a local electricity may be communicated in any part of its surface by the contact of an electrified body; and the parts thus electrified may afterwards be distinguished from the rest by the attraction which they exert on any small particles of dust or powder projected near them; the manner in which the particles arrange themselves on the surface indicating also in some cases the species of electricity, whether positive or negative, that has been employed; positive electricity producing an appearance somewhat resembling feathers, and negative electricity an arrangement more like spots. The inequality in the distribution of the electric fluid in a nonconductor may remain for some hours, or even some days, continually diminishing until it becomes imperceptible.

If we suppose a quantity of excess fluid to exist in a spherical conducting body, it will be almost entirely collected in a tiny space next to the surface, while the internal parts remain barely overcharged. We can ignore the actions of the portion of fluid that is only involved in saturating the matter, as well as the effect of the matter that is neutralized in this way, since the excess fluid is repelled as much by the one as it is attracted by the other; we only need to consider the mutual actions of the particles of this surplus fluid on each other. It can then be shown—in the same way that the force of gravity is demonstrated—that all the spherical layers further from the center than any given particle will have their total action on it canceled out by the balance of their forces, and that the effective repulsion of the inner layers will be the same as if they were all concentrated at the center. Therefore, this repulsion will push the particles of the fluid toward the surface as long as it exists, and nothing will hinder the accumulation of the excess fluid there until it is cleared from the area around the center. In the same manner, it can be shown that if there is a deficiency of fluid, it will only occur in the outer parts, while the central parts always remain in a state of neutrality. Since the amount of electric fluid removed from a body in any typical experiment is only a very small fraction of the total it contains, the deficiency will also be found in a very small portion of the sphere next to its surface. Even if the body is not spherical but of some other form, the effects of electricity will still be mainly confined to its surface. This proposition was investigated very convincingly by Mr. <term>Cavendish</term>; and it was afterwards more fully shown by Dr. *Gray’s* experiments that the capacity of different bodies for receiving electricity depends much more on their surface area than on their solid volume. Thus, the conductor of an electrical machine will contain almost exactly as much electricity if it is hollow as it would if it were solid.

If two spheres are joined by a small cylindrical conducting substance, equilibrium will be reached when the effects of the excess fluid in the spheres on the total fluid in the cylinder are equal; that is, when the surfaces of both spheres are electrified to the same degree. (Plate XXXIX. Fig. 551.)

In this distribution, we find a very characteristic difference between the pressure of the electric fluid and the common hydrostatic pressure of liquids or simple elastic fluids. These exert a pressure proportional to their size on every surface situated similarly; however, the electric fluid exerts a pressure on small and angular surfaces that is greater, in proportion to their size, than the pressure on larger parts. Thus, if the electric fluid were generally kept in place by atmospheric pressure, that pressure might easily be too weak to prevent its escape from any prominent points. However, it does not appear that this pressure is the only cause preventing the escape of the electric fluid. Nor is it certain that this fluid can pass through a perfect vacuum, although it has not yet been proven that a body placed in a vacuum is perfectly insulated. Whatever the resistance may be that prevents the loss of electricity, it is always more easily overcome when the electrified substance is more pointed and the point is more prominent. Even the presence of dust is often unfavorable to the success of electrical experiments because of the great number of pointed ends it provides.

The general effect of electrified bodies on each other, if their size is small compared to their distance, is that they are mutually repelled when in similar states of electricity and attracted when in different states. This is a consequence immediately derived from the mutual attraction of excess matter and excess fluid, and from the repulsion supposed to exist between any two portions of either matter or fluid; it can also easily be confirmed by experimental proof. A neutral body, if it were a perfect nonconductor, would not be affected either way by the proximity of an electrified body. For while the total matter it contains remains just saturated with the electric fluid, the attractions and repulsions balance each other. When a positively electrified body approaches a neutral body, the excess fluid repels a portion of the natural quantity from the nearest parts of the neutral body, causing it to accumulate at the opposite end. Meanwhile, the matter that is left deficient attracts the excess fluid of the first body in such a way that it becomes more concentrated near the second body than elsewhere; as a result, the fluid of this body is driven even further away, and all the effects are intensified. The attraction between the excess fluid of the electrified body and the deficient matter of the neutral body is stronger than its repulsion for the fluid that has been expelled from it, because the square of the average distance to the matter is smaller than the square of the average distance to the fluid. Therefore, in all such cases of <term>induced electricity</term>, an attraction is produced between the bodies involved. A similar attraction will occur under opposite circumstances when a neutral body and a negatively electrified body approach each other.

The state of induced electricity can be illustrated by placing a long conductor a short distance from an electrified substance and pointing it toward it, and by suspending <term>pith balls</term> or other light bodies from it in pairs at various points along its length. These will repel each other because they become similarly electrified at the two ends, which are in opposite electrical states; however, at a certain point toward the middle, they will remain still, as the conductor is perfectly neutral there. It was from the location of this point that <term>Lord Stanhope</term> first deduced the true law of electrical attraction and repulsion, although <term>Mr. Cavendish</term> had previously suggested the same law as the most likely hypothesis.

The attraction thus exerted by an electrified body upon neutral substances is strong enough—if they are light enough—to overcome their <term>gravitation</term> and pull them up from a table at a small distance. The repulsion, which takes place between two bodies in a similar state of electricity, is the cause of the currents of air which always accompany the discharge of electricity—whether negative or positive—from pointed substances. Each particle of air, as soon as it has received its electricity from the point, is immediately repelled by it; and this current has also been supposed to facilitate the escape of the electricity by bringing a continual succession of particles that are not already overcharged.

If two bodies approach each other, electrified either positively or negatively in different degrees, they will either repel or attract each other according to their distance. When they are very remote, they exhibit a repulsive force, but when they are within a certain distance, the effects of induced electricity overcome the repulsion which would necessarily take place if the distribution of the fluid remained unaltered by their mutual influence.

When a quantity of the <term>electric fluid</term> is accumulated on one side of a <term>non-conducting substance</term>, it tends to drive off the fluid from the other side; and if this fluid is allowed to escape, the remaining matter exerts its attraction on the fluid which has been imparted to the first side, and allows it to be accumulated in a much greater quantity than could have existed on an equal surface of a <term>conducting substance</term>. In this state, the body is said to be <term>charged</term>; and to produce this more readily, each surface is usually coated with a conducting substance, which serves to convey the fluid to and from its different parts with convenience. The thinner any substance is, the greater quantity of the fluid is required for charging it in this manner, so as to produce a given <term>tension</term>, or tendency to escape. But if it is made too thin, it will be liable to break; the attractive force of the fluid for the matter on the opposite side overcomes the <term>cohesion</term> of the substance, perhaps forcing its way through the temporary <term>vacuum</term> which is formed.

### LECTURE LIII.

When a connection is made in any manner by a conducting substance between the two coatings of a charged plate or vessel, the equilibrium is restored, and the effect is called a shock. If the coatings are removed, the plate will still remain charged, and it may be gradually discharged by making a connection between its several parts in succession; however, it cannot be discharged all at once for lack of a common connection. Therefore, the presence of the coating is not absolutely essential to the charge and discharge of the opposite surfaces. Such a coated substance is most usually employed in the form of a jar. Jars were formerly filled with water or with iron filings; because the instrument was made known primarily through the experiments of Musschenbroek and others at <term>Leyden</term>, it was called the <term>Leyden phial</term>. But at present, a coating of tin foil is commonly applied on both sides of the jar, leaving a sufficient space at its upper part to avoid a spontaneous discharge, which would often occur between the coatings if they approached too near to each other. A ball is fixed to the cover, which has a connection with the internal coating, and by means of which the jar is charged, while the external coating is allowed to communicate with the ground. A collection of such jars is called a **battery**, and an apparatus of this kind may be made so powerful, by increasing the number of jars, as to exhibit many striking effects by the motion of the <term>electric fluid</term> in its passage from one surface to the other.

The conducting powers of different substances are involved not only in the ease with which the motions of the <term>electric fluid</term> are directed into a particular channel, but also in many cases of its equilibrium, and particularly in the properties of charged substances, which depend on the resistance opposed by <term>nonconductors</term> to the ready transmission of the fluid. These powers may be compared by determining the greatest length of each of the substances to be examined through which a spark or a shock will take its course, in preference to a given length of air or any other standard of comparison. The substances which conduct electricity most readily are metals, well-burned charcoal, animal bodies, acids, saline liquors, water, and very rare air. The principal <term>nonconductors</term> are glass, ice, gems, dry salts, sulfur, amber, resins, silk, dry wood, oils, dry air of the usual density, and the <term>barometrical vacuum</term>. Heat commonly increases the conducting powers of bodies; a jar of

## LECTURE LIV.

### ON ELECTRICITY IN MOTION.

**The** manner in which the <term>electric fluid</term> is transferred from one body to another, the immediate effects of such a transfer, the causes which originally disturb the equilibrium of electricity, and the practical methods by which all these circumstances are regulated and measured, require to be considered as belonging to the subject of electricity in motion. Among the modes of excitation by which the equilibrium is originally disturbed, one of the most interesting is the galvanic apparatus <note>an early form of the electric battery, such as a voltaic pile</note>, which has been in recent years a very favorite subject of popular curiosity, and of which the theory and operation will be briefly examined, although the subject appears to belong rather to the chemical than to the mechanical doctrine of electricity.

The forward motion of the electric fluid through conducting substances is so rapid that it is performed in all cases without a noticeable interval of time. It has indeed been said that when it is very weakly excited and forced to pass to a very great distance, a perceptible portion of time is actually occupied in its passage; but this fact is somewhat doubtful, and attempts have been made in vain to estimate the interval employed in the transmission of a shock through several miles of wire. We are not to imagine that the same particles of the fluid which enter at one part pass through the whole conducting substance, any more than the same portion of blood which is thrown out of the heart in each pulsation arrives at the wrist at the instant that the pulse is felt there. The velocity of the transmission of a spark or shock far exceeds the actual velocity of each particle, in the same manner as the velocity of a wave exceeds that of the particles of water concerned in its propagation; and this velocity must depend both on the elasticity of the electric fluid and on the force with which it is confined to the conducting substance. If this force were merely derived from the pressure of the atmosphere, we might infer the

The author compares the rapid movement of an electric shock to the propagation of a wave, noting that individual particles do not travel the entire distance themselves.</summary>

density of the fluid from the velocity of a spark or shock, compared with that of sound; or we might deduce its velocity from a determination of its density. It has been supposed, although perhaps somewhat hastily, that the actual velocity is nearly equal to that of light.

When a conducting substance approaches another that is electrified, the distribution of the electric fluid within it is necessarily altered by induction before it receives a spark, so that its further end is brought into a state similar to that of the first body. Hence it happens that when the spark passes, it produces less effect at the further end of the substance, while the part presented to the electrified body is most affected because of its sudden change to an opposite state. But if both ends approach bodies in opposite states of electricity, they will both be strongly affected when the shock occurs, while the middle of the circuit undergoes very little change.

The manner in which the electric fluid makes its way through a more or less perfect nonconductor is not completely understood. It is doubtful whether the substance is forced away on each side so as to leave a vacuum for the passage of the fluid, or whether the newly formed surface helps to guide it on its way; and in some cases, it has been supposed that the gradual communication of electricity has rendered the substance more capable of conducting it, either immediately or, in the case of air, by first rarefying it. However this may be, the perforation of a glass jar by an overcharge and that of a layer of air by a spark appear to be effects of the same kind, although the charge of the jar is principally contained in the glass, while the layer of air is perhaps little involved in the distribution of the electricity.

The actual direction of the electric current has not in any instance been fully ascertained, although there are some appearances which seem to justify the common designations of positive and negative. Thus, the fracture of a charged glass jar, caused by a spontaneous explosion, is well-defined on the positive side and splintered on the negative side, as might be expected from the passage of a foreign substance from the former side to the latter; and a candle, held between a positive and a negative ball, although it apparently vibrates

We cannot, however, rely much on any circumstance of this kind, for it is doubtful whether any current of the fluid which we can produce possesses sufficient momentum to carry with it a body of noticeable size. It is, in fact, of little consequence to the theory whether the terms positive and negative are correctly applied, provided that their meaning remains determined; and that, like positive and negative quantities in mathematics, they are always understood as states that neutralize each other. The original opinion of <term>Dufay</term>, regarding the existence of two distinct fluids—a <term>vitreous</term> and a <term>resinous</term> electricity—currently has few advocates, although some have thought such a supposition is supported by the phenomena of the galvanic decomposition of water.

When electricity is simply accumulated without motion, it does not appear to have any effect—whether mechanical, chemical, or physiological—by which its presence can be discovered; the acceleration of the pulse and the advancement of the growth of plants, which have sometimes been attributed to it, have not been confirmed by the most accurate experiments. An uninterrupted current of electricity through a perfect conductor would perhaps also be imperceptible in every respect, since the best conductors appear to be the least affected by it. Thus, if we place our hand on the conductor of an electrical machine, the electricity will pass off continually through the body without exciting any sensation. A constant stream of galvanic electricity passing through an iron wire is, however, capable of generating a considerable degree of heat; and if it is transmitted through the hands of the operator, it will produce a slight numbness, although in general some interruption of the current is necessary to provide an accumulation sufficient to produce noticeable effects. Such an interruption may even increase the effect of a single spark or shock; for example, gunpowder is more easily ignited by the discharge of a battery passing through an interrupted circuit than through a series of perfect conductors.

The most common effect of the motion of the electric fluid is the production of light. Light is probably never caused by the passage of the fluid through a perfect conductor; for when the discharge of a large battery renders a small wire luminous, the fluid is not wholly confined to the wire, but

There is always an appearance of light whenever the path of the fluid is interrupted by an imperfect conductor; nor is the apparent contact of conducting substances sufficient to prevent it, unless they are held together by a considerable force. Thus, a chain conveying a spark or shock appears luminous at each link, and the rapidity of the motion is so great that we can never observe any difference in the times of the appearance of the light in its different parts. So, a series of luminous points, formed by the passage of the electric fluid between a string of conducting bodies, represents at once a brilliant delineation of the whole figure in which they are arranged. A lump of sugar, a piece of wood, or an egg may easily be made luminous in this manner; and many substances, by means of their properties as solar phosphori, retain for some seconds the luminous appearance thus acquired. Even water is so imperfect a conductor that a strong shock may be seen in its passage through it; and when the air is sufficiently moistened or rarefied to become a conductor, the track of the fluid through it is indicated by streams of light, which are perhaps derived from a series of minute sparks passing between the particles of water or of rarefied air. When the air is extremely rare, the light is greenish; as it becomes more dense, the light becomes blue, and then violet, until it no longer conducts. The appearance of the electrical light from a point enables us to distinguish the nature of the electricity with which it is charged: a pencil of light, streaming from the point, indicates that its electricity is positive, while a luminous star with few diverging rays shows that it is negative. The sparks exhibited by small balls, differently electrified, also have similar varieties in their forms according to the nature of their charges. (Plate XL. Fig. 552.)

The production of heat by electricity frequently accompanies that of light and appears to depend in some measure on the same circumstances. A fine wire may be fused and dissipated by the discharge of a battery; and without being perfectly melted, it may sometimes be shortened or lengthened, depending on whether it is loose or stretched during the experiment. The more easily a metal conducts, the shorter the portion of it which the same shock can destroy; and it has sometimes been found that a double charge of a battery has been capable of melting a quadruple length of wire of the same kind.

<page-num>672</page-num>
<header>LECTURE LIV.</header>

The destruction of a glass tube that contains a fluid in a capillary bore, when a spark is passed through it, is the natural consequence of the conversion of some particles of the fluid into vapor. But when a glass jar is perforated, this rarefaction cannot be supposed to be adequate to the effect. It is remarkable that such a perforation may be made by a very moderate discharge when the glass is in contact with oil or with sealing wax, and no sufficient explanation of this circumstance has yet been given.

A strong current of electricity, or a succession of shocks or sparks transmitted through a substance by means of fine wires, is capable of producing many chemical combinations and decompositions. Some of these may be attributed merely to the heat which it occasions, but others are wholly different. Of these, the most remarkable is the production of oxygen and hydrogen gas from common water; these are usually released at once in such quantities that, when recombined, they will reproduce the water which has disappeared. However, in some cases the oxygen appears to be released most copiously at the positive wire, and the hydrogen at the negative.

When the spark is received by the tongue, it generally has a subacid taste; and an explosion of any kind is usually accompanied by a smell somewhat like that of sulfur, or rather of fired gunpowder. The peculiar sensation which the electric fluid causes in the human frame appears in general to be derived from the spasmodic contractions of the muscles through which it passes, although in some cases it produces pain of a different kind. For instance, the spark of a conductor causes a disagreeable sensation in the skin, and when an excoriated <note>abraded or stripped of skin</note> surface is placed in the galvanic current, a sense of smarting, mixed with burning, is experienced. Sometimes the effect of a shock is felt most powerfully at the joints, because of the difficulty which the fluid finds in passing the articulating surfaces which form the cavity of the joints. The sudden death of an animal as a result of a violent shock is probably due to the immediate exhaustion of the entire energy of the nervous system. It is remarkable that a very minute tremor, communicated to the most elastic parts of the body—in particular to the chest—produces an agitation of the nerves which is not unlike the effect of a weak electricity.

<page-num>673</page-num>

# ON ELECTRICITY IN MOTION.

The principal ways in which electric equilibrium is primarily destroyed are simple contact, friction, a change in the form of aggregation, and chemical combinations and decompositions. The electricity produced by the simple contact of any two substances is extremely weak and can only be detected by very delicate experiments; in general, it appears that the substance which conducts more easily acquires a slight degree of negative electricity, while the other substance is positively electrified to an equal degree. The same distribution of the fluid is also usually produced by friction, with one substance always losing as much as the other gains; and commonly, though not always, the poorer conductor becomes positive. At the moment friction is applied, the capacities or attractions of the bodies for electricity appear to be altered, and a greater or lesser quantity is required to saturate them; upon the cessation of this temporary change, the resulting redundancy or deficiency becomes perceptible. When two substances of the same kind are rubbed together, the smaller or the rougher one becomes negatively electrified. This is perhaps because the smaller surface is heated more, due to its undergoing more friction than an equal portion of the larger one, and thus becomes a better conductor; it may also be because the rougher surface is inherently a better conductor than the smoother one, and may have its conducting powers increased by the greater agitation of its parts produced by the friction. The back of a live cat becomes positively electrified regardless of the substance it is rubbed with. Glass is positive in most cases, but not when rubbed with mercury in a vacuum, although sealing wax—which is generally negative—is made positive by immersion in a trough of mercury. When a white and a black silk stocking are rubbed together, the white stocking acquires positive electricity and the black negative, perhaps because the black dye makes the silk both rougher and a better conductor.

Those substances which have very little conducting power are sometimes called <term>electrics</term>, since they are capable of readily exhibiting the electricity that friction excites on their surfaces; there it remains accumulated, so that it may be collected into a conductor. Meanwhile, the surfaces of substances with greater conducting powers do not as readily absorb the fluid from others with which they are rubbed, since they may be supplied from the internal parts of the substances themselves when their altered capacity requires it. Thus, glass, when heated to 110° Fahrenheit, can only be excited with difficulty, as it becomes an imperfect conductor:

Vapors are generally in a negative state, but if they rise from metallic substances, or even from some kinds of heated glass, the effect is uncertain, probably on account of some chemical actions which interfere with it. Sulfur becomes electrical when cooling, and wax candles are said to be sometimes found in a state so electrical when they are taken out of their molds that they attract the particles of dust floating near them. The tourmaline and several other crystallized stones become electrical when heated or cooled; it is found that the distribution assumed by the fluid bears a certain relation to the direction in which the stone transmits light most readily, with some parts of the crystal being rendered always positively and others negatively electrical by an increase of temperature.

The most remarkable phenomena attending the excitation of electricity by chemical changes are those which have lately received the name of galvanic. Some of the effects which have been considered as belonging to galvanism are probably derived from the electrical powers of the animal body; the rest have been attributed by Mr. Volta and many other philosophers on the continent to the mere mechanical actions of bodies possessing different properties with regard to electricity. Thus, they have supposed that when a circulation of the electric fluid is produced through a long series of substances in a certain direction, the differences in their attractions and their conducting powers—which must remain the same throughout the process—keep up this perpetual motion, in defiance of the general laws of mechanical forces. In this country, it has been generally maintained that no explanation founded on such principles could be admissible, even if it were in all other respects sufficient and satisfactory, which the mechanical theory of galvanism certainly is not.

The phenomena of galvanism appear to be principally derived from an inequality in the distribution of the electric fluid, originating from chemical changes and maintained by means of the resistance opposed to its motion by a continued alternation of different kinds of substances; this provides a much stronger obstacle to its transmission than any of those substances would have done alone. The substances employed must neither consist wholly of

solids nor of fluids, and they must be of three different kinds, possessed of different powers of conducting electricity; but whether the difference of their conducting powers is of any other consequence than as it accompanies different chemical properties, is hitherto undetermined. Of these three substances, two must possess a power of acting mutually on each other, while the other appears to serve principally for making a separate connection between them: and this action may be of two kinds, or perhaps of more; the one is oxidation, or the combination of a metal or an inflammable substance with a portion of oxygen derived from water or from an acid, the other sulfuration, or a combination with the sulfur contained in a solution of an alkaline sulfuret <note>An alkaline sulfuret is what is now commonly called an alkaline sulfide.</note>.

We may represent the effects of all galvanic combinations by considering the oxidation as producing positive electricity in the acting liquid, and the sulfuration as producing negative electricity, and by imagining that this electricity is always communicated to the best conductor of the other substances concerned, so as to produce a circulation in the direction thus determined. For example, when two wires of zinc and silver, touching each other, are separately immersed in an acid, the acid, becoming positively electrical, imparts its electricity to the silver, and hence it flows back into the zinc: when the ends of a piece of charcoal are dipped into water and into an acid, connected together by a small tube, the acid, becoming positive, sends its excess fluid through the charcoal into the water; and if a wire of copper be dipped into water and a solution of alkaline sulfuret, connected with each other, the sulfuret, becoming negative, will draw the fluid from the copper on which it acts; and in all these cases the direction of the current is truly determined, as it may be shown by composing a battery of a number of alternations of this kind, and either examining the state of its different parts by electrical tests, or connecting wires with its extremities, which, when immersed into a portion of water, will exhibit the production of oxygen gas where they emit the electric fluid, and of hydrogen where they receive it. These processes of oxidation and of sulfuration may be opposed to each other, or they may be combined in various ways, the sum or difference of the separate actions being obtained by their union; thus it usually happens that both the metals employed are oxidizable in some degree, and the oxidation, which takes place at the surface of the better conductor, tends to impede the whole effect, perhaps by hindering the passage of the fluid through the surface. Instead of the release of hydrogen, the same causes will sometimes occasion a deposition of a metal which has been dissolved, will prevent the solution of a metal which would otherwise have been corroded, or produce some effects which appear to indicate the presence of an alkali, whether volatile or fixed. All these operations may, however, be very much impeded by the interposition of any considerable length of water, or of any other imperfect conductor. (Plate XL. Fig. 556.)

It is obvious that since the current of electricity, produced by a galvanic circle, facilitates those actions from which its powers are derived, the effect of a double series must be more than twice as great as that of a single one: and hence arises the activity of the pile of Volta <note>The Voltaic pile, the first chemical battery.</note>, the discovery of which forms the most important era in the history of this department of natural knowledge. The intensity of the electrical charge, and the chemical and physiological effects of a pile or battery, seem to depend principally on the number of alternations of substances; the light and heat more on the joint magnitude of the surfaces employed. It is unquestionable that the torpedo <note>An electric ray.</note>, the *gymnotus electricus* <note>The electric eel.</note>, and some other fishes, have organs designed for the excitation of electricity, and that they have the power of communicating this electricity at will to conducting substances in their vicinity. These organs somewhat resemble in their appearance the plates of the galvanic pile, although we know nothing of the immediate arrangement from which their electrical properties are derived; however, the effect of the shock they produce resembles in all respects that of the weak charge of a very large battery. It has also been shown by the experiments of Galvani, Volta, and Aldini that the nerves and muscles of the human body possess some electrical powers, although they are much less involved in the phenomena that Galvani initially attributed to them than he originally supposed. Consequently, many philosophers have been inclined to consider the excitation of electricity as always caused by the inanimate substances employed, and the spasmodic contractions of the muscles as merely very delicate tests of the influence of external electricity on the nerves.

Mr. Davy is inclined to infer from his experiments that all the attractions which cause chemical combinations depend on the opposite natural <term>electricities</term> of the bodies involved; since such bodies are always found, by delicate tests, to exhibit marks of different types of electricity when in contact. Their mutual actions may be either increased or destroyed by increasing their natural electrical charges, or by electrifying them in an opposite way. Thus, an <term>acid</term> and a metal are found to be negatively and positively electrical with respect to each other; by further electrifying the acid negatively and the metal positively, their combination is accelerated. However, when the acid is positively electrified, or the metal negatively, they have no effect whatever on each other. The acid is also attracted, as a negative body, by another positively electrified body, and the metal by a body negatively electrified, so that a metallic salt may be decomposed in the circuit of <term>Volta</term>, with the positive point attracting the acid and the negative point attracting the metal. These attractions are so strong that they carry the particles of the respective bodies through any intervening medium in a fluid state, or even through a moist solid; nor are they intercepted in their passage by substances which, in other cases, have the strongest <term>elective attractions</term> for them. <term>Alkali</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, and <term>alkaline sulfurets</term> are positive with respect to the metals, and even more so with respect to the acids; hence, they have a very strong natural tendency to combine with the acids and with <term>oxygen</term>. <term>Hydrogen</term> must also be considered as belonging to the same class as the <term>alkalis</term>.

Suppose now that a plate of <term>zinc</term> decomposes a portion of water: the oxygen, which has a negative property, unites with the zinc and probably tends to <term>neutralize</term> it and weaken its attractive force. The hydrogen is repelled by the zinc and carries its natural positive electricity to the opposite plate of <term>silver</term>. If the two plates are made to touch, the energy of the zinc plate is restored by the electricity it receives from the silver. It receives it all the more readily because these two metals, whenever they are in contact, have a tendency to become electrical—the zinc positively and the silver negatively. Mr. Davy, therefore, considers this chemical action as destroying, or

From modifications of this counteraction, he explains the effects of <term>galvanic combinations</term> in all cases. Thus, in a circuit composed of copper, <term>sulfuret</term>, and iron, the fluid tends to pass from the iron toward the sulfuret, and from the copper to the iron, in one direction; in the opposite direction, it tends to pass from the copper to the sulfuret with a force that must be equal to the sum of the other two, since there would otherwise be a continual motion without any mechanical cause and without any chemical change. However, the action of the sulfuret on the copper tends to destroy its <term>electromotive</term>—or rather, <term>electrophoric</term>—power of directing the current toward the sulfuret, and its combination with the sulfur makes it either positively electrical or negatively <insert>REESE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</insert> electrical to a less significant degree. Consequently, the fluid passes, according to its natural tendency, from the copper to the iron, and from the iron to the sulfuret. 

In a third case, when copper, an acid, and water form a circuit, the natural tendency is from the acid to the copper on one side, and from the acid to the water and from the water to the copper on the other. Here, we must suppose the first force to be only slightly weakened by chemical action while the third is destroyed, so that the first overcomes the second. The circulation is thus determined, although very feebly, in a direction such that the fluid passes from the acid to the copper. 

When, in the fourth place, the combination consists of copper, sulfuret, and water, the tendencies are, first, from the copper to the sulfuret and from the water to the copper; and secondly, from the water to the sulfuret. In this instance, a chemical action must be assumed to occur between the oxygen of the water and the sulfuret, which lessens the electromotive tendency more than the action that takes place between the sulfuret and the copper does, so that the fluid passes from the copper to the sulfuret. This current even has enough force to prevent any chemical action between the water and the copper, which would tend to counteract that force if it took place.

Mr. Davy has observed that the decomposition of the substances employed in the <term>battery of Volta</term> is of much more consequence to their activity than either their conducting power or their simple action on the other elements of the series. Thus, sulfuric acid—which conducts electricity better and dissolves metals more readily than a neutral solution—is nonetheless less active in the battery because it is not easily decomposed. ...extended his research and the application of his discoveries to a variety of natural as well as artificial phenomena. There can be no doubt that he will continue to make such additions to his experiments as will be of the greatest importance to this branch of science.

The operation of the most common electrical machines depends first on the excitation of electricity by the friction of glass against a leather cushion. This cushion is covered with a metallic amalgam, usually made of mercury, zinc, and tin, which—besides being useful in supplying electricity readily to different parts of the glass—probably undergoes a chemical change that releases some electricity. The fluid thus excited is received into an insulated conductor by means of points placed a short distance from the surface that has recently undergone friction; from this conductor, it is conveyed by wires or chains to any other parts as desired. Sometimes the cushion, instead of being connected to the earth, is itself fixed to a second conductor which becomes negatively electrified. Either conductor may contain a jar within it, which can be charged immediately by the operation of the machine when its internal surface is connected either with the earth or with that of the jar contained in the opposite conductor. The glass may be in the form of either a circular plate or a cylinder; it is uncertain which arrangement provides the greatest quantity of electricity from the same surface area, but the cylinder is cheaper than the plate, less prone to accidents, and appears to be at least as powerful. (Plate XL, Figures 558, 559.)

The plate machine in the Teylerian Museum, used by Van Marum, produced electricity (when worked by two men) with an attraction that was noticeable at a distance of 38 feet, made a point luminous at 27 feet, and produced sparks nearly 24 inches long. A battery charged by it instantly melted twenty-five feet of fine iron wire. A few years ago in the Pantheon in London, Mr. Wilson also had an apparatus of remarkable size; the principal conductor was 150 feet long and 16 inches in diameter, and he used a circuit of 4,800 feet of wire.

The electrophorus derives its operation from the properties of induced electricity. A cake of a non-conducting substance, commonly made of resin or of

...sulfur is first excited by friction and becomes negatively electric. An insulated plate made of a conducting substance, when placed on it, does not come into close enough contact with it to receive its electricity directly, but instead acquires through induction an opposite state at its lower surface and a similar state at its upper surface. Thus, when this upper and negative surface is touched by a substance connected to the earth, it receives enough of the electric fluid to restore the equilibrium. When the plate is then raised, the influence of the cake no longer continues, and the electricity that the plate has received from the earth is imparted to a conductor or to a jar. This operation may be continually repeated until the jar has received a charge of an intensity equal to that of the plate when it is raised. Although the quantity of electricity received by the plate is exactly equal to that which is emitted from it at each alternation, the spark is far less noticeable. This is because the proximity of the cake increases the capacity of the plate, while the tension, or force impelling the fluid, remains weak. At the same time, the quantity received is sufficient—once the capacity of the plate is diminished again—to produce a much greater tension when at a distance from the cake. (Plate XL, Figure 560.)

The condenser acts to some extent on the same principles as the electrophorus, as both instruments derive their properties from the effects of induction. The purpose of the condenser is to collect a weak charge of electricity from a large object into a smaller one, so as to make its density or tension sufficient to be examined. A small plate, connected with the object, is brought nearly into contact with another plate connected to the earth. Generally, only a thin layer of air is placed between them, but sometimes an insulating varnish is used; however, this method is prone to some uncertainty due to the permanent electricity that the varnish sometimes acquires through friction. The electricity is accumulated in the plate of the condenser by the attraction of the plate connected to the earth. When this plate is first separated from the object being examined and then removed from the opposite plate, its electricity is always of the same type as that which originally existed in the object, but its tension is increased so much that it becomes more easily detectable. This principle has been applied in various ways by different electricians, and the use of the instrument has been made easier by several secondary arrangements. (Plate XL, Figure 561.)

Mr. Cavallo's multiplier is a combination of two condensers; the second or auxiliary plate of the first, like the plate of the <term>electrophorus</term>, is movable. It carries a charge of electricity—opposite to that of the substance being examined—to the first or insulated plate of the second condenser, which receives it repeatedly until it has acquired an equal degree of tension. When the two plates of this condenser are separated, they both exhibit an electricity much more powerful than that of the first condenser. The force is, however, even more rapidly increased by the instruments of Mr. Bennet and Mr. Nicholson, although it has been suggested that these instruments are more prone to inconvenience because a larger portion of electricity attaches to the first plate of the instrument; this leaves a certain quantity of the charge for a very considerable time, which is not easily separated from it. Mr. Bennet employs three varnished plates laid on top of each other, but Mr. Nicholson has substituted simple metallic plates that only come very close together, so that there can be no error from any accidental friction. In both of these instruments, the second plate of a condenser acquires an electricity opposite and nearly equal to that of the first. By means of this, it brings a third plate very nearly into the same state as the first; and when the first and third plates are connected and insulated, they produce a charge nearly twice as great in the second plate, while the first plate becomes at the same time doubly charged. Thus, by each repetition of this process, the intensity of the electricity is nearly doubled: it is therefore almost impossible for any quantity to be so small as to escape detection by its operation. (Plate XL. Fig. 562, 563.)

The immediate intensity of the electricity may be measured, and its character distinguished, by electrical balances and by electrometers of different constructions. The electrical balance measures the attraction or repulsion exerted by two balls at a given distance by the magnitude of the force required to counteract it; and the most convenient way of applying this force is by the torsion of a wire, which has been employed for this purpose by Mr. Coulomb. The quadrant electrometer of Henley indicates the mutual repulsion of a movable ball and a fixed column by the divisions of the arc to which the ball rises. These divisions do not exactly represent the proportional strength of the action, but they are still useful in ascertaining the identity of any two charges, and in informing us how far we may venture to

...proceed in our experiments with safety. The same purpose is served, in a manner somewhat less accurate, by the electrometer, which consists of two pith balls or two straws that are made to diverge by a small amount of electricity. Mr. Bennet’s electrometer is even more sensitive; it consists of two small strips of gold leaf hanging from a plate, to which the electricity of any substance is transferred by contact. A very weak charge is enough to make them spread apart, and it can easily be determined whether the electricity is positive or negative by bringing a charged stick of sealing wax near the plate. The approach of the wax tends to produce, through induction, a state of negative electricity in the far ends of the leaves; consequently, their divergence is either increased or diminished depending on whether the charge was derived from negative or positive electricity. A strip of gold leaf or tin foil, attached to the inside of the glass covering the electrometer opposite the ends of the leaves, prevents the transfer of any electricity to the glass, which might otherwise interfere with the instrument's operation. When the balls of an electrometer stand at a distance of 4 degrees, they seem to indicate a charge nearly 8 times as great as when they stand at one degree. A charge 8 times as great in each ball produces a mutual action 64 times as great at any given distance, and at four times the distance, a quadruple force; in the same way, a separation of 9 degrees is probably derived from an intensity 27 times as great as at 1 degree. In Lane’s electrometer, the magnitude of a shock is determined by the amount of air it is forced to pass through between two balls, the distance of which may be varied as desired; the power of the machine may be estimated by the frequency of the sparks that pass at any given distance. It appears from Mr. Lane’s experiments that the quantity of electricity required for a discharge is simply proportional to the distance between the surfaces of the balls; the shocks are twice as frequent when this distance is only 1/24 of an inch compared to when it is 1/12. Mr. Volta says that the readings of Lane’s and Henley’s electrometers agree directly with each other, but it seems difficult to reconcile this result with general theory. Sometimes the force of repulsion between two balls in contact is resisted by a counterweight of a specific size; as soon as this weight is overcome, the balls separate and complete a circuit which discharges a battery. For this reason, the instrument is called a <term>discharger</term>. (Plate XL. Figures 564–568.)

# LECTURE LIV.

...imperfect state: we know little or nothing of the internal nature of the substances and actions involved in it, and we can never predict, without previous experiment, where or how it will be triggered. We are completely ignorant of the makeup of bodies that gives them different conducting powers; we have only been able to draw some general conclusions regarding the distribution and balance of the supposed electric fluid from the laws of attraction and repulsion it appears to exert. There seems to be some reason to suspect, from the phenomena of cohesion and repulsion, that the pressure of an elastic medium is involved in the origin of these forces; and if such a medium truly exists, it is perhaps closely related to the electric fluid. Few now doubt that the general causes of electrical and galvanic effects are identical, and in this country, the main phenomena of galvanism are universally considered to depend on chemical changes. Perhaps, also, time may show that electricity is significantly involved in the essential properties that distinguish different types of natural bodies, as well as in those minute mechanical actions and influences which are probably the foundation of all chemical processes; but at present, it is hardly safe to venture a guess on such an obscure subject, although Mr. Davy’s experiments have already, to some extent, justified the boldness of this suggestion.

## LECTURE LV.

## ON MAGNETISM.

The theory of magnetism bears a very strong resemblance to that of electricity, and it must therefore be placed near it in a system of natural philosophy. We have seen the electric fluid not only exerting attractions and repulsions, and causing a peculiar distribution of neighboring portions of a fluid similar to itself, but also excited in one body and transferred to another in such a manner as to be perceptible to the senses, or at least to cause noticeable effects in its passage. The attraction and repulsion, and the peculiar distribution of the neighboring fluid, are found in the phenomena of magnetism; but we do not perceive that there is ever any actual excitation, or any perceptible transfer of the magnetic fluid from one body to another distinct body. It also has this striking peculiarity: that metallic iron is very nearly, if not absolutely, the only substance capable of exhibiting any indications of its presence or activity.

To explain the phenomena of magnetism, we suppose that the particles of a peculiar fluid repel each other and attract the particles of metallic iron with equal forces, diminishing as the square of the distance increases; the particles of such iron must also be imagined to repel each other in a similar manner. Iron and steel, when soft, are conductors of the magnetic fluid, and become less and less permeable to it as their hardness increases. The groundwork of this theory is due to Mr. Aepinus, but the forces have been more particularly investigated by Coulomb and others. The same objections apply to these hypotheses as to those which constitute the theory of electricity, if considered as original and fundamental properties of matter. Furthermore, it is difficult to imagine why iron, and iron only—whether apparently magnetic or not—should repel similar particles of iron with a peculiar force that happens to be an exact balance to the attraction of the magnetic fluid for iron. This is obviously improbable; but the hypotheses

The doctrine of the circulation of streams of the magnetic fluid has been justly and universally abandoned, and some other theories, much more ingenious and more probable—for instance that of Mr. Prévost—appear to be too complicated and too little supported by facts to require much of our attention.

The distinction between conductors and non-conductors is, with respect to the electric fluid, irregular and intricate; but in magnetism, the softness or hardness of the iron or steel constitutes the only difference. Heat, by softening iron, must consequently make it a conductor; even the heat of boiling water affects it to a certain degree, although it can scarcely be supposed to alter its temper; but the effect of a moderate heat is not as significant in magnetism as in electricity. A strong degree of heat appears, from the experiments of Gilbert and of Mr. Cavallo, to destroy completely all magnetic action.

It is perfectly certain that magnetic effects are produced by quantities of iron incapable of being detected either by their weight or by any chemical tests. Mr. Cavallo found that a few particles of steel, adhering to a hone <note>a whetstone used for sharpening razors or needles</note>, on which the point of a needle was slightly rubbed, imparted to it magnetic properties; and Mr. Coulomb has observed that there are hardly any bodies in nature which do not exhibit some marks of being subjected to the influence of magnetism, although its force is always proportional to the quantity of iron which they contain, as far as that quantity can be ascertained; a single grain being sufficient to make 20 pounds of another metal noticeably magnetic. A combination with a large proportion of oxygen deprives iron of the whole or the greater part of its magnetic properties; <term>finery cinder</term> <note>a type of iron slag or oxide produced in a forge</note> is still considerably magnetic, but the more perfect oxides and the salts of iron only in a slight degree; it is also said that antimony makes iron incapable of being attracted by the magnet. Nickel, when freed from arsenic and from cobalt, is decidedly magnetic, and the more so as it contains less iron. Some of the older chemists supposed nickel to be a compound metal containing iron, and we may still venture to assume this opinion as a magnetic hypothesis. There is indeed no way of demonstrating that it is impossible for two substances to be so united as to be incapable of separation by the art of the chemist; had nickel

Had it been as dense as platinum, or as light as cork, we could not have supposed that it contained any considerable quantity of iron; but in fact, the specific gravity of these metals is very nearly the same, and nickel is never found in nature except in the vicinity of iron. We may therefore suspect, with some reason, that the hypothesis of the existence of iron in nickel may even be chemically true. The aurora borealis is certainly to some extent a magnetic phenomenon, and if iron were the only substance capable of exhibiting magnetic effects, it would follow that some ferruginous particles must exist in the upper regions of the atmosphere. The light usually accompanying this magnetic meteor may possibly be derived from electricity, which may be the immediate cause of a change in the distribution of the magnetic fluid contained in the ferruginous vapors that are imagined to float in the air.

We are even less capable of distinguishing with certainty in magnetism than in electricity between a positive and a negative state, or a real redundancy of the fluid and a deficiency. The north pole of a magnet may be considered the part in which the magnetic fluid is either redundant or deficient, provided that the south pole is understood in the opposite sense: thus, if the north pole of a magnet is supposed to be positively charged, the south pole must be imagined to be negative; and in hard iron or steel, these poles may be considered unchangeable.

A north pole, therefore, always repels a north pole and attracts a south pole. And in a neutral piece of soft iron near the north pole of a magnet, the fluid becomes so distributed by induction as to form a temporary south pole next to the magnet; the whole piece is, of course, attracted because of the closer proximity of the attracting pole. If the bar is sufficiently soft and not too long, the farther end becomes a north pole, and the whole bar becomes a perfect temporary magnet. But when the bar is made of hard steel, the state of induction is imperfect due to the resistance opposed to the motion of the fluid; hence, the attraction is less powerful, and an opposite pole is formed at a certain distance within the bar, and beyond this another pole similar to the first; this alternation is sometimes repeated more than once. The distribution of the fluid within the magnet is also affected by the vicinity of a piece of soft iron; the north pole

A weak magnet is capable of receiving a temporary induction of a contrary magnetism from the action of a more powerful one, its north pole becoming a south pole on the approach of a stronger north pole; but the original south pole still retains its position at the opposite end, and restores the magnet nearly to its original condition after the removal of the disturbing cause.

The polarity of magnets, or their tendency to assume a certain direction, is of even greater importance than their attractive power. If a small magnet, or simply a soft wire, is balanced on a center point, it will arrange itself in such a direction as will produce an equilibrium of the attractions and repulsions of the poles of a larger magnet; acting as a tangent to a certain oval figure passing through those poles, the properties of which have been calculated by various mathematicians. This polarity may easily be imitated by electricity; when a suspended wire is brought near the ends of a positive and negative conductor that are placed parallel to each other, as in Nairne’s electrical machine, its position is perfectly similar to that of a needle attracted by a magnet, for which those conductors represent the poles. (Plate XLI. Fig. 569.)

The same effect is observable in iron filings placed near a magnet, as they adhere to each other in curved lines by virtue of their induced magnetism, the north pole of each particle being attached to the south pole of the particle next to it. This arrangement may be seen by placing the filings either on clean mercury or on any surface that can be agitated; and it may be imitated by scattering powder on a plate of glass supported by two balls which are oppositely electrified. (Plate XLI. Fig. 570.)

The polarity of a needle may often be observed when it exhibits no noticeable attraction or repulsion as a whole; and this may easily be understood by considering that when one end of a needle is repelled from a given point, and the other is attracted towards it, the two forces, if equal, will tend to turn it around its center, but will completely cancel each other’s effects with respect to any progressive motion of the whole needle. The magnets which we have considered so far have a simple and well-defined form; but the great compound magnet that directs the mariner’s compass—and which appears to consist mainly of the metallic and slightly oxidized iron contained in the internal parts of the earth—is probably of a far more intricate structure, and we can only judge its nature from the various phenomena derived from its influence.

The accumulation and the deficiency of the magnetic fluid, which determine the location of the poles of this magnet, are probably in fact quite diffused; however, they may generally be imagined, without much error in the result, to center in two points: one of them nearer to the north pole of the earth, the other to the south pole. In consequence of their attractions and repulsions, a needle—whether previously magnetic or not—always assumes, if freely balanced, the direction necessary for its equilibrium. In various parts of the globe, this direction is differently inclined toward the meridian and toward the horizon. 

Hence arises the use of the compass in navigation and in surveying: a needle, which is balanced with the freedom of horizontal motion, assumes the direction of the magnetic meridian, which for a certain time remains almost unchanging for the same place; and a similar property is also observable in the dipping needle, which is movable only in a vertical plane; for when this plane is placed in the magnetic meridian, the needle acquires an inclination to the horizon, which varies according to the location of the place with respect to the magnetic poles. (Plate XLI. Fig. 572, 573.)

The natural polarity of the needle may be illustrated in some measure by enclosing an artificial magnet in a globe; the direction of a small needle, suspended over any part of its surface, is determined by the position of the poles of the magnet in the same manner as the direction of the compass is determined by the magnetic poles of the earth, although with much more regularity. In either case the whole needle is scarcely more or less...

A bar of soft iron, placed in the position of the <term>dipping needle</term>, acquires a temporary state of magnetism from the earth by <term>induction</term>, which may be reversed at will by reversing its direction; but bars of iron, which have remained long in or near this direction, assume a permanent <term>polarity</term>; for iron, even when it was at first quite soft, becomes a little harder over time. A natural magnet is nothing more than a heavy iron ore which, in the course of ages, has acquired a strong polarity from the great primitive magnet (the Earth). It must have lain somewhat detached and must possess little conducting power in order to have received and to retain its magnetism.

We cannot calculate the true position of the needle for all places from any assumed position of two or more magnetic poles; and even in the same place, its direction is observed to change over the course of years, according to a law which has never yet been generally determined. Although the variation which has been observed at any one place since the discovery of the compass may perhaps be understood through some very intricate mathematical expressions, less reliance can be placed on any calculations of this kind, as there is reason to think that the change depends more on chemical than on physical causes. Dr. Halley indeed conjectured that the earth contained a nucleus, or separate sphere, revolving freely within it—or rather floating in a fluid contained in the intermediate space—and causing the variation of the magnetic meridian; and others have attributed the effect to the motions of the celestial bodies. But in either case, the changes produced would have been much more regular and universal than those which have been actually observed. Temporary changes of terrestrial magnetism have certainly been sometimes caused by other factors; such causes are, therefore, most likely to be involved in the more permanent effects. Thus, the eruption of Mount Hecla was found to disrupt the position of the needle considerably; the aurora borealis has been observed to cause its north pole to move
