...6 or 7 degrees to the westward of its usual position; and a still more remarkable change occurs continually in the diurnal variation. In these climates, the north pole of the needle moves slowly westwards from about 8 in the morning until 2, and in the evening returns again. This change has, with great probability, been attributed to the temporary elevation of the temperature of the earth to the east of the place of observation—where the sun’s action takes place at an earlier hour in the morning—and to the reduction of magnetic attraction resulting from the heat thus communicated. In winter, this variation amounts to about 7 minutes; in summer, to 13 or 14.

As important as the use of the compass currently is to navigation, it would be even more valuable if its declination from the true <term>meridian</term> were constant for the same place, or even if it varied according to any discoverable law. This is because it would provide an easy method for determining the <term>longitude</term> of a place by comparing an astronomical observation of its <term>latitude</term> with another measurement of the magnitude of the declination. And in some cases, it may even now be applied to this purpose, where we have a collection of recent and numerous observations. Such observations have been arranged from time to time in charts, which are furnished with lines indicating the magnitude of the declination, or variation, at the places through which they pass. These begin from the <term>line of no variation</term> and proceed on opposite sides of this line to show the magnitude of the variation to the east or west. It is obvious that the intersection of a given parallel of latitude with the line showing the magnitude of the variation will indicate the precise location of the place where the observations were made.

The line of no variation passed through London in 1657 and through Paris in 1666; its northern extremity appears to have moved continually eastwards, and its southern parts westwards; and it now passes through the middle of Asia. The opposite portion seems to have moved more uniformly westwards; it now runs from North America to the middle of the South Atlantic. On the European side of these lines, the declination is westerly; on the South American side, it is easterly. The variation in London has been, for several years, a little more than 24°. In the West Indies, it changes only slowly; for instance, it was 5° near the island of Barbados from 1700 to 1756. (Plate XLI. Figures 574 to 576. Plates XLII. XLIII.)

The dip of the north pole of the needle in the vicinity of London is 72°. Consequently, the lower end of a bar standing upright—such as a poker or a lamp iron—always becomes a north pole. Because the temporary south pole of a piece of soft iron is at the top, it is somewhat more strongly attracted by the north pole of a magnet placed above it than by its south pole. The distribution of the fluid in the magnet itself is also slightly more favorable to the attraction when its north pole is pointing downwards. It is obvious that the magnetism of the Earth's northern magnetic pole must resemble that of the south pole of a magnet, since it attracts the north pole. Therefore, if we considered the nature of the fluid’s distribution rather than its location in the Earth, we would call it a south pole. Although it is impossible to find locations for two—or even a larger number—of magnetic poles that will correctly explain the direction of the needle on every part of the Earth's surface, the dip may still be determined with reasonable accuracy by assuming that a small magnet is placed at the center of the Earth and directed toward a point in Baffin’s Bay (at approximately 75° north latitude and 70° longitude west of London). The variation of the dip is so slight that a very slow change in the position of this theoretical magnet would probably be enough to produce it. However, the operation of such a magnet, according to the general laws of the forces involved, could not possibly account for the very irregular arrangement of the curves indicating the degree of variation or declination. A general idea of these might perhaps be obtained by assuming there are two magnetic poles situated on a line a considerable distance from the center of the Earth, but this hypothesis is not accurate enough for us to rely on it. (Plate XLI. Fig. 577, 578.)

The art of making magnets consists of a proper application of the attractions and repulsions of the magnetic fluid. By using the different conducting powers of various kinds of iron and steel, one can produce and preserve a distribution of the fluid in a magnet that is best suited to displaying its unique properties.

We may begin with any bar of iron that has stood in a vertical position for a long time, but it is more common to use an artificial magnet of greater strength. When one pole of such a magnet touches the end of a bar of hard

iron or steel; that end assumes, to some degree, the opposite character, and the opposite end the same character. But in drawing the pole along the bar, the first end becomes neutral and later acquires the opposite polarity; meanwhile, the second end has its force at first slightly increased, then becomes neutral, and finally becomes opposite to what it first was. When the operation is repeated, the effect is at first somewhat destroyed, and it is difficult to understand why the repetition adds significantly to the unequal distribution of the <term>magnetic fluid</term>; however, the fact is certain, and the strength of the new magnet is for some time increased at each stroke, until it has acquired all that it is capable of receiving. Several magnets, made in this manner, may be placed side by side, and since each of them is nearly equal in strength to the first, the whole collection will produce together a much stronger effect. In this manner, we may obtain from a weak magnet others that are continually stronger, until we arrive at the greatest degree of polarity of which the metal is capable. It is, however, more usual to employ the process called the <term>double touch</term>: placing two magnets with their opposite poles near to each other, or the opposite poles of a single magnet bent into the form of a <term>horseshoe</term>, in contact with the middle of the bar. The opposite actions of these two poles then combine in their effort to displace the <term>magnetic fluid</term>, and after the magnets have been drawn backwards and forwards repeatedly, an equal number of times to and from each end of the bar with considerable pressure, they are at last withdrawn in the middle in order to keep the poles at equal distances.

Iron filings, or the <term>scoriae</term> from a smith’s forge, when finely <term>levigated</term> and formed into a paste with linseed oil, are also capable of being made collectively magnetic. A bar of steel, placed red hot between two magnets and suddenly quenched with cold water, becomes magnetic to some degree, but not as powerfully as it may be rendered by other means. To preserve magnets, it is customary to place their poles in contact with the opposite poles of other magnets, or with pieces of soft iron, which—in consequence of their own <term>induced magnetism</term>—tend to favor the accumulation of the magnetic power in a greater quantity than the metal can retain after they are removed. Hence, the ancients imagined that the magnet fed on iron.

There is no reason to imagine any immediate connection between magnetism and electricity, except that electricity affects the conducting powers of iron or steel for magnetism in the same manner as heat or agitation. In some cases, a blow, an increase of temperature, or a shock of electricity may slightly speed up the acquisition of <term>polarity</term>; but more commonly, any one of these causes impairs the magnetic power. Professor Robison found that when a good magnet was struck for three-quarters of an hour and allowed to ring in the meantime, its efficacy was destroyed, although the same operation had little effect when the ringing was impeded. Thus, the continued exertion of the <term>cohesive and repulsive powers</term> appears to favor the transmission of the <term>magnetic fluid</term> as well as the electric fluid. The internal agitation produced in bending a magnetic wire around a cylinder also destroys its <term>polarity</term>, and the use of a file has the same effect. Mr. Cavallo has found that brass generally becomes much more capable of being attracted when it has been hammered, even between two flints, and that this property is again diminished by fire. In this case, it may be conjectured that hammering increases the conducting power of the iron contained in the brass, and thus renders it more susceptible to magnetic action. Mr. Cavallo also observed that a <term>magnetic needle</term> was more powerfully attracted by iron filings during their solution in acids—especially in sulfuric acid—than either before or after the operation. Others have not always succeeded in this experiment, but there is nothing improbable in the circumstance, and there may have been some actual difference in the results, dependent on causes too minute for observation. ## LECTURE LVI.

### ON CLIMATES AND WINDS.

The science of meteorology relates mainly to the natural history of the air, and to such temporary changes in the earth and sea as are produced by causes that are not purely mechanical. The subject is of a very complicated and intricate nature; it includes many effects derived from causes that belong separately to every department of physics which we have examined so far; and although it has occupied the attention of several eminent philosophers, we cannot yet boast of having made any great progress in it. Whether we shall ever be able to develop our theories to such a high degree of perfection as to provide us with much information applicable to the purposes of daily life, to agriculture, or to medicine, is at present uncertain; although some advantage has already been derived from the readings of meteorological instruments, and the theoretical science is in many respects much more advanced than has commonly been supposed. We shall divide this extensive subject into two parts: the first relating mainly to the effects of heat on the atmosphere, including the phenomena of winds; the second to the nature and consequences of evaporation, including atmospheric electricity, and the effects of subterranean fires and fiery meteors.

The variations of temperature in different parts of the earth's surface must be examined first, since they are not only of considerable importance in themselves, but are also among the primary causes of other changes in the state of the winds and weather. These changes are measured by thermometers of various kinds, which have already been described; but, for meteorological purposes, some additions are frequently made to the simple thermometer. In <term>Six's thermometer</term>, the tube is bent twice so as to return in a parallel direction; the bulb is in the form of a long cylinder, and

...is usually filled with spirit of wine, which is in contact with a portion of mercury occupying the lower part of the tube; this is followed by a second portion of spirit. The mercury carries an index on each of its surfaces, which is held in its furthest position by a weak spring; consequently, it shows the greatest degree of heat or cold that has occurred since the last observation. The indexes are made of iron or steel and may be brought back to the surface as desired by using a magnet; they are carried up by the mercury, more by its capillary action than by the difference in their specific gravities. A similar effect is obtained in Rutherford's arrangement of a pair of thermometers—one with mercury, the other with spirit of wine—placed in a horizontal position. One index is outside the surface of the mercury, and the other is within that of the spirit. Since the thermometers are facing in opposite directions, both indexes may be returned to their places simply by raising the end of the instrument. Self-registering thermometers have also sometimes been constructed to keep an even more accurate record of all temperature variations that have occurred; they do this by tracing a line on a revolving barrel, which shows the temperature at every moment during the entire time of their operation. (Plate XLI. Figures 579, 580.)

The climates of different parts of the earth's surface are unquestionably due, in large part, to their position relative to the sun. At the equator, where the sun is always nearly vertical, any given part of the surface receives a much greater quantity of light and heat than an equal portion near the poles. It is also even more affected by the sun's vertical rays because their passage through the atmosphere is shorter than that of the oblique rays. Regarding the sun's mean altitude alone, it appears from Simpson's calculations that the heat received at the equator over the entire year is nearly two and a half times as great as at the poles. This proportion is nearly the same as the ratio of the meridian heat of a vertical sun to the heat received at an altitude of 23.5°, in the middle of the long annual day at the poles. However, the difference is made even greater by the effect of the atmosphere, which blocks a larger portion of the heat at the poles than elsewhere. Bouguer has calculated—based on the assumption that heat and light behave similarly—that in latitude 45°, 80 parts out of 100 are transmitted at noon in July, while only 55 are in December. The heat intercepted by the atmosphere is perhaps not entirely, but very nearly, lost in relation to the climate of the

neighboring places. It is obvious that, at any individual place, the climate in summer must resemble the equatorial climate to some degree, as the sun's altitude is greater, and in winter it must resemble the climate of the polar regions.

While the earth is warming at any particular spot, the heat thrown off by radiation into the atmosphere—and from there into the empty space beyond it—together with the heat transmitted to the internal parts of the earth, must be less than the heat received from the sun. When the earth is growing colder, more heat must pass off than is received; but whenever the surface temperature is stationary, neither increasing nor decreasing (as at the times of maximum and minimum heat), it is obvious that the heat received from the sun must be exactly equal to the heat that is thrown off. This quantity may be estimated by the degree of cooling at night; and from this, Mr. Prévost has very cleverly deduced the proportion of the sun's heat reaching the surface of the earth at the latitude of Geneva in July and in December, which he finds to be a ratio of 7 or 8 to 1. This result agrees very well with a calculation based on the length of the day, the sun's altitude, and the interception of its rays by the atmosphere.

In London, the temperature generally varies between day and night by somewhat more than 5° and less than 20°. In January, the mean daily variation of temperature is 6°, in March 20°, in July 10°, and in September 18°. Therefore, says Mr. Kirwan, we may understand the reason for the great frequency of colds in spring and in autumn.

Some philosophers have supposed that the earth becomes progressively warmer over the ages, while others have imagined that its heat is being exhausted. Both of these opinions generally appear improbable. The more heat the earth receives by day, the more it throws off, both by day and by night; so that in the course of a few ages, the heat must probably have reached its maximum. Local changes may indeed arise from local circumstances; for example, the climate of America is said to have become considerably warmer since a large part of its surface was cleared of its dense forests by human labor. Judging from the descriptions of the ancient writers, it appears that even in Europe, the winters were formerly much colder than they are at present. If, however, Dr. Herschel's opinion regarding the variation of the sun's heat is

The sea is less heated than the land, partly because a greater quantity of water <term>evaporates</term> from it, and partly because the sun's rays penetrate to a considerable depth and have less effect on the surface. Additionally, the water is mixed by the agitation of its waves and currents with the colder water below. It is also cooled more slowly than the land, since, when the temperature of the surface particles is lowered, they become heavier and sink to the bottom. For similar reasons, the sea is colder than the land in hot climates and by day, and warmer in cold climates and by night. These circumstances, however, nearly balance each other, so that the <term>mean temperatures</term> of both are equal, with the sea's temperature being merely less variable. Although the process of <term>evaporation</term> must cool the sea, when the vapors are <term>condensed</term> without reaching the land, their <term>condensation</term> must compensate for this effect by an equal release of heat.

There is another cause which perhaps contributes in some degree to the production of cold in temperate climates: the alternation of freezing and thawing. Mr. Prévost observes that <term>congelation</term> (freezing) takes place much more suddenly than the opposite process of <term>liquefaction</term> (melting); consequently, the same quantity of heat must be more rapidly released in freezing than is absorbed in thawing. Since the heat thus released is inclined to dissipate in all directions and little of it is retained by neighboring bodies, more heat is lost than is gained by the alternation. Therefore, where ice has once been formed, its production is redoubled in this manner. This circumstance must occur wherever it freezes—that is, on shore, in latitudes above 35°. It appears that from about 30° to the pole, the land is somewhat colder than the sea, and increasingly so the further it is from it; nearer the equator, the land is warmer than the sea. However, the process of <term>congelation</term> cannot by any means be the primary cause of the difference, and it is probable that the different <term>heat capacity</term> of earth and water is significantly involved in it.

Since the <term>atmosphere</term> is very little heated by the passage of the sun's rays through it, it is naturally colder than the earth's surface;

and for this reason, the highest areas of land, which are the most prominent and the most exposed to the effects of the atmosphere, are always colder than locations closer to sea level. The northern hemisphere is somewhat warmer than the southern, perhaps because of the greater proportion of land it contains, and also to some extent because its summer is longer than that of the southern hemisphere. For although it was observed long ago by Simpson that the sun's varying distance compensates exactly for the earth's varying speed in its orbit—regarding the total quantity of heat received on either side of the equinoxes—Mr. Prévost has shown that, in all probability, the same quantity of heat must produce a greater effect when it is applied more slowly. This is because the portion lost by radiation from a heated body is greater as the temperature rises. 

Therefore, because of the eccentricity of the earth's orbit, the North Pole is turned toward the sun seven or eight days longer than the South Pole, and so northern winters must be milder than southern ones. Yet the southern summers, though shorter, should be somewhat warmer than the northern ones; in reality, however, they are colder, perhaps partly due to the much larger proportion of sea—which balances the temperature to some extent—and partly for other reasons. The relative intensity of the southern summer and winter is not precisely known, but on the island of New Georgia <note>Likely referring to South Georgia Island in the southern Atlantic</note>, the summer is said to be extremely cold.

Northern ice extends about 9° from the pole, while southern ice extends 18° or 20°, and in some parts even 30°. Floating ice has occasionally been found in both hemispheres as far as 40° from the poles, and sometimes, it is said, even at latitude 41° or 42°. Between 54° and 60° south latitude, snow remains on the ground at the seaside throughout the summer. The line of perpetual <term>congelation</term> (freezing) is three miles above the surface at the equator, where the mean temperature is 84°; at Tenerife, at latitude 28°, it is two miles high; at the latitude of London, a little more than a mile; and at 80° north latitude, it is only 1,200 feet. At the pole, according to the analogy deduced by Mr. Kirwan from a comparison of various observations, the mean temperature should be 31°. In London, the mean temperature is 50°; at Rome and Montpellier, a little more than 60°; on the island of Madeira, 70°; and in Jamaica, 80°.

Thus, it has been observed that when the weather is clear and a cloud passes over the place of observation, the thermometer frequently rises a degree or two almost instantaneously. This has been partly explained by considering the cloud as a covering, preventing the escape of the heat which is always radiating from the earth and reflecting it back to the surface; the cloud may also have been recently condensed and may itself be of a higher temperature than the earth. Mr. Six <note>James Six (1731–1793), the English inventor of the maximum-minimum thermometer.</note> has observed that in clear weather, the air is usually some degrees colder at night and warmer by day close to the ground than a few feet above it, but that in cloudy weather there is less difference. It is possible that this circumstance may be derived from the difference in the amount of evaporation from the earth's surface, which causes a different degree of cold in different states of the atmosphere.

The motions of the air, which constitute winds, are generally dependent, in the first instance, on variations of temperature. They are so accidental and uncertain that they are subject to no universal laws; however, as far as any regularity can be observed in their recurrence, it may in most cases be sufficiently explained.

The principal phenomena of the periodic winds may be reduced to six distinct categories: first, the general tendency from the northeast and southeast toward the equator in latitudes below 30°; second, the deviation of this tendency from the exact position of the equator; third, the prevalence of westerly winds between 30° and 40° or more, especially in the southern hemisphere; fourth, the local modifications to which these general effects are subject; fifth, the monsoons, which vary every half year; and lastly, the diurnal changes of land and sea breezes.

With respect to the general tendency of the trade winds toward the west, it may be sufficiently explained by Hadley's theory of the difference in the rotational motion of different parts of the atmosphere, combined with the currents caused by the greater heat at the equator. For the sun's rays, expanding the air in the vicinity of the equator and causing it to ascend, produce a current in the lower parts of the atmosphere; these rush southward and northward toward the equator in order to occupy the place of the heated air as it rises. And since the rotational motion of the earth is...

Dr. Halley supposed that the air was made in some measure to follow the sun around the earth, simply by means of the expansion of the atmosphere, which takes place immediately under it, and accompanies it around the globe; but it does not seem evident that the air could have any greater tendency to follow the sun than to meet it. Astronomers have, however, deduced an additional cause for an easterly wind from the attractions of the moon and of the sun, which appear, from the laws of gravitation, to have a slight tendency to retard the rotary motion of the atmosphere: and a similar instance has been observed in the motions of the atmosphere of the planet Jupiter, by means of the appearances of spots of different kinds on its disk, some of which seem to revolve less rapidly than the body of the planet. At so great a distance, the influence of the sun's heat must be comparatively inconsiderable, and the lack of a tendency in the spots toward the equator appears to show that the atmosphere in which they float is not put in motion by the same causes which we have supposed to be most concerned in the production of our own trade winds. It has been remarked that the friction of the atmosphere, thus retarded by the attraction of the sun and moon, must in the course of ages have impaired the uniformity of the earth's diurnal motion; and it has been observed, on the other hand, that even this effect would be partially counteracted by the gradual filling up of valleys, by means of the descent of the surface parts of mountains, which, at a greater distance from the center, were revolving with a rapidity somewhat greater than the valleys in which they are deposited; but probably neither of these changes would become sensible in millions of years.

The second circumstance is easily explained by the greater heat of the northern than of the southern hemisphere; so that instead of coinciding with the equator, the neutral portion of the atmosphere lies between 3° and 5° of north latitude; the northeast wind not reaching the equator, and the southeast continuing about 3° beyond it. Where northern and southern currents meet, their joint effect must naturally be to produce a due east wind; but in some parts of the ocean, temporary calms and irregular squalls have been observed to take the place of this easterly wind, which generally prevails in the neutral parts near the equator.

<insert>REESE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</insert>

The third fact, that is, the frequency of westerly winds between the latitudes 30° and 40°, has not yet been sufficiently explained. The most probable cause of this circumstance is that the current of heated air, which we have until now neglected, and which passes in the upper parts of the atmosphere from the equator each way toward the poles—and which, being the opposite of the trade wind, must be a southwest and northwest wind in the different hemispheres—becomes cool enough here to descend and mix with the lower parts of the atmosphere, or to carry them along by its lateral friction. While it descends to complete the circle necessary for supplying the current to the equator, its motion with respect to the horizon must become at a certain time due west, since the cause which stops its progress northward has no tendency to impede its motion eastward. Outward-bound East India ships generally make their easting in about 36° south latitude. It is probably also on account of the rotary motion of the earth that southwest winds are more common in our latitudes than southeast, and northeast than northwest.

Among the local modifications to be considered in the fourth place, we may reckon the greater indistinctness of the third effect in the northern than in the southern hemisphere, a circumstance which is explained by the more irregular distribution of sea and land; for between 30° and 40° south latitude the ocean is scarcely anywhere interrupted. In lower latitudes also, near the west coast of Africa, the winds are so much deflected toward the land as to become in general westerly instead of easterly.

The monsoons, which constitute the fifth remarkable circumstance, are so called from a Malay word meaning season. They are caused by the peculiar situation of the continent of Asia on the north side of the equator. From April to September, the sun having northern declination, the heat on this continent—a little north of the tropic—is very intense, and the general current is consequently toward the north. Both these winds are, however, variously modified by the particular situations of the islands and continents. From October to March, on the contrary, the sun having south declination, the southeast trade wind stops at 10° south latitude; the trade winds on the north side of the equator are, as usual, northeast; and beyond the equator they become for some degrees northwest, the circumstances being the reverse of those which happen in the summer months, at greater distances, on the other side of the equator. (Plate XLII. XLIII.)

The last fact is the simplest of all. The land and sea breezes are produced by the ascent of the air over the land in the daytime, while the land is hotter than the sea; and its descent at night, when the land has become colder: hence the breeze comes from the sea by day, and from the land by night.

The violent agitations of the air, which constitute hurricanes and whirlwinds, occur more commonly in tropical climates than in others. The causes of these storms are little understood: their course is said to be generally opposite to that of the trade winds; but tornadoes, which are less regular hurricanes, originate indifferently from every quarter.

The variations of the weight of the air, which occasion the winds, and other changes in its density, which are the effects of the winds themselves, are indicated by the height of the barometer, which is in general more variable as the winds are more liable to sudden changes. Hence, in the neighborhood of the equator, the height of the barometer is scarcely ever a quarter of an inch more or less than 30 inches, which is very nearly its mean height at sea level in every part of the globe: in Great Britain, it is sometimes as low as 28 inches, but never higher than 31. We have already seen that the elevation of any place above the sea reduces the height of the barometer according to a law which is determined by the general

<header>ON WATER AND WEATHER.</header>

## LECTURE LVII.

## ON AQUEOUS AND IGNEOUS METEORS.

The phenomena originating from the evaporation of water constitute a large proportion of the subjects of meteorology: they are materially influenced by the diversities of climates and winds, which we have lately considered; and they appear to contribute to the electrical changes, which form a principal part of luminous or igneous meteors: nor is the action of water wholly unconcerned in many of the effects of subterranean fires, which have also a slight connection with atmospheric electricity; and it has been conjectured that the only igneous meteors, which appear wholly independent of any of these phenomena, may originate from volcanic commotions in other worlds.

The action of heat appears to detach continually from the surface of water, and perhaps of every other liquid, and even solid, a certain quantity of vapor, in the form of an invisible gas; but when the space above the liquid is already charged with as much vapor as can exist in it at the actual temperature, the vapor, thus continually thrown off, either remains suspended in the form of visible particles, or falls back immediately into the liquid. This is the simplest mode of explaining the continuance of evaporation, under the pressure of any dry gas, however dense, and its apparent suppression in the presence of moist air, however rare. Sometimes also, when the temperature of the liquid is elevated, so that minute globules either of steam or of air rise through it, some visible particles are projected upwards by each globule, and continue to float in the air; this appears, however, to be an irregularity unconnected with the principal process of slow evaporation.

The quantity of vapor, which can exist in the space above any portion of water, has been supposed by Deluc, Volta, and Dalton, to be wholly independent of the nature, the density, or even the presence of the air or gas

We may easily imagine that the smallest distance at which the particles of water, constituting vapor, can exist without coming within the reach of their mutual cohesion, is the same, regardless of whatever other particles may be scattered through the intervening space. It appears, however, more consistent with some experiments to suppose that the presence of air at its usual density allows the particles of water to approach a little nearer together without cohering. Consequently, the maximum quantity of moisture that can be contained in a cubic foot of air at a given temperature is not exactly the same as would make a cubic foot of pure vapor, but is always in a certain proportion to it. It seems to follow from the experiments of Saussure, compared with those of Pictet, that the weight of the vapor contained in a cubic foot of air is about one-half greater than that of a cubic foot of pure vapor at the same temperature.

When the air near the surface of the water has become thus saturated with moisture, evaporation proceeds very slowly, the vapor being precipitated as soon as it rises. But if the air is continually changed, so that the moistened portion may be removed and dry air substituted for it, the process will be greatly expedited. Such a change may be effected either by wind or by the natural circulation caused by any elevation of temperature communicated by the water to the neighboring air. But when this circulation is prevented, evaporation is much diminished, although the temperature may be considerably elevated. In moderate exposures, the depth of the quantity of water evaporating in 24 hours from any surface is expressed, according to Mr. Dalton's experiments, by the height of the column of mercury equivalent to the force of steam at the given temperature, deducting, however, the effect of the elasticity <note>In this context, "elasticity" refers to vapor pressure or tension.</note> of the moisture already existing in the air.

Since the quantity of moisture which the air is capable of receiving is greater as its temperature is greater, we may obtain a natural measure of the quantity which it contains by reducing it to the temperature at which the moisture begins to be deposited. Thus, if we take a glass of cold water and add some common salt or some muriate of lime <note>Now known as calcium chloride.</note> to it, we may cool the air near it so much as to cause it to deposit a part of its moisture on the glass. By measuring the temperature of the water when the precipitation begins,

Mr. Dalton estimates the true state of the air with respect to moisture in this way: if the glass begins to be moistened when the water is at 40°, he infers from the known <term>elasticity of steam</term> at that temperature that the quantity of moisture contained in the air is equivalent to the pressure of a column of mercury about a quarter of an inch in height. If the actual temperature of the air is 50°, and the corresponding elasticity of steam is a little more than one-third of an inch, the daily evaporation in such air will amount to about one-ninth of an inch, totaling 40 inches for the entire year. In fact, however, the air is usually more humid than this, and the average evaporation across all of England is, according to Mr. Dalton, only about 23 inches.

In hotter climates and in specific situations, evaporation may be considerably greater. The Mediterranean Sea, being surrounded by land, is heated more than the ocean, and the winds which blow over it are drier; consequently, its evaporation is greater than that of the Atlantic, and its specific gravity is increased by the higher proportion of salt. Because of this, at the Straits of Gibraltar, a current flows inward at the surface and outward near the bottom, for the same reason that air—when it is denser in a hallway than in an adjoining room—blows a candle toward the room at the bottom of the door and draws it toward the hallway at the top. Had there been a continuous inward current through the Straits at all depths, the Mediterranean must, in the course of ages, have become a solid block of salt. It is indeed remarkable that all lakes into which rivers flow without any further outlet are more or less salty, as are lakes in general near the sea; but where a river flows through a lake into the sea, it must necessarily, over time, have carried the salt of the lake with it, if any had ever existed.

Experiments on the deposition of moisture, like those of Mr. Dalton, are prone to slight inaccuracies on account of the effects of an apparent <term>elective attraction</term>, by which some substances seem to attract humidity at a temperature a little higher than others. For example, a metal surface often remains dry in the neighborhood of a piece of glass that is covered with moisture. It is certain that some substances attract moisture from the air even when the quantity it contains is incomparably less than what would saturate it, since it is on this circumstance that the construction of hygrometers depends; and it is probably by a property somewhat si-

It is, however, only necessary to use, for Mr. Dalton’s experiment, a substance which has a very weak attraction for moisture; and any kind of metal will perhaps be found sufficiently correct in its indications.

It has been observed that a piece of metal placed on glass usually protects the opposite side of the glass from the deposition of dew as well. Mr. Benedict Prévost has shown that, in general, whenever the metal is placed on the warmer side of the glass, the humidity is deposited more copiously either on the metal itself or on the glass near it. When it is on the colder side, it neither receives the humidity nor permits its deposition on the glass; however, the addition of a second piece of glass over the metal destroys the effect, and a second piece of metal restores it. It appears that, due to its properties regarding radiant heat, the metallic surface produces these effects by preventing the easy communication of either heat or cold to the glass.

The quantity of invisible moisture contained in air may be estimated, to some degree, from the readings of hygrometers, although these instruments have so far remained in a state of great imperfection. A sponge, a quantity of caustic potash, sulfuric acid, or a stone of a specific nature has sometimes been used to determine the degree of moisture in the air, from which the substance acquires a certain increase in weight. A cord dipped in brine, or the beard of an oat, is also often used for the same purpose: the degree to which it untwists due to the effect of moisture is shown by an index. However, the extension of a hair or of a slip of whalebone, which have been used by Saussure and Deluc, appears to be more certain and accurate in its indications. The hair hygrometer more quickly reaches the degree corresponding to any given state of the air, but it seems to reach the maximum limit of its scale before it reaches perfect humidity. Meanwhile, the whalebone hygrometer appears to show a greater change upon immersion in water than from the effect of the moistest transparent air, which some have also considered an imperfection. Both of these instruments are impaired by time and develop opposing errors, so that an average between the two is more likely to be correct than either one separately. Their readings are always widely different from each other, and the average appears to approach much closer to a natural

Mr. Leslie employs a very delicate thermometer, of which the bulb is moistened, for measuring the dryness of the air by the cold produced during evaporation when the thermometer is exposed to it; but this mode of estimating the quantity of moisture appears to be liable to considerable uncertainty. (Plate XLI. Fig. 581.)

In order for the scale of a hygrometer to be perfectly natural, it should express, at all temperatures, the proportion of the quantity of moisture in the air to that which is required for its saturation. Thus, at 100 degrees, it should imply that the slightest drop in temperature would produce a deposition; at 50 degrees, it should mean that the air contains only half as much water as would saturate it; or, assuming the thermometer is at 52°, that a deposition would be produced in it by a drop of 17°. If we know the actual temperature and the temperature at which the deposition takes place, we may find the reading of the natural hygrometer by the proportion of the corresponding elasticities of steam. The average reading of the natural hygrometer in London is probably about 80°; that of Deluc's hygrometer, with proper corrections, being nearly 70°: so that a drop of 6° must usually be sufficient to cause a deposition of moisture.

The quantity of water actually contained in a cubic foot of air saturated with moisture appears to be about 2 grains at the freezing point, 4 grains at 48°, 6 grains at 60°, and 8 grains at 68°. According to Saussure’s experiments, the density of the vapor mixed with air in this way is about three-fourths as great as that of the air itself; consequently, moist air is always a little lighter than dry air, and even more so as the air is warmer, provided that it is saturated with moisture by the presence of water. It follows from the properties of moisture determined in this way that if any two portions of perfectly humid air at different temperatures are mixed together, there must be a precipitation. For example, if a cubic foot of air at 32° is mixed with another at 60°, their common temperature must be 46°. If they are saturated with moisture, they must contain 8 grains of water when separate; but when mixed, they will be 2° too cold to contain the same quantity, since air at 48° can only contain 4 grains for each foot. It has been supposed that such mixtures frequently cause precipitation in nature. Thus, it often happens that the breath of an animal, which is transparent in itself, becomes visible when mixed with a cold atmosphere

When visible vapor has been deposited in this way from transparent air, either through cold or mixture, it generally remains suspended for some time in the form of a mist or a cloud. Sometimes, however, it appears to be deposited immediately onto the surface of a solid in the form of dew or hoar frost; for it is unlikely that the crystalline form in which hoar frost is arranged could be derived from the union of particles already existing in the air as distinct clusters.

The dew commonly deposited on plants is derived partly from vapors ascending from the heated earth in the evening—since it is then found on the internal surface of a bell glass—and towards the morning, from moisture descending from the air above as it begins to cool. Sometimes, however, in warmer weather, the dew begins to descend in the evening; the French call this <term>serein</term> <note>evening dew falling from a clear sky</note>. The humidity deposited by mists on trees, and by moist air on windows—generally on the inside, but sometimes on the outside—they call <term>givre</term> <note>hoar frost or rime</note>.

Mists are sometimes said to consist of particles other than pure water; these are called dry mists, and they have been thought to blight plants. Such mists are sometimes accompanied by a smell resembling that produced by an electric spark. Rain falling after a dry season deposits particles of foreign matter brought down from the atmosphere, once the water is allowed to stand. Indeed, there must frequently be many different kinds of substances floating in the air; the wind has been known to carry the <term>farina</term> <note>pollen</note> of plants as far as 30 or 40 miles, and the ashes of a volcano more than 200 miles. It only requires the size of any substance's particles to be sufficiently reduced to make them incapable of falling at any significant speed; when this velocity is very low, it may easily be overcome by any random movements of the air. The diameter of a sphere of water falling at the rate of only one inch per second would need to be one six-hundred-thousandth of an inch, which is about the thickness of the top of a soap bubble at the moment it bursts. However, the particles in mists are incomparably larger than this, as they would otherwise be completely invisible as separate drops; the smallest particle that could

But it is very probable that the resistance opposed to the motion of particles so small may be considerably greater than would be expected from a calculation derived from experiments made on a much larger scale, and their descent consequently much slower.

When the particles of a mist are united into drops capable of descending with a considerable velocity, they form rain; if they are frozen during their deposition, they show the appearance of a perfect crystallization and become snow; but if the drops already formed are frozen, either by means of external cold or on account of the great evaporation produced by a rapid descent through very dry air, they acquire the character of hail, which is often observed in weather much too hot for the formation of snow.

It cannot be doubted that there is a connection between the drop in the barometer and the fall of rain; but no satisfactory reason has yet been assigned for this circumstance; nor is it possible to foretell, with certainty, that rain will follow any changes in the height of the barometer that have been observed. The immediate dependence of rain, or of any other atmospheric phenomena, on the influence of the moon, appears to be rendered highly improbable, not only by mathematical calculations of the effects of the moon's attraction, but also by the irregularity of the very observations which have been cited in favor of such a connection. But however uncertain the ultimate causes of rain may be in general, their effects in some places are sufficiently constant to be attributed to permanent local circumstances, and in particular to the periodical recurrence of similar winds.

In low and level countries, clouds may often begin to descend from the upper regions of the atmosphere and may be dissolved again by the warmer air below; but when they descend in an equal degree among mountains, they fall on the earth; and besides the quantity of water which they provide for vegetation, and that which is carried off by evaporation, they afford, by means of springs and rivers, a constant supply for the use of humans and other animals in distant parts. The upper regions of the atmosphere are, however, by no means the principal sources of rain in ordinary climates, since a gauge placed on a very high building seldom collects more than two-thirds as much rain as another standing on the ground below; and the effects of mountains in

The Abyssinian rains are the causes of the inundation of the Nile; they last from April to September; but for the first three months the rain is only in the night. The inundation, in Egypt, begins at present about the 17th of June; it increases for 40 days, and subsides in the same time; but the ancient accounts, as well as some modern ones, assign a longer duration to it. The river Laplata <note>The Río de la Plata in South America.</note> rises and falls at the same times as the Nile. The Ganges, the Indus, the Euphrates, the river of Ava or Pegu <note>Likely referring to the Irrawaddy River in modern-day Myanmar.</note>, and many other large rivers, have also considerable inundations at regular periods. In many other countries there are seasons at which the rains seldom fail to recur; and sometimes the periodical rains are different in different parts of the same country. Thus the coast of Malabar, which is to the west of the Gate mountains, or Gauts <note>The Western Ghats mountain range in India.</note>, enjoys summer weather, without rain, from September to April, while that of Coromandel, which is on the eastern side, experiences all the rigors of its winter; being at this time exposed to the influence of the northeast trade wind. Vicissitudes of a similar nature are also observed on the north and south sides of the island of Jamaica. The mean fall of rain in London is about 23 inches; at Exeter, which is nearer to the Atlantic, 33; the average of England and Wales is 31.

The evaporations and precipitations, and probably also the condensations and expansions, which take place on a large scale in the atmosphere and in the clouds, cannot fail of producing changes in their electrical qualities; and these changes appear to be the principal sources of the phenomena of thunder and lightning. The clouds, when electrified, being more or less insulated by the interposition of the air, exhibit attractive and repulsive effects, and are discharged by explosions, either among themselves, or communicating with the earth, in the same manner as bodies which have been electrified by artificial means; they also sometimes produce, in the neighboring parts of the earth, and in the animals on its surface, a state of induced electricity; and in this case the returning stroke, or the sudden restoration of the equilibrium, when the electricity of the nearest clouds is imparted to the more remote, may be fatal, without any appearance of an immediate discharge, at the place where the animal stands.

<header>### LECTURE LVII.</header>

We cannot, however, by any means precisely determine in what manner all the electrical phenomena of the atmosphere are produced. It appears from the experiments of Beccaria and Cavallo that the air is generally positively electrical, and most significantly so in cold and clear weather; in cloudy weather, it is more slightly so; and during rain, the air is generally in a negative state. Mr. Read has found that air filled with foul vapors of any kind, and in particular the air of confined rooms, is almost always negatively electrified. The electricity is more easily communicated to an electrometer in an elevated location, and in damp weather, than in other circumstances; a candle is also very useful for collecting it. When a wire is connected to a kite and run along the string, we may frequently obtain sparks from it a quarter of an inch long.

We find a complete and interesting description of the effects of a violent thunderstorm in a paper by Mr. Brereton, included in the *Philosophical Transactions*. The event occurred in September 1780, at East Bourn <note>Now known as Eastbourne.</note>, in a house occupied by Mr. Adair; it was built of stone and faced the sea. About nine o’clock on a very stormy morning, a black cloud approached the house; several balls of fire were seen to drop from it one after another into the sea, and one in particular, appearing like an immense skyrocket, broke against the front of the house in different directions. Mr. Adair was standing at a window on the first floor with his hands clasped together and held against the middle of the frame. His hands were forced apart, he was thrown several yards onto the floor, and he remained for some time speechless and motionless, though not unconscious. His clothes were badly torn; several metal items on his person were partially melted, while others in apparently similar circumstances—and specifically a silver buckle—escaped damage; and his skin was badly scorched and torn in many places. All of the glass in the window, and a pier mirror near it, were completely destroyed and scattered about the room; most of the furniture was broken to pieces, and all the bell wires were melted. In the room above this, a lady and her maid were driven to a far corner and rendered unconscious for some time, but they were not injured. In the room below, two servants who were near the windows were struck dead: both their bodies turned black; one of them had a wound near the heart, and neither of them became stiff after death. A third servant, who was a little behind one of them,

To guard against such dreadful accidents, Dr. Franklin’s great invention of metallic conductors may be very advantageously employed; for, when properly fixed, they provide a degree of security that leaves very little room for apprehension. A conductor should be extended deep into the earth or connected with some well or drain; it should be of ample dimensions and, where it is thinnest, made of copper, since copper conducts electricity more readily than iron. In one instance, an iron conductor four inches wide and half an inch thick appears to have been made red-hot by a lightning strike. It seems to be of some advantage for a conductor to be pointed, but this circumstance is of less consequence than has often been supposed. Mr. Wilson demonstrated some experiments in which a point was struck at a greater distance than a ball, and he therefore argued against the use of pointed conductors. Mr. Nairne, on the contrary, showed that a ball is often struck in preference to a point. But it has been observed that if a point attracts the lightning from a greater distance, it must protect a larger area of the building. It is easy to show, by hanging cotton or wool on a conductor, that a point repels light electrical bodies, and that a pointed conductor may, therefore, drive away some fleecy clouds; but this effect is principally derived from a current of air repelled by the point, and such a current could scarcely be expected to have any perceptible effect on clouds as distant as those involved in thunderstorms. To escape personal danger in a thunderstorm, the best precautions are to avoid high ground and all exposed situations, as well as staying away from conductors. Being near windows, mirrors, fireplaces, and trees must always be considered hazardous.

It has been suggested that a sudden condensation of the air caused by cold, accompanied by a deposition of moisture and spread by the continued cause—through the cold created by expansion—frequently produces the sound of thunder without any lightning and without any electrical activity; however, it does not appear that this opinion is well-established.

<summary>This page discusses the utility of Benjamin Franklin's lightning conductors, the debate between pointed and blunt conductors, and safety advice for avoiding lightning strikes. It also briefly mentions an unproven theory regarding the production of thunder without lightning.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of natural phenomena and their relation to electricity, moving from the use of lightning conductors to the scientific causes of waterspouts, the aurora borealis, earthquakes, and volcanoes.</meta>

<page-num>716</page-num>
<header>LECTURE LVII.</header>

The phenomena of <term>waterspouts</term>, if not of electrical origin, appear to have some connection with electrical causes. A waterspout generally consists of large drops, like a dense rain, much agitated, and descending or ascending with a spiral motion, at the same time that the whole spout is carried along horizontally, generally accompanied by a sound like that of the crashing of waves. Spouts are sometimes, though rarely, observed on shore, but generally in the neighborhood of water. They are commonly largest at the top; sometimes two cones project, one from a cloud and the other from the sea below it, to meet each other, the junction being accompanied by a flash of lightning. When the entire spout has exhibited a luminous appearance, it has perhaps served to conduct electricity slowly from the clouds to the earth. Some of these circumstances may be explained by considering the spout as a <term>whirlwind</term>, carrying up drops of water which it has separated from the surface of the waves; and the remainder may perhaps be deduced from the cooperation of electricity already existing in a neighboring cloud.

It is doubtful whether the light of the <term>aurora borealis</term> may not be of an electrical nature; the phenomenon is certainly connected with the general cause of <term>magnetism</term>. The primitive beams of light are supposed to be at an elevation of at least 50 or 100 miles above the earth, and everywhere in a direction parallel to that of the <term>dipping needle</term>; but perhaps, although the substance is magnetic, the illumination which renders it visible may still be derived from the passage of electricity at too great a distance to be discovered by any other test.

<term>Earthquakes</term> and <term>volcanoes</term> appear to originate in chemical changes that take place within the substance of the earth. They probably have little further connection with electricity, other than as causes which occasionally destroy the <term>electrical equilibrium</term>; for although some authors have inferred, from the great velocity with which the shock of an earthquake is transmitted from place to place, that its nature must be electrical, others have, with greater probability, attributed the rapid succession of the effects to the operation of a single cause acting at a great distance below the earth’s surface. There are, however, some circumstances which indicate such a connection between the state of the atmosphere and the approach of an earthquake as cannot easily be explained by any hypothesis.

<summary>This page explores the scientific theories behind waterspouts, the aurora borealis, earthquakes, and volcanoes, examining how they may or may not be linked to electrical and magnetic forces. The author suggests that while some atmospheric events are clearly electrical, geological events like earthquakes primarily result from internal chemical changes.</summary>

# ON AQUEOUS AND IGNEOUS METEORS.
<sig>VOL. I. 4 U</sig>
The shocks of earthquakes and the eruptions of volcanoes are, in all probability, variations of the effects of a single common cause; the same countries are susceptible to both of them; and where the shaking produced by an earthquake extends further than there is any reason to suspect an underground disturbance, it is likely propagated through the earth in nearly the same manner as a noise is conveyed through the air. Volcanoes are found in almost all parts of the world, but most commonly in the neighborhood of the sea, and especially on small islands; for instance, in Italy, Sicily, Iceland, Japan, the Caribbean, the Cape Verde Islands, the Canaries, and the Azores. There are also numerous volcanoes in Mexico and Peru, especially Pichincha and Cotopaxi. The underground fires, which are continually maintained in an active volcano, perhaps generally depend on sulfurous combinations and decompositions, like the heating of a pile of wet pyrites, or the reaction of sulfur and iron filings; but in other cases, they may perhaps more closely resemble the nature of common fires. A mountain of coal has been burning in Siberia for almost a century and has likely undermined the neighboring country to some degree. The immediate cause of an eruption appears to be very frequently the entry of water from the sea or from underground reservoirs. It has often happened that boiling water has been discharged in great quantities from a volcano, and the force of steam is perhaps better able to produce violent explosions than any other power in nature. The consequence of such an entry of water into an immense collection of burning materials may, to some extent, be understood from the accidents which occasionally happen in foundries; for example, an entire furnace of molten iron was recently blasted into the air in Coalbrookdale by the effect of a flood which suddenly overflowed it.

The phenomena of earthquakes and volcanoes are thoroughly illustrated by the detailed accounts of those which have happened at different times in Italy, sent to the Royal Society by Sir William Hamilton. The earthquake which devastated Calabria in 1783 was fatal to about 40,000 persons, continuing its destruction for more than three months. It destroyed the towns and villages occupying a circle of nearly 50 miles in diameter, located between 38 and 39 degrees latitude, and extending almost from the western to the eastern coast of the southernmost point of Italy, besides doing considerable damage to places at much greater distances from its origin, which is supposed to have been either immediately under the town

This island, as well as Mount Etna, had smoked less than usual before the earthquake, but they both showed signs of an eruption while it continued: Etna toward the beginning, and Stromboli at the end. Before each shock, the clouds were usually motionless for a certain time, and it rained violently; lightning and sudden gusts of wind also frequently accompanied the rain. The principal shocks appeared to consist of a sudden elevation of the ground to a considerable height, which spread somewhat like a wave from west to east. Besides this, the ground also had a horizontal motion backward and forward, and to some extent in a circular direction. This motion was accompanied by a loud noise; in one instance, it continued for ten seconds without interruption, and it shook the trees so violently that their tops nearly reached the ground. It affected the plains more strongly than the hills. In some places, the earth emitted luminous exhalations, which Sir William Hamilton thinks were electrical rather than igneous. The sea boiled up near Messina and was agitated as if by a massive discharge of vapors from its bottom; and in several places, water mixed with sand was thrown up to a considerable height. The most general effect of these violent commotions was the destruction of buildings of all kinds, except for the light barracks made of wood or reeds, which the inhabitants fled into as soon as they were aware of their danger. The beds of rivers were often left dry while the shock lasted, and when the water returned, it overflowed their banks. Springs were sometimes dried up, and new ones broke out in other places. The hills that formed the sides of steep valleys were often split by deep chasms parallel to the valleys; and in many cases, large portions of them were separated and moved by the temporary deluge to places half a mile or a mile away, with the buildings and trees still standing on them. In this manner, hills were leveled and valleys were filled up. But the most fatal accident of this kind happened at Scilla, where such a large portion of a cliff was thrown into the sea that it raised an immense wave. This wave carried off more than 2,000 inhabitants who were gathered on the beach, and even extended its formidable effects to the opposite coast of Sicily, where several people perished in a similar manner.

In March 1767, Vesuvius began to throw out a considerable quantity of ashes and stones, which raised its summit in the course of the year no less than 200 feet, forming first a little mountain of pumice stones within the crater, which by degrees became visible above its margin. On the morning of the 19th, clouds of smoke were forced, in continual succession, out of the mouth of the volcano, forming a mass like a large pine tree, which was lengthened into an arch and extended to the island of Caprea <note>Modern Capri</note>, 28 miles off: it was accompanied by much lightning and by an appearance of meteors like shooting stars. A mouth then opened below the crater and discharged a stream of lava, which Sir William Hamilton ventured to approach within a short distance, imagining that the violence of the confined materials must have been exhausted; but on a sudden, the mountain opened with a great noise at a much lower point, about a quarter of a mile from the place where he stood, and threw out a torrent of lava, which advanced straight towards him while he was involved in a shower of small pumice stones and ashes and in a cloud of smoke. The force of the explosions was so great that doors and windows were thrown open by them at the distance of several miles: the stream of lava was in some places two miles broad and 60 or 70 feet deep; it extended about six miles from the summit of the mountain and remained hot for several weeks. In 1794, a still more violent eruption occurred: it was expected by the inhabitants of the neighborhood, as the crater was nearly filled and the water in the wells had subsided. Showers of immense stones were projected to a great height, and ashes were thrown out so copiously that they were very thick at Taranto, 250 miles off; some of them also were wet with salt water. A heavy noxious vapor, supposed to be carbonic acid, issued in many places from the earth and destroyed the vineyards in which it was suffered to remain stagnant. The probabilities of such an event, in the whole course of time, are however so small that we have no reason to be apprehensive of the chance of it occurring in the future, for it is not enough that a comet should approach so near to the Earth as to be very powerfully attracted by it; its motion must also be directed almost in a straight line towards the Earth; otherwise it might only be deflected into a new orbit and go off again, without having caused any other disturbance than a partial overflow of the sea.

The face of the globe has also been very significantly changed in the course of ages by the gradual operation of the sea and of rivers. The sea has encroached in particular parts and retired from others; and the mouths of large rivers, running through low countries, have often been variously modified by a deposition and transfer of the matter washed down from the land. At Havre the sea undermines the steep coast and recedes at Dunkirk, where the shore is flat: in Holland, the Zuiderzee was probably formed in the middle ages by continual incursions of the sea, where only the small lake Flevo had before existed; and the mouths of the Rhine have been considerably altered, both in their dimensions and in their directions. The mud, deposited by large rivers, generally causes a Delta, or triangular piece of land, to grow out into the sea; thus the mouth of the Mississippi is said to have advanced above 50 miles since the discovery of America; and the sea has retired from Rosetta above a mile in 40 years. The mouths of the Arno and of the Rhone consist also in great measure of new land.

The meteors called shooting stars are observed to move in all directions, as well upwards as downwards, although they frequently seem to have a tendency towards a particular quarter in the course of the same evening. Other igneous meteors, which closely resemble the largest of these in their appearance, are sometimes observed to fall to the earth, either whole or divided into parts; and after their fall, certain stones have been found which have been supposed to have descended in a fiery state. Mr. Howard has confirmed that almost all these stones agree in their general characteristics and in their chemical analysis, especially in the fact that they contain nickel. It has been conjectured, both in this country and on the continent, that they have been emitted by lunar volcanoes, and it has been observed that since they would find little or no resistance from the very thin atmosphere of the moon, they would require a projection velocity only four times as great as that which a cannonball sometimes receives in order to rise into the sphere of the earth’s attraction. Their heat and combustion may quite likely be derived from the great condensation they must cause in the air immediately in front of them, and even their friction might easily produce enough electric light to make them visible in the dark. Among many such substances projected from the moon, it is probable that only a few would be directed toward the earth, and many more would be made to revolve in ellipses around it, becoming tiny satellites too small for human observation, except when they enter far enough into the atmosphere to produce an appearance of light resembling that of a shooting star; but it is scarcely probable that their velocity could ever be at all comparable with that which has been attributed to these meteors. There is, however, no difficulty in supposing, on the other hand, that the wandering substances which may be moving through empty space with a velocity equal to that of shooting stars may be slowed down so much when they penetrate deep into our atmosphere that they make only a moderate impact when they fall on the ground; and if we suppose the meteors to be of one kind only, they must be referred to the category of shooting stars rather than to that of the products of lunar volcanoes; although the undulating motion sometimes observed in these meteors seems to be somewhat inconsistent with the progress of a heavy body moving by its natural inertia in a straight line.

# LECTURE LVIII.

## ON VEGETATION.

It may appear idle to some persons to attempt to reduce the outlines of natural history into so small a compass as is required for them to become a part of this course of lectures; and it would indeed be a fruitless undertaking to endeavor to communicate a knowledge of the particular subjects of this science, even in a much longer time than we shall bestow on it. But many naturalists have spent a great portion of their lives in learning the names of plants and animals, and have known at last less of the philosophy of the science than might have been told to them in a few hours by persons who had observed with more enlarged views and who had reasoned on general principles. And we shall perhaps find it possible to collect into a small compass the most useful information that has been obtained so far respecting the laws of animal and vegetable life, as well as the foundations of the methods by which the most accepted systematic classifications have been regulated.

The surface of the earth, both sea and land, is occupied by innumerable individuals, constituting an immense variety of distinct species of animated and inanimate beings, included in the three grand divisions of natural bodies. The mineral kingdom consists of such substances as are composed of particles either united without any regular form, or collected together by <term>accretion</term> or external growth only. When mineral substances crystallize, they often imitate the form and almost assume the external appearance of vegetables; but their particles are never extended to admit others between them, and to be thus enlarged in all their dimensions; their growth is only performed by the addition of similar particles upon the surface of those that have already been deposited.

Vegetables derive their existence, by seeds or otherwise, from a parent

There is indeed in the crystallization of minerals a slight resemblance to a reproduction or generation, when a small portion of the substance serves as a basis for the formation of subsequent crystals: but this portion becomes a constituent part of the crystal while it preserves its original form; a seed, on the contrary, is a substance naturally and completely detached from the plant, and containing within itself the simplest rudiments of a new individual, which is afterwards evolved and enlarged. Sometimes, however, vegetables are propagated by means of bulbs, or by spreading roots, by slips, or by grafted scions, without a seed detached in the regular manner; but in these cases the new plant is much more identical with the old one than when it is raised from a seed, being, as it were, a continuation of the same existence. Plants are nourished in great measure by means of their roots; and sometimes, where they are without roots, their nourishment is probably absorbed by all parts of their surface.

Animals are distinguished from vegetables by the reception of their food, for digestion and assimilation, into an internal cavity constituting a stomach. The existence of a stomach, designed for the digestion of food, appears to be the best, if not the only criterion of an animal. Some vegetables, indeed, have a power of catching and detaining animals by curling up their leaves so as to cover them, such as the *drosera* or *sundew*, and the *dionaea muscipula*, or *catchfly*; but this mechanism can scarcely be intended for their immediate nourishment, at least the leaf can scarcely be supposed to assume the character of a stomach. It is true that we imagine all animals to have sensation, and all plants to be without it; and if it were possible to distinguish decisively between sensation and irritation, the distinction would supersede every other: but in many cases it is extremely difficult to say where sensation is present, and where irritation only produces the same apparent effects. We cannot be sure that the *hydra*, or fresh water polypus, or the *trichurus sol*, an <term>animalcule</term> described by Dr. Shaw, feels any sensation of pain when it is divided into two parts; at least the pain seems to agree remarkably well with its constitution, for it lives and thrives with increased vigor as two distinct animals. On the other hand, many plants are easily stimulated to perform motions which have the appearance of muscular actions influenced by sensation: the sensitive plants close or depress their leaves in consequence of agitation or of

A zoophyte is an animal absolutely fixed to one place; and the *vallisneria* is a vegetable possessed of a certain limited power of locomotion. A plant chooses, by preference, to turn toward the light; and it has been known that an ash tree on a wall, when no longer capable of being supported by the wall alone, has concentrated all its force into the production of one large root, descending to the ground. Some of these circumstances may be explained without recurring to anything like volition; but, as far as we know, the same explanations might be applied to some animal motions. And although it is very possible that there may be a certain limit where the influence of mind and sensation ends and the laws of vegetable life alone prevail, the point of division is not marked strongly enough to allow it to form a defining characteristic in an artificial system. It has been asserted that some worms are nourished by absorption only, without the assistance of a stomach; thus hydatids, which are supposed to be animal in nature, appear to be simply bags of a fluid without any visible opening; but a few doubtful cases of this kind can scarcely be sufficient to invalidate the general position that all bodies decidedly animal have a cavity for the reception of food. There are usually also some chemical distinctions in the component parts of animals and vegetables: animal substances commonly contain greater proportions of azote or nitrogen, and of phosphoric acid; but there are some exceptions to this observation; for example, the *carica papaya*, or papaw, contains nearly the same principles as are usually found in substances of animal origin. In general, we may readily distinguish a small portion of an animal from a vegetable substance by the smell produced in burning it. According to common language, we say that minerals have growth only, though not always; that vegetables grow and live also; and that animals have sensation, as well as life and an increase of magnitude.

Mineralogy is a branch of natural history so nearly allied to chemistry that it cannot be completely understood without a previous knowledge of that science. It may, therefore, be more properly considered as belonging to a course of chemical rather than physical lectures.

<header>LECTURE LVIII.</header>

The vegetable kingdom presents us with a highly interesting spectacle through its variety and elegance; but the economy of vegetation appears to be little diversified, although it is poorly understood. With respect to the apparent perfection of their functions and the complexity of their structure, we may consider all vegetables as belonging to two principal divisions: in one, the seed is prepared with the assistance of a flower, having its stamens and its pistils, with petals or a calyx; while in the other, the preparation of the seed is less regular and conspicuous, and therefore such plants are called *cryptogamous*. In some of these, there is a slight resemblance to the flowers of other vegetables, but on the whole, the class appears to form one of the connecting links between the three kingdoms of nature; its physiology is probably simple, but it has been little examined. The herbs, palms, shrubs, and trees, which constitute the numerous genera of flowering vegetables, exhibit the greatest diversity in the forms and arrangements of the organs of fructification, while they all have a general resemblance in their internal economy.

Every vegetable may be considered as a collection of vessels in which, by some unknown means, the watery fluids absorbed by its roots are subjected to peculiar chemical and vital actions, and exposed in the leaves to the influence of light and air; so as to be rendered fit for becoming constituent parts of the plant, or of the peculiar substances contained within it.

The first process in the germination of a seed is its absorption of moisture and its undergoing a chemical fermentation, in which oxygen is absorbed, and a part of the mucilage contained in the seed is converted into sugar; a substance probably more nutritive to the young plant. The radicle shoots downward, and the seed leaves, or cotyledons, which are generally two, although sometimes more or fewer, raise themselves above the ground, until in a short time they die and drop off, being succeeded by the regular and more mature leaves.

In every transverse section of a vegetable, we commonly discover at least four different substances. The parts next to the axis of the tree or branch consist of medulla or pith, which is supposed by some to be the residence of the vegetable life of the plant; but a tree may live for many years after be-
