...ing, being largely deprived of its <term>medulla</term>. The pith has a loose, light, and spongy texture; it extends a branch into every branch and leaf, where it also appears to serve as a reservoir for moisture. The pith is surrounded by the woody part, which is composed of fibers more or less tightly packed together; these do not actually branch into each other to any great degree, although there is reason to suspect some lateral communication between them. In many trees, these are interrupted at certain intervals by fibers in a radiating direction, forming what is called the silver grain. Like the bones in animals, the wood constitutes the strongest part of the plant; and like them, it is also equipped to some extent with vessels. Some have even supposed that the fibers themselves are distinct tubes, while others believe that the spaces between them serve as vessels, but neither of these opinions is currently accepted. The wood consists of a number of concentric layers or strata formed in successive years. The external part, which is formed last, is called the <term>alburnum</term>, or white wood, and this part is the most vascular. The bark surrounds the wood; in trees, this also consists of several layers produced over as many years. The external parts usually crack, allowing us to observe the number of layers at their divisions, though only the inner layer is of immediate use. This layer is called the *<term>liber</term>*; since this material was once used instead of paper, the Romans also called a book a *<term>liber</term>*. The bark consists of fibers of the same kind as the wood, but more loosely connected. It is covered by the cuticle, which expands significantly as the plant grows, but eventually cracks and has its function replaced by the outer layers of bark. Between the bark and the cuticle, a green pulpy substance, or *<term>parenchyma</term>*, is found; this seems analogous to the *<term>rete mucosum</term>*, which is found between the true skin and the cuticle in animals. Mr. Desfontaines has observed that in palms and several other natural orders of plants, the annual deposit of new matter is not confined to the external surface, but takes place in various parts of the plant, as if it were composed of several ordinary stems joined together.

There are three principal kinds of vessels in the different parts of plants: first, the sap vessels, which are found in both the wood and the bark, although their nature appears to require further examination; second, the air vessels, or *<term>tracheae</term>*, which are composed of single threads wound into a

spiral tube, like the spring of a bell, and capable of being easily uncoiled; these, though they have been called air vessels, and supposed by some to serve the purposes of respiration, are described by others as containing, during the life of the plant, an aqueous fluid: and they are probably little more than sap vessels, with an additional spiral coat: they are not found in the bark, nor in all species of plants; and it has therefore been inferred that they are not immediately necessary to the growth of the plant. The third kind are the <term>proper vessels</term> of the plant, which are generally arranged in concentric circles, and appear to be unconnected with the sap vessels, and to contain the milky, resinous, and other peculiar juices, which are found in different kinds of plants; for the sap is nearly the same in all—at least it is independent of the gums and resin, which often distinguish particular plants; it contains a certain portion of mucilage, and probably in some plants, such as the sugar maple, a considerable quantity of sugar. Mr. Mirbel has also made a number of still more accurate distinctions respecting the structure of the different kinds of vessels. The circulation of the sap is not completely understood; when an opening is made near the root of a tree, it flows most copiously from above: when near the summit, from below. Dr. Hope actually reversed the natural course of the juices of a tree, without changing its position; by <note>grafting</note> a willow with two others, he completely united its existence with theirs, and then, removing its roots, he found that its growth was supported by the juices of the two others. A tree may also be actually inverted, and the upper part will take root, while the lower puts out branches and leaves.

Plants perspire very considerably, and also emit a quantity of gases of different kinds; they generate a slight degree of heat, which may be observed by means of the thermometer, and by the melting of snow in contact with them. The growth of every tree takes place at the internal surface of the bark; not only is the bark itself formed there, but the wood is also deposited by the bark. For Dr. Hope separated the whole of the bark of a branch of willow from the wood, leaving it connected only at the ends, so as to constitute a hollow cylinder, parallel to the wood; and he found that new layers were formed within the bark; and in another experiment a part of the wood, deprived of the bark, although protected from the air, was only covered with new bark as it grew over from the old bark above and below. rings, which register the age of the tree, are very easily observed when it is cut across; sometimes as many as 400 have been found in firs, and oaks are said to have lived 1,000 years.

Mr. Knight has inferred, from a great variety of experiments, that the sap, either usually or universally, ascends through the wood into the leaves, and then descends through the bark to nourish the plant. The leaves seem to be somewhat analogous to lungs, or rather to the gills of fish: for plants have a need for air, and it has been found that even seeds will not germinate in a vacuum. As the lungs of animals appear to be concerned in forming the blood, so it may be inferred from Mr. Knight's experiments that the sap first ascends to the leaves through the external fresh wood or <term>alburnum</term>, and through the central vessels of the young leaves and branches (derived from the alburnum and accompanied by the <term>spiral tubes</term>); and after being perfected by exposure to light and air in the leaves, it descends in the bark and serves for the secretion of the alburnum and of the internal layers of the bark, being conveyed probably by two distinct sets of vessels. The sap, thus prepared by the leaves in the summer and autumn, is supposed to leave its extractive matter in the tree throughout the winter in such a state as to be ready to unite with the aqueous juices which ascend from the root in the succeeding spring. The internal parts of the wood, having served the purposes of vegetation, are hardened and perhaps dried up, so as to be afterwards principally subservient to strength alone. By subsequent experiments, Mr. Knight has also found that when a branch hangs downward, the sap still appears to proceed from the part of the bark which is uppermost; so that the direction of the force of gravity seems to be concerned in determining the direction of the motion of the sap. There appears also to be some reason to suppose that mechanical means assist in the protrusion of the sap and the consequent growth of the tree; for if a tree is agitated more by the wind in one direction than in another, its diameter will be greatest in that direction.

The process of <term>grafting</term> depends on a remarkable property of the growth of vegetables; if the cut surface of the inner bark of a small branch, or cutting, is placed in contact with that of the branch of another tree, they will unite sufficiently for the nourishment of the cutting—provided, however, that the nature of the plants is not too different. kind occurs in animal life, where a tooth has been transplanted into the socket of another, or where the spur of a rooster has been inserted into his comb.

Plants have their natural lifespans, whether of only a few days, as in the case of some fungi, of one year, of a few years, or of many centuries. They also have their diseases; they are often infested by insects, as seen in the gall of the oak and the woodruff of the rose, or by microscopic organisms of a still lower order, which are either the causes of smut in corn or are constantly associated with it. Through unnatural and overly lush cultivation, they become sterile and produce double flowers instead of fruits and seeds. When deprived of sufficient moisture or nipped by frost, their leaves and branches often die; and if the plants recover their vigor, a separation is brought about by a natural process resembling the shedding of decayed parts in animals. However, when the entire plant dies, the dead leaves continue to cling to it. The annual fall of leaves in autumn appears to be a natural separation of nearly the same kind, which takes place when the leaves are no longer needed—the growth of the plant having stopped and their functions no longer being required.

Succulent plants generally die when the outer skin is removed, but this is not the case for all other plants. Air appears to be harmful to vegetables where it is not natural for it to be; from this arises the benefit of Mr. Forsyth's method of completely excluding air from the wounded parts of trees, by which means their damage is often largely repaired, and they acquire new strength and vigor. Sometimes a reduction in the size of a tree immediately increases its fertility; its energy being more concentrated by pruning its useless branches and leaves, it produces a larger quantity of fruit using the sap that would otherwise have been spent on their nourishment.

The Linnaean system of plants is admittedly more of an artificial than a natural one; however, it is extremely well-suited for practice, and its universal adoption has produced the most important improvements in the science of botany. Of the 24 classes into which Linnaeus has divided the plant kingdom, 23 are distinguished by the forms of the flowers and fruit, and the 24th by the lack of a regular flowering. The first ten are named from <term>monandria</term>, in order, to <term>decandria</term>; then follow <term>dodecandria</term>, <term>icosandria</term>, and <term>polyandria</term>. These names express the number of the <term>stamina</term>, or filaments, surrounding the seed vessel; and the orders are derived in a similar manner.

...from the number of pistils, or little columns immediately connected with the seed vessel; and named *monogynia*, *digynia*, and so forth, as far as *polygynia*. These classes generally differ little in their natural characteristics, except for the twelfth, *icosandria*, which is characterized by the attachment of the filaments to the green cup surrounding the flower, and which includes the most common fruit trees; this class has, however, been incorporated by some later botanists into the next. In the third class we find most of the natural order of grasses; the fifth, *pentandria*, is by far the most numerous of any; the sixth contains the lilies and many other bulbous plants. The 14th class, *didynamia*, is recognized by two longer and two shorter filaments; it is perfectly natural and includes flowers similar in their structure to the foxglove and the dead-nettle. The 15th class, *tetradynamia*, is also strongly characterized, even by chemical properties; here, two of the filaments are shorter than the other four. Cresses, radishes, and many other acrid and ammoniacal vegetables belong to this class, as well as the turnip and cabbage, which, when cultivated, become mild and nutritious. The class *monadelphia* contains a few plants similar to the mallow; they are known by the union of the filaments at their bases into a cylinder. The filaments of the next class generally have nine united and one separate, which is why the class is named *diadelphia*; it contains the papilionaceous flowers, which somewhat resemble a butterfly in their form, like the pea and other leguminous plants, broom, furze, and acacia. The 18th class, *polyadelphia*, has the filaments of its flowers united into several masses or bundles, such as the *hypericum* or tutsan. The next class is perfectly natural and contains the composite flowers, which have a unique union of the summits of the filaments; it is named *syngenesia*. Sunflowers, daisies, and artichokes are familiar examples of plants in this class. The 20th class, *gynandria*, though it contains the natural family of the orchids, has been omitted by some later botanists; here the filaments are fixed on the pistil or, more properly in the arums, within the pistils. The three following classes—*monoecia*, *dioecia*, and *polygamia*—differ from the rest by having some flowers with filaments or stamens <note>referred to in the original as "chives"</note>, and some with pistils only, either on the same plant, on different plants, or mixed with flowers of more common construction. Most forest trees belong to these classes, but the distinctions that separate them from other classes are not always uniformly preserved; for this reason, many later botanists have stopped using them. The plants of the last class, *cryptogamia*, are exceedingly numerous; they include the families of ferns, mosses, algae (or membranous weeds), and

<term>fungi</term> or mushrooms, fill up its extensive departments; some have also separated a part of the <term>algae</term> under the name of <term>hepaticae</term>, or gelatinous weeds. In this class, the methods of reproduction are extremely various; some of the <term>fuci</term> and <term>confervae</term> approach so much in their general appearance and mode of growth to corallines and zoophytes that they seem to form an obvious connection between the lowest ranks of the vegetable and animal kingdoms; while other plants of the class are scarcely distinguishable by their appearance from some of the productions of the mineral kingdom.

The French have introduced Jussieu’s botanical system into very general use. The most prominent feature in this system is the division of all the genera into a hundred natural orders, which are also arranged in fifteen classes. Jussieu begins, like Linné, with the separation of <term>cryptogamic</term> from <term>phanerogamic</term> plants; the seeds of the <term>cryptogamic</term> plants, which form the first class, lack <term>cotyledons</term> or seed leaves, and all other plants are distinguished into those that have seeds with one and with two <term>cotyledons</term>. Depending on whether the stamina or filaments are inserted below the pistil, on the calyx, or on the seed vessel, the first description of seeds provides three distinct classes. The plants which have two <term>cotyledons</term> follow, and are divided into <term>apetalous</term>, <term>monopetalous</term>, and <term>polypetalous</term>, based on distinctions regarding the corolla or flower leaves, which are somewhat arbitrarily understood; and lastly <term>diclinous</term>, from the separation of the stamina and pistils. The first three of these divisions are subdivided according to the insertion of the stamina and the union or separation of the <term>antherae</term> which they support into ten classes, making, with the four already mentioned, fourteen, to which the <term>diclinous</term> plants add a fifteenth. The orders are determined without any particular limitation of the parts from which the characteristics are taken. This system is of acknowledged merit as a philosophical classification of the natural orders of plants; such vegetables as nearly agree in their habits and appearances are brought more uniformly together than in the system of Linné. Hence, in the arrangement of a botanical garden, or in a treatise on the chemical or medical properties of plants, it might be employed with advantage: but for the practical purposes of botanical investigation, it appears to be utterly unfit, since its author has sacrificed all logical and systematic laws to the attempt to follow nature through analogies, which are often discoverable only with great difficulty and which are seldom reducible to methodical definitions.

## LECTURE LIX.

### ON ANIMAL LIFE.

The functions of animal life are not only more complicated within the same individual than those of vegetation, but they are also more diverse across the different classes into which animals are divided; as a result, the <term>physiology</term> of each class is governed by its own peculiar laws. We are indebted to Linnaeus for the first expansion of our views regarding the different classes of animals, and perhaps for the most convenient arrangement of the animal kingdom, even though his method has never been universally adopted by our neighbors on the continent.

A considerable portion of the mass of all animals is composed of tubular vessels which originate in a heart. With the assistance of their own muscular power, the heart propels either a colorless transparent fluid or red blood through the <term>arteries</term> into the extremities of the <term>veins</term>, through which it returns again to the source of its motion. Both <term>insects</term> and <term>vermes</term> (or worms) have circulating fluids that are slightly warmer than the surrounding environment and are generally colorless; however, insects have legs equipped with joints, while worms have nothing more than simple <term>tentacula</term> in place of legs. Fish have cold red blood, which is exposed to the influence of the air contained in water by means of their gills. The <term>amphibia</term> receive air into their lungs, but their blood is cold like that of fish; in both of these classes, the heart has only two regular cavities, whereas the hearts of animals with warm blood have four. In the latter, the entire contents of one pair of cavities are required to pass through the lungs in order to reach the other pair. Among warm-blooded animals, the <term>oviparous</term> (egg-laying) are birds and are generally covered with feathers; the <term>viviparous</term> (live-bearing) are either quadrupeds or <term>cetaceous</term> animals and are provided with organs for suckling their young.

Each of these classes of animals is subdivided by Linnaeus into different

These, with very few exceptions, have teeth fixed in their jawbones; and the orders are distinguished by the form and number of these teeth, except for the order of cetaceous fishes, which is identified by the fins found in place of feet. The distinctions of the teeth are somewhat minute, but they appear to be connected with the animal's way of life, and they are reasonably natural.

The first order, *Primates*, contains humans, monkeys, and bats; the second, *Bruta*, includes, among others, the elephant, the rhinoceros, the anteater, and the *ornithorhynchus* <note>the platypus</note>, an extraordinary quadruped recently discovered in New Holland <note>Australia</note>, with a bill like a duck and sometimes teeth inserted behind it; however, there are some suspicions that the animal is oviparous <note>egg-laying</note>. The order *Ferae* contains the seal, the dog, the cat, the lion, the tiger, the weasel, and the mole—most of them beasts of prey; the opossum and the kangaroo also belong to this order, though the kangaroo feeds on vegetables even though its teeth are like those of carnivorous animals. The fourth order, *Glires*, includes beavers, mice, squirrels, and hares; the fifth, *Pecora*, includes camels, goats, sheep, and horned cattle. The sixth order, *Belluae*, contains the horse, the hippopotamus, and the hog. The cetaceous fishes, or whales, form the seventh and last order: they live in the water, enveloped in a thick clothing of fat—that is, oily matter deposited in cells—which enables their blood to maintain its temperature despite the external contact of a dense environment that is considerably colder.

Birds are distinguished from quadrupeds by their laying of eggs; they are also generally feathered, although a few are somewhat hairy; and instead of hands or forelegs, they have wings. Their eggs are covered by a calcareous shell; they consist of a white, or *albumen*, which nourishes the chick during incubation, and a yolk, which is suspended within it so as to keep the side where the tiny embryo of a chicken is located constantly facing upward, nearest to the mother sitting on it. Birds are divided, according to the form of their bills, into six orders: *accipitres*, such as eagles, vultures, and hawks; *picae*, such as crows, jackdaws, hummingbirds, and parrots; *anseres*, such as ducks, swans, and gulls; *grallae*, such as herons, woodcocks, and ostriches; *gallinae*, such as peacocks, pheasants, turkeys, and common fowls; and, lastly, *passeres*, comprising sparrows, larks, swallows, thrushes, and doves.

The amphibians are in some respects very closely related to birds, but their blood is little warmer than the surrounding medium. Their respiration is not necessarily performed in a continuous succession of breaths, since the whole of their blood does not pass through the lungs; thus, circulation may continue without interruption in other parts, even though it may be impeded in these organs for lack of respiratory movement. They are very tenacious of life; it has been asserted on good authority that some of them have lived many years without food, enclosed in hollow trees and even in the middle of stones, and they often retain signs of life for some days after the loss of their hearts. Their eggs are generally covered with only a membrane. They sometimes have an intermediate stage of existence in which all their parts are not yet developed, as we observe in the tadpole; in this respect, they resemble the class of insects. They are now universally considered to be divided into only two orders: *reptilia*, such as the tortoise, the dragon (or flying lizard), the frog, and the toad—all of which have four feet—and the animals belonging to the order *serpentes*, which are without feet. Most of the *serpentes* are perfectly harmless, but others have fangs through which they instill a poisonous fluid into the wounds they make. In England, the viper is the only venomous serpent; it is known by its dark brown color and by a stripe of whitish spots running along its back, but its bite is seldom, if ever, fatal to humans.

The first three classes of animals have lungs for respiration, as we have already seen, and receive air through the mouth. Those which have gills and red blood are fishes, residing either in fresh or in salt water, or indifferently

Of the six orders of fishes, four have regular gills supported by small bones; and they are distinguished, according to the location of their ventral fins, into *apodes*, such as the eel and lamprey; *jugularis*, such as the cod; *thoracici*, such as the sole and perch; and *abdominales*, such as the salmon and pike. These distinctions appear to be perfectly artificial, although they are useful in a systematic arrangement. The two remaining orders are without bones in the gills: those of the one are soft, and those of the other are cartilaginous or gristly. These are the *branchiostegi* and *chondropterygii* of Artedi, which Linné, by mistake, classified among the *amphibia*. The sunfish, the lumpfish, the fishing frog, and the seahorse belong to the former, and the sturgeon, the skate, and the shark belong to the latter order.

Insects derive their name from being almost always divided into a head, thorax, and abdomen, with very slender intervening sections, although these divisions do not exist in all insects. They are usually oviparous; they breathe, but not through the mouth. They have a number of small orifices on each side of the abdomen through which air is received into their branched tracheae, and if these are blocked with oil, the insects suffocate. Instead of bones, they have a hard integument or shell. Their mouths are formed in extremely varied but generally very complicated structures. Fabricius made these parts the basis of his classification; but because of their smallness in most species, the method is, in practice, insuperably inconvenient. The only way in which such characteristics can be rendered really useful is when they are employed in the subdivision of the genera, as determined by more conspicuous distinctions. Insects most frequently have jaws, and often several pairs, but they are always positioned so as to open laterally or horizontally. Sometimes, instead of jaws, they have a trunk or proboscis. In general, they pass through four stages of existence: the egg; the larva, or stage of growth; the pupa, or chrysalis, which is usually in a state of torpor or complete inactivity; and the imago, or perfect insect, in its reproductive capacity. After the final change, the insect most frequently takes no food until its death.

The *monoculus* is a genus including the little active insects found in pond water, which are scarcely visible to the naked eye, as well as the Molucca crab <note>the horseshoe crab</note>, which is the largest of all insects, being sometimes six feet long. Besides these, there are several genera of wingless insects that are parasitic and infest the human race as well as other animals.

The *vermes* <note>worms and various other invertebrates</note> are the last and lowest of animated beings, yet some of them are not lacking in either size or beauty. The most natural division of *vermes* is into five orders: the *intestina*, such as earthworms and *ascarides* <note>parasitic nematodes</note>, which are distinguished by their lack of movable appendages, or tentacles, from the *mollusca*; the *mollusca* include such as the dew snail <note>likely a slug</note>, the cuttlefish, the sea anemone, and the *hydra*, or freshwater polyp. The *testacea* have shells of one or more pieces, and most of them inhabit the sea and are called shellfish, such as the limpet, the periwinkle, the snail, the mussel, the oyster, and the barnacle. The order *zoophyta* contains corallines, sponges, and other compound animals, united by a common habitation that has the general appearance of a plant, although it is of animal origin; each of the little inhabitants, resembling a *hydra* or polyp, imitates with its extended arms the appearance of an imperfect flower. The last order, *infusoria*, is hardly distinguished from the *intestina* and *mollusca* by any character other than the smallness of the individuals belonging to it, and their spontaneous appearance in animal and vegetable infusions, where we can discover no traces of the manner in which they are produced. The process by which their numbers are sometimes increased is no less astonishing than their initial production; for several of the genera often appear to divide spontaneously into two or more...

The <term>volvox</term> and some of the <term>vorticellae</term> are remarkable for their continual rotatory motion, probably intended for the purpose of straining their food out of the water; while some other species of the <term>vorticella</term> resemble <term>fungi</term> or <term>corallines</term> in miniature.

Among the animals of these different classes, the more complex animals are informed about the qualities of external objects by the senses of touch, taste, smell, hearing, and vision. A few <term>quadrupeds</term> are incapable of seeing: the <term>mole</term> has an eye so small as to be distinguishable only with difficulty; and the <term>mus typhlus</term> <note>the greater mole-rat</note>, supposed to be the <term>aspalax</term> of <term>Aristotle</term>, has its eye completely covered by the skin and integuments, without any opening. Birds have hearing but no external ears, or <term>auriculae</term>. <term>Insects</term> appear to lack organs of smell; but it is not impossible that their <term>antennae</term> may serve the purpose of hearing. Many of the <term>vermes</term> are totally destitute of sight, and some lack all the organs of sense; none of them have either ears or nostrils. The external senses of warm-blooded animals are usually subject to a periodic state of inactivity at night, called sleep. It is said that fish never sleep; and it is well known that some animals pass the whole of the harshest part of the winter in a state nearly resembling their usual sleep.

In animals whose physiology approaches that of the human system, the process for supporting life by nutrition begins with the mastication of the food that has been received by the mouth. The food thus prepared is conveyed into the stomach by the act of swallowing; but in ruminating cattle, it is first lodged in a temporary receptacle and more completely masticated at leisure. In the stomach, it undergoes digestion, and being afterwards mixed with the bile and other fluids poured in by the liver and the neighboring glands, it becomes fit for providing <term>chyle</term>, or nutritive juice, which is separated from it by the absorbents of the intestines during its passage through the coils of a canal nearly forty feet long. Together with the <term>chyle</term>, all the watery fluids that are swallowed must also be absorbed and pass through the thoracic duct into the large veins entering the heart, and from there into the general circulation, before they can arrive at the kidneys, by which the superfluous parts are expelled. We must therefore suppose that when the florid arterial blood is, by some unknown means, converted, in the extreme ramifications of the arteries, into the purple <term>venous blood</term>—to return to the heart by the converging branches of the <term>veins</term>—there is a much more considerable release of heat than in the conversion of venous into arterial blood by the absorption of oxygen and nitrogen in the lungs. The red particles in the human blood are about 1/2000 of an inch in diameter, somewhat oblong and flattened; they usually have the appearance of a dark point in the center, but there is some reason to suspect that this is merely an optical deception. In a few animals they are a little smaller, but in most of the <term>amphibia</term>, they are much larger and flatter than in man. While the lymph remains fluid after the blood has been withdrawn from the vessels, these globules tend to settle and leave it semi-transparent; hence arises the appearance of a <term>buff coat</term> on blood left to coagulate, which is thinner or thicker, depending on whether the globules are sooner or later arrested in their descent.

In what manner these reciprocal impressions are transmitted by the <term>nerves</term> has never yet been fully determined: but it has long been conjectured that the medium of communication may bear a considerable analogy to the <term>electrical fluid</term>; and the extreme sensitivity of the nerves to the slightest portion of electrical influence, as well as the real and apparently spontaneous excitation of that influence in animal bodies—which have been demonstrated in recent years by <term>galvanic experiments</term>—have added very significantly to the probability of this opinion. An extremely slender fiber, made of a substance capable of conducting electricity with perfect freedom and enveloped in a sheath of a perfect nonconductor, would perhaps serve to communicate an impulse in very nearly the same manner as the nerves appear to do. Indeed, nothing could be more fit to constitute a connecting link between material and immaterial beings than some modification of a fluid which appears to differ very considerably in its essential properties from the common gross matter of the universe, and to possess a subtlety and an activity which entitle it to a superior rank in the order of created substances.

When all the functions of animal life are carried on in their perfect and natural manner, the animal is said to be in health: when they are disturbed, a state of disease ensues. The diseases to which the human frame is liable are so various and irregular that they cannot easily be reduced to any systematic order. <term>Dr. Cullen</term> has divided them into four classes. <term>Febrile diseases</term>, which constitute the first class, consist principally of an increase in the frequency of the pulsations of the heart and arteries, together with an elevation of the temperature, the whole animal economy <note>the body's internal biological systems</note> being at the same time in some measure impaired: they are often accompanied by unnatural or irregular actions of the vessels of particular parts, constituting local <term>inflammations</term>, which were formerly considered a derivation of diseased humors <note>fluids believed to control health</note> falling on those parts: thus, a <term>pleurisy</term> is a fever, with an inflammation of the membrane lining the chest. The incapacity of a part to perform its functions upon the application of a natural stimulus—or perhaps more frequently the incapacity of the nerves to transmit to it the dictates of the mind—constitutes a <term>palsy</term>: such derangements, and others, by which the actions of the nervous

A general derangement of the system, without fever or any specific weakness of the nerves, constitutes the class of cachectic diseases, such as atrophy, consumption, scrofula, and dropsy. Besides these diseases, we have a fourth class, consisting of local affections only, such as blindness, deafness, tumors, and luxations <note>dislocations of joints</note>.

Despite the labors of men of the greatest learning and genius, continued for many centuries, it must be admitted that the art of healing diseases is still in a state of great imperfection. Fortunately, however, for mankind, we may observe in almost all cases where the offending cause is discoverable, and where the system is not at once overwhelmed by its magnitude, a wise and wonderful provision for removing it by a mechanism that is admirably simple and effective; and it is reasonable to conclude that where the cause is more obscure, the same benevolent Providence has employed agents equally well-suited for counteracting it, although their operations are completely beyond the reach of human understanding.

# LECTURE LX.

## ON THE HISTORY OF TERRESTRIAL PHYSICS.

Throughout all of nature, we discover a tendency toward the multiplication of life, activity, and enjoyment. Man is placed at the head of terrestrial beings—the only one who comprehends and can trace, even in a faint outline, the entire plan of the universe. We have seen the innumerable luminaries that enliven the vast regions of immeasurable space with their brilliant but distant emanations of light and heat. Revolving around them at smaller intervals, and cherished by their fostering influences, are their planets and their comets; the former maintaining nearly equal distances, and the latter ranging more widely from the upper to the lower regions, without limits to their numbers or their motions. Having conjectured what might possibly exist on other planetary globes, we descended to our own and examined its structure and the proportions of its parts. Next, we studied the general properties of the matter within our reach, and then the specific substances or qualities that are either not material or are distinguished from other matter by very remarkable properties, as we found them involved in the phenomena of heat, electricity, and magnetism. We afterward examined the combinations of all these in the great atmospheric apparatus of nature, which serves for the display of meteorological phenomena. The forms and the laws of animal and vegetable life have been the last objects of our inquiries; but the magnitude of some departments of natural history, and the obscurity of others, have prevented us from entering into any of them more than superficially.

We have already taken a historical view of the gradual advancement of astronomy. With respect to the other sciences included under the category of physics proper, the progress of discovery has generally been slow and frequently accidental. The ancients had little or no substantial

knowledge of any part of physics, except astronomy and natural history: their opinions were in general mere speculations, derived from fancy, and inapplicable to the real phenomena of nature. Opinions such as these will only require to be examined so far as to enable us to trace the imperfect rudiments of discoveries, which were only completed after intervals of many ages.

The Chinese are said to have been acquainted with the use of the compass more than 3,000 years ago; but in such accounts, it is impossible to ascertain how far the spirit of national vanity may have induced a historian to falsify his dates. It has been conjectured that the death of Numa, like that of Professor Richmann, was occasioned by some unguarded experiments on the electricity of the atmosphere, which drew on him the effects of a passing thunderstorm. If, however, the fact was such, the experiments must probably have been suggested rather by an accidental discovery of light on the point of a spear, than by any rational opinions respecting the nature of the ethereal fire.

Thales is the most ancient of the Grecian philosophers who appear to have seriously studied the phenomena of nature. He supposed water to be the general principle from which all material things are formed, and into which they are resolved; an opinion which was without doubt suggested to him by the obvious effects of water in the nutrition of plants and animals. He particularly noticed the properties of the magnet, which had been previously observed to attract iron, as well as the effect of friction in exciting the electricity of amber; and he attributed to both of these substances a certain degree of animation, which he considered as the only original source of motion of any kind.

Anaximander appears to have paid some attention to meteorology; he derived the winds from the rarefaction of the air, produced by the operation of heat. Thunder and lightning he attributed to the violent explosion or bursting of the clouds, which he seems to have considered as bags filled with a mixture of wind and water. The same mistaken notion was entertained by Anaximenes, who compared the light attending the explosion to that which is frequently exhibited by the sea when struck with an oar.

<meta>This page continues the historical survey of ancient natural philosophy, moving from Thales’ theories on water and electricity to the diverse atomic and elemental theories of Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Democritus, Heraclitus, and the metaphysical systems of Plato and Aristotle.</meta>

# LECTURE LX.

Pythagoras, as great as he was in some other departments of science, reasoned regarding physical effects in a manner too mathematical and visionary to allow him much claim to be ranked among those who have studied to investigate the minute operations of nature.

Anaxagoras was so far from confining himself to the supposition of four elements, which was most generally accepted by the philosophers of antiquity, that he imagined the number of elements to be nearly, if not absolutely, infinite. He conceived that the ultimate atoms composing every substance were of the same kind as that substance, and his system was therefore called the **homoeomeria**; it perhaps erred less from the truth than many of the more prevalent opinions. Democritus, adopting the views of Leucippus, proposed a still more correct theory of the constitution of matter, supposing it to be ultimately homogeneous to such an extent that the weight of its atoms was proportional to their bulk. He asserted that the forms of these atoms were different and unalterable; that they were always in motion; and that besides their primitive difference of form, they were also susceptible to a variety in the mode of their arrangement. The space not occupied by the atoms of matter he considered to be a perfect vacuum.

As Thales had supposed water to be the first principle of all things, and Anaximenes air, so Heraclitus fixed on fire as the foundation of his system, attributing to it the property of constant motion and deriving all kinds of grosser matter from its condensation in different degrees. This doctrine was wholly unsupported by anything like reason or observation.

Plato introduced into philosophy a variety of imaginings which resembled the fictions of poetry much more than the truths of science. He maintained, for example, that ideas existed independently of the human mind and of the external world, and that they composed beings of different kinds by their union with an imperfect matter. It is observed by Bacon, in his essay on the opinions of Parmenides, that the most ancient philosophers—Empedocles, Anaxagoras, Anaximenes, Heraclitus, and Democritus—submitted their minds to things as they found them; but that Plato made the world subject to ideas, and Aristotle made even ideas, as well as all other things, subservient to words; the minds of men beginning to be occupied, in

It concludes with Francis Bacon's critique of how Plato and Aristotle prioritized abstract ideas and language over the observation of nature.</summary>

those times, with idle discussions and verbal disputes, and the correct investigation of nature being wholly neglected. Plato held, however, some correct notions regarding the distinction between denser and thinner matter based on its greater inertia; and it would be extremely unfair to deny a very high degree of merit to Aristotle's experimental research in various parts of natural philosophy, and in particular to the vast collection of real information contained in his works on natural history. Aristotle attributed absolute lightness to fire and gravity to the earth, considering air and water to be of an intermediate nature. By gravity, the ancients generally seem to have understood a tendency toward the center of the earth, which they considered to be identical to the center of the universe; and as long as they held this opinion, it was almost impossible for them to suspect the operation of a mutual attraction in all matter as a cause of gravitation. The first traces of this more correct opinion regarding it are found in the works of Plutarch.

Epicurus appears to have reasoned as soundly regarding many particular subjects of natural philosophy as he did absurdly regarding the origin of the world and of the animals that inhabit it. He largely adopted the principles of Democritus regarding atoms, but attributed to them an innate power of affecting each other's motions and of swerving in such a manner as to constitute—through the diversity of their spontaneous arrangements—all the varieties of natural bodies. He considered both heat and cold to be material; he thought the heat emitted by the sun was not absolutely identical to light, and even went so far as to conjecture that some of the sun's rays might possibly possess the power of heating bodies and yet not affect the sense of vision. In order to explain the phenomena of magnetism, he imagined a current of atoms passing in certain directions through the magnet and through iron, which produced all the effects by their interference with each other. He attributed earthquakes and volcanoes to the violent explosions of trapped air.

Among all these opinions and conjectures, there is scarcely any one that was scientifically established upon firm foundations. Some isolated observations had a certain degree of merit; and we find many interesting facts relating to different departments of natural knowledge, not only in Aristotle, but also

Protagorides of Cyzicum, who is quoted by Athenaeus, relates that in the time of King Antiochus, it was common, as a luxury, to cool water by evaporation; and it is possible that the custom may have been introduced from the East, where even ice is frequently made today by a similar process. Others among the ancients had remarked, according to Dr. Falconer, that water usually froze more easily after having been boiled; and it is possible that other isolated observations of a similar nature may occur to those who have the curiosity to research them.

The thirteenth century may be considered the date of the revival, if not the beginning, of physical discoveries. Our countryman, Roger Bacon, was one of its principal figures: he appears to have anticipated the work of later times in his knowledge of chemistry, as well as many other parts of natural philosophy. The polarity of the magnetic needle is described in some lines attributed to Guyot, a French poet who lived around 1180; however, some people believe that this description was actually written by Hugo Bertius in the middle of the following century. It is generally believed that the compass was first used in navigation by Gioja of Amalfi around the year 1260; he is said to have marked the north with a fleur-de-lis as a compliment to a branch of the French royal family then reigning in Naples. The deviation of the needle from the true north is mentioned by Peter Adsiger, the author of a manuscript dated 1269. The poet Dante, who flourished at the close of this century, distinguished himself not only through his literary pursuits but also his philosophical ones; among his many works, we find an essay on the nature of the elements.

The learned and massive works with which Gesner and Aldrovandus enriched the various departments of natural history may be considered to include most of what the ancients had done in investigating the <term>economy</term> <note>the internal organization or functional systems</note> of the animal world; however, their works appear more like collections of what others had asserted rather than their own original observations.

The first writer whose observations on the properties of natural bodies excite our attention by their novelty and importance is Dr. Gilbert of Colchester. His work on magnetism, published in 1590, contains a large collection of valuable facts and ingenious reasoning. He also extended his researches into many other branches of science, and in particular into the subject of electricity. It had been found in the preceding century that sulfur, as well as amber, was capable of electric excitation, and Gilbert performed many further experiments on the nature of electric phenomena. The change or variation of the declination of the needle is commonly said to have been discovered by Gellibrand, a professor at Gresham College, in the year 1625; but it must have been inferred from Gunter’s observations made in 1622, if not from those of Mair, or of some other person, as early as 1612; for at this time the declination was considerably less than Burrows had found it in 1580.

<insert>
<image-desc>Circular library stamp in the right margin reading: REESE LIBRARY OF THE UNIVERSITY OF CALIFORNIA</image-desc>
</insert>

At the beginning of the seventeenth century, Lord Bacon acquired the deserved reputation of a reformer of philosophy through his praiseworthy efforts to dismantle the incorrect modes of reasoning that had dominated the schools; however, his own immediate discoveries were neither striking nor numerous. In 1620, regarding heat, he proposed an opinion that appears to have been new at that time, inferring from a variety of considerations—which he detailed very minutely in his *Novum Organum*—that it consisted of:

> “an expansive motion, confined and reflected within a body, so as to become alternating and trembling; having also a certain tendency to ascend.”

A similar opinion regarding the vibratory nature of heat was also suggested around the same time by David Gorlaeus, and it was later adopted by Descartes as a part of his hypothesis concerning the constitution of matter. Descartes imagined matter to consist of atoms of various forms, possessing no property other than extension, and deriving all its other qualities from the operation of an ethereal and infinitely elastic fluid, which was continually revolving in different types of vortices.

A much more significant step than the proposal of any hypothesis concerning the nature of heat was also made around the year 1620 by Cornelius Drebel, who appears to have been the original inventor of the method for measuring degrees of heat with a thermometer. The utility of the instrument remained, however, quite limited due to the lack of an accurate method for adjusting its scale,

<header>LECTURE LX.</header>

And it was not until the close of the century that Dr. Hooke's discovery of the permanence of the temperature of boiling water provided a correct and convenient limit to the scale on one side, while the melting of snow served for fixing a similar point on the other; although there would have been no great difficulty in forming a scale sufficiently natural from the proportion of the expansion of the fluid contained in the thermometer to its whole bulk.

It was about the year 1628 that Dr. Harvey succeeded in demonstrating, by a judicious and conclusive series of experiments, the true course of the circulation of the blood through the veins and arteries, both in the mature state of the animal and during its existence as an embryo. Servetus had explicitly asserted, in his work on the Trinity as early as the year 1553, that the blood performed a complete revolution in its passage through the lungs, beginning and ending in the heart; and Cisalpinus had even expressed some suspicions in 1569 that the circulation of the whole body was of a similar nature; but neither of these authors had advanced any satisfactory proofs to confirm their opinions.

In the middle of the seventeenth century, the barometer was invented by Torricelli; the variation of atmospheric pressure was discovered by Descartes; and Pascal performed several experiments on the difference in its magnitude at different places, which tended to illustrate the principles on which the method of determining heights by barometric observations is founded.

What Gesner and Aldrovandus had previously done regarding the animal kingdom was performed, a century later, for the vegetable world by John and Caspar Bauhin, whose works—as collections of all that was to be found on record respecting the distinctions and properties of plants—have not yet been superseded by the latest publications. Our countrymen, Ray and Willughby, also contributed much new matter to the stores of natural history in all its departments; and their labors, as well as those of Tournefort and Réaumur, are of even greater value, as they were far more diligent than their predecessors in distinguishing truth from fiction.

<page-num>749</page-num>
# ON THE HISTORY OF TERRESTRIAL PHYSICS.

The foundation of the most celebrated of the philosophical societies of Europe renders the latter half of the seventeenth century a very interesting period in the history of natural knowledge. The Royal Society of London and the Academy of Sciences of Paris have always been the most distinguished of these; and the Florentine Academy *del Cimento*, although its labors were not of long duration, produced in a short time a very copious and interesting collection of experiments relating to various subjects of physical research. In the Royal Society, Boyle, Hooke, and Newton were the most industrious as well as the most successful investigators of natural phenomena: the elementary doctrines of chemistry, the nature of combustion, the effects of heat and cold, and the laws of attraction, repulsion, and cohesion were attentively examined and discussed. The expansion of water, caused by a reduction of its temperature near the freezing point, was first observed by Dr. Croune, although his experiments were considered by Dr. Hooke to be inconclusive. The attention of the society was directed by Newton to the phenomena of electricity, some of which had been particularly noticed a short time before by Guericke; the mode of making electrical experiments was greatly improved by Hauksbee; this accurate observer also investigated the nature of capillary attraction with considerable success. Early in the following century, many of the members of the Academy of Petersburg followed the example of other societies with great industry, and the experiments of Richmann on heat were among the first and best fruits of their researches.

Dr. Halley employed himself, with the most laudable zeal, in procuring information respecting the variation of the compass; he undertook a voyage around the world for the express purpose of making magnetic observations, and he published a chart of variation adapted to the year 1700. He also collected many details respecting the trade winds and monsoons, and he endeavored to explain them by a theory which has been adopted by some of the latest authors, but which is in reality much less satisfactory than the hypothesis proposed some time afterward by Hadley. His magnetic investigations were continued with great diligence by Mountaine and Dodson, who published, at different periods, two charts representing the successive states of the variation. Euler, Mayer, and others have attempted, in later times, to discover such general laws as might be sufficient to determine the magnitude

The science of electricity was diligently cultivated in the middle of the last century by Stephen Gray, Dufay, Winkler, Nollet, Musschenbroek, and Franklin. As early as 1735, it was remarked by Gray that “the electric fire seemed to be of the same nature as lightning,” and their identity was afterwards more strongly asserted by Winkler and experimentally demonstrated by Franklin. The shock of a charged jar was first discovered by Kleist in 1745; and the experiment was repeated by Lallamand and Musschenbroek, who described its disagreeable effects on the sensations with an exaggeration that was not the most philosophical. The theory of the nature of the charge was the second great improvement made by Dr. Franklin in this science.

The introduction of the Linnaean system of botany and zoology is to be considered as bringing near to perfection the logic and phraseology of natural history; nor has its celebrated author wholly neglected the philosophy of the science. The number and the diligence of his successors have already furnished the different departments of natural history with a much ampler store of observations than could easily have been expected from the short time which their labors have occupied. Buffon had merit of a different kind, and though his imagination was too little regulated by mathematical accuracy, the elegance of his writings has made their subjects highly interesting to the general reader. Among other modern naturalists of great respectability, Spallanzani, Daubenton, Degeer, Geoffroy, Pennant, the Jussieus, Lacepede, and Haüy have particularly distinguished themselves by the importance of their discoveries and the accuracy of their descriptions.

The absorption of heat during the conversion of ice into water appears to have been separately observed by Deluc, Black, and Wilke about the year 1755. On this experiment, Dr. Black principally founded his doctrine of latent heat, supposed to be retained in chemical combination by the particles of fluids. Dr. Irvine and Dr. Crawford explained the circumstances somewhat differently, by the theory of a change of capacity for heat only. The elegant hypothesis of Aepinus concerning magnetism and electricity, founded largely on the theory of Franklin, was advanced in 1759. Our venerable countryman, Mr. Cavendish, had invented a similar theory and had entered in many respects more minutely into the details of its consequences without being aware of Aepinus's work, although the publication of his paper on the subject was 12 years later. Lambert, Mayer, Coulomb, and Robison have also pursued similar inquiries, both theoretically and experimentally, with great success. The electrophorus of Wilke and the condenser of Volta are among the earliest results of developing a rational system of electricity, and Mr. Cavendish's investigation of the properties of the torpedo <note>The torpedo is a species of electric ray; Cavendish's work helped prove that its "shock" was identical to man-made electricity.</note> may serve as a model of accuracy and precision in conducting experimental research.

The speculations of Boscovich concerning the fundamental properties of matter, and the general laws of the mutual action of bodies on each other, have been considered by some impartial judges as deserving the highest praise; they remain, however, in almost all cases, speculations only. Some of the most complex of them, being intended to explain facts which have perhaps been much misunderstood, must consequently be both inaccurate and superfluous.

The attention of several experienced philosophers who are now living has been devoted, with much perseverance, to the difficult subject of hygrometry <note>The science of measuring the humidity or moisture content of the atmosphere.</note>. Deluc's experiments have offered us a very useful comparison of the hygrometrical qualities of various substances. Saussure has investigated, with great labor, the readings of the hygrometer and the thermometer as they relate to the presence of a certain portion of vapor contained in air of various densities; and Pictet has determined some similar circumstances regarding vapors of different kinds entirely unmixed with any air. [Expe]riments, however, have generally been too little supported by facts to be entitled to universal adoption.

For some years past, the scientific world, as well as the general public, has been much occupied and entertained by the discoveries of Galvani, Volta, and others, regarding the operations of the <term>electric fluid</term>. The first circumstance that attracted Galvani’s attention to the subject of <term>animal electricity</term> was the twitching of a frog that had an "armed" nerve—that is, a nerve laid bare and covered with metal—when a spark was produced nearby. A person acquainted with the well-known laws of <term>induced electricity</term> might easily have foreseen this effect; it proved, however, that a frog prepared in this way was a very delicate <term>electrometer</term>, and it led Galvani to further experiments. It has been shown by Volta that an entire frog may be convulsed by a degree of electricity which affects an <term>electrometer</term> only very weakly; but when prepared in Galvani’s manner, it will be agitated by a current one-fiftieth as strong, which cannot be detected by any other means without the assistance of a <term>condenser</term>. Galvani, however, found that a connection made between the armed nerve and its muscle, by means of any conducting substance, was sufficient to produce a convulsion without the presence of external electricity. From this, he concluded that the nerve and muscle, like the opposite surfaces of a <term>charged jar</term>, were in opposite states of electricity, and that the connection produced a discharge between them. He observed, however, a considerable difference in the effects when different metals were used to form the circuit; and this circumstance led to the discovery of the excitation of electricity by means of a combination of different inanimate substances alone, which Mr. Davy attributes to Fabroni, Creve, and Dr. Ash. It was, however, still more satisfactorily demonstrated by Volta; he at first supposed that all the phenomena observed by Galvani were derived from effects of this kind, but upon further examination, he was obliged to admit the independent existence of animal electricity. This industrious and ingenious philosopher has the sole credit for the invention of the <term>pile</term> or <term>battery</term>, which has rendered every other mode of exciting <term>galvanic action</term> comparatively insignificant.

### ON THE HISTORY OF TERRESTRIAL PHYSICS.

A pile was constructed by Mr. Carlisle, and its remarkable effects in the decomposition of water were jointly observed by himself and Mr. Nicholson. The actual existence of <term>animal electricity</term>, as asserted by Galvani and Volta, has been confirmed to some degree by the experiments of Aldini, the nephew of Galvani. A number of separate observations, of considerable merit, have also been made by Pfaff, Ritter, Cruikshank, Wollaston, Fourcroy, and many other chemists, both in this country and on the continent. But Mr. Davy's recent experiments must be considered to exceed in importance everything that has been done on the subject of electricity since the discovery of the <term>pile of Volta</term>. The conclusions which these experiments have enabled him to form regarding the electrical properties of substances that have the strongest tendencies to act chemically on each other, and the power of the <term>electric fluid</term> to modify and counteract those tendencies, have greatly extended our views of the minute operations of nature and have opened a new field for future investigations. I hope that I shall be pardoned by astronomers for having inserted, on this occasion, the figure of a <term>galvanic battery</term> in a vacant space among the constellations near Pegasus; it must now be acknowledged to have as much claim to such a distinction as the electrical machine and the chemical furnace.

The recent experiments and speculations of Mr. Dalton on various subjects belonging to different branches of physics have tended to place some parts of the science of meteorology in a new light. It is true that many of his hypotheses are assumed quite arbitrarily; some of them are clearly contrary to experiment, and others to analogy and probability. At the same time, his remarks appear in some cases to be either perfectly correct or to lead to determinations which are sufficiently accurate for every practical purpose. I have attempted to borrow some hints from Mr. Dalton's ideas, which I have incorporated into a more acceptable system; and by comparing his experiments with those of many other philosophers, I have deduced some methods of calculation which may perhaps be practically useful—specifically a simple rule for determining the <term>elasticity of steam</term>, and a mode of reducing the readings of <term>hygrometers</term> of different kinds to a natural scale.

...years by the Royal Society to the author of the most valuable discovery concerning heat or light, marks a period less remarkable than the first awarding of the medal to himself, and the second to Mr. Leslie. Count Rumford’s numerous experiments on the production and transfer of heat are highly important, both for the benefits that may be gained from their practical application and for the help they provide us in investigating the fundamental nature of heat. Mr. Leslie’s discovery of the various properties possessed by different types of surfaces regarding the emission and reception of radiant heat is in every respect highly interesting; and the number and variety of his experiments would have earned him even greater praise than he has received if they had been described more simply and in more detail. Perhaps, however, none of the modern improvements in theoretical science deserves a higher ranking than Dr. Herschel’s discovery of the separation of heat from light through refraction. Mr. Prévost has made some accurate remarks on the experiments of other philosophers concerning heat; and his own theory of radiant heat, along with his original investigations into the effect of solar heat on the earth, have significantly helped to clarify the subject of his research.

The general laws governing the rise and fall of fluids in capillary tubes and between various types of plates had been established long ago by the experiments of Hauksbee, Jurin, and Musschenbroek. Many other circumstances depending on the same principles had been examined by Taylor, Achard, and Guyton; and some progress toward a theory of the shapes assumed by the surfaces of liquids had been made by Clairaut, Segner, and Monge. In an essay on the cohesion of fluids read before the Royal Society in the year 1804, I reduced all effects of this nature to the combined operation of a cohesive and a repulsive force that balance each other. I assumed only that the repulsion increases more than the cohesion as particles approach each other, and I have had the satisfaction of discovering in this manner a perfect connection between many facts that were not previously thought to have the slightest relationship with each other. Almost a year after the publication of this paper, Mr. Laplace read a memoir on capillary tubes to the National Institute in which, as far as he pursued the subject, he precisely confirmed the most obvious of my conclusions;

although his method of calculation appears to be by no means beyond criticism, as it does not include the consideration of the effects of repulsion. If my paper had been fortunate enough to attract Mr. Laplace’s attention before his memoir was presented to the Institute, he perhaps would have extended the results of my theory with the same success that has consistently characterized his work in every other department of natural philosophy.

When we reflect on the state of the sciences in general at the beginning of the seventeenth century and compare it with the progress made in all of them since then, we will be convinced that the last two hundred years have done much more to promote knowledge than the two thousand years that preceded them; and we will be even more encouraged by the consideration that perhaps the greater part of these advancements has been made within only the last fifty or sixty years. We therefore have the satisfaction of seeing the knowledge of nature not only in a state of progress but even advancing with increasing speed; and the universal spread of an interest in science appears to promise that, as the number of its practitioners increases, new facts will be continually discovered, and those already known will be better understood and more beneficially applied. The Royal Institution, along with other similar societies, will have the merit of assisting in the dissemination of knowledge and in cultivating an interest in its pursuit; and the advantages arising from the general introduction of scientific studies, and from the adoption of the practical improvements depending on them, will amply repay the efforts of those who have been active in establishing and supporting associations so truly commendable.

### PLATE I.

Fig. 1. If point A is assumed to move in a straight line toward B, AB is the direction of its motion. P. 21.

Fig. 2. The lines AB, BC, and CD are the successive directions of point A as it moves from A to D in the figure ABCD. P. 21.

Fig. 3. The tangent AB is the direction of motion for point C, moving along the curve CD, at the moment it arrives at E. P. 21.

Fig. 4. As the square AB moves on the board CD, such that points E and F describe the parallel lines EG and EH with equal velocities, the plane AEFB is in rectilinear motion with respect to the surface CD. P. 24.

Fig. 5. The cycloid ABC and the trochoid DEF are the results of the rotational motion of points B and E around the center of the wheel, combined with the progressive motion of the wheel along the base AC. P. 24, 44.

Fig. 6. AB is a fixed bar, and CD is an arm that slides upon it. ECF is a thread passing around the pulley at C, which is either fixed to the pin on the slider F or passed over the pulley G and fixed again at H. The arm turns around the same axis that carries the pulley at C and can be fixed by means of the screw cut into the axis, while two other screws keep it steady by pressing on the slider beneath it. Point I describes, through its compound motion, the oblique line KI. P. 24.

Fig. 7. The diagonal AB of the parallelogram CD is the joint result of the motions represented by its sides AC and AD. P. 25.

Fig. 8. The line AB may be simply drawn in the direction AB, or it may be traced by the equal motions AC and AD of the arm and its slider, or by the unequal motions AE and AF. P. 25.

Fig. 9. The body A, moving uniformly along the line AB, first approaches point C and then recedes from it, as if repelled. P. 27.

Fig. 10. When AB and AC approach each other and coincide, the diagonal AD becomes equal to their sum. P. 30.

<column-break/>

Fig. 11. Atwood’s machine. The boxes A and B, containing equal weights, are connected by the thread ACB, which passes over the pulley C. This pulley is supported either on friction wheels or by the points of screws, one of which is visible at D. The box A is made to descend either by a flat weight placed on it or by the bar E, which is intercepted by the ring F; the box continues to descend until it strikes the stage G. The distance is measured on the scale HI, and the time is measured by the pendulum K, which may be kept in motion by a clock escapement with a weight. The machine is leveled using the screws L and M. P. 31.

Fig. 12. If the time of a falling body's descent is represented by any portion AB of the base of a triangle, the velocity will be proportional to BC (which is equal to AB). The space described during the infinitely short time DE will be proportional to the area DEFG, which is expressed by the product of BC and DE. Consequently, the entire area AEF represents the space described in the time AE, and AHI represents the space described in the time AH. However, AHI is half of the square HK, and AEF is half of the square EL: the distance is therefore always proportional to the square of the time and is equal to half the distance that would be covered in the same time at the final velocity. P. 32.

Fig. 13. The whirling table. The arms AB and CD are made to revolve on the axes EF and GH by a string passing over the wheel I; either the upper or lower pulley of each axis can be used as desired. The stages K and L, with their weights, are placed at specific distances from the center using the racks or teeth below them. They move along the arms by means of friction wheels resting on wires, and they raise the weights M and N using threads that each pass over two pulleys. P. 35.

Fig. 14. If a body revolving in a curve ABC, driven by a force directed toward D, covers the portions AE, BF, and CG in equal times, the areas ADE, BDF, and CDG will be equal. The velocities at A, B, and G will be inversely proportional to the perpendiculars DH, DI, and DK. P. 36.

## PLATE II.

**Fig. 15.** The ball **A**, rotating around the point **B**, and being drawn toward it by the thread **BC** with a force that can be changed as desired; its velocity may be observed to vary according to its distance from point **B**. P. 37.

**Fig. 16.** The curve **ABCDE** is an ellipse; **E** and **G** are its foci, **AD** its major axis, and **CE** its minor axis. P. 37.

**Fig. 17.** The horizontal range, **AB**, of a body projected at an elevation of 45°, is greater than **AC** or **AD**, which are the ranges of bodies projected with the same velocity at a greater or lesser elevation. If the parallel lines **EF** and **GH** are always proportional to the squares of **AE** and **AG**, the curve **AFH** will be a parabola; and such is the path of a projectile. P. 39, 40.

**Fig. 18.** The path of a ball moving quickly through the atmosphere nearly resembles the curve **AB**. P. 39.

**Fig. 19.** The ball **A**, having descended along the groove **AB**, describes the parabola **BC**, passing through the rings **D** and **E**. P. 40.

**Fig. 20.** The cylinder **A**, weighted at the axis, descends along an inclined plane more rapidly than the cylinder **B**, which is weighted with an equal weight at its circumference. P. 42.

**Fig. 21.** The balls **A**, **B**, and **C** descend along the planes **AD**, **BE**, and **CF**, which are of equal height, in times proportional to their lengths. The upper surfaces of the slides **AD**, **BE**, and **CF** are slightly grooved. P. 43.

**Fig. 22.** The balls **A**, **B**, and **C** descend in equal times along the chords **AD**, **BD**, and **CD**. P. 43.

**Fig. 23.** The same ball, descending from equal heights at **A**, **B**, or **C** by different paths, will rise to the same height at **D** on the opposite side of **E**. P. 43.

**Fig. 24.** The thread **AB**, moving between the cycloidal cheeks **AC** and **AD**, describes the cycloid **CED**,

<column-break/>

and the balls **B** and **E**, descending from any two points of the curve, will meet at **E** in the same time that the ball **G** falls from a point nearly 1/4 of **AE** above **A**. The distance traveled by the pendulum in descending is always proportional to the height **HI**, to which a body starting from **E** and rotating uniformly in a circle will rise in the same time. The circle **EI** lies outside the cycloid **CED** and is somewhat less inclined to the horizon at equal distances from **E**. P. 44, 45.

**Fig. 25.** The ball **A**, descending from **B** in the curve **BA**, arrives at **C** before the ball **D** moving in a straight line on the plane **BC**. P. 46.

**Fig. 26.** When the balls **A**, **B**, and **C** are made to rotate using the whirling table, they are always found in the same horizontal plane. The joint connecting them with the axis is shown at **D**, as seen from above. P. 47.

**Fig. 27.** The equal oscillations represented by **AB** and **CD** form, when combined, the circular revolution **AEB**; the unequal oscillations **AB** and **FG** form the ellipse **AHB**; the position of the body is always determined by combining the <term>versed sines</term> of two circular arcs that increase uniformly. P. 47.

**Fig. 28.** As the rotation of the balls **A** and **B** becomes more rapid, they move outward, and the point **C** is lowered. P. 48.

**Fig. 29.** The mass of body **A** being 1 and that of **B** being 2, and **AC** being twice the length of **BC**, **C** is the center of inertia. P. 51.

**Fig. 30.** The balls **A** and **B** are suspended by long threads, which allow them to move in the arcs **AC** and **BD**; the ball **A** has a hole through it in a horizontal direction and contains a spiral spring, which is held by the thread **E**. When released by burning this thread, the spring strikes the ball **B** so as to cause each of the balls to move through an arc where the chord is proportional to the weight of the other ball. P. 52.

## PLATE III.

**Fig. 31.** The center of inertia of the bodies *A*, *B*, *C*, *D*, may be determined either by finding *E*, the center of inertia of *A* and *B*, and assuming a body equal to their sum to be placed in it, then determining *F* from *E* and *C*; and *G*, the point required, from *F* and *D*; or by first finding *H* and *I* from *A*, *C*, *B*, *D*, taken in pairs, and dividing *HI* in due proportion at the same point *G*. P. 54.

**Fig. 32.** The point *A* being the center of inertia of the bodies *B*, *C*, *D*, *E*, the products obtained by multiplying *B* by *BF*, *C* by *CG*, *D* by *DH*, and *E* by *EI*, are equal, when added together, to the product of the masses of all the bodies by the distance *AK*; all the lines drawn to the plane *FI* being parallel. P. 55.

**Fig. 33.** The weights *ABC* will remain at rest when they are in the same proportion to each other as the respective sides of the triangle *DEF*; *DF* being parallel to *EG*. P. 61.

**Fig. 34.** The bodies *A*, *B*, remain in equilibrium when their center of inertia *C* is immediately below the point of suspension *D*. P. 61.

**Fig. 35.** The system of bodies *A*, *B*, *C*, is at rest when the center of inertia *D* is immediately below the point of suspension *E*. P. 61.

**Fig. 36.** The bodies *A*, *B*, remain at rest when the center of inertia *C* is immediately above the point of support *D*. P. 61.

**Fig. 37.** The bodies *A*, *B*, remain at rest when the center of inertia *C* coincides with the fulcrum or point of support. P. 61.

**Fig. 38.** The irregular body *AB*, remains at rest when the center of inertia *C* is immediately below the point of suspension *D*. P. 61.

**Fig. 39.** *A* being the center of gravity of the board *B*, *C*, the point of suspension being *D*, *E*, or *F*, the position of the vertical line will be *DA*, *EA*, or *FA*. P. 62.

**Fig. 40.** The equilibrium of the vessel *A* is stable;

<column-break/>

that of the vessel *B* is tottering <note>unstable</note>, the path of the center of gravity having its concavity upwards in the first, and downwards in the second. P. 62.

**Fig. 41.** Paths of the center of gravity of an oval. P. 62.

**Fig. 42.** Paths of the center of gravity of a body resting on a sphere. P. 62.

**Fig. 43.** *A*, the path of the center of gravity of a body standing on a flat base; *B*, the tottering <note>unstable</note> equilibrium of the same body inclined. P. 63.

**Fig. 44.** The effects of a certain inclination of a wagon, loaded with light and heavy materials, are represented at *A* and *B* respectively. P. 63.

**Fig. 45.** The suspension of a weight from a rod projecting over a table. P. 64.

**Fig. 46.** *A* shows the path of the center of gravity of a loaded cylinder on an inclined plane; *B* shows that of the center of gravity of a double cone moving towards the more elevated end of a triangular surface. *C* is an elevation <note>a side or front view drawing</note> of the double cone. P. 64.

**Fig. 47.** *AB* is a lever of the first kind, the forces acting on different sides of the fulcrum *C*; *DE* is of the second kind, the forces being applied at *D* and *F*, on the same side of *E*. P. 65.

**Fig. 48.** A force applied at *A* may be held in equilibrium by a triple force, applied in the direction *BC* either at *B* or at *C*, or in a direction perpendicular to the arm *CD* at *E*; *DE* and *DB* being each one-third of *AD*. P. 67.

**Fig. 49.** A force, acting at *A* on the lever *AB*, has a great mechanical advantage in turning the lever *CD*; but when the levers are in the position *BE*, *DF*, the force acts with a similar disadvantage. P. 67.

**Fig. 50.** The diameter of the cylinder *A* being three times as great as that of *B*, the weight *C*, or an equivalent force applied to the winch *D*, will support a triple weight at *E*. P. 67.
