# PLATE V.

**Fig. 65.** By means of the movable inclined plane AB, of which the height AC is one-third of the horizontal length BC, the weight D, acting horizontally, supports a triple weight E acting in a vertical direction. P. 71.

**Fig. 66.** AB being one-fourth of BC, the rope AB must exert a force of tension equal to one-fourth of the weight C in order to support it, assuming the surfaces are without friction. But if the friction of the end of the beam AC were equal to one-fourth of the pressure, it would support the weight C without any other force, whatever its magnitude might be. P. 72.

**Fig. 67.** AB being half of BC, or one-fourth of CD, the force extending the rope CD each way is equal to the weight E. P. 72.

**Fig. 68.** The thin wedge AB, of which the height is one-fifth of the length, being rolled around the cylinder C, forms the screw D, by means of which the weight E is capable of supporting a weight five times as great as F. P. 72.

**Fig. 69.** A is a screw, and B is the nut belonging to it. P. 72.

**Fig. 70.** The endless screw AB acts on the teeth of the wheel CD. P. 72.

**Fig. 71.** The distance between the threads of the interior screw is four-fifths of that of the exterior or perforated screw, and this distance is one-thirtieth of the circumference. Hence, the weight A is capable of sustaining a weight B 150 times as great as itself. P. 73.

**Fig. 72.** The apparatus for experiments on collision. Those balls which are not employed may be left behind the graduated arc, as at A and B; some of the strings have balls of half the weight of the others, while others have a small dish C, on which balls of clay, or of wax softened with one-fourth its weight of oil, may be supported. P. 76.

**Fig. 73.** If the ball A strikes the ball B in the oblique direction AC, the ball B will be impelled in the direction CD perpendicular to the surface of contact; and the velocity EC being resolved into EF and FC, the part FC will continue unaltered; and if the balls are equal, the part EF will be destroyed, so that the ball A will move after the impact in the direction CG, except for the effect of any accidental dis-

<column-break/>

turbance which may be derived from the resistance of the surrounding bodies. If we imagine a ball at C in contact with B, in the direction DB, we may aim a blow at the center of this ball in order to drive the ball B to D; and if B happens to be situated anywhere in the semicircle DCG, the motion of A after the impulse will be in the direction BG or GB, if there is no resistance. When the ball H is reflected by a fixed obstacle, such as by the cushion of a billiard table at I, its velocity KI may be resolved into the parts KL and LI; the part KL continues, and may be represented by LM equal to KL; the part LI is converted into IL in a contrary direction, which when combined with LM makes IM, the angle LIM being equal to LIK. We may find the proper direction for striking any ball by reflection if we suppose a ball N in contact with the nearest point of the cushion, and making NO equal to MN, aim at a ball supposed to be at O. In the same manner, if we wish to impel the ball P in the direction PQ by a stroke of the ball R after reflection at S, we first place a ball at T behind P, and determine the direction RS by aiming at a ball U, as if we wished to strike a ball at T with a direct impulse. But in the case of a billiard ball, the rotation of the ball around its axis, which is not destroyed by the collision, will cause the ball to move—on account of the friction of the table—in a direction different from its first direction: thus the ball C will not go on to G, but will strike the cushion between C and D; and the ball H, after reflection at I, will proceed in a direction a little nearer to N than IM; so that the imaginary ball O ought perhaps to be placed as far from the cushion itself as M, in order that the ball may be struck after reflection. P. 82.

**Fig. 74.** Mr. Smeaton's apparatus for experiments on rotatory motion. P. 84.

**Fig. 75.** The movable center of suspension being fixed at the distance of 5 inches from one of the balls and 7 from the other, the vibration is performed at the same time as that of a pendulum 37 inches long. P. 85.

**Fig. 76.** The three weights, supported on wheels, being drawn up the three inclined planes at the same time by the action of three other equal weights, the middle weight arrives first at the top, the length of its plane being twice the height. P. 88.

**Fig. 91.** A <term>sector</term>. The scale of equal parts is marked L. As AB is to AC, so is BD to CE; and if any line BD is placed with its ends in the third division of the scale on each leg, the distance CE between the seventh divisions will contain 7 equal parts, of which BD contains 3; and the same is true of any other numbers. **Fig. 96.** A <term>micrometrical scale</term> made by Troughton. The compound microscopes A and B are fixed nearly at the required distance on the scale C: A is then made to point exactly to a division of the standard scale D by means of the screw E, and B to another division, at the required distance, by means of the screw F, the fractional parts being added by the turns of the screw G. The scale D is then removed, and the object to be compared with it is put in its place. P. 112.

movable stud C; the screw D fixes it in its angular position. It is also capable of motion around the axis EF, which is fixed by the screw G. P. 113.

**Fig. 100.** Illustration of the principles of <term>perspective</term>. A being the position of the eye, and BC the plane of projection, if AD is parallel to EF, GH, and IK, then D will be their <term>vanishing point</term>, and ED, GD, and ID their whole images; AL being parallel to EM and IN, L will be their <term>vanishing point</term>, and EL and IL their whole images; and AO being parallel to PQ, O will be its <term>vanishing point</term>. P. 115.

**Fig. 101.** A being the center of the picture, AB the horizontal <term>vanishing line</term>, AC the vertical line, and D the <term>point of distance</term>, if a <term>ground plan</term> EFGH of any figure on the horizontal plane is placed in its true position with respect to IK, the bottom of the picture, the <term>vanishing points</term> of all its lines will be found by drawing DL, DM, DN, and DO parallel to those lines respectively; and the whole images of the lines will be PL, QM, KN, and IO, determining, by their intersections, the figure RSTU, which will be the projection of EFGH. The plan may also be drawn in an inverted position below the line IK, and the <term>point of distance</term> taken above A instead of below it. P. 115.

**Fig. 102.** AB being the whole image of the line represented by AC as a <term>ground plan</term>, and D the <term>point of distance</term>, we may find E, the image of the point C, by drawing CD; or we may make BF=BD and AG=AC; FG will then also cut AB at the point E. P. 116.

# PLATE VIII.

**Fig. 103.** The heights of the houses, windows, doors, and figures are determined by lines directed to the center of the picture; the true height is measured on the lines AB and CD, where the objects are supposed to touch the plane of projection. The distance EF, and all other parts of lines perpendicular to the picture, are measured by laying off the lengths of the originals, such as GH, on the line AC, and drawing lines IEG and IEH from I, the point of distance; in most cases, this point will be further from the center of the picture than it is shown here. The line KL, and others parallel to AC, may be measured with the assistance of any point M on the horizontal line, by laying off the distances NO and OP on AC, or simply by reducing the scale in the proportion of MP to ML. P. 116.

**Fig. 104.** A circle rendered in perspective by means of a surrounding square, with the points of contact found by bisecting the sides. P. 116.

**Fig. 105.** Two perspective drawings and two orthographic projections of a cube in different positions. For the orthographic projection, where the ground plan is ABCD, the image of any point A or B may be found by drawing AE and BF perpendicular to the ground line; EG and FH parallel to the line assumed for the direction of the center of the picture; and AG and BH parallel to the line of direction of the point of distance. The intersections G and H will then be the points corresponding to A and B. P. 116.

**Fig. 106.** A is the orthographic projection of a sphere, along with some of its circles; B is the stereographic projection of the same circles. P. 117.

**Fig. 107.** A balance made by Fidler for the Royal Institution, which closely resembles those made by Ramsden and Troughton. The middle column A is raised as desired by the lever <note>original: "cock"</note> B, and carries the round ends of the

<column-break/>

axis in the forks at its upper part, in order to remove the pressure from the sharp edges of the axis within the forks. The scales are occasionally supported by the pillars C and D, which are raised or lowered by turning the handle E. The screw F serves to raise or lower a weight within the conical beam, by which the position of the center of gravity is regulated. The extent of the vibrations is measured on the graduated arc G. P. 125.

**Fig. 108.** A balance for illustrating the different kinds of equilibrium. When the scales are hung on the middle pins, A and B, which are on the same horizontal line as the beam's support, the equilibrium is neutral, as the weights act as if the center of gravity coincided with the point of suspension. If the scales are hung on the lowest pins C and D, the center of gravity will be nearly on the line CD, and its path will be the curve E, which is concave upward; but if the scales are hung on the pins F and G, the path of the center of gravity will be convex upward, and the beam will overset. In reality, the true paths of the center of gravity would be nearly along the curves H and I, situated between the weights in the scales, but these are similar to the other curves. P. 125.

**Fig. 109.** When the equilibrium of a balance is unstable <note>original: "tottering"</note>, the lower weight acts with the greatest advantage: thus the effect of weight A is reduced in the proportion of BC to DC by the slant of the arm CA, while weight E acts on the full length of its arm CF. P. 125.

**Fig. 110.** If ABC is a semicircle, and BD represents a given weight, and AD its counterweight in one of the scales of an unequal balance, then DC will be the counterweight in the other scale. It is obvious that AC is more than twice as large as BD. P. 126.

### PLATE XI.

**Fig. 148.** A machine for examining the <term>strength of materials</term>. The force is applied by using the <term>winch</term> *A*, which winds up the rope *BC*. This rope passes over the first pulley and under the second, which is positioned directly under point *D*, where the force acts on the piece *EF* to be broken. The pulleys slide on two parallel bars fixed in a frame, which is held down by a point projecting at *G* from the <term>lever</term> *GH*; this lever is graduated like a <term>steelyard</term> and measures the force. The piece to be broken is held by a double <term>vice</term>, *I*, *K*, with four screws (two of them hide the other two in the figure). If a wire is to be torn, it may be fixed to the cross bar *LM*; a substance to be crushed must be placed under the <term>lever</term> *NO*, with the end *N* receiving the rope and the end *O* being held down by the click, which acts on the double <term>ratchet</term> *OP*. The lever is double from *O* to *Q* and acts on the substance by a loop fixed to it by a pin. P. 151.

**Fig. 149.** The outline of a <term>column</term> diminished by one-fifth of its diameter, shown in two different ways. Side *A* is an arc of an <term>ellipse</term>, of which the semidiameter *AB* is the lesser semi-axis, joined at *A* to a straight line *AC* that is one-third the length of the column; the part *AD* is cylindrical. Side *DE* is a <term>cubic parabola</term> and may be drawn mechanically by fixing a straight ruler *EF* in such a position that *DF* is twice the diminution at *E*, and then bending it to *D*; the diminution is everywhere proportional to the cube of the distance from *D*. These two methods are compared in a contracted scale at *G*: the outer line represents the first method, and the next line represents the second; the third line, which is nearest to *G*, is the <term>conchoid of Nicomedes</term> recommended by <note>Sir William</note> Chambers and said to be found in the columns of the <note>Roman</note> Pantheon, with the curve beginning at the base. <note>Andrea</note> Palladio fixes the ruler at *A* and bends it to *H*, which makes the curvature abruptly greater at *H*. P. 158.

**Fig. 150.** A section of Mr. <term>Smeaton</term>'s <term>lighthouse</term> at the <term>Eddystone</term>. P. 159.

<column-break/>

**Fig. 151.** Mr. <term>Smeaton</term>'s mode of uniting tiers of stones by wooden pins and wedges. P. 160.

**Fig. 152.** A string of beads suspended in <term>equilibrium</term> from two points and remaining in equilibrium when in an inverted position. The ends are supported by two pieces which slide backwards and forwards and are fixed by screws; the string is also tightened by turning a pin. P. 161.

**Fig. 153.** A system of bars hanging in <term>equilibrium</term> and supporting each other in the same form when inverted. P. 161.

**Fig. 154.** *A* is a chain loaded at equal distances with other chains of such a length as to represent the depth of the materials pressing on an <term>arch</term> of the form shown by the first chain, holding it in <term>equilibrium</term>. *B* is an <term>arch</term> of a similar form. P. 161.

**Fig. 155.** A comparison of the curves which have various advantages for the construction of an <term>arch</term> supporting a horizontal road. The solid line is an elliptic arc, somewhat less than half the <term>ellipse</term>. The outside curve, which is also continued furthest down, is the one calculated for resisting the pressure of materials acting like a fluid or in the manner of wedges. The second dotted curve is for supporting the pressure of the materials above each part, assuming they act in a vertical direction only. The third is a circular arc, forming one-third of a whole circle. The fourth is part of a <term>logarithmic curve</term>, which is of nearly equal strength with respect to the tendency of the materials to give way for want of <term>lateral adhesion</term>. The fifth is composed of parabolic curves, showing the outline which would be strongest for supporting any additional weight placed on the middle of the arch. If the height were greater in proportion to the span, as usually happens in practice, there would be less difference between these curves. With the <term>radius of curvature</term> at the summit being *AB*, the <term>horizontal thrust</term> is equal to the weight of the portion *ABCD* of the materials.

# PLATE XIII.

**Fig. 166.** Joints for a <term>tie beam</term>. The joints at A and B cannot be more than half as strong as the entire beam, even assuming the adhesion produced by the pressure of the bolts is as strong as could be required. The joint at C is called a <term>dovetail joint</term>; its strength is a little less than that of A and B, but the adhesion is more easily secured, since a force tending to separate the beams must tighten the joint. P. 167.

**Fig. 167.** Joints for a <term>tie beam</term>. The joint A, if sufficiently tight, may possess 2/3 of the strength of the beam. The joint B might be as strong as the beam if the adhesion were great enough, but it would be difficult to apply sufficient pressure to create such an adhesion; if the beam were subject to much shaking, the joint would be a very bad one. P. 167.

**Fig. 168.** A good joint for a <term>tie beam</term>; the adhesion is secured by a slight reduction in strength. P. 167.

**Fig. 169.** A, a simple <term>scarfed joint</term>, which may be tightened by a wedge at the center; it is not strong. B, a <term>scarfed joint</term> which is much stronger. P. 167.

**Fig. 170.** A joint for a beam supporting a weight by its <term>transverse strength</term>. The junction might be made, if necessary, by means of a third piece, the limits of which are marked by the dotted line. The strength is only slightly diminished by the joint. P. 168.

**Fig. 171.** A beam supporting a weight by its <term>transverse strength</term>, joined to another by means of a third piece of half the depth, <term>spliced</term> or <term>fished on</term> below the beam, and secured by pins and by blocks or <term>joggles</term>. The strength is a little greater than that of the original beam. The dotted lines show the proportion in which the layers (strata) are extended or compressed, with the lower part of the original beam remaining in its natural state without sustaining any pressure as far as one-fourth of the depth and a little further. P. 168.

<column-break/>

**Fig. 172.** A joint for a beam pressing obliquely against another. The dotted lines show the form of the <term>tenon</term>, which may occupy a considerable part of the width of the beam. The upper strap, A, is in the most common position, but the lower one, B, appears to provide greater strength, as it presses the beams more closely together without any danger of damaging or buckling them; it also has the advantage of having a firmer hold of the lower beam. P. 169.

**Fig. 173.** A joint for a horizontal beam suspended from a vertical one: the end of the <term>tenon</term> being expanded by wedges, and the whole secured by a strong strap. The tenon ought not to be wide, since it reduces the strength of the horizontal beam. P. 169.

**Fig. 174.** Straps that are bent so as to deviate from the straight lines joining their extremities to the degree represented here have their strength reduced to about one-seventh of what they would have if they were straight. Thus, A B is only one-seventh as strong as C D, assuming the material is inflexible. P. 169.

**Fig. 175.** The simplest form of a roof. A B and A C are the <term>rafters</term>, and B C is the <term>tie beam</term>; the weight of each half being represented by A B or A C, the thrust in the direction of the rafters will be A D, and the horizontal thrust each way will be B D or C D. It is obvious that A D will be at its minimum when B A C is a right angle. P. 170.

**Fig. 176.** A common roof with <term>braces</term>. A B is the <term>king post</term>, and B C and B D are the braces. P. 170.

**Fig. 177.** A <term>curb</term> or <term>mansard roof</term>, the rafters of which hold each other in equilibrium. A B and C D are <term>queen posts</term> helping to support the tie beam. The piece A C acts as a <term>strut</term> in supporting the pressure caused by the weight of the tie beam. The heads of the queen posts are not thickened much, in order to avoid changes arising from the unequal contraction of the wood. P. 170.

Fig. 189. The form of a wheel or pulley on which a broad strap runs, the surface being convex; the wheel that drives it is of a similar form, but only its upper part is shown in the figure. P. 175.

Fig. 191. The teeth of two wheels, formed into involutes of circles, described by uncoiling a thread from the dotted circles; the point of contact of the teeth is always in the straight line that touches both circles. P. 176.

Fig. 192. Two surfaces formed into involutes of circles, revolving in contact with each other; the equidistant lines drawn on them continue to meet each other throughout the revolution. P. 176.

Fig. 193. The pinion A is of the kind called a spur wheel; B is a crown wheel, or a contrate wheel. P. 177.

Fig. 194. The wheel and pinion are both beveled; the faces of the teeth are directed toward the point A. P. 177.

Fig. 195. Two wheels slightly eccentric, acting on each other. P. 178.

Fig. 196. An eccentric contrate wheel, acting on a long pinion. P. 178.

<column-break/>

Fig. 197. A machine for cutting the teeth of wheels. A is the wheel whose teeth are formed by the revolving saw B, turned by the wheel and pinion C and D by means of the handle E. Meanwhile, the frame that holds the saw—moving on hinges and resting on a spring—is pressed down by the handle F, its position having been previously adjusted by the screw G. The large plate H I contains a number of concentric circles, variously divided by points into which the end of the spring I sinks at each step, so as to fix the apparatus in the required position. P. 178.

Fig. 198. A chronometer for measuring minute portions of time. As the axis AB is turned, either by the handle A or by the weight C, the balls D and E fly outward and move the weights F and G further from the axis; as a result, the increased effect of friction slows the motion when it becomes too rapid. Meanwhile, the barrel H is turned with the axis and is allowed to descend as the thread at I is uncoiled, so that the point K, which is pressed against it by a spring, traces a spiral on it that is interrupted whenever the pin K is touched. P. 191.

Fig. 199. The fusee of a watch or clock, the general outline of which forms part of the hyperbola A B, in which the distance of each point from the axis C D is inversely proportional to its distance from the line D E. P. 192.

# PLATE XVI.

**Fig. 200.** A fusee with an auxiliary spring, for continuing the motion when the watch is wound up. The action of the mainspring turns the fusee in the direction A B; the fusee acts on the ratchet wheel A B C by means of the click B, and this wheel drives the toothed wheel D E by the spring C B A, which is supposed to be seen through it. When the watch is wound up, this spring forces back the wheel A B C against the click F, which serves as a fixed point, while the other end continues to act on D E, and to maintain the motion. P. 193.
**Fig. 201.** The escapement wheel A B, moving in the direction A C B, impels the pallets D, E of the crutch or anchor, alternately in opposite directions. P. 194.
**Fig. 202.** A is the escapement wheel, B and C are the pallets of the common watch escapement. P. 194.
**Fig. 203.** The deadbeat escapement. The teeth are first received on the flat or rather cylindrical surfaces A, B, on which they rest until the pendulum arrives near the middle of its vibration, when the teeth begin to act on the inclined surfaces terminating the pallets. P. 195.
**Fig. 204.** The horizontal escapement, for a watch. The tooth A rests first on the external surface of the cylinder, B C, and then impels it by its inclined face, in the direction B C; it afterwards falls on the concave surface D E, and lastly impels the cylinder in the contrary direction. P. 195.
**Fig. 205.** The duplex escapement. A B is the pallet, through which the cylinder and the tooth which rests on it are supposed to be seen, the point of the tooth being about to escape from the notch towards C. The short tooth D next impels the point of the pallet, and the long tooth E falls on the cylinder. It first rests on the convex surface, and then drops into the notch, which causes a slight recoil in the wheel, and passes by, the tooth F being beyond the reach of the pallet; but on its return, the tooth falls again into the notch; and when it escapes, the pallet is impelled as before. P. 196.
**Fig. 206.** Mr. Mudge's watch escapement. A, the escapement wheel, and one of the subsidiary springs, seen from above; B, a general view of the balance, with both the subsidiary springs, seen from one side. The point of one of the teeth rests at C on the end of the pallet, which is bent so as to detain it until the pin D, which is attached to the balance, sets it at liberty by striking against the arm E: this arm is then carried on by the balance to the end of its vibration, and impels it on its return, until the pallet meets the next tooth. The other spring acts alternately in the same manner, but in a contrary direction. P. 197.

<column-break/>

**Fig. 207.** An improvement on Mr. Cumming's escapement for a clock. The tooth A is seen resting on a flat surface at the end of the pallet B: it is disengaged by the descent of the opposite pallet into the position in which it is represented, the pallet B being impelled by it at C. This pallet continues resting on the flat end of the tooth, until the pin D of the pendulum strikes against the arm E, which is carried before it, and impels the pendulum in its descent, until the pallet B acquires the situation in which the opposite pallet is represented, and sets that pallet at liberty from the tooth E, which has raised it. The situation and magnitude of the weights G, H, may be adjusted at pleasure. P. 197.
**Fig. 208.** Mr. Arnold's watch escapement. The pin A, projecting from the verge or axis of the balance, moving towards B, carries before it the spring B, and with it the stiffer spring C, so as to set at liberty the tooth D, which rests on a pallet projecting from the spring. The angle E of the principal pallet has then just passed the tooth F, and is impelled by it until the tooth G arrives at the detent. In the return of the balance, the pin A passes easily by the detent, by forcing back the spring B. The screw H serves to adjust the position of the detent, which presses against it. P. 197.
**Fig. 209.** Mr. Earnshaw's escapement. A is the unlocking pallet, B the spring on which it acts, C the detent, holding the tooth D by a pin; E is the point of the principal pallet first impelled by the tooth F, G is the tooth next locked, and H the adjusting screw. P. 197.
**Fig. 210.** A gridiron pendulum, consisting of three bars of iron, and two of a mixture of zinc and silver. P. 200.
**Fig. 211.** A compensation balance, as employed by Arnold. The outside of the hoops A, B is of brass, the inside of steel: the weights C, D are screwed backwards and forwards, in order to obtain the requisite degree of compensation. The weights E, F, are employed to regulate the mean rate of the watch, and G, H, and I, for adjusting it to all positions with respect to the horizon. P. 201.
**Fig. 212.** The compound plate A B rests on two supports, which are adjusted to a proper distance by turning the double screw C; the bending of the plate by heat raises the bar D, which supports the pendulum, while its effective length is determined by a fixed clip, which is seen below the plate. P. 217.

P. 212.

Fig. 224. A pair of friction wheels, supporting one end of the axis of a wheel. P. 214.

Fig. 225. The center of the wheel A B, passing over the obstacle C, describes the path D E; that of the larger wheel F G, the path H I, which is less steep. P. 214.

Fig. 226. The center of the wheel A B describes the curved path C D in passing over the obstacle E, while that of the larger wheel F G has an angle at H. P. 214.

Fig. 227. The wheel A B, moving on a soft road towards B, has to overcome the resistance of the earth at C. P. 215.

Fig. 228. A section of the wheel of a carriage, a little dished, or inclined outwards. P. 217.

Fig. 229. A B and C D being the straps or braces by which a coach is suspended, if the center of gravity is at E, F, or G, it must move, when the carriage swings, in the curve passing through the respective point. P. 218.

Fig. 230. The mode of harnessing two horses so as to make them draw conveniently together: when either horse advances so far that the bar A B assumes the position C D, the foremost horse has the disadvantage of acting on a lever equivalent only to E F, while the other horse acts on E C. P. 218.

Fig. 231. A sugar mill. The axis A is turned either by animal force or by water: the liquor is collected in the trough B and runs off in the channel C. The openings D are for the purpose of adjusting the axes of the rollers. The canes are supplied by the hands of the workmen. P. 221.

Fig. 232. A glazier’s vice. The opening in the middle shows the form of the section of the lead which is drawn through it. P. 223.

Fig. 233. A forge hammer, raised by the plugs projecting from an axis, either at A or, more conveniently, at B, and thrown forcibly against the wooden spring C. P. 224.

Fig. 234. An engine for driving piles, based on Vauloué’s construction. The horses, drawing at A and B, raise the

<column-break/>

weight C, held by the tongs D, fixed in the follower E, which are opened when they reach the summit by being pressed between the inclined planes F and G, so as to let the weight fall. At the same time, the lever H is raised by the rope I and presses on the pin K L, so as to depress the lever M N and draw the pin O out of the drum P Q; the follower then descends and uncoils the rope, its too rapid motion being prevented by the counterweight R, acting on the spiral barrel Q. The motion is regulated by the fly S, the pinion of which is turned by the great wheel T. P. 226.

Fig. 235. The rollers of the slitting mill. P. 228.

Fig. 236. A simple plough. A is the coulter, for dividing the ground; B the share, fixed on the mould board C, for turning it to the right hand; D is the rest, and E and F are the handles. P. 229.

Fig. 237. Section of a threshing mill. The corn is drawn in by the rollers or feeders A and B: it is beaten by the revolving beaters C and D, and the straw is drawn out by the rakes E and F, which discharge it at G; the grain falling through the arched bottoms H I and I G, which are formed like sieves. P. 233.

Fig. 238. A corn mill, with some of the improvements made in America by Mr. Ellicott and Mr. Evans. The corn, being poured into the funnel A, is conveyed by the revolutions of a spiral B C to C, from where it is raised by the chain of buckets C D to be cleaned by the revolving sieve E and the fan F; it is then deposited in the granary G, which supplies the funnel or mill hopper H; this, being constantly agitated by the iron axis of the upper millstone, shakes it by degrees into the perforation of the stone; it escapes, when ground, at I, and is conveyed, by means of the carrier K L and the elevator L M, to the cooler N, where it is spread on a large surface; it passes afterward to the bolter O and is received in the bin P, from where it is taken to be packed in sacks or barrels. Q represents the surface of a millstone, cut into furrows, in order to make it act more effectively on the corn. P. 234.

**Fig. 244.** The weight A may be supported by the pressure of a small quantity of fluid, either by making the surface of the vessel B C very large and the height of the tube D E moderate, or, while the vessel F remains of a moderate size, by making the height of the tube G H very great. P. 263.

**Fig. 245.** The pressure on any small part of the side of the vessel A B, at C or D, may be represented by the lines C E and D F, and the total pressure on the side by the triangle B G, of which the center of gravity is at H; and if the side A I be supported by a single prop, it must be placed at the point K, the height of which is equal to that of H. P. 265.

<column-break/>

shown at A and B will have a certain degree of stability, but if they sink, as at C, they will overset. However, a beam of the breadth shown at D will always float securely. P. 267.

**Fig. 251.** The bottle A, containing air and mercury, has the tube A B fitted into it: and when the jar C D, in which it is enclosed, is exhausted by means of the air pump, the elasticity of the air in the bottle forces the mercury up the tube. P. 270.

**Fig. 252.** An instrument for showing the buoyant effect of the air, called by Boyle a <term>statical baroscope</term>; the index A shows, on the scale B C, the degree to which the ball D is forced to descend by the reduction of the weight of the air. P. 272.

**Fig. 253.** The line 0 denoting the natural density of the air, the line 1 A next above it shows the degree to which the air is expanded at the height of a mile, and 1 B the density of the air at the same height: in the same manner, 10 C shows the expansion of the air at the height of 10 miles, and 10 D its density; and 5 E, below the line, shows the density which it would acquire at the depth of 5 miles below the earth’s surface. The lines A C and D B E are of the kind called <term>logarithmic curves</term>. P. 272.

**Fig. 254.** The box or basin in which the mercury of the common barometer is contained: A is a float for adjusting the height by means of the screw B, which operates on the leather that forms the bottom of the cavity. P. 276.

**Fig. 255.** A jet or stream of a fluid, passing through an opening in a thin plate in any direction, and contracted after its escape due to the lateral motions of the particles that flow toward the stream, following nearly the directions of the lines drawn here. P. 280.

**Fig. 256.** A stream flowing through a short cylindrical pipe, compared with another flowing through a widening conical pipe; the directions of the motions of the particles appear to be nearly similar in both cases. P. 281.

**Fig. 257.** In an experiment by D. Bernoulli, the water flowing through the conical pipe A drew up water through the tube B from the vessel C; in another by Venturi, the water flowing through the cylindrical pipe D raised water through the tube E. P. 281.

**Fig. 258.** A siphon, through which a fluid runs from the higher vessel into the lower one. P. 283.

**Fig. 259.** A fluid flowing through a vertical pipe and filling a vessel to a height nearly equal to the length of the pipes, while it is discharged through a similar horizontal pipe. P. 284.

**Fig. 260.** Underground cavities with outlets in the form of siphons, through which they do not begin to discharge any water until they are nearly full; the lower one will then continue to run until it is empty. In the meantime, either of them may maintain a constant stream through other passages. P. 285.

P. 289.

**Fig. 264.** A series of waves spreading out from a center A and striking a fixed obstacle BC; they are reflected by it into the same form as if they originated from the center D, at an equal distance on the opposite side of the surface BC. P. 289.

**Fig. 265.** An apparatus for observing the motions of waves created in a fluid poured into the trough AB by the vibrations of the elastic wire C, which is loaded with a movable weight D; the shadow of the waves is thrown on a screen E by the lamp F, passing through the bottom of the trough, which is made of glass. P. 290.

**Fig. 266.** A series of waves, spreading out from the center A and passing through the opening BC, extends on each side so as to fill the space BCDE, while they affect the areas outside this space much less noticeably. P. 290, 458.

**Fig. 267.** Two equal series of waves, spreading out from the centers A and B and crossing each other in such a way that, in the lines pointing toward C, D, E, and F, they cancel out each other's effects and the water remains nearly smooth, while in the spaces between them, the water is agitated. P. 290, 464.

**Fig. 288.** Mr. Woltmann’s hydrometrical fly. The plates A and B are adjusted by experiment to move exactly or very nearly at the velocity of the wind, with a few degrees allowed as compensation for the slowing effect of friction. This pipe has a small opening at the bottom which limits the size of the stream discharged into vessel G, the end F being considerably larger. Tube H serves as a gauge to measure the velocity at any given time. Page 319.

**Fig. 309.** The common suction pump. Page 333.

**Fig. 310.** A bag pump, with the bag or puff A being extended and contracted by the motion of the piston. Page 333.

**Fig. 311.** A lifting pump, where the piston rod AB is drawn up by a frame. Page 333.

**Fig. 312.** A suction pump, converted into a forcing pump by the addition of a leather collar at A. Page 333.

**Fig. 313.** A fire engine, based on a design similar to some machines described by Ramelli. AB is the piston, working within a cylindrical barrel and moved by the handles CD. When the end C is lowered, the water enters through the valves E and F and is discharged at G and H; when D is lowered, the water enters at I and K and is discharged at L and M into the air vessel N, from which it is expelled by the pipe O. The pipes P and Q may be joined together if required. Page 334.

**Fig. 314.** From Ramelli. The wheel AB, rotating in the direction BA, carries a portion of water C between itself and the sweep DE; this is intercepted by the slider F and forced up the pipe FG. Page 335.

**Fig. 315.** From Ramelli. The roller A, rotating within the reservoir BC (which is nearly cylindrical), carries with it the slider DE, which is made to sweep

<column-break/>

the internal surface of the cylinder from C to F by means of a projecting surface acting on the end D, so that the water G is forced through the pipe F. Page 335.

**Fig. 316.** From the collection of Mr. Servière. The wheels A and B carry, during their rotation, a quantity of water from C to D, or from D to C, depending on the direction in which they are turned. Page 335.

**Fig. 317.** Mr. Gwynn’s patent water engine. The valve A is kept in contact with the roller or piston C—partly by the spring B, but even more by the pressure of the water. The piston revolves within the box DE and sweeps it from E to F, so that the portion of water G is forced into the pipe F during each half of a revolution; or it is drawn from F to E when the roller rotates in the opposite direction. Page 335.

**Fig. 318.** A chain pump. Page 335.

**Fig. 319.** The mechanism of Höll’s acting pump. In the position of the stopcock AB shown here, the water flows out of the barrel C, and the piston D is allowed to descend. The rod E then turns the stopcock, and the barrel C communicates only with the pipe F, which fills it and forces up the piston until the stopcock is turned back to its former position. Page 336.

**Fig. 320.** The hydraulic air vessels of Schemnitz. The reservoir A being filled with water and B with air, and water being poured into the funnel C, the air in B acts through pipe D on the water in A and forces it up pipe E. Page 337.

**Fig. 321.** With A being the high-water mark and B the low-water mark, the vessels C and D are filled at high water from below, while the air is allowed to escape through a stopcock opened by the fall of the ball F. At low water, air enters vessel D at B; and before the next high water, the water C will be forced up the pipe E. Page 337.

**Fig. 322.** The fountain of Hero. Its operation resembles that of the hydraulic air vessels in Fig. 320, but here the pipe D ascends. Page 337.

**Fig. 323.** The hydraulic ram of Montgolfier. When the water in the pipe AB has acquired sufficient velocity, it raises the valve B, which stops its passage; consequently, part of the water is forced through the valve C into the air vessel D, from which it rises through the pipe E. Page 338.

## PLATE XXIV.

Fig. 324. The cupping instrument of Hero. The cavity A was partly exhausted by applying the mouth repeatedly to the pipe B, the stopcock B being turned after each application. When the stopcock C was opened, the air at D in contact with the skin was also rarefied, and the effect of suction was produced. P. 339, 353.

Fig. 325. Mr. Cuthbertson’s air pump. When the piston rod A is depressed, it leaves the piston B a little behind it, so as to make an opening between two conical parts which are ground together, and the air escapes from the lower part of the barrel into the upper part; when it is elevated, the whole piston is raised, and a wire, which slides through the axis of the rod, raises a small valve at the bottom of the barrel, which leads to the receiver C by the tube DE. The air is forced from the upper part of the barrel through a valve in the oil vessel F, from which the oil runs back, when it overflows, by a tube leading to the mouth of the barrel; and if this tube is stopped by turning its cock, the air may be condensed into a receiver fixed at G. At H is a long gauge, with a barometer immersed in the same basin of mercury. The piston rod, which is hollow, has a perforation a little above A to admit the oil, in order that the wire may work freely in it. P. 340.

Fig. 326. The two flies <note>In this context, "flies" refers to revolving vanes or fly-wheels used to demonstrate air resistance.</note> A and B being caused to revolve with equal velocities by the descent of the weight C, they continue to move for an equal length of time in the vacuum of the air pump. P. 341.

Fig. 327. The air in the bottle A expands when the receiver B is exhausted, and causes the water to rise in a jet. P. 341.

Fig. 328. A pear gauge; to be suspended in a receiver by a hook like that which is shown in fig. 325. P. 342.

Fig. 329. A condenser, with screws, for confining the receiver. A is a gauge for showing the degree of condensation; B is the piston of the syringe, with a valve of the best kind, which is conical and is confined by a spiral spring. But in common, the valves are made of leather, with a plate of metal to strengthen it. P. 342.

Fig. 330. A diving bell. A is the forcing pump, B a stopcock for letting out the heated air, C a strong glass for giving light, D a float for the security of the diver. P. 343.

Fig. 331. Laurie’s hydraulic bellows. When the vessel A is raised, the air enters at the valve B; when it is depressed, the valve B shuts, and the air is forced through the pipe CD, which conducts it to the reservoir E, where it is confined by the valve F, and forced by the pressure of the water through the pipe G. P. 343.

Fig. 332. Mr. Watt’s gasometer. The pressure is regulated by the magnitude of the weights A and B, which act by the spiral fusees C and D, so as to sustain a part of the weight of the inverted vessel, represented by the exterior dotted line. The gas is admitted at E or F, and is delivered at G. GH is a gauge for show-

<column-break/>

ing the height of the water within and without the movable vessel. I is a cock for letting off the water. P. 344.

Fig. 333. The shower bellows. The stream A, passing through the strainer B, carries with it a quantity of air through the pipe C, which rises to the upper part of the air vessel D, and is discharged by the pipe E. P. 344.

Fig. 334. The centrifugal bellows. By the revolution of the fly, the air is caused to enter at A, and is discharged at B. P. 345.

Fig. 335. The original steam engine of Savery. The vessel A being filled with steam from the boiler B, and the stopcock being turned, the steam cools and is condensed, and water is forced into its place by the pressure of the atmosphere, through the valve C: the steam is then readmitted, and forces the water to ascend through the valve D and the pipe DE. The vessel F acts alternately with A. P. 347.

Fig. 336. The common steam engine of Newcomen and Beighton. The steam being admitted into the cylinder A below the piston, the weight B is allowed to descend: a jet of water is then admitted by the pipe C, which condenses the steam, and the pressure of the atmosphere then depresses the piston: a part of this water is admitted by the pipe D into the boiler, in order to keep it sufficiently full. P. 347.

Fig. 337. Mr. Watt’s steam engine. The steam, which is below the piston, is allowed to escape into the condenser A by the cock B, which is opened by the rod C, and at the same time the steam is admitted by the cock D into the upper part of the cylinder; when the piston has descended, the cocks E and F act in a similar manner in letting out the steam from above and admitting it below the piston. The jet is supplied by the water of the cistern G, which is pumped up at H from a reservoir: it is drawn out, together with the air that is released from it, by the air pump I, which throws it into the cistern K, from which the pump L raises it to the cistern M; and it enters the boiler through a valve, which opens whenever the float N descends below its proper place. The pipes O and P serve also to determine the quantity of water in the boiler. The piston rod is confined to a motion nearly rectilinear by the frame Q; the fly wheel R is turned by the sun and planet wheel S, T; and the strap U turns the centrifugal regulator W, which governs the supply of steam by the valve or stopcock X. P. 349.

Fig. 338. Mr. Symington’s steam boat. A is the boiler, B the cylinder, C the piston, D the condensation pipe, E the air pump, F stampers for breaking ice. P. 349.

Fig. 339. An air gun. The air is forced by the syringe A into the cavity surrounding the barrel, from which it is discharged by the valve B, which is opened either immediately by the action of the trigger C, or by a spring, which is bent by cocking the gun, and set at liberty by the trigger. P. 351.

Fig. 357. The right half of the human larynx. ABC is the outline of the cricoid cartilage, DEFGH of the thyroid, and I K L of the arytenoid cartilage; M is the epiglottis, NK the upper ligament of the glottis, OP the lower ligament, and Q the trachea. P. 400.

Fig. 359. Sections of the pipes employed by Kratzenstein for producing the sounds of the different vowels; generally by means of a larynx resembling the mouthpiece of a reed organ pipe, but in the case of the vowel *I* by simple inflation through tube B. The pipe for *U* produces the sound *O*, except when it is nearly closed. P. 401.

Fig. 360. The <term>vox humana</term> organ pipe, with the mouthpiece common to reed pipes in general; the lower part in contact with the tongue is nearly semi-cylindrical. The tongue is adjusted to the proper pitch by means of a sliding wire, which regulates the length of the part that is free to vibrate. P. 401.

Fig. 361. The mouthpiece proposed by Kratzenstein for imitating the human voice; the tongue A passes freely in and out of the tube, which is more than half of a cylinder, as seen at B. P. 401.

Fig. 362. The form of the <term>regal</term> organ pipe. P. 401.

Fig. 363. A front view and section of the open <term>diapason</term> organ pipe made of metal. It is tuned by opening or contracting the upper orifice. P. 402.

Fig. 364. A is a front view of the flute organ pipe, made of wood, which is tuned by a plug. B is a section of the pipe. P. 402.

Fig. 365. A stopped <term>diapason</term> organ pipe, made of metal. It is tuned by altering the position of the pieces on each side of the mouth. P. 402.

Fig. 366. A chimney pipe. P. 402.

Fig. 367. A spindle-shaped organ pipe, contracted at the top. P. 402.

Fig. 368. A is the form of a <term>cromorne</term> pipe, B is a trumpet pipe; both have reed mouthpieces. P. 403.

<column-break/>

Fig. 369. A ray or pencil of light A B, C B, falling on the surface D E. A portion of the light is reflected, and another portion is transmitted in the direction BF, BG, so that B G is equal to BC, and BH to BI. C I K and G H L are lines perpendicular to D E at such distances that B K is to B L in a certain proportion; this is the proportion of the sines of the angles of incidence A B M and C B M to those of the angles of refraction F B N and G B N. BO and BP are the reflected portions of the rays. P. 411.

Fig. 370. A method of determining the position of a refracted ray, which is particularly convenient for refractions at spherical surfaces. A B C is any circle, either touching the refractive surface at A, or being itself a section of the refracting substance. If another circle D E F is drawn on the same center, having its diameter related to that of the first as the sine of the angle of incidence is to that of refraction, and a third circle G H I is smaller than the first in the same proportion as the second is larger; and if the direction of the incident ray K A is continued to D, and LD is drawn from the center, cutting G H I at G, then A G will be the direction of the refracted ray. If this ray passes out of the denser medium again at B, its direction BM may be found by drawing LIF, and FBM will thus be truly determined. P. 411.

Fig. 371. A ray or pencil A B, refracted at B to C, and there reflected by a perpendicular surface into an opposite direction C B, will also return in the direction B A; a portion of it is reflected in the first place to D, and in the second to E. P. 412.

Fig. 372. A pencil A B passing through a substance CD contained between parallel surfaces continues its course in the direction EF, parallel to AB. P. 413.

Fig. 373. The ray A B, entering the medium CD through the transparent substance EF contained between parallel surfaces, acquires the direction GH, parallel to IK, into which LI is at once refracted. P. 413.

Fig. 374. The appearance of a prism, of which the lower surface is divided into a bright and a dark portion, separated by a colored arch ABC. P. 414.

**Fig. 375.** A is an actual focus of diverging rays, B is an actual focus of both converging and diverging rays, C is a virtual focus of converging rays, and D is a virtual focus of diverging rays; A and B, B and C, and C and D are conjugate foci to each other, with respect to the refractions of the three lenses. **Fig. 382.** The pencils of light A and B are refracted by the convex lens C in the same manner as they would have been by the circumscribed double prism D E; and in the same manner, the concave lens F resembles the prisms G and H in its operation. P. 417.

**Fig. 383.** A, a pencil of parallel rays, made to converge by a double convex lens of crown glass to the center of curvature of one of its surfaces. B, a double concave lens, causing the rays to diverge from the center of curvature. C and D, a planoconvex lens, in which the principal focus is at the distance of one diameter. P. 417.

**Fig. 384.** The lenses represented by the shaded surfaces are equivalent in their effects to those where the sections are shown by the dotted lines; the figures at A and B are of equal thickness in the middle, and at C at the edges as well. P. 417.

**Fig. 385.** At A, a radiant point and its image are both situated at the distance of twice the focal length from the lens; at B, one is more remote and the other is nearer; and C D is to D E as E F is to F G; D and F being the principal foci of the lens. P. 418.

**Fig. 386.** The oblique pencils of rays A and B, and

<column-break/>

the direct pencil C, are supposed to be brought to their respective foci in the same plane D E. P. 419.

**Fig. 387.** The square A intercepts all the light proceeding from point B which would fall on the surface C D, which is four times as large and placed at double the distance. P. 421.

**Fig. 388.** The box of Count Rumford's photometer. The lights, being placed at proper distances on the graduated arms or tables A and B, throw equally dark shadows of the cylinders C and D on a white surface at E F. The wings of the cylinders serve to make the shadows of equal width. The shadows are viewed through the aperture at G. P. 421.

**Fig. 389.** Dr. Wollaston's instrument for the measurement of refractive densities. A is a rectangular prism of flint glass, under which the substance to be examined is attached; B C is a rod, or ruler, 10 inches long; C D and D E are each 15 85/100 inches. When the sights at B and C are so placed that the division between the light and dark portion of the lower surface of the prism is seen through them, the rod F, which carries a vernier, shows the index of the refractive density, which, in the situation represented here, would be 1.43. P. 421.

**Fig. 394.** A is the virtual image of the candle B, formed by the concave lens C, and is smaller than the object. P. 422.

**Fig. 395.** When the object A is placed in the principal focus of the convex lens B, a virtual image is formed at an infinite distance, which subtends—when viewed from C or from any other point—the same angle as the object subtends at the center of the lens. P. 422.

**Fig. 396.** The object A being placed a little within the focus of the lens B, a virtual image C is formed at whatever distance is most convenient to the eye; this image subtends the same angle as the object from the center of the lens, and therefore appears somewhat more magnified than when the object is in the principal focus. P. 422.

**PLATE XXVIII.**

**Fig. 397.** An imperfect image of an external object, projected in a dark room in an inverted position, by light traveling in straight lines through a small aperture. P. 425.

**Fig. 398.** A portable camera obscura. *A* is a lens, *B* is a mirror placed at an angle, throwing the image onto a plate of ground glass, *C D*. *E* is a movable cover, and *F G* is a screen attached to it for blocking out external light. P. 425.

**Fig. 399.** A camera obscura which projects an image downward by means of the mirror *A* and the lens *B* onto the surface *C*, where it may be seen through the aperture *D*. The surface *C* has the curvature best suited to receive a perfect image of a distant object at every point. P. 425.

**Fig. 400.** A proposed arrangement for a solar microscope, adapted to a south-facing window. The mirror *A* is moved by a hinge into the position required for the time of day, and while the instrument is in use, it is only turned around the axis *A B*, which is parallel to the axis of the earth. The mirror *C* is fixed; it receives the beam of light from *A* and throws it on the object through lenses *D* and *E*, whose joint focus is near the magnifying lens *F*. This lens projects an inverted image of the object onto a screen at *G*. If the focus of the condensing lenses were behind the object, as at *H*, the light would likely be concentrated into a spot on the screen at *I*. P. 426.

**Fig. 401.** A proposed arrangement for a phantasmagoria. The light from the lamp *A* is directed by the mirror *B* and the lenses *C* and *D* onto the painted slide at *E*, and the magnifier *F* forms the image on the screen at *G*. This lens is fixed to a slider that can be pulled out of the general support or box *H*. When the box is moved back on its wheels, the rod *I K* lowers the point *K*, and by means of the rod *K L*, adjusts the slider so that the image is always clearly projected on the screen *G*. When the box moves toward the screen—so that the images appear to shrink and vanish—the support of the lens *F* allows the screen *M* to fall and block part of the light. The rod *K N* must be equal to *I K*, and the point *I* must be at twice the focal length of the lens *F* in front of the object, with *L* being directly under the focus of the lens. The screen *M* may have a triangular opening to uncover only the middle of the lens, or the light may be blocked in any other manner. P. 427.

**Fig. 402.** The construction of the astronomical telescope. *ABC* and *DEC* are the central parts of the bundles of rays coming from the edges of the visible field through the middle of the objective lens. P. 427.

**Fig. 403.** The outermost bundles of rays in the double or compound microscope. P. 428.

**Fig. 404.** The outermost rays in the Galilean telescope, or opera glass. P. 428.

**Fig. 405.** *A* shows the directions of the outermost rays in the common terrestrial telescope of Rheita. If only two eyepieces were used, as at *B*, the field of view would obviously be more narrow. P. 428.

**Fig. 406.** Dr. Herschel's forty-foot telescope. *ABC* is the path of a ray of light, reflected by the mirror at *B* to the eyepiece *C*. *D* is a chair in which the observer sits. *E* is a movable gallery on which several people may stand. *FG* is a smooth surface on which the bottom of the telescope is made to roll, while its opening

<column-break/>

is raised or lowered by the pulleys at *H* and *I*. *K* is one of two rooms or huts for the accommodation of the observer's assistants. The wheels under the frame serve to turn the entire instrument around its center. P. 429.

**Fig. 407.** The Newtonian telescope, showing the direction of the central rays. These are not the rays by which the object is actually seen, because they are blocked by the small mirror, but they provide the simplest way to determine the size of the field of view. P. 429.

**Fig. 408.** The assumed path of the central rays in the Gregorian telescope. P. 429.

**Fig. 409.** The assumed path of the central rays in Cassegrain's telescope. In this case, the rays actually represented would not only be blocked by the small mirror, but they would also fall on the hole in the large mirror. However, they serve equally well to determine the size of the field. P. 429.

**Fig. 410.** The assumed path of the central rays in Dr. Smith's microscope. The rays traveling directly from the object are blocked by a screen. P. 429.

**Fig. 411.** *A*: the dotted line represents the curve called the caustic of a concave mirror, in which rays coming from a distant point (in the section shown in the figure) would be collected. *B*: the dotted line is the caustic of a convex mirror. If the eye is assumed to be at a great distance from the hemispherical mirrors *C* and *D*, the images of distant objects in all directions will be found between the dotted curves; the distance between those curves shows the degree of visual confusion. The images of distant objects in all directions formed by the small concave and convex mirrors *E* and *F* are found between the dotted circle and the straight line touching it. P. 430.

**Fig. 412.** The effect of a field glass in a compound microscope; the inner lines show what the size of the field would be without it. P. 431.

**Fig. 413.** The manner in which Mr. Ramsden used a plano-convex lens in the eyepieces of his telescopes and in his double magnifiers. The curved dotted line shows the image of the straight line (divided into equal parts) which is formed by the larger lens in the focus of the smaller lens through which it is viewed. P. 431.

**Fig. 414.** An achromatic telescope with a triple objective lens and with Boscovich's achromatic eyepiece, consisting of two similar lenses; one of these is three times as large as the other in every dimension, and their distance apart is twice the focal length of the smaller lens. P. 432.

**Fig. 415.** The dotted lines *AB* and *CD* represent two images of the same object formed by rays of different refractability passing through a simple objective lens. These are brought, by the effect of the lens or field glass *E*, into such positions and sizes that they span nearly the same angle from the eyepiece *F*. P. 432.

**Fig. 416.** *A* represents Mr. Ramsden's divided eyepiece micrometer; the two parts are moved simultaneously in opposite directions by turning the pinion *B*, until the two ends of the distance being measured appear to coincide. P. 433.

**Fig. 417.** Dr. Maskelyne's micrometer, made with a double achromatic prism *A*, showing two images *B* and *C*. The different parts of these images are made to coincide by moving the prism back and forth along the axis of the telescope. Mr. Ramsden believes that any substance placed in this way must greatly interfere with the telescope's perfection. P. 433.

**Fig. 427.** A triangular figure, exhibiting in theory all possible shades of colors. The red, the green, and the violet are single at their respective angles and are gradually shaded off toward the opposite sides; a little yellow and blue only are added in their places in order to supply the lack of brilliancy in the colors 

<column-break/>

which ought to compose them. The center is gray, and the lights of any two colors which are found at equal distances on opposite sides of it would always very nearly make up white light together, such as yellow and violet, greenish blue and red, or blue and orange. P. 441.

**Fig. 433.** A complicated system of halos. From Lowitz. The arcs A, B, and C were colored and, like all the other colored parts, had the red toward the sun. D and E are two <term>anthelia</term> <note>luminous spots opposite the sun</note>. P. 444.

**Fig. 434.** The figures of two complicated flakes of snow. From Nettis. P. 444.

P. 445.

### PLATE XXX.

Fig. 436. A section of the human eye. A is the cornea; B the aqueous humor, in which the uvea hangs; C the crystalline lens; the ciliary processes are located between it and the uvea; D the vitreous humor; E F G is the choroid coat, lined by the retina; H I K the sclerotica, and L the optic nerve. P. 447.

Fig. 437. A picture painted on the retina in an inverted position, seen by dissecting off the sclerotica and choroid behind it. P. 448.

Fig. 438. Since the apparent shape of the sky is nearly like the curve A B C, the sun or moon at A or C appears to be much larger than at B. P. 454.

Fig. 439. The red square A, enclosing a green square, produces—if viewed attentively in a strong light—a spectrum resembling B, which is red inside and green outside; this appears when we look soon afterward at any white object. P. 456.

Fig. 440. The spot, which is tinted with black lines only, appears to have a purple hue when placed upon the yellow ground. P. 456.

Fig. 441. A gray spot on a purple ground appears to have a greenish-yellow or olive hue. P. 456.

Fig. 442. The manner in which two portions of colored light, admitted through two small apertures, produce light and dark stripes or fringes by their interference, moving in the shape of hyperbolas; the middle ones are, however, usually a little dilated, as at A. P. 465.

Fig. 443. A series of stripes of all colors, at their appropriate widths, placed side by side in the manner in which they would be separated by refraction, and combined together to form the fringes of colors below them, beginning from white. P. 465.

Fig. 445. The internal hyperbolic fringes of a rectangular shadow. P. 467.

# PLATE XXXII.

**Fig. 471.** **A** represents the sun, **B** the earth, and **C** the planet Mars. Supposing Mars and the earth set out together from **D** and **E**, the angle **DAC** was determined by Kepler through calculation, and the angles **BAD** and **ABC** by observation; from these, it was easy to construct the triangle **ABC** and to find the proportion of **AB** to **AC**. P. 505.

**Fig. 472.** The solar system, representing the form and proportions of the orbits of all the primary planets and of three of the comets. The parts of the orbits represented by solid lines are to the north of the ecliptic, and the dotted parts are to the south; the letters **A** and **P** denote the aphelion and perihelion. The point in the center, which should be only 1/700 of an inch in diameter, represents the sun. The figures of the respective planets show their comparative magnitude, while the magnitude of the sun is represented by the innermost of the graduated circles which enclose the whole: they

<column-break/>

are placed according to their actual positions on the 14th of June, 1806. The letters **MD** show the mean distance of the comet of 1759, being placed at the extremity of the minor axis of the ellipse in which it must be supposed to revolve. P. 514.

**Fig. 473.** The orbital periods of the different planets, represented by lines of different lengths. P. 514.

**Fig. 474.** The comparative velocities of the different planets, represented by lines which show the number of English miles traveled in a second, on the scale marked on the lowest line. P. 514.

# PLATE XXXIV.

**Fig. 486.** Supposing the gravitating body **A B C** revolves on the axis **A C**, the fluid column **B D** must be longer than **E D** in order to support its pressure. P. 519.

**Fig. 487.** If **A** represents the position of the sun, **B** that of the earth, and **C** that of the moon, and if the ratio of **A D** to **A C** is the same as the ratio of the square of **A C** to the square of **A B**, then **A D** will represent the sun’s attraction acting on the earth. **C D** represents the disturbing force, which, together with **A D**, makes up **A C**, the total force acting on the moon. It is obvious that when the nodes are in any oblique position, such as **E F**, and the force is directed to some point **D** between **B** and **A**, the force **C D** will tend to lessen the inclination while the moon moves from **G** to **H** and ascends from **E** toward **C**. This causes the node **E** to move back toward **G**. When the moon is again descending toward **F**, the inclination will be increased and the node **F** made to recede toward **H** until the moon arrives at **H** and the force becomes directed to a point on the other side of **B**. The nodes only advance while the moon is between **H** and **F**, or between **G** and **E**. P. 520.

**Fig. 488.** A body attracted toward the center **A** and descending from **B** in the ellipse **B C D** has the inclination of its orbit to the revolving radius (**A B**, **A C**, **A D**) constantly changing until, at **D**, it becomes perpendicular to it. however, when the force increases more rapidly, the radius does not become perpendicular to the orbit until it arrives at **E**, and the line of the apsides **A D** moves forward to **E**. P. 521.

**Fig. 489.** **A** represents the position of the limit of light and darkness on the earth’s surface at the vernal equinox, **B** at the summer solstice, and **C** at the winter solstice. **E Q** denotes the equator, **N** the north pole, and **S** the south pole. P. 525.

**Fig. 490.** **N E S W** being the horizon and **Z** the zenith, **E A W** shows the sun’s apparent path in London at the time of the equinoxes, **B C D** at midsummer, and **F G H** at midwinter. These are projected orthographically, as if the circles were described on the surface of a globe and viewed from a great distance. The circle **I K L** is the boundary of twilight, assuming it is 18° below the horizon; its intersections with the sun’s path show the beginning and end of twilight, as at **I** and **K**. P. 527.

**Fig. 491.** The rays of light, coming in the direction **A B**, are bent by the atmosphere so as to arrive at **C** and illuminate a part of the atmosphere there. This is visible, by means of a second refraction, to a spectator at **D**, and causes the first and last twilight. P. 527.

<column-break/>

**Fig. 492.** Venus is at its greatest elongation, or angular distance from the sun **A**, when situated as at **B** with respect to the earth at **C**. It is stationary at **D** when it moves with the same velocity as the earth with respect to the direction of the earth’s motion; the line **E D** is then more oblique with respect to a fixed line than either before or after. P. 527.

**Fig. 493.** **A B C D** is the apparent path of Venus for the year 1806, assuming the sun **E** revolves around the earth **F**. The places of the sun and planet are marked for every four weeks. P. 527.

**Fig. 494.** The apparent path of Saturn in the heavens for the year 1806, referred to its proper place with respect to the ecliptic. The figures denote the positions at the beginning of each month. P. 527.

**Fig. 495.** The small figures represent the phases of the moon in different parts of its orbit. The smaller detached figures show the appearance of the moon as seen from the earth; the larger ones show those of the earth at the same times as seen from the moon, which are always the reverse of the moon’s appearance. At **A**, the moon is new; **B** is the first quarter, **C** the full moon, and **D** the last quarter. **A** and **C** are sometimes called the syzygies, and **B** and **D** the quadratures. P. 528.

**Fig. 496.** **A** shows the moon passing through the earth’s shadow, which is divided into three parts: the perfect shadow, the true shadow, and the penumbra. At **B** and **C**, the moon is shown passing through the section of the shadow. P. 529.

**Fig. 497.** The path of the moon’s shadow passing over the earth in the solar eclipse of 1764, assuming the earth revolves on its axis at the same time. The line **A B** is the part in which the eclipse appeared annular, **C D** being the breadth of the whole shadow or penumbra. P. 529.

**Fig. 498.** The shadow of the moon falling on the earth. Since the true shadow does not extend to the earth here, the cone formed by the continuation of its outlines marks the extent of the areas in which the eclipse appears annular. P. 529.

**Fig. 499.** The termination of the moon’s disc in a solar eclipse. From **Dr. Herschel**. P. 529.

**Fig. 500.** The apparent magnitudes of the planets, assuming that of the sun or moon is equal to a circle one foot in diameter. Where there are two figures, one shows the mean apparent magnitude and the other the greatest. P. 531.

**Fig. 501.** The apparent magnitude of the sun as seen from the different planets; for Mercury, the magnitude is shown by the size of the earth in fig. 497. P. 535.

# PLATE XXXV.

**Fig. 502.** With A B being the Earth's axis, the circle A C B is the meridian of the place C, and C D represents the plane of its horizon. P. 537.
**Fig. 503.** The effect of the obliquity of the ecliptic on the equation of time is shown by the difference of the angles A B C and D B E, which are subtended at the pole B by equal portions of the oblique circle A E. P. 538.
**Fig. 504.** With A B being parallel to the Earth's axis, the 12 planes passing through it at equal angular distances mark the hour lines of an equatorial dial on the circle C D perpendicular to it, and those of a horizontal dial on the horizontal surface E F. P. 538.
**Fig. 505.** A method of constructing a dial on any given plane. A B C is the elevation of the pole or, more generally, the angle which the surface makes with the gnomon A B. The circles are divided into equal parts, and 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are the hour lines, with B being the position of the gnomon. The reason for this construction will become clear by comparing the circle in the previous figure with the ellipse that is formed on the horizontal surface. P. 538.
**Fig. 506.** A dial for a pointed gnomon, or obelisk, drawn on a horizontal surface. P. 538.
**Fig. 507.** A mural quadrant with its telescope; A B is the plumb line for adjusting the instrument, and C is the counterweight for the telescope. P. 542.
**Fig. 508.** A portable transit instrument. A and B are screws for adjusting the axis by vertical and horizontal motions; C D is a spirit level, which may occasionally be hung on the telescope by the pins E and F. G is a small graduated arc to be viewed through the microscope H for measuring elevations of a few degrees. P. 542.
**Fig. 509.** A transit circle, resembling Mr. Wollaston's, with a horizontal circle by which both altitudes and azimuths may be measured. A is a microscope for viewing the plumb line, B is another for reading the divisions of the horizontal circle; C and D are spirit levels. P. 542.
**Fig. 510.** A zenith sector with its telescope, which usually has a reflecting prism for its eyepiece, like that of the Newtonian telescope. P. 542.
**Fig. 511.** The marine octant, introduced by Hadley. The method of taking the common or front observation is shown by the lines drawn to the Sun and Moon; the back observation is shown by the two stars. A is a dark glass

<column-break/>

to be used in observations of the Sun, and which may be fixed at B when required. P. 542.
**Fig. 512.** With A B being the position of the Earth's axis, if the angle C B D (the altitude of the body D) is measured, and we subtract from it the elevation of the celestial equator C B E, the remainder will be the declination E B D. P. 542, 543.
**Fig. 513.** The angle A B C is the Moon's horizontal parallax, and D B C is the parallax when it is elevated above the horizon D E at the angle B D E. P. 543.
**Fig. 514.** The position of the Earth during the transit of Venus in June 1769. A spectator at the North Cape was carried from A to B during the transit, and the transit appeared to him to last while Venus moved from C to D. The island of Otaheite, on the contrary, which is situated on the lower part of the illuminated hemisphere, was carried from E to F, and the duration of the transit there lasted only while Venus moved from G to H. Consequently, the rotation of the Earth was compared with the difference between the orbital motion of Venus and that of the Earth. P. 544.
**Fig. 515.** A planisphere closely resembling that of Professor Bode. The outer circle is fixed to the chart and is divided according to either the degrees of the ecliptic or the days of the month. The graduated circle immediately inside it is divided into 24 hours and is fixed to a circle of pasteboard, from which the circle N E S W (representing the horizon) is cut; this space is filled with thin varnished paper with circles of azimuth and altitude engraved on it, which is carried around with the hour circle. P. 567.
**Fig. 516.** A diagram showing the length of the day and the times of sunrise and sunset in any part of the world within a few minutes. The time of year is found on the graduated circle representing portions of the ecliptic, and the latitude is found on the middle line; by following the concentric circles of declination until they meet the horizon passing through the given latitude, the line drawn from the pole through this point will intersect the equator at the point showing the length of the day or night. Thus, on the first of March at latitude 50° North, the length of the day appears to be nearly 10 and a half hours, meaning the sun must rise about 37 minutes after six; but at latitude 85°, the sun never sets on that day. P. 567.

# PLATE XXXVIII.

Fig. 519. A scale of the height of different parts of the earth's surface above sea level, in English feet and miles, and in French <term>toises</term> <note>A French unit of length equal to approximately 6.39 feet</note>. P. 574.

Fig. 520. **A.** The dotted ellipsis shows the section of a spheroid, which would be the form of the earth and sea if it were always in a state of equilibrium with the attraction of a distant body; the shaded ellipsis shows the actual form assumed in consequence of its rotation around its center, the depth of the sea being less than 13 miles. **B.** If the surface of the sphere were supposed to be flattened and the tides spread upon it, they would assume the form of the waves shown here. The dotted straight line shows the mean height, which is a little above the surface in the principal sections of the spheroid, although not universally. **C.** The nature of the tides of lakes, the surface being regulated by that of the dotted line at **B**, nearly agreeing with it in direction, as at **D**, when the lake is narrow and deep, but differing from it, as at **E**, when it is shallower. P. 579.

Fig. 521. The progress of the tides from the Atlantic through the channels surrounding the British islands; the lunar tides occur in any part of the shaded lines nearly at the hour after the moon's <term>southing</term> <note>The time when the moon crosses the local meridian, reaching its highest point in the sky</note> which is indicated by the figure next to it. P. 582.

Fig. 522. The lines **AB** and **BC** represent the heights of the lunar and solar tides, and the angle **ABC** represents twice their angular distance; or, with **ADC** being simply the angular distance, the line **AC** shows the 

<column-break/>

height of the compound tide, and the angles **BAC** and **ACB** represent its distance from the lunar and solar tides respectively. P. 585.

Fig. 523. The two unequal tides represented by the elevation of the ellipsis above the smaller circle may be considered as composed of two equal tides cut off by the dotted circle, and the single tide between the two circles; just as the tides **B** and **C** create the unequal tides at **D**. P. 587.

Fig. 524. The first and second curves represent two equal semidiurnal and one diurnal tide, which together would make two unequal tides. The third and fourth represent the same tides six hours more advanced; when these are combined, the first and third cancel each other, but the second and fourth together compose the fifth, or a large diurnal tide. P. 587.

Fig. 525. **A.** The ancient system of the world, adopted by Ptolemy. **B.** The arrangement supposed by some other astronomers. P. 590.

Fig. 526. The Egyptian system of the world. P. 590.

Fig. 527. The system of the Pythagoreans and of Copernicus. P. 592.

Fig. 528. The method used by Ptolemy to represent the inequalities of celestial motions; the small circle is carried around the circumference of the larger one while the luminary revolves within it, so as to describe the dotted curve. P. 595.

Fig. 529. The Tychonic system of the world. P. 597.

## PLATE XXXIX.

**Fig. 530.** The repulsive force of two particles of matter, placed at the distance A B or A C, is represented by the ordinates or perpendiculars B D and C E, drawn to the curve D E, assuming the force is inversely proportional to the distance; however, the law of the force appears to be more nearly represented by a curve like F E. The line D F G shows the magnitude of the cohesive force, which overcomes the repulsion at the distance A G, and is balanced by it when the particles arrive at the distance A B or A H. The dotted lines represent the nature of the changes made in the lines F E, D F G, and F H by an increase in temperature. P. 619.

**Fig. 531.** The general direction of the cohesive force acting on a particle of a liquid at A being represented by A B or A C, that of the repulsive force will be D A or E A; in order to maintain equilibrium, the forces B F and C G, making together H A, must be supplied by the pressure or reaction of the internal parts. P. 620.

**Fig. 532. A.** The transverse section of a drop, supposed to be of considerable length and flat at the sides: the curvature of the outline is everywhere proportional to its distance from the horizontal line A B. **B**, a round drop, where the concavity at the horizontal line is equal to the convexity that would be found by cutting off the drop horizontally; the sum or difference of the curvatures is everywhere proportional to the distance from this line. P. 621.

**Fig. 533.** The solid AB having half the attractive power of the liquid CD, the surface of the liquid will remain horizontal: for the attractions will be represented by DA, DE, and DC; and of these, DA and DE make DB, and DB and DC make DF, which is vertical. If the solid is more attractive, the forces will be combined nearly as at G, and if less attractive, as at H. P. 622.

**Fig. 534.** The form of the surface of a liquid in contact with a plane and vertical side of a solid that is wetted by it. The height of the ascent of water is about one-fourth of that which is represented here. P. 622.

**Fig. 535.** The form of the surface of a liquid elevated between two plates that meet at A and are at a little distance from each other at B; about one-third of an inch, assuming the liquid is water. P. 623.

**Fig. 536.** The height at which water will stand in tubes of the form and magnitude that are represented here. P. 623.

**Fig. 539.** The actual elevation of a portion of water in contact with a horizontal surface that is wetted by it. P. 624.
